I've had The Isle for a little while now, so it only seemed like a good idea to write a review. This game is a huge work-in-progress, but even with that I find it every fun and entertaining. The controls are easy to understand and there's a rather large selection of playable dinosaurs to choose from to keep the game interesting, not to mention the humans that may be released soon. The frequent updates are also something nice to look forward to.
However, it is important to consider the fact that this game is still in Early Accsess, which means a ton of bugs. Some of these bugs can be rather irritating, but the devs are quick to fix them. Speaking to the developers, some of them can get rather snappy, so it's best to just leave them to do their job. Some of the games mechanics require a lot patience to deal with, such as the infamous leg breaking. You should also consider that you will die often if your someone who does not enjoy that aspect of the game.
Is The Isle worth twenty dollars? If your patient and okay with dealing with bugs, easily-annoyed devs, and an irritating community for the time being, yes. I see that the game is worth that, and things get more exciting when you read about Dondi's plans for the game in the future. If your not as patient but you still want this game, wait. It's still in Early Access and full of issues that will be resolved later.

Sheltered is a lot of fun... for a while. I'll explain that later.
But first lets look at the game itself. You live in a shelter set in a post-apocalyptic area that is, of course, irradiated. You can get rad poisoning, food poisoning, basically any kind of poisoning. (including cookie poisoning... not really.) You explore (go on expeditions) this area and get supplies from the many question marks on your map. They can be houses and caves and such. But you can also meet others in the wastes, and depending on where you are they can be friendly or hostile. In these human encounters you can recruit, trade, bully (essentially fight), or flee. Trading is pretty-self explanatory, just click on the things you want, and then give them something that has the same amount of value points as the other item does. Bullying is basically just killing the person for what you want. Fleeing is also self-explanatory. Recruiting is pretty easy to do as often times the people you meet are desperate.
Now onto the mechanics.
Since it is a post-apocalyptic wasteland you need food and water. Water is obtained through rain and expeditions. Food is obtained through expeditions and traps that you can set outside. You will also need gasoline to fuel your shelter. Yes, you have lights and things. You can build more rooms in your shelter to expand room for more buildings. You build, build, build, build, build, build, until you can build no more. You can get quests from people and give them things.
But that's about it. Don't get me wrong, I love the game, but I didn't get that much playtime out of it. I am stuck at a point where I can do about anything because I have such a large water supply, and enough resources to get food from animals. Again, I do not think this game is bad, but I just don't know what else to do.

Intro:
I honestly thought I would just be replaying the movies. It is aptly named Back to the Future: "THE GAME." There is enough material in the first 30 minutes of gameplay to warrant a weekly Television Show. With that said, if you haven't seen the movie (WTF? - It is possible I am told.) Go see it first. The game story relies HEAVILY on the fact that you've seen the movie 'more than once.' It is absolutely made for fans of the movie and not designed for people who will not get the references. You could play it and solve the puzzles but it wouldn't be half as fun. In my opinion this was definitely made for die-hards as expressed in the tremendous detail and love of the franchise. xD~
Game Review: (pros and cons)
Graphics: "Cartoony" style. Simple and quaint. A cool twist on beloved characters.
Sound: Fantastic! High Quality. The voices are stellar and when the theme hits it gives you goose bumps.
Interface: Point, Click and Grab. Simple and straight forward. Dialogue text. ... Clever Puzzles. Object Manip. (*Note: Some people have reported sporatic issues of not being able to: ? - move to a certain spot, problem clicking and/or manipulating a certain item/element in the game world, etc. Obviously if this occurs on an object needed to continue the story it would be a major problem. ~ I myself have thankfully not encountered any of these issues.)
Story: Here's the kicker for me... I bought this game as a die-hard fan with an open mind of expecting any and everything. (Mild Spoiler Upcoming...) In the first 30 seconds, I thought I was simply going to be replaying the game (it was just the intro... duh xD~) and I was fully satisfied with the thought that I would just be playing out the movies. ~ It's Not. ~ It is a totally unique and original story. There is enough material in this game to write an entire Television Drama series. From the best Sci-Fi that we are all familiar with; Guess what? As George Lucas found out the hard way... It's not the pretty graphics, it's not the 3D interface with a bunch of peripheral toys, it's not the high priced actors and the gorgeous women. What is the 'IT' Factor that makes something so spectacular? It's the writing. Always has been, always will be. And this game HAS IT! =) If the writing sucks, the 'whatever it is' tanks. It's that simple. You can throw all the money in the world at something but if you don't pay someone with a brain five bucks to write a good story, people are going to know it and they are going to know it QUICK. Unfortunately in these days, =) like plutonium, good writers are a 'little hard to come by.' xD~ What is/was a $10 steam sale game; hits upon a Serious IDEA. They only made three movies. This should Really be made into a TV television series drama. (NBC/Universal I'm talking to YOU!) Quantum Leap part 2 so to speak. Guy who bounces through time with his buddy. They already have all of it; it's all on the Paramount lot, even the costumes. It would take nothing more than a producer with the nerve. I'm sure there's a demand. All of the cost is taken care of because the props are all there. It would be... SO EASY it's unbelievable. The only thing they NEED: are Writers. =) So... you heard it here. xD~ To be cliche: Well, here's hoping the idea doesn't magically vanish. At least 'The Future' is: whatever we make it, so we'll have to make it a Good One, ALL of US! ~ Enjoy Life the best you can, wherever you are, because we're all stuck In "Good'Old" Two Thousand and Fifteen.
Conclusion:
If you don't have B2tF: The Series to watch on NBC...

Apotheon is the second game developed by Alien Trap Games, the same people who developed Capsized. Apotheon is a 2D side scrolling action RPG game based on Greek mythology where your home has been destroyed by the Gods of Olympus, you have to ascend Mount Olympus and defeat the Gods
It is a simple game, but has a lot of mehcanics that need to be learnt slowly. I love Apotheon's storyline as I love Greek mythology, and seeing all the Gods, such as Poseidon, Zeus, Hades and many more in Apotheon, made me really happy seeing them in a videogame
The game's mechanics teach you not to button mash when it comes to combat, you have to strategically plan your attacks, and if you don't or fail to plan them correctly, then you are liable of being killed. The combat is simple, plan your combat correctly, strike the enemy until his/her healthbar reaches to zero, but as mentioned before its not that easy
Overall, the game is not easy. It has the same amount of difficulty that Capsized offered, however, there isn't a huge difficulty spike as Capsized had
The music is wonderful and made me feel like I was on Mount Olypmus during the Greek times. The voice acting was really good, hearing every single character talk in the game was a nice addition
Apotheon also offers a free to play multiplayer portion which is seperate to the main game, however, for me personally, I cannot understand why Alien Trap Games made a multiplayer version so late and seperately, the multiplayer is bare bones, hardly no one plays it, whenever there is a match it always keeps on disconnecting and personally, Apotheon's multiplayer is a waste of time...
Apotheon is a nice game to play in short bursts, it is not an easy game, but certainly not as unforgiving as Capsized. Apotheon Arena (which is the multiplayer portion of Apotheon) is a waste of time downloading and playing

I'm not really a fan of shooters that are based off of historic wars. War stories typically don't intrigue me and I usually find them to be repetitive and dull, which means games like this need to have superb gameplay in order for me to enjoy it. Fortunately, Sniper Elite V2's gameplay delivers.
The game takes place in Berlin. It's 1945 and nearing the end of World War II. The Americans are gathering the best of Germany's rocket scientists and V2 programme architects for Operation Overcast. You assume the role of Karl Fairburne, an american sniper sent out to make sure those scientists don't end up in Russia's hands.
Unlike other modern day shooters, Sniper Elite V2 doesn't focus so much on going in guns blazing. Instead, it focuses on stealth and strategically timing your shots in order to complete your mission unnoticed and unharmed. As you can probably tell by the title, this is a sniping game. It's largely focused on sniping your enemies from distances while staying in cover. Sniping out enemies with your rifle is so satisfying thanks to the x-ray effect. When you pull the trigger, a short slow-motion cinematic shot will begin showing the bullet penetrate your enemy. For example, if you shoot your enemy through the eye, it'll show the bullet penetrating the eye and coming out of the back of the skull. Even after doing this for hours, it never gets old. You're always trying to get that next great headshot. However, it's not all about sniping. There will be times when an enemy soldier will be alerted by the sound of your rifle and you'll have to defend yourself in other ways. The game allows you to carry three weapons at a time. This usually consists of one rifle, one pistol and one machine gun. The game also allows you to carry various equipment such as trip wires, land mines, dynamite and even rocks to distract your enemies. With so many options, the gameplay definitely makes up for it's lack of interesting storytelling.
The game also has different collectibles to pick up throughout each level if you care about that sort of thing, but it's up to the player and isn't necessary in order to complete the game. It's a nice additional feature that encourages the player to explore every corner of the map. 
If you're a fan of third-person shooters, stealth games, or if you just love sniping, I'd definitely check this out. I'd also recommend getting the DLC packs for this game as they contain extra missions and weapons. I can't say the additional weapons are worth it because I didn't find myself using them that often. However, the four additional missions should add on a few more hours of fun if the base game left you craving more.

I'd like to think most gamers at least know what Doom is all about and why people like it, but I'll go ahead and lay it out.
This is my favorite shooter game in the world, and one of my favorite games period. It nails the logical progression of difficulty in terms of enemy placement and quantity as well as map layout. This game is so replayable -- it's actually among the first few games people had the idea of speedrunning. If you're not out for speed, then you can kick the difficulty up a notch or try and get every secret. Every weapon has a distinct application (save for the handgun) and feels satisfying to use. Fantastic gunplay.The Doom engine itself is divine, one of the best I can think of. The game is as challenging as you want it to be, anywhere from♥♥♥♥♥♥easy (I'm too young to die!) to brutally hard (Nightmare)
You can't ignore the music and graphics either. Some of the best, most appropriate game music and graphics that have aged incredibly well.
The atmosphere in Doom is absolutely flawless. Never does the game fail to make me feel like I've got a monstrous task ahead of me. Sometimes you'll be anxious to activate a switch that is so obviously a trap and you don't know if you can make it out alive, but you have to activate it anyway if you want to progess. At others, you'll channel the badass nature of your space marine avatar and let nobody out of your clutches. You're supposed to feel like this is a hell (heh) of a task to take on, but also that you're exactly the man for the job, and that's exactly the feeling Doom gives me.
With only select Bethesda ARPGs coming even close, Doom is probably the most modded game in the world. There are countless megaWADs, level packs, and gameplay-altering mods. And you can bet your sweet♥♥♥♥♥there's multiplayer mods available, each with level packs and gameplay mods of their own. Mods are coming out faster than you can probably play them, so don't worry about running out of content. With the base game and all these mods that have been coming out since the early '90s, anyone who gets a kick out of this game can easily get hundreds of hours of enjoyment out of it.
Basically, Doom is one of the most polished, most well-designed games on Earth (and Mars, and Hell) and I could play it forever.

There's been many simulation games that try to show off that they have the most realistic car physics or realistic collisions. Those games have either died out, or were just created and every pupular youtuber plays it then goes back to more popular games. Beam.NG Drive however is different. Very different.
Just before I start talking about why this games spectacular, let me just clarify that if you don't like driving or simulation games, this ain't your cup of tea. This game feels to be made for the ones who just like driving cars.
Beam.NG Drive has a revolutionary physics engine, it can make crashes based on weight, durability of the material, how many parts the car has, segments of the frame or chassis, and the speed at which you're going. It's amazing how fast and how accurate the physics can be. These guys worked on another physics-based car game named Rig of Rods in 2006, so you know when they have phisics in a game, it will be top notch.
For the tinkerers out there, Beam.NG Drive's customizability outperforms any car customization game or feature of any type, and doesn't gimp any of the parts down to "General Customizations", and so in other words, it's your dream game. You can select from a huge amount of parts. Some things you can change are Differentials, Transmision Gear Ratios, Driveshafts, Axle Types (Solid and Independent most commonly), Wheel hubs (and assortment of lugs on the hub varing from 4 to 8 lugs.), Radiators, and so much more that i'm not going to cover here.
The driving system is realistic as well, and don't be suprised that you flip over or spin-out on your first time driving. It is reccomended that you play with a gamepad or steering wheel but a keyboard can work too. It's meant to drive as a normal, everyday car (Unless if you dont get a normal car. *Duh*) , so going too fast or turning too much may result in a over or under steer. It will take time too learn the basic moves to drive. I'd reccomend doing situations first before doing freeroaming or career (When it comes out).
For those people who like graphics or don't have powerful pc's, I got good news for both of you guys. The graphics are really good on max, still look decent on lowest, and it is a cpu intensive game, not a gpu intensive game. Don't let the "Intensive" part of that sentence fool you, I can run this on a Surface Pro 1 just fine at lowest with 30 fps, 720p. Or for a better example, a Intel Core 2 Quad is all you need for this game. The gpu can even be a GT 610 if you want.
Lastly, for the modders. They fully support mods, and the community is thriving and growing bigger daily. Cars, Maps, Parts and more are avalible on Beam.NG's website.
Beam.NG Drive is a master at what genre this game is in. It is a simple, yet extremely advanced car game, with the best physics i've ever seen on any car game. Get this game whenever you can. I bet you'll enjoy it.
I give Beam.NG Drive a 10/10.

If anyone cares to read, here's what I thought.
For Honor... is a mixed bag for worse....
The gameplay and design of the game is fresh and exciting, no doubt. It feels as if fighting games have finally reached the third demension comfortably and innovatively without any kind of gimmick. It's addictive and always has you wanting "that next good match". Soime of the duels you'll have will be tense and exciting.
The aesthetics and animations are very pleasing to look at. Even running around feels good, watching your character move in and out of ducks and jukes with natural ease. It's pleasing.
Aside from all of the obvious positives, there are quite a few negatives...
As I'm sure you all know, the Peer-to-Peer connections... It speaks for itself.
If you're not familiar with PtP connectivity however, it's simply direct connections between players PCs instead of a server. As I'm sure you can imagine, this causes a hoard of issues, ranging from twitchy, teleport-y fights, match drops, host advantages (despite Ubi swearing there isn't) and even lagswitches and DDOSers.
For a game that requires split second timing and reactions, unreliable PtP is extremely counterintuitive.
If you're a fan of balanced games, this isn't the game for you.
Outside of duels, your gear for your character can effect different stats, such as attack, defense, stamina usage and so on. If you play anything 4v4, you can put your gear to use, changing the playstyle of your character. Grinding to good gear is lengthy and can take some time, especially if you avoid the microtransactions in a... ahem... full priced game.
However, the only REAL gear to go for is the gear that affects your revenge stat. You can essentially gear your character to be hit nigh but a few times, block a few attacks to where you can activate revenge and boost yourself to be able to kill players in 2 to 3 hits. Everyone does it and it's not very fun.
Variety is the spice of life, you know.
Speaking of which, variety is NOT something you'll find in the duel modes. If you don't enjoy the high leveled gear idea, then most people would think to go to the duels and brawls. 1v1s and 2v2s that do not use gear. Sadly, these a ridden with their own plague, that of light classes.
Now, some say light classes aren't all that bad, but I must beg to differ. Light classes are the easiest to pick up and understand, the fastest and in some cases the hardest hitting, aside from maybe one or two other classes. Their dodges have invincibility frames on them, which can in some cases, allow them to dodge mid-combo and hit you, despite you just wailing on them.
Despite that, even if I'm wrong about light classes being slighty, SLIGHTLY better than the rest, it's almost all you'll ever see in duels.
I decided to entertain myself one night and did 50 duels, back to back, a new opponent every time.
I am not f*cking kidding you, eight, EIGHT of those 50 had someone playing something other than a light class, and SIX of those eight times, it was Nobushi.
So, essentially, 2 out of 50 times I fought against someone who was considered a "medium" class.
Lastly, the bugs, the most prominently being the guardbreak bug. If someone is to attempt a guardbreak on you, and you input ANY input into the game before the proper timing, which is much tighter than beta mind you, it'll cancel your ability to tech.
Yes, the game thinks you tried to tech too early by hitting your eft thumbstick or what have you, and it denies you the tech.
This can lead to some pretty frustrating strings of guardbreaks, where your enemy can string free hits on you.
No word on the fix as far  as I know, or if it will be addressed.
---
So, essentially you have a game with a fresh concept and addictive gameplay, ridden with horrendous, actually horrendous, peer-to-peer connection issues in-game and even in-menu, gameplay dulling bugs and terrible lack of variety in character choice either from them being too strong or too easy to play.
It's like trying to play streetfighter 3rd strike online with p2p connections, but everyone just chooses Gill and exploits a free hit bug.
It's not fun anymore.
I've honest to god gotten tired of it, and I'm not one to put down a game often. I beat Ninja Gaiden 1 and 2 on master ninja for god-sakes.
It's just... too frustrating. You try and try to do your best, but most, if not all of the time, you'll have the game telling you otherwise. I've been beaten without being able to guard any attacks, I've watched executed enemies rollback and gain half of their health back after being dead, while running around with NO HEAD. I've slaughtered people with poor connections, watching them guard and parry me yet still taking full damage.
Hell, I've even seen people get pushed off cliffs, only for them to float back up onto the cliff to toss the guy who threw him off back down.
It's... it's a warzone, by every sense of the word. Mad, chaotic, and full of bad blood.
I would NOT reccomend this game in it's current state. It's just too damn flawed to have a consistant good time. For me, 1/5 matches have me feeling good, if that even. It just gets worse the more upset you get.
I doubt they'll ever change it from P2P to dedicated servers. It'd cost them more money than they're willing to spend in it's long term 5 or so year plan.
I doubt they'll ever balance the gear score, because as of now they have no alternative and I personally think they're afraid that if they do, they'll lose a lot of the "casual" audience.
I doubt they'll ever balance the classes properly either. Again, afraid to lose the "causal" audience and afraid to be hung, drawn, and quartered for not listening to the crying masses. Bad classes like lawbringer are being ignored, yet decent classes like Raider, Valkirie and PEACEKEEPER of all classes are getting BUFFED.
Explain THAT one to me.
---------------------------
TL;DR
Game is terribly flawed and isn't worth the frustration as of now. Expect it to remain this way for as long as it lives, because it's already losing players.

Most satisfying driving and most satisfying destruction in any game I've ever played, all down to some really impressive soft-body physics technology.
This game is not for everyone, though. It doesn't offer passive entertainment (cutscenes, "xp", social aspects). It's an unfinished car sandbox, and you'll need to meet it halfway. For enthusiasts and Top Gear fans, this is very exciting, and probably the richest, freest experience you can find in car games.
It's possible to get very, very serious about this game, with custom parts and deep tuning possibilities. But it's also fun to just run hot laps in some preconfigured sports car (or hot hatchback, or a lifted van, or trashy 90s buick—every carchetype you could want is here). There's no line between casual and hardcore driving: you'll be doing timed point-to-point rallycross down a canyon one minute, the next minute you'll intentionally slip off the road and go tumbling down it, just see the glorious vehicle carnage.

SOMA is one of the most philosophical, incredible, and darkest games I have ever seen. The game is reminiscent of novelist Michael Crichton's
, but is even more profound, disturbing, and mind-blowing. It's just incredible. Explore a horrific underwater civilization filled with fascinating backstory, and monsters that render you genuinely helpless. Use the world around you to solve puzzles that make you think. Run for your life. Explore the deep ocean and the extraordinary technological world filled with functioning airlocks, televisions, computers, tablets, and much more. The sound effects mesmerize you, and the music is solid as well. This world feels so
. When you go underwater, you feel like you are there, and when you are in an airlock, you almost feel the water rise around your legs as you wait to go out into the sea. Absolutely incredible, with a plot that never ceases to surpise you. This is no "Outlast underwater;" it focuses not on external monstrosities, but those that lie inside. SOMA is definitely one of the most excellent horror games ever created. Recommended.

I've thrown a pro's and con's and also my own experiences at the bottom.
PROS-
-Good, social game to make you feel in a different roleplay world which stands out from the rest.
-Nice variety of dinos to choose from. There are few but they are such good starts with good skin textures. (Much better ones coming soon!)
-Decent size server player count with big map. You're always going to come across another player so don't feel too lonely.
-Animations and sounds look real nice and sound nice. Most importantly, sounds and movements register upon interaction THANK GOD!
-Basic survival game that you control being the hunter, the pacifist, or a neutral scavenger! :)
CONS-
-High settings will wreck your gameplay! Low settings still look decent so not to worry.
-Some attacks don't go through when you're in a certain position or you get hit by an attack when you're not near your rival. Gets a bit bothersome and unfair.
-Eating with herbivores is pretty bugged. There is no guide to what eats what, it's a figure it out yourself thing.
-Not that many social interactions but enough to get your dino heard. (The way people show their friendly is NUM. 2 and a fast crouch and up LOL) There should be more like bowing or standing ground!
Those are honestly the only things a regular player will experience. KoS is normal because, well, dinosaurs. Unless there's a stego killing everyone in a herd who are also stegos then that is annoying. It's not that horrible of a problem unless you keep trying something and dying because then now it's your fault. lol. People will group kill you, carnivores will protect herbivores, whatever. Let them do what they're doing. Not everyone is in the same mindset of your gameplay.
Experience-
I'm mainly an Allosaurus. The best time I had was when there was a wall of Herbivores and circle of Carnivores getting ready to battle because it was a fight for Spawn Lake. Me, being a sneaky snake, crouched in trees and bushes in a far left circling behind the herbies. (Not herpes).. The best part, 4 allo's saw the idea and crouched along with me. With the wall of herbies distracted, we got right up behind them, roared, then charged. Once the Carnivores saw that, they charged also. It was a full fledge ambush! There was roaring, jaws snapping, feet stomping and hearts stopping. It was around 25 carnivores and the rest herbivores (Highest person count server I forget which one). We lost the battle but it was very intense and cinematic.
That actually lasted for 2 hours and the adrenaline was just there the whole time. This just shows that no matter what, you're going to be addicted to this without knowing. Everytime I re-enter the server, there are always intense conflicts like that having a different setup and plot.

Overall, I beleive this game has great potential. It's already fun, with amazing graphics (something you usually don't get in EA games) and an active community. You will spend a long time limping around a far-too-large map though, so be warned. I highly suggest this game if you like dinosaurs, cause for me that's at least half the entertainment value.

I loved this game since I started playing it in December. I wanted to wait to put up any kind of review because I was concerned about the direction of the game. Here are some observations and opinions of mine.
The Good:
-Be a dinosaur! With an expanding roster of available animals!
-The dinosaurs look really good and the animations are pretty good (although some are better than others).
-Devs update the game and are clearly very dedicated to the project. I'm talking 1-5 updates per week, although lately they've been more back-end updates that dont directly translate into game content. A LOT has been added since I first started playing.
-The players are great! It's fun getting to know other players and adding them to the friends list and playing the game with them. Even random people in-game can make it a real blast to play!
The Bad:
-Dino balancing is very much a WIP. A dino that can be OP one week can be unplayably weak the next. Rex overpopulation combined with their power currently makes this an almost Rex-only game as of this writing, but when I first started playing it was the Shaunt that was OP. Balancing the dinos will be an ongoing challenge and it's to be expected in an early access game, but I thought I should mention it.
-The Devs' attitude. I don't dislike the devs but they have a reputation for being "unprofessional." Your miliage may vary on this one, as they do seem to have as many white-knight suck-ups as they have haters. I guess what bothers me is the "if you don't like the game then GTFO" response to constructive critisism that I've whitnessed.
-The players! There are some real ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s in this game, just like all games. Made worse by internet anonymity and you can't see players' names in game anymore. People also have different ways they play the game and everyone gets their feathers ruffled by it.
-Punishing Difficulty. While all the above "bads" can be said of most any game, this one is pretty specific to The Isle. The game has been getting progressively harder since "launch" and it feels like it's getting rediculous at this point. The leg breaking thing went too far, but better maps could potentially solve that problem. Now that carnivores apply a bleed on top of their base damage, surviving as a herb doesn't feel challenging, it feels impossible. These could be simple balancing issues, but the devs have stated over and over that they intend for this game to be punishing by design, so I don't expect things to get better but worse. I think it's a bad idea and will doom this game in the long run to a very small playerbase that burns out quickly.
-Design Decisions and Direction. There are some non-player-friendly aspects of the game which may be part of the "punishing difficulty" issue and may not. Huge maps that take forever to travel, 15-30 minute real-time healing. These things all start adding up to sap the fun out of it and make the game feel like work more than play. Spawn locations are way too far from areas of interest. The potential that nude human models may be added in the future concerns me as well. I'm not a prude myself but I'm worried that younger players might have their access to the game jeopardized just to satisfy the devs' "wouldn't it be cool" approach to the issue.
The Ugly:
-The Devs wanted me to buy, but don't want me to play. This goes hand-in-hand with "dev attitude" and "Game direction." The devs have a certain playerbase in mind in terms of who they are trying to appeal to, which to me seems to be 14-17 year old males who want a hardcore gaming experience. Floppy♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥in games aren't "edgy" or "cool" to me, and I would rather the game be fun than a punishing waste of time, so the devs say that I can pretty much go f-myself. It's their goal to make people like me stop playing and they've said as much in their streams.
-The game has been virtually unplayable for months. Ever since "saving" was introduced, the servers have been crashing constantly, almost like clockwork, the server will crash and kick you out of the game. I gave the game another shot today, after not playing for a while, and in 15 minutes of playtime I was kicked out twise by server crashes. When it takes 15 minutes on a good day to reach a population of dinos, and then longer to form a group, this many crashes with such alarming regularity is a game breaker, and that the problem has existed for so long and still hasn't been resolved makes me think that it may never be resolved and I should just pack my bags.
So that's it. I've had a blast playing and the game is probably still basically fun, but I wouldn't know because I no longer have any meaninful play sessions due to the amount of time it takes to do something in-game combined with the constant crashing. Now that chat has range, I can't spawn in and ask in chat where people are so I can join up, because they're 15 minutes away in real time travel and can't hear me, and by the time I got there anyways the game would crash and we'd start all over. The overall "fun-ness" of this game goes a long way but it's been getting less fun and more frustrating over time.

Firstly I thought it wouldn't be good like a Splinter Cell game; but it actually surprised me. It is better than I could ever imagine! A must have for any stealth game fan, mostly if you like WWII games also. It is as good as a Splinter Cell game, if not even better in some aspects.
Recently I played the Hitman series and it was obvious where Velvet Assassin got its inspiration; although this game isn't an "assassin sandbox" as Hitman is, that fits the theme very well. Not every game should have that kind of openess, which to be honest, turned some Hitman levels into a chore. You can indeed kill your targets using many tricks, and if everything else fails, you still can rely on your silenced pistol, just make sure to hide the body afterwards. It has some good hide mechanics too, including the good old pick at a corner and hide into or behind bushes.
Velvet Assassin uses a checkpoint save system, but they are well distributed, and even if you must replay a big chunk of some level, it isn't a frustratingly hard game; it has its chalenge bits, but everything is very well balanced.
The game has a dark tone, which fits perfectly with its WWII settings, it runs very well even with the minimum requirements, and it's extremely solid (I didn't find a single bug within my 2 playthroughs); it has astonishing sound FX too, including weapons sounds, environments, the usual guard-talk and a great soundtrack. I can't recommend this one enough for the stealth game funs.

I've always been a fan of Arma games for their attention to detail and realism and I've had my mind blown over the years to see just how much more detail and realism they can capture in their titles. This one has really little to no flaws in any department whatsoever. Quick n' Dirty review.
Graphics: 10/10 - Runs smooth as butter even on my not-so-stellar GTX770 with modest graphic settings and still looks amazing.
Sound/Audio: 10/10 - The environments sound alive and the crack and whiz of the bullets really help immerse you in the game.
Controls: It's Arma - If you didn't know, I can't explain it. If you know, then I don't have to.
Gameplay: 9/10 - Went to a 9 because some issues are present in online play. Server performance varies and a lot of them are locked due to restrictions on content you own. If you buy it all or download it all, no issues then you can assume 10/10 score.
Campaign: It's Arma - It's really difficult to score this because for a lot of people the campaign is going to feel boring. It's a lot of you running around doing actual stuff with very little run n' gun like you find in most newer CoD games. They did put in a fairly impressive campaign that took me I think about 6 to 8 hours to beat, but again that's up to the player, because I took my time and had to step away to dad/husband stuff. The core of the game I feel is online though.
MODS: It's Arma - There are more mods than bullets fired in all of human history. It might be an exaggeration but not by much. Mods, simply put, make Arma what it is. There are enoough Mods in the community to make this game a new experience pretty much whenever you want. From Altis Life to crazy deathmatch crap you really have no shortage of new content for free.
Overall rating is just you simple need to buy it. If you're a fan of the series and don't already own it then buy it. If you're not a fan or this is your first Arma game you're thinking of trying then definitely do so. You don't need to own any of the prior games to really get into this. This is definitely one of those games you can play for a while and come back to down the road over and over again.

I am very much conflicted when writing this review, this game has so much potential and great assets. The main problem I have is that it is made of pure potential, and only that. Its essentially an expensive garrys mod for serious fps roleplayers, but it tries to market itself as a milsim. These are my top 3 issues with the game:
Actually joining a game:
Not only is it extremely hard to hop on a gamemode besides 3 servers for King Of The Hill, but 99.99% of any other gamemode either has zero players or REQUIRES buying each and every single ♥♥♥♥♥♥ DLC (which might I add costs $120+ total) along with upwards of 7 unique mods per server.
Physics:
The physics of this game can be extremely unpredictable which is not acceptable at all in a game that markets itself as being extemely realistic. The game has been out for over three years now and some of the bugs and flaws are honestly baffling, like breaking a helicopter's rotor blades will cause it to float around the map like Kirby and vehicles will randomly explode when being towed.
Necessity for tons of friends:
Most servers have only small communities of friends on them that are playing PvE missions that are up for about as long as the group of 20 people feel like playing. Its not very fun to have to join servers of people who will go "who the ♥♥♥♥ are you" and kick you from the server after having to download all their mods to join at all.
Tl;dr dont buy this game unless
-You are ok with playing $120 worth of content once a week for about 2 hours with friends
-You have over 70 online friends ready to hop on to a server at all times
-You have a spare terrabyte for all the mods you need to get to be able to play this game in any meaningful way

his game stays true to the feel of the old games in that you can still talk to people between missions, and explore the world a little bit. The guns are a lot more effective and easier to use, and the darkness powers are stronger, more varied, easier to use, and are implemented very well into the combat. You can carry one main weapon, such as a shotgun or an assault rifle, and two side arms, such as pistols and small SMG's.
You can control both the dark tentacles with a button press. One grabs enemies, weapons, and items. The other is used for executions, and demon-arm slashes into enemies.
If you liked the first one, or are looking for a new kind of shooter, get this game!

Back to the Future is an enjoyable point ‘n’ click, featuring a great adventure and an astonishing cast, but it couldn’t deny it was a TellTale game even if it wanted to: all of the studio’s old trademark design elements are there in abundance.
Before TellTale switched to creating interactive cinematic miniseries, they were largely known for their classic style point ‘n’ click adventure games. Back to the Future: The Game was one of the last ones that used this format.
In a sense, this was a match made in heaven, since the movie trilogy itself was one of the last large-budget adventures on the big screen. It was a large task to try and match it, but for the most part, the creators did a good job.
The story begins not so long after the movies, when Marty finds Doc’s distress signal sent from 1931. This sets off a chain of events that involve a run-in with another troublemaking Tannen, and a woman who accidentally becomes young Doc’s girlfriend, leading him on a path that results in Hill Valley turning into a police state. And the episodes themselves have even more twists and cliffhangers, keeping up your interest.
On the other hand, it needs these tricks to keep you in the game, because like all old TellTale titles, it is very slow, and most of the events take place at one location (in this case, the town square). The studio’s formula is also present in full force: all episodes have the same structures and similar solutions to similar problems, always including a multi-choice puzzle where you need to run back and forth until you stumble upon the right combination.
The dialogues were always TellTale’s strong point, and Back to the Future is no exception. The entire series is a love letter to the movie trilogy, and the return of Christopher Lloyd (and Michael J. Fox for a few lines at the last episode) really helped to make you feel that this is as close as we can get to a fourth film without an actual fourth film.

Let me start this review off by saying I think this is a fantastic game. However, for what it costs I wish I could undo my purchase and wait for it to go on sell. I've completed a playthrough and most content I care about in 8.7 hours according to steam.
The Good
-Great Soundtrack: Supergiant always does a fantastic job with this.
-Fun and visually interesting world: Another staple of supergiant.
-The story: While walking a fine line between too slow and not immersive enough I found it to be a lot of fun and genuinly cared about it for a long time. Only towards the end did it become "meh".
The Bad
-The game is one part visual novel and one part mini game: I can't help but feel this game tried the usual "give the best of both worlds" and ending up giving me the "worse of both worlds" instead. I constantly found myself getting annoyed that I would either have to trodge through a bunch of dialog I didn't care about or complete another mini game to get to the bits I did. I wish they had spent more time streamlining the story and gave the mini game more depth (More items, characters, challenges?)
-The story: After completing what I would call chapter 1 the story becomes a bit interesting but all together too slow and the traveling in this really immersive world became a chore more than an adventure. Game designers! Please don't reuse maps/content!
-Mini game: After awhile I didn't care about the mini game at all or upgrading anything. I put the dificulty to the max and used all of dificulty increasers and it just didnt matter. The characters while diverse were not interesting enough, nor was their mastery/trinket system. I truely believe this was the weakest part of the game.

One of the better tactical games out there.  Several out there will tell you otherwise because of a few reasons.  Some complain about the graphics being dated, well I am an old school gamer from the Atari 2600 days so lemme say that great graphics do NOT make great gameplay.  I'd rather have a blocky ugly game that plays great than some photo-realistic crap that simply isn't fun just pretty to look at.  Another group of players will say there's no varity in weapons, equipment, etc.  Folks being a former active duty U.S. Marine I can tell ya that in the real world you don't always get "varity"  you get what your issued and make it work.  You improvise, overcome and adapt.  Those are the two biggest complaints I see from some reviews, most of these only have one sentence and in no way justify their complaint on the game in any way.  There is plenty of weapons and equipment and as you unlock harder difficulties you'll fond plenty of challenge and replayability.  There's no one way to beat each scenario, you can try different approaches each time and see which works best.  Graphically the game is just fine and reminds me of the models used in the original Rainbow Six, whuch was way better  than its better looking sequels.  Plus this is available for iOS now so you can play on the go.  I think multiplayer is the only thing I'd add or improve in the game at all.  I highly recommend this title to any fans of urban combat, close quarters simulation.  One of the best, period.

Soma is a psychological horror/survival horror/exploration game that asks the very important question of what it means to be human and what IS a human. Set in a failing undersea facility, the player takes the guise of Simon Jarrett. Simon wakes up from a brain scan after a traffic accident to find himself in PATHOS II with no idea how he got there or what is going on. But he soon learns that things are bad and they are going to get worse. Through Simon’s journey through the different sections of the facility we learn the reasons behind what happened to the facility and shy Simon is there through computer files, logs, radio messages and interaction with some of the insane(?) robots and AI that inhabit the facility.
Along with robots, there are “things” that inhabit the facility. You can’t fight these enemies and all you can do is run, hide or hopefully outwit them. If you are caught by one of them they can hurt or kill you. The survival horror in Soma is very much in line with “Amnesia: The Dark Decent”, an earlier game by the same company.
The Good
There is a lot to recommend in this game. It is VERY atmospheric and makes good use of its setting most of the time. The questions the game raises are important and are explored through the story.
The Bad
Some of the characters aren’t drawn as well as they could and at times I find Simon being so dense a problem. At one point he is flat out TOLD something (an important plot point as well) but he seems to ignore it. While the main plot is well written some things connected with it don’t make sense if you think about it a little and some things are never really explained. The biggest problem I have is the survival horror aspect. This is also known as “running away from monsters and hiding”. Frankly while the monsters are well designed (when you can get a good enough look at them) just don’t anything for me. Part of it that I’m not scared all that easy and my mind works on the idea “If it can hit me, I can hit it back.” I found the monsters irritation enough I downloaded a mod so they wouldn’t attack me. For me, it made the game much better.
I liked the game in many respects and what they attempted. Most of my problems stem from me not being big in the survival horror aspect. sm

Wow. Just finished the game, and boy is has to be the darkest game I've ever played. No, I don't mean literally dark like Doom 3, but rather, dark in terms of premise and storyline. I don't want to say much about the plot because it is the key draw for playing the game. Everything else ranges from "meh" in quality to pretty decent, while the ideas behind the plot are an 11/10, and the plot itself is good enough. The only gripes I really have about the storyline are concerning named characters, because there are a lot of names getting dropped in recordings you'll hear, and it's hard to keep up with who is who or what certain characters did and why. To make matters worse, sometimes it was difficult to understand some of the voices in recordings, which certainly didn't help with the mess.
The gameplay was alright. If this game didn't have the plot and philosophical shenanigans going on that it does, I probably wouldn't have finished it because the actual gameplay is pretty so-so. You walk around a bunch, interact with equipment, solve a small number of puzzles, and do stealth stuff. I love stealth, and this game has some of the worst stealth I've ever seen in a game. Most of the time, you just crouch, look away from the enemy, and sit perfectly still...even in bright light while it's looking right at you, and the things just waddle away like idiots. They are very annoying and I never enjoyed this element of the game despite having been a fan of Alien Isolation; another first person game where you hide from but don't fight a monster. Actually playing the game just wasn't fun for me. It was all about the story, character interactions, and philosophical questions that get brought up.
The game took me about ten hours to complete, which was long enough. I would've been fine if it'd ended a couple of hours sooner, but it didn't outstay its welcome to the extent that the aforementioned Alien Isolation did for me. I was ready for this game to end, and before to much longer, it ended. The story and philosophical matters are quite dark and twisted. Maybe it has a terrible ending; maybe a happy one? I shan't spoil it, but there is certainly dark stuff about...oh, and do watch after the credits.
If you enjoy really thinking about things and sci-fi existence/humanity "stuff," and a pretty good storyline, you'll likely get something you'll like out of this game. It's not great or an absolute must-play for most people, but my curiosity was gnawing at me and I just had to see this game for myself.
In closing, I would like to point out that if you think you guessed a big plot twist from the trailer, the thing you think is a massive plot twist is just an early-game twist that is hinted at and built up to, revealed within the first couple of hours. I assure you there's much more interesting stuff going on than just that one twist the trailer pretty much gives away. It's just the groundwork for the philosophy I spoke of. I know I'm being cryptic about the plot, but honestly, there's not much other reason to play this game than for the story/character/philosophy aspects.

I never wrote a review before, but I feel like writing one for "The Isle".
So where to start? I suppose most know what this game is about, or at least what it is planned to be about, since, as many other reviewers already mentioned, the gameplay is so barebones as of right now that it's barely even bones. Walking, eating, drinking and communicating is the entire extent of the current abilities of any dinosaur you decide to pick as your character (humans are not yet implemented).
Although interesting situations can occur together with other players, playing alone, especially on a not-so populated server is about as captivating as watching a cat sleep. There are a few hotspots on the given maps (which are anything but good, but since no professional mapper created them I do not necessarily consider this as really negative), where people either do nothing, or basically turn the entire area into a huge Deathmatch zone.
Well, when I got the game in December (I think) development seemed to be going into a really good direction. Nice/handy features were implemented, it ran quite good (even on my PC, which leans towards the lower end of the hardware requirements) and it felt like the game was going to be a lot more fun within a few months. Half a year later, it does feel changed, but not actually improved. New dinosaurs and maps were added, foliage models were changed and so on, while the actual gameplay remained the same. In order to create a "hardcore" survival game, things like broken legs were implemented (which would be a fun feature if it weren't for the following), apparently without giving thought to the fact that a day is limited to 24 hours, since for the biggest among the dinosaurs healing a broken leg can take 2+ hours of ingame time and make no mistake, you can't log off and it continues healing. I am glad that people in school and the developers seem to have enough time at their disposal to be able to wait that amount of time, but I oftentimes do not even have the time to play two hours and I am certain many people agree with me when I say that spending those waiting for your character to heal is not what motivates me to play this game. Optimisation, server stability and other important things are seemingly unaddressed still/only now starting to get addressed.  I don't pretend to be savvy when it comes to game development, but it feels like books are being put onto an unfinished shelf.
Even a bad game can be fun online with friends or a bunch of cool strangers. Unfortunately, "The Isle"'s community is about as toxic as it gets. The developers encourage this behaviour, whether intentional or not is not for me to judge. Criticism, no matter how polite or well thought out is usually silenced either by the forum moderators, a developer (oftentimes through mockery), or an entire group of people who immediately form a defensive phalanx against anyone who dares criticise any individual of the developer team, despite being mocked by them themselves, but to each their own.
Contributing to the game has (as far as I am aware) officially been made impossible since (again, as far as I know) the main developer stated that he is not going to listen to any input since he is going to create the game only the way he wants it, just as a heads up for anyone who might think they will perhaps get their ideas considered, since they support the game during its EA phase.
I would further go into the atrocious handling of the community and marketing, but I feel like this review is long enough already.
So now the progression system has been added, which is supposed to be the main feature of the dinosaur side in the final product. Good news right?
Well, it would be if it were at least somewhat finished. Half of it. A quarter even. Right now it pretty much forces the carnivores (starting as Herrerasaurs) to cannibalise each other constantly to progress to an inferior dinosaur that often gets killed by other Herrerasaurs again, which means the player who managed to progress already has to start again from the bottom, because there is no way to save any progress as of now. Carnivores also starve within a very short amount of time, resulting in anything but an actual surviving "simulation", but rather a deathmatch on a timer. Water can barely be found and is usally fiercely protected by the one or two players who managed to reach a high tier of carnivore, thereby turning the area into no man's land for anything smaller than them. In addition to that, neither the game's own, nor server performance was notably improved (in fact they seem to have gotten a lot worse), thus the combat usually turns out to be a laggy merry-go-round until one (or often both) of the combatants dies due to bleeding. All of this of course implies that you even find another player in the first place, since AI dinosaurs are still not a sight on the isle.
A new map was added and while it is a bit better than the previous ones, it still has plenty of obvious flaws that further decrease the playability of this new mode. The fact that the new map is also several times larger than the already large previous maps also denies casual players (those who do not have the time to play for 5+ hours in one go) a somewhat easy access, since only those who have enough time and the will to sink hours upon hours into memorising the map will have a general idea of where they are upon spawning (which is atrocious at best) as of now.
None of this would be so bad if you could still switch over to the old "Sandbox" mode, where you could just choose whatever dinosaur you desired to play and get going, however for some reason it was decided to remove this mode until the progression mode is finished (in a move to force the playerbase to "test" the new mode it appears), which could, based on its current state, very well take several months, thus driving people who do not wish to submit themselves to such an ridiculously imbalanced and badly done gamemode away from the game, but as I already mentioned in this review, it does not seem to bother the developers all too much.
Once again, it feels like little to no thought was given about the consequences of a feature implementation.
All in all, I can't recommend it right now, especially not for the current price. I will edit this review if things change in the future, but for now this is my personal view of things as of July 2016.

Let's start this review by saying this is one of the best RPG of all time, from back in the days where RPGs were done right, with proper dice rolls and level up mechanics. Not the watered down Action/Adventure style of modern days.
I played this way over a decade ago and even in the rushed out version (without the Restored Content Mod) it was almost as good as KOTOR1
After so many years my original windows copy would not even be able to start without crashing, so I wondered for a while to get a Steam version, but I was worried that after all this time, the outdated graphics would turn me off.
But when I realized that the KOTOR2 Steam version, (unlike KOTOR1) is sort of a remastered version with widescreen, higher resolutions and xbox controller compatibility (which was always odd to me why both KOTORs didn't have it since they are console ports) paired up with a dirt cheap price made me decide to get it just to have it in my library....
was I in for a treat...
...after installing a few mods: Restored Content Mod is a must, also TLS Backdrop Improvements and M4-78 Enhancement Project add content and better visuals... then a few reskins and armors.
Playing this on a big screen with controller, console style, was very enjoyable even just in the Prologue and early stages on the Peragus Mining Facility which is by far the dullest part of the game since you are just discovering what happened and you don't even have a lightsaber!
Well 6 hours later at about 5 am I was still investigating what happened and I didn't put the controller down till I killed HK-50 just like I did 12 years ago...and this time I really wanted to experience him on my team...but once again the impulse to kill him took over... aaah the anger...
Bottom line: if you played it a long time ago, it's definitely worth going back to memory lane especially if you never experienced the added content, if you never played it and you like RPGs this is a must play to remind you what an RPG should be like. And yes the outdated graphics were completely offset by an engaging story and great RPG mechanics.

Numerous reveiwers have compared this game to FTL: Faster Than Light. Oh if only this were true! FTL is a true gem of a game, with balanced gameplay and eliciting a constant feeling of imminent peril. It is perhaps the best game ever created.
Sheltered is a micromange-heavy grindfest entirely lacking balance. If you can survive the first week or two (which is essentially just a case of storing enough water, and not doing anything really stupid like walking outside without a hazmat suit) it quickly becomes a case of grinding for items without any sense of danger. Admittedly this may not be the case if you select more-balanced attributes for your family, unfortunately I seem to have stumbled upon the over-powered traits almost immediately.
But there remains hope. There are the makings of a good game here. With just a little work (better balance, more varied content) Sheltered could become a good game. Implementing some sort of long-term effect for the morality choices made by the player could also be very interesting. But as it is, Sheltered does not feel ready for release.
Key critical issues appear below.
Most of your time is spent micro-managing your survivors: every task except stat restoration must be manually initiated - repairs, training, crafting, tending plants, etc. Even taking medicine or using bandages requires user input. (I have lost count of the number of times an ill or injured family member has died simply because I did not see their negative status, given this mechanic). With small numbers of survivors this microing gets tedious; with larger numbers I expect it becomes impossible. This could be fixed either by improving the automate mechanic to automate these tasks as well, or by allowing the player to instruct a survivor to continually perform a certain type of task whenever they do not have needs to take care of.
Another big time-sink is inventory management, trying to maximise the items you bring home or purchase in a trade due to limited storage space. This could be improved by adding a colour-coding scheme for inventory management, e.g. colouring the background of an object green if it will take an empty inventory slot, yellow if it will be added to an inventory slot already containing other objects of the same type, and red if there will be no space in the inventory.
With strong characters (easily achievable - see balance below) exploring the world is just a case of grinding without thinking: search every location, fight every encounter (at least, those the game lets you - I want the option to kill traders and would-be recruits - in fact anybody!), with no risk to your survivors.
With strong characters, the different options available in combat are rarely required; simply melee each enemy in turn, or empty your clip into them once you have firearms. Steal, subdue, defend all seem underpowered. The early game may require a little caution (just in case you end up outnumbered) and the late game may be very different - I have no idea, I got bored of the grindy mid-game.
As for getting strong characters, this is also far too easy: simply select Courageous and Troubled for any character you wish to send on expeditions and send them out in pairs, as this will give them two guaranteed (and a third very likely) high-power hits each - none shall stand against this.

Another example of where Steam needs a neutral button.
Short:  I would recommend this game if you love the movies more than tight gameplay or it's on sale.
Long:  I haven't played an adventure game like this since the old LucasArts ones.  The story is decently well-crafted thus far and the voice acting and direction is tremendous.  My issues with the game are MOSTLY technical:
1) The camera is obnoxious and spastic at times.
2) The movement controls curiously keep their memory as you walk despite the 'stage' changing orientation.  For instance, if I travel from a north/south stage to an east/west stage walking 'right' and Marty ROTATES 90 degrees in the transition, I would expect when my frame of reference changes that the 'right' arrow key continues moving Marty to the 'right' of his new orientation.  This isn't the case and you end up with some stages where you are pressing the right arrow key to move 'down and to the left' for instance because of some quizzical initial orientation during the transition.
3) Poor continuity in parts.  In the first episode you choose a 'fake name' to give someone back in time.  When I saved and later reloaded my game, the game had forgotten my choice and I was momentarily concerned maybe I had missed something.  Nope.  Thinking 'well that must be the default' I was proven wrong again when the name changed to another option in EP2.  For a game literally all about the 'details' that seems really... lazy?
4) Every episode apparently has its own 'game' shell which requires you to change ALL your settings each time you play a new one.
Here's where the line between 'technical' and 'design decision' get a bit blurry though:
5) The inventory randomly deletes certain items which, fine, I wouldn't need a key to one door later in the game provided I never go back.  However at one point you get a tool and a few minutes later when you are presented with a situation where the tool is a good solution, it is mysteriously missing.  It didn't get removed via story elements, just deleted from the inventory because the 'scene' changes.
6) The puzzle solutions are not robust.  Whittling down the gameplay, you must select the right choices in the right order.  Dialogue options do not 'matter' in the sense that saying 'smart' things (maybe offering some dialogue that's generic and some that, if you were paying attention earlier in the game, would give you an advantage) makes no difference.  It's somewhat disappointing that there does not appear to be more than one way to solve any puzzle, just in some cases you can solve a few concurrent puzzles in a different order to the same outcome.
Here's where it's mostly a minor gripe with the story, though:
7) The game (thus far) obviously plays homage to the original trilogy, however it almost entirely avoids it.  It would have been nice to at least have had better 'woven' timeline.
Overall, it's a game worth the sale price if you are an afficionado and I don't regret picking it up for ~$6 even if I struggle to f inish with some of the technical oddities.  I would not recommend it for full price, however.

A average, maybe even decent game and with the little amount of sniper games available, it might be worth it. But for me, the bad definitely outweighed the good and I often got tired of it or dropped it for a while out of frustration, not at least with the terrible autosave system. If you buy it cheap on sale (personally I got it for free in a short promotion offer on steam), it isn't a waste, but the money could be used so much better and for an older (and short) game it is quite expensive.
The good:
- Quite good sniper mechanics including wind and bullet drop (meaning that you often have to fire a bit over and to the left of the target to hit it, which is realistic).
- Kill cam shows you the bullet penetrating your target in x-ray.
- You can hit grenades in enemy belts and make them explode.
- Graphics are quite good.
The bad:
- The third person looks provide you with a hell of a camera angle, often meaning that you can't see an enemy if he's right in front of you and you are standing close to a wall.
- No real training possibilities meaning you need to practice shooting on the go. This is a problem in a sniper games as it means that you will newer really master how to hit a far away target precisely where you want to, that is, to calibrate the wind and bullet drop. At least not until you are almost finished with the game anyway.
- The autosave is very bad and means some place that you might need to play through half an hour of combat again if you die. Also, to me it seems like some places, the enemies kept coming closer and closer every time I restarted at checkpoint giving me very little time to react and therefore dying a lot of times.
- There is a general lack of genuine good sniping positions. Most positions are of the kind where you would be dead in five minutes in real life. In real life, a good sniping position is NOT sitting behind a small box in the middle of the road, but a place where you can fire without being spotted and then move to another good sniping position before you fire again. This is more or less impossible in this game.
- While stealth is a possibility, most parts of the game more or less enforce you to chose between rambo or rambo-ligth approaches. A real sniper doesn't stand in one position blasting down 15 enemy soldiers firing in on him or assaulting a compound with a submachine gun killing off 50 soldiers.
- There should be a more realistic game mode whit less help for when you want a challenge. In this you should be able to set off your own landmines and trip-mines if you don't pay attention to where you put them and there shouldn't be bullet lines to help you spot where people are shooting at you from.
- The plot is bad and extremely right-wing USA coldwar hawkish. You fight to liberate nazi war criminals as long at they will help the USA build weapons or kill them if they want to do the same for the USSR. You don't assist in winning the war, on the contrary you actually delays the advance of the Red Army thereby prolonging the war and the suffering of both soldiers and civilians in the war zone or living in areas still under nazi control. Actually, you even kills lots of allied soldiers of the red army.
- There are a few bucks in the game, but when they happen, they are major. Like a wagon full of German soldiers not moving at all while I stand right next to it killing them one by one.
- There is no real aiming with other weapons than the sniper riffle, no real use of iron-sight but instead a cross point with a large spread of bullets, even at very close range .... like 1 meter.
- The game is too split up in "zones". Meaning that you can't really lure most enemies away from the small area they start in. It would be cool if you could fire at them, luring them to follow you into a building which you had filled with traps offering you a more realistic way of taking out a lot of enemies and making landmines and the like much much more practical usable in this game.
Also, the game is quite short, which can be both a good and a bad thing in my opinion.

Let me start this review off by saying I think this is a fantastic game. However, for what it costs I wish I could undo my purchase and wait for it to go on sell. I've completed a playthrough and most content I care about in 8.7 hours according to steam.
The Good
-Great Soundtrack: Supergiant always does a fantastic job with this.
-Fun and visually interesting world: Another staple of supergiant.
-The story: While walking a fine line between too slow and not immersive enough I found it to be a lot of fun and genuinly cared about it for a long time. Only towards the end did it become "meh".
The Bad
-The game is one part visual novel and one part mini game: I can't help but feel this game tried the usual "give the best of both worlds" and ending up giving me the "worse of both worlds" instead. I constantly found myself getting annoyed that I would either have to trodge through a bunch of dialog I didn't care about or complete another mini game to get to the bits I did. I wish they had spent more time streamlining the story and gave the mini game more depth (More items, characters, challenges?)
-The story: After completing what I would call chapter 1 the story becomes a bit interesting but all together too slow and the traveling in this really immersive world became a chore more than an adventure. Game designers! Please don't reuse maps/content!
-Mini game: After awhile I didn't care about the mini game at all or upgrading anything. I put the dificulty to the max and used all of dificulty increasers and it just didnt matter. The characters while diverse were not interesting enough, nor was their mastery/trinket system. I truely believe this was the weakest part of the game.

Rayman Legends is the best platformer of this decade. Everything in it has such a touch of affection and detail that it constantly wows the player with it's unique style. Common background elements could have been hung in an art exhibit, enemies interact and animate in a variety of ways that boggles the mind that a team of animators took the time for such a trivial thing. And its platforming is exceptionally tight. The game ramps up in its difficulty in such a way that near the end you're more than prepared for its Lost Levels echelon of difficulty. It hearkens back to the older days of platforming, while at the same time discarding old standards like lives and poor checkpointing. It's constant fun, not tedium. Rayman Legends is what a modern Mario game should have been, and it surpasses the old bastions of platforming on every front.
And the music, sweet potato the music. When this game rolled out its series of trailers I was worried that it was just rehashing the songs of the previous title. But no, no no no. Another clever rouse on their part. There was a moment, I think around the third world, where I just had to put the controller down and appreciate how they had integrated the music into the stage. It's that good. In Origins the special stages were exceptionally difficult, particularly the Tricky Trunk levels. While Legends is no cakewalk, the trunk levels have been superseded by musically timed levels. It's understandably strange to jump and hit to the tune of Eye of the Tiger, but not unwelcome. But there's more than just those special stages, there's a huge variety of levels that leave the player with a myriad of options, all fun. There's a Gradius clone with mosquito mounts, time trials, wall running, a whole host of others.
There are criticism, and if you've made it this far into this recommendation I guess I could give them to you. The game has the same problem as its predecessor in that once you've collected all the baubles and creatures, there's really nothing else for you to do than the multiplayer stuff or to farm for days to unlock a skin for your character. Once you complete the main story, all that's really left is tying up loose ends, and it feels a little lacking in reason either than tying up loose ends in this game is still quite fun. Also, the introduction of touch based gaming in the series has been replaced by button prompts. Unless you're playing on a system that utilizes the touch, then some of the Murphy levels feel cheating, as entire swaths of gameplay get replaced by hitting the Y button.
But these are minor peeves. The game is still fun. It's a labor of love, and it shows it, bleeds it. I think, if you have the opportunity, that Rayman Legends is really worth your time.

I thought I would give this game a try for 30 mins.... but spent the whole night playing it. It is a very tactical turn based shooter that forces you to consider kill zones, weight of fire, flanking and cover.
It seems very minimalist, but very smooth, slick and stable as a game. The initial simplicity of the game disguises how complex the tactics will become.
As the missions get harder you realise its all about the real tactics of Close Quarters Combat ... you need maximum fire power on your enemies, whilst denying the enemy of the same. You need to move forward aggressively to take the initiative but not kamikaze into enemy fire. You need to exploit cover, but flank your enemy so they are being fired upon from multiple directions.
.... and with every map you are forced to chose between splitting your forces, and getting better possibilities of flanking action, but by doing so, you split up your squad, and reduce their weight of fire.
There is also an RPG aspect to the game. As you level up you unlock weapons and earn money, which you can spend on buying kit for you squad. As your progress you can buy better guns, armour, helmets, and accessories for your weapons, consumables for your missions and vanity items like clothing and face masks. You have to chose wisely though as often it a choice between better low level kit across the squad.. or one great upgrade for one guy. Spending your money wisely is part of the game.
Im really surprised how great this game is ... its a brilliant tactical shooter.

SOMA is an atmospheric sci-fi psychological horror experience that will make you question yourself, and what it is to be human.
I don’t want to say too much about the story, since I don’t want to give any spoilers. Much of the story is told with audio files, and character interaction, but there is more to learn if you want to take the time to explore, and discover written logs for more backstory. The story was extremely well done, and I enjoyed all of it. The experience was definitely a memorable one.
The game is not a horror in your typical sense. It’s not loaded with jump scares like a lot of other horror games, but instead it relies on the eerie, immersive atmosphere, and the potential presence of creatures to keep you on your toes. I didn’t really feel scared, or have my heart racing like parts of Amnesia made me feel.
The creatures in SOMA were very strange, and creepy. You can’t look at them for very long, or most of them will attack. You have no weapons, and you have to run, and hide if you catch their attention. There is a visual effect that shows you when monsters were near, and I would hide and be waiting, and I could tell that the creatures were getting closer, thinking to myself “please go away…”
Some parts of the game, made me feel like a horrible person; the things the games makes you do, and the choices that the games lets you make on your own. It really made me think about the value of life, and sometimes made me questions my very own thoughts, ideals, and decisions.
The game took me about 12-13 hours (I played the first few hours offline), exploring as much as I could. Since the story is linear, I don’t feel the need to replay it. It’s been over a week since I played SOMA, and I still feel guilty thinking back to some parts of the game, and that stuff is going to stay with me a while.
I’ve wanted to play SOMA since it was released, and I’ve had a few people suggest that I play it, but I was hesitant to spend the full price, so I waited for a sale, but I would not have been disappointed if I had paid full price. A game that makes me reflect on the things I did, and the choices I made for days and weeks after playing... just wow… SOMA was an amazing game, and I highly recommend it for those looking for a psychological horror story.

Finally completed SOMA and I would highly recommend this game if you like survival horror & sci-fi games.
~ No Story spoilers ahead ~
Much like the Amnesia games before it, in SOMA your job is to navigate your way through places, avoiding creatures and collecting the odd object / reading notes to solve a rudimentary puzzle or two to progress. The game is pretty linear, with the exception of a few interweaving corridors scattered throughout where you sneak around the unsavoury beasts that lurk in this eerie and atmospheric tale. If you’re not familiar with the Developer’s past titles, that’s fine: narratively speaking it is a solo story and not connected to anything they’ve done before. I found the plot intriguing and very enjoyable. Not going to give anything away as I like to go into these sort of games with knowing little and coming away surprsied, but If I had to give you a hint of what to expect then... no, not going to tell you ^_^
Enemies cannot be killed: you can run, hide, distract and avoid. There are a variety of non-inventory objects that you can pick up to throw to distract the creatures; this may aid in your escape and allow for misdirection so you can continue your progression throughout the game. If you get caught, you get one more chance to proceed near from where you left of, albeit injured and slower than before. You can heal yourself at points through the game, but if you get caught for the second time in a row then the game ends and you have to restart from the last checkpoint. Checkpoints and health are fairly frequent and I didn’t find the game altogether difficult / frustrating when compared to other games in the genre.
There is also a community Mod feature whereby you can play other people’s creations: to date there are few game mechanic changes and fully playable sections of horror. I can only hope the popularity of the mods increases over time.
Overall the excellent story had me hooked , the tense sections of hide and seek, & the odd heart thumping chase sequence made this a very enjoyable outing. There perhaps isn’t much to bring the player back for a replay unless you are interested in diving back into the story. I’d give the game an 8/10

Velvet Assassin is a WWII-based 3rd person game and is basically a simplified version of known stealth games like Splinter Cell.
Due the game taking place in the 1940s, there aren't any nifty gadgets to assist you, so the shadows are your most valuable tool. Ammo for the few weapons you find in the levels is rare, but since the shooting mechanics are horrible that doesn't even matter anyway.
Moving through the levels without being spotted requires a certain amount of tactics and timing, but luckily, by whistling, you can lure enemies into dark places to take them out silently with a variety of brutal takedown animations.
The biggest drawback of the game is the save system. With no manual saves, you have to rely on the rarely placed checkpoints, which - due the nature of the game - can be a very tedious and frustrating task, especially when going for an unarmed full-stealth playthrough.
VA is a game you *can* get, but you certainly won't miss out on anything if you don't.
