I have to say - I never write reviews, but I think Pyre deserved one so I'm going to go ahead and give it a whirl.
What can I say about this game?  Honestly, I didn't know what I was going into - my expectations were literally "From the creators of Bastion" - which was just a little indie game that I thoroughly enjoyed some years back.
This game really has no good comparisons that I can honestly think of.  It is RPG-like in nature in the fact that you build a team of characters that have vastly different playstyles and abilities, and you are able to level them up (5 levels) and choose traits for each level to increase/alter some of their individual abilities.  You also find/buy talismans throughout the game and can equip 1 per character.  Some are worthless, and some are VERY OP in my opinion if leveled up (you can increase the level of the Talismans with Stardust which increases the effectiveness of whatever each talisman does).
The basic storyline of the game is you are a group of exiles trying to escape back to the Commonwealth where you were exiled from.  You do this buy winning battles (called Rites) against other groups of exiles.  I don't want to go too deep into it, but it's a decent story for what it is.
This is a combat heavy game - and it's pretty fun.  It's basically a "game" where you try to burn out the other teams Pyre.   You do this by taking a ball like object in the middle of the map and getting it into their Pyre.  Each team member has different ways of doing this.  You can have 3 people on the map at the same time that you choose before the Rite starts.  Every character has individual strengths and weaknesses attributed to making them good offensive or defensive players.  There are an endless number of combinations that you can try based on the number of characters you have, the talismans you equip to them, and the choices you make in their progression with traits.
What I enjoy MOST about the game is the re-playability.  In my first run, the game took me about 4 hours to get through to the "end" - but it was not the end at all, in fact, it was just the beginning.  Without ruining the story I will say that each time you finish a run through this game you will lose one of your exiles (returned to the Commonwealth), and then go through it again.  The first run was relatively linear, but from that point on the game opens up and you are able to fly across the map to each objective more or less as you choose.  On the way to each objective you will have choices you can make to forage for items/coin, mentor individual characters to raise experience, or study the Rites to provide individual bonuses to your players for the next Rite.
All in all, I had no expectations coming into this game other than I liked the developer - but they blew me away.  I played this until I had to go to sleep last night and I will likely continue again daily for 4-5 hours until I'm "finished" with the game.  I see it as having a solid 20-30 hours, which is well worth the price of entry.

Ok, this game is bad. There are a few decent aspects, but they are overshadowed by all the negatives.
-There are no dedicated servers, meaning that everything is P2P hosted. This can lead to a multitude of issues. I have played indie games with better servers than this game, which is rediculous.
-The matchmaking in this game is really bad. I mean REALLY, REALLY bad. You get matched with not only people of a much higher skill level than you, but also people who have WAAAAAY better gear than you, giving them an actually statistical advantage over you. You would think that in a game with gearscore, you get matched with people of a similar score to you. NOPE. Almost every game I have played, I have been matched with people who are far beyond me in terms of both gear and skill. This is the fundamental problem with the game, and ruins the entire multiplayer as a result.
-As a result of the matchmaking, most of the fun of this game for me comes from the single player campaign, and playing multiplayer matches against bots instead of players. There are problems with both of these. First, the single player campaign is NOT offline. You must be online to play it, and this is rediculous, considering the fact that the co-op campaign is optional. Can someone remind me again why I need to be online to play by myself? Inexcusable, and disappointing. Playing against bots is fairly fun, except their skill level is all over the place, and the reward you get in terms of steel (in-game currency) and experience, is pathetic compared to PvP. The bots are easy to win against, most of the time, except occasionally, you will get a bot who wipes your entire team by himself, and has revenge mode up permanently. Expect to be playing bots (who might be sloths with sticks, or literal gods of war with the power of foresight) for a whole day to get half of what you would have playing against players, who are once again, overleveled, and will outmatch you 9 times out of 10.
-You might have trouble getting steel to upgrade your characters, since you will lose many PvP matches, netting you minor benefits, or will win bot matches, which still give you scraps. You can of course purchase steel as a microtransaction, which should immediately indicate to you how money-hungry Ubisoft is, and how little they have tried to distance themselves from the rest of the industry. This micro-transaction garbage is what I see in F2P games, not full price AAA titles. I paid 40 dollars for a game. I expect to get everything in it, with relative ease, and should not be able to pay more to get it faster. This is rediculous. It encourages poor business practices, and treats consumers more like wallets, and less like people. If you think this is excusable, you are encouraging the development of poor consumer willpower. No normal person should be expected to play for hours on end to scrounge up enough steel to get all the unlockables in this game, when anyone else can just pay for it. Outrageous.
-The mechanics are fun, and it feels fun to play almost every character in the game. The only problem is, that you will rarely find a moment in regular play where you get to experience the full potential of the character you are playing. It happens maybe once or twice every three hours, where you actually get revenge mode and solo kill two opponents. Most of the other times however, you get gangbanged by multiple oppenents, and can't do anything. Many of the characters also currently have some fairly overpowered moves or combos, that no one should be expected to be able to avert. Really good players make use of these moves CONSTANTLY, and as a result the mechanics of the game can get VERY overwhelming, very quickly. I would love to practice against players my level, and actually get good at these mechanics, but if you saw what I said about matchmaking, that is currently impossible.
For Honor is a AAA game, with a huge budget, and the fact that it has issues like this is insane. No one should defend this game. It is yet another example of Ubisoft's failings as a game producer, and unless it gets fixed soon (which is unlikely), it should go down in history of what happens when a great concept gets turned into a pile of refuse. Do not buy For Honor. Do not support Ubisoft. Forget this game, and do not make the same mistake I did.
This game gets a 2/10. It has a great concept, and many good mechanics, but the product as a whole is executed horribly. Any redemmable aspect of the game is buried under a pile of garbage, and an unfair grind to get through it all.
For Honor is a bad game, and brings dishonor to the game industry.

Been wanting to write my own review for some time now and between my schedule, some mild procrastination and just plain sitting on the fence on things, I believe now is the right time for it. First off I want to say this game as it is holds so much potential it's silly, it could easily become something amazing with just a few more pushes in a few directions it's heading, that being said there are a few factors weighing it down that need to be addressed which I intend to do so in detail here. Bare in mind a bit of it is opinion and personal stance but I'm used to fire by now so feel free to disagree but I will also be adding a few extras towards the end for others, new and looking into the game or otherwise, to keep in mind.
Pros:
1: Current and future plans and fitting a niche. As stated above, the game has potential. There aren't many games out there that allow players to play the dinos (Ark with mods yes, PC:E, etc and eventually Saurian.) But none quite (yet) with the models, smooth animation and realistic details as the dinos of the isle, let alone with the idea of progression backing them. That alone attracted me to the game at first and I feel could make it very unique out of so many other games out right now.
2: Survivability. It always adds an ever changing twist to games, you never know what will happen and you must fight to survive, I for one enjoy survival games and the sheer unpredictability they pose and this is another reason why the isle caught my eye.
3: Multiplayer. Going off to play with people from every walk of life and at every corner of the globe is always a plus in general as it always makes for interesting interactions with both sides of players or just grouping up with friends and exploring.
4: Community. The community of the isle is very much a double edged sword but for now I will say that there are many passionate players who genuinely care for the game, it's genre and dinosaurs in general, I see it in the fan art, I see it in their forum posts and I most certainly see it in those few who strive to actually help other players. These people are the glue that hold a community together.
Cons:
1: Data pests. Early access is early access, bugs are to be expected and anyone thinking otherwise is just fooling themselves but these bugs are rather impressive, when something messes up it messes up well and there is the glaring fact that, before the bug tracker reporting bugs wasn't handled in the best way it should have been and has lead to some stress between players, mods and devs.
2: Server issues. As with above it's to be expected there will be down time with servers but even for early access this shouldn't be as big of an issue as it is as seen with other early access games. To those looking for hours of endless map wandering and exploring you'll be disappointed. Servers overload and crash at the drop of a hat, or rather at the drop of too many dinosaur bodies piling up.
3: Gamplay, or lack there of. Currently the only selling point, and that's being extremely generous, is getting to run around as a dinosaur in massive maps, if in a free for all, pvp environment. Core mechanics such as the progression system or server type structures aren't even in the game yet and while one could argue the game is still being developed, I find this to be a major red flag when other early access games have those bedrock features already in place by the time they go into early access. From my observations it feels like they're developing the game backwards and have no actual frame work for the game in mind, this plus my points below only add to the growing concern many are bringing up for the game and it's legitimacy.
4: Extreme miscommunication and horrible behavior. Good communication between developers and their community is of the utmost importance with early access games, after all that's why we've been given the opportunity to even have early access. To give and exchange feedback, suggestions and so on while also getting to try the game while it's still being developed and give our input on it accordingly. However, it becomes discouraging and downright worrying when you constantly see posts explaining that the devs rarely even look at the forums, suggestions or other concerns from their players and do so with complete disregard. Again, one could argue it's the place of the mods to handle these things but that's both missing the point and helps very little when there's an obvious miscommunication between them and the devs alone given observed and recorded responses.
This coupled with the blatantly rude, childish and unsavory, callous and uncivilized behavior and harassment both on and off the project from some mods, devs and even the lead creator of the game adds to the list of red flags and leaves more then a sour taste in the mouths of many, many players who have voiced their concerns in both the forums, the reviews and elsewhere. All of which needs to be taken into in depth consideration both for current players, newbies looking to buy/support the game, and above all, the developers and Dondi themselves/himself.
[UPDATE]:
One of the devs has stepped forward to issue an apology to the players and other devs for their behavior, of which I (among others) have accepted. I hope to see more positive steps like this in the isle's future.
5: Community: A community can make or break a game in many ways and despite the praise I gave to a part of it above, the larger, more vocal side has made it's way onto my list of cons. As with any online community there will always be trolls and generally unfriendly people but this section isn't about them. This section is about those who publicly shame and ostracize other players for simply asking a question, for having an outlook and opinion that differs from theirs to the point that they take misguided, personal insult from it and lash out and who fall into the "Stop liking what I don't like!" category.
While it's one thing to simply disagree with another player regarding gameplay or even suggestions, it's a whole other can of bull to outright shun new players simply for being new, or to verbally beat down on and look down upon those who enjoy a different style of gameplay then their own. There is a very obvious tribal mentality festering away at the isle's community and any of those who don't instantly fall in line with it are cast out, publicly insulted and told to leave (even by devs and mods). Many, many people are doing just that, leaving because of how bad it is. To say this side of the community is toxic is a gross understatement.

TLDR - Amazing art, music and story and fun 3v3 battles - but if you don't like visual novels it is highly unlikely you will enjoy this game.
I absolutely love Pyre, but it is very different to Supergiant's other games in that it plays more like a visual novel with an rpg/sport mix battle in between reading sections - called the rites. The rites are a 3v3 battle to get an orb into the opponent's base (pyre) while avoiding them getting the orb into your pyre. The catch is that you only control one player at a time, which sounds off, but actually works very well and fits in with the narrative. Not to spoil too much, but the idea is that the three must be act as one.
The visual novel style is a big change from their other games. However, I think the art, music and narrative effectively draw you in to the story so that the rites really feel meaningful. I genuinely want to win these rites for the freedom of my party (friends?) and every time a rite starts I ponder who should take part in this challenge. Should it be X because they are longing for battle, or Y because I feel they really suit the situation. The game is full of small choices like that which can add up to something much bigger and I think it is great.
It is worth noting that the rites can actually be quite complex at high level play, and I would recommend putting the AI on hard to really experience some of the nuances of battle! This can lead to some awesome moments of "holy crap I just did that!", and frustrating moments of "Oh boy I just messed up!" - against easier AI I think these moments might be missed which would be a shame.
All in all, I really enjoy this game!

There is a lot of skill involved in playing the game itself, from learning when to block and to figure out the best way to hit your opponent during combat.  If you enjoy games you have to endure, this is the one for you.  It isn't easy and it isn't for laid back gamers.  The hardest part is playing games alone, so make sure you have friends that will play with you and you will do well.
For Honor isn't about a single persons honor, it is the honor of the faction you choose.  Many people scream, no honor, when they get teamed up on, but it is in Dominion and Team Death match, which is team based game play.  For those who want honorable fights, go do duels or brawls, as they are 1v1 and 2v2.   The game itself is plagued with people who quit the game because they are losing or they get teamed up on, which we all know they are poor losers.  I wish there was a thing in place to discipline those that quit.

I was honestly hoping for the"Remastered" (or at least an episodic packaged version free for old owners) version being released on Steam as on the Xbox One/PS4. Since today would be the day to market something like that--and they didn't--I'm guessing that it will never come to Steam.
All I can say about BTTF is that it's Back to the Future Part 4. Instead of being a movie, you get an old-school adventure game. And even if you do not like Adventure Games or you have never watched a BTTF movie, I would still recommend this game.
(I played this game before watching any of the movies. Also, this was my first TT game and the first Adventure Game I wanted to finish on my own. I loved it.)
I don't feel the need to review Back to the Future as in-depth as Tales from the Borderlands. It's an old-school puzzle game with TellTale's dialogue variation system. That means puzzles, puzzles, puzzles--and no QTEs--only more puzzles and laughs. But if you enjoyed the humor of TFTB, you'll probably enjoy BTTF for what it is as well.
The puzzles can be a little too cryptic at times, but they have a sense of self-awareness and a sense of direction to keep you from getting completely lost. I still don't think they're all as great as Grim Fandango, but you won't be doing anything absurd like in the old King Quest games.
The only downsides I should mention, besides you have to install every episode separately and open the next episode as a new program, is that being an earlier TT game the controller is not the best option to play with. Perhaps the Remastered version fixed it, but you should stick with a KB&M.
Also, don't go in expecting a choice-simulator game like recent TT games. This is a game before The Walking Dead became their new formula.
You have variations in dialogue, superficial ones, and there is no deviation on your paths. I don't think this is a negative, but it is something people will expect from TT. I prefer BTTF to stay the way as it is as the characters remain consistent. Some characters from the film's cast return to their roles (Christopher Lloyd as Doc) while others have great imitators (David Kaufman as Marty McFly.)
The first two episodes are a little slow and full of fanservice, but midway into EP 2 and from there-on the game gets really crazy with its time-travel storyline and shows some great character development of its cast. And the ending will leave you in smiles.

While I wouldn't necessarily compare the game to X-Com, neither new nor old, it is hard not to draw some parallels, considering both are Turnbased Tactics games. Breach & Clear has more in common with Frozen Synapse than it does have in common with X-Com though.
The gameplay is rather simple. Enemies are randomly seeded into a map, where they will do their terroristy things like inspecting the carpet in an otherwise empty room, and you are tasked with clearing the bad guys, finding a hostage/bomb or escaping to an exfil location. The random seeding of the enemy gives the game quite a bit of replay-ability.
Each level has one or more entry points and you as the player are tasked with dividing your 4 people team among the entry points and then go from there. You plan each move in its entirety and then once you have planned it, you execute said plan. Covering all the angels, trying to use cover to your advantage or throw flashbangs or regular grenades into an area to deal with the enemy.
The game's simplicity is also its strength. Nobody ever said that chess was a boring game because it had a bunch of simple rules and Breach & Clear is like that as well. You do have a couple tactical options but for the most part its simple facing, facing and positioning, that wins the day.
Graphically the game isn't impressive, but being a spiritual successor to Frozen Synapse it is still a step up from a blue backdrop and green and red enemies. Also I can't quite put my finger on it, why I am liking this game more than I did Frozen Synapse, but I also couldn't name any real difference between the two other than Breach & Clear having the more appealing aesthetic.
Breach & Clear also offers a class and level system, with your team getting more experienced and unlocking more abilities. And there is a shop allowing you to buy new unlocked weapons, equipment and cosmetic items.
All in all a solid game with, at the very least, the early missions taking about 10 to 15 minutes tops.

Breach & Clear is a small squad based tactical simulation.
You manage a Squad of 4 soldiers to fulfill different technical scenarios.
- Terrorist hunt (clear all hostiles),
- Bomb Squad (Find and defuse one or multiple Bombs)

Overall it is strangely addictive, I do highly recommend the game.

SOMA is an atmospheric sci-fi psychological horror experience that will make you question yourself, and what it is to be human.
I don’t want to say too much about the story, since I don’t want to give any spoilers. Much of the story is told with audio files, and character interaction, but there is more to learn if you want to take the time to explore, and discover written logs for more backstory. The story was extremely well done, and I enjoyed all of it. The experience was definitely a memorable one.
The game is not a horror in your typical sense. It’s not loaded with jump scares like a lot of other horror games, but instead it relies on the eerie, immersive atmosphere, and the potential presence of creatures to keep you on your toes. I didn’t really feel scared, or have my heart racing like parts of Amnesia made me feel.
The creatures in SOMA were very strange, and creepy. You can’t look at them for very long, or most of them will attack. You have no weapons, and you have to run, and hide if you catch their attention. There is a visual effect that shows you when monsters were near, and I would hide and be waiting, and I could tell that the creatures were getting closer, thinking to myself “please go away…”
Some parts of the game, made me feel like a horrible person; the things the games makes you do, and the choices that the games lets you make on your own. It really made me think about the value of life, and sometimes made me questions my very own thoughts, ideals, and decisions.
The game took me about 12-13 hours (I played the first few hours offline), exploring as much as I could. Since the story is linear, I don’t feel the need to replay it. It’s been over a week since I played SOMA, and I still feel guilty thinking back to some parts of the game, and that stuff is going to stay with me a while.
I’ve wanted to play SOMA since it was released, and I’ve had a few people suggest that I play it, but I was hesitant to spend the full price, so I waited for a sale, but I would not have been disappointed if I had paid full price. A game that makes me reflect on the things I did, and the choices I made for days and weeks after playing... just wow… SOMA was an amazing game, and I highly recommend it for those looking for a psychological horror story.

Finally completed SOMA and I would highly recommend this game if you like survival horror & sci-fi games.
~ No Story spoilers ahead ~
Much like the Amnesia games before it, in SOMA your job is to navigate your way through places, avoiding creatures and collecting the odd object / reading notes to solve a rudimentary puzzle or two to progress. The game is pretty linear, with the exception of a few interweaving corridors scattered throughout where you sneak around the unsavoury beasts that lurk in this eerie and atmospheric tale. If you’re not familiar with the Developer’s past titles, that’s fine: narratively speaking it is a solo story and not connected to anything they’ve done before. I found the plot intriguing and very enjoyable. Not going to give anything away as I like to go into these sort of games with knowing little and coming away surprsied, but If I had to give you a hint of what to expect then... no, not going to tell you ^_^
Enemies cannot be killed: you can run, hide, distract and avoid. There are a variety of non-inventory objects that you can pick up to throw to distract the creatures; this may aid in your escape and allow for misdirection so you can continue your progression throughout the game. If you get caught, you get one more chance to proceed near from where you left of, albeit injured and slower than before. You can heal yourself at points through the game, but if you get caught for the second time in a row then the game ends and you have to restart from the last checkpoint. Checkpoints and health are fairly frequent and I didn’t find the game altogether difficult / frustrating when compared to other games in the genre.
There is also a community Mod feature whereby you can play other people’s creations: to date there are few game mechanic changes and fully playable sections of horror. I can only hope the popularity of the mods increases over time.
Overall the excellent story had me hooked , the tense sections of hide and seek, & the odd heart thumping chase sequence made this a very enjoyable outing. There perhaps isn’t much to bring the player back for a replay unless you are interested in diving back into the story. I’d give the game an 8/10

Bought this game 14 hours ago, haven't stopped playing it since. Enough said?
Seriously though, this game is fantastic for the following reasons:
- Solo queueing in quickplay is a pleasent experience, mainly due to the fact that the community is here to have fun.
(Sure you will still get the bad eggs every now and then, but the good eggs make up for it 100x over)
- Quick and easy fun, load it up and hop into a game and instantly you're having fun. What more could you ask for?
- Jason is an amazing experience, playing as him is wonderfully satisfying.
- Survivors are incredibly challenging but rewarding to play, you eventually get good at juking Jason and stunning him and it makes the game much easier.
- Perks add great depth to the game, I can't wait for them to add even more perks then there already is to make certain builds more viable.
- Every match is different, it really is a refreshed thrilling experience each time.
- Like I said earlier, if your friends don't own the game yet then solo queueing is incredibly fun still.
- I'm probably forgetting some stuff, as i've been up for over 14 hours playing this game.
- Very easy to make new friends in this game. Experience a fun round with a certain lobby? Add em up!
Cons:
- First and foremost, the PRICE! $40 is very steep for a game like this, if they dropped it to $30 it would seem more reasonable. That being said, I am very glad I decided to take a gamble with this purchase because it has provided me with some amazing fun. $40 is steep for being an indie game.
- Maps/Killers, this is a little knitpicky. As this is an indie game afterall and I feel this generation of gamers is simply spoiled by the amount of content AAA titles provide us these days, but there's a lack of maps/killers for the price tag. This is something that can change with future updates/dlc.
- The severe rarity of being a killer, you will find yourself suffering from killer withdrawals in between killer procs, I wish there was a way to be killer more often but there simply isn't. It seems that's just how it is, because I can't think of a way they could improve this as everyone would want to queue as killer and survivor roles would be increasingly difficult to fill.

This game is one of the most fun and challenging shooters on Steam at the moment, especially with friends. It is difficult to get into and learn all the maps, callouts, camera locations, etc. However, once you get to grips with this game, it feels extremely satisfying to get kills and win games with your squad. You'll praise yourself for getting cheeky peeks and winning intense clutch moments, perhaps outsmarting the enemy and shooting them through a wall after scanning them with your drone. You'll think of so many different ways to approach a situation with the many unique operators you will unlock over time. This game makes for many great moments that wouldn't really be possible in other shooters and these experiences will leave you feeling like a badass.
Beyond gameplay, the extensive customisation you can give to your weapons through the many different stylish camos and cute charms makes you want to show off your guns to your friends and say "I love that guy's gun" to your squadmates during a round ending killcam. The introduction of Alpha Packs also means the camos, charms and outfits that are either expensive or discontinued are surprisingly easier to get and you'll get cosmetic items you didn't even know you wanted.
On the other hand, this game is developed by Ubisoft, which means (like most of their other games): amazing concepts, relatively poor execution. The only reason this game has stuck around for so long is because Ubisoft actually tried fixing it over time instead of letting it die out like their other online multiplayer games. All the great things about this game I listed above only apply when this game actually works like it's supposed to (which can sometimes prove really inconsistent). Ubisoft clearly don't have much of an idea when it comes to fixing the many issues with this game; the recent Operation Health (which had us miss two new operators and a whole map) was supposed to fix a lot of the game and yet it seems the updates post-Operation Health are doing a better job. Operators like Blitz and Ash are still broken in their own ways, hit detection is still very inconsistent, spawn peeking is still an issue, the ranked system is still in beta after god knows how long. If this game had a development team that was passionate about the game, it would flourish, however, I just don't get the feeling Ubisoft are giving this game their all. In all fairness, once you get hooked into this game, chances are you'll overlook any issues you encounter, anyway.
This game is a (mostly) great tactical shooter that I would definitely recommend to any fans of the genre.

I reviewed the game in 4/2015, whereas this was my original review:
----
I play Survarium since early closed beta and it started off really promising with a lot of potential. This potential was not used at all. Despite the game exists already since late 2013 all features player wanted are still missing like freeplay and coop. Right now it is just a lobby based arena shooter with a horrible grind and no long term motivation.
The gameplay lacks balance, same goes for the match making. In addition it is very poorly optimized.
----
The only thing that has changed so far is that the optimisation is far better now. However there is another huge problem: Devs added bots to the game, which seems nice at first, because it might be a step in the freeplay direction, but the actual reason might be, that otherwise the match queues would be even longer. Especially in mid tier ranks there are only matches (at night time of EU timezone) with bots and two human players per team - and guess, what bots are by script not capable of? - Playing the objective (well in that regard it is a quite good copy of human teammates at least).
In addition to that, the devs once promised that all guns will be obtainable ingame without paying real money. This promise was not directly broken, but the borders of obtainable ingame were pushed really far, so that you need tons of luck and time to get the weapon dropped as a reward. For a long time this was just the case with one single gun, which was endurable back than, sadly the same procedure is now used with a couple of other guns as well.
In the entire time from 4/2015 to now 2/2017 nothing big contentwise has happened:
Some weapons and items were added, one "new" gamemode (which is just a variation of capture the flag) was added, some maps got some vegetation added and thats it - over one and a half year and nothing substantially new was given to the players.

Back To The Future: The Game is heavy.
Episode 1 feels like classic BTTF1. Very rewarding for fans of the series, full of lots of references. Everything you could want from the reintroduction. Some things are new, and other things are still tied to the original series. The introduction of Young Emmett “Doc” Brown is a nice addition to the series. The puzzles are fine, but not the main appeal.
Episode 2 feels like classic BTTF2, during the past timeline. This is where the game starts to stand on its own, rather than relying on a heavy dose of nostalgia. This episode further develops the characters of the game, introducing the major conflict of the game. The puzzles are much better, and far more logical than the puzzles of Episode 1.
Episode 3 feels like classic BTTF2, during the alternate present/future timeline. Continues the story established in Episode 2, while allowing the player the opportunity to see an alternate version of the cast of the original movie.  This cast manages to hold true to the classic personalities, while giving the characters a new reality to react to. The puzzles feel very heavy handed when compared to the previous two episodes. They rely far more on trial & error, over logic or clear direction like the previous episodes' puzzles. The highlight of the puzzles in this episode would be the heavy metal guitar battle.
Episode 4 doesn't feel like a classic BTTF movie. But this is not a bad thing. By this point, Young Doc learns how to stand on his own two feet, which is also what happens with the story. It no longer needs the safety net of the classic movie trilogy any more. While this episode might have the worst and most tedious puzzle in the game, conversely the story is one of the highpoints of the entire game. Asking heavy questions like “Is it worth hurting a friend, to do what is right?” and “How do you deal with someone that has given up hope?”. This episode manages to juggle these types of questions, while still advancing the story into the final chapter. By the end of episode 4, this story has truly become its own, and worthy of the BTTF name.
Episode 5 resolves all the stories created from Episode 1 through Episode 4, and at the same time it feels like classic BTTF3. This episode, by far, has the best puzzle in the game. This puzzle actually advances the plot, rather than being that annoying thing that stops the story from progressing. As this episode gives closure to the game, it pays homage to the series, with the ending that ties back into the classic BTTF1 ending.
If I would have known that the writer of the movies helped write this game, I would have played it years ago. The gameplay isn't the main attraction here. The reason anyone would play this game, is for the story. While the story is VERY linear, this is not a negative. We are more interested in allowing Marty to fix the timeline, over having a heavy focus on gameplay or a branching narrative. This game is going for a cinematic presentation, and it would never be considered a bad goal to aim for, as it is creating its own spot in the BTTF legacy alongside the trilogy of movies. It knows how to do a proper BTTF story, while still breaking new ground worthy of being included in the canon of the series. The Young Doc storyline shows us that no matter what influences the future, you will still become the heavy hitter that you were always destined to be. There are so many great references and parallels to the movie trilogy, it feels rewarding to fans of the series, as we are not ignored for a new vision of the universe. It really respects the original trilogy, which is rare for a video game based in a movie universe. This game manages to create new classic BTTF moments, without completely relying on constant references to the movies.
It has the “classic” Telltale problem with reading the previous episode's gamesave for the choices you made in the previous episodes. Luckily the number of times the later episodes check the gamesave is minimal, so it is only a minor annoyance. It's best to just choose the first “cover name” for Marty, because that is what the game defaults to, if it fails to correctly check the first gamesave for the name you have actually chosen. This allows for your immersion to not be broken, while bypassing the problem of Telltale's bad programming.
There is a heavy amount of heart and joy in this game, and it is safe for all members of the family to share. Because of this fact, it is a true sequel to the BTTF trilogy, and has earned the title of being called Back To The Future Part 4.
Back To The Future Part 1 – 10/10
Back To The Future Part 2 – 9.7/10
Back To The Future Part 3 – 9.9/10
Back To The Future Part 4 – 9.8/10
Happy Back To The Future Day! I hope we all ended up creating a better future for ourselves, than Marty did today in the original BTTF2 timeline, before he learned his lesson in BTTF3.

I enjoy this game very much! It plunges the player into a magical pre-historic world with great graphics and a fun community. You can interact with others, choose and customize your own dinosaur, and explore the world to the fullest extent. It has an aspect of survival, where you must fend for yourself, and find resources. It is fun and enjoyable, and I recommend it to anyone that wants to enter that awesome time period.
However, I have noticed a lot of negative reviews on the game, and most were about how it is buggy or doesn't have enough content. I mean, sure it would be neat to fly around as a dimorphodon, and sure, the Trex's animations may not be perfect, but I would like to point out that it is an early access game, and it is not complete as of now. If you did buy the game, and are not happy with its current state, I hope you understand that animation and game-developing takes time, and we should not rush creators to hurry. The game is fabulous so far, and they have done an amazing job with it. So, calm down, and enjoy what we have so far, and be patient for what is to come.
To end the review on a happier note, this game is amazing... It runs smoothly, the graphics are beautiful and the maps are huge. The gameplay is great, and you can perfectly simulate the calming life of a Trike, or run around and slaughter people as a T-rex, whichever suits your style. An amazing game for early access, and a must-play for anyone even remotely interested in prehistoric environments and creatures. I do recommend this game!

This is the first review I have written for any game, this game has compelled me to do so. The game itself, the content of action-packed fighting, is all that I could have hoped for. The game modes are fun, and I feel the classes are moderately well balanced overall. From story, to pvp, the battles are exciting, thrilling, and intense. The real issue that comes with the game are the connection issues. The peer to peer system really has let many people down. I can not begin to tell you how frusturated most players are with it week one. At times, I will have hours of uninterrupted play, while at other times I will be booted from game after game. Even inviting friends to create a group seems to take five minutes instead of what should take seconds. The online system they have simply does not do the game justice. There are other small issues I have with the game, only being able to prefer "elimination" over "skirmish" when I have an "elimination" specific quest for one. The cash shop they implimented seems unwarranted as well, truly the cash shop has nothing of value to offer that I could not just get from playing the game as is. I can really over look all these other minute issues, but the online problems really take this from a great game to just an "alright" one. Which frankly, saddens me greatly, for this type of game is really my jam. I sincerely hope they fix the peer to peer, otherwise I really do not want to recommend this game.
Edit: You can now choose between elimination and skirmish, good to know.

Here's my review for, Breach & Clear !! **Early Review (2h gametime)** (7.6 out of 10.0) Overall.
Before you start reading (this review is kinda long) you can just take a look at my
to see what this game is about.
Now to my review :
First Look: I didn't know what I'm about to witness of playing this game because I don't play simulator games so much. And especially tactical simulators.
My first run was near 2 hours.
I enjoyed this game and played the first mission, 5 times.
This game has very much to offer in terms of difficulties,missions,equippments,replayability,roles and ofcourse the main reason we purchae this game - tactics.
Gameplay:
Gameplay is very simple once you get used to it (I got used to it very fast and the tutorial was short and clear).
You have 4 characters, each one has same options and your role is to control them.
Besides that, there is the map itself which has easy acess to it (all you need to do is to move the cameras to your like, and manovering the soldiers on the map.)
Me as a hardcore tactical fan player I like to complete each mission on the best side so it took me around 15-20 minutes to complete a mission but after you do the same mission few times you do it faster and easier, and while still enjoying the mission. (8/10)
Cons: 1) Repetetive. 2) Full Members each mission (Annoying thing is you can only use all 4 members and not 2 or 1 or 3.)
Gameplay Styles:
1) Go loud and use breaching equippment / Loud weapons / Frag grenades etc
2) Go quiet and use silencers / lock picks / Flashbangs etc
3) Split your team through the rooms or work with all of them togather in each room.
4) Enjoy your time in investing and planning each mission to your liking and your own tactical strategy.
5) Difficulties - 5 Difficulties. (8.5/10)
Graphics:
Only saw one map so far but each room looks realistic with objects and tactical props (Walls/Big Closets etc that can block the A.I view so you can take cover behind them). (5/10)
Cons: 1) Lack of FPS. I get this is a sim game but they did add fps moments but I'm not feeling it cuz it's only in start/end of the mission. it would be better if we could switch between FPS and Map-Look modes of the cameras but oh well I guess it will take the tactical-strategy element of this game.
Equippment:
What can I say about this one..
4 Sections - Weapons , Gear , Headset , Consumeables.
There is an in-game store (Buy/Sell items from the money you've earned in each mission).
In each section there are many things to buy include Vests/Guns/Gun Parts/Suit Colours/Camos/Grenades etc..
Some of them are locked, you need to unlock them as you progress through the game.
There are also stats like Speed/Accuracy/Noise etc in some of the equippments. (7/10)
Cons: A bit more organized menu would be better, and there are some items I don't think I will use.
RPG Elements:
I should talk about this one cuz there are 6-7 special op teams you can choose from.
6 Roles to choose from and stick them to your soldier. (Not sure yet if each team has different roles or not)
Stats in equippment items and Money to invest in equippment.
Level up system to your soldiers. + XP.
Choose how your soldier will look like, and colour your guns. (6/10)
Enjoyment: (9/10) I'm sorry but this is one of the best tacticla simulators I've played.. I can invest all my time in this game figouring out different tactics/ways to approach into the enemy.
Repetetive: (6/10) It is but still you enjoy playing this game.
Replayability (9/10)
Frustraiton (1/10) - Early review but as long as you know what you do in this game.. You're fine.
Boredom (0/10) - Nothing so far.

Long before there was Candy Crush, there was Bejeweled. This is a simple, casual game with a grid that requires you to shift colored jewels and match them into lines of 3 - 5. You can only shift 2 jewels if it will result in a line of 3+ matching colors. Very easy game, but where this game blossoms is all of the mini games / variations of it. Dozens of modes, all centered around making lines. There is classic mode that has you going through levels making lines, lightning rush, which has a very limited time and you need to collect time ups to keep going, diamond mine, where you need to match lines near the bottom rock to destroy the rock and progress further down. Bejeweled poker which every line is like a hand gains you something similar to a card in poker. Butterfly mode has you making lines with jewel butterflies to keep them from reaching the top of the screen where it will be an end of game. There is also a never ending zen mode, which is just like classic only without levels that break the flow of what you have going. Finally, there is an ice breaker mode which forces you to keep up with rising and freezing water. Once a line gets frozen enough its game over.
In a way, I prefer Candy Crush, because they have focus on levels, rather than letting you free to pick modes to play. I just feel overwhelmed with all of the choices and just end up playing 'classic' mode for the most part. On a plus side, unlike Candy Crush, there are no micro transactions. You've bought the whole game and need to unlock the modes.
Bejeweled 3 has a level system that keeps track of all of your points throughout all of your games and a high score amongst your friends. That seems to be my real driving force to play the game, just to beat my friend's high scores and since every time you play, you start with a random grid of jewels, its got something to do with luck as well as skill.
I can recommend the game, but I could recommend it more on the phone. I just feel there are better games I could be playing on my PC than something as simple as this. Tetris sold Gameboys, not  Nintendo Entertainment Systems.

Apotheon is fun. The artwork is beautiful, the gods and mythos interesting, the gameplay is fun, and there's both enough challenge and slack to appeal to higher and lower skill levels. The game is not long in terms of its main story (it took me 9 hours total), though it can be fun to explore a bit and try to get the acheivements, or just bash some enemies, so there's potential to pad the run time, or replay.
The game does have its faults though. For me, the controls were spotty most of the time. Areas that required precise and agile platforming were absolutely horrible, and when combine with the pressure of combat made for an entirely unenjoyable experience. The controls also prevented me from enjoying all that Apotheon's combat had to offer, since I could never actually do anything more advanced than flail a spear at my enemies. Also, the game will hard crash at times. The crashes usually occur when loading in a new area or cutscene, and the auto-saver does a pretty good job of covering you so that it's a simple matter of rebooting and hitting continue, but it's not perfect, and you might have to completely redo a boss battle if it fails (I did).
In summary, the controls are imprecise and problematic, there are issues with hard crashes, but Apotheon will deliver what it promises, namely unique and interesting mythological Greek gameplay.

Match-3 is about as basic as games get. Seriously, it's the first type of game most people are tasked with creating in game design school. So you've got to make an exceptional match-3 in order to deserve any praise for the task. The two most praised names in match-3 are Puzzle Quest, renowned for turning match-3 into a remarkably fun RPG, and Bejeweled.
The original Bejeweled was far more basic than Puzzle Quest, featuring a basic match-3 until you have no more matches gametype, and a time attack mode. These persisted into Bejeweled 2, which got a little creative on us, adding in a puzzle mode, some secret extra modes to spice things up, and special gems for matching 4 or 5 gems at once. Still not as unique as Puzzle Quest, but getting there.
So what sets Bejeweled 3 apart?
Two things, really. Game modes, which have evolved immensely from the previous two installments, and presentation. The game plays
. Matching feels great. Explosions feel
. The sound effects and vocal work both sound great. Everything is easy to figure out and menus are not a pain to navigate. B3 is even pleasant to look at.
As for the game modes, the match until you can't match anymore (Classic) and time attack (Lightning) return once again. Endless mode returns from Bejeweled 2 in the form of "Zen Mode", which is basically the same exact thing as Endless Mode (no end to the game, play as long and as poorly as you please), only with the addition of a set of gimmicky zen features (such as sound and visuals to help control your breathing, and relaxing background noise of the nature variety). Puzzle Mode is gone, and now replaced with a much cooler Quest Mode. In this mode, you are given five set of eight different missions to complete, which can range from quick snippets of one of the game's hidden modes with set goals, to special gametypes unique to this mode, involving things like uncovering artifacts in sand, balancing the number of red and blue gems matched, and turning the entire playfield gold.
I mentioned hidden modes, and yes those are back. Only this time, they're much easier to unlock than in Bejeweled 2, because I guess PopCap realized that keeping people playing longer through added functionality might work better than expecting them to play nearly 300 levels of Endless Mode in order to unlock the basic time attack mode, but with altered scoring.
The hidden modes of B3 are much better than B2's offerings, as well. Poker Mode is unlocked through Classic Mode, and kind of... well okay, Poker sort of sucks, really. It would be nicer with a larger board or a gem drop algorithm that's slightly more in your favor. In this mode, you try to complete poker hands by making five matches in a row. As you go, skulls will appear over the next-lowest non-skulled hand in the hand info box to the side. You can clear these skulls off by getting enough points, but if you match a hand with a skull over it, a coin flip determines whether you keep playing or game over. And this is what I'm talking about. It really seems as though they added the coin flip in in lieu of making the game a little more playable. It's fun, but sometimes you just don't get enough good gem drops to make decents hands, for several hands in a row.
Butterflies Mode is much more fun, and is unlocked by playing Zen Mode for only a little while. In Butterflies, butterfly gems float up the board one space every time you make a move. If they reach the top and stay there for too long, the board freezes and you lose, but you can clear them by matching them with other gems. Ice Storm has you fighting off continuously rising pillars of ice by matching gems in their columns. Horizontal matches don't lower the pillars much, but can hit multiple at once, whereas vertical matches will only hit one pillar, but will drop it to the bottom of the screen. Special gems have varying results.
Diamond Mine is my favorite mode to play. In this one, you have block of dirt on the bottom of the screen, and must clear them by making matches next to them or hitting them with special gems. Clearing all rows above a certain line drops the line down further and adds precious seconds to the timer. As you dig, you'll collect gold and ancient artifacts which will add to your score.
Also, there are star gems now. Created for making a horizontal and vertical match with one gem, these take out the entire row AND column that they occupy when matched.
The leaderboards are interesting, and took me a little while to figure out. I initially thought they had glitched up. Turns out, your top score is saved as your Steam display name, and all lower scores are saved under your in-game name. None of my friends have played this yet, but I'm willing to assume that only your top score is displayed on your friends' boards, but your own extra scores are there for you to personally see and improve upon.
My biggest complaint is simply an issue that comes with the match-3 territory, and that's that sometimes you'll lose for just no good reason at all. This ties into my complaint with Poker Mode. The issue is that sometimes you'll desperately need a thing that just won't drop, or you need to make a match on the opposite side of the board, but the gems seem to only want to fall in a pattern which keeps you on the wrong side and oh look time's up. I would rage if I cared more.
If you want match-3 with an adventure and a story, Puzzle Quest is the way to go. If you just want to match gems and maybe do it in some unique and fun ways, then Bejeweled 3 is the best way to do so that I have personally found.

Sheltered is a fairly easy game to play.  If you were looking for a hardcore survival game in which every turn could be your last; you may want to look elsewhere. This is recommended to those who just want to relax and explore the world while crafting interesting special items from schematics that you could possibly find out in the wasteland.
Although this game is easy, you can still find yourself playing and losing all track of time.
Negatives:
There are still a few bugs in the game.  One current game breaking bug in which I show in my video below, my expedition team sprite is in the base but they are actually exploring and now they cannot return at all and I have lost my people.
Once you are in your normal routine this game will become quite mundane quickly.
There's no real need to upgrade everything in the base right away. As long as you have enough people around to fix the durabilities of whatever needs it, you'll be fine.
No real story to go on.  You're just tasked to keep up your shelter all the while managing who comes in and out.
You will find that instead of "surviving" that you're just waiting around for the right amount of materials to craft your next item, which for some uncanny reason you won't find for many many days.
Food and water is trivial and many more items seem worthless (like books and records and stuffed bears) after just a couple of weeks game time.
Positives:
This game does a good job keeping you playing as there is a ton of cool stuff to craft.  Although some of them are absolutely unneccessary it does add fun factor to the game.
Your party gain experience in their base stats and will level up enabling them to perform their functions better.  This gives a good incentive to keep people around who are good and will only become more overpowered over time.
Overall:
Truthfully there's nothing wrong with this game... it's just painfully easy. The reason why I am not recommending this game is that it's just a "forgettable" game.  This is one of those times in which I wish I could rate this a 5 out of 10.

When I first played this game I was a little disappointed. I love Bastion and Trasistor, but this game didn't seem like it will capture me in the same way. It seemed like this is just a glorified visual novel. The rites, which are the gameplay of the game seemed not very fleshed out and lacking depth. After completing the game though I must say that it is hard to say for me which of the three games from Supergiant is my favorite (but it probably is Transistor :P).
My favorite part of this game is a certain decision that you will have to make several times throughout the game, because the choice is a little dilemma. Choosing one way could be argued is selfish, while the other is for the greater good. I hope that is how the choice was intended to be, because sometimes it didn't feel exactly like that, but most of the time it worked really well. These choices will make every playthrough of every player very different.
The game has a lot of replay value. Apart from these big choices, there are a lot of smaller choices, that don't affect the main story in any way, but add slight nuances to each playthrough and make it unique. The game achieves this by being very text heavy though, which could be a negative for some people, but I must say that for me, someone who never reads a book and english is not the first language, I had no problem with the reading and actually really enjoyed it, which is simply because it is really well written.
There was one narrative "thing" that was a little annoying that happened multiple times, which is that you expect something to happen, but then the text says that it's not happening for some reason and that is surprising, but a second later it happens anyway. I don't know what the point of that is, building fake tension? Maybe make clear that this time something is different? I don't know, it was a little irritating.
The best part of this game are clearly the characters and the music, both of which kept me motivated and kept me playing, sometimes even for more than three hours, which is very rare for me in other games. The music will remind you of Bastion and Transistor very quickly, but it still has its own identity. It is also the biggest soundtrack Supergiant made yet, which made the extra purchase for the soundtrack even more worth it.
I didn't like every character, but none affected the experience negatively. What I would maybe criticize is that the characters barely make any decisions, with very few exceptions. They mostly do what you expect and follow your lead, which is fine, but the game could be a little more surprising. Another thing I would criticize a little is that the game recycles too much content for my taste. After the first cycle you will visit the same areas and play on the same arenas multiple times. They always try to have some twist to keep it fresh, but for the 13 hours it took me to complete the game, I don't feel like there was enough, but this is just a minor criticism.
One thing I love about Supergiant is how they handle difficulty. I don't think any of their previous games have actually difficulty levels, this one does, but it's more a very rough decision. You can fine tune your difficulty more with modifiers that you unlock with time, just like in Bastion or Transistor. Doing this also gives you a little more experience points too, although not really a relevant amount. I have to say though that when you play on the hardest difficulty it sometimes gets very chaotic and hectic. Sometimes it led me to moments where I didn't know what exactly happened, or I wanted to do something but had trouble with the controls because I had to react so fast. Maybe a smaller problem if you play with a controller.
The rites are alright. Not amazing, but definitly not bad. Not a huge fan of the masteries and the talisman. Some are cool and interesting, but more just give you passive bonuses. Also there are some which introduce a new button out of the blue, I always forgot to make use of those, because the game never teached you that button (it is like a "taunt" button by default) and it also never reminds you to use it. During your journey you will also often get temporary bonuses like "+1 Hope", which is cool, because it is also always related to the narrative somehow, but these bonuses are so minor that you will never notice a difference.
Anyway, all I can say is that I love the game. It has a very fair price too. The soundtrack is brilliant. I can't stop thinking about the characters. Play it.

I'm going to write this game a positive review because I believe this game needs the recongition. What makes this game fun is how absurd it can be.
Yes, you can get screwed over very easily.
No, Jason is not broken and neither are the counslers
The point of playing as the counslers is that you're going to have your own little adventure where you can either find the items that will get you out of the mess of being stalked by the killer Jason, or you're going to get found quickly and he'll beat you to death. There are a bunch of ways to escape jason, even to the point that if you're out of options, just play hide and seek against him (of course I wouldn't suggest that until 4-5 minuets are left). When you start a match your not sure what will happen, and that's what's fun. It's sort of like how every holocaust surviver has their own story to tell, but the reality is that some don't make it (dark example but I can't think up a better one).
Jason's is straight forward, It's fun to stalk and kill people (welcome to any video game). It might feel ridiculous to have to chase someone around because you can't run, but that's the point! There is suppose to be suspense when jason is after you. Think of how in the movies, Jason doesn't always go straight for the immediate kill. There is a chase where the helpless try to do whatever it is that they can do to try to live. Playing Jason means that you have to abuse what you can do and what they cannot. there is no "mana" so use 'em if you got 'em.
The jist of how you enjoy this game is to get in character, you're gonna get chased and you're gonna get killed or make it out by an inch of life. Let yourself get wraped up in the moment of a chase or stalking. If you can't bring yourself to feel that when then it may not be for you. But hell is it a lot of fun for me. Thank you IllFonic and Gun Media for making a game that makes you feel like your in the movies.

Ok, have played much more now (up to unlocking
- fairly sure that the time played is incorrect, feels like much longer. Muuuuuch looonger, experienced advanced aging while playing).
The major issues are:
Visual novel / main map:
Pacing - the start of the game introduces concepts / play styles
slowly. You also end up sending a character
very early on, removing them from the rest of the game - meaning, in practical terms, you'll want to meta-game this & dump a weak / bad character rather than a stronger one. You only really understand this afterwards, however. Likewise, you unlock
early on - it is used for a couple of maps then rendered entirely pointless - the first chapter literally shows you the entire map in a linear fashion, so don't expect surprises from then on.
There are large parts of 100% pointless busy work: when you
you have to fly between maps. There are a couple of "interest points" (which mean a couple of fluff lines of text / codex page) but otherwise it's pure filler. It has no role at all, no real freedom, it's just there as an interactive (ish) "look at the pretty map". Which is fine the first time... the seventh time? Zzz.
Due to the nature of the Visual Novel part, you'll find yourself making trite choices - 100% each conversation there's an obvious "be best friends and get a bonus" options. You will take them. Friends are magic. Friends always do X. Oh, and someone needs to point out to the writer that "Freedom from Fear" can also equal "Genocide is Good" the way they've worded it, for the record. The philosophy is at High School level.
Now, the major major issue: the actual gameplay.
#1 Feedback / control is loose / non-precise. Lost count of the # times a jump was slow or the stamina bar wasn't quite full enough (which has no feedback) for a dash or a block. The AI, of course, doesn't suffer this issue often leading to annoyance. Given the AI is controlling three players at once, while you only control one
, not even rudimentary AI / dodging, this can get quite annoying.
#2 The playfields are tiny - one character can literally jump 1/4 of the length to score instantly. This leads to quick scores / speed > any other tactic. Why bother passing? Exactly.
#3 The characters are not balanced
. There are characters with skills / stats / abilities that 100% are better than others. Meaning when dumping characters, you'll want to dump the bad ones first unless you're playing for the narrative.
#4 Pacing in the game parts: glaaaacial. Loading screens / resets / narration / scoring animations
last longer than the play-time (5-10 seconds to score, esp. in early games or with fast upgraded characters, see #3). This isn't related to computer specs (i7, 16 gig ram, 970GTX, Win10), it's deliberate. Oh, apart from: there's no 3-2-1 / countdown to the ball being released - not a great design mechanic.
#5 You can throw the ball at characters, forcing them to hold it while they're mid animation for blocking / using a special ability. Guess how exploitable this is? Yep...
.
#6 The RPG lite stuff doesn't really appear to do much in practical terms. I've upgraded a talisman to level 20 (which then vanished when that character
, thanks for nothing you ungrateful sod) but playing with much lower level heroes, as long as they're the fast ones, doesn't really change the experience.
~

In 1994, Doom took the world by storm, and taught the gaming industry how to create violent, beautiful first-person-shooters using cutting-edge technology. Sadly, this is the only major takeaway we saw from the breakaway game, many of the elements that made it--in my opinion--the greatest first person shooter ever made, having been lost to time.
What you'll find in this package is the 1995 re-release of the classic original for IBM PC, with all the major updates to that point, including the bonus fourth episode "Thy Flesh Consumed." The game is certainly gorgeous, with lovingly crafted visuals and sound for the era, but what makes this game truly timeless is the unrivaled gameplay. Each and every stage is designed such that it resembles no real, believable space, which gave the level designers carte-blanche to create environments which served no purpose other than empowering the gameplay; the weapons are all designed such that each provides a unique tactical approach, with very little overlap; and the bestiary on display is among the most varied in any video game, first person shooter or otherwise. The monsters in Doom provide not only their own unique tactical considerations, but multitudes by little more than creative combination and placement.
Doom is much more than a simple historical curiosity. As someone who never touched a single game in the the series until 2009, I am living proof. You owe it to yourself to become a part of this great experience.

Pyre is a fantastic visual novel with some interesting gameplay elements that contains a story with the motto of "If we're gonna have cliches, might as well pick the best ones and make you care about the characters along the way." The visual style as per usual of supergiant is unique and colorful, granted unlike bastion and transistor there weren't nearly as many "I could use this as a desktop background it's so good" moments.
The gameplay in between the visual novel segments is like if you crossed Diablo with basketball, and it works surprisingly well.
There is a versus mode after you complete the campaign that I'm positive would have been extremely successful had it online multiplayer capabilities, but alas, this was a huge missed opportunity since the foundation of what's here probably would have sparked an entire community, assuming they could keep up with the balancing and such. Perhaps that's why they didn't do it, however, as there are a lot of characters to balance in versus mode. At least you can play local multiplayer, but I don't really have anyone to do that with these days. I'm sure it's tense and fun though considering my experience with expert difficulty AI.
Finally, the soundtrack. It's great. That being said, this game didn't have as many memorable tracks in it as bastion and transistor did, but there were a few that really stuck out. My favorites were "In The Flame", "Thrash Pack", and "Downside Ballad".
In my opinion, this game is among the best I've played recently, though if you weren't already a fan of Supergiant like me despite how different this game is from the other games I'm not sure it'd sway people who didn't like bastion and transistor. After all, some people might be turned off by the fact that this is visual novel first and game second, but as someone who reads a lot of those anyway, I didn't mind.

This is my first Telltale game I have played. I just bought the whole collection. Now let me start off with this: I have never been an adventure game fan. This is why I have stayed away from Telltale games. However, hearing just wonderful, awesome, best game ever reviews I finally let my guard down and purchaseed THEM ALL! Here is my verdict so far.
TL;DR - Adventure game still aren't for me.
Wow, that was a really easy, yet expensive lesson, for me to learn. In a FPS if I shoot someone, they die. If I shoot their arm, they die. If I shoot their face, they die. If I shoot their leg... you get the picture right? Of course you do, you've played FPS b4. Adventure games suffer from constantly having to do exactly what someone decided was the right thing always and conforming your mind to be set completely in track with that person's idea of mindset.
Basically, in adventure games, if I shoot your leg first, but the programer thought I would aim for the arm, they do not die. If I shoot the arm, but there was a hint to shoot the face, then leg, then face, then arm, they do not die. You see why I do not like adventure games? I can't just play them. I have to spend hours figuring out every nuance that some other geek decided was the right way.
BttF is no different. 1.5 hours in and I'm just clicking on every highlighted item, in a static world, wondering what logic the programer decided would work to make a damn barrel of alchohol fall from a shelf. AND THAT is exactly why I wish I had never bought any Telltale game. Definately not ALL OF THEM!
So much buyer's remorse! What have I done?!

The Isle is a game where you play as a dinosaur and run rampant on an island. Depending on the server or workshop mod(s), the gameplay experience may vary. There's a lot of very toxic and clearly quite small children, but there's also plenty of mature, and rather adultish people you can find too, making the community not all that bad. One of the main criticisms of the game is the Dev's, which in my opinion is ridiculous due to the fact that they use twitter polls to get what they're going to update next most of the time unless it's a bug fix. The devs do listen to the fans but can be harsh when enforcing their rules, and a lot of people aren't used to devs acting like robots that never respond to them I guess. Anyways, the game itself is great. It requires a hefty computer to play and unfortunately more optimization won't come until the future because of how big of a game and a project this game is and how much work needs to be done. So incase you have a bad computer, either wait until gameplay optimization arrives, or get a better computer. There's not that many options in that area right now. The dinosaurs and animations are phenomenol. It's easily one of the best games of the century just in the graphics department if your computer can handle it on maximum graphics. The gameplay is great, but the AI needs refinement before it's finished and I acknowledge that. If you don't like people KOSing you, I recommend a server called "The Isle RP/Realism" It's not as much Chat RP as much as it is just Realism, since you don't need to follow any form of normal "RP" things in the chat, and rather you just have to act as that dinosaur would have in a real environment. Servers like that I personally find a lot of fun. Most of the community is pretty good, but there are low points. All in all, it's a good game with great animation, and has realistic dinosaurs and models. I definently recommend it to anyone interested in the genre.

You know, it's funny. Rayman was once considered "just another platform game" but now with Sonic running underwhelming sequels and Mario failing to do anything new or creative since Mario Galaxy, it's Rayman whose ultimately on top and destroying them with what is hands down one of the best examples of a platform game in over a decade.
The first thing you'll notice about Rayman is the atmosphere. With beautiful hand-drawn artwork and polish that is truly unrivaled, the game gives off an immediate great first impression. Fortunately it doesn't stop there.
Lead by great music and fantastic level design, Rayman Legends manages to snag your attention and hold on to it for dear life. Constantly changing things up, every world adds new concepts and eases them in with an old-school "learn by doing" approach.
With that said, it should be said that this game can get very hard. It starts out easy but very quickly ramps things up. This is of course expected of a Rayman game and wouldn't be one without being as punishing as it is beautiful.
And the best part of it all is... content. The game has a ton of it and it all holds up to the same level of quality. If you're even the slightest bit interested, you'd be a fool not to buy it. Easily my game of the year for 2013.

I really wanted to give episode 1 a 'thumbs down'. I don't want to turn people off to the game though. As a whole, the BttF game is great. Episode 1... is not.
There are many problems. Generally related to bugs. I experienced them constantly in episode one. (Luckily none of these appear in the other episodes!) I have a lot of complaints. That will be the focus of this review. However, I still recommend the game as it has a great deal of entertainment value.
Often I would be unable to click on certain people or objects. The game would randomly decide I hadn't clicked on what I clearly did click upon. Instead, it would pick a random clickable person/object instead. Sometimes mouseover caused odd results. The pop-up text (on-screen description) would rapidly flash between what was highlighted by the cursor, and a nearby object.
The dialog trees are all messed up. It seems like a part of the story was removed... or maybe it's just bugged. I'm not sure. I would frequently find that the dialog I was part of was way ahead of the story. Events (cutscenes) were always in order. The dialog rarely was.
The story itself, is good. It is very much a BttF-style story. The character models were given a distinctly cartoony appearance. There is also a lot of adult humor. (The kind you should expect based on the film series.) This is sharply contrasted with the fact that the characters look like they originated in a modern animated film. (See: The Incredibles, Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs, Frozen, etc.) They kind-of look like anime versions of the real-life actors of 'Back to The Future'.
The mouse controls are poor. You have to hold Left-Mouse-Button(LMB), then drag to make your character walk. If you want to run, you have to hold RMB. However, if you hold RMB before you hold LMB, then you don't run. I can use the keyboard to walk, but I'm not sure how to run. Which means I'm stuck using the mouse for just about everything in this game.
Probably the most disappointing thing is that animation was reused from the 'Sam & Max' games. Marty walks with the exact same motions as Sam. When people are talking, their mannerisms will follow the same patterns used in 'Sam & Max'.
Lastly I want to mention that if you have a Nvidia card, you'll need to turn on 'Antialiasing - Transparancy'. If you don't, the shadows will look terrible. Personally, I find them so bad that it distracts me from the game. Then again... it might just be my particular video card. You never know.
Most of these problems do not carry to the subsequent episodes. So, I happily recommend this.

One of the best games of 2013, if not the best platformer.
Every square inch of this game oozes heart, soul, charm, and whimsy.
The sheer amount of content puts many other games to shame: want to play single player? It's there. Want to obsessively collect items and trinkets? They're in there, but not in a way that makes it tedious. Want to play a simple yet hilariously competative multiplayer game? Kung-Foot, the Shaolin Soccer simulator you always wanted is in there. Want a single player platformer with tight controls, great physics, amazing art and incredible music and sound design? It's there. Want to play the same with four players? You can do that too. Want daily and weekly challenges that you can play time and again to top the charts and compete against your friends? It's there.
There is way too much to do and way too much fun to be had. If you missed out on Rayman Origins, just get Legends as it even includes updated versions of the best levels from Rayman Origins that you can play! It really does have it all!
