The world is amazingly well realised and rivals the likes of Mieville for originality and imagination. I don't want to spoil anything, but there are story and design concepts I loved within the first 5 minutes of gameplay.
The meat of the gameplay is a slick 3 vs 3 ritualised sports game, almost a cross between basketball and rugby, where you control one character at a time whilst the others remain wherever you left them, projecting a defensive aura, which temporariliy banishes opponents when they come into contact with it. Without going too indepth into the mechanics they seem to be elegant and well executed.  I've seen a few classes so far and they are all distinct whilst having a unified set of controls. There are level ups, items, and lots of events.
I could not get into Bastion or Transistor but this game has it's hooks in me in a way no other game has in years. I'd highly recommend you take the plunge.

The game has amazing polish.  The artstyle, sound, and animation is second to none.
That being said, Rites are incredibly lacking in substance.
Of the four stats applied to every character, quickness is clearly the most important (the one that actually wins games).  The others are meager at best.
The paltry 8 mastery talents available to heroes (at the time of writing) is insultingly simple and imbalanced, as there are clearly superior options.
Being defensive is suicide in this game since offense can literally overcome EVERYTHING a defensive character can do, and reliably at that.  As a result you can absolutely steam-roll the AI, even at higher difficulties, if they try to be defensive.
All in all, trying to combine the mysticism of fantasy with the everyday mundane-ness of basketball doesn't really serve either of the two.  The technicality of basketball is disserviced by the whimsy of fantasy, and the magic of fantasy by the mundanity of basketball.
It's a lot like trying to mix oil and water.

For instance, the very first "puzzle" is apparently to discover where an omni-tool is hidden in the room -- after all, the only interactive elements in the room refer to an omni-tool. If the compulsive (and reinforced) action is to do "something" and the "hint" is to do something entirely dfferent, your game design has failed.
SOMA continues to present this failure throughout the game. And despite the interestesting narrative and story, I cannot recommend this as a game.

7/10
Plenty of fun, but about as deep as a thimble.
The Good
--- Tons of fun. Extremely satisfying to clear a level of badguys in like 14 seconds of "real time"
--- Just like the old Rainbow Six before they dumbed it down, (minus the Rainbow Six first-person mode)
--- Passable graphics and sound. Good enough for what it is.
--- Randomly generated enemy locations thwart attempts at replaying with prescience.
--- Flanking seems to remove the need for dice rolls. I hate dice rolls. Strategy games should win or lose on strategy, not dice rolls.
--- Levels can be replayed in a variety of different modes: Terrorist Hunt (standard), Defuse the Bomb (capture and hold), and Escape. These add a lot of really awesome replayability
--- Heavily moddable equipment, but I kinda wish it were more moddable, and that there were some way to save loadouts
--- Enemy AI isn't totally dumb. Uncoordinated, perhaps - but its how I would expect them to act in the face of marines kicking down the door. (Dive for cover, unload magazine at doorway)
THE BAD
--- Clunky User Interface, with some frustratingly annoying problems.
--- No story, plot, or characters. Just a series of, what are essentially just "puzzles". Puzzles solved with guns and grenades, true... but the puzzle is always: "Get all the Marines to flank all the terrorists as quickly as possible", just with new environments each level.
--- Guns are pay-to-win, which is a bit silly for a game touting its realism. I would expect realistic prices, not having guns that "unlock" when your navy seals reach a certain level, and like super-sci-fi versions from some of the company's other games
--- Gameplay mechanics are more reminiscent of tabletop than real tactics. Cover can't be thwarted (except with grenades), so its all about getting baddies in a crossfire. I suppose there's nothing strictly -wrong- about this, except that (once again) it flies in the face of the vaunted realism
--- A lot of the equipment is a bit silly. You might get a gas assist system that increases damage by 3 but increases noise by 3, then add a silencer that decreases noise by 3 but also decreases damage by 3. Somehow I feel that the net benefit of something should be greater, not just even-out
--- Soldier customization is rather bad. You may find yourself doing the same thing over and over. Like if you want to switch out for close range for a particular level and then switch back afterward, you need to go back and replace every single item. There are no preset or savable loadouts. Depending on your level of customization, this can be quite tedious. For example: all my soldiers have helmets and armor painted black (paint applied separately), and guns with 6 unique enhancements. The guns and all the enhancements also have to be painted black (etc).
IN CONCLUSION
Fun, but not perfect. I really wish they'd add a plot like Splinter Cell or something. Something in-line with what they're trying to do, but make it more interesting. UI and the market/loadout could really use a lot of work. Otherwise pretty solid!

military strategy game with lots of potential and managed to do most of the things right too.
pros-
engrossing! -every time its a new experience. even though the maps are (seem to be) small there are many variables that can provide great replaybility. and after a few minutes you'll WANT to master every map or try it with different loadout or different classes in your squad or just turn up the difficulty level/perma death.
music- not many tracks but enough to create that sense of urgency and tension.
perma death- level up a soldier to level 15+ and then see him die hurts a lot.
progression- unlike many other games where level progession is usually just about higher number in stats, here you can see the difference between leveled squad member and a rookie.  devs have done good job but*(see cons)
cons-
difficulty spikes- play a map 15 times with perfect strategy - spike the difficulty and see your team getting hammered! the AI literally becomes stupid (like wont shoot while moving when the enemy is strolling right in front of them, their range shortens, enemy AI become bullet sponges even when they have no armor and snipers just become invincible unless you are 4-5 paces away) every now and then you feel that enemy sucker punched you below the belt.
absolutely no in-game help- there is one kinda useless tutorial. it teaches only the basic movements. there is no ingame notifications (even about features like market place, upgrading gear etc.) i saw the market 1st time i started the game after that the game never offered/mentioned that i can visit the market place and buy stuff in between maps(and game sucked me in so much that i completely forgot about it). i played 1st four maps(repeated a few times too) and when i came back to main menu i saw the marketplace. another example- i bought a sniper rifle (probably one of the costliest gun) and had no idea how to properly use it(no tutorial). when my 2 snipers died i decided to go back to assault rifle but couldn't sell the sniper :/ really disappointed coz snipers(enemy snipers too) are awesome in this game if used properly. yet another eg. i bought 4 suppressors and 2 different guns(2 each) only to realise that one gun model doesn't support silencer & it wasn't mentioned on the gun's profile page :( which is bad coz money is hard to get in this game AND IT IS VERY IMPORTANT!
no lone-wolf mode- every time a squad member dies the game forces you to go to squad menu(in main menu) to choose a replacement. only way to play lone wolf is to keep giving 'hold' command to rest 3 soldiers which is time consuming.
2nd-tier perks - they just come wayyyyyy tooo late. you get them when you are rank 30 :( and reaching rank 30 is really time consuming. i have just one guy at level 17 and now the progress is really slow.only way to level him fast is to make him kill max. enemy which means putting him at high risk and sooner or later the enemy sucker punch them.(i have lost 2 level 15 guys already)
inconsistant point awarding ?!- i am not 100% sure about it but i don't understand how points are awarded after each mission. and the difference here is not of 50-100 points.
Overall i would recommend this game to every one who loves strategy military games. if you liked xcom or older rainbow 6 games pls give it a go.

This is not a bad game, but it isn't good enough to warrant a definition recommendation.
So far I'm a couple of hours in.
- Combat is floaty and underwhelming and some attacks take a lot of time to 'wind up', which is especially frustrating against fast moving enemies. This is especially annoying in my current level filled with fast moving wolves.
- Navigating between weapons in a fast paced combat is difficult and fiddly, but I'm on a controller. There isn't a function to map different weapons to D-pad, so you have to navigate to a menu item whilst being attacked in real time.
- Boss fights are either not challenging, or a grind fest. For example, the boss I'm on has turned me into a deer and I have to dodge her arrows. Too bad she teleports - There's no real strategy involved for this boss match at least.
- While the levels are visually distinct in colour themes and have good immersive music, they offer no variation in terms of gameplay. Most places have interchangeable map design.
- Because each level is its own 'zone', there's little internal variation *within* levels, it's difficult to locate oneself and explore. The fast running and scrolling means you can move fast through the level, but actually counteracts exploring.

Not at it's current state anyways.
Only 30 minutes or so in and I can already say "meh."
Good things, it has loads of potential. I loved the classic star wars space battles, and I feel like this could be the new battle. Oh, and the gun controls seem fairly real. Like, having to angle your shots.
That it? Yes. At it's current state, the only thing it can show for itself is potential. Would a bank loan you money on that promise? No.
Things that could be tweaked:
- The game lacks immersion. I don't feel like I am a part of the action.
- Design of the interior of ship: Meh. Not really all that cool.
- No real soundtrack. It may not need one though.
- Enemy ships are in this divide between ships that blow up easy and ships that take forever. It doesn't feel like my weapons do anything to the ships my size. Only 10% of the ships I fight I can kill in a snap of a finger.
- Upgrades are way to common, and I feel like they don't really help.
- I kept getting the same upgrades for two weapons all the time. What makes it worse is that they were max upgraded. The two weapons that were max upgraded only make up 1/3 of the weapons I have, why do they make up 99% of the upgrades I receive?
- Weapons aren't clear as to "Which is better." If the two I kept getting upgrades for were the ones that dealt the least damage, then I understand why the game wants to give me more of those.
- I can literally sit there and shoot. I am not forced to move until I get one hit or two. Shouldn't I always be in motion?
- I don't feel like what I am controlling is anything. It doesn't really exist.
- Repetitive combat. No real story or campaign.
- Took me to level 3 to finally know that "T" was target.
- ^^ No tutorial
- I got torpedoes, but I have no honest idea how to get to it.
- Missile are endless. Is that a good thing or bad? I don't really know. Depends on where they want to go.
- Engine max upgrade makes it really hard to control your ship. If they put in a throttle or something, it'd make it easier.
Things that are utterly bad:
- Price. At it's current state, it is not worth $5. I am lucky I got the 80% off deal and got it for $1.
- Wait, seriously? $5 for this? It feels early dev not released.
- I feel like this is more of an arcade game.
I hope that the creators are working on this game, because I have faith in it. I also hope that they already had plans to fix these things.

I just shot some things, flew to another mission ("enemy ships detected in area!", "Defend the friendly ship!", etc...) and that was it.
The thing is, the game engine is actually pretty good. Movement feels fine, weapons behave real enough that you have to lead your shots, but not so much that you can't still hit anything. It looks pretty good, and with some shading and lighting tweaks, could look fantastic. Some minor sound effect stuff too (the generic weapons fire sounds are very repetitive and could use something to make them less so).
But in the end, it doesn't really do much of anything. Shoot, fly, next mission. Shoot, fly, next mission. Shoot, fly, next mission.
Add a basic campaign mode or something. Then it would be worth keeping. I'll check back in a year or so, see how things have improved.
Overall, I'm cautiously optomistic about the game, but it needs to add more content.

While toted as a high quality combat system, For Honor is a waste of hard drive space. It certainly looks good on paper, but the actual appeal is lost the moment you hit multiplayer.
Combat
The combat system is elegantly designed in simplicity, with layers of complex nature. The problem? It's easy to break by simply spamming certain attacks, which ruin 9/10 of the playable characters. I don't know how many times I've taken on 1v4 and killed all 4 enemies, just because they want to fight and I just want to spam left click. Additionally, throwing people into instant-death hazards is WAAAAAY too easy. It's usually unblockable, near instant, and has a HUGE range.
Multiplayer
Never, have I ever seen a more toxic community. This game is 100% filled to the brim with the worst kind of people. Have a question? Trolled. Have a request? Trolled. Try to help an ally? Trolled harder. Win? Trolled. Lose? Oh you better believe you'll be trolled. This game's community is the worst, and that's coming from a LoL/Smite/Overwatch player. Additionally I love how they implemented an in-game voice feature that I've never once seen anyone use once. No communication then a barrage of typed insults by keyboard cowboys about how no one else is talking, well Buttercup? You're not either.
Singleplayer
By far the best feature in this game, as it plays exactly as expected. Too bad the AI is dumb as a board and boring repetitive.
Sound
Beautiful... I actually have no complaints about music or sound, I just would suggest making it so that if you're knocked into something like an iron gate, you don't get the same sound effect as being knocked into a stone wall. It seems off somehow.
Controls
Eh... not bad? I mean it's like someone took a game, then plastered a fighting game on top of it. Every character has special button combos and methods to play, which for some people is nice I guess. For me though it means it's a waste of time. I mean seriously, that's 12 different ways to fight I have to remember if I want variety in who I play as.
Characters
Actually pretty well thought out, I like the diversity of the roster, I just wish their buttons were more similar. On this note though I HATE the Revenge function. Each character gains ... revenge-meter?... based on certain things, such as taking damage, blocking, parrying, etc... When it's full, they gain half their health back, become unblockable, and take less damage. That's cool and all, but I've seen and used my meter multiple times in a VERY fast paced fight. It fills so fast that it just serves the purpose of extending a fast-paced interesting fight into a slow grindy samey fight.
Menus
My god... please... consolidate these nightmare enducing black holes you call menus. Do you know how long it took me to get comfortable with where things were? For instance, to practice against an unmanned bot that auto-heals and allows you to practice your attacks: Multiplayer > How to Play > Train > Level 0 Bot.
Ok why is it multiplayer? Why isn't it just on the main menu?:
Multiplayer
Train
How to Play
etc..
These menus are absolutely abismal and the controls to maneuver them are attrocious. I know this game was originally intended to be a console game, but when you ported it to PC you should you know... take that into account.

I'd recommend the game, it's short, but there are a lot worse ways you could spend a dollar on 1-2 hours of entertainment.
There are 50 levels in the game, and they range in time from a few seconds per level, to a few minutes.  The early levels are super easy, as the game teaches you how to play by introducing features one at a time.  The game is refreshingly minimal.  Indeed the title screen is also level one.  You are not told how to play, you just start playing, and as new features are introduced, you are not shown or told how they work.  You just try things out to see how they work.  If you make a mistake, the level starts over, which is no big deal, because the early levels take so few moves to complete.  The final few levels allow you to make up to 3 mistakes, since they are more complicated, though you'll not likely need to use them if you're careful.
The game has one achievement, awarded for beating all the levels.  I felt that was kind of lazy of the dev actually.  Once you've added code to support one Steam achievement, you can easily hook up several.  It doesn't ruin the game or anything, but it just sticks out to me.
Overall, it's a fun playthrough, but does leave you wanting more.  The final 5 or so levels feel like what the majority of the game should have been like.  Additionally, I felt like I was about 35 levels in before I even had to think about which button I clicked first.  Having said that though, if a game leaves you wanting more, not because you feel ripped off, but because you enjoyed the time you did have, then it's probably doing something right.  And the game's totally worth the non sale price in my opinion.
If there were more levels in the form of DLC I would likely buy them right away.

When I read a book, I deem it good based on how it impacts me. Like a good book, that you simply cannot put down, Pyre enchants me in a mysterious way, it has an essence that pushes me on to see what lies ahead in the journey of our heroes.
I liked Bastion a lot, and I love Transistor even more. So the expectations were high. So  far, Pyre has lived up to these expectations and more.
Beautiful graphics aside, the game boasts a phenomenal soundtrack, which is as expected, and an interesting and challenging gameplay in the form of the Rites. Unique characters and a compelling story drives the player forward onto uncovering the stories of the characters and the story of the game itself.
Update :
After completing the story, few thoughts come to mind. What would have been different, had our heroes chosen a different path in life? Maybe we would have never gotten together to go on this incredible journey to find our freedom.
Certain aspects of the story lingers even after finishing the game, just like when you may go back to read the last few pages of that last good book you read over and over again. From here on, there's only a few options that remain. Either you find another venture that's just as enticing, or you simply sit tight and jump back on the same one once again. There are only a handful of games that have left me with such a lingering impression, and I am happy that Supergiant Games' latest work of art has managed to attain a position in that list.
Pyre is a truly wonderful experience, a journey that I will, from the bottom of my heart recommend.

I hate visual novels with a passion but I /LOVE/ this game.
I think they're bland, unattractive and all around cannot hold my attention - clicking one button just doesn't do it for me. But almost five hours into Pyre and I can say it is NOTHING like a visual novel, (apart from long segments of talking and a few choices you are presented with,) in that it isn't boring.
Supergiant scores another masterpiece, fantastic soundtrack, amazing lovable characters and things that will make you laugh and cry all at once.
The segments of the game that function as a world/character/story building VN are not boring and manage to capture my attention, and although the gameplay for the Rites is COMPLETELY different from what Bastion and Transistor was like it manages to stress me out in a way that has me on the edge of my seat wondering if I'm going to lose the Rite. Losing in this game (haven't lost yet on normal) appears to have an impact on the story and listening to the banter between each character is fantastic.
Buy this game.
If you liked Bastion or Transistor, buy it.
If you didn't like Bastion or Transistor, buy it.
If you love Visual Novels, buy it.
If you hate Visual Novels, buy it.
Supergiant never fails to bring something fantastic to the table, can't wait to beat Pyre.
EDIT: ON HAVING BEAT THE GAME
The ending was lackluster, but throughout the rest of the story all was fantastic. Still 100% reccomend.
Enjoy :))

I will update this review when I finish the game.
I've got about 3 or so hours into the game so far, and I can say pretty comfortably that it's very good. I'm a massive fan of Supergiant's prior works, so I was willing to give the game a shot despite having reservations on the concept, and I'm glad I did. The story and the marriage of all of its elements is what makes this game truly special. Supergiant knows how to make an interesting story and world, building and supporting it with everything they have at their disposal. Music, visuals, writing, and gameplay are all built with that story and experience in mind. So far, Pyre is no different.
Pyre's gameplay loop can be somewhat compared to The Banner Saga's. Half the game plays as a choice-based visual novel. Talk to your characters, make choices about your travel, and make choices in relation to your supplies and what actions you may take between Rites. The second half are the Rites themselves, a psuedo-sport combat game where you control three of your party members to deliver an orb into the enemy's pyre. Whichever team destroys the others' pyre wins. It's a simple concept that is made interesting with the large cast of party members who all act differently and can be levelled in different ways. Party members can also be equipped with Talismans that afford them certains buffs. Overall, these two gameplay halves serve each other well.
Overall, I've been seriously enjoying this game. It would have been nice to have voice acting for all the characters, but what's there is very good. The story has kept me very engaged, which is somewhat surprising as I don't generally care for text-heavy games like this. Ultimately, while I can draw comparisons to other games, such as The Banner Saga, there's nothing quite like Pyre. I commend Supergiant Games for continuously trying new and interesting ideas and being so good at what they do they can make it work as well as they have here.

I don't understand any of the hate this game is getting, people exaggerating the conncetion issues immensely, I've disconnected from maybe 1 in 30 games, which Is too many, but far from terrible. The gameplay is fun and very skill based, those who say there is too much spam in the game simply aren't very good as once you get good enough spam is easily beaten with a good pary or guard break counter. The classes are diverse and play quite differently even down to things like the way they block and go into different guards. While more gamemodes would be appreciated the ones we have are good, with 2 v 2 and 1 v 1 being the best modes. Those who complain about needing to buy gear clearly haven't paid any attention to the game, as gear levels are only applied in 4 v 4 gamemodes, the idea being that you hone your skills in 1 v 1 and 2 v 2 (as well as level up and unlock gear) before jumping into dominion (domination in other games) and elmination modes. If I had to guess why this game is getting so much hate I'd have to say that it's one of those cases of people jumping on the bandwagon, there are some people here who have less than 20 hours giving negative reviews, which is no where near enough time in the game to make a proper decision. If you look at the 'points' they make they are usually just rehashed from YouTubers or other people telling them how bad the peer to peer is, when in reality although there are some issues it is far from terrible. Finally the campaign is lacking I will admit, but when you compare it to games like Rainbow Six and Overwatch it is very much appreciated that one was included. Think of it as more of an additional tutorial, which you do get rewards for. To conclude I would give the game an 8/10, or a 7/10 at worst depending how unlucky you are with the peer to peer, for most it should'nt be much of an issue.
TL;DR The game is a fun medieval combat game with diverse classes. People are exaggerating the peer to peer issues and while the campaign is lacking it is much more than what contemporary games are offering and will give you some nice rewards. 8/10, 7/10 if you do happen to get unlucky with peer to peer.

Sniping is always great fun so any game that offers plenty of it has to be a good thing. The sniping in SNIPER ELITE V2 is (as I understand it) pretty realistic. It includes all the conditions that would effect such a task in the real world, including bullet drop, wind speed and direction, body movement etc. There’s no denying the satisfaction when you score a hit, especially a headshot, and this is often augmented by the enjoyable spectacle of the bullet flying through the air in slow-motion towards its target. Personally, I could have lived without the kill-cam’s depiction of the victim’s injuries, but this is only a game so let’s not get too wrapped up in the ethics. Less successful is the close-quarter combat that you are sometimes forced into. The cover-based stealth system is less sophisticated than in some games (Deus Ex: Human Revolution, for example) and aiming at close range can be problematic. This, coupled with a ridiculously keen-eyed AI, can prove frustrating. The graphics are good to very good, with the ruins of a war-torn Berlin particularly well depicted. The story is rather fractured due to the mission-based gameplay but SEV2 isn’t really about story, its about honing your long-range shooting skills, and this it does well.

Doom is something everyone should play. It is one of the earliest games in the FPS genre and it is also one of the best. The story is very simple, there are two research bases set up on the two moons of Mars, Phobos and Diemos, the scientists there are working on a new teleportation project to get from one moon to the other instantly. Something goes horribly wrong, a gate to hell is open, and everybody is killed exept for one lone space marine. You must fight through hordes of demons on both moons and eventually hell. That's all there is to it. \ You have many weapons at your disposal including your fists, a chainsaw, a pistol, a shotgun, a chaingun, a rocket launcher, a plasma rifle, and the almighty BFG 9000. Your goal in each level is to solve puzzles, get keycards, hit switches, kill tons of demons, kill a boss now and then, and then get to the exit. Doom cam out in 1993 and this version on Steam is the Ultimate Doom from 1995. It has a new fourth chapter that will really test your skills. Age has not detracted from this game and if your somebody that only plays games a few years old at best because you only want the newest stuff than that is your loss because I would take this game over Black Ops or Ghosts any day. While this version may not come with multiplayer you can just download skulltag online and fix that right up. Happy gaming.

This was one of the most addicting games I've ever played. I usually don't like this style of game and I wasn't expecting much when I purchased it, but I was quite impressed.
The amount of customization is enough to keep you occupied for hours. There are several special forces factions to choose from, each having a minor stat boost to differentiate from the others. You can customize every soldier in your squad, unfortunately you do have to pick from premade looks but there's so many that it's not that big of a deal. After you've given your soldier his look you can pick one of the classes/roles, each having their own bonuses and skills that unlock as you level the soldier up. Then there is gun customization, there are a lot of guns to choose from, though it can take a while to unlock some of them. Unfortunately most of the guns are just different versions of the same gun with different stats. Furthermore you can equip scopes, lasers, flash lights, triggers, grips, and even change the gas system. After you have your soldiers outfitted with guns there are several helmets, vests, camos, etc. to choose from. It's really amazing for such a small game to have customization that rivals games like Battlefield.
The gameplay is fun and thoughtful planning is your best weapon. Once you get a handle of the game the earlier difficulty levels can become sort of a faceroll, but don't worry there's multiple difficulty levels and you can tell a difference on each one. If you want to make it even harder on yourself you can select the permanent death option which is exactly as it sounds, contrary to the regular mode where your soldier will just be out of that battle but back again after the mission is over. I've always been a fan of hardcore modes in games so this was a great feature for me, though it caused me some pain a few times when I had almost max level soldiers die, then had to replace them with a fresh level 1.
My only issue with the game is there is I guess you could say an "OP" gun. I will not list which gun this is as I don't want to ruin anyones experience with the game. But once I outfitted all four of my soldiers with this gun the game was too easy even on the hardest difficulties.
All in all, a surprisingly impressive game. 9/10

If you are looking for deep tactical gameplay (as this game is advertised), then stay away, you won't find that here.
That said, the game still offers good casual entertainment, if you enjoy leveling up your guys and unlocking new equipment, give it a spin.
Quick run-down of the gameplay if you need help deciding if it is for you:
You first create a squad, you can decide between some well-known specops units like DEVGRU, SAS, KSK and so on. What unit you select decides the starter attributes of your guys, one will have their special ability trained up nice, other will have reaction time up, other accuracy etc.
Then you run through the missions, and I really mean run, as once you discover the one tactic that works 100% of the time against the AI, you'll just breeze through. Not much depth here, and the occasional weird glitch with your guys running backwards or facing a wall for no good reason.
Your guys gain experience, and you get money, so in-between you level up your guys (in the end, it doesnt matter much what squad you made, they'll all end up the same just look different), buy them some new weapons and gear.
You can upgrade weapons to modify their stats, but here you'll end up again with all the same upgrades as there is one good combination.
Sounds like not much, but it is a decent enough time-killer, pick it up when it is on sale.
In case 3d is not that important to you, I'd suggest to take a look at 'Door Kickers', that one has tactical gameplay down to perfection.

I have begun a project to review all of my games on steam. I do it in alphabetical order, and I just realised that the first three games are horror games… well then. anyways, let the review begin.
You know what’s funny? The first time i played this game, i was around ten years old, and didn’t get scared by it. Now, replaying it many years later, there was actually some parts that genuinely scared me! Amnesia was the first horror game I ever finished, and it is one of the most important horror games to date, since a lot of modern horror games takes a lot of inspiration from this game, for example Outlast. As far as I know, this game invented the run and hide type of horror games! When it was released, everyone talked about it, and it quickly built up a fanbase. But has the game aged well? Let’s find out!
*STORY*
You play as Daniel, who suffers from amnesia. (Well, that explains the title!) Actually, he chose to forget about his past. Why? You’ll have to play the game yourself to see, but beware. The story is actually quite disturbing. There’s a lot of reading to do if you want to know everything, but i actually think it’s worth it. It has the best story of any horror game I’ve played, or at least I think so, because I didn't read the story in outlast, so I have no idea if it was good or not!
*VISUALS*
This game takes place in a really dark castle. The castle looks pretty good, but it gets a bit boring after a while. The entire game takes place in the castle, and the design of the place never really changes. There is a few places that stands out from the rest near the end of the game, but other than that it is just more castle. I find the main monster to look pretty goofy. It isn’t very scary looking at all. There is another monster later in the game that looks a lot creepier, but it is just in a small part of the game! The first couple of hours you don’t get a good glimpse of the monster, and your imagination runs wild on how terrifying it looks. That is exiting, and you're waiting in anticipation to see it. But when you do, you'll get mildy dissapointed. It’s a shame that it looks as goofy as it does, because the build up is really good!
*GAMEPLAY*
This game is what i like to call a run and hide horror game. There is no way to attack or kill the monster, and all you can do to save yourself is to run and hide. The game works like this: You start by finding a big room. This room is safe. There won’t be any monsters in this room. From the room, you have access to some levels. Every level has an area to explore. There is often a puzzle for you to solve. When you finish the puzzle, the monster will enter the level, and you have to make your way out without getting killed. Once you have done all of the levels around the big room, you can get into the next one, with new levels to explore. Rinse and repeat through the whole game. This makes the game really repetitive. Thankfully, the game is very short. It took me seven hours on my first playthrough, and four hours on the second. The game isn’t long enough to get annoying, and that’s fine. The best part of this game if you ask me, is the sanity system. If you look directly at the monster, you'll lose your sanity. If you’re in the dark, you’ll lose your sanity. If something spooky happens, you’ll lose your sanity. When your sanity decreases, scary stuff will happen. For example, pictures will change to a much scarier version of the picture. When your sanity meter is all the way down, you will fall on the ground and walk very slow for a while, which is awful if you’re being chased by a monster. What makes this system so good, is that when hiding from the monster, you have to be in the dark, or else the monster will spot you. But when you’re in the dark, your sanity will drop! This makes hiding a scary thing to do. Another good part of the game is the lantern, or the oil. Your lantern needs oil to light up. There is not a lot of oil in the game, and I spent the entire game being scared of running out of it. There's also tinderboxes hiding around the world, which you can use to light candles, but i didn’t use them often. by the end of the game, i had about 40 tinderboxes left. You can also pick up a lot of items. There’s a couple of puzzles you have to pick up and throw items to solve, but for the most part it’s useless. I do like it though, and it is one of the things i missed the most from a machine for pigs, but more on that in my next review.
*VERDICT*
Amnesia: the dark descent is a good game. It has a lot of cool mechanics and basically created the run and hide genre, for better or for worse. The monster might not be scary, but the atmosphere is! The biggest downfall is that the game never really changes, and is the exact same game from start to finish. But the game is relatively sort, so it didn’t affect my enjoyment of the game to much. overall, I’ll give this game a:
7/10
It is a classic in the horror genre, and while it has some problems, It’s still a ride worth taking!

While the game on itself is cute and stuff, there are number of serious issues which stops me from recommending this game.
First, and the most importaint, the game is not nearly optimized at all memory-wise. It just loads all it's resources to the memory at once. The game definitely would not work on 4 GB machine. It barely works on 8 GB machine in fact.
Next, the game can't handle mouse. If you are playing in windowed mode, eventually the mouse cursor, though hidden, will move outside the window, and the next time you click you will switch to different program. This makes game unplayable in windowed mode. In the full-screen mode, if you do not move the mouse for a while, it will hide the cursor, moving it to the center, making it inconvenient to navigate through the menu.
Gameplay-wise, while the graphics are good, the game is not very addictive. There are apparently no inertia for ships, so you can just rotate arbitrary. You also need to hold shift to just fly forward. Relative object speed is not very high, making the game not really immersive. Wanted to feel like Luke Skywalker, flying into the fray and shooting stuff? Tough luck.
While I understand it is an early access, and this may change in the future, there is currently no long-term goal between levels, making you feel like you just repetitively shooting static stuff.
The game really does have a potential, but it will take a lot of work to see it to fruition. I would also note that the slow process and concentration on visuals adds to the risk of seeing the game eventually abandoned, unfortunately.

I was so excited to find out that Catan online had been updated. The visuals are simple but greatly updated from the original. I read the other reviews indicating the requirement for pay but im ok laying down a few dollars for a good game.  I fired it up and was immediately lost. The GUI is mysteriously cryptic and devoid of labels. All functions rely on meaningless icons that must be hovered over to get a detailed description for understanding. After starting a random match I was faced with the game board visual with little to no reference as to what I was seeing and what I should do. Nothing about the controls are intuitive to a veteren player of any multiplayer online game. Small obscure icons appear and disappear quickly as various plays are made during each turn which can only be identified in more detail by hovering over them before they go away. One example of this poor control design is during trades. When a trade is offered, a large window pops up, covering much of your view, displaying all 5 resources for both the trader and you - whether you have the resource or not. It's up to you to decipher which row is yours and which is the trader, there is no indicator identify which is which. A simply directional arrow down (to reference a resource being offered to you) and one pointing up (to signify what you are going to give). You must quickly scan each resource and look for a small white number that indicates how many, if any, the trader wants and is offering. It is very easy to miss that the trader may have requested multiple types of resource. Don;t like the trade? Too bad. You have to open a new window and re-offer a brand new trade without being able to reference the map and think through your decision based on the type of resource requested and what you need. Why? Why so much needless clicking for even the simpest tasks? Why all the clutter of useless information and icons with no words? Why couldn't they just pop a small window that indicates the specific resource requested and the specific resource offered? Why display a bunch of additional resources with a value of 0? everyone complains that turns take too long and this is a good reason why. Even the turn indicator is difficult to identify at a glance. Let's say it's the blue player's turn. The turn indicator shows an arrow in the blue box over the avatar, but it is a darker shade of blue. Why not white? I spent 30 minutes on my first game and the farthest player was only at 5 points. I feel like the controls take too many clicks and require too much thought that it interrupts your strategy resulting in unnecessarily lengthy turns. In any case, I am terribly disapointed in the exectution of this game. They have incurred a huge tragedy on this game that I played for free for years. This is a cartoony, childs iphone game. If you are a pc gamer or a fan of the original online game, then I would pass. Save yourself the disappointment.
Update: 8/26/17
So a Catan community rep has commented on this review stating "I have to ask. Did you play the tutorial?". This alerted me that I need to clarify something. My negative review is not based on whether someone can learn this game on their own without a tutorial. This review is rooted in two major problems. 1 is that this is not settlers of catan, it's clickers of catan. I am a big fan of practical and EFFICIENT interfaces. This game utilizes neither. One of the useful indicators to determine how efficient a task is, is how many clicks it takes to accomplish it. Let's just say I lost count.
Example: During normal gameplay you can only see the top card you are holding in your hand. The other cards are obscured. You want to see all your cards? Click on them. Nope, sorry. It just zooms in, still displaying the top most card. Click again, my friend. Now you can see a VERY large display of each type of card. But I'm sorry, it's so big, you can't see the board. You must now click elsewhere on the screen to zoom them back down to it's beginning state. 4 clicks to accomplish something that should automatically be visible at all times. Why so difficult? Well, that's ok because you can recognize the type of card by it's border color, right? Wrong. Sheep and wood are both green, albeit two slightly different shades. So maybe it doesn't bother you, but it bothers me. I find myself often checking whether I have sheep of wood.
Issue number two: labels. Why not? What did words ever do to you? Words are good. They are the basis of human interaction for thousnads of years and it seems like we all turned out pretty good. PErsonally, I prefer PC games over other formats like consoles or mobile devices because of the superior interface made possible by the access to a keyboard and a 22" screen. Probably not everyone is like that but even on the first screen you can immediately recognize that this game is meant for a tablet. 80% of the real estate on the openeing screen is just blank artwork, not even used. The icons themselves are just meaningless symbols.The trade icon is a bag with an arrow around it. Huh? You have to hunt around and read tooltips. Want to exit? There is no quick exit feature. You must click on your avatar in the menu screen to be offered an option to exit and then you must also confirm. In game is even worse. Yes the tutorial, briefly, explains how to accomplish the most needed tasks but does nothing to explain any of the icons displayed except for the trade icon. There are a number of other icons that display throughout the match, indicating various actions that are happeneing and sometimes they only appear for a few seconds. Want to know what they mean? sorry, you will have to brush over them and read the tooltip before it disappears.
For these reasons, I will not recommend the game. Not everyone will care about the concerns I brought up and don't have a problem with them. But for the people out there who want to play a well constructed game using a well constructed interface, than they should look elsewhere. When playing a competative game with time limits and running rank ladders, I expect more thought than was put into it. Tasks should center around quick and precise completion so that turn meter time does not get wasted. Does this clarify my complaint, Catan Universe Rep? All this is to say - yes. Yes I played the tutorial.

I am writing this review based on gameplay conducted on the 28th of August
GAMEPLAY – My rating: 7.5/10
PROS:
-	Gameplay is very nostalgic, reminiscent of a late-70s arcade space shooter like Asteroids or Space Invaders.
-	Massive improvements since release in July.
-	Enemy health/shield indicators
-	Enemy indicators
-	Targeting boxes with windage targets to help land shots from a distance.
CONS:
-	No looting system.
-	No ship customization.
-	No difference in ships; i.e. nothing to upgrade to or purchase with in-game currency
AUDIO – My rating: 8/10
PROS:
-	Not earbleedingly loud
-	Semi-smooth transition from menu to space to fight
-	Weapons have distinct sounds
CONS:
-	No “muffle” effect from being in space
-	Soundtrack can seem abrupt from one level to another
CONTROLS – My rating: 7/10
PROS:
-	Much improved since July/initial release
-	Hard mode controls are very intuitive
-	Has multiple modes of input: Mouse/Keyboard, Gamepad or Joystick
CONS:
-	Lacks small immersion aspects, like ship floating after letting go of the thrusters
-	Normal mode still feels slightly slow to respond to player input
GRAPHICS – My rating: 8/10 (on high end graphics card)
PROS:
-	Beautiful graphical fidelity
-	Large battles, lasers, explosions, do not seem to drop framerate
CONS:
-	My graphics card (1080) was at 90% load all the time
-	No option to limit FPS
-	No graphics settings outside setting display ratio and bloom quality
LONGEVITY – My rating: 7/10
PROS:
-	ShilohGames is really listening to the community and implementing realistic feedback.
-	Easy to play for short periods of time
-	Very nostalgic feel
-	Would work very well in an arcade
CONS:
-	No multiplayer
-	No looting system
-	No reward system
-	Nothing for players to “earn” from gameplay outside a score
Overall rating: 7.5/10
In the end, I’d rate this game an overall 7.5 out of 10. There are a lot of great things about Disputed Space and I believe ShilohGames is one of the most active indie developers I’ve seen in a long time. It really feels as if it should be in an arcade somewhere with players vying to have their names at the top of the scoreboards.

Review of "Episode 1: It's About Time"
"You built a time machine out of a De Lorean??" The conversation between Marty McFly and 'Doc' Brown seems very familiar but something isn't quite right. And it ends up with our time travelling heroes getting stuck in Prohibition Era Hill Valley. Along the way they meet Marty's grandfather Arty, Principal Strickland's aunt, and a 17 year old Emmett Brown. The game is presented with lovely looking 3D cartoon graphics and a voice cast including Christopher Lloyd reprising his role as Doc Brown. The actor playing Marty totally nails the teenage Michael J. Fox voice too! The story is supervised by Bob Gale who co-wrote the films with Bob Zemeckis and, you know, it really does come off in the spirit of the films. (If perhaps on the fan service side of things.)
The game plays out like most point-and-click adventure games. You move Marty around the environment and interact with specific elements or characters to move the story along. The philosophy for the game seems to be that the story is important above everything. In this regard, the puzzles are never overly difficult or distracting from the story. The player is never penalised for their actions which means you are free to go through all the character responses which are often amusing. To this end, Back to the Future: The Game ends up being a bit more interactive fiction than a game as such. And that's not necessarily a bad thing. The story and acting are engaging and you find that you want to move along as well.
Playing the game isn't very different to many adventure games. I've always found the genre a bit clunky to move around in and while the developers at Telltale Games add a bit of polish to make the controls a bit forgiving, I find it's really an endemic fault of the genre. I was extremely pleased to find that there was gamepad support for the game and I could take advantage of Big Picture Mode. The gamepad is usable, and I used it for about half of the game, but it is also quite clunky to use.
Probably the only thing that really bothered me about the game were the few intense scenes where the music swells up and scene gets busy. There is a sense of urgency in the scenario but because the adventure game is to some degree turn based it's difficult to satisfy that urgency. It becomes a little frustrating and you kind of want to turn all the sound off so you can concentrate on the puzzle you're supposed to be solving.
Otherwise Back to the Future: The Game, Episode One is a delightful little game and I look forward to playing the subsequent instalments.

When I read a book, I deem it good based on how it impacts me. Like a good book, that you simply cannot put down, Pyre enchants me in a mysterious way, it has an essence that pushes me on to see what lies ahead in the journey of our heroes.
I liked Bastion a lot, and I love Transistor even more. So the expectations were high. So  far, Pyre has lived up to these expectations and more.
Beautiful graphics aside, the game boasts a phenomenal soundtrack, which is as expected, and an interesting and challenging gameplay in the form of the Rites. Unique characters and a compelling story drives the player forward onto uncovering the stories of the characters and the story of the game itself.
Update :
After completing the story, few thoughts come to mind. What would have been different, had our heroes chosen a different path in life? Maybe we would have never gotten together to go on this incredible journey to find our freedom.
Certain aspects of the story lingers even after finishing the game, just like when you may go back to read the last few pages of that last good book you read over and over again. From here on, there's only a few options that remain. Either you find another venture that's just as enticing, or you simply sit tight and jump back on the same one once again. There are only a handful of games that have left me with such a lingering impression, and I am happy that Supergiant Games' latest work of art has managed to attain a position in that list.
Pyre is a truly wonderful experience, a journey that I will, from the bottom of my heart recommend.

I hate visual novels with a passion but I /LOVE/ this game.
I think they're bland, unattractive and all around cannot hold my attention - clicking one button just doesn't do it for me. But almost five hours into Pyre and I can say it is NOTHING like a visual novel, (apart from long segments of talking and a few choices you are presented with,) in that it isn't boring.
Supergiant scores another masterpiece, fantastic soundtrack, amazing lovable characters and things that will make you laugh and cry all at once.
The segments of the game that function as a world/character/story building VN are not boring and manage to capture my attention, and although the gameplay for the Rites is COMPLETELY different from what Bastion and Transistor was like it manages to stress me out in a way that has me on the edge of my seat wondering if I'm going to lose the Rite. Losing in this game (haven't lost yet on normal) appears to have an impact on the story and listening to the banter between each character is fantastic.
Buy this game.
If you liked Bastion or Transistor, buy it.
If you didn't like Bastion or Transistor, buy it.
If you love Visual Novels, buy it.
If you hate Visual Novels, buy it.
Supergiant never fails to bring something fantastic to the table, can't wait to beat Pyre.

I will update this review when I finish the game.
I've got about 3 or so hours into the game so far, and I can say pretty comfortably that it's very good. I'm a massive fan of Supergiant's prior works, so I was willing to give the game a shot despite having reservations on the concept, and I'm glad I did. The story and the marriage of all of its elements is what makes this game truly special. Supergiant knows how to make an interesting story and world, building and supporting it with everything they have at their disposal. Music, visuals, writing, and gameplay are all built with that story and experience in mind. So far, Pyre is no different.
Pyre's gameplay loop can be somewhat compared to The Banner Saga's. Half the game plays as a choice-based visual novel. Talk to your characters, make choices about your travel, and make choices in relation to your supplies and what actions you may take between Rites. The second half are the Rites themselves, a psuedo-sport combat game where you control three of your party members to deliver an orb into the enemy's pyre. Whichever team destroys the others' pyre wins. It's a simple concept that is made interesting with the large cast of party members who all act differently and can be levelled in different ways. Party members can also be equipped with Talismans that afford them certains buffs. Overall, these two gameplay halves serve each other well.
Overall, I've been seriously enjoying this game. It would have been nice to have voice acting for all the characters, but what's there is very good. The story has kept me very engaged, which is somewhat surprising as I don't generally care for text-heavy games like this. Ultimately, while I can draw comparisons to other games, such as The Banner Saga, there's nothing quite like Pyre. I commend Supergiant Games for continuously trying new and interesting ideas and being so good at what they do they can make it work as well as they have here.

Sheltered is so much fun, that I spent way too many hours playing it when I should have been sleeping. Don't be fooled by the simpler design of this game, as it actually adds a lot to its charm. In the beginning you start out confused and lost as you struggle to keep your family alive and well. Every tiny decision you make, even mild, will somehow matter when that one unit of water could have prevented one of your characters from dying.
When you play more, the more you actually learn how you are supposed to do things the right way. Generally I really like the fact that the tutorial is ambiguous, this adds to the fear and confusion of what a real apocalypse would feel like. Intelligent players will enjoy the challenge of figuring things out for themselves, while others may find this annoying.
The pet feature is one of my favorite aspects with the game, as they add a lot of fun, and can prove to be extremely important in the future. I hope to see different pets added in the future, parrots, turtles, rabbits, and even cows could all have their own odd little perks. Skins on certain animals would also be awesome too, having a black cat, or a pug dog could add to the personalization and attachment to the creature.
Cons about this game would mainly lie on the lack of dialogue, and affects of recruiting certain people. Dialogue is often repeated and the same from every character, it would definitely be more interesting to see if what some says depending more on the traits you chose prior. Not to mention the fact that I got bored of the exact same diary entries all the time as they were almost all the same. Adding some diversity would really help enhance this.
-spoiler alert (kind of not really)- Time to address the pink elephant, the cannibal that randomly ends up being completely normal. I'm sure a lot of you have come accross this, you accidentally recruited someone who actually seems super suspicious by saying your family sounds delicious. Well it REALLY is irritating when you find out there is literally no repercussions for this, sure they might eventually leave and mess with something if they start dying from lack of supplies, but so does EVERY other survivor you recruit. Proper repercussions from certain actions would avoid strange conflictions like this. -spoiler end-
I also wish there was another way to defend yourbase other than the reinforcing of the door, or traps. Otherwise they come in and everyone, even courageous people, curl up in a ball and let the intruders take everything, even if said intruders actually is only one person. To be honest there are people who would just get too scared to react, but there are a lot of people who would defend themselves and attack the intruders. Maybe I'm just not doing things right, but it would be nice.
Those are the only things that particularily annoy me, but every game has flaws. The fact that even some people lose sanity over time is interesting, and the amount of details and features put into the game are really just amazing. A long time ago in a Galaxy far, far away someone had the idea of creating a turn-based RPG based around events in the Star Wars universe.  Star Wars Knights of The Old Republic was released and it was brilliant!
But this posed a problem, any sequel would need to be equally as good.  No easy feat.
The sequel was released, KoTOR II, and possibly the most polite way to describe it was 'disappointing'.
DO NOT play this game without the restoration Mods!  If it had been allowed a full development cycle, and had not been rushed by the publishers, this would have been a more than worthy successor to the original.
The 'complete' story is brilliantly written, the voice acting astounding, particularly Kreia, and the total effect is to drag the player gloriously into the story.  The story is far more provocative and engaging than the original.  Gone is the stark choice between light and dark, here we have shades of grey and choices are far less clear cut than in the original.  There are a number of times the game makes you want to act against any alignment you have chosen to pursue and engenders empathy in situations that would in lesser games be black and white.
It still has its bugs, movement keys often fail after combat and cut-scenes can sometimes break, but neither of these is enough, while being undeniably irritating, to prevent the game being an immersive and rewarding experience.
Definitely worth a buy but the Mods really are a must!

As you can tell by my profile picture, I like this game. I play it again every few years. It's really amazing to see how different first person shooters were when id software was the only one's doing it and had nothing to compare to. You don't look up or down, aiming in the vertical plane is done automatically. There is no commanding officer shouting orders through a radio. The story is told in the instruction manual and by a paragraph at the end of each episode. No need to reload weapons. DOOM was made with one goal in mind: shoot everything and anything that moves. Usually when you play a really old game, you think about how good it would be with modern graphics, but with DOOM there is some sort of uniqueness about its graphics, you don't seem to mind.
Bottom Line: DOOM is absolute carnage. A must play.

I played Amnesia a few years after its hype died down and wasn't very impressed. I saw what people liked, but didn't think much of the game itself. However, it did have enough potential that I kept an eye on the studio. When SOMA came out, I was very excited to check it out and see what this studio's next game was.
SOMA was surprising in a lot of ways. It is incredibly story-focused to the point that some people call it a  walking simulator. I  don't think this is a  bad thing, as it has one of the best stories I have seen in a video game. It found a way to make a sci-fi plot new and interesting  and actually tackles new ideas that I've never seen in other sci-fi stories. The places it goes are incredibly dark and extremely interesting. They kept me playing and clamoring for more.
The one downside this game has  is its actual gameplay, sadly.  Whenever a monster shows up, they are far more annoying than actually scary. They get in the way more than anything. There were times where I would be trying to read e-mails on a computer to get more cool story bits and monsters would come and interrupt me. Don't even get me started on the awful visual effects that get stuck on your screen when you take damage. I heard there was a mod that removes the monsters and honestly, I think that would be the best way to play the game.
Overall, I absolutely recommend the game for its story, despite the flawed gameplay bits. I would say this is a must play

Breach and Clear is good for what it is, a squad level turn based strategy game(though it meshes real time mechanics into it). That's the short version.
The long version is that this game does well to cover a market that really isn't thriving right now. For so long strategy games have been more about commanding large armies rather than smaller squad levels of highly specialized soldiers. The few that do attempt this are either outdated or poorly executed. Breach and Clear provides a breath of fresh air to a genre that seemed stuck for a long time.
I will admit, the gameplay is rather simpe and somewhat repetitive, but still will suit true strategy/military genre fans out there. You are allowed to control 4 man squads of some of the world's best specialized combatants (American Special Forces, Army Rangers, Navy SEALs; German KSK; British S.A.S.; Russian Spetsnaz; Canadian JTF2). In this squad creation of whatever force you decided to pick(you cannot mix and match, if you pick Rangers, all four members of that squad are Rangers, but you can create multiple squads), you create four operators each with default skills and loadouts(the loadout is by default the M4A1 SOPMOD, the skills vary somewhat based on what kind of force you pick. Special Forces, for example, will have higher health stats by default). Upon creating a squad, each member of the team you create must be assigned a role, and depending on this role he will have special abilities and skills(the fireteam leader provides bonuses to his squad as well as being able to draw enemy fire, for example). As you complete missions, your soldiers will  earn experience, thus allowing them to upgrade certain stats, such as health, movement speed, accuracy, etc. Also, with each successful mission, you earn moeny to buy new gear and weapons for your operators(only qualm I have about the guns is that they are almost all American used weapons, most of which AR-15 derivatives, so there's not a whole lot of variation there).
When you start a mission, you are given an aerial view of the area of operation(this is the main viewpoint for te entire game). This will allow you to examine the area before sending your guys in. Once content with what you see, you can select which entry points you want your guys to stack up on(most maps will have at least two entry points, though there are several that have just one). You can divide your team to tackle multiple entries and cover more ground, or you can keep your units together and lessen the risk of one of them going down. When you send the guys in, you have a movement stage, where you coordinate where you want your guys to go, what direction they cover, what actions they should do, etc. Once you got all that figured out, you can execute, and your guys will follow your orders to the best of their ability. Be mindful, when you activate this and they start moving, the enemy starts moving to, and will therefore react to your guys, this is where turn based strategy meshes with real time strategy. Assuming that your team is well equiped and your tactics are sound, you should be able to complete the missions without many casualties.
So the gameplay, unfortunately, doesn't vary much. The same principle is applied over and over. But the gameplay is solid and once again those who enjoy this kind of commanding style will be pleased. Overall, I'd give it a solid B rating. Could be more varied in terms of gameplay mechanics, but what it does offer is well rounded and well executed.

To this day, almost 30 years since the release of this game, there's been only one FPS that is as good as this, and that's the entire half-life series.
This game isn't a rails shooter. It's not a trip through disney land. It's a "cozy" maze based shooter. You're in the middle of a non-linear level with limited ammo and horrors from hell, but it feels good.
This game makes you feel the entire world is burning up around you, but you have the power to fight back. Hence, "cozy".
Just an incredible game.
If this is your first time going through this on a modern machine.
Pick up gzdoom and the two mods I mentioned above and you're in luck. There's probably a newer version of brutal doom by the time you read this, so get the latest one, but even going through the game once in vanilla is probably fine, but you'll still want to go through the vanilla version in gzdoom because dosbox doesn't always play friendly with the latest OS.

SOMA reminds me of Canadian author Robert J Sawyer's science fiction, so perhaps it's no coincidence the game's prelude is set in Toronto. From that moment forward, I suspected I would enjoy this game. I did.
I completed the game in about 13 hours, only referencing a walk-through in two or three tough spots. The AI was fairly predictable, but there were a couple of challenging encounters. This isn't a game you play for complex or deeply satisfying play mechanics. It's a few systems more sophisticated than a "walking simulator" like Dear Esther, but not much.
You play SOMA for the story. At turns SOMA tells a tale that is suspenseful, deeply shrouded in mystery, heartbreaking, and morally challenging. Players will either reinforce or reframe their conception of what it means to exist as a person.
The voice acting is top-notch. The graphic design and execution are excellent. But, the story is phenomenal.
Highly recommended.

Breach & Clear is a tactical turn based strategy game similar in execution to XCOM. You take command of a special forces squad of your choosing, and plan your attack on objective based missions (terrorist hunt, bomb defusal or extraction). You have a reasonably wide selection of weapons available, though weapons used by some special forces are absent from the game. Enemy engagements are always lethal, as there is no option to simply incapacitate. The inability to set timings is also detrimental to tactics.
Overall the game is entertaining enough to keep you playing for hours, but it lacks scope and depth in comparison to tactical predecessors such as Deadline (1996, Millennium Interactive). The graphics and audio are good, but I'd like to see some destructability, and a greater range of weapons and consumables (no smoke grenades or CS gas?).

I've barely got my hands on the game, but absolutely love it so far. I found this game really suits me for cuople of reasons.
One is that it's not overly complicated. You can easily learn and master the controls and fundamental gameplay in minutes after the tutorial. Each missions are not too long, just enough for my rather short concentration. Now, that does not mean this game is shallow. It will give you quite a bit of options you can take, as well as tactical challenges you will need to work around.
Second is the Stats/Gear system. You can build your own squad with operators with different class, stats, and gear. Since there are 6 classes and only 4 operators can be in a single squad, you will need to adjust your strategy depending on what kind of operator is available.
The third is the overall "tacticoolness". If you are firearms/military enthusiast, you will probably appeciriate this game. Most of gears and wepons dipicted in game is realistic, as well as appropriate. Authentic weapons and tactical gears from manufacturers such as Surefire, LaRue, First Spear, LBT, etc... are availble at your operators disposal and you can kit up your team of real-life global warfighters, ranging from 75th Ranger Reg., German KSK, Canadian JTF2, Russian Spetznaz, and everyones favorite, SEAL/DEVGRU. You can outfit Army SOF with BALCS and DCU, give the seals JPC and Airframe helmets. Sadly there are not too many variations at the moment. I hope the devs add more choice of weapons and gears.
Some ways, this game really reminds me of Medal of Honor: Warfighter. Gameplay aside, you can feel that the creators of both gmaes defnitely put a lot of effort into military authenticity. However, the gameplay is enjoyable, but ordinally and really not outstanding.
Overall, I reccomend this game to anyone looking for casual tactical game and like guns and operators operating operationally.

This (TL:DR) review is more meant as feedback to the creator(s) with some suggestions of what may make the game more immersive for the player, as it is still in Early Access.
Despite "not recommending this game in its current state" I still enjoy it and find its ship designs and lasers to be pretty cool, and it has a lot of potential. I am a big fan of large capital ship space battles, and I think if you can also admire the designs of those kinds of ships you will still get some enjoyment from what this game offers as of now. However, beyond the ship designs being cool and the combat being "just okay" it feels very Early Access still, with little to the levels beyond blasting away at the main enemy capital ships that appear and fending off smaller fighter planes.
This can still be enjoyable, but it could use more immersion. The sound effects while decent seem sparse. Some kind of speed or UI indicator beyond the very miniscule 'shake' your view does while using your speed boost would add to the effect of using that ability, maybe some vignetting or blurring around the edges of the player view? Or at the least a "boost sound"
Your boost also seems to be a bit wonky in that it will work sometimes and then at others it seems like I have to click the stick in a few times to get it to register. Your ship feels quite slow overall when moving at its default speed.  The controls on Xbox One USB controller take a bit of getting used to, with LT mapped to moving your ship backward and RT mapped to moving your ship forward, with rotating your ship on the dpad. In the control options the creator(s) note that being able to remap the buttons will (??) be coming in a future update, so maybe this will alleviate some of the control issues and make the game feel more fluid than it does in its current state. That being said, you do get used to it after awhile.
Something that I enjoy in this genre of game and I think this game would benefit largely from are "radio chatter" style portraits popping up during the combat, from friendlies and enemies. I realize this may be out of range of the creator's budget, with voice acting etc.. but I think it would make the game more immersive and make the enemy capital ships seem more adversarial / boss-like than ... placeholder floating big enemy.
The enemy capital ships health is very ambiguous and you're just kind of plunking away at them until they explode. A portrait popping up of an enemy saying "I'm in trouble now..." or something along those lines would do well to further immerse the player and also make them aware of what's going on that the limited UI doesn't seem to portray.
Your own ship's health seems a bit vague as well right now, whereas a computer AI voice for the ship (i.e. "shields low" "damage critical" etc..) would warn the player and also add some to the immersion.
The text used in the game ("enemy ships detected in nearby area" "earth is under attack" etc) looks very generic.
Although you have a variety of weapons to cycle through it's not very clear which do better to lower the enemy fighters' shields or actual health, and you're just left to kind of assume which may or may not be more effective.
All these criticisms aside, the game just recently released and it looks quite good, with the colorful flares of the firefights going off and the large capital ships floating by with planets in the distance. I just think the game could use more immersion via a variety of sound effects (more 'hit' noises, steam, rockets/turbos boosting -yours or others-, whatever..) and the aforementioned portraits or radio or AI chatter. As-is right now you're just kind of thrown into an area to float along and blast away at the enemy capital ship until it explodes and then you're warped to the next area to the do the same thing. I enjoy what's there, but I'm also a big fan of this kind of setting (large capital ship space battles) so I may be biased to forgive the game's shortcomings otherwise. I can't help but imagine that ripping by an enemy capital ship while your booster is roaring (or their engines are making some kind of sound beyond just floating along silently...) as their portrait pops up lamenting you would add to the overall fun/immersion rather than it just being a pretty straight-forward, quiet experience.
I hope the creator continues to refine what is here! I enjoy the look of the game and think the overall premise is cool, I just think more effects to immerse the player would go a long way.

Never before has a game re-created a child's curiosities with such precision, such detail, that this simulator almost seems too real.

In all, I very highly reccomend this game for it's educational purposes, and it's nostalgic feeling of playing with dolls.

You know, after enjoying Transistor and Bastion so thoroughly, for some reason, I didn't think Pyre would really be on the same level as those two games. The gameplay, at first glance, whilst interesting, didn't seem too engaging.
...But the more and more I play Pyre, the more I think I'm wrong. This game - whilst it has a slow story->gameplay->story pace not all may enjoy - is actually shaping up to be one of my favourite games of all time. Allow me to explain why. (And if you don't like long-winded reviews, you'd better find another one haha).
Pyre is an inspiring, lovingly-crafted, and clever game of quality I've only experienced in few games. When it comes to a mixture of creativity, quality, and a genuine love for the product they're producing, Supergiant has proved to me they're one of the best companies out there in that regard. Whilst I'm not one to read every inch of lore, I love being immersed in a certain setting, getting a feel for characters, and really feeling 'part of the game'. Pyre absolutely excels in that regard.
The gameplay itself appears simple at first, but there are many layers of complexity to it which I think would make it a really excellent multiplayer game. I won't fully go into details, but it's basically like playing top-down basketball made a lot more exciting with excellent graphics, sound design, and with a selection of many characters spicing up your different 3v3 matches with their own abilities. There are honestly tons of ways you can play, with characters such as the slow and powerful Jodariel offering an aggressive/defensive playstyle, or the super speedy Rukey allowing you to quickly rush down the celestial ball. Matches can get tense: seriously tense, if you find yourself getting thrashed by the AI (thankfully that's only happened to me once).
I wouldn't go as far as to say the gameplay is flawless (though it is very very good). Even at max difficulty, whilst I'm sure things are getting harder, I find it rather easy to repeatedly 'rush down' the celestial ball with fast characters. It would be nice to see a level of difficulty above the 'hardest' one that already stands for crowds looking for a true challenge. That said, if you lose a match, as far as I know, you don't just 'restart'. That loss goes down in history forever, so it's pretty intense. You /can/ restart a match if you lose, but... I'd sort of recommend against that, really.
Also, I'd love to see online multiplayer in this game, but unfortunately, I don't think it'll be possible to impliment it. It offers local multiplayer, though, and an 'arena mode' if you just want to hunker down into some gameplay and ignore the story.
Gameplay aside, another very big strength of this game is its characters. As you meet them (and yes, you meet more than the initial trio as you go along), you slowly begin to learn more and more about them. All of their dialogue is carefully written, and if you like seeing a lot of dialogue from a seemingly huge lineup (a bit like Fire Emblem), then this is a game for you. I also love how there's loads of little 'hidden interactions', and the game sometimes gives you 'multiple-choice options' that I'm sure will accomodate
The best thing about this game overall, though, for me at least, is the creativity of its design. I don't know if I'm the only one, and it's sort of unrelated, but I'll be going into university to do a Game Design & Writing course. I've always thought that, being a writer, I'll always be the 'useless' one of a game creating team when it comes past the design/ideas stage. This game, however, has encouraged & inspired me to think otherwise. The writing in this is truly superb, well-thought out, and it's funny how much a few little words on a screen can make you think and inquire about a character that... well... doesn't actually exist. And there are so, SO many multiple choices and ways you can go about this game, I can't even begin to imagine how many lines of dialogue were actually written for Pyre.
Oh, and this game costs not even half of what I'd be willing to pay for it. If you're cautious of your money, whilst I haven't completed a full playthrough yet, I am very, VERY sure this is worth your money.
So, waffling aside, what would I rate this game? Personally, it gets a 9.8/10 (which may as well be 10/10) from me, and I'm rare to give games I even consider 'good' anything higher than an 8.
I'd only recommend against buying this if you're someone who doesn't like story-driven games, or someone who gets annoyed when they're pulled out of gameplay and just can't bring themselves to care about characters at all. If you're one of those people, whilst I think you're missing out, I'd definietely say your money is better spent elsewhere.
