In the modern age of first person shooters such as CoD and Battlefield with their stylized presentation and Quicktime events it is a welcome and joyous occasion when you can fire up a game of Doom and be sucked in like it was 1993 all over again.
On the outside Doom is just another retro shooter trying to survive in this modern world. With it’s pixelated 2.5D graphics, midi soundtrack, inability to jump or duck or even look in 3 dimensions, you would think that it would have been long forgotten in a wash of newer, flashier combat games, but that’s where Doom really shines. In its minimalistic nature, Doom makes you forget what it doesn’t have and focus on what it does have: amazing gameplay.
Doom doesn’t hold your hand. Right from the start you are thrust into a foreign Martian world with a pistol and the hope of survival as you are faced with ever increasing opposition which comes in the form of possessed Space Marines and demonic creatures straight from the depths of hell, and over time that’s exactly where you go. Through the game you get access to bigger and badder weapons but also find larger and more dangerous enemies such as the Cyberdemon and the Spiderdemon-both a mix of demonic flesh and futuristic machine a perfect parallel to the twisted world around them-to use them on. Through it all, superior level design and your wits are what separate you from the dead marines at your feet. The levels unobtrusively lead you into your next surprise encounter all the while providing the cover needed to save you from near death. One thing they don’t do is raise that veil of atmosphere that Doom lays on you. All of the pieces fit together wonderfully in this game to give you the perfect immersive experience.
Of course, one of the biggest reasons this game is still relevant today is the still thriving community of modders who create everything from single levels to entire modifications for the game that give you new weapons, enemies, graphics, sounds, levels, game mechanics… even huge multiplayer and coop levels. And it’s all free.
If you are looking for an adrenaline rush or just want to run screaming down memory lane, look no further than Doom.

Well folks, they've done it again!
Pyre is a game that plays a bit like an interactive visual novel with some choice-and-consequences, sprinkled with a sports type mini-game mechanic to push the story. If you're wondering what the vibe here is, I'll just say that it feels closer like Bastion than Transistor.
The way of traversing is through a Jrpg-like map in which you utilize a wagon (essentially a mobile base/stronghold). You can make upgrades or other things to along your jouney. There are some events that take place to challenge players as well and keep things fresh and interestimg.
The rpg element applies to your "team" whom you are able to level up for combat or outside of combat. Characters level up by rank and after "rites" (rites are the game's unique sport-like replacement of a battle). Characters have their own strengths, weaknesses and movement.
Combat isn't as nearly as satisfying as it was in Bastion or Transistor but it's nore rewarding still and it's more unique than the prior games from Supergiant. Where this game excels is story... This is mostly story-based, and it has alot of character development throughout the game.
Animation is beautifully done, the graphics are purely 2D but so well done that they'll trick the human eye into thinking they are being rendered. Artistically it's undeniably Supergiant's best work to date. Colors are there, detail isn't as great as Transistor or Bastion but stylistically it just pops more.
Characters are likable so far, just as likable as Red or Kid. The world feels hostile, almost a Mad Max feeling mixed with some sort of carnivale fantasy experience. There are dog-people.... yes... dog-people and other weird creatures for you to meet.
There is more replayability here than the other games and you can tell that already from just a few minutes of playing it. Although, I can't talk about it as it would spoil things.
As far as voice-acting, all the characters (except the announcer/commentator) talk in some kind of gibberish as far as audio. Text is well written and very easy to get into the story through that.
Soundtrack is still just as good as ever. Music is up to par with Bastion and Transistor. Though not as atmospheric, it's more lonely.
TLDR:
Pyre's trailers didn't exactly explain the game very well but when you play the game it will all make sense. It's a worthy addition to Bastion and Transistor in my opinion.

As the millennial age broadened gaming to a wider audience, more and more big franchises from the 80's and early 90's began to adapt themselves in bigger budgeted games.  When news of a Back to the Future adventure game created by Telltale surfaced, there was an explosion of fan interest into how it would turn out. They were not disappointed.
The story takes place after the movie. Marty goes back in time to rescue Doc Brown, who landed himself in jail in 1931. During this inital event, he comes across many past characters of Hill Valley, including a young Doc Brown. As the story progesses, both Marty and Doc travel back and forth through time to fix an even greater mess on the timeline then the one in Back to the Future II. Needless to say, it gets heavy.
Very few of the movie's original cast returns, which is a shame. While the voice actors perform wonderfully, it is obvious that they are filling in for who didn't return. The exception is the voice actor for Marty, who is so convincing that many fans won't notice if not told out-right. It's his performance that make this game feel like a direct continuation of the movie.
The game isn't as polished or long as more recent Telltale Games such as The Walking Dead or The Wolf Among Us, so adventure game fans won't find much challenge. There is, however, just enough content to satisfy any fan of the series and is very well worth a purchase.

Pretty great idea, and breath-taking models. They do appear to be straying away from the modern bird-like models however, and they are now starting to look more like they do in Jurassic Park (Although that isn't exactly a bad thing). Game seems to run fine for me, and its a fun experience. Although the game does currently have MANY major flaws.
1: Servers
Massive Multiplayer games like these need good servers, and when you seem to crash out of you're game every 30-40 minutes it just ruins the fun you and your friends are having. Not to mention that many of ther servers are flat out dead, and with only about 30 to choose from, you will more often then not find yourself in one with only 10 people because the main servers are full with around 50-70 players capped.
2: Map
The map FEELS small. I have yet to find how small it really is, but I always spawn next to the wall (Which is just a drop off into nothing). This coupled with the very dense hills you traverse through, make it so you can never see any mountains in front of you, so the map just appears to end almost everywhere. This makes the game feel VERY small. Although the Misty Vally map is a perfect polar opposite of this, with plateaus and deep valleys, filled with fog and well mist, make the map feel open and spacious. I hope to see later maps go follow this example, or better yet, just try to make the current maps feel more open.
3: Chat
When you choose a dinosaur, your chat box is now exclusive to that type of dinosaur, and you can't see the other chat. This is bad in its own ways, but mainly it makes the game feel very empty. I can see where they are coming from with this, making it so you and other species can't communicate with one another and give away position. I think that instead of locking my species, they could lock it by Carnivore and Herbivore. This way, the game is still keeping the the division between species well enough that herds can't be exposed by others in the group, and the chat can be more easily used between these groups.
Thats about all I can think of off the top of my head, I didn't talk about anything like the camera, or ping issues (Beside Servers) because those will al be fixed in due time. I would just hope to see more "design" being placed into gameplay and immersion instead of pumping out new dinosaurs every other week.
Have these be fixed, and the final product be as smooth as I hope it becomes I would give it a 7 or 8/10. I just ♥♥♥♥ing love dinosaurs.
Although as the game is currently I would give it a 5/10.

I just finished playing through one complete game (you play until every member of your team dies) of Sheltered.  Sheltered is a very emotionally involving game.  In many games (if not most) I could care less if my character dies.  Dying is an inconvenience at least and an annoyance at most.  In Sheltered, on the other hand, I really care about what happens to my characters.  They are tough cookies!  At first I thought they would all be dead around Day 6 (they lived until Day 18) but I found the items I was looking for just in time and continued on.  Later in the game my first character died, one of my recruits, in a fight against someone in an area being explored in the Wastelands (the name given to the areas outside the shelter).  I tried running away repeatedly without success and even though I "disarmed" the attacked, he picked up his knife immediately on the next turn, and stabbed my character with it until he died from his injuries.
In terms of game mechanics, Sheltered is one of very few "crafting" games that I was able to just pick-up and play.  The crafting system is very well covered in the game without any tutorials, although I believe there was a tutorial option that I played through.  Hovering you mouse above any item, even "grayed-out" uncraftable (based on current ability) items reveals what is required to craft the item.  Best of all, the game starts you off with enough items to get crafting some basics right away.  I won't give away any spoilers in my review as 1) it is fun to learn as you go along and 2) you will learn from your experience playing this game.  My very first playthrough lasted 2 hours and was made much better by the in-game "automation" feature you can use for your characters.  Automation makes them automatically do what they need to do (i.e. eat, sleep, drink) without you constantly watching over them.  While occaisionally harsh in terms of how it punishes you for bad decisions, Sheltered is nevertheless one of my favorite "apocalyptic survival management" games.  Recommended if you like challenging yourself occaisionally to see how long you can "make it" in a game situation.  I am pleasantly surprised by the quality and playability of this game.  Recommended.  4/5

I don't recommend the game. KOTOR II will waste your time. It's almost playable, but it never is enjoyable.
The story is worth reading about. It's a much more interesting story than KOTOR on paper while remaining true to the tone of Star Wars if moving uncomfortably distant from it. Your character is an acolyte to Revan during the Jedi Civil war and now cut off from the force by the Jedi council on Dantooine. You seek them out on planets, moons, and space stations, them diagnosing your wound, then fading into death or shame. It is the best Star Wars story never told, never told at the failure of a diceroll RPG to convey the subtle horror that is finally sharpened to pain on a razor's edge. Were it a film I'd watch.
As a game KOTOR II doesn't seem to know what it's doing. It provides a revamped workbench system that allows you to finetune your team's specs according to the circumstances in which you and your gang find yourself. If you engage with this system in any sincere way you will spend hours boosting numbers that have already enlarged with every level up. The levelling system and indeed the player design stage asks me to predict what skills I will need, so I ask myself such questions as: "will I meet a droid companion later on who removes the need to boost computer or repair skills?" or, "does this person seem like a swordfighter or a healer or a marksman?" and always "what does it really matter?" The answer to the last question is "not at all, Sam", since the game becomes oddly easy and favours enormously the use of Jedi party members quite early.
Unlocking doors is a matter of equipping the right stuff and waiting, a business that draws my mouse to the exit button. I don't see how this is true to Dungeons and Dragons, in which experience I suppose you might be able to imagine solutions to locked doors, using your dexterity or strength or intelligence. Attributes do not widen your scope of options, they increase the likelihood of the only option being succesful, so the difference between you and a solution is always the defecit of whatever skill score the obstacle requests. You do not have to think to beat this game. It feels enormously unclear what effect anything will have, while there are so many statistics I feel like I'm reading the raw code of the matrix. These integers mean, all said, not much.
Many weapon or damage types are not used or resisted by the enemies in the game. Heat armour, for example, is almost pointless as you're not likely to face a plasma grenade with enough constancy that you should change clothes on the suspicion of fire. Even if electrical weapons validated a rubber suit I don't feel like pausing and changing into it mid battle, all the time. I don't think are supposed to do this necessarily, it being possible to draw any enemy's fire by attacking it. If your Zabrak friend is wearing the blast-proof jacket, have him fight the flamethrower droid while you shoot sonic waves to throw off the sniper's aim. Such strategy is fun to enact. I would remove the character modification aspect so that an augmented sword-fighter does not cut balance in two. The strategy required should become more complex as the game progresses, not dissolved in an ether of force powers and flurry.
On the side there are bugs. Quests don't work sometimes, creating certain armours crashes the game, and always you feel the truth to be so true: the game isn't finished. The visuals are atrocious, the "planets" like abandoned shopping malls. I guess it's to be expected, since the game runs on an iPhone. Play it on an iPhone, if you're going to play it at all, because the furtiveness with which you scurry around on the train or the bus will match with your neurosis as you arrange points here and there, floating up ramps that lead somehow down.

One of my favorite games.
I have well over 200+ games played pre-steam+ followed the games development since late 2013.
If you are looking for a post-apocalyptic shooter with NO ZOMBIES- then this is the game for you.
[THE GOOD]
-Maps feel big and open-ended. (There are also some small maps). Lots of little paths to take in each map, lots of little places to find and explore.
-Sounds and Visuals
I love the weather effects in this game, very atmospheric and really helps to engulf the player in the world of survarium. Turn up the sound and play with headphones :).
The game is very rough, but at the same time the sounds and visuals in the game are incredibly tight. Every step, each bullet fired sounds amazing. Smoke, fog and particles in this game look fantastic.
-Lots of guns to play with and each gun plays very unique. No gun is really the same, some are similar but each has its own feel. Earning a new weapon feels satisfying and rewarding.
-The shooting machanics are great: Things like bullet drop and velocity are real, for instance you do less damage per bullet depending on the distance of your target. Shooting through wood or thin walls are also a factor, and I love this about the game. Each round fired from your weapon feels responsive, and landing those hits is very rewarding.
-Unique post-apocalypse atmosphere. A very dark and gloomy future where plants have overgrown the earth...never heard that one before. I like it :) feels almost like stalker or metro 2033 in way.
-Looking for artifacts and using them is fun and feels differnent them most games.
[The Bad]
-Slow development. Still waiting on lots of features promised a long time ago.
-Slow match-making due to small community (hope steam helps with this)
-Slow grind for end-game gear can take weeks if not months to earn all weapons/gear.
-No free-play(open world game-mode) yet :( (Planned for this year, heres hopeing :))
-Not very well optimized for systems yet, pushes your graphics card and CPU to its limits even on low/medium settings. High system requirements, the listed requirments appear to low.
Overall this game is very enjoyable and I reccomend you try it!

Prepare to be disappointed. This game is a thin layer of tasty whipped cream covering a big pile of steaming manure. The problem is that you get through the cream quite fast.
The cream:
Very pretty graphics. Models, textures, shaders are all done with great attention to detail and are a pleasure to look at.
Good sound design, immersive soundscape.
Different weather modes for maps. It's very interesting to play the same map during a sunny sunset and during heavy rain.
The gunplay is quite nice. Shooting feels punchy
The manure:
Edit: Ok, the point about being advertised as an MMO is no longer valid as the description was changed and is now clear that it's a pvp.
It is NOT an MMO, and there are no survival elements. It's a very fast, run&gun, 8 vs 8 twich shooter played on very small maps.
Because of the size of the maps weapon range has been reduced greatly - assault rifles 60m, smg 40m, sniper rifles 100m.
Most games quickly degrade into spawn involuntary butt love (i can't say grape on steam). One team  camping just outside the other's team spawn and shooting everything that tries to go outside. This is caused by small sizes of maps, bad map design, and pretty bad match making system.
It's not pay to win (yet, there is a p2w feature creep though), but it's pay not to grind endlessly. The dev's argument against p2w is that every premium weapon can be dropped after a match. In fact you have better chance to win lottery than dropping any premium weapon apart from socom.
Undelivered promises. The game is basically built on them. Weapon customization? It's being made for a year now, and all Vostok Games can show for it is a video of a graphic designer with an exploded view of a gun. Free roam mode? All you will see is some concept art.
Arrogance of the community manager. From consistently avoiding answering questions about any burning issues, to straight up lies about servers, and inability to admit mistakes (quote from him: we can't admit mistake if we planned it) - he doesn't know the difference betwee making a mistake and doing something by mistake.
Insanely overpriced microtransactions. I can only assume that the developers are baffled by the phenomenon of people wanting to spend real money for in-game items and can't figure out how to do the microtransactions right. The cosmetics (camos, decals) are both ugly and expensive, the premium guns have ugly textures slapped on and cost up to 50$. Instead of lots of cheap items there are very few expensive ones.
All in all, come back in a year, and see if there was any improvement. I want to think that VG will be able to pull this game up from it's current state, but I don't quite believe they can do it.

First and foremost, I got this game for like 3,74€ or whatever, and for that price it's right on the mark. The normal price of 15€, however, is way, way out there for a product like this. That's why the thumb down.
The female voice in the opening sequence is talking about how this is "the most advanced tactical simulator which revolutionised the world of urban combat and is used throughout the world for training puposes in various military forces" etc. Well that's just utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, like claiming Paranormal Activity is actually composed of real life footage. I would describe this piece of software as a "silly little game", rather than a tactical simulator, and if this is "most advanced" I really wouldn't want to see what the less advanced versions look like.
Basically you have a team of four dudes (why is it always four? the SAS apparently assaulted the Iranian Embassy in London with some 30 soldiers, against six terrorists. The Russian military assaulted the Moscow theatre in 2002 with some 200 men if I remember correctly...), who you will use to clear rooms of enemies in scenarios which last about 2-15min of real time, and some 7-40 seconds of game time (talk about blitzkrieg! :D) There aren't any terribly complicated tactics or techniques involved, you can tell your men to walk from waypoint to waypoint, stay still, or throw a flashbang or a granade. Firing at enemies is automatic. You give commands to your men simultaneously while the game is paused, and then press OK and the gametime advances by some 5 seconds or so, during which you have no control over what happens. After the 5 secs it's another order-giving turn in pausemode, and so on. There is no command to wait for two seconds and go, which means that when you're about to assault a room you either throw in a flashbang first and wait until the next turn to go in, by which time the effect of the band has already worn away. Or, you can charge in right away with another soldier while another man is deploying the bang, which means that the guy assaulting the room has already dispatched all the baddies and maybe taken some damage himself by the time the flashbang goes off.
Completing the missions give you experience which improves your soldiers, and money which you can use to buy new gear and weapons. Some of the gear is strictly cosmetic, and has no impact on gameplay, such as sunglasses or uniforms in funny camos. For some reason one of the bulletproof vests is by far the best, with a +145 bonus to health (or something like that), while all the others have something like +20 bonus to health. And the superarmour is not even the most expensive one, and it has no drawbacks... :D and yeah, in the true videogame fashion, the soldiers have a simple numerical value of health, which means that it doesn't matter how much lead they eat during a mission, if they finish with at least 1 health left they are ok in the next mission. Incredibly advanced and realistic.
So yeah, all in all, it's a casual little tactics game, with hardly any real substance and very little flavour or immersion. Maybe the devs made the opening video first, and actually intended to make a realistic tactics simulator, but once they had the graphics somewhat ready they just thought "f*ck it, anyone fancy a pint? Just wrap it up and publish it on Steam." I'm glad I only paid that four Euros for it.

Apotheon is one of my favorite platformers, period.
The music and art are absolutely SUPURB. I highly recommend playing this game with good headphones, because it's worth fully sinking into. It's gorgeous, thematic, with great voice acting and a pretty good, fitting story (if you've played God of War, it will feel really familiar).
There is a wide variety of weapons, and they are all interesting in their own right. Because of the way weapons degrade in the game, I ended up trying all of them at least once, out of curiosity or necessity. The combat using said weapons is incredibly satisfying; the sound effects and the tight hitboxes really drove every hit home. Some parts of the game were definitely more challenging than others, and it never felt frustrating.
My only problems with this game have to do with the inventory management/controls, and slight bugginess. You can hold a very large number of weapons at a time, and it can be really tedious to equip the one you are looking for. You have to have the right type equipped (melee, ranged, tools, or support) and then scroll with the scroll wheel until you reach the right one. You can't really find what you want unless you take your eyes off of the action, which I didn't like at all. Also, the wide variety of weapons and potions in the game can feel a bit excessive at times. I used many of the weapons (and enjoyed the variety from a historical/mythological standpoint), but I rarely touched any support potions other than the healing one, which has its own hotkey.
There are also a few bugs in the game, but none of them were totally game-breaking. They would either cause crashes or a need to restart (due to an invisible wall or something), but the game would continue from a very recent checkpoint.
Apotheon is not perfect, but it is also really, really good. I wholeheartedly recommend it. After seeing this game, I couldn't stop thinking "why didn't I think of this?! It's such a good idea for a game," and it's well-implimented. I doubt it will happen, but I would love to see more; with Egyptian hierogliphic art!

I decided to rewrite my original review from being an asinine review "too spoopy -1/10" to a serious review.
This game is actually well made. It's absolutely horrifying in singleplayer because you have to simply sit in an RV at night and listen for these fast approaching footsteps in the woods before this creature, the Rake, comes out of the woods and tries to kill you before running off once again.
Multiplayer isn't so bad though. Well, that actually depends on how you look at it. It's pretty spooky but running around with your friends shooting at the little naked white man is hilarious.
The game also isn't going for cheap horror. It is some hardcore psychological warfare at night in singleplayer but also has very basic jumpscares that aren't really jumpscares.
It's a good game.

The combat isn't lacking in any way for me. If you like games with a lot of mindgames and mixups, I highly recommend this to you. The only way this is lacking is the customization of your hero. You can modify their appearance by changing the color of their gear, adding patterns, etc. But the armor itself is tied to stats, so in some scenarios you have to choose between looking cool and having proper stats. People complain about the micro-transactions, but I don't see why this is a problem. They're just a side option if you have money and are willing to pay. You can accumulate steel just fine without the transactions, and the pacing of how fast you unlock stuff is actually very well done. When I bought this game, I played it for around 13 hours day one. Super good.

After a year and 130+ hours in-game, I can say I recommend Rainbow Six: Siege. After a rough start, it has come a LONG way. I began this game a year ago. This game they gave us was very different. When I saw what they were selling instead of the amazing tactical game they had demonstarted, I was very skeptical. I wasn't about to buy a game that was not advertised for $60. I thought I wasted $35 on this game that was going to die soon. I had at the time only played the game 8 hours in an entire month. Then I saw Ubisoft began updating the game with hopes of saving it. I came back to the game, and while it was not what I wanted, it was a massively improved game. The operators had been balanced, lighting was fixed, and new operators were being released. The game continues to deliver in every aspect that it did well on originally and further continues to improve its balancing aswell as releasing new operators. I can safely say that Rainbow Six: Siege is worth the purchase. However, try to buy it on a sale. The game is worth no more than $40.

One thing to keep in mind is that you have basically no control over anything, unlike Telltale's later games like Walking Dead and TWAU.  Every choice you make is either meaningless, or a filler answer until you reach the one you need.  But that is my only critisism of the game, and apart from that, I loved everything!
I would highly recommend this game for anybody who likes story-rich games, or just anybody who likes Back to the Future.  It's a lot of fun, a wonderful story, and an all round enjoyable game to play!  I really hope they make a second series at some point!

Physics are great and crashing is always fun but the major downside of this game is it's lack of edibility and the fact that the world edit tool makes it extremely hard to get that perfect smooth banked turn that you want or that perfect flat drag strip. Another huge downside of this game is the updates. They barely add anything content wise (such as new cars, new maps, new objects, etc.) the worst part is that they break almost every mod you had installed. The mod installing process is already annoying enough, instead of having a highly efficient and helpful steam workshop, they chose to put all the mods on their own website which you must then install yourself.
I'll have to give this game a 5/10. Coming from a person that really loves cars and creating their own things in games, this game just doesn't have the creative aspect that I'd like to see in it yet, it's more of a play what you can find if you can't mod. I'm going to try and keep this review as unbiased as I can for those who want an honest interpretation of the game.
Do not jump into this game thinking that what you see, is what you get. This game is in early alpha and features are being added all the time. What is meta gameplay now, will not be the same in a few weeks. Species will be added, maps will change, and each new feature added will bring with it a whole new level of difficulty. If hardcore survival is not your thing, I'd turn away now because this game is only going to get harder as time goes on. And frankly, that's not a bad thing.
But it is something you'll need to understand before buying this game. Something which, apparently, a lot of people did not consider before buying and reviewing. This game was never mean to be easy, and you'll need to keep an open mind about it as it develops further. Bleeding, starvation, broken bones, and limping are all perfect examples of this. Each of these features added a whole new level of difficulty to the game and because of it, people were forced to adapt to different playstyles to survive. My point is if you can't adapt, don't purchase the game right now.
Humans will be added in the future, and this open world game is only going to get bigger. Imagine the Skyrim map, Final Fantasy open exploration, and the hardcore survival of Day-Z all combined into one.

I played Amnesia, Outlast and Dead Space so i'm used to this kind of game. For this review I will give the pros et cons and compare Soma to these games.
Pros:
- The story is great, even if the robot-intelligence theme is used a lot these days, I think Frictional Games used it very well in a new philosophic perspective.
-The puzzles are nice... not too easy, not too hard, and you have a great feeling of accomplishment when you find out what to do and you can move on. I didn't have to look online to find out what to do.
- Nice details in the informative aspects of the game (the pictures, notes and recording you find). It helps to create a good atmosphere and immersion.
- The narration is excellent.
- The atmosphere is great.
- There are hard decisions to make and you have to think about it. I liked it.
- There are a lot of times in the game where I had the feeling of being lost and vulnerable, but I always find out naturally where to go and never got stuck. Consequently, I think the game is well done for that.
- The end is very good.
Cons:
- The length of the game. In my opinion, it is relatively ok for this type of game, in which there are stressfull moments and a deep story, but I understand it can be expensive at full price for a 11-13h game (I did it in 12.7 hours and I looked at everything possible). I will play it again someday and I will mod it of course.
- The graphic are mostly good, but It seems like they didn't put the same effort on everything. Some objects are very well defined and others not.
- The horror in the game is also mostly good, but it could have been better. It is not the main aspect of the game like it is for Amnesia. The story and atmosphere is way more important and it think it's ok like that.
- I don't know if it's my computer of something, but the game lagged sometimes when I was switching a zone to another.
Conclusion:
I would give 8.7/10 to Soma. It is a great game and I don't regret my buy at all. To compare it to Amnesia, Outlast and Dead Space, I would say that each game has his main aspect and it's a question of taste.
For a pure-horror game, Amnesia is still the best for me. The atmosphere and horror are so great, but the story is not very good.
Outlast is also pure-horror, with better graphic, but I prefer the style of Ammesia. Outlast horror is hardcore... mostly chase and non-stop stressfull moments. It can be annoying sometimes.
Dead Space is my least favorite of the 4 games. The gameplay is nice, the story is ok and the horror aspect is not strong compared to the others... and its EA...That's all I have to say.
Soma has by far the best story, narration and details in everythings. It has also the best atmosphere with Amnesia, depending on the kind you prefer. Even if it will not revolutionize the genre like Amnesia did, it is the best game of the 4 in 2016 for sure.

This game. Where do I even begin with this game? OK what I'm going to tell you first, you're here, you're obviously somewhat interested in this game,
Soma is sci-fi psychological horror-game developed and published by frictional games, the same studio which brought us Amnesia: the dark descent.
You're playing as Simon, a car crash survivor diagnosed with a brain damage which will kill you in a few months. The game begins with Simon waking up to go get a brain scan. Simon goes to the building where the doctor told him to go, meets up with the doctor and sits in the scanning chair. The scanner covers Simons eyes and a brief static let's him know that the scan is complete. However, when the scanner is lifted from Simons face he finds himself somewhere else Somewhere different...
+ The story is amazing, immersive and has you wanting more for each minute that passes by
+ The atmosphere is really what you would expect from a psychological horror game, it is spooky. If you've played Amnesia: the dark descent, that's it.
+ Great voice acting
+ Beautiful scenery
- some really slow parts where you basically just walk from point a to point b, they are really few though so they hardly drag the score
- Some crashes when entering new locations, basically fixed by rebooting the game and just continue from where it left of. Does ruin the mood, but nothing that makes the game not worth playing.
SOMA is what Amnesia: a machine for pigs should have been. An amazingly immersive experience filled with a thrilling story and characters that you actually feel for. The scenery is beautiful, the monsters are terrifying and most importantly, like i've said many times, the story is super well made.
SOMA gets a 9/10 from me, one of the greatest story driven horror games I have ever played. Buy this game.

First thing I noticed is that the game is almost pitch black. Player is given a lantern to help see but it runs out of fuel almost as soon as you light it regardless of how much oil it has. This leaves you with the option of fumbling in the darkness for the whole game or just adjusting the brightness in the options. You can make it so bright that you don't need the lantern at all, so I just did that.
It has the most illogical and convoluted puzzles of any game I've ever completed. It hides essential objects under other objects with no hint that they're there, indicating that you need to lift up and check under absolutely everything in the game (thousands of objects) or fail to progress.
At one point there's a
Exploration is the main element of the gameplay. Finding items to open doors and operate machinery. Necessary parts are strewn across an immense castle that encompasses the entire game. That works well in some games but not here because it's impossible to know what you actually need, leaving you to search huge locations accessible through multiple long load screens for a mystery item rather than just doing it in one specific place.
Textures repeat from the first area to the last - everything looks the same. Some games do this on purpose and execute it in a clever way but it's done in Amnesia because this is a cheaply made indie game. It looks♥♥♥♥♥♥
Simple things like functional controls are beyond it. There's a scene where the player
Like Skyrim, it's one button to grab an object and another to manipulate it. Unlike Skyrim, when you grab something heavy here
and try to move it, about 90% of the time it won't budge. If you stand at the side of a lever, hold it and press down, the lever will move up, so you have to be directly in front.
Health items are available but mostly pointless because health recovers automatically. The game doesn't limit savepoints so if you die you'll just restart outside the area you were in, which means you lose a few minutes' progress at most (I died a couple of times and lost about one minute's progress each time). One time I died it teleported me to the next area of the game, even though I hadn't successfully finished the previous area.
Sanity is a stat similar to health. The game explains that if your sanity drops too low, it will have significant negative consequences. I ignored this mechanic altogether and suffered no negative consequences. Lighting your lantern, candles and torches restore sanity; I didn't do any of those things and I was fine.
The game is most effective when it gives you an easy puzzle in a limited area and has a roaming monster in the same location. It makes the simple task intense because it feels like you know what to do but you could be ambushed at any time. This kind of thing was done much better in Outlast.

Just to clarify, my recommendation is very limited.  Though this game was worth getting, it left me feeling a little disappointed.
First of all, the story was good, the pacing was good, and I really liked the sanity aspect to this game (with Eternal Darkness being the only other game I'm aware of that has anything to do with sanity).  In terms of total amount of time feeling afraid and uneasy, I don't think there was another game that topped such a feeling for me.  Unlike the sequel (A Machine for Pigs), this game wasn't annoyingly dark or dark "because its scary".  The darkness served a purpose, and I didn't find myself struggling to see where to go the whole time.  I actually felt a real threat from the enemies in this game, too.
However, there are some things that either made the game less fun, less scary, or less interesting:
* There were way too many oil bottles and tinderboxes.  I probably could've beat the game on my first try not using any tinderboxes, after acquiring the oil lamp.
* Your character loses sanity so quickly and easily once in darkness.  Even when your sanity level is clean, he still gets pulsating vision and grinds his teeth when in darkness for a few seconds.
* Though the sanity effects available were nice, I'd like to have seen more hallucinations when going insane.
* I don't really see the point in the health meter.  You get way more health potions than you'll ever need, and most of the injuries you receive during the game are either fatal or would be easy to recover from in real life.
* The story ended somewhat abruptly.  It's not so much that the ending was bad, but anti-climactic.
* I overall felt the game was too easy.  Sure, some of the puzzles had enough of a challenge to them, but the constant darkness and slow running pace made figuring them out a lot more tedious than they needed to be.
* I suppose what would've made the game harder is if you didn't have the option to save wherever you wanted, or at the very least, if some of the enemies just never go away.  It's much more stressful when there's always something lurking and you don't know it is there.

Okay. So where to start. With one word; No.
Gameplay: 4/10
It plays like Catan. Its luck, hand management and risk mitigation. You can go entire games getting rubbish rolls unable to do anything, or if you figure out certain placements (especially on the Freeboard), win every time.
Trading is simplistic; theres no counter offers, theres no choosing which person you trade with. You throw out an offer (3:1 or w/e) and the first to click yes, gets it. Even if that person is someone you DONT want to trade with, as it may give the victory. The Timer forces you to play Blitz style, and if you have a good hand of cards and need a long turn (talking multiple trades, multiple roads, settlements, cities or Developments), you'll be♥♥♥♥♥♥out of luck with 90seconds. Especially when other players can wait out YOUR timer, during trades.
Graphics: 7/10
Nothing to scoff at, but simple enough, could do with more intuitive "obviousness", you can highlight a segment to build off board or you can highlight a space. The latter isn't made clearly possible until you spot it by chance.
Trade window takes up too much room on the board and hides things like unbuilt pieces, but you can click off and return to the trade if need be.
Sound: 4/10
Repetetive music. Mute it after an hour and stick your own on. Piece soundsare as you expect.
Cost: 5/10
The cost to buy the game out right WOULD be considered respectable, especially in comparison to the actual board game (£15 vs £50) IF it included all the necessities you get from the board game. But a lot of it is cut down and limited (see Gameplay;Trading).
Monetisation/DLC: 2/10
On the F2P side, its bad. Mostly because of one thing; ONE UNCHANGING BOARD.
Because theres one singular board, there IS a few preset ways to win everytime. Notably, sheep abuse. 3/5/8 + sheep port breaks the freeboard and it becomes a mad rush for a player to nab one this spot. Its bad because its sheep on 3/8 and grain on 5. This gives you almost everything you need to 2:1 trade at the port for ANYTHING and if anyone robs from you theyre liable to get nothing but worthless sheep. It removes any need to trade and opens up the ability to solo any build requirement, Developments, Roads, Settlements and cities become trifling. There are a few other similar spots, but this is the biggest offender especially when paired with any other 6/8. (6/stone/wood or 8/brick).
Thats just how its affected gameplay. Money wise on the Scrolls and cosmetics, scrolls are the only way for Freebies to play with friends Free Match is with random people only.
Totals: 4,7,4,5,2.
GRAND SCORE: 4.4 BELOW AVERAGE - Would Not Recommend.
How to Improve:
1 of these: Give Free 2 Play the option to play with friends who are also F2P or Give PAID players the option to invite Free Players (meaning only one person in a group has to pay) but maintain the Free limitations.
This for certain: Randomised Board.

Only 2 cameras on the entire map are actually useful, and they're in the most obvious locations (right next to the camper), the others are there for the lol's. The pig camera, if you can't guess, is the most useless of the lot. Last but not least, the Rake is like taking the fear factor of someone like Mike Tyson, and giving him the punching force of Miley Cyrus. He doesn't do enough damage to be even remotely scary.
How could the devs remedy this?
-More damage from the Rake.
-More diverse/interactive nights.
-More/freeplace camera locations.
-Differnt selections of maps.
-Multiple Rakes.
-Different creatures.
All in all, it's not a BAD game. It's good for one or two playthroughs where your adrenaline is elevated. After that it's only good to scare your friends when they might come by for a visit. Would I pay 5$ again? Probably not. Do I regret buying the game? No. 5/10

I was instantly drawn to this game,  more than a year before it released, when I saw its art style, and the combat looked right up my alley as well.  I can say with certainty that it was worth the wait.
Combat is timing-based, and depending on what weapon you're using timing will change, as will the damage per swing.  Some enemies may be fast enough that certain types of weapons won't land a hit, so you'd better be able to think on your feet.  As for weapons, there are a LOT of them, with decent variety in playstyle.  There is also a crafting system for health items, fire jars, temporary speed, and other such powerups, giving you good reason to seek out all the little pick-up-ables that can be found amoungst pots, jars, and crates.
The world is *large*, open, and PACKED with locked doors and little dungeons.  Definitely in the "Metroid-vania" genre.  As a completionist, I'm wondering how in the world I'll finish this game, with those tantalizing little "X-out-of-Z chests unlocked" indicators teasing me - so many locked doors to remember to open.
The hub world is interesting, having a group of "police" that you'll need to avoid whilst you lock-pick into merchant's houses in search of loot, or try to take that tempting little statue.  You'll want to run and hide until your alert meter cools off if you're seen being a trouble maker, lest you be first warned with a fine of 20 gold, then straight up executed if you're caught again not long after.
Boss fights are satisfying, music is fitting, story is fun.  Fair disclaimer though, I'm not finished yet, so I can't say if I like the ending.
If I have one complaint about the game itself, it might be that the voice acting is perhaps the only thing not fully fitting with the style (it's not BAD, it's just not as "Greek" feeling as the rest of the game is), as it might be more enjoyable to just have text bubbles and imagine the voices.  Still, the speaking is good for the lazy who prefer not to read.

By now it's likely that you've heard of Apotheon's art style. If not, it is the single most remarkable thing about this game. The whole thing is designed to look like an ancient Greek vase, and it is most effective. The primary colors are orange and black, to resemble the clay and dark ink of the artifacts, with blue on the protagonist's armor and red on those of the enemies, along with occasional changes in background color as is appropriate for each setting (Green for the forest, blue for the sea, and so on.) The art style and animation generate a terrific atmosphere, as well, ancient and mystical and desolate and hopeless. Aesthetically, Apotheon is an absolute masterpiece and deserves every mote of the attention it's gotten.
The story is also excellent. With the dawning of the Iron Age, the Gods of Olympus are none too pleased with the direction that humanity has taken, and like Zeus's Christian counterpart, have decided to punish mankind with extinction. Demeter makes it so that nothing will grow, Poseiden stirs up the seas, Apollo denies the Earth light, and Artemis keeps the forests wanting for game. Enter Nikandreos, the hero. He wakes as his home village, Dion, is under attack by raiders. After defending the Temple of Hera from the outsiders, the Queen of Olympus charges Nikandreos with overthrowing Olympus and saving mankind. I won't say any more. While this isn't a game with a great many twists and turns, the development of the story is something you should uncover for yourself. The key here is that the developers really know their stuff when it comes to the Hellenic gods. Each one you meet fits their classical characterization to a tee, and this creates a number of great scenarios, my personal favorite being the Artemis boss fight. None of the gods are simplified or lionized as they have been in a great many modern sources, (God of War or Disney's Hercules this is not) and many of them have aligned against Zeus' abandonment of humanity. In addition, there is a liberal scattering of passages from classical Greek sources throughout the game, each placed to give you a clear impression of the particular obstacle or characters you'll be facing shortly. All in all, while the story itself may not be groundbreaking, it's well researched, well written, and creative, and is a joy to watch unfold.
The gameplay is where Apotheon falls a little flat. Most of the time it's fine, your classic action platformer with just enough backtracking and exploration that it could be called a Metroidvania (Though that doesn't quite fit). There are two hubs, the Agora and the Acropolis, with a shop, and each is connected to three major levels each based around a particular god, as well as both having two optional gods each: Aphrodite and Dionysus in the Agora and Hermes and Hephaestus in the Acropolis. These aren't required for the core plot but they are fun, help flesh out the world and each bestows you with a useful upgrade.
The place where the game falls short is the combat, specifically. I enjoyed it, don't get me wrong, but it was simply clunkier than it had to be. Essentially, you have three attacks, an uppercut, an overhead strike, and a thrust, in addition to a shield bash. With the exception of the shield bash, which is done by pressing the middle mouse button with the shield up, the rest are far too difficult to pull off consistently or accurately. For example, the overhead attack is done by moving the mouse up and attacking, the uppercut involves moving it down, and the thrust is done by keeping it still. The problem is, the mouse is also used for aiming the attack and controlling the direction Nikandreos is looking. Couple that with highly mobile enemies, a problem that only worsens late in the game with the introduction of flying enemies, and this means that you'll have a hard time predicting exactly how your strike will come out or where it will go. The best thing to do is "trade blows", attack, shield, attack, shield, and so on and so forth. However, this can be problematic in the frequent case that you're facing more than one enemy. At that point, I just used the bow and cheesed everything.
This isn't fatal, and once you get the hang of it, can be pretty fun. It's just something that will catch you by surprise and can annoy you throughout the game. The other thing to know about the combat is the weapon system. This is not a negative point, but it will be a turn off for some players. Rather than having set weapons that you unlock and can use indefinitely, you have a wide selection of weapons that will break after some use. This has two effects on gameplay: First, you must be a generalist. You can't just stick with the Doru (Spear) or Xiphos (Sword), unless you want to put a great deal of effort into making sure you always have decent durability. Second, you have to learn to preserve the most powerful weapons for the situations where you need them, like you might save the BFG ammo in Doom rather than using it on an imp. As I said, it's not a mark against the game, it's just something not everyone will like.
Is Apotheon a masterpiece? Certainly as a work of art. As a game, no, there's plenty of room for improvement. However, while it isn't perfect, it's still a very good time. Hell, the aesthetic alone is worth any gamer's time. I recommend it without reservation. Check it out, I think you'll like it.

UPDATE 1:
Since I've gotten more experience, I feel I should write an update on how it'll be to play with more experienced players. First thing I want to address is how buggy the game is. They fixed most of the exploits, but a lot of bugs are still in the game, as well as wonky hitboxes. As a counselor, if you have even just another experienced counselor with you and you both have weapons, you can kite Jason almost indefinitely until he gives up or you run out of weapons. As Jason, this can be incredibly frustrating sometimes. However, the majority of the time in quick play this will not happen due to lag or simply not having enough coordination. Another aspect of play as and against Jason I should mention is the grab range. While it doesn't have much range on the side, it is incredibly long when extended forward. This means he could grab you 5 meters away, or he could miss you while you're right next to him. Rolling perks is slightly frustrating as well due to the glacial CP gain, and the odds of rolling a good perk. Another major problem with the game at the moment is the lack of English speaking players that largely populate the Australian servers. This might not be true for the American servers, but it is very prevalent in the AU servers. However, despite the frustrating buggy mechanics and lack of English speaking players, if you find a good group to play this game with it's still a lot of fun.
ORIGINAL REVIEW:
Despite being plagued by server issues during the launch period, it seems that the devs have finally fixed those issues. Finally, the core game can shine through without being brought down by those server issues. Playing as a counselor or Jason is lots of fun, just so long as you're playing with other somewhat competent counselors. People say that Jason is OP, which to some degree is correct, but he's meant to be an unstoppable killer. Additionally, juking IS possible, so if you're skilled enough you can juke around Jason and jump into a nearby house to regain your stamina and go for round 2 to buy your teammates more time. There are numerous ways to escape, and teamwork is needed, so a mic is strongly recommended.  Playing as Jason is just brilliant. Nothing can quite match the thrill of putting beartraps around a house and hearing the terrified person inside screaming through the voice chat. Now that the server issues have been fixed, I would recommend this game.

The servers I've played on were really laggy, despite having a few servers with a ping of 30-50. Progression as the herbavores is really easy, since you can benefit off of the environment.
Graphics: 6/10 Dinosaur models look pretty good, but the fog and uninspired landscapes dull the experience.
Sound: 7/10 The ambient noises are nice, and the calls of distant player controlled dinosaurs and approaching footsteps do a good job of helping you stay aware of your surroundings.
Gameplay: This is where it falls flat, there's still a lot to be done to make this game enjoyable. I hope they can find a balance between challenging gameplay and fun, but right now it's not there.

I'd say this game has earned a positive review, though an extremely tentative one.
It's fun and certainly forces you to make some tough choices, but the annoyances pile up quickly. It plays like the love child of The Sims, This war of mine and Fallout Shelter in terms of gameplay and it basically works fine. Keep your little people fed and send them into the wasteland for crap to make into a dining table.
This is where things start to fall apart.
The basic things, like wood, plastic and wool, are far too hard to find. I kept finding crap for upgrades I had absolutely no use for when all I wanted were some hinges to build a furnace. This is a particularly annoying problem right away, because once you've built a shower, toilet and sleeping bag, you're basically entirely out of room in your shelter and you'll have to build another room. If the gods have chosen not to grant you sand, limestone or just cement, you're gonna be stuck not building anything for quite a while.
In short, the drop rate for basic loot like nails or nylon needs to be raised and the rate for stuff that's only useful in upgrades or later contruction needs to be lowered a bit.
Furthermore, there is absolutely no point in talking to anyone. You can take stuff with you to trade, but your extremely limited inventory makes that a bit of a gamble. Forget about fighting anyone too, unless you have clearly superior gear. An enemy who gets the first hit is liable to take off half your health.
Again, it's generally fun, but there's a few aspects that take the fun out of the game very quickly.

It probably goes without saying that Amnesia: The Dark Descent is a good game. As others note, the sound design is fantastic and monsters are exquisitely monstrous. Alongside this, the castle setting goes a long way to creating this uncomfortable feeling of lurking inhumanity that was at the heart of many, if not all, European castles.
However, Amnesia does have its faults. Frictional doesn't always seem to know how to mete out its excellent sound design. The game is basically gushing with it to the point of what I found to be an unintended discomfort. I went from being tense at first due to the eerie soundscaping to being so accustomed to it that the groans and creaks were akin to forgettable muzak at a clothing store. Castle Brennenburg went from a truly unsettling place to a shop of spooks, where I was stopping by the creep stalls to figure out how to stir up the scares.
In other words, Frictional would have done better to hide the eerie sounds for when you started losing sanity, and created more moments where you could make mistakes in play. They actually do this for some of Daniel's mumbling to himself, should you find yourself in the dark and/or staring at monsters too much, but these aren't nearly as compelling as the cries and growls.
Alongside this, the castle is a wonderful setting, which much could have been done to capitalize on its creepiness, but instead it's relatively normal for much of the very beginning part and even towards the end of the first half, as you've only seen one particularly strange setpiece to make you go, "What the hell?" Instead, they opt for the general dimness that a castle without adequate staffing would probably appear to have. This overwhelming darkness then presses you into a game of scouring for fuel and tinderboxes simply to see well and not have Daniel going off his rocker from a fear of darkness which is never really developed.
After all, Daniel is afraid for reasons that he made himself forget, and despite the first note vaguely indicating what's pursuing him, that doesn't seem sufficient to explain his getting anxious in any dimly lit place. So how could a castle be made creepy even when well lit? Think of any classic haunted castle setups. Painted portraits' eyes following you, distant silhouettes that can be mistaken for ghosts, suits of armor rattling here and there as if someone's within, so on and so forth. Overdone, but done with the right touch, and you could do a little more than the creaks and groans of Amnesia.
Despite all these critiques, there's no denying that Amnesia is as already mentioned, a good, solid game, and many of the negatives I mention here are likely only there to the extent that they are due to Frictional's difficulties during the time they were developing this title. I imagine they wanted more peculiar and striking scary moments, but had to make do, and they certainly did in a lovely way with this work.

Disclaimer: I'm writing this review because the Uplay servers went down for most of the day and, after the community managers reported the servers were back up, are still down specifically for For Honor while other Ubi games are back up. I'm reasonably well tilted at the moment (45 degrees?), as is the community that was planning some tournaments this weekend.
Actual Review: Probably the most fun melee combat game I've played, ruined by terrible UI and ugly networking.
+Combat is third-person like a Dark Souls game but has inputs, combos, throws, counters, and feinting mindgames like a AAA fighter; characters are reasonably balanced at low-mid tiers
+Amazing animation and artwork
+Character customization options are robust and there's a large variety of options to make yourself look badass
+Various practice modes and different AI levels so you can learn against bots or set up custom games with friends
+A few different game modes ranging from 1v1 duels with strict rules to more open escalating battlefields with ability level-ups similar to MOBA games
+Singleplayer mode (the voice acting, dialogue, and story randomly range from bad to average, and the collectibles are more annoying than fun - BUT it does have a singleplayer mode and it gives you reasonable rewards that carry over to multiplayer).
-Game requires an online connection so you can't play even the singleplayer campaign or practice modes if, say, the servers go down all day as they have been Feb 25/17
-Connectivity is♥♥♥♥♥ Easily 25% of games have some kind of interruption due to a laggy connection, someone leaving the match, random disconnects, and even basic stuff like the matchmaker trying to join you into a game that's already full
-Matchmaking is inconsistent, typically unbalanced, and unclear how it assigns teams; it queues you with the same players and teams after each match instead of balancing teams or rotating out your opponents
-There are several game modes, but a couple have a shared queue so you don't always know what mode you'll get until you're in the match; makes it a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to do daily quests ("Orders") which require X number of games/kills in a specific game type. You can specify a preference (not a guarantee), but see my comment about inconsistent matchmaking above.
-UI isn't optimized so it requires excessive menu diving to get to everything, menu buttons are just plain text, gear comparisons are annoying, and the stats screen is never accurate. During matchmaking, you can't do anything else but stare at loading screens while waiting for other players to join or choose their gear. In-game text chat only supports a couple lines of text and you can't access it from every screen, much like you can't get to the Escape menu in every screen.
-Party members are randomly removed from the party during the matchmaking process or just don't show up as online on Uplay. Often you quit as a party only to have the party be completely disbanded. This is on top of the connectivity issues outline above.
-You're still reading this? Okay: I could write a 5000 word essay on the networking and lag issues with the game, but others have done so on Reddit already if you want to check out the For Honor subreddit. Most notably, you'll see some characters teleporting around occasionally, and *very* frequently, you'll see someone guard your hit and take damage at the same time as your game and the opponent's game are not entirely in synch. Once or twice I have killed someone and had it register in the UI only to have it reversed an instant later. For reference, I have green NAT status (you're assigned a colour depending on your network accessibility - green good, red bad) and don't encounter this issue with other games. This game does not use dedicated servers (it uses a P2P system that's supposed to be better than regular P2P systems, see the Dev tech post on Reddit), so if you have a problem with that, 100% don't buy.
-The gear system can be considered Pay-To-Win for 4v4 game modes. The 1v1, and 2v2 duels only use gear for cosmetics and aren't affected by this, but all the 4v4 modes are (custom games can be configured to enable/disable gear bonuses). Players can purchase in-game currency for real money, and then purchase gear chests to randomly receive rewards in addition to those everyone randomly gets at the end of a match. You still must play a character to a certain level to unlock the best gear (maybe 10-20 hours worth in my experience), but then you can use real money to spam buy gear until you get what you want and upgrade it to max. The gear makes stat changes to your character that can make you significantly stronger than a default character. This would NOT be an issue if the matchmaker was better, but currently you can end up matched against players that can 1v4 your team if the gear balance is lopsided.
Background & Progress:
I've played this game in the tech alpha and two of the closed betas, the open beta, and live, and basically none of my gripes with the networking/UI have improved. Ubi has done a couple very minor patches since release (about 2 weeks ago) to address character issues and bugs from the open beta, but broke about as much as they fixed. Also, it's cross platform so *everyone* has to wait weeks for fixes while changes are tested and released in the XBone pipeline.
Community managers appear to be active on Reddit, Twitch, and Discord, so it *seems* like they care about the game to support it long term, but it’ll be difficult to maintain a community if players have to deal with terrible networking in-game and larger Uplay-wide outages like today.
Normally I don't care enough to write a review like this, but the actual GAME is really good. I just can't get to it as much as I want because of the Uplay cockblocks. I feel like the UI/social aspects could be overhauled pretty easily since it's so barebones (and it’s likely stayed that way as a low priority item to get the game to ship on time), but the networking is so sketchy and can’t possibly be a quick fix. Does the community (or you, possible purchaser) have enough tolerance to live with it?
I can't currently recommend this game at this price until at least a few of the issues are resolved.

Overall, this game is definately good, however some parts could use improvement. This review may be a bit lengthy, I try to address all aspects of the game.
First of all, aside from the rest of this review, I have noticed many complaints about the board being the same in free to play mode. This is quite obviously because most free to play users are new to Settlers of Catan. This free to play board is like the starters map in the real life verison of the game. It is specifically designed to balance the quantities of every resource. To people who are already good at Catan, it may seem trivial to win on that map. But if free to play users who had not played before were given random maps, they likely would get frusterated at the difficulty of the game. When you haven't played Catan before, it can be quite annoying to be trying to build a settlement when wheat is only available on 2, 12, 10, and 4. If your main complaint about the game is the non-changing board, just spend the small amount of money to unlock the base game.
Cost: 7/10. The free version of this game is certainly a plus. Being able to download the game and try it out at no cost definately made me more likely to play. After about 3 games, I determined it was worth it to purchase the base game, and I certainly intend to buy both expansions soon. Comparred to the real life board game, this version is significantly cheaper and more fun to play. Not only is it free to play at first, you are basically guaranteed to have opposing players. No need to schedule an afternoon to play the game with friends when I can get on my computer at any time and start a game. The only part I don't like is the shop's catan gold and scrolls mechanisms. The catan gold seems like a pointless addition just to get me to waste more money somehow. I'd prefer to be able to click on the expansion I want and just purchase it, not buy this catan gold first. The scrolls are nice that they are given free, but I definately do not recommend spending extra money on a limited time trial.
GUI and Graphics: 8/10. Coming from real life catan and the alternate
, the graphics took me a while to get used to. For the most part it was fairly intuitive, click the spot where you want to put the settlement (the double clicking thing is a bit weird), click the trading menu to trade, click to dice to roll them, etc. However, the development cards were a bit confusing. Since the resources are given automatically, and other buttons are always on screen, it was weird that development cards are treated as a 3D entity on the table. Also by default, you are zoomed in far enough that you can't even see them, I had to ask someone in chat. The graphics as a whole were good, not extremely impressive, but they do not distract from gameplay in any significant manner. One weird aspect of the board, however, is the fact that the ocean tiles are not the usual frame. I own the third edition catan art, so it is normal for me, however for players used to 4th and 5th edition art, it won't look correct. I personally am a fan of the individual tiles, as long as they are virtual and don't slide around. I also find it helpful that player's pieces are visible on the table, so I can see just how many roads each player has left when competing for longest road.
Trading: 5/10. The trading menu unfortunately does take a while to get used to. Now that I have played it enough, it begins to make sense, however some major aspects have been left out. For example, there is basically no way to do counter offers, or propose a trade when it is not your turn. The closest I could find to proposing a trade, is using chat or setting your own preffered trades. This displays a tiny icon next to your name, with what you are willing to give, or what you want. Unfortunately, I tend to forget to update this, so I may be asking for wheat well after I gain access to it. Also, I have not seen any other players make use of this feature (it is quite hidden and not useful), and no trades offered seem to be relevant to my preferences. I still continue to use it, but it seems basically useless. Another problem is the lack of counter offers. If someone proposes a trade, and I want say 1 more wood to go with it, I have to attempt to quickly type so in chat. Unfortunately, they usually end the trade and their turn before I can finish the message. This is a serious error in the diplomancy aspect of the game. One problem I have seen complaints about is the inability to direct your trade at one player. I do not think this is a problem, however, because you are not forced to accept the trade from a person if you don't want to. You propose, they accept, then you must accept once more the person you wish to trade with. So if player A, about to win the game, accepts your trade, and player B rejects it, the game does NOT force you to trade with player A. You can cancel the trade despite their willingness to accept.
Starting Games and Player Matching: 9/10. When you want to start a game, you can select the game, the varieties (Base, Harbormaster, etc.), elo, and karma. Your karma rating is affected by if you completely finish games, or leave early. If you select to only match with players of a simmilar karma rating, you won't get paired with those annoying players who start a game then disconnect immediately. Even without this setting, however, I have had very few problems with people ending games early. If they do so, the game provides another helpful feature where they will automatically be replaced by an AI. You can also match with players of a simmilar elo, which is basically an overall skill rating. So if you are annoyed with playing less skilled strategists, you can make the game a bit more challenging by playing those at your level.
Overall: 7.25/10. The overall game is very fun to play, and much better than real life catan. With the game set up for you, and resources automatically delivered, game speed is significantly increased, letting you spend hours mastering your catan strategy. With only some minor improvements, the game could become even better. But despite the few shortcomings, it is still certainly worth the money to unlock at least the base game. I would like to see future updates in the trading mechanism, and some changes to the shop, but the game is certainly still playable and fun.

This is a great Squad Tactics, turn based strategy. When you load up a game, it'll ask you to make a Squad. First you choose what kind of Special Forces you want your dudes to be: US Navy Seals, Germany's KSK, Canada’s JTF2, UK's SAS, and if you get the DLC, you can play as the Green Frozen Synapse guys too. After that, you choose each one of your 4 guys portrait/face, which is pretty limited, and their class, such as weapon expert, medic, direct assault, etc., which governs what kind of skills you can use in game and what kind of passives they have. You can name your squad too.
Once you're in the game, you have your squad move through the level eliminating terrorists. If you've ever played Frozen Synapse, moving around and killing is like that, but less in-depth. Click where you want to move, and where you want him to face when he get's there. You can click along his path and have him look in a different direction when he get's there. You can also have them throw grenades and other equipment if you've purchased them(more on this in a bit). You do this with all 4 squad members, click 'breach', which starts the turn, and they'll all do their orders immediately, shooting at enemies that enter their line of site. A 'turn' is pretty much 5 seconds, and clicking Breach will have them carry out orders and shoot people for 5 seconds before time stops and you can issue another set of orders Some have skills and passives, like the Weapons Expert has 'Suppressive Fire', which does what it says. The Intelligence class can see all around them, a 360° range of vision for a fairly short distance, about 5 feet. Normally, a soldier has  the standard 40°-45° cone line of sight in front of them(no distance restrictions), simulating a person's eyesight. The Intelligence class has this stanard 45° cone, plus a much smaller 360° view, which extends maybe 10-ish feet. This is great for when an enemy is in a place you didn't expect. Normally a soldier will turn around by himself and shoot back at an enemy that shot him, but that's a precious few seconds of getting wailed on. The 360° view let's the Intelligence class immediately start to turn around the second he enters his range. You'll still get hit since you'll still have to turn around, but the chance of dying has been drastically lowered.
After each mission you get money, experience, and a 1-4 Star rating depending on how well you did,  Experience will level up a soldier, and when he levels, you can put 5 points into one of their stats. Each class has some stats all on their own, like the Intelligence Class has a stat that increases his 360° view distance. All Classes have some similar stats though, like all have a 'Moving Speed(distance you can travel in one turn). 'Accuracy', 'Health', and 'Reaction', which is how long it takes for them to 'lock on' to the enemy and start shooting. All stats can be increased to 100, and each stat starts at around 45-55. The type of squad, such as US Seals/German KSK/UK SAS/etc, plays in here too. Each type has a beginning bonus to one of their stats. I believe either the US Rangers or Seals starts with their Accuracy at 75. Each squad type has a bonus, and that bonus can pretty much aid in your preferred play style.
As for money, You get a $200-ish bonus for completing a mission for the first time, and I think $200 per Star(rating), at least on normal difficulty(4 modes). There are other bonuses and penalties that reward/subtract too. Anyway, in the main menu there's a Marketplace, where you can buy new clothes, armor, helmets, weapons, all sorts of weapon attachments, and consumable items. Most of these items will offer some sort stat boost, like scopes increasing accuracy and armor(vests) increasing health. This isn't Door Kickers btw, where buying the gun once unlocks it for free use with everyone else. If you want your 4 squad members to wield that shiny rifle, then you'll need to buy that shiny rifle 4 times. I wasn't  mocking Door Kickers btw. I love that game too. If you're short on cash, and there's a particular level you like, you can simply do that level a few times to earn money. Just keep in mind that you'll only really earn money for the amount of stars you get on that run(4 max). So at most, on normal difficulty at least, you can only get $800 max, and you'll probably have some of that subtracted due to taking damage or taking too long. The prices are not ridiculous btw. They're not expensive, but you won't be buying everything in the first hour(or week).
There are a good number of missions to do, and lots of gear and weapons to get and play around with. I definitely recommend this game.

Preface:
I’ve played Catan on Android before and played the beta version of Catan Universe. After they’ve moved the client to Steam I signed up here to download.I’ve not played PlayCatan before that some are mentioning here, but from the screenshots I found, I believe this was some 90s version of the game.
The game:
If you are familiar with Catan, you’ll feel right at home. I like the visual style that is really similar to the latest edition of the board game. Free content is limited to the base game in multiplayer on a fixed map with 3 players. Also you can play the tutorials (these are quite good for beginners imho) and the Catan card game introduction. However that one doesn’t have tutorials yet, so you’ll need to check the card rules in the almanac and the game rules on the Catan website.
Free and paid content:
The game uses an in-game currency for purchases and has a secondary currency in so called scrolls. You can use these to temporary unlock expansions, so it’s basically a trial. You get some gold and scrolls for signing up and you get some scrolls for levelling up your character. You get experience for levels every game you play and also from the tutorials. You get another five scrolls at level five (you’ll reach that really quickly), so after you’ve used the 2 scrolls from registration, you can unlock other expansions for some more days.
The game and expansions are quite cheap compared to the board game. Depending on what you like, you can get bundles including the base game and the seafarers and cities and knights expansions for 12-15 dollars with some extras like experience boosters. This is much cheaper than a single board game expansion and with the online mode and coputer player support (after you’ve at least purchased the base game set) there’s always something to do.
There’s also some customization options available for the game (new models for settlements, roads etc.) and for the player avatar. Some of those are unlocked while levelling, others seem to be exclusive purchases.
Pros and cons:
It’s my favorite board game Catan and provides all important expansion sets and uses all original rules. I use a 3 year old Asus Laptop with an Nvidia graphics chip and it runs smoothly. I’ve had no crashes like some other users reported. I wish there was a tutorial for the card game as well. It seems interesting enough for two players. Payment is a bit clunky in steam, as I had to get money into the steam wallet first. The default timer in multiplayer is quite fast, however I’ll rather play two fast games than one slow one, so it’s fine with me. Newbies to Catan will need to play the tutorial to get into the game first though. Free content is very limited and there is no way to unlock actual game content by playing except temporary via scrolls. However as pricing is fair (although a bit clunky as mentioned above), I rather have this than some of the usual f2p grinding.
