A well-rounded game whose uniqueness runs much deeper than just its highly-stylized visuals. Apotheon's basic elements are shared with countless other games-- the platforming, combat, exploration, and quest-based advancement elements will feel immediately familiar to many gamers-- but its creators have clearly put a lot of time and love into building a novel experience on top of that common foundation. The game's numerous scenarios provide varied challenges that demand equally varied approaches; at numerous points, it's very clear that the game's designers and developers took the time to create something striking in terms of both visuals and gameplay, rather than falling back to what would have been the 'easy' and expected thing to do. All throughout the game, I continued to be surprised and pleased by the unexpected new mechanics introduced just to make a single boss-fight or puzzle or challenge really stand out and adhere to its deity's theme.
Apotheon's not flawless. At points, its physics-based combat system can get clumsy and repetitive and easily exploited, its take on the Greek pantheon is sometimes unsatisfying and shallow and burdened by modern stereotypes unreflective of the source material, and its equipment system sometimes feels designed to punish the player for using the equipment they want to use. However, the overall experience, mood, and visuals really do bring something unique and enjoyable to the table, and I feel I got more than fair value out of the time and money spent on this game.

The game also offers a plethora of melee and ranged weapons to use according to occation or to your liking.
Story wise
Level design is generally good and unique which helps to retain players' interest. On the other hand the total game length is rather short.
In addition, as in every platform game, there is some puzzle solving, alas not complex enough (or at all) in many cases.
As for the art style, a simple glimpse says it all. The use of ancient greek vase artwork for a 2D platform game is not only convinient for this genre but it bonds extremely well with both the theme, story and gameplay.
Overall its a very good 2D platformer and certainly its worth its price value, though it needs a little bit more features and content.

Telltale makes genre games, and this is one of those. I feel like it's solidly representative of pre-Walking Dead Telltale- kind of a mediocre-to-good game that never really impresses. It's a 5 episode series, about 10-12 hours in length. It's a point and click adventure game with some QTE-ish action sequences sprinkled around. It's never really challenging but sometimes interesting.
The plot's decent, typical hop-around-in-time BTTF faire, but they manage to make the gameplay pretty samey despite the time difference. The high point is probably the whole dystopian-future Citizen Brown plot, which is a pretty decent departure from the tone of the series. Maybe that's why it works.
The music is great, of course, it's the BTTF soundtrack, but it really starts to wear out its welcome the 20th time you hear the main theme or "back.. in.. time.." They managed to find a voice actor who can do a pretty passable Marty, even.
The game's loaded with fanservice, so I'd say that if you're a fan of BTTF it's easily worth a play, and that you might not enjoy it very much if you aren't. The gameplay isn't that great to carry interest beyond that.

The idea of remaking classic arcade games is somewhat of a niche these days. Dark Matter grabs this niche and propels us back to 1979 when Asteroids was released in arcades. The game is simple: each level takes place on one screen and our objective is to destroy everything that moves. Most of these are meteorites but later on enemy ships will appear, too.
We can use thrusters to move when the going gets rough; leaving the screen on one side makes our ship reappear on the opposite one. As we destroy objects our weapon receives upgrades; we can also collect multiplier pickups to increase our score. Reaching a new score milestone gives us extra lives and bombs; the latter can be used to eliminate everything in a large radius once and for all.
The game has simplistic graphics (a low resolution is applied) we cannot change as well as built-in achievements (i.e. these are not logged separately on our Steam profile). A campaign mode offers dozens of missions that increase the difficulty level gradually but I find this and the related "story" in the form of a text unnecessary - this game is all about surviving as long as possible and its challenge mode gives us the opportunity. The accompanying music throughout, too, serves its purpose.
This game is a throw-back to the golden era of arcade games. I would love to play another version of this with revamped, HD graphics and some more achievements; in the meantime, this version will do.

This game is my favorite post-apocalypse survival / hoarding simulator to date! Mirroring games such as This War of Mine and even in the more distant past, the Oregon Trail series, Sheltered puts you in the position of moving your family into an underground bunker to toil through the days following the nuclear apocalypse. Even though in Early Access, this game offers a lot already and should hopefully prove to be even more promising as time goes on. Here's a quick run-down:
PROS
- A whole slew of resources to gather and use toward crafting and survival
- Many customization options, including expanding your shelter, placing many different craft stations, all the way down to painting the walls and adding some decor
- Frequent recruitment opportunities to turn your small family group into a formidable fighting force
- A few quests to enjoy - mainly gathering resources for desperate people or fighting off thugs who try to extort from you
- A fairly large map to explore
- An automation feature that lets your shelter dwellers go about their business and take care of their needs so you can pay attention to more important things
- Many aspects of your shelter to micromanage and tweak (great for the business/management gamers)
- A leveling system for your characters to increase their stats and become more invaluable to you
- Decent, turn-based fighting scenarios when your party encounters hostiles
- Active devs and frequent updates
- OK price at $15.00
CONS
- Some bugs, none of which are game breaking from what I've encountered, though annoying
- Not enough trading opportunities
- Questionable continuity or end game (as of now, you play forever without a conclusion)
- The camper van, which you painstakingly have to find parts for to make functional, will disappoint you by how inefficient it is to take on supply runs (guzzles more gas than it's worth)
- The stats "Trauma" and "Stress" are thus far vague and hard to understand what triggers them and how to reduce these negative stats
- Somehow, everyone knows how to fix and build anything in your shelter, even the kids. Negative points on realism (but how great would it be if we were all that mechanical - we'd all get some serious s**t done in our lives)
- Things in your shelter need fixed all the time - perhaps way more often than they should. This should be nerfed a little so it isn't a constant chore
SUGGESTIONS
- Add more quests or a main campaign storyline to make the game more compelling
- Have the camper van not chug so much gas to make it worth fixing
- Trade stations or more trading caravans coming to visit your shelter
- Shelter defense: How about having your group fend off occasional raids or adding in traps to keep your bunker safe?
- Additional maps
- More items to craft and even greater customization
- Automated shelter doors, so you don't have to always let your group members in manually
- Include bios, a backstory, and greater stats customization of characters
Thus far, the game has been strangely addictive and I look forward to more additions and polishing from the devs at Unicube and Team 17
Grade: 8/10

ENGLISH REVIEW
[>[>[> I no longer recommend this game, but cannot paste this here nor can I change the rating to negative due to how Steam reviews work. Please check the comments section of this review for more info about this. <]<]<] Original review follows below:
Survarium is an ongoing project that is still officially in beta (albeit in the international open beta stage now), growing since the start of development in 2012. Recently, groups of scammers have appeared in the media who have insolently tried to use the renown of the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series to get some quick money by impersonating the old developers, but don’t worry – the studio behind Survarium (that is Vostok Games) is genuine. It is based in Kiev, Ukraine and it really was formed by some of the former employees of GSC Game World. Their aim is to create an online spiritual successor to the Stalker games, but one that has its own character and avoids the copyright infringement problems of that trilogy.
As for the game itself, it is a first-person shooter which currently has only one game type called “Teamplay” – though there is some variety in terms of objectives, as Teamplay is divided up into three separate modes: the first revolves around competing against an opposing team in capturing batteries and carrying them to your team’s base; in the second one you have to vie for control over strategic points on the battlefield; as well as the third and last mode, which is your typical team deathmatch. Teams are made up of eight people each, totalling up to sixteen players per match. The gunplay is slower and thus feels slightly more realistic than the average shooter, whilst the gorgeous maps of reasonable size make for engaging battles, during which the authentic firearm sounds go splendidly well with the immersive ambient soundtrack.
Generally, the game has evolved quite a bit through gradual little steps – it now has four distinct factions, personalised loadouts, clans and squads, side missions to complete during PvP matches, plenty of varied weapons and equipment to choose from, different ammunition types, decals and a choice of materials to customise your outfit with, artefacts to collect in-game that give you temporary bonuses, a rudimentary skill point system for your character, etc. It has also become a much more stable game than it used to be, with less glitches and crashes. However, the main feature that everyone is waiting for is the “Freeplay” game mode, which will bring larger open world maps that will provide an environment for session-based nonlinear survival gameplay (à la Stalker or DayZ).
At this moment in time, Survarium has few features on offer that would separate it from other F2P competitive shooters. It resembles S.T.A.L.K.E.R. aesthetically since it is post-apocalyptic fiction and most of the game’s maps have an Eastern Bloc feel to them, but the gameplay is less interesting and doesn’t have much in common with the beloved Slavic classics that we all know. Unfortunately, the creators at Vostok have stumbled a few times too by making numerous wrong decisions, such as dividing the game’s growing international community (along with all the clans and friendships formed within) into three regional servers or by almost continuously marginalising the non-European segments of their fanbase. Nevertheless, the game in its current state is at a decent level of quality, but with Freeplay due later this year along with the implementation of many other promised features to come… let’s just say that the best is yet to come.

UWAGA: Mam mało godzin nabitych w tej grze, bo gram w nią od 2014 roku, czyli zanim została wydana wersja na platformie Steam.
Survarium to trwający projekt, który jest wciąż w becie (aczkolwiek już w etapie światowej „bety otwartej”), rosnący od rozpoczęcia przedsięwzięcia w 2012 roku. Niedawno w mediach pojawiły się grona oszustów, którzy bezczelnie próbowali użyć sławy S.T.A.L.K.E.R.a, aby szybko zarobić trochę pieniędzy poprzez podszywanie się pod znanych producentów, ale bez obaw – studio, które stoi za Survarium (tj. Vostok Games) jest szczere. Mieści się ono w Kijowie, na Ukrainie i naprawdę zostało założone przez część byłych pracowników z GSC Game World. Ich celem jest stworzenie gry sieciowej, która ma być duchowym spadkobiercą Stalkera, tworząc przy tym własną tożsamość, unikając problemy z naruszeniem praw autorskich tamtej trylogii.
Jeśli chodzi o samą grę, jest to FPS, który obecnie ma tylko jeden rodzaj gry o nazwie „Gra Zespołowa” – tym niemniej istnieje kilka odmian pod względem celów, gdyż Gra Zespołowa podzielona jest na trzy odrębne tryby: pierwszy polega na konkurowaniu z wrogą drużyną o to, kto zbierze najwięcej baterii i doniesie je do własnej bazy; w drugim walczymy o kontrolowanie punktów strategicznych na polu bitwy; oraz trzeci, który jest typowym „team deathmatch”. Poszczególne zespoły składają się z ośmiu ludzi, co w sumie wynosi szesnastu graczy na mecz. Sama rozgrywka toczy się wolniej, niż w przeciętnej strzelance, dzięki czemu wydaje się bardziej realistyczna, podczas gdy przepiękne mapy, zresztą o rozsądnym rozmiarze, pozwalają na zajmujące potyczki, w których autentyczne brzmienie broni palnej pasuje świetnie do wciągającej ambientowej ścieżki dźwiękowej.
Z upływem czasu gra zmieniła się znacznie, choć działo się to stopniowo. Ma ona teraz cztery frakcje, spersonalizowane „loadouty”, klany i brygady, poboczne zadania do wykonania podczas meczów PvP, mnóstwo rozmaitej broni i ekwipunku do wyboru, odmienne rodzaje amunicji, dostosowanie wyposażenia poprzez naszywki i wybór tkaniny, artefakty z tymczasowymi bonusami do zebrania podczas rozgrywki, rudymentarny układ punktów umiejętności dla postaci, itd. Gra stała się również dużo bardziej stabilna, niż niegdyś była; z mniejszą ilością „glitchów” i „crashów”. Jednak główna rzecz, na którą wszyscy czekają, to tzw. „Swobodna Gra”, która udostępnić ma nam większe mapy typu otwarty świat, gdzie toczyć się będzie prawdziwa walka o przetrwanie na podstawie nieliniowej rozgrywki (jak w Stalkerze albo DayZ).
W tej chwili Survarium nie posiada zbyt wielu cech, które odróżniłyby grę od innych konkurencyjnych strzelanek w rodzaju „free-to-play”. Estetyka przypomina tu gry z serii S.T.A.L.K.E.R., ponieważ uniwersum Survarium także przynależy do gatunku fantastyki postapokaliptycznej i większość z map w grze ma atmosferę powiązaną z blokiem wschodnim, lecz sama rozgrywka jest mniej interesująca i nie ma wiele wspólnego ze słowiańskimi klasykami, które wszyscy znamy i kochamy. Niestety sami twórcy z Vostok potknęli się już kilka razy, podejmując nieprawidłowe decyzje, chociażby dzieląc międzynarodową społeczność (łącznie ze wszystkim klanami i przyjaźniami, które w niej powstały) na trzy serwery regionalne, czy też wielokrotnie marginalizując swoich fanów spoza Europy. Niemniej jednak, produkt w obecnym kształcie jest na przyzwoitym poziomie, ale biorąc pod uwagę, że tryb „Swobodna Gra” jest przewidywany jeszcze w tym roku razem z wieloma innymi obiecanymi funkcjami… możemy powiedzieć, że to, co najlepsze jeszcze przed nami.

Thinking about getting The Guild 3 when you saw it being hyped for 2017? Try The Guild 2 while you wait! This is one of those diamonds in the rough that has so much replayability you can't help but keep digging it back up out of your old games bin to give it another go.
I bought this game in the box long before it was ever on Steam and played it with the original (buggy) version for hours years and years ago. I've replayed it a few times and now I've gone ahead and bought it a second time on Steam as a way to support the Devs and easy access to the beta patch (4.211) that fixes so many of the issues I found with the game years ago.
The graphics are dated, the AI is wonky at times, and the voices of the NPCs can sometimes be a little silly but that's part of the fun of it. When you forgive those minor details and really dig into it, you will find it's actually quite a complex game that not only offers you the freedom to play however you want on a medieval map of your choice, but requires you to strategize, think and plan ahead for the success of your dynasty. You can start out as a lowly crofter and work your way up in titles and politics until you become a highly respected member of the city, the mayor or beyond to nobility. Or maybe you'd rather go a more nefarious route as a rogue? A devout scholarly clergyman? Whatever you choose, you'll find your goal: Outsmart the other dynasties in various ways to overthrow their businesses, their corrupt members, and trade monopolies. How you choose to do that is up to you ... Destroy their founders, run them out of town, run them out of business, or marry their only daughter to worm your way into their family and take over! It's all up to you how you decide to become a medieval legend!
I just adore this game and am happy to finally have it on Steam to keep me occupied while waiting for them to finish up The Guild 3 which is going to do everything The Guild 2 does but better and look amazing too!

Scary survival adventure game. Less is sometimes more, and a glimpse of a monster, or just the knowledge that one may be near, trumps a horde of ghouls chasing, as far as being scary. I was pleasantly surprised that there were no areas where sneaking around a monster would feel frustrating or bothersome, like the wolves in Penumbra: Overture. Hiding from a monster once is often enough, and it will shuffle off, possibly not seen again. I think I got past at least one possible encounter without ever coming across the monster, but that doesn't mean it was any less scary. Once again, our mind can conjure scarier things than what our eyes can show us.
Unlike Penumbra, you can save your game on exit, should you ever feel like it's being too intense, and if you happen to die a save point is always at hand. Combined with low difficulty with avoiding monsters, the game seems to agree with me that the repetition can be the biggest fear killer.
Besides the scary bits, Amnesia is first-person adventure game with pretty straightforward puzzles, an excellent atmosphere and sufficiently mysterious story being told through journals and returning memories.
The game turned 7 years old last month but it aged very well, and I can recommend it, as someone playing it for the first time. (And yea, 2010-2017 is nowhere as big jump as '03-'10, much less '96-'03)

This game is just fantastic.  It's simple, accessible, straightforward, and it will scare you- not just cheap jump scares, though there are a few, they will usually be followed by a genuine fear and panic as you seek to escape, outwit or hide from the thing that scared you.  I've heard complaints that there isn't a lot of replay value, but I argue that it's worth going through a few times.  But it does reach the point after your fourth or fifth playthrough that you begin to have memorized where the scary parts will be, where the necessary objects to proceed are hidden, and how best to avoid danger.  After a few playthroughs it becomes fairly easy to never find yourself in danger once you really have a feel for the AI and when and where danger will strike.
All that being said, the first playthrough of this game will be unforgettable for you, and the second and third times around will lead you to find things you missed before, and the included DLC, Justine, is equally thrilling.  If you are a fan of horror games and have not played this game, you need to.  If you're not a fan of horror games, you should play this game anyway.  The fact that this game was crafted by a small team yet attains AAA quality (or better), delivering on an unforgettable and thrilling experience, makes it worth every nickle.  Play this game.

The concept behind the story amazes me. It brings forth so many moral questions and interesting sides of the shere concept of morality, that it really makes you think. The horror factor of the game was completely ignored by me as I soaked in every piece of information I could find. If any monsters hindered me of getting information, I will be sad.
The transisions in the story are made superbly well, and the discovery of how real everything is, is the most fun thing about the game.
If you like stupid monsters that don't see you if you stick a chair in their face, and like the middle age and a madman on the quest of vengeance, go play amnesia.

If you know what a runner is you're halfway there, if not, I'll explain. A runner is, simply, about moving as long as possible through an obstacle course. The game moves you forward and it is up to you to simply jump to avoid obstacles or traps that will end your run. That's really it.
So with several modes and single screen two player, Canabalt is about as straightforward as it gets. As you progress things move faster, but this can be helped a little by allowing your character to collide with occasional chairs or crates sprinkled in your path.
This is a strictly no-frills game that does what it sets out to do.

You are a raider! Legendary!

N.B. my recommendation for this game depends entirely on the the fact that I picked it up for 4$. If I had paid full price for this game, I would probably feel a little more lukewarm about this. Now that that's out of the way...
This game really shines in its mechanics. There is a strong incentive to be careful, plan ahead, and make the right choices in terms of tactics and equipment. Moreover, there are multiple paths to success, and the variety of maps makes it difficult to confine yourself to a single strategy.
As compared to other turn-based tactical games (I'm thinking X-Com: EU in particular), the action plays out in a very satisfying way. Simultaneous movement of your troops and enemies adds a lot of realism to the game. The ability to choose firing angles along your path, rather than picking targets with hit percentages, really gives you the sense that you're in control, not the RNG. The cover system is excellent, with flanking angles being the default rather than an option. Stealth is a viable option with suppressors and a welcome addition to the game.
Unfortunately, this game does have some issues. Most glaring, and something that puts a bit of a damper on the strength of the gameplay, is that the AI is
bad at adapting to you. I've often seen the AI deliberately take a flanked position en lieu of something which offered full protection. Higher difficulties do not seem to increase intelligence but buff enemies. Alert states seem a bit off, since enemies only really react to seeing you, instead of, say, being alerted when the person in front of them is dropped by a gun with a silencer on it.
The most glaring flaw of this game is customization and the menu system. For a game whose selling point is massive customization, the system feels far more shallow once you actually delve into it. There are clear winners in attachments and upgrades, so you end up sticking to those when you can afford them. The menu system for upgrades is by far the worst feature of this game. Having to unequip each upgrade and then confirm the unequip so that you can switch weapons and put those upgrades back on is clunky and slow. Doing it once is bad, doing it for each of your four soldiers (and then back again after a mission) is torturous. In addition, the cosmetic features of your soldiers reduce to face gear and camo patterns. X-Com may not have the depth of this game's tactical play, but I felt way more invested in my individual troops in that game.
Aesthetically speaking, the game isn't much to look at. The graphics are sloppy, but since you're spending so much time zoomed out, it hardly matters. What you see conveys what you need to know, and that's fine. Less fine are the sounds. I get that they're sticking to realism, but none of the sound FX seem to have the necessary 'weight', if that makes sense.
TL;DR if this game is on sale and you need a quick fix for realistic tactical combat, this is a game for you. It's loads of fun for a little while and outshines its contemporaries in its mechanics. There are some areas that seriously require polishing, but if you can overlook those, you'll have a ball.

I bought this on Steam just so I could write a review of it, and maybe push id in the right direction with sales. I have actually played this game for hundreds of hours. I probably play it for at least 10-20 hours per year, for every year of my life.
Let me make one thing perfectly clear: nostalgia does not factor into this game's enjoyment. Doom still has a very active community, and new mods come out all the time. Thanks to Carmack's programming, Doom made modding a staple of PC gaming, and it hasn't gone away. Getting older has made me see more of Doom's flaws, but I don't really like it any less.
Doom is far from perfect. Unlike modern corridor shooters, which almost completely abandon the principles of level design, Doom is made or broken by its level design. There are a few different level designers that worked on Doom, and once you've played enough you can tell each of them just by playing their levels, even if you don't know their names. This means that level design is inconsistent, and therefore you're going to really like some levels and hate others. Most people who played Doom as a kid forgave the bad levels because, well, they were kids. If you're new to Doom, it's best to start at the beginning and play Episode 1 of Doom 1. This is widely regarded as one of the best, if not the best, set of levels for Doom, designed by John Romero. They're coherent, look nice (relatively speaking) and have well-placed secrets. Oddly enough, Doom 64 has one of the best sets of levels and plays like any of the other classic Doom games; google "Doom 64 Absolution" and you can easily find a total conversion mod that basically allows you to play Doom 64 on your computer once you have Doom. Thanks, Midway!
Virtually every level can be summed up by "find keys, throw switches, open doors." This sounds bad, but again, it can either be tedious or enjoyable depending on the level's design. I must stress that the player should use their automap (tab key) here. Doom's levels are not afraid of having many twisting paths, and it's quite easy to get lost without it. Helpfully, switches are usually recessed into the wall slightly, which clearly marks them on the automap. If levels truly become tedious, don't be afraid to skip them by typing "IDCLEVXX", where "XX" is a two-digit number following the convention of episode number, then level number. i.e. IDCLEV14 changes to episode 1, level 4. Each episode has 9 levels. I won't lie to you, there are a few quite truly bad levels in Doom, but fortunately id left this cheat code in. Be careful, it starts the level as if you'd started a new game, which means you lose all your weapons except the pistol, and start with 100 health and 0 armor. However, all Doom levels are designed with pistol start in mind, so you should be able to manage with enough skill. Doom should be enjoyed on a level-by-level basis; remember, there is almost nothing in the narrative that ties these levels together. If you really hate a level, you should get used to the idea of just skipping it.
The guns... well, everyone knows how the guns work, since they were the basis for almost every shooter arsenal until Unreal came out, notable exception being Rise of the Triad. They're quite well-balanced, actually, with the exception of the pistol, which becomes useless once you get the chaingun. The shotgun and chaingun are good at long range. The super shotgun is probably the best all-around weapon in the game, although it doesn't appear until Doom 2. The rocket launcher and plasma rifle are high-power weapons meant to break out against threatening hordes of monsters, and the BFG is there when nothing else substitutes.  Every one of them has a place in your arsenal, although depending on the levels you're playing, you may be using one a lot more than the other due to ammo distribution.
Doom is famously narrative-light. Romero makes a good effort to portray "realistic" military base locations, but the game's somewhat ridiculously deep story penned by Tom Hall was thrown out in short order - trust me, if you'd have read it, you would agree that it is quite over-the-top for a fledgling shooter made in 1993. The inconsistency between levels means that the ultimate choice to abandon any hope of telling a story beyond the intermission text screens was probably for the best. There are a few key events that happen in the plot, but they mostly happen at the end of or between episodes.
Overall, I highly recommend Doom for anyone who enjoys shooters but hasn't played Doom before. I also recommend Doom for anyone who is new to shooters, since it was also designed for that audience. If nothing else, it will give them an appreciation for where the genre has come from. This game still holds up very well today, especially with the active modding community.
HOWEVER: If you do buy this game, do NOT run it as-is from Steam's library. To run the game on modern systems, it comes packaged with DOSBox, which simulates the MS-DOS environment. The emulation can slow down your computer considerably and ironically make running the game more difficult. You should instead download and install one of the many "source ports," which are redesigns of the actual game engine to make it compatible with modern computers. ZDoom is a good and popular choice. Some "purists" swear by Chocolate Doom, which faithfully recreates the game, merely updating it to allow it to run on modern hardware without such niceties as OpenGL or mouselook.

“how do you Do It?”
Even the title of Nina Freeman, Emmett Butler, Decky Coss, and Joni Kittaka’s Global Game Jam project seems to reflect on the difficult relationship between American culture and sex. For a lot of people even referring to sex AS sex is seen as taboo and embarrassing, and so sex becomes “It”, so common as to singularly embody a pronoun in the right context.
Living in such a puritan society, we’re taught that sex is something dirty that you don’t talk about in normal conversation. It’s a natural, pervasive aspect of our lives, existing everywhere in media, and advertisements, and the pornography which takes up the entire other half of the internet not filled with cats, but nevertheless we’re taught to pretend it doesn’t exist.
It’s a society that shames women for being sexually active, and men compete for the number of people they’ve slept with. Sex is simultaneously considered evil and as a sort of prize to be sought after, creating an environment of unhealthy relationships and abuse if you should stray from the clear sexual path society has planned for you. And yet still, you don’t talk about “It”.
how do you Do It? is as pure a representation of our collective attitude toward sex as I’ve ever seen. It embodies our early innocence and curiosity toward intimacy, and also the anxiety associated with exploring it before even knowing exactly what sex is. Shoving two dolls together attempting to recreate the act of sex without being caught by a mother who had just stepped out, I found myself reliving the sort of terrified curiosity of being a child wondering what the “It” everyone seems to be talking and refusing to talk about is. I became jumpy and nervous about how I’d explain this should someone walk in on me playing it, even as I recognized how silly that was given the content of the game.
how do you Do It? is so completely innocent and “clean”, yet it managed to pull out the feelings of embarrassment and impurity that had been ingrained in me throughout my entire childhood, and even now can’t seem to entirely shake. It’s a simple game, maybe not even a very good one (though as polished as you would expect something built in three days), yet its existence is important.
In a medium that almost always shies away from sex or uses it for solely exploitative titillation, a game that actually has something to say about sex and how we view it deserves at least the minute of your time this takes to complete. You might even learn something.

Back to the Future: The Game consists of five episodes which are a sequel to the movie trilogy.
Doc Brown the inventor of the time machine has gone back to the '30s and he will die via mob justice. Now its up to you to change his fate, but as we learned from the movies, screwing with the past mucks up the future. The goal is to make sure the Hill Valley of 1986 is just how Marty left it.
Telltale fail miserably at making their own circa 1931 Hill Valley anything more than a studio lot full of comedy gangsters.
The gameplay is traditional adventure stuff. You walk around as Marty, talk to citizens and use items to solve puzzles. Unfortunately the puzzles are very easy, uninspired and boring.
The characters are just as bland, also most of the characters are cardboard nobodies. At least, in some cases, the acting is good. On the most basic level, the actors sound like the original characters.
The graphics do not render smoothly and the worst part is that these tech problems distract from the cinematic gameplay.
The sounds of the game are pretty decent. Music is mostly in the background and not too distracting and actual sound effects also take a backseat in favour of the voice acting. The voice acting is definitely the best part in the game.
If you are a big fan of the movies, then you could think about getting Back to the Fute: The Game. However, if the franchise does not really appeal to you, then this game may not be in your interest because the game practically relies on the player knowing the characters and the setting.

ENGLISH REVIEW
[>[>[> I no longer recommend this game, but cannot paste this here nor can I change the rating to negative due to how Steam reviews work. Please check the comments section of this review for more info about this. <]<]<] Original review follows below:
Survarium is an ongoing project that is still officially in beta (albeit in the international open beta stage now), growing since the start of development in 2012. Recently, groups of scammers have appeared in the media who have insolently tried to use the renown of the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series to get some quick money by impersonating the old developers, but don’t worry – the studio behind Survarium (that is Vostok Games) is genuine. It is based in Kiev, Ukraine and it really was formed by some of the former employees of GSC Game World. Their aim is to create an online spiritual successor to the Stalker games, but one that has its own character and avoids the copyright infringement problems of that trilogy.
As for the game itself, it is a first-person shooter which currently has only one game type called “Teamplay” – though there is some variety in terms of objectives, as Teamplay is divided up into three separate modes: the first revolves around competing against an opposing team in capturing batteries and carrying them to your team’s base; in the second one you have to vie for control over strategic points on the battlefield; as well as the third and last mode, which is your typical team deathmatch. Teams are made up of eight people each, totalling up to sixteen players per match. The gunplay is slower and thus feels slightly more realistic than the average shooter, whilst the gorgeous maps of reasonable size make for engaging battles, during which the authentic firearm sounds go splendidly well with the immersive ambient soundtrack.
Generally, the game has evolved quite a bit through gradual little steps – it now has four distinct factions, personalised loadouts, clans and squads, side missions to complete during PvP matches, plenty of varied weapons and equipment to choose from, different ammunition types, decals and a choice of materials to customise your outfit with, artefacts to collect in-game that give you temporary bonuses, a rudimentary skill point system for your character, etc. It has also become a much more stable game than it used to be, with less glitches and crashes. However, the main feature that everyone is waiting for is the “Freeplay” game mode, which will bring larger open world maps that will provide an environment for session-based nonlinear survival gameplay (à la Stalker or DayZ).
At this moment in time, Survarium has few features on offer that would separate it from other F2P competitive shooters. It resembles S.T.A.L.K.E.R. aesthetically since it is post-apocalyptic fiction and most of the game’s maps have an Eastern Bloc feel to them, but the gameplay is less interesting and doesn’t have much in common with the beloved Slavic classics that we all know. Unfortunately, the creators at Vostok have stumbled a few times too by making numerous wrong decisions, such as dividing the game’s growing international community (along with all the clans and friendships formed within) into three regional servers or by almost continuously marginalising the non-European segments of their fanbase. Nevertheless, the game in its current state is at a decent level of quality, but with Freeplay due later this year along with the implementation of many other promised features to come… let’s just say that the best is yet to come.

UWAGA: Mam mało godzin nabitych w tej grze, bo gram w nią od 2014 roku, czyli zanim została wydana wersja na platformie Steam.
Survarium to trwający projekt, który jest wciąż w becie (aczkolwiek już w etapie światowej „bety otwartej”), rosnący od rozpoczęcia przedsięwzięcia w 2012 roku. Niedawno w mediach pojawiły się grona oszustów, którzy bezczelnie próbowali użyć sławy S.T.A.L.K.E.R.a, aby szybko zarobić trochę pieniędzy poprzez podszywanie się pod znanych producentów, ale bez obaw – studio, które stoi za Survarium (tj. Vostok Games) jest szczere. Mieści się ono w Kijowie, na Ukrainie i naprawdę zostało założone przez część byłych pracowników z GSC Game World. Ich celem jest stworzenie gry sieciowej, która ma być duchowym spadkobiercą Stalkera, tworząc przy tym własną tożsamość, unikając problemy z naruszeniem praw autorskich tamtej trylogii.
Jeśli chodzi o samą grę, jest to FPS, który obecnie ma tylko jeden rodzaj gry o nazwie „Gra Zespołowa” – tym niemniej istnieje kilka odmian pod względem celów, gdyż Gra Zespołowa podzielona jest na trzy odrębne tryby: pierwszy polega na konkurowaniu z wrogą drużyną o to, kto zbierze najwięcej baterii i doniesie je do własnej bazy; w drugim walczymy o kontrolowanie punktów strategicznych na polu bitwy; oraz trzeci, który jest typowym „team deathmatch”. Poszczególne zespoły składają się z ośmiu ludzi, co w sumie wynosi szesnastu graczy na mecz. Sama rozgrywka toczy się wolniej, niż w przeciętnej strzelance, dzięki czemu wydaje się bardziej realistyczna, podczas gdy przepiękne mapy, zresztą o rozsądnym rozmiarze, pozwalają na zajmujące potyczki, w których autentyczne brzmienie broni palnej pasuje świetnie do wciągającej ambientowej ścieżki dźwiękowej.
Z upływem czasu gra zmieniła się znacznie, choć działo się to stopniowo. Ma ona teraz cztery frakcje, spersonalizowane „loadouty”, klany i brygady, poboczne zadania do wykonania podczas meczów PvP, mnóstwo rozmaitej broni i ekwipunku do wyboru, odmienne rodzaje amunicji, dostosowanie wyposażenia poprzez naszywki i wybór tkaniny, artefakty z tymczasowymi bonusami do zebrania podczas rozgrywki, rudymentarny układ punktów umiejętności dla postaci, itd. Gra stała się również dużo bardziej stabilna, niż niegdyś była; z mniejszą ilością „glitchów” i „crashów”. Jednak główna rzecz, na którą wszyscy czekają, to tzw. „Swobodna Gra”, która udostępnić ma nam większe mapy typu otwarty świat, gdzie toczyć się będzie prawdziwa walka o przetrwanie na podstawie nieliniowej rozgrywki (jak w Stalkerze albo DayZ).
W tej chwili Survarium nie posiada zbyt wielu cech, które odróżniłyby grę od innych konkurencyjnych strzelanek w rodzaju „free-to-play”. Estetyka przypomina tu gry z serii S.T.A.L.K.E.R., ponieważ uniwersum Survarium także przynależy do gatunku fantastyki postapokaliptycznej i większość z map w grze ma atmosferę powiązaną z blokiem wschodnim, lecz sama rozgrywka jest mniej interesująca i nie ma wiele wspólnego ze słowiańskimi klasykami, które wszyscy znamy i kochamy. Niestety sami twórcy z Vostok potknęli się już kilka razy, podejmując nieprawidłowe decyzje, chociażby dzieląc międzynarodową społeczność (łącznie ze wszystkim klanami i przyjaźniami, które w niej powstały) na trzy serwery regionalne, czy też wielokrotnie marginalizując swoich fanów spoza Europy. Niemniej jednak, produkt w obecnym kształcie jest na przyzwoitym poziomie, ale biorąc pod uwagę, że tryb „Swobodna Gra” jest przewidywany jeszcze w tym roku razem z wieloma innymi obiecanymi funkcjami… możemy powiedzieć, że to, co najlepsze jeszcze przed nami.

There are some other ships, too, but the focus is more on killing asteroids.  You can play Asteroids online in a web browser now, for free, so there's really no purpose to this game existing on Steam.
Graphics are slightly improved over 1979's Asteroids.   Not much, however, and it's the year 2016, so one would have thought 45 years of development in the silicon age should yield better improvements.   Not for these guys!  No widescreen support, no support for high res monitors (not even 1080p).
Failing both gameplay and technical categories, there's no way at all to recommend this game.   If you like the genre, try out Star Control 2, or any number of better alternatives.

This game is garbage. I'm sorry to say that, as I was really excited to see something like this come out. Here's the rundown;
The Good:
- The idea is there. The game is based on a fairly interesting idea, and the lore is scattered around in randome places for you to discover and connect yourself. This is a nice touch if you like stories.
The Not-So-Good:
- The optimization is absolutely horrid. The game runs at the same framerate for many, regardless of their settings, and turning off special options like ambient occlusion, which makes a world of difference in almost every other game, changes next to nothing performance wise. If the game looked like Crysis or Metro it could be forgiven. Unfortunately, it cannot.
- The graphics themselves are an actual issue here. This is a serious problem, as I have seen games with pretty horrible visuals by todays standards that are still, at the very least, charming. This game has doorways designed for hobbits inside some apartments, while the entryway was twice your size. Buildings often clip through eachother and block doorways of one another, with several instances of a door from one building being sealed with the next door neighbor's wall. Graphics aren't an issue for me, but when it looks like you spent a few hours just throwing things onto the map, it can really ruin the atmosphere.
- The community. I won't go as far as to say that everybody in this game is a KoS player, but... I've only ever run across KoS players. If you're looking to survive with some other players, look to DayZ or Rust. Much better shot of not being instantly shredded with those.
If you really must have the game, I would wait until it is on sale for at most 4.99. It isn't worth the current 9.99 price tag.
Rating:   3/10

Differen't, Interesting and Genuinly Funny
After building a reputation of scaring the Weebie Jeebies out of us It was time for Frictional Games to try something differen't and I'm happy to report that they pulled it off.  SOMA is an altogether Lighter offering (Think of this as the Star Trek 4 of Frictional Games) that concentrates on a Story which actually makes sense by the half way point, there is no "Open to Interpretation" element here which is a refreshing change.
Without giving too much away  The Earth has been wiped out and Humanity has been saved by having their minds uploaded to a "Matrix" style Database called The ARK.  Other People have had their minds placed inside various Machinary but have no idea that they are no longer Human, or refuse to accept the fact that they are now Robots, which results in some Intelligent and Witty writing and interactions very much like that of "Short Circuit" and "Marvin The Paranoid Android".
As per usual the Humor and exploration is suplimented by encounters with various "Insane" Robots that need to be avoided not fought with, but these come across as more adorable than scary (with the possible exception of the one in the diving suit right at the end).  The reason they are attacking is never quite explained but this is truly the only weak point in the Story.  I have to say this came across as very forced, and indeed, seemed to come out of a completely differen't game.  SOMA could easily have excluded these "Scary" elements without harming the Game or the Story and certainly not the progression or the way it it told.
The Scenary is by far the best realised of Frictional Games and has a Retro 1970's "Patch Work" look to it with Clunky Computer Keyboards, Wires and Huge Chunks of Circuit Board all over the place in the style of The Nostrmo and Battle Beyond The Stars.  There is even an adorable little "R2-D2" type companion that follows you around helping you get through rusted doors and tight places.
This is an Exellent Page Turner of a game that holds interest to the very end.  Very differen't from Amnesea and Penumbera but Huge Fun.

For a general-purpose car physics engine, this makes for some really fun and challenging rally racing. I'm in the far minority of reviews here, not recommending it for the crashes. I try not to crash in this, any more than I already crash in Dirt Rally. I really like the feel of the car handling, making allowances for a lack of specific focus on laser scanned tracks (Assetto Corsa) or rally-focused surface modeling. That said, I'll reiterate that this is still really fun and challenging rally racing, even for an engine not focused on it. Plus I love the idea of building a game/engine working from first principles and organically evolving real-world results and vehicle/environment interactions.
Remember what the devs said -- they're focused on the mechanics. The graphics at first don't look polished. But there's a level of fidelity in car body deformation on major or minor dings that I dig -- it's not the same canned response for damaged bodywork when I prang an obstacle. The angle of impact and shape of the colliding object all naturally shape your car's response and deformation. I mean duh, of course, it's what they designed it for. And they're rightfully proud of how car bodies respond in going over rough ground. Pretty cool.
Totally recommend, even without the crashes.

Amnesia: The Dark Descent is an ironically unforgettable horror adventure.
Your name is Daniel.  You live in Mayfair.  Something is hunting you.
These are the only things you can remember of your life as you wake up on the cold stone floor of Castle Brennenburg.  Stumbling down the abandoned and worn down hall will eventually yield a discovery.  A letter FROM you TO you explains that your past self has purposefully put you in this groggy and amnesiac state.  It confirms that something is hunting you and that nothing can stop it.  This Shadow will follow wherever you go.  Finally, the letter makes a request.  The Daniel of the past urges the confused Daniel of the present to descend into the castle's lowest sanctums, to find Baron Alexander, and to kill him the old man.  The letter does not justify this murder, but orders Alexander's death all the same.
Traveling through the castle will slowly dole out Daniel's past as scattered journal pages, sudden memory surges, and full on flash backs reveal a tale of desperation, fear, and the lengths men will go to secure their future; no matter the cost.  Dipping into to a twisted amalgamation of science and magic makes for an original and grotesque tale of rediscovery as you explore Alexander's relationship with Daniel and just what kind of man Daniel used to be.  It's all supported by quality acting and a genuine feeling of mystery as you take the pieces where you can get them and assemble the puzzle.
The Dark Descent also features a side story: Justine.
Waking up in a dark cell as a wheezing monsters stumbles away from the locked door, a girl finds herself challenged to get through the sadistic Justine's Cabinet of Perturbation.  The short story doesn't have much to offer, but makes for a neat distraciton.
Set in the first person; Amnesia is a simple game based not around combat and character building, but stealth and environment interaction.  A solid physics engine connected to the mouse allows players to pick up and manipulate objects, levers, doors, and more.  The inventory screen keeps track of key items of use that Daniel will gather along the way as well as his general health and interestingly; sanity.  Injury in Amnesia can be easily remedied with specially brewed drinks scattered along the path, but sanity is something entirely different.  Daniel finds himself a broken, scared, and utterly lonely man as monsters hunt him and the castle haunts him.  Unsettling or super natural events and scenes will cause Daniel's mind to unwind as his vision begins to blur and shift and his motor skills become sluggish.  The monsters that stalk the halls are so horrific that the mere sight of one is enough to damage Daniel's fragile mind.  Even worse, Daniel suffers a phobia; a fear of darkness itself.  Players are challenged to hide from enemies they can't look at by hiding in the dark that they can't stand to be surrounded by.  Losing your sanity entirely will see Daniel collapse in mental anguish as his ears ring and he loses control of his speech; attracting attention to himself in his highly vulnerable state.
It's a novel approach to both health mechanics and stealth gameplay and it makes every second of stealth feel like it could go wrong at any moment; cranking up the anxiety.  The only way to mend Daniel's mind is to take part in mentally stimulating activities like solving puzzles and making progress towards the Inner Sanctum.  Players can creep through the game as slow as they like, but cautious speed can keep Daniel from losing his mind.
Devoid of weapons and unable to fight back; players have only two trusty tools for navigating the world.  An oil burning lantern must be kept constantly stocked to be of any use, and tinderbox's can be collected to light torches, candles, and other potential sanity saving fire sources.
Physics interaction also plays into enemy interactions.  Players can slide themselves into empty wardrobes and close the doors to just a peek as they wait for threats to pass.  They can throw objects at pursuing monsters, but at best this will only stun them a second as they bash the item aside and continue the chase.  Doors have to be opened manually by pulling them opening and closed.  Accidentally pushing on a pull door as a screeching threat is actively rushing up from behind is a horror experience so simple that it's perfect.
A myriad of puzzles in the game require the collection and proper use of items around the castle as you repair machinery, brew tonics, and remove obstacles in the environment.
Mercifully, the game is shorter than I expected and can be completed in a day if you know what you're doing, but given that every sound in the game could be a potential threat; most first time players will see their time padded a bit as they fearfully slink along and feel their way out.
Justine's gameplay features much, much more obscure puzzle solving and enviroment traversal.  Each of its three "challenges" tests different facets of the player's psyche as they can solve each one in two ways with varying out comes.  The monsters in these chambers have been blinded, but hunt even the smallest sound; and to increase the challenge of the incredibly short story, death is permanant.  If you can't hack it the first time, you'll have to give it a full shot all over again.  The puzzles themselves are quiet interesting and probably wouldn't be so neat if they were easier to decipher the answers to.
By far Amnesia's weakest point is its visual presentation.  Although consistent and thematic, the graphics lack any sort of fidelity or flair.  Even when you reach some genuinely neat areas, they just don't exactly pop.  Visually the monsters are unique and horrifying but the general surroundings just don't have much to really look at and appreciate.  Except for that spooky statue in the Back Hall.  That thing is pretty neat.  Sound design is in excellent form though.  Stones can be dragged across the ground and will audibly grind across it.  The thick doors of the castle close with an appropriate hefty thud.  And the sound of filling your lantern with oil is strangely gloopy and satisfying.  Voice acting isn't ALWAYS on point, but is stellar for the most part.  Alexander in particular is a stand out performance.  Music mostly takes  a back seat to the wind blowing down the hall and the the general sound of insanity roiling around inside of Daniel's head, but the occasinal and simple tunes can range of scary and oppressive to actually rather comforting.

You play the role of a cryptid/fortean event hunter that is attempting to trap/kill his mother-in-law in a forest - 10/10 would kill a relative again : ]
Ok, so that was a jokey review that doesn't say much for this game.  Well, the true part is that your character is on a quest to discover the truth behind anomalous events/creatures - do these events exist/are these creatures real?, etc.
You have a number of motion activated trap cameras at your disposal that you can place on trees and even wild pigs (giggles like a little girl) that will aid you in finding your mother-i....er......the 'creature' once night falls.  You can also set feed and bear traps to aid you as well.  Thankfully you can skip the day segments and get right to the good stuff.  Now for the real problem with this game: the creature, or Gibbering Alien Man-Child (GAM-C) as I like to refer to it, takes 5,000 shotty rounds and/or bear trap encounters to kill it.  Ok, so it doesn't take quite that much damage.....but it is truly absurd just how much damage it actually does take.  I mean seriously, a couple well-placed shots to the head with your shotgun (yeah, I said shotty earlier though they call it a rifle in the game - it clearly is a shotgun, though there is apparently a rifle at some point, at least in multiplayer maybe...don't know, haven't played this game too much) should do the trick bu apparently the developers wanted to make this thing more difficult than Patriarch in Killing Floor on HoE difficulty.
Regardless, it's a pretty fun game and using the cameras and waiting breathlessly for the GAM-C to appear can be quite fun.  Just don't expect too much going in with only a $5 price-tag.

Simon Jarrett volunteered to have a brain scan taken using a new technique and hopes that'll help doctors find a treatment for the condition he's been suffering after a near fatal car crash: once the process starts he finds himself in a dark, abandoned station that'd not be out of place in a sci-fi movie.
Soma deals with Simon's journey through the facility as he attempts to figure out where he is and how to survive the situation he's in: the game is a fine psychological horror with an appropriately dark, disturbing plot and powerful atmosphere, the actual gaeplay and writing might falter slightly at times but nothing detracts from what is a super experience.
-good graphics and great art style make the underwater facility a believable and ghostly place to be in
-excellent sound design, the ambient sounds are especially great: the voice acting is also very good
-great atmosphere, the facilities and places you explore all give a sense of eeriness and loneliness
-a very nice story that slowly unfolds as you progress through the game
-effective monster design
-puzzles are pretty straightforward affairs set in appropriate places, they're believable, make sense and require some thought without being too hard
-a good length at around 10 hours
-not a model of optimization, some fiddling is required to get a smooth framerate on certain systems (setting vsync to adaptive seems to help alot)
-a few buttons or elements required for puzzles could be easily missed as they seem to not stand out enough from the rest of the environments
-certain monster encounters can become annoying obstacles due to cryptic behaviour and/ or taking places in cramped spaces
-visual distortion due to monster presence and/ or low health can be a bit too much at times
-some dialogues seem to push certain themes a bit too forcefully in your face and, as a result, feel forced and unnecessary
SOMA is probably Frictional's best game so far, imho, possessing unrivaled atmosphere, a great setting and accessible yet satisfying puzzles. Its plot is also good per se and contains interesting reflections on human identity and its persistence, something that might give decent food for thought to philosophically inclined players. The PATHOS-II facility is a creepy place thanks to its level design and the superb sound effects, there's a great sense of abandonement and estrangement as you explore its rooms and slowly uncover what happened there. Just like in previous games from the same dev you can expect to encounter some truly disturbing imagery both in actual scenes and in the reports scattered around the station.
The writing and dialogues can become a bit too heavy handed at times, as if Frictional was afraid their you'd miss certain meta concepts if they aren't obviously and clunkily thrown on your face every now and then. It can get midly annoying but thankfully the overall plot and its themes are good and interesting enough to make those moments easily forgivable. Monster encounters are generally decent affairs, I personally feel they're not really "scary" but can certainly be very tense when you're playing cat and mouse with a baddie in dimly light hallways: each enemy type has different strengths and weaknesses and it's generally up to you to discover what they are through trial and error. This can become slightly annoying if you can't make sense of an enemy's reaction and are forced to face it amongst small corridors with little space to hide or run. Honestly, my advice is to simply look up a guide if you feel an enemy has become an unnecessary obstacle.
I certainly recommend SOMA to any fan of the psychological horror genre, even more so if you're a fan of Frictional's previous games, its shortcomings are easily forgiven once you're taken by the plot and it's a journey worth taking.

I bought this on Steam just so I could write a review of it, and maybe push id in the right direction with sales. I have actually played this game for hundreds of hours. I probably play it for at least 10-20 hours per year, for every year of my life.
Let me make one thing perfectly clear: nostalgia does not factor into this game's enjoyment. Doom still has a very active community, and new mods come out all the time. Thanks to Carmack's programming, Doom made modding a staple of PC gaming, and it hasn't gone away. Getting older has made me see more of Doom's flaws, but I don't really like it any less.
Doom is far from perfect. Unlike modern corridor shooters, which almost completely abandon the principles of level design, Doom is made or broken by its level design. There are a few different level designers that worked on Doom, and once you've played enough you can tell each of them just by playing their levels, even if you don't know their names. This means that level design is inconsistent, and therefore you're going to really like some levels and hate others. Most people who played Doom as a kid forgave the bad levels because, well, they were kids. If you're new to Doom, it's best to start at the beginning and play Episode 1 of Doom 1. This is widely regarded as one of the best, if not the best, set of levels for Doom, designed by John Romero. They're coherent, look nice (relatively speaking) and have well-placed secrets. Oddly enough, Doom 64 has one of the best sets of levels and plays like any of the other classic Doom games; google "Doom 64 Absolution" and you can easily find a total conversion mod that basically allows you to play Doom 64 on your computer once you have Doom. Thanks, Midway!
Virtually every level can be summed up by "find keys, throw switches, open doors." This sounds bad, but again, it can either be tedious or enjoyable depending on the level's design. I must stress that the player should use their automap (tab key) here. Doom's levels are not afraid of having many twisting paths, and it's quite easy to get lost without it. Helpfully, switches are usually recessed into the wall slightly, which clearly marks them on the automap. If levels truly become tedious, don't be afraid to skip them by typing "IDCLEVXX", where "XX" is a two-digit number following the convention of episode number, then level number. i.e. IDCLEV14 changes to episode 1, level 4. Each episode has 9 levels. I won't lie to you, there are a few quite truly bad levels in Doom, but fortunately id left this cheat code in. Be careful, it starts the level as if you'd started a new game, which means you lose all your weapons except the pistol, and start with 100 health and 0 armor. However, all Doom levels are designed with pistol start in mind, so you should be able to manage with enough skill. Doom should be enjoyed on a level-by-level basis; remember, there is almost nothing in the narrative that ties these levels together. If you really hate a level, you should get used to the idea of just skipping it.
The guns... well, everyone knows how the guns work, since they were the basis for almost every shooter arsenal until Unreal came out, notable exception being Rise of the Triad. They're quite well-balanced, actually, with the exception of the pistol, which becomes useless once you get the chaingun. The shotgun and chaingun are good at long range. The super shotgun is probably the best all-around weapon in the game, although it doesn't appear until Doom 2. The rocket launcher and plasma rifle are high-power weapons meant to break out against threatening hordes of monsters, and the BFG is there when nothing else substitutes.  Every one of them has a place in your arsenal, although depending on the levels you're playing, you may be using one a lot more than the other due to ammo distribution.
Doom is famously narrative-light. Romero makes a good effort to portray "realistic" military base locations, but the game's somewhat ridiculously deep story penned by Tom Hall was thrown out in short order - trust me, if you'd have read it, you would agree that it is quite over-the-top for a fledgling shooter made in 1993. The inconsistency between levels means that the ultimate choice to abandon any hope of telling a story beyond the intermission text screens was probably for the best. There are a few key events that happen in the plot, but they mostly happen at the end of or between episodes.
Overall, I highly recommend Doom for anyone who enjoys shooters but hasn't played Doom before. I also recommend Doom for anyone who is new to shooters, since it was also designed for that audience. If nothing else, it will give them an appreciation for where the genre has come from. This game still holds up very well today, especially with the active modding community.
HOWEVER: If you do buy this game, do NOT run it as-is from Steam's library. To run the game on modern systems, it comes packaged with DOSBox, which simulates the MS-DOS environment. The emulation can slow down your computer considerably and ironically make running the game more difficult. You should instead download and install one of the many "source ports," which are redesigns of the actual game engine to make it compatible with modern computers. ZDoom is a good and popular choice. Some "purists" swear by Chocolate Doom, which faithfully recreates the game, merely updating it to allow it to run on modern hardware without such niceties as OpenGL or mouselook.

Dark themed Grecian Metroidvania.
If the above sentence piques your interest then look no further than Apotheon!
Set in the wildly creative ancient Grecian times where Zues and his fellow gods and goddesses rule over the kingdom of man. You play as Nikandreos, a simple peasant armed with the responsibility to protect his beloved home town of Dion. Hera is there to meet you at the city's temple and tells you to vanquish the gods of Olympus. Thus begins an epic quest of godlike conquest. Mount Olympus can be seen as the world hub where you can explore different parts of the city, visit markets, break in to houses and even uncover a long buried secret or two.
The primary structure of the game is to enter a God's domain through one of the game's two main hubs. Inside each domain is a vastly unique set piece where you must display skills related to the god at hand. For example, in the Forest of Artemis you will be tasked to hunt legendary beasts and possible become a beast yourself in your ultimate quest to take on Artemis herself! Likewise, in Poseidon's realm, you will have to brave the seas that the old god controls himself to calm the spiteful deity's wrong doings. Each area really does have a life of it's own even if it uses the same art style throughout. Another piece of conversation of its own is the art design.
I have never seen anything like this game's visual design. It's a 2D-open world-sidescroller at heart but the way it is presented just bursts with originality. It is hard to explain but just looking at the screen shots gives you an idea of paintings come to life. The breathing vivid colors of these pieces come to life give a sense of wonderment and otherworldly experiences like no other metroidvania. The different domains of gods use this visual style by shifting color palettes perfectly to suit the environment you are in. From the warm orange glows of the central hub Agora to the soft off-white blues of Poseidon's sea palace to the muted dismal tones of Hades, the worlds are brought to individual life from this masterful design. The gameplay is engaging and does not get old even to the very end of Nikandreos's arduous quest to become one with the gods.
The central gameplay element is exploring the realms of the gods and combat. Combat is simple yet intuitive as the popular deterrent to the norm of button mash is once again ill advised. Nikandreos attacks in concentrated swings, swings that drain a stamina bar which will cause him to take large amounts of breath in order to wind up another attack if he is not given some time to rest. Enemies do the same, where the have timed attacks and can shield/roll/fly/backpedal/ and charge at their opponent with little hesitation. While the combat is rather easy, I found the reactive style to be quite satisfying all the way through. Spear pieces flesh, sword slashes at sinews, and clubs bludgeon skulls. The instant ragdoll and sound of your foes dropping their weapons as their last breath leaves there sorry bodies is something to take in again and again.
The other side of the game resides in the player following certain laid out quests in order to gain audience with the god of that domain. You will encounter secrets, puzzles, and platforming challenges as the game plays out. Each challenge is presented in some unique way that never makes you tire of the formulae at hand.
There is a multiplayer that is both local and online, and while this is always welcomed I can see this being only a quick side interest to the major deal that is the single player campaign. There are also two difficulties with the last being unlocked after completing the game. I am curious to see how the increase challenge plays out and could easily provide more replay value for the hardcore Apotheoner.
I can easily recommend Apotheon at it's full asking price of $15.00 USD. If you love metroidvania games then you will NOT be disappointed with Apotheon offering to the table!

Twenty years! Twenty years we'd waited to find out what happened to Marty after events in final instalment of the Back to the Future Trilogy.
And then, finally, Tell Tale stepped into the breach to satisfy our craving with their 5 part episodic adventure,  Back to the Future:  The Game.
But was it worth the wait or should the franchise have remained a fond memory, unsullied by this digital resurrection?
When you fire up episode one, the aptly titled "It's About Time" , You'll find yourself (Marty) standing in the familiar Twin Pines Mall Parking Lot with Doc and Einstein.
The Delorean is hooked up to a remote control, It's nearly 1:21 AM, October 26th 1985 and Einstein is about to become the worlds first time traveller.
The recreation of this scene from the first movie does an excellent job of sucking your right into the Back to the Future universe. You'll find yourself quoting the lines from the movie, comfortable that you've been here before and you know what is coming next...
It's here that the story throws its first curveball.
Things don't pan out the way you expected, and its at this point that you know it's not just the nostalgia that's keeping that big grin on your face. This isn't just a trip down memory lane, This is Back to the future 4!
Whatever you've got to tell me, I'll find out through the natural course of time.
The "Present Day" Time line in the game takes place in 1986, a few months after the end of the final movie in the trilogy, although it won't be long before the game has you heading back in time to help Doc out.
Let me say now that, for the most part, the story in this game is excellent. It may get a little silly towards the end, but then you'll be so invested that it just won't matter!
In the spirit of avoiding spoilers, I'm not going to cover any of the story in this review, but I will say that if you enjoyed the movies, you will enjoy the twisted, rollercoaster of a narrative that awaits you here.
So we know we know there's a cracking story waiting for you here, but how does it look?
It looks just fine.
Released at the end of 2010, the graphics show their age a little, but they're perfectly serviceable.
The characters we know and love are all instantly recognisable and their facial expressions are spot on.  As I said, it looks just fine.
The voice acting here is of the highest quality.
Christopher Lloyd reprises his role as Dr Emmett Brown and whilst Michael J Fox doesn't provide the voice for Marty McFly in the game, A.J. Locascio, the actor who fills his vocal shoes, does an outstanding job of sounding every bit the Marty McFly we know from the movies.
The superb Michael J Fox, does make a cameo appearance later in the game, providing voices for past and future McFlys.
The musical score is also true to the movies, I defy any Back to The future  fan not to be swept up in the atmosphere of the game when the theme start playing.
So this is a Tell Tale game, should we expect a quick time event extravaganza like the disappointing  Jurassic ?
Thankfully No. Back to the future s game play is a pleasing mix of puzzles , searching for items and picking your way through the snappily written and often funny dialogue options.
The writing is witty, the atmosphere is spot on and the continuation of the story is worth the price tag alone.
If you're a fan of the franchise, then you owe it to yourself to play this game.
If you haven't seen the movies (shame on you) then you should go and watch them first, go on... "make like a tree and get out of here!"
Whilst some chapters play out better than others and the ending is a little "silly" I still have no hesitation in recommending Back To The Future: The Game.

I saw this game featured on the Autumn sale and seemed like a decent game for the 5$ asking price.
The best way to describe the gameplay is a mix of Frozen Synapse Lite and XCOM. Units move along a path you designate and face in specific directions, engaging any enemy they see. Unlike Frozen Synapse your units can take cover behind objects and units in cover are much more durable as in XCOM. There is a major emphasis on flanking and use of grenades to flush out enemies. The game offers three game modes based around the same set of maps. The first one is straight up Seek and Destroy where you move through a level and clear it of enemies. The second involves getting to and defusing explosives. And in the third mode your units start in the middle of the level and must fight their way clear.
The game is not without issues and lacks polish in many areas. The game's mobile origins are very clear in the setup of the interface and the level-based progression system. One point in it's favour is a detailed options menu for controlling sound and game resolution. Something which many games lack, especially mobile ports.
When you first start the game up it immediately forces you to create a team of soldiers. First by picking the unit they come from (Navy Seals, JTF2 etc) and a class for each character of the 4-man team. However since you haven't even done the tutorial yet you will have no idea what stats do and what classes mix well together. Annoyingly each class has a set of perks you can't even see until you make a squad and examine a soldier's stat page.
Every soldier starts with a set of basic equipment matched roughly to what they would use in real life. You can upgrade each soldier by unlocking and then purchasing new equipment. Progression is linear in that later more expensive equipment is better in every way. Weapons can also be upgraded with components such as a new trigger or gas system to modify the statistics. However these upgrades can easily produce weapons that break the game or weapons that deal no damage at all. In all honesty whatever assault rifle your men start with is perfectly adequate and most of the specialist weapons like the light machine gun or shotgun are useless.
Soldiers can also wear various clothing and body armour, but this is another area where the lack of polish shows. Hats can clip through hair and beards. No matter what they are equipped with your soldiers have a tan coloured pistol belt that probably won't match the other things they wear.
The third mission type is extremely silly. The premise of having your men escape the level is good, but the implementation is terrible. Your men start scattered around the level with each man in a mexican standoff with 1-3 gunmen standing not 10 feet away. 90% of the time all you have to do to win the level is to hit the end turn button, watch your men gun down everything and then spend a couple turns moving them to the exit. Personally I just pretend this part of the game doesn't exist and stick to the first two mission types.
--
All in all I would recommend this game for sale price only. There is fun to be had, but don't get into it expecting Rainbow Six. The developers are working on a new game called Breach and Clear: DEADLINE which promises to be an improved version of the game built with the PC in mind instead of the mobile platform. Sales of this game can only help them in that endeavor.

Why do I keep coming back to Doom? It's old, blocky, and tough. It makes me jump in my chair. It fills me with dread every time I have to round a new corner. I spend half the time playing it just cowering in corners waiting for enemies to find me. It makes me feel pathetic.
I keep coming back though, because of that visceral feeling. An arcade game on the PC, realized in full 3D, which exists in its raw form within Doom. It is pure and powerful and awesome.
The fact that a pixelated game created two decades ago can still scare me pretty good, can still engage me enough to make me worry about what's around the next corner... that is a testament to the staying power of Doom.
Play Doom. It might upset you, or scare you, or freak you out. But you'll be a better person for it, having witnessed one of gaming history's finest.

I tend to be rather verbose with my reviews so I will attempt to keep this one short.
I complete the single player game this weekend on normal difficultly, I have not played the online multiplayer so this review will be standing on the merrits of the single player alone.
Bare in mind that I was using an X Box pad, I would not recomend playing without some sort of controller.
Pros
- Good story even with silent protagonist, manages to create its own plot while been very loyal to source material.
- Great artwork and level design, music is atmospheric but you won't remember it after leaving the game.
- Moderate difficulty platforming, secrets can be spotted with careful eye or by paying attention to map.
- Antifrustration features in final level, respawning you on platform if you are unlucky enough to be knocked off platforms.
- Auto Save everytime you enter an area.
- Good selection of weapons, shields and usuable items though some do seem a little pointless at times.
- Fast load and save times, remarkably so compared to the usual 45 seconds to 2 minute wait I've had to put up with in more recent games.
- No issues with controller input, worked from the start with no problems
Cons
- Frequent Crashes to menu when changing areas which then usually followed by a crash to desktop when attempting to continue game.
- Combat whilst fun can quickly grow tiresome at times since foes can backpeddle as fast as you can move and the combat system doesn't favour big group combat with difficulties in aiming and swapping weapons.
- Selecting weapon/item method is clunky if you don't wish to pause everytime due to the large amount of items to scroll through.
- Summons are not avaliable in many areas when you want them most.
- Two or three side quests are a little vague if your achievement hunting.
- Story isn't entirely clear for people with a lack of knowledge in Greek mythology and may make the ending seem weak.
- The Olympian achievement. Seriously I just spent 11-12 hours beating your game and you want me to replay the whole thing on a new unlocked difficulty? With nothing else new apart from dying really quickly? This is a crappy throw back to old gaming, either have the Olympian difficulty unlocked from the start or make it a new game +.

This is a game about family and its survival, rather than the usual cliché of killing monsters in a post-apocalyptic world. From the point at which you create your cast, assigning them names and traits, to when they pass away and you have to make the difficult decision of whether to harvest their body just to keep your other members alive… you’ll feel the emotion of the household, and guilt at knowing you perhaps could have done better by them.
Sheltered’s downside is that it becomes a little repetitive after a few hours. It’s possible to have your expedition party automatically take care of any encounters out in the wilderness and to semi-automate some actions back in the bunker; but reducing your level of control in this way could result in some unwanted outcomes. I also like to have an end objective and it wasn’t entirely clear whether there was something I should be working towards, or if it was just a case of surviving as long as I possibly could.
Saying that however, this is an addictive title despite still being in early access. I ended up playing for three hours after planning to only spend an hour with Sheltered on my first go, and managed to survive for a total of twenty-four days before I called it quits for the evening. It's just a shame we had to eat the cat.
