You spend your time in the shelter controlling your family and taking care of their needs, this can also be set to auto pilot. When in your shelter people can approach it asking for refuge or wanting to trade. Then you have the scavenging side of the game, you can send parties of 2 into the wasteland to look for loot. When you do this they leave the shelter area and will radio if there is a problem, if there happens to be a problem in the wasteland (pfft its likely :P) You can take control of the situation which will put you were your scavengers are, these can be from people wanting to kill you, join or trade. With your newly scavenged loot there is a crafting side to the game were you can start decorating your shelter and provide a better life for your family.
This game is still in early access, with active devs, they just released an update last week or so with some new items and bug fixes. This game was a fantastic surprise for me. The first I believe I'd even heard of series was when the third game released. I played the first couple of missions of this one in single player, but it was too much fun to pass up playing co-op mode with a friend.
Sniper Elite makes sniping enemies and objectives loads of fun. Between the slow motion shots and the x-ray shots of bullets flying through your targets, it makes for quite the satisfying shooter. Unfortunately, but understandably the x-ray slow motion shots are missing from co-op play, but they still have the slow motion for completing special objectives and the close up shots when you tag enemies from a distance. I only played the first two or three missions in single player, but from what I could tell there are the exact same number of enemy forces when playing co-op with a friend.
Missions usually end in the assassination of a specific target, followed by fighting for your life as troops start incoming from every direction, leaving you to take them out from your nest. Vehicles, such as tanks and troop transports usually have small targets that you get to snipe at to take them out, always encouraging you to engage from a distance. So, in essence, as expected, each mission is built around sniping, even though they do leave you with shorter range guns, traps, grenades and other options. There is also a bit of a stealth mechanic allowing you to throw rocks to distract guards, though my friend and me never really found this as too viable an option while playing in co-op.
If you decide to play this game, do it justice and play on sniper elite difficulty. Wind and bullet drop really enhances the game.

As a longtime fan of Frictional Games, I knew what to expect when I bought SOMA, and I'm happy (I guess) to say that I got what I expected but, if I'm honest, this time around I didn't care so much for the endless crouching behind cover and not looking at the creatures that always seem to know more or less where you are. This was creepy in Penumbra, and I'm pretty confident that the stress of all those hours playing Amnesia:TDD resulted in some amount of long-term psychological damage. However, the monsters in SOMA aren't very scary and, on top of that, they feel overused and almost unnecessary. I found myself hurrying recklessly through the hide-and-seek parts of the game just so I could continue with the main story, which is really the great thing about SOMA.
One quick way to explain SOMA is 'Bioshock meets Amnesia:The Dark Descent'. Except that Rapture has been overrun by technodemons and looks like a hellscape straight out of Harlan Ellison's 'I have no mouth and I must scream'. As the protagonist, you are confronted with questions of existential horror at every turn: Who are you? Your conscience? What is the physical meaning of conscience? I can't get into any further detail without spoiling the story but, in my opinion, this is exactly the juicy bit of SOMA. It helps that the writing and voice acting were done competently, so the characters feel real, and their reactions genuine and believable. When horrible things happen to them, you feel it. And as the credits rolled at the end, I was overcome with the discomfort of being repeatedly made to think about stuff that most people just routinely flip under their mental carpets. Time, humanity, death, the self. It's all there, and it's a blow to the back of the skull. But if you enjoy having your brain tickled that way, SOMA is definitely for you.

For a general-purpose car physics engine, this makes for some really fun and challenging rally racing. I'm in the far minority of reviews here, not recommending it for the crashes. I try not to crash in this, any more than I already crash in Dirt Rally. I really like the feel of the car handling, making allowances for a lack of specific focus on laser scanned tracks (Assetto Corsa) or rally-focused surface modeling. That said, I'll reiterate that this is still really fun and challenging rally racing, even for an engine not focused on it. Plus I love the idea of building a game/engine working from first principles and organically evolving real-world results and vehicle/environment interactions.
Remember what the devs said -- they're focused on the mechanics. The graphics at first don't look polished. But there's a level of fidelity in car body deformation on major or minor dings that I dig -- it's not the same canned response for damaged bodywork when I prang an obstacle. The angle of impact and shape of the colliding object all naturally shape your car's response and deformation. I mean duh, of course, it's what they designed it for. And they're rightfully proud of how car bodies respond in going over rough ground. Pretty cool.
Totally recommend, even without the crashes.

I never write reviews, but this game was so good that I had to. Here are the most important points:
1) Graphics/art - I've never seen anything like it, unless you want to count the ancient Greek art it's based on. Seriously, just watch the preview video - its beautiful. Very crisp, with interesting uses of color and good detail. The creators even include readable stone etchings in the game that have real passages from ancient Greek literature, further adding to the atmosphere. The best way to say it, I think, is that the game has a feel of authenticity about it. You can really tell that the creators did their homework, and I think they did a fantastic job of giving the Greek mythos life.
2) Music - Also fitting in with the setting, you will feel like Odysseus while you're listening to this soundtrack. War drums, chanting, full orchestrated scores - it's got it all. The tracks for the boss battles have a very epic feel to them; they really lend to the idea that you're fighting Gods.
3) Gameplay -  Probably the other "best" from this game besides the art/music. I've never seen another game in this genre implement such a wide variety of weapons so well. You will have at your disposal quite a few ancient Greek weapons, including spears, swords, clubs, bow & arrows, javelins, greek fire, and a lot more. You can wield most weapons with a shield as well as throw them, and you can evasively roll back and forth to try and manuever into a better position or get behind your enemies. When you combine all of these elements, combat is very engaging and fun. Usually in games of this type, I find myself using one or two weapons that are clearly superior to the others, but that isn't the case here. I can honestly say that I used every weapon class in the game effectively, and I think that using all of the different weapons is part of what makes this games so fun. I can only speculate that the creators realized this early on, which is why the weapons have durability that runs out decently fast - it forces you to experiment.
The other aspect to the gameplay I wanted to mention is the scenario variety. Each boss battle, especially, and to a lesser degree, each quest, presents different sorts of challenges to the player. There is almost always more to it than "hit this enemy until he dies" or "go to this location and pick up this item." The level designs themselves are very unique, so often just getting through the level can be the most interesting part.
4) Collectibles/side quests - Some games suffer from having nothing else to do outside of the main questline, while others suffer from overloading the game with collectibles and time-consuming sidequests. In my opinion, this games walks the line well. There are 2 achievements for collecting - 1 for getting all of the unique weapons in the game, and one for opening all of the chests(lockboxes) in the game. The weapons, however, are often found in the chests, so really you can focus on just finding the chests, which are not terribly difficult to find if you are constantly looking out for breakable walls and making sure to explore every area thoroughly.  The sidequests available range from simple tasks to fairly complex series of events that require trips to multiple areas. I didn't find any of the sidequests to be frustrating, which is a mistake a lot of games make.
5) Minor points:
- Each piece of armor you get permanently increases your total armor points, which basically acts as a second pool of hitpoints. However, you keep all of your old armor pieces, and since the increase is permanent, you can freely switch between armor pieces with no penalty. I found this to be very progressive and pleasing.
- There is a multiplayer mode, though I cannot comment as I haven't tried it
- A 3rd difficulty unlocks after you beat the game, Olympian Difficulty. Beating the game on this difficulty earns you the last achievement.
6) Negatives: not many for this game.
- I did have one save become irrevocably corrupted at one point, and it crashed the game whenever I tried to load it. Luckily, the autosave saved the day for me. Hopefully this isn't a widespread issue.
- The character movement can be a little clunky & hard to get used to, and I hate that the character stops running whenever I hit stairs. I highly recommend playing with a gamepad, though this may vary if you're used to using a mouse/keyboard all the time.

This is a point and click game based on the Back to the Future movie franchise. It has everything going for it, the music straight from the movie, the nostalgia, the amazing voice cast and the immersion that lets you explore a lot from the movie. This is some good interactive fiction and a point and click was the way to go to tell a story. The only real problem here is the genre just isn't all that fun.
The story has you going back in time as Marty McFly from the movies to find Doc Brown and really puts a focus on Doc's youth instead of the movies that put the focus on Marty's family and him saving it. Most of the characters are here from the movie, Marty, his dad George McFly, Doc Brown, Einstein the dog and of course Biff Tannen. It introduces more characters, but they're not the stars. Biff's voice actor could have sounded more like Biff, but Marty's voice actor is fantastic and Doc is played by Christopher Lloyd as always.
Since this is a modern point and click game that lets you walk around an area instead of being confined to one screen like the older version of the genre. You'll be able to collect items and use them. That's one of the problems, the tedium of using the items. Going into the item menu, selecting the item, using the item and if you fail then you need to do it all over again. Over and over. , You'll be figuring out what dialog choice you need to make, which character to distract so you can do something with them gone. At least with this and other modern point and click games they accentuate what to click on.
I can't say the game is fun and to be honest it feels like a chore to sit through the story. There aren't any crazy moments like in the movie so much as dialog and wandering around. I can't imagine non gamers that are fans of the movie franchise sitting down to enjoy this game and play it all the way through. I can't imagine gamers saying wow that was fun, unless this was the 90s when point and click games were more accepted, before technology left them behind.
For the most part, the game is a series of cut scenes to say even the simplest of things. Potentially over and over again. There is some interactivity when you chat with someone, but it feels more like how much flavor dialog do you want to hear? There is always a logical choice with dialog and there are no wrong choices, so much as do you want to listen to all 3 - 5 responses or pick the most logical one to get it over with and progress? There are no real consequences like in Walking Dead where it can change characters and or events. You'll always get through the game. There is no death, there is no failure, there is just pressing on until you figure out what to do next.
I've always been a big fan of the Back to the Future movie franchise, and I really enjoyed my first play through of Walking Dead, which is also from Telltale Games, but this game is a chore. The story and the nostalgia just aren't enough to make me want to see what happens next.

Breach & Clear is the kind of game that is easy to learn, but takes some serious skill to master. While you will spend a lot of time staring at the different locations to put your limited team, once you end the turn and the action starts it's over in a flash. Getting sub 15 second clear times on multiple room levels is one of the fuzziest feelings I've gotten playing a turn based game and the game does a good job of trying to teach you the idea of efficiency of movement.
If you, like me, grew up playing the OLD Rainbow Six games, then this will feel very familiar, as you plan out the movements of your team every turn and then they rush to execute that plan. Play with Permadeath on, it adds an element of stress in the later levels when there's some very hard to handle corner and hall combinations that the enemy will easily take advantage of even on the easier AI settings. Great game, 9/10.

What's the first thing you think of when you think of ancient Greece?  No, not that!  Get your mind out the gutter, you degenerate!  Okay, what's the second thing?  Right!  The awesome myths of heroes and gods!  You think of Odysseus blinding the cyclops, Zeus overthrowing the titans, and... uh, Heracles mucking out some stables!  Yeah, that's the ticket.
With all these feats of heroism wouldn't it be sweet if there was a video game that took place in ancient Greece, so that we too could test our mettle against these gods and monsters?  What's that?  God of War?  No, no.  That won't do at all.  I'm talking about something that wasn't pushed through the filter of what thirteen year old boys think is cool.  Something that's got fun gameplay, sure.  But something that keeps it classical, you know?  Preserves the tone and character of the myths.  Fortunately for us, we've got Apotheon.
Assuming you've at least looked at the screen shots, I don't need to sell you on Apotheon's visual aesthetic.  It just looks great.  Bold black character models, flattened in profile, placed on warm background colors and intricate patterns do an excellent job of making you feel like you're playing an ancient Greek vase come to life.
It's clear a lot of work was put into Apotheon's visuals, but I'll admit, I almost passed on Apotheon, since I was concerned there might not be any substance behind the style and very little was said about it when I first had a look.  It's too easy to fall into the "art game" trap, these days.
I grew still more concerned in a different way when some of the voice acting for the early game's enemies intruded on the stately visuals with an out of place cockney sounding accent.  And still more worried when it introduced the main conceit of the game as "the gods have taken their gifts from man and it's up to you to overthrow them one by one."
Ugh.  Groan.  Spit.  We're really doing the God of War thing?  We're really giong to treat the Olympians as one big boss rush?  No concern for all the gods' benevolent qualities?  No mention of the heroes they helped, the customs they preserved?  Just gonna treat them as absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥♥all the time?  Ladies and gentlemen, I will confess that I was genuinely worried that upon my descent into Hades I would find the big man himself putting on his best James Woods playing Hades-as-the-Christian-devil before a meat-head slam down as the hero against an irredeemable evil.
But, mercifully, for its couple of worrisome first impressions, Apotheon never went that route.  Yes, you do play as the mortal hero, Nikandreos, on his quest to conquer Olympus and steal the gods' powers.  And, yeah, that concept's a little off-base from the mythology, but Apotheon always manages to treat the source material with a great deal of knowledge and respect and it gets all of the points for that.  Aside from the odd intro enemies, the voice acting is good and, I would say, necessary for presenting the extreme personalities of the Greek gods.  Most importantly, their characters are preserved.
Oh yes, your encounter with Ares will be a slaughter-fest bordering on supernatural Hulkamania, but that's befitting the charcter of Ares.  Your meeting with Hades on the other hand is one of a number that pass without violence and with a lot of understanding for your plight.
And just to ensure that the fight-the-gods premise is pulled off with panache, Apotheon makes sure to vary its gameplay to suit the gods' realms and keep each climactic encounter with the gods themselves true to their characters.  I knew, for instance, that I was in for something special when my showdown against Artemis took the form of a demented game of tag, with the role of hunter and prey switching as I navigated the level.
In Poseidon's realm you get to ride a goddamn horse!  People who know about mythology just came!
Sorry, I got excited there.  The fundamental gameplay for Apotheon is fairly simple.  You can attack with an absurd variety of ancient weapons: spears, swords, axes, pitchforks, bows, javelins, rocks, the power of love, an arrow that's three arrows, a flying saucer, a sword on fire....  Look, it's a big list, okay?  And you can block with a shield if you have one equipped.  You can adjust the angle of your attack with melee as well as ranged weapons to sneak blows past enemy shields.  But despite the extreme variety of weaponry, your equipment will break on you mid-battle.  Normally, I'd question the setting's decision to make equipment out of paper mache, but it was the bronze age, I guess. Combat gets fairly frantic as you and your opponents are smashing each others' shields and you dodge roll around like Sonic the effin' Hedgehog while you scramble to pull out your next favored weapon.
It's gets a bit metroidvania-ish with you being able to explore large areas of Olympus right out of the gate.  There are lots of secrets to find and reasons to backtrack, athough the game is about as good at rewarding the player as someone saying "open your mouth and close your eyes."  More on that later.  It's also a bit step platformer-y, with movement focused on jumping and climbing around on your environment.  Nothing really unique, but it works.
There are some RPG elements where you can buy upgrades to speed and damage with various weapon types, but it's minimal.  You start with everything you need right out of the box.
But it wouldn't be like an ancient urn without some cracks in it, would it?  The core gameplay is weak when it comes to precision.  I found that the arrow telling me where I was aiming with my ranged weapons only had a token resemblance to where my attack was actually going and that made a few puzzles that relied on that precision tedious.  The sheer volume of weapons can also quickly become a hindrance.  Yes, you will need a lot of weapons since they break quickly.  But it sucks to cycle through your huge inventory looking for the next spear weapon in the heat of the fight, especially since they aren't placed next to each other for some reason.  It also makes one wonder why Nikandreos can't drop some swords and axes to hold more spears if you happen to have been giving him more proficiency with them.
On the huge inventory note, there's also a crafting system that feels a bit gratuitous.  Yes, the potions and things you can make are useful.  But so often, I found myself overburdened with materials that only had one or two specific uses, I couldn't help but wonder, "Is this necessary?  Could you maybe have just given me the final product instead of making me go through this extra flow-breaking step."
And as I've briefly mentioned, Apotheon doesn't seem to know how to reward questing and exploration.  I did one side-quest for an optional god and ended up with something that increased the duration of poison damage.  There aren't any weapons that do poison damage. No, really, I didn't find any and I found everything.  You also get a grappling hook for another elaborate sidequest that allows you to explore absolutely ♥♥♥♥-all you couldn't without it.  Generally, there's very little reason to go after all the secret treasures.  Odds are you've found one or two weapons you really like and that chest is going to contain those special sling bullets you are already maxed out on because you never use them or a backstabbing dagger in a game without real stealth mechanics.
But for its flaws, Apotheon's gameplay feels shield-shatteringly epic and suits the mythology well.  I'm always happy to pick some nits, but the broad strokes are exactly what they need to be.
Indeed, short of including butt-stuff mechanics, I'd say that Apotheon has everything you need to get the full experience of epic Greek mythology.  It's certainly the best take on the subject material I've seen to date and it's just good fun.

If you're a big fan of the original Back to the Future trilogy, you need this game. No, seriously, you NEED this game. Period. The storyline is incredibly good and feels authentic to the original movies, pushing the characters in interesting directions that I hadn't expected. It takes place after the movies, and as Marty McFly you'll end up traveling back to prohibition era Hill Valley after discovering that a prolonged absence by Doc Brown is due to his having been murdered back in the 30's. As expected, traveling back in time to save him leads to unexpected alterations in the timeline and a frantic hustle to fix one mess, only to create another. Overall it's very cleverly written and worthy of the franchise.
Aesthetically, the game takes a more stylized cartoonish approach to the characters rather than attempting realism - something that I personally rather enjoyed. And the voice acting - hoo man the voice acting is amazing! Christopher Lloyd reprises his role as Emmet Brown, and though Michael J Fox does not reprise his, the person who fills in as Marty does such an amazingly good impression that I literally could not tell the difference. Seriously, I was genuinely shocked to learn it hadn't been Fox voicing him. Best yet, Fox returns for a couple of cameo roles in the final episode.
From a gameplay standpoint, it's a point-and-click adventure with pretty simple puzzles. Overall its approach is straight forward and only a small handful of times did I find myself getting hung up on a puzzle - however, the puzzles aren't really the point so much as that you're involved in an interactive movie, and this is made very clear by the fact the game has a hints feature that will outright TELL you the answers if you're well and truly stuck, allowing you to breeze through the story at a pace that's already hardly broken by frustration. At least, not in terms of the puzzles themselves. This isn't to say this game isn't without issue - things like movement is a bit buggy and aggravated me quite a bit, especially when switching between sceneries. The inventory is also kind of annoying the way it makes you have to scroll through it instead of having all items available at once. As inconvenient as this can sometimes be, it's hardly enough to detract from what makes this game shine.
Seriously, if you're a fan of the movies, put this in your collection. You'll thank yourself.

This game plays great either with your mouse (no keyboard at all) -OR- a controller.  With the mouse, it's actually pretty easy to control your ship.  Left mouse button is fire, Right mouse button is your thrust, and the middle mouse button is your bomb which you'll need to conserve and use sparingly and in those do-or-die moments.  With a controller, you'll only use the left stick to point your ship, buttom button is fire, right-most button is thrust, and top-most button is your bombs.
This game has two game modes.. An objective mode where you clear waves of rocks and enemy spaceships that get progressively harder and an endless challenge mode where you the enemies and rocks never stop, you just keep playing trying to achieve a high score and the game ends when you eventually run out of lives.
Sadly, high scores for this game are only kept on your local computer.  Missing a internet based high score list to compete against would have been a nice feature, and makes this game feel like it's missing something important.
More and higher graphics resolution options (especially for widescreen monitors) should also have been here.
I do love how enemy ships, even early on have pretty good AI and will try and flank you from multiple angles, and might even turn away from you and "run" at times.
All-in-all, this is one of the best Asteroid re-makes I've ever played, even though the graphics are certainly no where in the ballpark of shinier options like Geometry Wars and Super Stardust.
Even with the missing universal high scores and graphics options (which I hope the developer adds later) .. I give this game an 8.5 out of 10.   For $5 USD, it delivers a solid arcade action game that would make it's grandfather, arcade Asteroids of 1979 very proud.

I'm still working through this game as of writing this, as I've gone through roughly 3 PC changes in the last few years.
Not to beat around the bush, but I do view Quake 1 as the superior game of the two (and yes, I do know about the naming issues making this game a sequel in name only). In spite of that, and some other minor complaints, this is one of my "unwinding" games, untainted by nostalgia.
I never played Quakes 1-3 as they came out; I never had a PC powerful enough, and I was always more in the Doom camp, Doom II being the very first FPS and "proper" PC game I ever played. However, after buying Quake 1 a while back, I immediately defected and wrote a glowing review for it.
Quake II, after the brilliant Lovecraftian mishmash that was 1, feels a bit strange to get into, especially after playing some more modern FPS's made after the genre had had more of its kinks ironed out. Level design, especially during portions of the game you're expected to retread levels with only a vague sci-fi-warehouse name that you're supposed to find after picking up the key item, is a particularly prickly bit for me. Luckily, it makes up for it with both tone and basically everything else.
Quake 1 had a heavy, oppressive, almost hopeless, sense of being a tiny human in an interdimensional grand plan orchestrated by an eldritch monster that neither understood nor particularly cared about you or your guns. That's all well and good, but Quake 2 completely eschews that (and in doing so, avoids tiring out the first game's premise) for run-gun-bunnyhop-rocketjump gameplay that pits your Lone Space Marine against an evil expansionalist society of nightmarish cyborgs. Serious series tonal shift? Yes. Good thing? Also yes.

If you're a fan of Quake 1, or really any '90s shooter, give this a try. If you dislike wonky series discontinuity throughout a franchise, you're gonna have a bad time.
As a VERY IMPORTANT side note, the game still relies on CD audio, which Steam doesn't include in this release. I STRONGLY recommend either using a 3rd party engine that supports the downloaded soundtrack files, like QuakeSpasm, or an analogous program to the Ultimate Quake Patch (for Quake 1), which patches in the music tracks and appropriate looping for you.

This game is absolutely amazing and I would recommend it to just about anyone. Regarding the game still being in early access, it's still a work in progress game! Bugs and glitches are constantly being fixed so us players won't have to worry about them anymore.
If you buy the game and complain how it's not working or the developers aren't doing a good job or there's a lot of bugs, there's no room to complain. There's a warning before you buy the game and even on the title screen stating you may encounter bugs and other problems! It's still in development!
DINOSAURS -- If you were into dinosaurs as a kid then you will definitely love them now. With the Isle you are able to become a dinosaur from a long list that are made or are currently being made. The models for these creatures are stunning and well made. There's no rushing through or sloppiness. Although there are just ground based herbivores and carnivores at the moment, later development will art reptiles, amphibious and avian dinosaurs.
MAPS AND ENVIROMENT -- Each map reminds me of huge games like Skyrim. Detail is everywhere and there is rarely a bare splotch of land to see. These maps are huge, holding landmarks to find your way, lakes, forests, mountain ranges, human camps, ruins, etc. Future development will add an enormous map, with hints that it's a couple times larger than Skyrim, which will allow for more people to join, more herds and packs, more outposts, more biomes, and even oceans for aquatic creatures. There are trees everywhere, actual grass on the ground predators can use to hide in, and bushes everywhere. With lower end computers, the grass may make one lag when you enter it though.
UPDATES -- This game updates a couple times a week usually, so if you like coming back to new things being added regularly, you'll enjoy it. With new updates come new bugs that the developers must fix though, so be patient when a new update comes out. All bugs will eventually be fixed.
BUILDS -- I believe the default build is now the build the developers use to test the things they add in the game for bugs before actually releasing it. For me, and playing this version, I like it. Being able to play new dinosaurs and things before they come out with an official update is cool. Not to mention it helps the developers find bugs and fix them in future updates. If you don't want an unstable gameplay, you can always change the version to Legacy in properties->beta->legacy for the last stable version that will only update when stable releases come out.
FUTURE -- As humans are planned, along with cannibals, progression systems of growth and taming and more, the future has a lot to hold! When the game is fully complete I'm sure it'll be amazing, and a favorite to just about anyone. I'm excited to see what it holds!

My review of For Honor:
Where to begin... This game is like going out for a nice steak dinner with your family at a really high end restaurant. The drinks are expensive, the decor is magnificent, the sides are superb and the steak you asked for has been aged for two weeks and was broiled at over 1800 degrees fahrenheit. Or rather, this is what the game COULD have been like.
This game is like going out for Jack in the Box at two in the morning, because everywhere else is closed. You immediately regret your decision and think of what you could have actually spent your money on.
My experience with this game... Well, to be quite honest I didn't even have an experience with this game. It is hard to have an experience with a video game if it doesn't even want to launch. Shocking, I know. I didn't think it was a big deal at first, I went through troubleshooting to see if I could alleviate the game's failure to launch, to include:
Validating the games files
Disabling my anti virus software
Adding exceptions to my anti virus software
Re-installing the game to my HDD
Watching an episode of Rick and Morty (Season 2, Episode 1) this step is crucial
Re-installing the game to the same HDD that the launcher is located on
Taking a shower, using Old Spice bodywash and Tea Tree Shampoo (Lather, rinse, repeat)
Un-installing and re-installing easyanticheat multiple times (no less than 30, give or take another 10)
Baked a pizza (pepperoni, this is very important)
Un-installing and re-installing Uplay
Watched an episode of Game of Thrones (Season 6 Episode 5, The Door) SPOILERS: HODOR DIES
Consulting the FAQs on both the Ubisoft forums and EasyAntiCheat website, none of which actually was helpful or insightful. Do not recommend.
I also submitted a trouble ticket to both Ubisoft and EasyAntiCheat, neither of whom were able to help figure out the issue. I suppose EasyAntiCheat is working, considering I can't even cheat if I can't access the game. Well done Ubisoft and EasyAntiCheat, bravo. Working very well 100%.
Now on to the grades I have given various aspects of the game:
Campaign: 0/10
I gave the campaign a 0/10 because I wasn't actually able to access the campaign. I am sure I would have been able to if the game had the capability to launch itself, but I wasn't able to determine whether the story had merit, if there was any character development, or if the dialogue was crisp. Sadly, the campaign gets 0 flurbos out of 10 possible. Not a good way to start off Ubisoft.
Graphics: 1/10
I gave the graphics a 1/10 because I wasn't actually able access the game due to its inadequacy and inabilty to actually function. It gets a single point because the splash screen the game gives me (before it gives me the launch error that I've seen 50+/- times give or take) was rendered wonderfully. I've never paid $60 USD for just a splash screen before, but unfortunately it is not able to make up for the rest of the game's dull appearance and mediocre attempts at being a joyful and exhilirating experience. Graphics get 1 Plumbus out of 10 possible.
Multiplayer: -69/10
I gave the multiplayer a -69/10 because the multiplayer functionality of the game was not accessible at the time. I believe this is due to the game's inability to start and perform its sole purpose in its life. It had one job, and now its back on unemployment, at least until it ends up at the bargain bin at your local Gamestop for tree-fitty ($3.50 USD). It would have been nice to wage war against my fellow gamers as a Samurai hopped up on cocaine and hookers, but alas, it was not meant to be. Multiplayer gets -69 shleemies out of 10 possible.
Conclusion: Don't settle for Jack in the Box. Go get the steak dinner (or tofu dinner, if you're into that) that you deserve. Also, I do not recommend this game. You are better off wasting your time inflicting minor/severe injuries onto your body, such as shooting yourself in the foot, peeling the flesh off your pinky, or cutting off your limbs with a lightsaber (PRO-TIP: Dress up as Obi-Wan and proclaim you have the high ground.)
If you have already purchased the game like I did (foolishly), know that you can get a refund for the lack of game you received if you haven't played it for more than two hours. (The .5 hours on record for me was the time accumulated just trying to get the game to run). My refund request was submitted and approved within a matter of 3 hours. THANK YOU STEAM!
Good day to you.

Apotheon
----------
A great platformer, its strong points are its beautiful design, music track and story. The game gives you a mood that you are exploring a mythic world and you are going to tear the gods from their rule.
The music accompanied with this game fits that mood perfectly.
You gather armor tiers and you can craft potions which may boost you or summon allies. The armor system is done pretty nice, once you gather higher tier armor, your total armor level expands. That means that once you can still wear your other armor purely for cosmetic reasons while retaining the armor level.
There is no experience or statistics system, but the game does not really need that.
You do get an array of weaponry with names that stem from ancient Greece. Spears are Doru, swords are Xiphos, etc.
The controls are a little floaty, but the developers have taken away frustrations that other platformers have. When you reach the edge of a platform, you hang off of it and you can gradually slide down or climb up.
Something I did not really like was the fact that you assault guards who clearly are not hostile to you unless you attack them first. It made me feel a bit like an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to attack them first just so I can progress in the game. But this is just my opinion.
Ingame, I missed the classic monsters like the Centaur, Pegasus, Minotaur, Manticore, Hydra and the Medusa Gorgon. I was hoping to fight those as well.
Furthermore the Steam achievements for Apotheon are a little too easy to gather.
----------
Nevertheless, Apotheon is a godly game and I really recommend it to anyone into Metroidvania games.

TL;DR
It's the Catan you know and love, but with a bunch of sub optimal interface decisions, poor optimization, and a few game breaking bugs. This game utterly fails to meet basic expectations for an online game. Right now this feels like an alpha or Early Access title.
Nitty Gritty
In approximately 1/3 games you'll run into connection issues. I'm not sure why their network seems to suffer so much for a turn based game of all things. When someone gets disconnected, it will halt and wait, it often takes a while for the game to figure out what happened and let the match continue.
Furthermore, giving a player a hit on Elo is a very poor way to manage disconnections. Primarily because the above bug does not appear to be related to intentional disconnection(afaik, they didn't seem intent on leaving). But also because this makes Elo not actually dependant on skill, thereby placing more skilled players with less patience(usually the main reason for disconnecting) against less skilled players who haven't done anything to deserve this.
As far as UI, there are a bunch of oversights. Luckily I happen to speak basic german, but the account creation screen when I first launched the game was in German. I imagine some people would have trouble with this. Even if they don't, it's a pretty good general reflection on the state of non polish this game has. Which is an absolute shame. Catan as a game is extremely balanced and probably my favorite board game of all time. But there are all sorts of things wrong here. I'm sure someone told the team some basic UI mantras like, "keep it simple". But simple should never supercede clear. When you log in it is completely unclear where you should click in order to exit the game. That's some pretty basic stuff, people. If it weren't for my overwhelming boner for the board game, this would be an absolute deal breaker. They spent time on making a 3d, real time rendered background, but not on basic user experience testing.
Now that I've brought up the 3d, let me mention that this game is generally appealing. They use the same music from the iPad version, which I find just as pleasant and non intrusive as ever. The tile and card art is identical to the board game. The title screen background is pleasant looking. The avatars are mediocre at best, with no variety. As far as I can tell they simply used a morph target and hair swap to change male to female, and it doesn't look good in either version. I don't know who they expect to buy these avatar add ons when they have such poor fidelity and design.
Now let's bring it back to optimization. There is no reason this game should not have been built first in a stripped down mode that can run on literally anything, then added the other features. I think the team must have failed to udnerstand their base value proposition, so i'm going to spell it out;
People are here to play *CATAN ON THE INTERNET*, that is ALL.
It's obvious they built this in UE4, since I can see some residual UI from the engine in here(lack of polish peeking through again), and I know it has its pretty PBR shader and fancy AO. But my laptop is burning up running this, while it is perfectly capable of running UE4 just fine.
Fix, optimize, THEN add microtransactions.
I haven't even gotten to the face that they have a very small number of maps....even though the original game has rules for randomizing the map already which they aren't using.....SMH.
I'll spare you the rest. If you're really curious, you can play some free matches online. I advise against purchasing the full game or any expansions until it's clear that they've put some elbow grease into this.
I find your lack of purchase disturbing.

Okay so I want to start with I just barely push this over to recommended over not.
I'd like to start with the good parts of the game as honestly there is a LOT of fun to be had. The combat is tight with a bit of a rough learning curve but I really enjoyed learning the class trying different jobs and finding the one I wanted to play the most. I even really enjoyed the PVP and I really not a fan of fighting players. The game is GORGEOUS. I found myself actually stopping during story mode and a few bit in PVP just looking at the detail and the environment. Even my character started to have sword wounds thru armor and their body.
The story mode was well done as a teaching tool. The story itself is pretty simple and nothing amazing. Heck from a narrative point I felt you could remove the viking chapter and the over all story would really not change. However, it lets you try out most of the jobs before you pay your steel for them. You learn the mechanics at a good pace. Hard mode for me was perfect balance. Even better playing the main story if you break the breakables you get free scavenger chests to gear up your champion once you hit multiplayer which is a great incentive. The tutorial both normal and advance also teach and give you a rather large amount of steel for completing them making them feel great as you learn but also progress.
I personally enjoyed the progression system as well though I wish it was explained better early on. As you level up you can get higher gear. You can't get rare gear until prestige one so you might accidently waste your hard earned steel and chests from the story if you use them before then. There are several narrative elements forming into large and complex story. There are also thought-provoking choices that don't have any impact on the story or gameplay but raise big questions to the player about moral and humanity. Most of the gameplay is about exploration, avoiding danger and solving puzzle to find the way to progress. You might even looking for more from Frictional Games.

I had seen mixed thoughts on this game, but thought I would give it a try.
I'm always very interested in ancient greek mythology, so that in itself is a major draw to this game. While the story is very reminiscent of another greek mythology game (*cough* God of War *cough*), the way it was presented set it on its own.
The art style is awesome, it's bold colors and just oozes with greek influence. It felt like I was playing a story book that was made by the ancient greeks themselves.  There is a nice variety of locals as well as your move throughout the story. While the graphics looked great, there were some slowdown issues with the framerate despite having a fairly powerful PC. They would come at random times, independant of what was going on during that particular moment.
The other part of the game that made it a very positive experience for me was the combat. Its difficult, it has a high learning curve (in my opinion), but its *satisfying*. Once you figure out how you have to space yourself for different weapon types, and how you have to actually aim your ranged weapons, it becomes very natural. I was FRUSTRATED at first, so expect that, but know the more you practice with it, the better the game becomes. You can't expect to just run in and kill everything without timing your attacks and blocks, or you'll die horribly (as I did at first).
There were a couple annoyances with the game I should mention too. For one, unless I missed some control, the map can't be moved around to search the area. This makes looking through a large map impossible, which is necessary sometimes when trying to figure out where treasure chests are, where an objective is located at specifically, or if you've already gone a certain way. Second, the weapon breaking system. It adds a degree of realism, and it allows you to try different weapons when one breaks, but it still was annoying. I enjoyed playing with the sword the most, but it always broke way too easily. I understand what the devs were trying to do with it, but it just detracts from the fun a bit in my opinion.
TL;DR
Overall, the game is a lot of fun, with great unique graphics, and very fun gameplay. The story is not very unique, but enjoyable. The map could use some tweaks, and the weapon breakage system detracts from the fun a bit. Still a highly recommended game!

Jason can murder anyone by himself without needing to sacrifice to some spider god in DbD, using either his trusty weapon (Different to each version of Jason), grabbing and tearing them apart with his bare hands, or finding a convienient object in the area...a fireplace to roast them, a window to smash them through, hell even just crushing their head in a door.

Use that free time to frantically search every cabin in the camp for car or boat parts, a working phone for a police escort, or even the secret components to silence Jason for good!
Each counselor has differeing stats and can be focused on hiding, fighting, repairing, or running, generally. Each Jason also comes with 4 unique grabs based on their unique weapon and unique 3 pros and cons each.

Very polished tactical shooter in vain of Frozen Synapse. Decent customization even though the weapon and gear models look too similar. The weapons are balanced and there are several nice levels which can be enjoyed in 3 modes: Terrorist hunt (kill everybody), Bomb Defusal, survival/escape.
Graphics are decent but not eye-popping. Far from it, actually. The human models all look pretty much the same even if you select different characters. Mediocre at best and could have used a more vivid style and color palette.
The gameplay itself is turn based tactical battles. about 70% of the maps are indoors and use tight corridors and covers to keep the action pumping and the rest are outdoors which focus more on tactical play and choosing the best ways to strike.
Your squad of 4 (which you can create yourself and customize) level up as you gain more stars in missions and more XP. You also receive money to purchase new weapon upgrades and gear. You choose specifically which attribute to level up for each soldier (e.g. accuracy, speed, special ability, reaction etc.). This all helps to give the game longevity as well as harder difficulty settings which make the game much more demanding. I'd also like to note that the music is pretty cool.
I only wish there was a "Restart Level" button in the pause menu because you need to go back to the main menu every time you choose to restart a level mid play.
All in all, a great bargain game and I'd say it's worth the full price even though there aren't many maps to play around in (there are new ones in a DLC though). But if you liked Frozen Synapse or want to give the games a try I think you'll like what you find here.

Whilst this game had massive server issues, you can't exactly blame the devs for being overwhelmed by it. They did/are doing everything they can to fix them.
Onto the gameplay:
Jason is OP, and that is perfectly fine. There really should be some changes though, because there's a difference between OP and broken. Jason being able to shift into a grab? Okay then. Jason being able to shift into a grab from outside your terror radius and insta-execute you without a chance of escape? Not okay.
The counsellors are at a major disadvantage right now, but thats mainly due to the fact that we're all noobs at the game. No-one knows what they're doing and, since Jason is much easier to learn, he's stomping most matches. In the future, when the counsellors are skilled and have good perks, the tables may very well flip.
The things I see that should change:
Combat stance being completely shot down by a grab. This could work by forcing Jason into a combat stance when you do. This could also let you sacrifice yourself to save your team, resulting in better teamwork.
Shift should have a grace period before you can grab again. This could stop people from instantly grabbing from a shift, and would make them use shift to instead go to the counsellor and hit them, or go infront and surprise them.
Right now, you can reverse-juke Jason very easily with the car. If you drive backwards and he morphs behind you, drive forward. He needs to shift within a second to actually get infront of the car. The cooldowns on morph for some Jasons, such as part 6, are too big to have a chance to catch up.
Finally, a little bug report. The bridge in Higgins (I think it's Higgins) can let people walk across the side of it, making them float above the water. Jason's hitbox is too big to go across, so the only way he can attack them is by throwing knives. If the councellor has packed up on first aid, Jason has no chance.

Canabalt isn't a bad game, but I don't recommend it because it's frustrating and not memorable.
When I say "frustrating", I don't mean to whine that it's hard.  I like hard games, but I like "Yes I did it!" hard, not "christ fckn finally" hard.  Canabalt is the latter - success in Canabalt is 10% skill, 90% getting lucky with the random level generator.  It's not a fulfilling experience when most of your deaths are caused by BS you couldn't have done anything about (like occasionally when you're jumping onto a building and it's completely destroyed except for a small platform, which is never where you land).  It would be a fun "I've got a few minutes to kill" game, except it's not really that fun.
Secondly, it's not memorable.  The whole game is the same thing, running and jumping.  The first five minutes are the same as several hours in.  It took 10 minutes to see every type of obstacle the game has, and a little over an hour to "beat" all the challenge maps and get all the worthwhile achievements.  What's worse, is I've already forgotten all of it - the game is always the same, so nothing ever stands out.
It feels like a flash game that you spend a couple minutes with then move on.  If it had something more - like a cooky story, or crafted levels instead of randomly generated - it might have been more enjoyable. As of the time of this review I've played 16 hours of Friday the 13th: The Game. I've given it fair amount of time and have played enough matches to share my opinion. First off, this game is immensely fun to play, from sneaking around as camp counselors to playing as the hocky-masked serial killer himself. There seems to be a lot of complaining that Jason is overpowered, which I don't really understand. From my experience it seems pretty balanced. I don't know what others expected when they bought a game about a supernatural serial killer, but you're not going to  be able to take him on by yourself, which fortunately, you won't have to as there can be up to seven other counselors on your side. There have been multiple situations where I have been able to outrun and evade Jason with a little help from another player. Which is the whole point of an asymmetrical multiplayer game. There are a few counselors to chose from, with clothing options and perks you can purchase with an in-game currency you get from playing. There are a few Jasons to chose from as well, as Illfonic have picked a few of the more popular iterations. The level up system works well and feels like it's got a nice pace to it.
That being said there are still a few glitches, from aesthetical glitchs such as hair behaving in crazy ways (pull it harder, HARDER!) to physics based issues (e.g., Jason being able to grab while turned the other way.) There are a few errors that pop up while you're in the menu as well, I wasn't able to buy perks for awhile. And there are only three maps and one game mode so far.
All in all, I've enjoyed my time with it so far. If you're into online multiplayer games and a fan of the Friday the 13th films, I  would recommend it.
And thanks for reading this novel of a review.

You can click to move the person to that location, but if you want to move them again you have to cancel their current action in their queue. I mis-clicked so many times just trying to figure out this system. I felt out of control over characters that needed CONSTANT MICROMANAGING. Thankfully, there is an auto feature that lets residents take care of their needs, but just selecting someone was such a pain. But if I need to be selecting these people a lot, selecting them should be much, much easier.

So most of your time is spent repairing things, which is to say, you have someone stand there for hours. No challenge to it, it's just annoying. The charm of Sniper Elite V2 is probably based off of it's satisfaction-- that is the satisfaction of getting a long range headshot and-- holy♥♥♥♥♥♥I just blew off his entire top half of his skull!
Beyond that gameplay wise it is a stepup from Sniper Elite 1 and that it's more hands on persay-- more hop-into-the-action feeling. My three main complaints with the game is that it is much more linear this time around, giving you less chances to explore and find multiple angles and camp spots-- which is a shame for a game like this. My second complaint is that the AI is still rather dim, as one alerted guard quickly turns everything into a game of "Muzzle Flashing Whack a Mole" but with more Nazis and crushed skulls. This ties in with my third issue and that the stealth in this game that could of been, lacks. Stealth in this game is basically there just to set your starting up area and get whatever position you want before the rest of the enemies are alerted. I don't think it's possible to play the whole game undetected, unless of course you want to stick to the welrod.
Due to the issues above, the idea of this being an open world exploritive sniper game kinda dwindles down into a bunch of mad quick-finger killing sprees, which isn't so bad because the game itself is fun.
It's not a bad game, it's just a very simplistic one, but nontheless it is quite enjoyable and worth a couple of hours to kill for sure.
Then there is the multiplayer...
The multiplayer is...surprisingly fun. The constant struggle for keeping your score, that fear and caution you get trying to hunt down the other player (unless there is a bunch, then it becomes a war-party of speed and reflexes) is so enjoyable and at times immersive, It makes the MP in this game worth a mention, because holy goddamn is it fun. Get friends, snipe eachother in the face, and laugh when you win.
Get it on a sale.

Not a review, just a comment about the feature list on the store page:
This game's main meat is its campaign. The playtime depends on how thoroughly the environment is explored for items/notes and how fast the puzzles are solved. It took me more then 15h with my cautious and thorough playstyle. The game also contains different endings based on your actions near the end of the game.
Alongside the main game comes the expansion "Justine" and "Remember", a short story collection in form of a PDF file, both accessible via the launcher (or directly in the game folder in case of "Remember").
Justine is a <1h short campaign consisting of 4 levels. It features permadeath, different endings and collectable notes.
Remember consists of five stories spread across 54 pages with some accompanying pictures.
Additionally fan made Custom Stories can be added to the game and accessed in the main menu.
Contains 17 achievements for the main game and Justine.
Almost full support. Creating a profile enables you to enter a name for the profile. Using a controller restricts you to the ingame keyboard that consist only of 0-9, A-Z and a-z. No symbols or special letters.
Also the primary keys (mostly mapped to keyboard/mouse buttons) can't be changed via controller. Only secondary keys.
There is a "subtitles" (for spoken text) and a "effect subtitles" (for effect voices) checkbox.
Seven languages are selectable in the launcher:
Português brasileiro, English, Français, Deutsch, Italiano, Russian, Español
I played it with English Audio and Subtitles. Aside from that I can't tell you which parts (audio, subs, CC) are actually localised. You might want to check
for that.
Almost all actions* are bound, but are not rebindeable.
*The dedicated actions "Lean Left" and "Lean Right" are not bound, but they are just shortcuts for the general "Lean" action combined with a direction.
The aforementioned Custom Stories can be created with tools given by the publisher, but they are not packaged with the game.

for more.

Quake 2 is one of my favourite FPS games from the '90s. It is nice to see it available in a digital format and playable even after 20 years of its release. Naturally, the graphics look quite dated but there are dozens of mods out there ready to provide you with the necessary remedy.
I remember using the Railgun here which became a franchise favourite (hardcore gamers always wanted to use this in Quake 3 against the A.I.-controlled bots). Also, from Doom the BFG weapon was included as perhaps the most devastating weapon in our assortment. As for the levels: objective-based they are and we have lots of wide, open areas. And finally some cutscenes explaining what is going on.
Forget Quake's dark fantasy environment and welcome a sci-fi milieu where mankind is fighting the Strogg civilization. I can't help but think of Star Trek's Borgs whenever I see some of the game's enemies. Our hero is the sole survivor of a crash and since he crash-lands at a key location on the Strogg home planet his superiors entrust him with solving their little problem once and for all. The title has nothing to do with the entity encountered in the 1st episode - the name was not changed as keeping the word made sales better.
Quake 2 had a fast-paced gameplay with really cool music (here non-existent, unfortunately, similarly to the issue experienced in Quake 1) and a long-lasting single player experience. A must-have classic and - for me - the best in the franchise.

I had seen mixed thoughts on this game, but thought I would give it a try.
I'm always very interested in ancient greek mythology, so that in itself is a major draw to this game. While the story is very reminiscent of another greek mythology game (*cough* God of War *cough*), the way it was presented set it on its own.
The art style is awesome, it's bold colors and just oozes with greek influence. It felt like I was playing a story book that was made by the ancient greeks themselves.  There is a nice variety of locals as well as your move throughout the story. While the graphics looked great, there were some slowdown issues with the framerate despite having a fairly powerful PC. They would come at random times, independant of what was going on during that particular moment.
The other part of the game that made it a very positive experience for me was the combat. Its difficult, it has a high learning curve (in my opinion), but its *satisfying*. Once you figure out how you have to space yourself for different weapon types, and how you have to actually aim your ranged weapons, it becomes very natural. I was FRUSTRATED at first, so expect that, but know the more you practice with it, the better the game becomes. You can't expect to just run in and kill everything without timing your attacks and blocks, or you'll die horribly (as I did at first).
There were a couple annoyances with the game I should mention too. For one, unless I missed some control, the map can't be moved around to search the area. This makes looking through a large map impossible, which is necessary sometimes when trying to figure out where treasure chests are, where an objective is located at specifically, or if you've already gone a certain way. Second, the weapon breaking system. It adds a degree of realism, and it allows you to try different weapons when one breaks, but it still was annoying. I enjoyed playing with the sword the most, but it always broke way too easily. I understand what the devs were trying to do with it, but it just detracts from the fun a bit in my opinion.
TL;DR
Overall, the game is a lot of fun, with great unique graphics, and very fun gameplay. The story is not very unique, but enjoyable. The map could use some tweaks, and the weapon breakage system detracts from the fun a bit. Still a highly recommended game!

This here, my review, is going to be, different. I plan not only to give my opinion but consider and somehow appeal to others opinions.
Let me start by saying that despite my original review (which was short and wrong on so many levels) i do not LOVE this game, but i do not hate it. It is fun at times when you have taken your time to learn the maps, the dino's, and just how the game works. For most this is a downside and i can understand why, most feel a game should be fun from the moment you start not after you learned everything, but what we forget is any game requires you to learn, the difference is that some games try to make your learning prosess fun, this game doesnt do so, but (in my opinion) with good reason. before i continue with my offtopic chatting i will like to say that as the game currently is i would have given this game a neutral raiting, unfortunetly that is not a option.
As i was saying before the game does not make the process of learning fun for the player but with a good reason. This a survival (slash horror when humans and canibals and such come) game that is ment to be very brutal, with the god given happiness of knowing that you can try again so long as your willing to. instead of "hey, you died? well good luck getting back to where you were on this server because now everyone can take your place!" some may disagree with this statement and believe me i know why, in progression (which is soon getting removed when the new gamemode is ready) if you die you must start back from the bottom, BUT, as i said. No one can take your place, if you are willing to take the time to try again you CAN reach the point at which you were again. This may change with humans but there not here yet so we will wait and see.
Speaking of humans, lets discuse something about them quickly, humans are a interesting bunch, with the information dondi has shared they will change the game greatly, so, where are they? I have seen two groups of people in the community, those who dont want humans, and those who are still asking "where are they?" then there's that side group off the second group who dislike the game because humans arent in yet. Dondi has said that the humans will be finished (if not already) and added AFTER everything the dev team want done with the dinosaurs is complete. For those of us who animate on any scale (2d, 3d, for game's, for youtube, ect.) will probably agree that dinosaurs are comparitivly harder to animate then humans, some may disagree but then again they either never animated a dinosaur before or are just really good at animating animals like dinosaurs. or im wrong and they are actually easy, thats very possible, personally i find them easy but thats only because i only animate dinosaurs, but i know people who find it rather difficult. anyways back on track. Dinosaurs still lack many things, proper turning animations, some cant swim, some that can jump dont have a jumping animation, yada yada yada. aswell most of the dinosaurs lack ther own mechanics, this is why i personally find playing apex's like rex and spino rather boring. right now dinosaurs lack there intended mechanics to make them fun, spino is supposedly going to be able to fish and walk on the bottom of lakes under water while rex can pick up and crush small creatures in its jaws, without these functions the animals become boring, always being stronger then all the other animals and tanky. by that point a apex may only fear another apex and even THEN nothing changes. to some it up quickly, dinosaurs need to be finished before humans can join the carnage.
A previous statement that leads me into this topic is, blanace. As this game currently stands, the dinosaurs are not balanced in most situations. I personally give this a pass as the animals, again, lack there intended and unique mechanics that MAKE them fun or balanced. Is there a way to fix the game currently so till these mechanics are ready the game is blanaced? well... no. you can nerf and buff things over and over and over but that will always create a new problem over and over and over. I understand others want balance now, but its not very easy to give them that when the mechanics needed to do so arent finished or implomented yet. So for the time being id say, fight what you know you can, and run from what you cant.
Another thing i see comonly talked about is gameplay. As it currently stands in the two original gamemodes (sandbox and progression) the process is simple. eat, drink, hide, reapeat. and in progression the process is reapeated until you can progress to the next dino. And in both death is not a issue because you can get back to where you were in either a few clicks or a quick nesting from friends or someone in the server. Nesting may be one of the only currently interesting processes in the game because once you nest someone you must (more like can but lets assume its necesary) care for another life ontop of your own, and make sure that child becomes a subadult so they can progg or respawn as a adult. BUT this will change, see, a new gamemode is coming. survival. sandbox will become a mod and progression will be lost in the winds of time. so what have the devs said about this new gamemode?
The new gamemode coming to the isle, survival mode, will become the enbodyment (im sure iv spelt that wrong) of what the game was intended to be, on a over extended reprisentation of dondi's words. The game will now have the fallowing function, you may start as any dinosaur you please from the ones available (once the gamemode is fully launched that will limit you to four dinosaurs for the time being, others will come when there mechanics are ready aswell as there lifestages. Which brings me to the next point, after you solect the dino you will not start as a full grown adult but instead a juvinile (if you are nested you start as a hatchling) and you must survive till you are a adult. a much different play as juviniles cant quite as easily commit the "stay in one place while reapeating a simple set of actions" gameplay style currently seen without a adult to protect them. once a dinosaur has reached adulthood they recive a unlock token, what does this do? well you can then unlock any of the other dino's you wish to play, and unlike progression, you will get to keep those dinosaurs for as long as the server isnt reset. meaning that even if you die, you can still play the dinosaur you unlocked. (disclaimer, you cannot unlock a new dinosaur then switch back to the first one you unlocked to get another token, you must complete the new dinos life cycle before you can get a new token.) with this new gamemode hopefully we can see more interesting gameplay, aswell, with the enitial limited playable dinosaurs, the team can focuse more on the dinosaurs unique mechanics and make things even more interesting.

Apotheon is a fantastic adventure/side-scroller. The art is beautiful, the story is great, the fighting system is pretty solid. There's plenty to do but not so much that you'll be overwhelmed. I usually don't feel led to accomplish a ton of side quests that only amount to extra loot or require a lot of running around, but something about Apotheon genuinely made me want to. Maybe it was the rich world the story takes place in, I'm not quite sure, but it was something I've found lacking in a lot of other similar games that give you free reign to explore.
Sure, the game has its setbacks. Sometimes you get absolutely bombarded by enemies and it gets repetitive or stressful, the default controls can be a bit awkward (especially if you're left-handed like me, even though I'm used to having to mess around with controls for Steam games), and the game has crashed on me a couple time, but it auto-saves frequently, so it's generally no big deal.
I also adore how the developers took so much time to research and properly implement different aspects of ancient Greek mythology, art, and culture into the game, you can tell a lot of love went into it. This game has made it into my top 10 favorite video games in record time, and I'm definitely looking forward to whatever the developer, Alien Trap is planning next.

Before I bought this game I had a quick scroll through reviews and most seemed to be one of two things.
OR
I agree with the latter. Both games feature turn-based tactical combat and squad customisation but that is where the similarities end. Instead of individual turns for squad members, you plan out the paths for your men, then you press the breach button and each soldier runs forth like a human weapon, pouring shots into balaclava-clad enemies. Each planning phase takes minutes but the actual real time mission plays out in a matter of seconds.
I started up the game and was presented with a choice of various world special forces to play as; each with their own minor differences. I chose the SAS because it was the obvious choice (who wouldn't want to be the SAS). You get to travel to various parts of the world conducting three different brands of mission. You kill terrorists, you defuse a bomb and kill terrorists, you kill terrorists. Despite the lack of variation between the mission types the different environments are fun and the basic narratives provided give you some context as to why you are shooting these terrorists/seperatists/diisgruntled blokes. There is a rudimentary leveling up system in which you can upgrade the various skills of each of your 4 squad mates including their class specific skills. The game also has two currencies. You gain star ratings for missions and stars unlock new missions and new guns while silver allows you to buy new weapons, weapon customisations, aesthetics, new gear and consumables. It's simple system but works rather well.
TL:DR -
+ Be the SAS
+ Bring Freedom to Heathen Terrorists
+ 8.5/10

- Not enough Content

Really fun squad-based strategy game. Says what it has and has what it says. Although the maps aren't randomly generated, there are quite a lot of them, and each time you play a mission on a given map the enemy placement is randomized, so there's solid replay value here. Building your squad is fun, and permadeath (which is option, but gives you a massive XP boost if you activate it) makes your decisions carry weight. Gun customization for your squad members is extensive; MUCH more than I'd have expected from a game of this type. Everything from the sights to the gas system to the trigger of every individual gun can be customized to suit your squad members' strengths.
In summary, excellent game. It can be even better, and I hope one day they'll make a game with procedurally generated missions, perhaps with an even greater variety of objectives. But even as it stands right now, this game was worth the price in my opinion.

It's the best thing out there for a room clearing CQB sim right now (at least until Door Kickers comes out).  The mechanics and engines are tight.  The character classes, skill development and kit building keep the gameplay interesting.  Each campaign has a distinct art style, and later campaigns introduce increasingly tricky scenarios including armored enemies, outdoor terrain, and entrenched marksmen.
The main downside is that I wish there was a narrative to it.  Each campaign is really just a set of five maps with the same art style.  You unlock campaigns as you go, and can bounce around as you please.  It's nothing like Frozen Synapse where the missions are plot driven.
As for other wishlist items, I'm sure destructable terrain would have been a pain to implement, but could have really changed gamplay.  There's also no multiplayer mode (like you'd even be able to find players for such a niche game?)  It's kinda strange you can't break-up or shuffle team-members short of getting somebody killed.  Having to build and separately level full teams is a grindy proposition should the player want to go that route.
For those unfamiliar with room-clearing, a more theory based tutorial might be better.  The devs designed the game to reward actual room-clearing tactics.  In room-clearing, the objective is to stay on the attack while not getting shot in th back.  If you're constantly camping behind cover, (like every-other game with a cover-dynamic encourages), you're not getting it.  Get away from the fatal funnel, stay agile, and learn how to sweep geometries.  If a room looks scary, toss grenade/flashbang before you breach.  Unlike the old Rainbow Six or the SWAT series, there's no incentive for restraint in this game (RoE, neutrals, civilians, surrendering enemies), so let the grenades fly.
All in all, it's good little single-player indie tactics game.  It's worth you time if you'd dig a fairly authentic room-clearing sim.

A classic. While the horror has worn out nowadays, the gameplay is still very fun. It's not too hard to pick up and play, as it's basically "Shoot things and pick up keys". Don't expect a riveting plot. There are "cutscenes" at the end of the episodes but they're mainly very basic and slightly snarky.
A recommendation I have is to download a source port (EG. ZDoom or Zandronum) so you can try the mods. The mods are the main things that keep me coming back. While the game itself is fair enough, the mods just add to the fun. Especially ones that replace weapons and monsters. Heck, I've made a few myself.
Expect lots of pixelated and cheesy gore with satanism that looks like stuff out of a 90s rock band. While back in the day it was shocking, it's mainly kind of corny. It doesn't effect the gameplay value, however.
Anyways, this is a good game and you should try it. If you like FPSes and don't just limit yourself to modern day shooters like CoD, you might like it.

A short but enjoyable deduction puzzle game.
Hook is extremely minimalist. In fact the menu screen is itself the first puzzle of fifty.  In each level you must carefully toggle switches so that when you push one of the dark circles (which you could think of as sending an electric pulse down that wire) then all connected wires will retract their "hook".  I call them "hooks" but it's hard to describe what that means.  They are the bolded lines you see.  If you make a mistake by trying to retract a hook that will run into another one, you start the puzzle again.
The game is paced extremely well, and even without a tutorial the game is immediately intuitive and new gameplay mechanics (switches mostly) are introduced at just the right times and the player is never left confused about how to proceed.
The visual aesthetic is perfect for the game.  Everything is black and white but you will never find yourself wishing the game was colourful.  Background music and sound effects won't grab your attention but they don't need to.
The only real downside is the game's length; People used to puzzle games will likely finish the game in under an hour, where they will get the game's only achievement!  The game is very cheap though so it's reasonable for it to be as short as it is.
Overall, highly recommended!

Canabalt is one of the first of the modern endless runners in the modern era.   I remember playing it originally on Kongregate in 2009.  So it's an old game, but the game published on steam is similar to the one that was originally put on Kongregate.
Canabalt is pretty simple.  You're a guy, you start running forward, and you slowly speed up, you try to avoid boxes and other things that might slow you down and you avoid falling off buildings. While simple in concept, there's a surprising amount of gameplay for the game, as well as strategies (for instance hitting a box may be helpful if you're moving too fast, but then you might not have enough speed to make a jump).
Instead of just the pure endless runner, which is contained here. Canabalt also includes a variety of different "zones" each focusing on a specific challenge, whether crashing through windows, dodging bombs, invisible roofs, or so on.  These zones are simple one offs, but some of them are quite challenging, and it helps the player to practice a specific skill.
Canabalt never really rises beyond it's relatively simple premise, however it offers a lot of challenge, and because the stages are random, it gives you a "one more try" type of feel.  There's a wonderfully developed two player mode which allows the players to compete against themselves or cooperate at the same time, it's up to the players to see who went farther, but the two scores are added together, so it's a collaborative experience.
I recommend the game to people who want a simple fast game, they can play endlessly.    It won't be for everyone, and at 3 bucks, the game might be pushing the price, but if you get into it, it can give you many hours of fun.  The different zones will likely take you an hour to beat just for achievements, and then to get the distance, there's a lot of challenge, so it can takes you quite a long time to beat.
