The one here on Steam is a port of the HD mobile version which was a port of the flash version.
There's only one control, which is the jump button. By default the jump button is set to the spacebar, LMB, and (A) button on a 360 controller. You can rebind all of those as well as the 2P controls available. The 2P is local only.
It's a 2D game through and through but you can turn on the "3D" settings which just makes the game 2.5D, as in it's played in 2D but the backgrounds and models are in 3D. They can get a little distracting and because this game's also part platformer, it can possibly make judging platform distance a little more of a task.
The music here's pretty nice but most of it doesn't seem appropriate for a game about running. Maybe for what's going on in the background but, it being a game, I'm more focused on what I'm doing than what's around me.
The concept of the game's very simple, which is just to run endlessly to the right as far as you can without dying via falling or exploding, the latter being a rare case. Your high score in this case is obviously how far you went from the starting point to where you died.
As you automatically run, all you're to do is jump from platform to platform avoiding pitfalls, boxes, and bombs. Pitfalls and bombs are obvious deaths but tripping hazards such as boxes & chairs are there to slow you down. Annoying, but those hazards can also be a life saver. The longer you run uninterrupted the faster you get until you hit a point where luck becomes a bit more of a factor than skill. Eventually you'll be going so fast that the next time you jump you'll likely still be in mid-air before the next platform even comes on screen, leaving you almost no time to do anything or even make a judgement on what to do next. That problem is supposedly accomadated by the hazards' ability to slow you down but unfortunately luck also plays a part here as well since there's a good chance that a box may not come to slow you down when you need it the most. If you're too slow because you've been hitting boxes in succession then there's a really good chance you won't be fast enough to jump to where you need to be as the only way to speed up is to keep running without interruption. In short, proper management of hitting the tripping hazards can very much help with survival.
The 2P is pretty weak and doesn't really encourage a fun time since either player can't help one another in any way, but only hinder.
It's a co-op based multiplayer somehow and you're on the same exact screen running together on the same path, only player 2 always has the slight disadvantage at the start of each run because player 2 is always slightly ahead of player 1, leaving player 2 to have less screen space than 1. If one player hits a tripping hazard then the other player goes ahead of them, leaving less and less screen space for the runner who just went ahead. After a certain time passes with both players not being interrupted by a hazard then the both of 'em end up to the left of the screen again, usually a little slightly apart than they were when they started.
If one player dies, for some reason the screen progressively scrolls impossibly faster. Your jumps look cooler because of how far you jump as a result but because you won't know what platform's going to come up next due to how fast the screen moves you'll eventually die. So if one player loses, the other's screwed as a result.
The score in the end is the sum of the distance both players have accumulated. You can play the 2P mode by yourself.
There are some other "game modes" available but all they do is make each hazard more abundant in each mode except for a couple where one mode makes the platforms invisible and the other has
platforms but
hazards. Basically each mode is the same exact thing with just a tweak or two to it.
It's a quick little time-waster and the game's alright at being that, but that's about it. No technical problems as far as I'm concerned either.
The flash version is still officially free on other sites, which is practically the entirety of this game.
Probably the only good reason maybe to actually buy this game is to support the developers and even then it's probably best to just stick with the mobile version.

I played on the mod KMQuake2 because it supports widescreen and high-fps.
(Hence the low amount of registered gameplay)
I really enjoyed playing this game. I will just mention my impression of the game here.
Gameplay is very well-balanced.  It keeps almost all the good things from Quake 1 in terms of weapons and pickups, and except for a few flaws, it is very well-done.There are a wide variety of enemies, that do not only range from weak to tough, but often have specific quirks and strenghts/weaknesses. This makes tactical gameplay possible. The typical progression is at hand in the campaign: Enemies are getting tougher, but you get also stronger weapons and resources. Also, for those unfamiliar with Quake 1, the game also features a heavier, more ammo-wasting weapon and a weaker, more ammo-preserving weapon for most types of ammo, which I really like. A cool new thing is that enemies dodge some of the stuff that is coming at them, which works pretty okay.
What I truly love about Quake 2 is that it really manages to balance things in a way that it is hard, yet fair. Actions have consequences, and that makes for particularly good gameplay at times. For example, I had a fight on an open field where I was very low on health, and I had a ton of ranged enemies coming at me. I recognized I was going to be in trouble, fled into a small, unknown corridor, fought one guy there and get health- and ammo-pickups, enabling me to recover and fight from a much more advantaged position because these enemies were quite clunky. However, some other enemies (like the berserker) would have been much more dangerous in small corridors. This way of fighting yourself out of situations is very cool to do and adds another layer to the gameplay.
Some minor cons about the gameplay are:
The removal of the airstrafing as seen in Quake 1, which makes movement less enjoyable.
Throwing grenades doesn't work well, so find a grenade launcher
Some enemies will shoot at you from great heights, resulting in you being very randomly shot from annoying places
On the other hand, enemies really don't  know how to deal with players attacking from a higher place.
Boss fights are a bit anti-climactic and often easier than some small hordes of usual enemies.
The game is aesthetically very different from Quake 1. Quake 2 chooses for a futuristic setting with some relatable places, instead of the more abstract gothic-style interdimensional setting from Quake 1. Graphically, I'd say Quake 2 is an improvement, with more detailed environments in general.
The level design is generally well done. Quake 2 features 'hub-gameplay': The game sometimes lets you run back and forth between places to hack systems, unlock keys, and other stuff, which can set off alarms and alerts more enemies on the way. The game definitely feels more relatable to a real place because of this. One minor con is that you sometimes have to figure out where to go and run around in desolate places because you killed every enemy already. There are still plenty of secrets, and the game lets you use the environment in fights, for example you can sometimes lower bridges to let enemies burn/drown instead of directly fighting them. There is a paperthin storyline in the game, but you can just as well ignore that.
NOTE: THE STEAM VERSION DOES NOT CONTAIN A SOUNDTRACK AT ALL!
I personally was not bothered by this, but I know the removal of the soundtrack is a bad thing for this version. Just putting it out there.
TLDR: Weapons/ammo/pickups similar to Quake 1, gameplay well-balanced & fair, yet challenging, Quake 2 has a science-fiction setting with more relatable places, and improves slightly on graphics.  The game lets you free in the way you play and is very enjoyable.

Nether is a MMO game where you play as a survivor in an intense and realistic post-apocalyptic version of Chicago. You can scavenge, craft, hunt and trade loot and you try to survive. This game sounds awesome, the game trailers look good, but Nether is quite a let down.
The first complaint I have about Nether, is the server selection screen. It's very laggy, and I had to wait 10 minutes before I could move my mouse to go and select a server. Once I selected a server, the server selection screen kept glitching out and I had to go and select the server again before I could actually jump into the game and play.
Once I got into a server, things only got worse. The graphics are average, not too bad yet not that great, and the character customization options are limited and not too great. Some of the game's textures were muddy and not very good, and found my self being able to walk through every object in the game except for cars, walls and floors which were solid at least.
Nether's combat is implemented alright, but the balance between enemies that instantly spawn and your player isn't too fair, and you need to get better equipment or else you will be killed pretty quick. The scavenging system is cool, and I liked how you need to find gun parts to craft weapons. The enemies' in their current state aren't too impressive, as their textures are muddy, and when they die they just sink into the floor.
Nether also doesn't give you any explanation of what is going on, or even how to play the game. Right when I started up the game it was showing a bunch of objectives to complete without giving me any explanation on how to complete them. Also, Nether lacks any sort of tutorial, which is not good news for new players. It just throws you in the game and expects you to know everything already.
Nether in a nutshell, is a buggy game that needs a lot of work. There is little here that is actually fun, but I'm hoping the developers will take the time to work on this game and deliver some new updates to the players, because this game has so much potential. I will update my review scores as the game is updated, but for now the game is difficult to recommend.

As stated above, I consider myself a individual well verse in Greek myth and it's Aesthetics. I say this in regard to why I think this game is probably the first of it's kind to seamlessly blend Greek iconography into a video game.
The art is immediately distinctive, and go's beyond just a pretty background
The art work is a stark reminded that this is actually how people; circa 500-300BC did ART, with some of the darker levels (Hades' realm for example) styled in old Athenian "BlackFigure' style, while the majority of the game plays in different palettes. The God's themselves are the stars of the show; with some being monstrosity tall and the ability to deal gigantic damage to boot, or the more cunning Gods, which use cunning or subterfuge to try and stop you.
I won't go into the story too much. The simple plot remains that the Gods have turned against humanity and Nikandreos, resident Greek villager turned Epic Hero must stop them from wiping them out. If this sounds cliche, that's because it is, but only to the modern eye. We live in a society where most media have butchered much of Greek Myth. This is not one of those pieces of media. Apotheon  reflecting a far older brand of storytelling.
Unfortunately, players will probably notice the game shares many of its narrative threads with God of War, but the differences pile up quickly. Where God of War sticks to video game tropes, Apotheon is content to ground itself in ancient myth. I find this to be a strike in Apotheon's favor.
In gameplay terms it's 2-parts Castlevania or Metroid, and 1-part Legend of Zelda 2. During this side scroller you'll forced to engage in combat and a little bit of platforming and open level design which scrolls in all directions. Each of the game's areas contains various objectives that must first be completed, then usually conclude against  the realms master as a boss, or trial.
The common pit falls of it's genre show through however. Too often you'll find yourself wailing on an enemy hoping that a good hit lands, or that you're weapon won't suddenly snap in two and you'll be left with only a dagger to poke at the giant Cyclops roaring for your nu**s. Another common problem I found was that sometimes, when both parties were melee focused, we'd be hacking at each other with neither hitting because the hitboxes didn't register super close hits.
Everything else seems to be good however. You can use a multitude of different weapons to kill your enemy's with including Spears, Bow&Arrows, Swords, Maces, Glaves, Hammers, Rocks, and explosives.
Soundtrack wise; it's passable. I found myself mildly surprised that a game with such insane visuals would have such a mediocre OST. To be fair however, soundtracks are often one of the harder development processes for Indie devs.
An exceptional oddity in our world of graphical powerhouses' like Crysis and Battlefield. This game to me looks better than all of them simply due to it's art style.
The combat is rock solid to, and the game boasts a fun story for you to keep you invested.
Slightly harder to justify at Retail price, but under any discount this becomes a steal. A definite recommendation to anyone with a passing interest in myth, Metroidvania, or looks for a fun distraction.

This game is really good but I dont wanna do a review. So heres how to make Enchiladas:
1 Preheat oven to 350 degrees F.
2 In a large frying pan at medium-high heat add a tablespoon of oil. When the oil is shimmering and hot (not quite smoking), add a corn tortilla to the pan. Cook it for 2-3 seconds, use a metal spatula to turn it over, and cook it for 2 to 3 seconds more. Lift up the tortilla with a spatula, add another tortilla underneath. Cook the second tortilla for 2-3 seconds, lift both tortillas, and add another tortilla underneath. Repeat the process with all the tortillas, adding more oil as needed. This way you can brown and soften the tortillas without using a lot of fat. It's important to pre-cook the tortillas because not only does cooking them help soften them for rolling, cooking them in a little fat helps develop the flavor of the tortillas. As the tortillas brown a little, remove them to a plate.
3 Heat olive oil in a large sauté pan on medium heat. Add the chopped onion and cook for 5-6 minutes, until translucent. Add the garlic and cook for a minute more. Add the crushed tomatoes. Add the green chiles. Add 1/2 cup of water. Add the oregano. Bring to a simmer and taste. If the sauce tastes too vinegary, add half a teaspoon of sugar to the sauce. Remove from heat.
3 Put a little olive oil on the bottom of a 3-quart casserole pan. Take a tortilla, cover 2/3 of it lightly with the shredded cheese, then roll up the tortilla and place it in the casserole pan. Continue until all tortillas are filled and rolled.
4 Add sauce to the top of the tortillas in the the casserole pan. Make sure the rolled up tortillas are covered with the sauce. If not, add a little water to thin the sauce to spread it more evenly over the tortillas. Cover the whole thing with the rest of the grated cheese. Put the casserole in the oven for 10-15 minutes or until the cheese melts.
Serve with sliced iceberg lettuce that has been dressed only with vinegar and salt. Garnish enchiladas with cilantro and sour cream.
Here is the full wiki for Enchiladas:
Enchiladas originated in Mexico, where the practice of rolling tortillas around other food dates back at least to Maya times. The people living in the lake region of the Valley of Mexico traditionally ate corn tortillas folded or rolled around small fish. Writing at the time of the Spanish conquistadors, Bernal Díaz del Castillo documented a feast enjoyed by Europeans hosted by Hernán Cortés in Coyoacán, which included foods served in corn tortillas. (Note that the native Nahuatl name for the flat corn bread used was tlaxcalli; the Spanish give it the name tortilla.) The Nahuatl word for enchilada is chīllapītzalli  which is formed of the Nahuatl word for "chili", and the Nahuatl word for "flute". In the 19th century, as Mexican cuisine was being memorialized, enchiladas were mentioned in the first Mexican cookbook, El cocinero mexicano ("The Mexican Chef"), published in 1831, and in Mariano Galvan Rivera's Diccionario de Cocina, published in 1845. An early mention, in English, is a 1914 recipe found in California Mexican-Spanish Cookbook, by Bertha Haffner Ginger.
Varieties - In their original form as Mexican street food, enchiladas were simply corn tortillas dipped in chili sauce and eaten without fillings. There are now many varieties, which are distinguished primarily by their sauces, fillings and, in one instance, by their form. Various adjectives may be used to describe the recipe content or origin, e.g. enchilada tapatia would be a recipe from Jalisco.
Varieties include:
Enchiladas con chile rojo (with red chile) is a traditional red enchilada sauce, composed of dried red chili peppers soaked and ground into a sauce with other seasonings, Chile Colorado sauce adds a tomato base.
Enchiladas con mole, instead of chili sauce, are served with mole, and are also known as enmoladas.
Enchiladas placera are Michoacán plaza-style, made with vegetables and poultry.
Enchiladas poblanas are soft corn tortillas filled with chicken and poblano peppers, topped with oaxaca cheese.
Enchiladas potosinas originate from San Luis Potosi, Mexico and are made with cheese-filled, chili-spiced masa.
Enchiladas San Miguel are San Miguel de Allende-style enchiladas flavored with guajillo chilies by searing the flavor into the tortillas in a frying pan.
A plate of enchiladas suizas.
Enchiladas suizas (Swiss-style) are topped with a white, milk or cream-based sauce, such as béchamel. This appellation is derived from Swiss immigrants to Mexico who established dairies to produce cream and cheese.
Enfrijoladas are topped with refried beans rather than chili sauce; their name come from frijol, meaning "bean".
Entomatadas are made with tomato sauce instead of chile sauce.
Enchiladas montadas, stacked enchiladas, are a New Mexico variation in which corn tortillas are fried flat until softened but not tough, then stacked with red or green sauce, chopped onion and shredded cheese between the layers and on top of the stack. Ground beef or chicken can be added to the filling, but meat is not traditional. The stack is often topped (montada) with a fried egg. Shredded lettuce and sliced black olives may be added as a garnish.

Working with such compelling proprietary content, Telltale, the reigning champions of turning licenced properties into enjoyable adventure games, could only do so wrong.  And they almost do that wrong, but they salvage a playable experience through a fun story, strong voice acting and writing, and impeccable faithfulness to the tone and spirit of the beloved Back to the Future franchise.
To stress, the gameplay itself is not the draw.  Puzzles act as minor speedbumps on the way to advancement of the story and dialogue.  The control scheme, identical to that of earlier Wallace and Gromit and Monkey Island offerings, clearly favors a console/controller over a mouse/keyboard setup.  The bulk of content is a bit too dialogue heavy which eventually causes the games to drag.   Unlike the aforementioned W&G and MI series that could rely heavily on absurdism humor in the dialogue, Back to the Future conversations are generally coherent --though certainly funny in their own way .  So a surfeit of quality writing and acting --especially by Christopher Lloyd! -- does truly feel like too much.
Nonetheless, the game gets a thumbs up, albeit a very tepid one.
Gameplay can be fun most of the time if i'm able to play. But I can feel this game getting really stale in a month or so.

My search for a historic game that is open-ended stops with The Guild II Renaissance.  The game is so non-restricting that open-ended is the best way to describe it.  It is a city builder/economic/RPG/strategy/medieval/criminal game.  Trust me when I say that this description doesn’t describe the game well enough.  Which is why I say that open-ended is the best way to describe it.  The only limits that I can find are the skills that your characters lack and the map sizes.
The only down side that I can understand some may find is learning the game mechanics.  There isn’t a good description of the game mechanics in the manual.  Holding down the RMB while hovering over anything in the game gives a description, but the description isn’t detailed enough to fully understand the mechanics of an action.
Example: Your thugs have an action button that says rob, but if you click that button you cannot select anyone to rob.  The thugs also have an attack button, and if you attack any non-family rogue unit they fight to the death (these types of units are the most common units to get in general fights with as they are commonly guards and attackers).  But every other character when attacked and loses the fight will be knocked unconscious.  It is when they are unconscious that you can select them to be robbed by you thugs.
Although I understand how some will see this as a negative quality, I have not found it too hard to figure out how most of the mechanics work.  I’ve been able to find solutions on the internet to anything I couldn’t figure out on my own.  Every time I find out how something works, the game only gets better.
I bought the game on sale for $2.49.  Now that I know how good this game is I would pay the full price of $9.99.  Ten dollars for hours of fun is well worth it to me.
I give this game 10/10.  The only other thing I can think to say is I can’t wait for The Guild 3 to come out.

I picked this up as part of the Telltale Games pack when it was on sale. I was mainly after the Sam & Max series so this was more of a bonus than anything.
Having finally got around to playing it I have to admit it's much better than I thought it would be. The attention to detail and the sympathetic way they have stayed faithful to the original premise makes it a pleasure to play. The story is fairly well constructed and (without giving too much away) the way the series ending pokes fun at itself made me chuckle. The whole series doesn't take itself too seriously and that is to its credit.
The good bits: The voice acting is superb. Christopher Lloyd! Even though Marty wasn't voiced by MJ Fox (who does do some cameos) I would not have known without looking. It is that good. The story holds together well with some nice plot twists not all of which are obvious.  It's a Telltale point-and-click adventure which I tend to like anyway. It doesn't penalise you for exploring or even trying something stupid. Fans of the films are going to appreciate the faithful reproduction of the BTTF universe with plenty of references to film trivia.
The bad bits: The graphics aren't exactly photo realistic but they are good enough in a cartoon spin-off way. Some of the puzzles are just a case of going through the motions rather than any significant problem solving ability. I don't think you'll get stuck very often so if it's a challenge you want then this might not be it. Each episode is probably only 2 or 3 hours of gameplay depending on how many of the dialogue options you explore.
If you like this type of game then you could do far worse. If there were a second season I would buy it although I might still yearn for a little more depth to the puzzles.  As I'm generally a miser when it comes to paying for games I'd say its full price is a little too high, but if you like this sort of game and see it in the sale I'd go for it. Recommended.

Good
The artwork - Absolutely beautiful. This is probably the prettiest game I have ever played.
The Story - The story is clever and is tight enough to be told purely through stuff that actually happens in game, so there is zero mucking around with a billion codex pages like some games.
Level design - Every level is challenging in it's own way, and no two levels will be resolved in the same situation, some will require a stealthy approach, some will require straight out bloodshed, and some will need brains rather than brawn.
Subject matter - This game delves far into greek mythology and is excellent in using it.
Combat - Combat is challenging, but if you take enemies as they arrive, it is usually quite manageable, and will leave you with a sense of accomplishment after the more difficult enemies.
Teaching the player - This game sort of throws the player right into the thick of it and teaches as it goes. It teaches everything you need to know without being too heavy or too light with the explanations.
Bad
Controls - With a keyboard the controls are somewhat clunky and some attacks, especially the bow, are very slow to respond. I even had some occurences where some of the more exotic weapons completely broke down, and prevented me from attacking, and one situation where I just stopped being able to block for no reason. The clunckiness of the controls also means that the platforming parts are usually a chore.
Weapons/Items - There are far too many weapons and items in this game. There's 4 different categories of melee weapons, and then probably 5 or 6 different types within each category, and you can usually carry at least one of each type. When you combine that with all the shields, arrows, slings, potions, traps, etc, your inventory is quite difficult to manage.
Finally, in my opinion the final boss fight area thing is utterly terrible. I found it so bad that rather than feeling like I achieved something, finishing the game just left a bad taste in my mouth. The entire section just completely ignored all the strengths of the game and used level designs and mechanics that emphasised everything that was wrong with the game.
However, with the exception of the truly awful ending, I thoroughly enjoyed this game, and I would recommend it.

Back to the Future: The Game serves as a well written sequel to the cult film franchise.
The game is a classic Telltale game, 3rd person adventure style with controllable walking and interactive objects while moving the plot forward. The plot across the five episode are well thought out. Marty travels to 1931 to find Doc, who has disappeared and is delcared dead in 1986. The main events of the game take place in alternate time period of 1931 and 1986 while also unraveling mysters of Hill Valley. And in the end, everything is actually tied up, from Edna and Tannen to discovering who Trixie Trotter really is and meating Marty's ancestors. The game does leave an ambiguity for a possible second season that Telltale haven't opened up about....yet.
The graphics are pretty standard for Telltale, a soft textures and average polygon models that sometimes look a little off. It does give a vibe of adventure in the style of how the characters were modeled though, I really like how Marty and Doc turned out.
Music and audio are great, nothing too special about them though.
Overall, this serves as a great add-on to the films and are just as scientific with theories new and old. Great game.

Firstly, this game was made in three days. I'll be taking this into account.
In lot of smaller games, the most part of the interest is in the gameplay itself. Here, however, the gameplay is just as interesting as the story and graphics. I'll explain why.
The very coherent story is compelling and realistic, while demonstrating the prowess of the developer's writing team. I won't spoil it here (I wouldn't be able to forgive myself), but a playthrough is relatively short, so you'll understand in no time.
This game manages to tell its story in a concise manner, using an inner monologue to explain the key themes thoroughly yet briefly. It even has time to include a reference to a movie.
The gameplay is where things get even better. Simplistic yet innovative, the controls handle well. Mobility in the game is non-existant, and yet this poses no problems. A traditional WASD setup with a couple of added buttons (that I'll let you discover for yourself!) allow for full control of the protagonist and the two side characters.
Graphically speaking, I had difficulty getting this game to run adequately on a 3000$ custom made gaming PC, however, once I scrapped it for a 15000$ PC the game handled well, disconcertingly well. There were times when I had to quit the game because the new age 3D graphics had me reeling and my eyes bleeding.
All in all, this is a stunning title, and free to play too. All we need now is a console release. 10/10 and highly recommended for GOTY.

Breach & Clear is an interesting marriage of Frozen Synapse's hybrid turn-based/real-time style of tactics gameplay with XCOM: Enemy Unknown’s customizable class-based soldiers and carefully-constructed mission levels, then given a Counter-Strike terrorists-vs.-special-forces makeover - right down to the almighty flashbang grenade.
Upon first starting up the game, the player will be greeted by a series of screens to set up their first squad.  They can choose from a variety of different special forces outfits from around the world, from the American Navy SEALS to the German Kommando Spezialkräfte, among others.
The player can choose the faces, names, and soldier classes for each member of their 4-man squad.  Each of the six classes has a unique role to play with their special abilities and passive traits, and having to choose which to bring and which to forego should be carefully considered, as it will significantly affect how you approach different situations from that point on.
Every mission starts by selecting which entry points to place the soldiers at before they storm the room, or otherwise enter the combat area.  Enemies inside rooms that have no open doors cannot be seen (conversely, every enemy in an outdoor area can be seen), meaning you will sometimes be storming a building blind.  As such, the player has to carefully survey the map layout, note cover near to every door, and account for every angle an enemy might be waiting at before breaching the entrance.  Sometimes it might even be favorable to split your team into two groups of two as opposed to keeping all four together.
At the start of each turn, the player will issue orders to all four of their soldiers during a “planning phase” - where to move (and along what path - an option XCOM sorely neglected), what direction to face, what inventory equipment or special abilities to use.  When everything is set, all four men will simultaneously execute your orders in real-time during an “action phase”, as will the enemies act.  Some of the enemies’ actions are proactive, and some are reactionary - especially in response to any grenades you throw.  This is unlike Frozen Synapse, where the enemy soldiers will follow their turn’s orders to a T regardless of what yours do.
This also leads to an important interesting factor introduced in Breach & Clear that XCOM notably fails to consider: noise.  Guns are loud, and if you hear a bunch going off in the next room, most militiamen would go check out what’s going on.  Every gun you give your soldiers and some modifications you can apply to said guns have a “noise” trait which affects how loud the weapon is.  The louder the guns in your squad, the more likely an unseen enemy in another room will come and investigate.  This can lead to some real “Oh shi-” panic moments if your men are caught flanked or out of cover when this happens, especially in areas with many closed doors and little cover - such as the living quarters on a cargo ship.  To account for this, the player must carefully position their soldiers to cover the squad’s flanks at all times, or trade in some lethality for low-profile, silenced guns.
There is a half cover/full cover system similar to the one in XCOM: different objects in the environment will either provide moderate or significant protection to the soldier behind it, depending on the object’s size.  There is one notable difference to XCOM’s implementation, especially on the higher difficulties: barring sniper rifles, soldiers shooting at each other from cover to cover will often have a very hard time actually scoring hits.  This forces the player to use all of the tools at their disposal to outmaneuver the enemy and gain flanking shots, rather than simply relying on a boosted aim stat.  This really strengthens the tactical depth of an otherwise relatively simple set of mechanics, which is great - it makes the fundamentals easy to grasp, but achieving victory is a very deliberate process that rewards planning and smart execution.
The soldier progression and customization system adds that XCOM-like personal attachment to your men.  As the player completes missions, they will unlock items for your men to use.  These items range from weapons and attachments to body armor and helmets to cosmetic-only elements like camouflage and sunglasses.  Each man can also be kitted out with two inventory items - typically a grenade of some kind or a medkit, or a revival defibrillator if your squad lacks a medic.
Completing missions will also earn each soldier XP.  As they level up, they will unlock new class-specific passive bonuses and, eventually, a powerful special ability that can only be used once per mission (for example, a Fireteam Leader can provide a “morale boost” that grants a large stat bonus to the entire squad for one turn).
Leveling up soldiers also allows the player to choose what stats to upgrade on a given soldier, whether it be how fast they can acquire targets, how far they can run in a turn, the effectiveness of their class bonus, etc.  This lets the player choose whether they want to make a squad of jacks-of-all-trades, or to specialize their soldiers to excel at certain things at the expense of others.  For example, Breachers (the grenade-tossing class that often leads the charge) might find specializing in health and target acquisition useful so that he can more effectively fight as he crosses open ground.
With the variety of mission environments offered by the game’s numerous mini-campaigns, collecting a range of gear - sniper rifles, machine guns, loud and silenced weapons, fast-but-light and slow-but-sturdy body armor, etc. - is important to maintaining a flexible force, especially considering that every level can be played in three different scenarios with varying levels of enemy numbers and emphasis on speed.  Overall, the persistent soldier system and surprising amount of content offers a considerable amount of gameplay for such a small title.
Despite all these features, Breach & Clear is not without its flaws.  The relative simplicity of the movement system compared to the one in Frozen Synapse - mainly the lack of an option to tell a soldier to wait a couple seconds before moving - can sometimes make synchronizing your soldiers’ actions difficult.  This is especially noticeable when attempting to follow a flashbang grenade into a room; it won’t stun your own soldiers, but it will give the enemy a moment to pepper your men with bullets as they enter before the grenade goes off.
Additionally (and this was an enormous gripe that I had with XCOM: Enemy Unknown, too), all the voiceovers are in a standard American English dialect, regardless of which international commando outfit your soldiers belong to.  Not only, but the vast majority of weapons in the game are ones used by the United States and Canada, despite the wide international breadth of options for the men themselves.  This can likely be attributed to the game originally launching with only American and Canadian task groups, with the others being added only later.  Given the size of the team making the game (spoiler alert: it’s pretty small), this is somewhat understandable, but it's still disappointing that I can't arm my Spetsnaz team with the latest Kalash AK-12s and have them bark responses in their native tongue - or at least in a cheesy Russian accent.
These blemishes, however, are relatively minor stumbles on what is, at its core, a very satisfying experience.  While the soldier progression system isn't quite as fleshed out as XCOM's, and the unit movement system not quite as intricate as Frozen Synapse's, the two fused together with the game’s own handful of unique features make a very fun and surprisingly deep tactics game that is both easy to pick up and complex to conquer.  For only $15, I would consider Breach & Clear worth checking out for any fan of tactics or small-scale strategy.

This is one hell of a game. 10/10. I love the strategy it takes to play this game; you can't just hand this game over to anybody and expect them to do great, there is a big learning curve that comes easily and will allow you to control every aspect of your characters. Not only do you tell your soldiers where to move, but also what path to take to get there, and what direction to face every step of the way. The character skills customization really allows you to get attached to your favorite characters and mourn when they die, permanently. The perma-death is an option though so you can choose how hard this game is for you and how strategic you have to force yourself to be. The controls are simple, but some of them you have to learn for yourself that the tutorial does not cover, like how not to open the door when you approach it and how to choose your path. Every mission earns you money and experience based on difficulty, speed, and overall skill and you spend that money equipping your squad with new weapons, attachments for your weapons, face masks, helmets, armor, clothing, and even the equipment they bring into the field. There are always multiple ways to complete a mission, and there is no set way of doing anything, you choose it all. I highly recommend this game to those looking for a great squad-based tactical game, to the fans of the XCOM and Shadowrun games, and anyone else who wants a game like this. If you want a typical FPS, control over just one character, or skill-less combat then I do not recommend this game to you.

A designer who understands the value of brevity & the efficacy of true minimalism as well as the complexity that comes with balancing so many elements.
The nature of the puzzles become perfectly clear through your interaction with it, no text offered and none needed. The learning curve is executed flawlessly. Rules are learned, mastered & retained before new rules are introduced.
A slight sense of dread at the beginning of each complex puzzle but resolve quickly takes over as the first element disappears from the screen after a succesful click. The gratification is immediate but it doesn't feel cheap. Resolve however, has a inverse relationship with tension. As you continue, the stakes are raised. If you ♥♥♥♥ up, you begin the level again.
Though tension excites but doesn't overwhelm thanks to its relatively short levels, soothing music, a neutral colour scheme and not obfuscating the screen with superfluous embellishment - though isn't devoid of character either. The formal qualities of the puzzles and the few necessary stylistic choices do not bore.
I like that there are no settings too - though it didn't scale properly in 21:9, so I did have to switch my resolution to 16:9.

Canabalt is a silent and modest game jam giant that was in the first wave of titles which drew attention to the emerging indie scene at the time. It was a groundbreaking game that popularized a subgenre of endless runner games, such as Race the Sun and BIT.TRIP Runner series in certain aspects. But does it still stand the test of time as a true classic?
Story wise, you are the Runner, an athlete who is running over the rooftops and is trying to avoid hitting any obstacle while there is an enigmatic, ongoing invasion happening. The story is minimal and its kept in the background, while the gameplay takes priority. Speaking of the gameplay, Canabalt shines in evoking rush of exhilaration through simple and tight controls: you only use one button in the game to jump. You can make light or high jumps depending on the force with which you push the button. There are various obstacles on tracks that are procedurally generated, which will cause the player more or less trouble, and sometimes will even help depending on the height of the jump and speed the player is running. Canabalt is a very fast game, where the speed of the protagonists progressively accelerates to ludicrous levels. Besides the endless main track, there are several modes of plays, each one focusing on one style of play and obstacle.
Visual presentation is still very good, with a minimalist and monochromatic graphics and a great attention to the details and animation that make Canabalt look vivid and evocative. There is only one, good music track that follows your ventures through the rooftops, and the sound is also minimalistic, but impactful.
But there are minuses in the game: there are many animation bugs that will pop up when you are reaching the maximum speed, that one music track is good but will get repetitive fast and procedurally generated course tracks aren’t as varied and interesting as they ought to be, and create that same-y feel in the long run, which is the game’s biggest letdown.
This was made by one man, and it is a stark achievement to be sure, but I can’t help but feel a little bit of indifferent to Canabalt. In the first hour of playing I was ecstatic and mesmerized, but the game shows all its tricks in less than 2 hours. After that, all that remains is the repetition and a ghost chase of getting back that feeling of being intoxicated with this game. Canabalt is a good game for the price developer is asking that simply runs out of fuel and magic tricks fairly quickly, a flawed classic.

You can pretty much sum up how great this game is just by observing how modern horror games draw their inspiration from the Amnesia series.
It really doesn't take a lot of words to explain what's so great about The Dark Descent, but here I go anyway!
To begin with, the sounds are so rich and textured, and they have a lot of depth. That's an element that's really key to any horror game, arguably the most important, and they really nailed it here. The voice-acting is phenomenal of course, where Sam Mowry and company really shine to make this game what it is.
Also, there's also a very full story associated with the game, which is something that's really rare to see as in most horror games to this day simply throw you into the world with no explanation whatsoever. The graphics aren't something to write home about, but in all fairness the game has been around for some time and somehow they fit the game just perfectly the way they are.
On the other hand, the game isn't as scary as some other games out there. Personally, I didn't mind that at all because like they say in the beginning of the game, it's important to let yourself become fully immersed in the atmosphere of the game, and sometimes in other horror games the developers try so hard to spook you that they don't create that same kind of feeling like in this one. On that same note, I do really appreciate how the game doesn't use cheap jumpscares whatsoever. Instead, you just pee your pants hiding in a wardrobe from hideous monsters.
Regardless of whether or not you play horror games, give this one a shot. It's a classic, and a must-play for anyone who can appreciate the experience of a well-designed game.

Apotheon is a platformer with an ancient Greek theme.  It is a very unique-looking game with an art style matching ancient Greek pottery.  You play a regular person, tasked with defeating the gods (led by Zeus of course) who have chosen to destroy humanity.  It's one of those games that shows how well thorough theming can work.  Everything about it is ancient Greek and well-researched to provide the best experience possible.
While the game may be a platformer, it deviates quite a lot from the norm.  You have a wide range of ancient Greek weaponry to choose from with various melee and thrown weapons as well as quite a few types of arrows and sling ammunition.  Weapons are realistically modeled so you must actually hit enemies with the blade in order to damage them and both you an enemies can use shields to block attacks.  While it may feel clumsy at first with long attack windups, you quickly get used to it.  The one major problem with the combat is that attacks are performed either overhead, underhand, or stabbing, but the game selects one at random when you attack.  This can cause a lot of incorrect attacks that miss your target and lead to some frustration.
The other major annoyance in the game is the movement.  While for the most part the platforming works fine, and the game even provides a ledge-climbing mechanic for when the jump is slightly too high, maintaining speed while running across a map is nearly impossible.  You speed up as you run but any time the slope of the ground changes, such as when you start climbing stairs, you lose all momentum.  In some places you can actually skip the stairs by jumping and land on another piece of ground of the same slope as you jumped from to maintain speed but very few locations offer that opportunity.  The game would have been better served by leaving out this feature altogether.
The game is structured in a non-linear way with several hub areas branching into areas with multiple objectives you have to complete before continuing.  It gives the game more freedom to allows for mini quests that take place across several areas.  It also allows easy access to go back to previous areas to find secrets you missed and complete achievements.  Each area is themed for a specific ancient Greek god while the hub areas act as towns, complete with town guards who will attack you if you break the law.
I was greatly surprised when I discovered that this game which I thoroughly enjoyed was made by the same developers as Capsized, a game which I found frustrating and poorly designed.  I hope they continue to make games of this quality in the future.

Apotheon was a little game that i'd never even known about up until its release. I believe I read a small review about it and shortly after checked out its Steam page. Immediately its art style hooked me as i've always been a fan of Roman and Greek mythology as well as their cultures. I also love the history and combat from the era and when I saw this game was done entirely in Greek mythology art style I decided I was going to go in blind on this game and just buy it there and then. It looked great and it met any expectations I had. It was a bit of a different game than I expected. Its a Metroidvania type game that is similar to a lot of the recent 2D platformers from the current era. Its challenging combat and beautiful art and animations immediately grabbed me and that was just the scratching the surface. As I got into the game I found it had more depth than I expected, varied weapons and items, fun secrets and side missions, great sound and voice acting and just a huge charm which made it feel so unique even though there are so many other Metroidvania games out there.
Everything in the visuals department sets Apotheon apart from other games and its amazing animation quality plays into the combat and gives it a very, very deliberate and visceral feel. They really did an amazing job on it and it stood out to me through my entire experience. Its a combat system that is a bit finnicky at first, is so satisfying once accustomed to and difficult to master. The combat I really feel makes this game worth playing and truly was handled perfectly to match the style of this game. Apotheon also controls fantastically, again it took a bit of getting used to because the game is animation heavy but once you get used to it the feeling of momentum from running and jumping just feels wonderfully on keyboard or controller. The same can be said for the combat as each blow landed feels visceral and has impact. The combat is deliberate, every attack commits your character to the action so the combat takes on a bit of a Dark Souls feel where some thought and patience is required to really accell at it. The game features a fairly large number of bosses each with their own challenges. The game never felt like it was getting stale as it threw in new twists to the combat at every turn with new enemy types and new level types to fight in. In one level you can barely see, its pitch black and you only have a torch to light the way a few meters in front of you. In another level you're battling mermen under water which restricts your ability to use ranged weapons accept for one which was made for the mermen's use. The voice acting is top notch and every God character has personality and identities. The story was well done and well told with lots of cool lore and history on the Greek Gods and every weapon and piece of armor has its own model and there are a lot of them. Theres a crafting system for consumables but its nothing to write home about. And each level looks beautiful and feels unique for the most part. The levels can blend together a bit because of how consistent the art style is but the color pallete is great and there are awesome contrasts and colors to give the game a really great feeling of majesty and beauty.
Pros -
-Great combat system. Satisfying and brutal, pretty easy to learn yet hard to master.
-Tons of different weapons, shields, items and armor each with their own unique models.
-Expansive levels with lots of secrets and items to be found as well as enemies to fight.
-Varied enemies.
-Great voice acting
-Strong, well told story.
-Beautiful art style and color scheme.
-Authentic feeling environment.
-Awesome final battle.
Cons -
-Weak crafting system.
-Boss fights can be unintuitive at first.
-Combat encounters can get a little repetative at times though not often.
-Normal difficulty isn't very challenging, I felt very overpowered by the end of the game.
All in all this game is absolutely worth $15 for my money. It was bigger, badder and better than I expected it to be. It lasted about 15 hours for 1 play through though, its probably realistically closer to 10-12 hours. It has multiple difficulty settings for extra play time as well as a multiplayer mode. I've not tried the Multiplayer so I can't speak for it but if it uses the combat system and runs smoothly I imagine its a lot of fun. I just bought this game not expecting the amount of detail and care that I found once I played it and it really suprised me. It was one of my favorite suprises in gaming in recent memory and I'd recommend it to anyone. It really is a fantastic Indie and is so masterfully crafted that it deserves more attention than its gotten.

This game has a pretty intense learning curve. I played through the tutorial fully and it doesn't tell you everything. Even if it did, you'd probably forget some information as you soaked in more. With 15 hours in I don't think I'm super qualified for a 100% true review...but seeing as the summer sale is just over the horizion, I want to put this on your watch list
After picking a map, a game mode [more on this later] and creating your character you get thrown into the game with no handholding. Every now and again you get little Tip popups but as I found, they are either useless or too vague to understand what it's referring to.
My character is a Rogue. So I will use him as an example to explain how to game works.
At level 1 you are only allowed to have one workshop building. Choosing which level 1 workshop to build depends on what profression you want. Each class has at least 4 [some more]. So let's say as a Rogue I want to be a pickpocket. I would build a Smugglers Den. You can use the Den to hire employees to aid you in your criminal affairs.
Each building gives special abilities. The smuggler's den allows for pickpocketing and burglary. Merc camp allows for extorting hush money from criminals not employeed by you. There is a lot more abilities but Steam does have a character limit.
Once you pick a building and start making money, it's best to consider carefully what to buy. The economy in this game seems to be bipolar. Some rounds I make tons of money, then Summer comes and I make pennies. Make sure you have at least 5k in your treasury for things you will need.
If playing solo, your money should be invested in profitable ventures. Building security measures in your house or buisness is worthless on certain difficulties for the AI may not even try to steal your stuff. What is worth while is buying rights. The more civil rights you have, the more you can partake in politics and own more buildings. Buying rights is super expensive, so it's best to save.
If playing multi [which can only be done in LAN or through Virtual LAN Emulators], It's highly advisable to buy as much building protection as possible. Burning down buildings, breaking into them and kidnapping other players is a danger you will face frequently if playing with aggressive players.
In both scenarios the most important thing to focus on.....is marriage.
One of the most clunkiest, unpolished feature of this game is marriage and children. This is extremely important because the goal of the game is to continue your Dynasty. Your first character will die eventually, not escaping it, so you have to have children continue your legacy.
Courting a person sucks. No way better to put it other than....it sucks. Your courting actions have a cooldown. Kiss her? cooldown on all actions. You can not kiss then hug then compliment NO you got to pick one then wait for a cooldown.
On top of this, each action seems to have a random effect. Sometimes you get 2 hearts on the progress to marriage meter, sometimes you get -10. Now performing these actions need to be constant. As soon as the cooldown finishes immediately do it again.
But there is only one problem. You gotta do this while you are micromanaging your buisness and paying attention to the world around you. And since the world is alive [kinda like the sims] the person you are courting is also doing random crap. So she could be alseep in her house and you can't go beguile her or whatever action you choose. This would be fine if it wasn't for the fact that time lowers the marriage progress bar. So since she is sleeping, her affection for you drops. THIS IS THE WORST FLAW OF THIS GAME. I HATE COURTING PEOPLE.
Thankfully once you get married, have sex a couple times, get some children....it requires less attention. You send your children to school then apprentice ship and eventually they will either take over your buisness or start new ones. You can let them do their own thing or put them in your control group and well....control them directly.
So this is where I will go into the game modes....
Dynasty: Ends when your dynasty dies out.....I don't think there is a end date but I havent gone far enough to see
Elimination: Ends when you're the last Dynasty alive. There is settings to change the amount you are competing against
Timed: ......well.....it's timed
Mission: Meet a specific goal to win
Late gameplay depends on the mode you choose. I typically play Dynasty mode till I get bored or die cause it allows for experimentation without too much penalty. Deep into Dynasty Mode is usually just expanding expanding and you guessed it, expanding. Depending on the map you may run out of building room.
Elimination is an intense gamemode depending on the amount of opponents and difficulty. After building some empire and marrying your wife....late game becomes a battle. What can you do to make your opponent dynasties burn out? Politics is the slow and more....legal way of gaining power over your enemies. I prefer burning down buildings or killing...much more effective if done without gaurds seeing.
I havent played the other game modes to answer to their late game.
I totally advise picking this game up on sale. For 2.49, it will give you large amounts of content and fun. Yes, there is a lot of clunky issues, none game breaking, but will make you face palm at times. If you want more information just let me know I will add it to the review. Thanks for getting through this review!

Back to the Future: The Game is a point and click adventure game which takes place roughly 6 months following the events of the third movie. In it, you play as Marty McFly, dealing with a variety of puzzles as he attempts to set right the past - largely dealing with the 1930s Prohibition-era Hill Valley.
This is a good game, but it feels like it could have been so much more. It was released prior to Telltale's The Walking Dead success, so it largely relies on their older formula of having a large inventory where you collect items, then use those items to solve puzzles, along with having a large number of items which can be interacted with, many of which are extraneous. There's nothing *wrong* with this, but given they were trying to provide a story more on-level with feature films, it ends up feeling like the gameplay is getting in the way of what they were trying to accomplish as opposed to complementing it.
Voice acting is excellent, the story was actually better than I expected (except for one or two areas which don't really "mesh" with how time travel is supposed to work in this universe). So basically, if you don't mind the way older point and click adventure games tend to play, and if you're not TOO invested in the storyline/mechanics of the BttF universe, it's probably worth a look.

If you enjoy realism and want to enjoy the game a bit longer I can recommend one of the many realism servers the community put up for players. Canabalt is a silent and modest game jam giant that was in the first wave of titles which drew attention to the emerging indie scene at the time. It was a groundbreaking game that popularized a subgenre of endless runner games, such as Race the Sun and BIT.TRIP Runner series in certain aspects. But does it still stand the test of time as a true classic?
Story wise, you are the Runner, an athlete who is running over the rooftops and is trying to avoid hitting any obstacle while there is an enigmatic, ongoing invasion happening. The story is minimal and its kept in the background, while the gameplay takes priority. Speaking of the gameplay, Canabalt shines in evoking rush of exhilaration through simple and tight controls: you only use one button in the game to jump. You can make light or high jumps depending on the force with which you push the button. There are various obstacles on tracks that are procedurally generated, which will cause the player more or less trouble, and sometimes will even help depending on the height of the jump and speed the player is running. Canabalt is a very fast game, where the speed of the protagonists progressively accelerates to ludicrous levels. Besides the endless main track, there are several modes of plays, each one focusing on one style of play and obstacle.
Visual presentation is still very good, with a minimalist and monochromatic graphics and a great attention to the details and animation that make Canabalt look vivid and evocative. There is only one, good music track that follows your ventures through the rooftops, and the sound is also minimalistic, but impactful.
But there are minuses in the game: there are many animation bugs that will pop up when you are reaching the maximum speed, that one music track is good but will get repetitive fast and procedurally generated course tracks aren’t as varied and interesting as they ought to be, and create that same-y feel in the long run, which is the game’s biggest letdown.
This was made by one man, and it is a stark achievement to be sure, but I can’t help but feel a little bit of indifferent to Canabalt. In the first hour of playing I was ecstatic and mesmerized, but the game shows all its tricks in less than 2 hours. After that, all that remains is the repetition and a ghost chase of getting back that feeling of being intoxicated with this game. Canabalt is a good game for the price developer is asking that simply runs out of fuel and magic tricks fairly quickly, a flawed classic.

A lot of people are ♥♥♥♥♥ing because an indie developer bit off more than they can chew, and they're trying to fix it.  Just not fast enough for the whiners.  A lot of people are ♥♥♥♥♥ing because they're Dead By Daylight fanboys and want to destroy the only other game in their genre, hoping it'll send all the F13 players to DbD (it won't).
Me?  I like F13.  Sure, there's some issues, I accept it's part of a Launch.  I've heard the same ♥♥♥♥♥ing from WoW players when a new expansion comes out, and that's with a multimillion dollar company doing that's done it numerous times.  Bugs happen in Launch week.  Servers get slammed, far more than the developers expected.  I was actually playing with no issues when Steam was the only platform. As soon as PS4 and XBone came online, that's when the problems started.
But how many people saw the Streamers playing during their 48 hour Early Access and decided "Hey, I wanna play this!" and bought it?   I know I did.
A lot of people are whining because they didn't back the game on KickStarter, so they don't get the Backer exclusive Jason.  I didn't.  And I don't particularily mind.
But hey, let's get to the review.
Friday the 13th: The Game is a 1v7 Horror thriller game set in third person over the shoulder.  It's designed to mimic what you've seen in horror movies.  To this end, Jason gets 2 movement abilities; Morph, and Shift.  Morph pulls up the map and lets him teleport nearby where he indicates.  It seems to be a random location within a radius of where you want.  Sometimes you appear where you wanted, sometimes you're about 20 feet away.
Shift causes Jason to disappear and rocket forward where the camera is facing while Shift is active.  You can't slow it down, you can't strafe during it, but you can cancel it early.
These two abilities are the ones that replicate the killer walking, the victim running, then the killer popping out from around a corner.  Or the victim stops, having evader their persuer...they look one way, they look the other, then the camera pans over and the killer is standing right next to them.
A lot of people don't get seem to understand this.  They just call it overpowered bull droppings.
Jason also gets Sense, which lets him detect fear in the counselors, causing them to glow red for him.  If a cabin is occupied, it will also appear red, but Jason can't detect WHERE in the cabin his prey is hiding.
The fourth active ability is Stalk.  Normally, when Jason is getting closer to a counselor, no matter which one is moving, the counselor will hear intense music, growing as the distance shrinks.   Stalk turns it off, allowing Jason to get the drop on someone.  Ideally, it'd be great to wait in place hunting someone, but that's just not feasble, really.
All together, these make Jason something to truly be feared.  As a counselor, it's likely you're going to die, unless everything goes right for you.  But isn't the point of a horror game to be scared?  You're in a cabin, looking for anything to help you; the car keys, a pocket knife, a weapon....and suddenly you hear the intense music.  You see Jason through a window, and he's heading straight towards you.  You can try to escape, and maybe you will.  Maybe you'll encounter another counselor, and together you can stun Jason and get a bit more distance.
Maybe you decide to be a hero, and lure Jason away from the weaker, slower counselor who is better at repairing the phone so they can call the police.  Sacrifice yourself, so others get a better chance to escape.
TL:DR;  Have I had bugs? Yes.  But I've also had a fair bit of fun, both as Jason, and as one of his victims.
I feel $40 is worth it for the game.  Go watch YouTube videos and Livestreams, see for yourself if you think you'd like it.
Just remember.. Indie developer, and Launch week.

At 50 levels, I beat "Hook" in maybe 2 hours. Just the right length for some casual gaming.

Already the better of the two RPG titles, this Steam release of The Sith Lords adds a very well done and much needed series of updates that breaths fresh life into the game and rekindles your enthusiasm for it.
The game itself features an active combat system that flows smoothly and brings life to the Star Wars universe with detailed animations and iconic abilities. Think Chrono Trigger without the speed stat and also you can move around I guess. The story starts off slow as can be expected with RPG's of its nature, really getting started about 2-4 hours from creating your character. From that point on it's an exciting ride that'll have you pushing your party to their limits against the light or dark, depending on your choices.
Speaking of choices, while this game has great voice acting and incredibly well written dialogue, the choices you make most of the time won't affect much more than your appearance and who's in your party. The ending will largely remain the same with the exception of light/dark side.
The original title was rushed to completion and the studio, Obsidian, barely saw any revenue from it. They would go through a similar process again with the followup to Fallout 3, New Vegas. I also consider New Vegas to be a better game than 3. Poor Obsidian. Due to this, much content was cut from the game, including the main side story of everyone's favorite Old Republic era droid, HK-47.
That brings me to the features that have been added to this release on Steam. The addition of Steam Workshop makes it easy to add in arguably necessary mods such as the restored content mod. This will add back in most of the cut content from the originally planned release and is highly recommended even for first time players.
Beyond that, HD resolutions and widescreen aspect ratios are now supported. As far as I can tell pretty much every resolution your monitor supports will be displayed as an option. There is also native support for Xbox controllers, which I think is a god send since the KB+M controls for the two KOTOR titles leaves much to be desired. That said, the support leaves a little to be desired and I end up having to use my mouse now and then anyway.
Thanks for reading and be sure to check out my workshop recommendations on this one!

However, while I wasn't that impressed with it's story, where it mattered to me was how fun it was. It's good fashioned Quake-style of gameplay intact and I couldn't find anything wrong with that.
If you felt the same way I did about where Quake as a series has gone since 2, may want to reconsider on giving this title a second chance.

Another game I recall from my childhood that I never really got very far into it. It sounds bizarre saying this, but my mom actually beat this game while she had time to burn in between jobs. I was more or less scared to get killed in any fps game, so I avoided it. Later on, I had a nostalgia for this game and so I swiped it after it was on sale. For about $2, it's hard to avoid purchasing.
So, let's start with the pros for late 2017:
-Still holds up in its single player campaign; pacing is good; doesn't particularly get boring
-Hard mode is the right difficulty. Sometimes you wonder why the Gladiators have such ridiculously accurate railgun blasts, so if you're like me and you want to keep reloading a save until you don't get hit by them at all, this might be a bit annoying, but all in all, there is nothing here that I would consider unfair or any spikes in difficulty
-Lots of guns; requires rationing of ammo types and thought about which weapon will work in which situation and enemy
-Variety of enemy types; AI is acceptable
-Secret areas, which most modern games completely lack
-Campaign is quite long
Cons:
-Hitting an enemy in the face seems to have no apparent difference to hitting them in their hand
-Sometimes you will find an area in which an enemy cannot move and you can just fire safely from your location using your blaster.
-Graphics look dated, but I am sure there are mods out there that can really fix this
-Color palette is drab. Like seriously drab. After about 10 hours through, you really feel a bit claustrophobic in terms of light and color, like you just want to escape to the surface. In a way, that is this game's strong point as the Strogg stronghold/ship is bleak and sterile, but it does become a pain as a player. I also had this problem to some extent when playing Resistance: Fall of Man, which had a very limiting color palette and was also aiming for bleakness in a hostile alien world, but that game had a more compelling story for an fps and remains more memorable to me despite that issue. That said, it probably owes something to games like Quake II and Half Life 1/2, so we can thank the makers of Quake.
-Story is basically irrelevant. It's good enough to get you through the game, but that isn't saying much. It really amounts to you single-handedly massacring an entire Strogg stronghold. And it's unclear who these guys are. They're this strange cyborg race in between man and machine, though it's not clear how exactly they stay alive if they're still biological organisms or what their purpose is, since they all seem intent on one thing, which is to kill you. Since they only seem to be doing someone's bidding, I can only assume they are under the control of a more intelligent sentient overlord. Only the end boss explains nothing and is just more of the same old same old. Speaking of which....
-End boss is really lame. You can basically stand behind a pillar, use any of your weapons when you step around the pillar, and then jump back behind the pillar while he starts blasting it
-Some of the weapons lack a bit of punch for what they are. The grenade launcher and rocket launcher in specific. This isn't a big deal though.
-Inventory UI isn't developed, so you often forget what items you have and what key you need to use any of them. I barely used any item on hard.
There are other issues with it that you can probably overlook, but something that does stand is its linearity. From this point of view, it's a standard fps. Barebones story to get you through the game, you're by yourself, you shoot the enemy, somehow you manage to kill about 1000 Strogg and their boss all by yourself and then you escape their fortress. But it's still a decent fps gameplay-wise.
Recommended if you like a solid fps, but can ignore a practically non-existent story. It was a reasonably enjoyable romp through memory lane for me personally, but it really isn't even a must-play for somebody who enjoys fps games, let alone games in general. If like me, you were curious how some of these 90s fps games you grew up playing held up now, it's worth looking at, but even then, there are plenty of good fps games that I would choose over this one.

All you really need to know going into Apotheon is this:
Mount Olympus is full of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. You are Nikandreos, humanity's last hope against Zeus and his family of mongrels.
In case you missed the thumbs-up, I like this game. Consistency is an oft-overlooked aspect of game-design. Apotheon's art-direction is essentially patterned after ancient Greek paintings. If you ever looked at some pottery and wondered "What if someone made a side-scrolling action game out of this?" this is about as close a result as you could imagine.
Going further, Apotheon's art-direction affects how the game is played. Everything animates in a very stiff manner. It's off-putting at first, and likely won't gel with fans of franchises such as Castlevania. This is what makes consistency such a double-edged sword. This game couldn't have its unique visuals AND the mechanics/animation of a traditional side-scroller, it would look weird.
Combat is all about commitment. Your defensive options are varied and effective at any moment. However, when you swing your sword, stab with your spear, or fire an arrow, you're going to be extremely vulnerable. Aiming & timing are essential; if both aren't true, you're going to take damage. While your skills can be upgraded, attacking is never instantaneous. Most of the time, you have to give your attack half a second to connect, and button-mashing is futile. Encounters tend to be short, as enemies can be killed in a few solid strikes. Furthermore, certain techniques (such as aiming for the legs) can force the enemies to crumple, leaving their head exposed to a critical strike.
The other interesting aspect of combat is that weapons are fragile. While it's expected that players will find armanents that suit their play-style, it's also common that they'll have to make do with what's available. This tends to keep every encounter fresh, since the player can't afford to exhaust their favorites. Thankfully, Apotheon is balanced in the sense that bosses or other tough enemies don't require the "best" weapons. The boss-fights are mostly unique, and tend to involve unexpected events. In short, intuition and reflexes are the weapons you should rely on. In my play-through I got by relying almost entirely on common weapons. In true Resident Evil fashion, I saved all of my best stuff for...that time after I beat the game and realized that maybe I should have used some of it. Perhaps on the harder difficulty I'll be a little less frugal. Hades, I didn't even touch the ability-boosting potions. Sure they provide temporary boosts, but that's still better than nonexistent.
Exploration is also a common element of this game. Each area has numerous secrets, most of which are hidden behind cracked walls and floors. Rewards are typically in the form of gold, weapons, and sometimes even God-granted powers. However, one aspect that is a bit disappointing is that there really aren't any powers that assist in exploration, or allow you access to new areas. Aside from bombs -- which are acquired as early as the first dungeon -- there aren't any techniques that allow Nikandreos to jump higher, fly, or reach areas he couldn't before. A side-quest unlocks a weapon called the Caduceus. It has a grappling mechanism that can be used on faraway objects, or even as a makeshift weapon. It's even possible (if a little finicky) to grab ledges to pull yourself onto. Unfortunately, this weapon can't be used to find new areas. Basically, this game is less Metroidvania than I expected, which is a little disappointing.
Apotheon shares innumerable commonalities with the genre, but it does just enough to stand out. Keep in mind though that the art-direction and its resulting combat is *sigh* not for everyone. Some gamers will discount it as clunky and cheap, and that's fine. Everything immediately clicked for me, so I had a pretty good time with the game.

UPDATE 12/11/16: ANYONE considering buying this game needs to read the "December Update."  It's a giant rant about how much the lead dev hates his customers.  He actually says in there that he doesn't really even feel like finishing the game.  Before I was just telling people not to buy it unless they find the hardcore stuff fun.  Now I'm warning people there is a real financial risk here.
Original Review:
60+ hours played.  I got the game after watching some YouTube videos.  It looked very fun in those so I gave it a shot.  And it WAS fun for the first week or so, until they introduced a leg-breaking mechanic which makes you sit around for 2 minutes to 2.5 hours (depending how big your dino is) for your broken leg to heal, during which time you can only crawl and most other dinos will view you as dead, which you basically are.  I've waited to see if it was intended to be this bad and now I've seen dev confirmation that it is.
I should have read the game description closer before buying and it's my fault for not doing so:
"Over time, the game will be updated to the point of intended hardcore functionality. As this happens, difficulty will gradually become more brutal and chances of survival become less likely."
I personally want more fun and less brutal in my games so I think this is where I get off.
Regarding polish, the game feels like an alpha currently.  You can play and probably not crash often, but disconnects are a little frequent and almost no part of the UI is good (there's a bar for Stamina, Food, & Water, but not for your health--and you do die when you get to 0).  You spawn in a random location and basically need to get to one of the lakes because that's where the other people are, a journey that can take 1-20 minutes if nothing bad happens to you on the way (see: leg breaking).  Short of memorizing the map, the only way to get to known places is to keep your debug screen up, which puts distracting writing all over the screen, while you watch 2 extra long coordinates at the top and try to keep going in the proper direction.  The lakes are largely bursts of massacres but that's pretty much all you can do at the moment.  Some people try to roleplay but it's ultimately silly when others will just attack you anyway.  I was a triceratops and resting next to another one in a herd of herbivores.  Then he got up and just killed me out of the blue before I could react.  Sweet, see you guys in 20 :)
I'll maybe re-assess at a later point but I wouldn't recommend it to my friends at the moment so I can't recommend it to anyone else.
And yes, the lead dev (at least) is quite brash.  It's not my cup of tea but I know some people think it's great so YMMV.

One of the better indie releases this year, for sure. It's an action platformer with unique controls and combat mechanics. The controls do take a bit of time to get used to, they could be a bit more precise and responsive, but once you get the hang of it the platforming shouldn't be any problem and the combat will become really fun. Especially during boss fights, which are really well thought out. The combat basically involves swiging your weapon and blocking with your shield at the right time and switching between your melee and ranged weapons when needed. Enemies are fairly competent too, so it keeps you on your toes and encourages you to try out all the special weapons the game gives you.
It's not quite metroidvania style as in you don't really gain additional mobility from killing bosses, but the game has two main hubs connected to several other areas you can complete in more or less any order you want. Areas will offer a lot of different challenges, the game never outlasts its welcome that way. The visual style is just plain amazing and the soundtrack is also very fitting, offering brilliant orchestral arrangements.
All in all an extremely good game. The only gripe I have with it is the fact that the controls aren't as finely tuned as they could be and the game, at least on my machine, suffers from performance issues on higher settings, while it really shouldn't.
