"Back To The Future: The Game" is a "point and click" adventure from TellTale Games, coming from the famous "Back To The Future" movie trilogy franchise. The game is composed of a total of 5 episodes, each of them smartly connected between each other (like a TV mini-serie).
As a fan of Back To The Future, I think TellTale did a really amazing job to be authentic to the movies. From a graphic standpoint, however, it looks different to the movie but it has that usual charm you can encounter in TellTale games that still make it classy enough to not complain about it.
From a gameplay perspective, you have to manage mouse control and keyboard for moving, which is bothersome to me, but it is still OK to manage. I am not a big fan of inventory that are not available right away in front of your eyes, which sadly this game have. I believe the inventory system a little annoying in the game.
Story wise, it is very likable and rather similar to the movie structure, which is great. Actually I tend to even prefer what TellTale did with Dr. Emmett Brown than on the movie, he looks more human and not only kind of like the crazy scientist he was on the movies... Also, Marty McFly is definitely a great hero to play with and he is super awesome in the game. I like the introduction of new characters like Edna Strickland, Trixie Trotter and another family member of the McFly with Arthur...
I am not a big fan of the chase sequence at the end of most the episodes, it is certainly reminescent of the movie endings but it lacks any fun gameplay in my opinion. I adore however some sequences such as in Episode 1 in Emmett's Lab, this was thought very smartly.
I definitely felt in love with this game, despite it not being perfect, it has some kind of funny and yet enjoyable adventure that I was expecting to have with Back To The Future for a long long time ago.

Artisticaly and technically speaking, this is one of the best games I have ever played. That's one hell of a phrase to throw around, but this game really earns it. This game went out to create the experience of being the hero greek myth and everything in the game goes to painstaking lengths to make sure you feel that way. The art is designed to look like it was painted on the side of a greek pot, where myths are so often seen painted, and everything seems to move that way as well. The voice acting is as good as one can ask for in an indie game and the music is brilliant. Youcan hear in the audio the epic and godly feel everythig is supposed to have. The combat feels very good and the need for skill is evident. Pulling off successful rolls into backstabs or taking down an dog as it jumps at you by throwing a well timed javelin is really rewarding.
But the best part of the game is by far the level design. A lot of research and love and a truckload of creativity went into the level design. It is perfect in that every area works by precisely the same rules but still feels entirely unique.  Your job is to gain the power of that god by fulfilling some task in their place on olympus and confronting them. Each area is desgned to reflect the god who lives there. For instance, Artemis lives in
Ares, aways the bloodthirsty, lives in
And Hades is built so be a sad, unsettling place where those you kill come back to life so as a result,
this gives the player the feeling that they don't want to be there long and forces them to run through the land of the dead for fear of joining them.
There are 7 different houses each with their own distinct feel which is what makes this game truly amazing and truly worth buying. The game was certainly not perfect and had quite a few flaws in terms of the execution of some of the fine points but artistically and design-wise, it is a masterpiece.

Let me get the worst bit out the way: In a game that focuses on exploration and object/environment interactions -when there is a bug that prevents you from moving forward - the player has no idea at first and instead feels he has missed something - back tracks, doubles over previously explored rooms. This happened to me once or twice, the worst being from a known bug when first trying to enter lambda. Really took away from the experience, but luckily...
However annoying that above was, I still highly recommend this game. The story is 10/10 - all my assumptions about the plot were wrong and I loved the game for it. There are some fantastic moments in the game, with the last third being some of the best. There is just not enough movies and games that deal with the abyss of the deep sea - I was truly inspired by how terrifying it would be to be lost down there. Moreover, the ideas presented make it a true scifi - moreso than what Hollywood calls scifi these days. Sci-fi asks questions and presents ideas in such a way that it should make you think long and hard about those ideas.
Also, the sound design must be praised, all the environment and ambient sounds were fantastic - constantly creating tension and a sense of unknown while giving life to every environment and stage within each chapter of the story.
This isn't a perfect game, but however occasionally frustating it is, this is a game that takes advantage of its medium - most games parody film in telling a story - this game shows how it can tell a story better than a film could.

Man, I hope you were there when Canabalt first appeared back in 2009. It was such a mystifying experience, playing this intense, engrossing Flash game on some random dude's website. I never thought I could be so entranced by a single-button game but the presentation absolutely made it and built on the hectic gameplay in the best way. They say it was the first of the endless runner genre, and even if it weren't, it would deserve a place of honor among them.
You'll never know who your hapless lady or fellow is or why their city is being annihilated by shadowy engines of destruction, but you won't have much time to wonder, either. Canabalt is a one-button game, and that button is jump. Your character runs to the right at an ever-increasing clip, and you need to jump them from rooftop to rooftop to billboard to girder to whatever else is in your path. Each run is randomized, with obstacles, crumbling buildings, windows, and occasional attacks from the marauding machines.
It's a simple premise, but the presentation takes it to another level. Set to pulse-pounding tracks, your journey through the chaos is all in silky-smooth, heavily-detailed gray-scale. Flocks of birds take flight as you charge past, the engines of destruction level buildings in the layered background, and stranger things still float past if you make it far enough. And if the presentation wasn't enough, there's a layer of strategy to the game as well. Letting your runner build up too much speed makes them hard to control, so sometimes you need to strategically hit an obstacle or two to slow them down.
Expanding on the original offering are eight challenge runs with different themes, like nothing but windows or no obstacles to slow you down. They each have a target distance to "beat" them which should keep you quite busy for awhile. Also included is a two-player mode that fully supports being played solo as a very interesting test of coordination. On top of all that is a full 3D mode that redoes the graphics in sharp polygons that still manage to stay true to the look and feel of the original. If infinite runners always struck you as thin on gameplay, you're bound to find plenty to do in this one.
There's not much negative I can say about Canabalt's triumphant return. A few of the obstacles, like the windows and walker legs, are quite difficult to overcome and can end some runs in frustration, but they hardly ruin the game. Outside of that, it's the same game that made a splash nearly a decade ago, with plenty of bells and whistles to justify a purchase. The original might be free, but if you have any love for infinite runners this will be a worthy addition to your library.

From the perspective of a player who's never played  Catan before this experience (real life or otherwise):
 
I love board games but somehow I've never had the chance to play Catan even though I've heard about it plenty of times.  So when I saw it was released on Steam and FREE TO PLAY I was very excited to give it a try.  I’d already read the negative reviews on the F2P model that the game employed so I can honestly say I was prepared for the available options as a non-paying customer.  I’ll run down my experiences with the game so far (4 hours played; maybe 10 games against computer and online?)
1.      Tutorial: Personally – tutorials can make or break an experience for me.  It’s tough to put into words but I didn’t like the tutorial for this game.  It felt “rushed” somehow but looking back I think it’s the way the user interface is implemented.  For the same of time-saving everything from the dice rolls to the card distribution is VERY FAST.  This makes sense for a veteran player who doesn’t necessarily need to see a slower animation of the dice rolling and cards being distributed but I think a concerted effort in showing these actions to a newer player could go a long way to player experience and satisfaction.  I honestly went and watched a YouTube video on how to play and then fooled around with an app on my phone to learn the mechanics of what was actually happening.  This occurred after #2.
2.      Free Online Match: I still felt very ill prepared but decided I’d learn as I go against live opponents on the available Free Online Match.  The matchmaking was relatively quick and the game started up without much waiting.  However, one opponent failed to connect I assume so he was replaced with an AI.  At this point I WAS LOST because of the not-so-friendly user interface (I’ll elaborate in a second) but I managed to make a few actions.  Around 8-10 minutes into the match my opponent and I encountered a bug that did not allow them to take an action.  Their only option was to forfeit the game which gave me the win.  I was happy for the win but I can only imagine the takeaway experience of the person who had to forfeit.
3.      User Interface: Lot to cover here which some of which may just be for the benefit of a new player:
a.      Please put a bigger and pronounced notification when it’s your turn.  A simple toggle in the middle of the screen saying: 1) Roll the dice or 2) Play a development card would go a long way towards the experience and game flow in my opinion.
b.      I’m stealing this one from the Catan app on the Android market but an Action Pane would be AWESOME especially for new players.  During my first game or two I was clueless how to proceed or even what my options were. 
 
I finally figured out I had to zoom out to pick up my roads, cities, etc. and then only later found out that I could just click the board if I had the necessary materials to take that action.
 
However, have an action pane that listed my options (Trade, Build, Buy a Development Card) and then gave me a breakdown of the necessary resources as I hover over them would be incredible and again I think it’d increase the satisfaction and help with game flow.
c.      The timer mechanic was very frustrating and confusing for me at first but after 5-6 games I learned to work within it.  However, it still feels very rushed sometimes especially as a new player and trying to work through your actions and trade opportunities.
d.      I would love it if after cards are distributed it’d leave a little indicator below each player for another 5-7 seconds showing what cards they just received.  Again, I know it’s there in the Game Log but for user experience I think it’d be helpful.  For a veteran it’s probably no big deal but I like knowing what cards everyone just got from a dice roll and it feels very rushed right now.  Just a few tiny cards and the count below each player would be helpful and inconspicuous.
4.      F2P vs Pay: I honestly have no problem with how the game is presented.  The price seems incredibly fair to me considering you can unlock the base game and all expansions for under $15 and have gold to spare.  I actually ended up purchasing the game so I could practice against the AI and play online against a friend.
Would I recommend this to a friend?  Absolutely.  In fact, I already did and we enjoyed a good game with each other against a couple AI.  He used one of the free scrolls to unlock the base game so we could play which, to be honest, I didn’t even realized was a possibility but kudos to the developers for throwing that little “carrot” into the game so he could try it out with me.  I’d recommend to any person who’s on the fence about purchasing the unlocked base game (for just a few dollars!) to use their 2 free scrolls to play the unlocked base game with or without a friend against the AI.
As I mentioned I’ve already purchased the base game plus the two expansions because I really wanted to unlock the single-player experience and I didn’t realize I could just use a scroll.  Not that I regret purchasing, though, because my satisfaction with this game went from around 30-40% in my first game or two to around 85-90% as I gained experience working with the UI and learning the rules/mechanics of the game.
Does the game need polishing? Absolutely.  I encountered the game-ending turn bug twice in maybe 10 games.  Fortunately both times it was barely into the game otherwise it would’ve been WAY more frustrating.  Also the user interface could take some notes from the Android Catan app for game flow and user experience purposes (see notes above).

'Knights of the Old Republic II: The Sith Lords' is the sequel to one of the best games of the 21st century. It had an awful lot to live up to, and I believe it did so surprisingly well.
Many of the companions are fun to interact with and bring along on your adventures. Players of the original 'KOTOR' will be pleased to find themselves reunited with more than one familiar face. One of the companions is simply awful, and barely deserves mentioning. The character I'm referring to is a droid-like drone, and you *won't* want him around for long. I have no further criticisms of the companion system, though; in fact, I'd say that a few of the player's sidekicks are outstanding. I'm chiefly thinking of Atton and Kreia - two characters you meet very early in the game - but it could be extended to several others.
The story is considerably more complex than the original game's. Some people will welcome this; others won't. I *did* welcome it, and found the network of plot twists and unforeseen developments to be fascinating. The RPG quality of the game also means that the twists may not occur on your playthrough, or that you may experience other developments that I haven't faced.
This game has two key antagonists - Darth Sion and Darth Nihilus. (This isn't really a spoiler as they're featured on most cover art!) I don't think that either of these two Sith Lords are quite as intimidating as the original game's Darth Malak, but the way in which they are written will really challenge your perception of the 'Star Wars' universe, especially where the Force is concerned.
The planets and other environments open to exploration are broadly as good as those in the first game, but I found it slightly disappointing that none of the worlds became quite as immersive or deep as Taris, the first planet the player experiences in the original 'KOTOR'. I view this rather negatively, but not all players will: some will welcome the lighter approach to the worlds of 'KOTOR II', as you can cover more ground in less time. My only other criticism of the landscapes of 'The Sith Lords' relates to Korriban. You may recall visiting this planet in the first game. I do, and I remember finding it considerably more interesting and enjoyable in that earlier game.
The side quests maintain the high quality set by the first game, you'll be pleased to hear. It should also be noted that there appear to be a greater number of them in this game, and many of them can be completed very quickly. They're absolutely worthwhile, though, as they often expand on the player's understanding of the various lands, characters and events experienced throughout the game.
Pazaak and swoop-racing both make a welcome return. Pazaak hasn't really changed a great deal (although I don't think NPC pazaak players are quite as easy to find), but the swoop tracks have been made significantly more challenging - and addictive! Overall, whilst 'KOTOR II' falls slightly behind the original game in certain areas, I believe that it actually surpasses it in others. The first one was a great game for RPG fans. The second one is a fantastic game for 'Star Wars' fans. It's definitely one of my greatest gaming experiences this year, and I have to recommend it to almost all gamers.

DISCLAIMER: I never played this back in the day. Why? I was 3 years old when this came out. I have no nostalgia for this game.
I played this for the first time a few years ago (around 2014), got to near the end, and despite enjoying it I somehow didn't finish this. Fast forward to a few days ago; I decided to start another playthrough, and have just completed the game a few hours ago.
Quake 2 was some of the most fun I've ever had in a single player FPS. It may even be THE MOST fun single player FPS I've played to date, and I've played and enjoyed the original Quake, both DOOM 1 and 2, Bungie's Halo games, Unreal, and the Half Life series among others.
Quake 2's gameplay is fast paced with very satisfying gunplay that, combined with the soundtrack, creates a constant feeling of raw power. The Super Shotgun, the Chaingun, the Grenade Launcher, the Rocket Launcher, the Rail Gun and the BFG10k are the best (and my most used) weapons in the game. The sound design and feedback of these guns are what makes the gameplay so good in conjunction with strafe-jumping at high speeds and gore-ing your enemies while doing so. The game's variety of enemies can be reduced to chunks of meat and metal depending on what weapon is being used, how close you are to them, and how many bullets you decide to empty into them.
The game is not without its downsides:
- You will sometimes find yourself lost and without enemies to slaughter. This is due to the lack of an in-game map that shows you your current position and where you need to be going. Instead, there's only a mission objective screen that can be opened by pressing [TAB] that gives two brief and shallow descriptions of your location and what to do. This is a strange step back considering there was a directional map in the first two DOOM games. Wandering around without enemies to gore can really make the game turn into a drag.
- Some of the weapons become useless or boring to use and feel like wasted inventory space and potential, specifically the Blaster (although this is the starting weapon), the regular Shotgun, the Hand Grenades and the Hyperblaster. Despite the Machine Gun being just the smaller version of the Chaingun, it still serves a purpose since you can control your rate of fire and conserve ammo better than the Chaingun, so I won't lump it in with the other lackluster weapons. The Hyperblaster was another weapon I didn't like to use mainly because of the sound and projectile appearance making it feel like a peashooter. When compared to the Plasma Gun in DOOM 1+2 and Quake 3, it doesn't hold a candle to how fun those were to use.
- The soundtack is great but repetitive.
Wrapping this up, I haven't been able to play any of id Software's new entries for Wolfenstein or DOOM 2016 yet (and I've heard and seen very good things) so I'll hold some reservations. Having played and completed Quake 2 in conjuction with seeing a lot of footage of DOOM 2016, I can see the influence that Quake 2 has on DOOM 2016. With Quake 2 not being an actual sequel to the original Quake, now taking place in an entirely Sci-Fi setting, I couldn't help but think that this felt more like a DOOM sequel despite originating as a new IP. If I haven't conveyed enough how timeless the gameplay is and unquestionably still holds up, it feels like playing DOOM 2016 on very low settings. Again, I have yet to actually play DOOM 2016, but the gameplay looks almost identical despite Quake 2 being 20 years old now.
Maybe that speaks to how last gen's console-oriented FPS titles took a lot of aspects backwards. Thankfully games like DOOM 2016, the new Wolfenstein games and even Titanfall 2 are proving that the PC versions of these games don't have to be compromised for consoles and their controller-based input methods, nor do they have to look at what Call of Duty is doing.
TL;DR: Play Quake 2. Especially if you played DOOM 2016. Fast paced combat, satisfying gunplay and brutal, high speed violence makes this my favorite single player FPS game to date.

Before political corruption, backstabbing, and gray morals became trendy thanks to shows like Game of Thrones and House of Cards, there was the Guild 2. It's clunky, buggy and unreliable, but it still ranks as one of my favourite games of all time, just because of how compelling the gameplay is. Starting out as a smalltime peasant, you toil, cajole and intimidate to move yourself up the ranks, expanding your business empire, prestige and family legacy. It's totally possible to play the game as a legit and honest merchant or farmer, working hard, going to church and doing what's right, but it's also possible to play the game as a corrupt merchant, who takes bribes, abuses his office and takes hostile actions on his enemies.
It's such a shame that the game never had the level of polish it sorely needed. I would wholeheartedly recommend playing with the available mega-mods by awesome modders such as McCoy and others, as these mods address many of the issues that were left unresolved in the game. Even so, expect UI issues, random crashes and other bugs. Having said that, I would still recommend this game highly if gotten at a discount, otherwise get ready for The Guild 3!

My review will be covering my opinion on the combat, because that's what matters most to me in a PvP-based game.
Water down the combat of games like Chivalry: Medieval Warfare and the Dark Souls franchise and you've got For Honor.
-Easy, satisfying one-hit mechanics that are designed to make you feel good for getting a kill.
-100% reaction based, which is a bit shallow in my opinion.
-Simple Rock+Paper+Scissors style with how some of the classes seem to work. Certain classes will simply have the advantage in certain scenarios, Paper beats Rock.
-Limited number of attack options, it's safer to play defensive and just [parry->guardbreak->guaranteed dmg].
-Most options in the game are lacking a "Risk vs Reward" system and seems to just favor "Reward".
All that being said, the game is still fun as hell and I do recommend it. It hits a niche that, currently, no other game on the market can. It's a unique game, and while severely flawed, is worth investing in.
Other reviews cover how bad the business model is, and how horrible P2P is in a 2017 game by a company with $3.4b Net Worth. But, many seem to blindly praise the combat and that's it. It's not perfect by any means, but the game has a fair amount of depth and I'm looking forward to see what all the heroes are capable of.

This game is, at it's core, really good. It is also, however, drowning in problems that won't be fixed. In this review i'll mainly be focusing on the negatives, but let me  say it once again: This game, underneath all it's blemishes, is REALLY GOOD, and that's why i recommend it.
-The game frequently breaks down for me if i minimize the game in order to check the web or what have you. When i return it'll often say "paused" in the middle of the screen, and no matter what key i push it won't unpause. the only way to remedy this is to quit and re-launch the game. it's never harmed my saves or anything, but it's annoying.
-Automation of trade. dear jeebus, this is annoying. this game requires a ridiculous amount of micro-management, and it's not by design. There are options so that, while being less efficient, you can set your businesses up to mostly run themselves, which is a staple of these industry types of games. however, leaving your businesses on their own is not only less efficient, which is understandable, but it's just plain broken. Left on their own, businesses will frequently leave employees doing nothing when they could be producing, your carts won't always go get the materials they need from your other businesses, (though sometimes they do) the carts frequently won't load ready to sell goods up on their own, and when carts DO go grab the materials they need to further production at their own place of employment, they'll often take sellable goods and drop them at the place they are collecting materials from, taking up valuable storage space and slowing down your income and forcing you to constantly check on everyone. EX: inn needs wheat to keep making beer, so it sends a cart to get wheat from your farm, but inexplicably loads thousands of dollars of valuable alcoholic beverages into the cart before leaving and drops them at the farm so it can make room in the cart for the wheat it needs, leaving money just laying around in the farm until you discover it there, where you usually need to tell the cart to come back to grab the beverages and then manually send it to the market, or use a farm cart to drive it back to the inn so that you can then manually load it into a cart so it'll take it to market where it should've gone in the first place. another EX: Windmill needs wheat to make more flour, so it grabs a bunch of flour, and, instead of taking it to the bakery which actually uses the flour, or, you know, maybe just not loading itself full of flour in the first place seeing as the reason it's leaving the windmill is to fill itself with a different item, it takes it and dumps it at the farm, and brings wheat back to the windmill, not only causing the same manual interference in order to fix as in the last example, but potentially starving your bakery of the flour it needs to function.
sometimes it makes even less sense. I frequently find goods have been transported randomly to other businesses that don't even actually PRODUCE the thing that they're after. Alcoholic beverages frequently end up at my bakery, which i'm pretty sure means that instead of going to the orchard to get honey or fruit, you know, where those things are produced, they're stealing them from the storage of the bakery which needs it's own supply of those things, causing a feedback loop of economic gear-jammage.
employee side, it's not even just the businesses that have problems. your thugs/guards, if left unmonitored, will often just abandon their patrol routes in favor of just standing in place for days/years.
-The pause function. Pausing this game in order to manage some things without time moving forward doesn't actually pause the game, it simply makes time move really slowly. this on it's own isn't a problem, and i would even think it were a neat idea, the march of time never truly stopping, forcing your hand to action, even if at a reduced rate.
However, it doesn't just slow down the game world. IT SLOWS THE WHOLE GAME DOWN. your interface is just as slow as the game world, meaning that while you do have more time to do stuff, actually doing stuff is also hit with latency. whilst slowed, clicking on something often takes the game 3-5 seconds to register. not seperating the ui from the game world in terms of the passage of game world time is absolutely ludicrous.
-You can only interact with women, mostly. in a life sim, this is a tad bummersome. The tutorial makes it seem like you can interact with a wide variety of people, but that's not the case. social interaction is almost entirely limited to wooing a bride, and once you've married, there's no reason to ever talk to her again. This isn't a huge problem, but it certainly makes the sim side of this game much less intersting.
All in all, this game can be a tad frustrating, lots of things could work better than they do, the tutorial could be a lot better, yadda yadda, the list goes on a bit. BUT! I still really enjoy it. bought it a few days ago and already i've got 16 hours in, a booming career as a patron and a couple of chiddrens that are almost all growed up. despite it's many flaws, if you think this game is up your alley, it probably really is. for every problem this game has there's something really neat about it to cancel the bad out.
At the time of posting this game is on sale for $2.49. My advice? pick it up on sale, enjoy yourself, and then check out the guild 3 when it comes out sometime this year. I know I will.

I have nearly 500 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews. An hour isn't very long to judge a game on, so think of this as more of a first impression, and take this review in the spirit in which it's given. Be sure to read other reviews from players who have spent more time in the game.
One Hour Reviews - Game 10
Apotheon
Purchase Date: 6/13/2015
Long ago on my Commodore 64, I used to play a game called The Return of Heracles, which had a similar Greek myth setting.  So when I saw this game, I was pretty much immediately sold on the setting and the art style looked awesome.  This is one of the rare games I bought on Steam that I ended up playing almost right away.
The game starts with some quick cut scenes explaning how Zeus has turned his back on mankind, and things are looking grim.   After that I found myself in a town being invaded by raiders, which is where the tutorial kicks in.
The controls are pretty simple.  I didn't check if the game supports a gamepad or not, but I played with a keyboard and mouse.  The keys move you around and perform actions, and the mouse is used for aiming.  I've played other games with this control scheme; it's not my favorite, but it does feel familiar, and isn't difficult to pick up.
Given the controls and the platform nature of the game, I was expecting the combat to be pretty simplistic.  Instead I was pleasantly surprised by the variety of weapons at my disposal.  Even better, the weapon differences are not just purely cosmetic.  Each weapon feels different.  Knives are quick and do small amounts of damage which add up over repeated strikes.  But after too many quick strikes I found myself gasping for breath.  Larger weapons do more damage but are slower, and can be trickier to hit with against a moving target.  A variety of ranged weapons are provided as well.
It isn't long before I am introduced to the crafting options in the game.  I got a couple of recipes, one to make a 'fire bomb' of sorts, and the other for making a 'healing potion'.  The components for making these can come out of random crates or from killing enemies.
I occasionally struggled with the map.  The map overlays the screen with a transparency effect that I sometimes had trouble distinguishing the map from the background.  I wished I could have had some control over the transparency here.  Otherwise though the map did a good job of highlighting the location of my current objectives and helping me find my way around.
One thing I appreciated was the run speed of my character.  The longer you run, the faster you get.  So for those times where I needed to run far across the map, it doesn't feel like it's taking forever.
As far as difficulty goes, the game starts out pretty easy.  The earliest fights are very simple and gave me a good opportunity to try out the different weapons.  At the end of the first area, I got into my first boss fight, where the game starts to ramp up the difficulty.  As I progressed into the next area, I started to encounter more of a variety of enemies, and I definitely noticed a continued increase in difficulty.  I found myself having to evolve my combat strategy as well.  Early on it was sufficient to simply stab enemies a few times before they could respond in kind.  But as the game progresses, I found myself leaping to dodge attacks, and having to approach combat more methodically, especially in some of the later boss fights.
The graphics options are pretty basic, but that makes sense given that this is a 2D platformer.  I did see the option to change my resolution, which for me is always the most important.
I ended my first hour of gameplay continuing to explore the forests of Artemis.  The game definitely gives you a decent amount of exploration.  It reminded me a little of Metroid in that regard.
Overall there really wasn't anything about Apotheon I didn't like.  I expect I'll be enjoying many more hours of fun in this game.  I can recommend this without hestiation.

So far, from many people, For Honor has recieved a bad rap in terms of reviews, so I thought i'd better write one of my own.
For Honor is a fantasy/realism based medieval fighting game that combines 3 of the best warriors in history (sword and spear obviously). The Samurai, Knights and Vikings. The game has a familiar feel to mortal combat and other street fighter games. The big open maps feel quite emmersive, and don't feel too claustraphobic like other games of this genre.
My initial feelings towards the game when I played the beta were fantastic. I had seen the trailer early last year and couldn't wait to become my childhood dream of being a knight. The combat system is brilliant. The moveset's of characters aren't extremely diverse howver, there is enough variation to keep your enemies on your toes.
However, when the game came out shortly after the beta, I had just spent money on other things, and this is where it was hard for me to make the choice to buy this game, as for lots of other people at the moment. $60 USD is pretty pricey and for that amount of money, I expect the game to be flawless. The peer to peer connection system isn't the greatest, as the game has to load in the middle of a battle most times when a player leaves the game. This is one of the turn-offs for many people.
So after I forked out the money from my already light wallet (I just built my first PC) I bought the game from what I experienced in the beta, and what I wanted to do in this game. Be a badass knight. And that's is where this game shines. The customisation of characters is amazing. There is so much detail in the colours of your characters, the armour, the engraving on the armour, the paint patterns, the symbols, the weapon customisation, the upgrading. This game really hits the spot when it comes to customisation, aswell as gameplay.
After spending over 30 hours on the game, I can without a doubt, say that this game is worth it. It's a beautiful, addicting game, that kinda pisses you off sometimes, as you loose your cool while you loose your head at the same time.
Would I buy it again? ...Yes!
Are there problems with the game? ...Deffinately some that can be fixed.
Do you recommend this game?... Deffinately

If you like the choice to be a dinosaur, or human and survival, look no further than The Isle. This game is still in early development, so a player only has the ability to play a herbivore or carnivore, for now. In the future, they are going to add playable humans (cannibals, tribals, mercernaries, etc.)
When you start out in the game, you have the ability to pick the species of dinosaur you want to play. The choices are Austroraptor, Carnotaurus, Tyrannosaurus, Allosaurus, and Suchomimus for carnivores, while the herbivores get the choices of Dryosaurus, Maiasaura, Triceratops, Puertasaurus, Shantungosaurus, Anklyosaurus, Gallimimus, and Diabloceratops. Your main goal for now is to survive. When you start the game, your food and water will be around half, while your stamina is full.
When I started the game, it took a little get used to manuevering my way around the map. Coordinates and landmarks are useful, when you have a certain destination to get to. The players in species chat, I find, can also be very helpful, when trying to find my way around in the game. At first, I played a Raptor, then dabbled a bit with Dryo... now my main dinosaur characters tend to be the Austroraptor and Allosaurus.
When getting more involved with the game, I find that some players of other species play fairly, while others will either kill on site, or kill for the hell of it. It is just like any other survival game, where some players tend to be kind, while others like to troll and cause havoc on the servers. As long as player finds a good group of people to play with, a player should be able to survive pretty well in the game.
Now, when playing the game, expect there to be some server crashes and restarts. They do tend to happen, and it does get frustrating at times. Some days are worse than other days, but playing the game, I find it worth it to deal with the crashes. After all, this game is still in development, so it is nothing unheard of.
Would I recommend the game in its current state? Well, if you want to experience surviving as a dinosaur, and don't mind the crashing, then yes. This game can be very fun to play, especially with a group of people. If you want to wait until the game is further developed, then that is fine too. I would recommend for a person (if they do not wish to spend the money for the game at this time), to at least have the game on their watch list. I have a good feeling about this game getting better, with progress from the developments, and there are new dinosaurs being added with the updates.

Classic. It's a word that is used often... And really, I think it's lost it's impact. Everything that holds nostalgic value in some way, shape and form is "classic". Whether jokingly admiring an admittedly BAD piece of media that you liked as a kid, or enjoying one of many similar games out there, ones that don't entirely speak for themselves; we all state that the things we like are "classic". In this case, the genre already existed in various, fledgling forms such as Maze War, and Spasim in the early 70's... All the way up to the venerable title Wolfenstein, a game that helped truly mold the genre at it's most basic values, by the very same company that crafted the leviathan trend-setter for the ages- the masterpiece I'm going to attempt to describe here. It was a title that, at the time, would have been mentioned of in hushed excited tones by the kids at school. A title that was so wildly different, the news media used its inferno-based imagery and its playstyle as a scapegoat for heinous crimes committed. A title SO revolutionary that every single developer creating games that followed in its footsteps were considered "clones"....And rightfully so, many were just carbon copying the EXACT ideals, or in MOST cases, even code, right from this legend. This was the mark of something different, in how was distributed, in how open and accessable much of the content was, and how people played games together: over the internet. The most classic game of this genre may not be the very FIRST of its kind, but the genre truly coalesced with one Big. ♥♥♥♥ing. Game. It's name is Doom. and it is classic. Even if you did not like doom, or grow up with it or even PLAY Doom... Go look up the definition of classic. While those things may be subjective, and that's why we're capable of throwing the label onto anything, it is undeniable that this game is the grandaddy of them all.
I've given a large enough intro, and i doubt anyone wants to ready the lofty and article-like writing of a giant nerd such as myself for hours, regarding a game that you probably don't even fully care for... So I'll break this down for you.
-The perspective had been done before (and then CONSTANTLY AFTER), but the quality and the art drawn in was revolutionary. It still holds up to this day with the right Source Mod (more on that later)
- The sounds, the lighting effects, everything it set out to do, such as running on lower end machines, and even looking and sounding better on NEWER ones, meant that the modular tuning and graphics engine design were brilliant, John Carmack crafted an amazing source code.
-The set up, a protagonist with no dialogue, the story elements cut, is another trend-setter for the genre. The creators intention despite the entertaining HUD, was to make YOU the protagonist, allowing you to relate more and create your own feeling for the nameless marine.
-Multiplayer. Coop with damage enabled, and deathmatch. Doom did it arguably first, or for the time, best.
-How the title was distributed: you got Episode 1 (sound familiar, Valve fans?) for free. 9 levels to play and enjoy nearly everything Doom offered. Free. If you enjoyed it? There were more to buy and enjoy. This leads to two gigantic pillars for which Doom stands as the father of FPS, and helped inspire Valve to do what they're loved for now-
The source code became open and free to modify a few years later. This allowed for countless mods using Ids revolutionary and modular "WAD" file format. - and for people to convert the source code to run on platform ports (source ports), so that this old DOS game can work on modern machines.... While enjoying mods that enhance and even modernize gameplay.
The best (well rounded) Source Port to download is GZDoom. Get that, buy this, and run your doom.wad through it. Tune the old graphics enough to clean them up, and relive the classic.
Once you're done, get some mods. I recommend:
Brutal Doom
Project MSX - (amazing HUD with modern mechanics, changes monsters)
Dark 7 - ( amazing mapset, play it with Project MSX)
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Those can get you started. And yes, GZDoom will allow you to look UP and DOWN with your mouse...Jump (which is cheating ;] ) and even crouch.
Enjoy.
Fun facts about Doom:
Not only was Valve likely inspired by their open distribution of the title, and source-code policies, but they got their start in game design thanks to Id software.
Gabe Newell and Doug Lombardi visited Id around the time of their next trend setter- the fully 3D Quake.
Id helped them start up by giving the entrepeneur coders the source code to Quake, Id Tech 2.... Which they then heavily modified and dubbed Gold Source.... Officialy GoldSrc. This engine powered Half Life.
When Gabe Newell was still working for Microsoft, he was the programmer that ported Doom over to Windows from DOS, in an attempt to get more people to accept the platform, as Doom was the most widely downloaded application of the era. It had been downloaded and installed more than Windows itself at the time.

Canabalt is, quite obviously, an inifinte running game. From what I've gathered, it was one of the front-runners of the genre. It is a port from mobile devices to the PC, and includes new 3D graphics. 2D graphics are enabled by default, but it's easy to switch back and forth. I found the 2D version easier to play, because the boxes have no shadowing, making it easier to determine exactly where they are located, and when to jump.
The colour scheme is rather dreary - variations of grey and black and white, all rather monochrome - however it is very clean. The controls, or rather, control, is as simple as could be, and the game is responsive. This is crucial since it is the core aspect of the game. There is enough variation and randomness in the game/level design to make things interesting. You have windows at varying heights you must jump through, buildings which crumble and start to drop as you land on them, and of course boxes to jump over. I was pleased to see that the boxes are not an instant death, but rather slow you down. Going too slow means you will be unable to jump high/far enough to reach the next building, but it can be useful if used correctly to slow down slilghtly.
There are something like 7-9 levels which feature different themes. On one, the building are invisible, and one must use the birds perched on the roofs to determine where to run and land. There are no boxes in this mode, thankfully; at least, none that I've encountered. Another features aliens randomly drilling into buildings, making it so that you have to (very quickly) alter your course to land on the drill bit, in the middle of the building. Another features a plethora of boxes. The one I found most interesting played with the windows mechanic, and required more estimation based on your speed to determine when to jump to fall enough to break through a window below you.
The randomised elements obviously make it so that no two runs are the same, but due to this, some runs will be much easier than others. In the end, the ever-increasing speed means the difference will still be based mostly on skill, however it could have some effect on the leaderboards, if that's something for which you're aiming.
In the end, this remains a port of a mobile game. The devs did well to price it under $5. This is something I'd purchase on a mobile device for $1, if I were interested in such games. I don't doubt that fans of this genre would enjoy this game, however I grew tired of it very quickly. I'll note that I did not venture into the multiplayer aspect of this game.
I received this game as part of a bundle, and wouldn't recommend it at full price. My short time spent with it gave me an impression of a game done well for its genre, but simply not enough to keep me entertained. It's hard to put a dollar-per-hour or dollar-per-unit of entertainment number on any game, as the first would be misleading, and the second... is very difficult to measure and describe.

Catan Universe is not a free to play game. It is still the standard buy-to-play model but with a cash shop for unknown reasons. At the start of the game, you are given 100 gold and 2 scrolls, and you can convert the scrolls into the demo.
While this game isn't Pay To Win, there is a cash shop. There are no purchasable in-game advantages despite having a cash shop. However, they make you buy gold at a rate of 3000 gold for $35. Using the gold, you can buy the base game, expansions, XP boosters and scrolls. Catan the Base Game costs 500 gold. The Big Bundle with the Seafarers and Cities and Knights Expansions (plus 3 Scrolls and 7 days XP Booster) costs 1600 gold.
Conclusion, the game is suspiciously like a Pay To Win Model but it's not. It's more of a trick to confuse you to pay more for in-game cash currency. Think of it as more of a deceptive practice. The original Quake two is one of most entertaining games ever made, and it is still fun in 2017. It's a bit too easy even on hard mode, but is otherwise masterfully made.
However, here's a review of the Ground Zeroes expansion because steam doesn't allow me to post this on the Ground Zeroes page itself:
" Some time ago I bought the other expansion for Quake two called The Reckoning and almost immediately thought that things couldn't get any worse. While not necessarily worse, Ground Zero is certainly not much less disgusting. It starts fairly well, and after an hour or two becomes obscenely bad.
Many reviewers here have mentioned the Turrets. There are no words to describe the Turrets. The Turrets ruin this expansion - period. It doesn't matter that the level design is solid, or that the levels are larger, more challenging and more loaded with enemies than in the original. The Turrets destroy any slight chance of Ground Zeroes being anything else than an offensively repulsive experience to the FPS gamers who are unfortunate enough to become its victims.
The other new features suck. The developers did absolutely nothing to even slightly improve id's work. The spider-like enemies are garbage. The new Icarus enemy variations are worthless. The new rapid fire rifle is complete filth - it feels like the Hyperblaster, but without important features such as damage and the ability to hit something, because, obviously, when an enemy crouches, bullets go through their bodies. The new grenade launcher is, well, a grenade launcher, but with a new color. The creativity of this expansion is admirable. As admirable as Imagine Dragons featuring Charlie Frigging Puth.
If this was the original Quake two, it would've become a sad, sloppy laughing stock instead of the legend it is today. John "Daikatana" Romero would be proud. "

Before I start, let me just say right now that I love games like this. These open-world, random, survival-type games. They really entertain me. Now on to the actual review, let's just say that I had the absolute hardest time with this game and attempting to get it to work. I'm going to go ahead and list the problems I had, and then go into detail with each:
1) Couldn't play the game when I bought it because the Nether website claimed that I "hadn't yet purchased Nether".
2) Couldn't play the game because the server list would freeze my game.
3) Couldn't play the game because the server (any server, by the way) would keep me in spectator mode.
In-Detail Descriptions:
1) Apparently, if you buy this game through Steam, Steam must verify with the PlayNether website that you have purchased the game. To play your Nether copy through Steam, you need to sync your Steam and Mbet accounts, which first requires you to purchase nether. See where I'm going with this? Though I purchased Nether, I couldn't play it for about 6 hours because Steam hadn't 'communicated' with PlayNether saying, "Hey, this person bought your game!"
2) Speaks for itself. Basically, just wait like 5 minutes. The developers are bad and didn't properly program threading into their system (makes sure your program doesn't hang while a user is waiting on a process to finish). It has to load ALL the servers before you can do anything.
3) Sometimes it would eventually load me if I waited long enough, sometimes it wouldn't. The longest I had to wait was about 8 minutes. I have found no threads as to what the solution to this problem is, if any.
I have found threads from back in Sept. and Oct. of 2013 that show the developers saying they know about these issues, and it's 2014 now. Half-way through it. The developers of this game are bad, and they should feel bad. Absolute waste of money, do not buy, .7/10.

Sniper Elite V2 is a 2012 tactical shooter video game developed by Rebellion Developments and published by 505 Games for the PlayStation 3, Xbox 360 and later Wii U consoles and a developer self-published version for Microsoft Windows. It is a sequel/remake of Rebellion's 2005 game Sniper Elite that takes place in the same timeframe and location—the Battle of Berlin in April–May 1945—but with an altered narrative. The game's story follows an American Office of Strategic Services officer who must capture or eliminate the scientists involved in the German V-2 rocket program while the Red Army invades. A prequel named Sniper Elite III was released in 2014 for current and new-generation platforms.

The amount of bitter disappointments I have wasted time and money on - the amount of games where so clearly a developer has had a brilliant idea, something incredible, and... it comes to nothing. My library is full of high-concept games that developers have obviously given up on, not up to the task of properly actualising the great idea.
I saw Apotheon when it first came out, and I thought 'beautiful, but I daresay that'll be it', and I ignored it. When in the steam sale it was something like £2.50, I thought 'why not...' How wrong I had been to judge and underestimate.
Everything is wonderful. The graphics are beautiful. The soundtrack is faultless, the voice-acting is brilliant. Level-design provides challenge but nothing is ridiculously difficult - it is well thought-out and achieveable.
Gameplay is very enjoyable - this is the most I've enjoyed a game in years, including games I've put dozens or hundreds of hours into. And as good as the gameplay is, it's made all the better by how much effort has gone into everything around it; as mentioned, the graphics, the soundtrack, the voice-acting... Everything works in unison to create something really special. Not to mention dozens and dozens of weapons to choose from, a nice level of customisation [tiered armour and several different top-tier helmets], sidequests...
There's niggles, but it's nothing truly annoying, just noticable - and nothing that isn't very fixable.
This is the game I would have given a foot to have played as a kid. I really can't believe something of this quality was so cheap in the sale.

You've read this before, it's Peer to Peer, so connections issues happens. You'll get kicked out from games from time to time. It's not a constant problem, but it's there, and you notice it.
Here's a more detailed reveiw:
Pros:
- Interesting and unique, and rewarding combat
- Different classes with unique abilites and feats
- Variable maps with usefull surroundings
· Depending on the map you can use surroundings your advantage
- Great visuals
- Satisfying sound effects
- Co-op Singleplayer
- Interesting crossplatform faction war
· After choosing which faction to fight for, either Knight, Viking, or Samurai, you will deploy War Assets after each game to an area where your faction is fighting. The area with most % of assets will win over the opposing faction and temporarily claim the land.
- Neat character customization
· You change pieces of your weapons and armour, all with different stats, these stats does not affect your actuall gear in some gamemodes, such as duel.
Cons:
- Peer to Peer
· There are no dedicated servers, meaning that you might experience lag or disconnects if the host has bad connection. Hopefully this will change later.
- Mediocore story
- No Honor
· The community is pretty salty, complaining about you using your surroundings to your advantage or teaming up against one player. Please understand that skillfull players are able to take on more than one player at a time.
- Season pass and microtransactions
· Ubisoft charging more money after paying the $60/60€/40£. This is of course optional, but with the microtransactions you can practiclly buy better gear instead of earning it.
- Multiplayer issues
· It sometimes tries to match you into full lobbies, or you will get instantly kicked from matchmaking.
· After games you will be given to option to keep on playing with the previous players, you may check in "Ready", if there are to few players you will be thrown out of matchmaking, and if you were in a group this group will be disbanded.
Summed up:
This game is really fun, darn, it's the most fun I've had with a game in a long time. The multiplayer issues ruins it though. They don't happen as often as you may think, but they are noticable. You will get kicked from time to time and you might sit in matchmaking for a while. However, when the game works, it WORKS, the combat is smooth, satisfying and rewarding. You also feel a certain weight behind your actions, and this helps with the combat. Because when you win you know that YOU are better than the person were facing.
Singeplayer is meh, it's just kinda there. You do however unlock some rewards for completing it. I recommend playing it Co-op on realistic for the best experience.
Even though this is mostly a positive reveiw, in the end I can't recommend it due to how poorly Ubisoft delivered the game with the huge muliplayer issues on launch and microtransations to give advantages in a $60/60€/40£ game.

Few movies hold the place in the public conscious like Back To The Future. Since their release in the 80's and early 90's, the Back To The Future movies have captivated generation after generation. There are probably several reasons these movies had such a massive impact and are still being watched today. One reason could be the loveable characters, and another could be that a lot of movies have used time travel as a plot, but Back To The Future was the first to really get it RIGHT.
I personally grew up watching the animated series on Saturday mornings, and watching Marty and Doc travel in time always was such a fun time for me. Then at a later age I watched the movies and they have since become three of my favourite movies ever. So naturally, when I heard there was a game coming out, and it was going to be an adventure game developed by Telltale, who have already been responsible for mostly single-handedly bringing the glory of graphic adventure games, such as Monkey Island and Sam & Max, back to gamers, I was pretty hyped. For some reason I waited until all the episodes had been done, which I don't regret since it made me able to get the complete experience right away.
To best describe BTTF The Game would be to call it a fourth movie. Story-wise, the game remains incredibly faithful to the canon established by the movies and the plot is very well-written and always seem to make sense within the rules established by them, though this could mostly be credited to the team using Bob Gale and Robert Zemmeckis as story consultants, making sure the continuity would never be broken in any severe way as this could really have ruined the game in a major way. I won't spoil the story for those who have yet to play this game, but all I can say is that it really feels like it could be the plot of a fourth movie, and it has enough twists and turns to keep each episode worth playing. A genious twist is that each episode ends on a cliffhanger that leaves you aching to play the next, and even the final episode has a bit of a teaser at the end, leading us to expect another BTTF game some time in the foreseeable future.
Another great aspect about the game is obviously the voice acting. While they couldn't get Michael J. Fox to reprise his role as Marty, they found a very great replacement in AJ LoCascio who sounds eerily similar to Fox. Thankfully, Chris Lloyd is back, great and funny as ever as the old Doc from the movies. It doesn't really feel like he has aged much in the last 20-30 years, and he does a great job bringing Doc back to life, though I doubt anyone else could really have done it. The acting feels natural and unforced and unlike many games where the voices could feel robotic and like they were simply reading a script, the voices in this game really adds tons of personality and flavour to the rich gallery of people that are featured thruout the episodes.
Those looking for realistic graphics though should probably look away from this game. The game opts for a more cartoony style that feels very reminiscent of Monkey Island, another franchise that Telltale has "reanimated". However, this isn't necessarily a bad thing as the animation is great and adds even more personality to the game and gives its a very unique charming style. I did notice some issues with the graphics though, such as black lines appearing randomly, however the game ran perfectly smoothly even with everything maxed out in 1080 HD resolution, so it did not detract too much from an otherwise enjoyable experience.
The controls feel highly reminiscent of a classic point-and-click adventure game where you use the mouse to make Marty look at things and pick them up or examine them. Everything has been simplified to a simple intuitive click of a button and the game feels really easy to play. The inventory screen is easy to use and you can make Marty examine items for clues and such. Another helpful feature in the game is the hint system, which greatly helps if one gets stuck, which often tends to happen with people who rarely play these games or are new to the genre. The game also lets you view what goal Marty has, which in of itself gives you a clue what to do.
Overall, I can't really find anything negative to say about this game. If you like adventure games like Monkey Island, Grim Fandango or Day of the Tentacle, then I highly recommend this. Not only does it continue the BTTF franchise in a way that no new movie ever could, it's also a blast to play and should give the fans of the movies tons of laughs and an overall great experience. Some moments felt a bit tedious, but in total it was a thoroughly enjoyable experience for me.
Summary:
Story: 10/10
Great story that sticks faithfully to the rules and plot points established by the movie trilogy, with great voice acting from AJ LoCascio and Christopher Lloyd as well as a whole cast of great characters.
Graphics: 9/10
Aside from a few glitches here and there, the graphics are great, colourful and with tons of personality. Has that typical Telltale charm that no one can replicate.
Controls: 10/10
Nothing bad to say as the game offers several control methods and all of them are a blast to play with.
Presentation: 9/10
A few moments in the game felt tedious, which detracted slightly from the overall experience, which was great.
Total score: 10/10
If you haven't played this, but love either BTTF or adventure games, then this is a must-have title.

Picked up this game in the Summer Steam Sale - I'd never heard of it before then, and wow, was I missing out apparently. This is one of the best platformers I've played in a while, and certainly the most distinctive in art style that I've ever played, period. The whole style of the game looks like any given scene from it could be painted on the side of a Greek vase, and it's this 2D art styling that really gives the game its unique quality, coupled with a solid soundtrack and voice acting, it really sell the 'world' of Apotheon.
The combat system is very solid (though it takes some getting used to) and there are tons of weapons, most of which you'll have to use because there is a breakage mechanism so you'll eventually (or quickly) bust your preferred one if you use it too heavily. Sometimes it can feel a little clunky, but when it works, it works well - there's nothing quite as amusing as smacking a cyclops in the back of the head with a boulder or trading spear thrusts with a demigod (or introducing Ares to 'sticky bombs'... heh heh).
If I had one thing to criticize, it would be that the game doesn't checkpoint except when you move between areas, so with the levels being very large, this can be a minor problem, at least early on when you might get murdered by beastmen in a swamp or something. You can save whenever you want out of combat, but this convenience feature actually feels like kind of a downside when the game is as immersive as Apotheon is. Popping out to the menu to save so you don't lose too much progress on an oops really breaks the rhythm of it.
But that's a minor problem in a game that's otherwise fantastic.

TL;DR: Great light strategy game that will be very addicting for the first few hours for most. In a nutshell, it is a turn based strategy game in which you must complete levels to unlock new and better stuff, to be able to accomplish new and harder levels! Standard procedure really.
Breach and Clear (B&C) is a port of what was original a mobile game (IOS, Android). It does have added content, however its origins still show through its simpicity. The graphics are decent and hold up to HD displays. but this the main improvement. It depicts multiple representations of real world Special Operations groups in a variety of environments, with the player being the commander that holds an eagle eye of the battlefield. The authenticity of much of the info in the game (such as the loading screen tips) is indeed relevant and true to modern day SOF, although the "tactics" the game pushes aren't necessarily completely accurate due to the reliance on user input of what to do.
Technical Performance: Although I am running this on "gaming" (albeit aging) hardware, it should hold up on almost any machine at a very nice framerate. There's really nothing intensive computationally in the game. Loading times between levels  are minimal. The only adjustable settings in the graphics section are antialiasing (up to 8x), game resolution/full screen, and vsync.
Starting out: There are 7 factions (squads) that you can choose from to customize, each with their own unique skill boosts. There's no context on why one might be better than the others, so it's essentially just luck. There's no reason to slave over the decision, I'd recommend just picking the squad you think looks the best aesthetically. You then select from a multitude of soldier types to fill your squad. This decision matters quite a bit as each has its own special abilities that have huge value on the battlefield. As long as you pick a variety (one of each), again don't think too hard about it. Afterward, you go through a relatively short tutorial that shows off the game's mechanics and basic strategies. Very easy to pick up, unlike some strategy games that overload my brain (and processor) from the get-go.
Entertainment value: I personally wore out most of the game around 10 hours, going through every mission (7 total) and sub level (5 per mission, making 35 total playable stages without DLC) at first on normal difficulty then attempting them on insane. I've found that insane generally is actually quite doable for the most part, although on some levels (especially on the "escape plan" gamemode) they are quite impossible to perfect. There are 3 game modes: terrorist hunt (eliminate all hostiles), bomb defusal (reach and defuse one or two bombs), and escape plan (get as many squads members as possible to a position on the map). Each gamemode reuses the same missions and sub-levels, however the initial position of your soldiers varies. The reuse of the stages does get tiring eventually, but each stage provides enough enough entertaininment for a few plays. At the end of each sub level, player performance is rated on a scale of 1-4 stars, 4 being perfect or somewhat close to it. Criteria (as far as I can tell) is the time spent and how many squad members went down during the course of the sub level (this is the larger of the two criteria). Stars actually matter as they unlock the ability to purchase new guns (all accessories and gear are unlocked at default. Completion of a sub level also awards a certain amount of money, which can be spent on better equipment (guns, gear, etc).
-As a little side note, it's interesting to see B&C incorporating a lot of big name brands into the game, such as but not limited to Crye Precision, Tyr Tactical, and Surefire. Even if the company doesn't have a nod, their equipment is still featured (LBT 6094, Giessele triggers, and a LOT more). This defintely is a seldom-seen feature that adds a authenticity.
One of the flaws I see in the game is the lack of thought as far as gun and equipment upgrades. It's somewhat 2-Dimmensional, as there is often a clear "X plate carrier is better than Y plate carrier in every category". It seems almost carelessly done, as it significantly dims the strategic value of many purchases. In the end, out of the 18 long rifles featured, I purchased maybe 10 of them, skipping from the default rifle (M4 carbine) to some of the higher end guns by patience and thriftiness.
Gameplay: Quite fun, but reptitive after everything worth buying is unlocked. Each turn is worth 5 seconds, and works in a way similar to Fire Emblem. You start each sub level by picking from 1-4 entry points that your troops can breach through, and work your way to the objective. Each soldier has a movement range, effective firing range, etc depending on their stats and equipment, so each squad member has the potential to be very diffferent from the next. Sub level design is actually quite thorough, albeit somewhat linear at times. Usually, there are a few ways to approach an objective, through different paths. Object placement is realistic, and although this sometimes does not work out tactically, the developers really try their best to keep gameplay relatively balanced. Experimenting with new unlocks in different situations also adds to replayability, however in the end there's really only a couple of guns that players might choose to switch betweeen as they are superior to all others. I feel that some of the elements of the game, such as stealth, do not matter in the end. The developers seemed to have added them in as they are viable in real life, but the way the game works makes it relatively ineffective and I end up shooting my way through every mission anyway.
Plot: There is no plot to B&C, not really even a true attempt at one, however this works out for the game. There are 7 "missions" that take place in different countries/stages, each with 5 sub-levels that have short descriptors which are essentially formalities.
User Interface: The UI is especially important for strategy games as it can be confusing for newer players who have not learned what each button does. However, B&C is a relatively simple game that, once you go through the initial tutorial, you've pretty much mastered the controls. Everything is very intuitive and well organized.

First to get this out of the way: No, this is not like X-Com.
Yes, both are somewhat turn-based strategy games, but they play vastly differently as in Breach & Clear you plan a turn for your entire 4-men team and then everybody executes these moves at the same time. Including you and the bad guys
That's not a bad thing, however. In fact, it's a pretty neat concept, although not entirely new.  It's always nice to see some varitey in the genre, and only few games handle their turns the way B&C does.
Hoewever, where B&C doesn't manage to hit the spot is the challenge.
In B&C most missions are either too easy or too hard.
If a mission is too easy, you simply ignore all the little intricacies the game has to offer, so for example you rarely if ever set waypoints or plan your men's field of view. Instead, you just charge in, gunning down every enemy on the way.
If a mission is too hard, this is often the game's fault, when the random generator for example places one of your men right in a room with four foes nearby, leaving him no chance for survival.
I still had fun with the game, but overall I can't recommend it wholeheartedly. There are just too many good (and better) strategy games out there.

I know Canabalt was instrumental in kickstarting the infinite runner genre, and I know I'm going to get a lot of hate for this, but I honestly can't recommend this PC port. It's not about the gameplay; the gameplay is fine, and always has been. But I found this port to be rife with technical issues.
This game is buggy. My
, this game is buggy.
You probably already know what Canabalt is, but if not, it's a very simplistic game where you play as a man running and jumping across rooftops, and the goal is to earn a high score by running as far as possible before inevitably making a mistake and dying. There's only one button used to jump, but you'll have to learn to aim and adjust that jump to hairpin perfection if you want to survive for long. You speed up the longer you run, and you can trip over boxes to slow down. Problem is, if you are running too slow, you won't be able to jump on rising I-beams in time or run across falling buildings, but if you're running too fast, you won't have time to adjust your jump to land on tiny platforms. So it's all about running into boxes when you need to, and maintaining a perfect pace, hoping the game doesn't throw anything too tricky at you. It's a good balance between skill and luck. Otherwise, that's pretty much it; if you're expecting a game with tons of content, this isn't it. But as far as low-investment casual games go, Canabalt is one of the most tried and true.
The graphics are stylish and gritty, and the whole immersive atmosphere of an alien invasion is probably the best part of the game. The Danny Baranowsky track "RUN!" is awesome and never seems to get old.
The new PC port adds some slightly better graphics, and extra features that weren't in the original mobile version. There's a new 2-player mode where you try to run alongside a friend, and your scores are added together for your final total. It's fun for a little while, and if your friend abandons you, it's easy enough to play as two players yourself; it's just one extra button, after all. There are also some new challenge modes, most of which are the same game but with some tweaks, like replacing all the random obstacles with one kind of obstacle. And of course, now we have Steamworks features like cloud synch, trading cards, leaderboards, and achievements.
Admittedly, it's much harder on a keyboard than it is on a touch screen to make the tiny tap-jumps which the game will sometimes require for your survival, unless you have very thin keys. Luckily, you can also use the mouse.
So what are my complaints? Well, here are just a few of the issues I ran into:
* The game is not alt+tab friendly at all. After returning from an alt+tab, I've had a wide number of glitches ranging from infinitely looping menus, to disappearing game objects, to soft-locked death screens.
* The game seems to hang a lot in the middle of the run, notably when kicking boxes. I assume this is due to the game buffering the different box kicking sound effects the first time they are played, but it has ruined many runs for me, especially during co-op.
* After some extended co-op sessions with two actual people, we have concluded that there is a bug which periodically causes one player's controls to make the other player jump, even if they're already in midair, causing an awkward and impossible midair jump. It's not something I noticed when controlling two players myself, but it became very apparent with an actual second player.
* Sometimes when you kick a box, another box somewhere else on the screen will mysteriously get kicked also. This is very apparent while running at high speeds on the "box tripper" challenge. This, combined with the "wrong player control" issue described above, indicates that there's some kind of pointer / memory corruption happening.
* On more than one occasion, I've restarted a run and all the buildings were gone, and I kept instantly falling to my death. When I tried to quit, the game soft-locked with a white screen.
* The Game Over menu is very lazily implemented. You can't merely press a button to restart the run, but you have to use the arrow keys or the mouse to select the "restart" option. The default option on the Game Over menu depends on where your mouse cursor is at the time you died; so if you make sure your mouse cursor is at the bottom-right corner of the screen while playing, then you can hit "enter" to restart the run when you die. Otherwise you might open the options or something.
* Kicking a box immediately after coming out of a roll from a high jump will sometimes cause the character's running animation to freeze, making him look like he's skating across the rooftops.
* Very wonky physics at high speeds; on at least two occasions I've jumped straight through solid objects at breakneck speeds, like when playing the "Panic" challenge.
* The jump button is the only button you can remap, despite the game menus using several other keys.
Overall, I just don't understand why something so simple as Canabalt can be screwed up and left without so much polish for a proper PC release. I mean, this is
a complex game; would it really have been that hard not to leave in so many bugs?
If you just want an occasional run across the rooftops in single player on your PC instead of your phone, this port seems to hold up in that regard -- although you can also just Google "Canabalt" and play a web version of it completely for free. I am just disappointed that what was supposed to be a definitive version of a great game is, in the end, just a lazy mobile port.
Achievement hunters: this is not an easy 100%. Not that there's anything wrong with that from a game design perspective (though some might raise objections that the game expects you to survive for 40,000 meters with so many random luck elements involved), but just don't expect to get the last few achievements unless you're very persistent and dedicated.

With the restored content mod, this is probably my favorite Star Wars game. Graphics, gameplay, sound etc. are all pretty out-dated, but the characters are excellent, story is engaging, and the RPG - mechanics solid. Kotor I and II both capture, IMO, the feel of the old movies, with great relatable characters and humor and so on, but still manage to do their own thing with the story. Plus, there's the dark side playthrough, which isn't completely independent, but still manages to feel different, like Mass Effect. Saying more would spoil much, I'll just say the player kills a lot more people as DS. The player also gets a different party member for light and dark, as well as another one for male and female main. There's a fair bit of replayability, especially if you love Star Wars. Also, there's a DA: Origins type influence system for party members, with serious rewards if played right.
It's pretty epic, I played it through maybe a dozen time when it came out, so my laudatory review might be tinged with nostalgia. Still, seeing an old favorite on steam, with a patch released some ten years after the original game came out, with workshop support of all things - as well as the fact, that the game is stable technically, and plays fine on Win 10, make it an excellent look into what a classic game of the sixth generation was like. Something of a testing ground for Dragon Age and Mass Effect, which stormed the industry, while Kotor turned into an MMO. Kind of sad, really.
No voice-acting for the player character, dated graphics, and wonky controls aside, it's a great buy. Also, the bit in the beginning on the mining station goes on for some three hours, but after that, the story starts to open up.
Warmly recommended for story, characters and writing.

The reviews for this game once again displays the average intelligence of a steam user.
This game is
as advertised.
This is what you get as a F2P player. The free game mode is basically matchmaking like in any other game, where you cannot select the map, expansions or any modifiers and is limited to 1 vs 1 vs 1. It doesn't allow you to create a custom game with your friends, that's a feature you have to buy the game for. Yes, there are micro transactions, but that doesn't mean the game is falsely advertised. You can literally play the base game infinitely on matchmaking without any restrictions. Any review that solely gives it a negative review because of this, is objectively wrong. People don't call Hearthstone Buy2Play either just because you have to pay for a singleplayer campaign, it still is F2P.
The game itself doesn't suffer from any major issues. What's definitely lacking is a native Anti Aliasing option and a rework of the trading UI, because the "Give" and "Take" regions aren't labeled, which forces you to guess if you have not memorized it in the tutorial.
There's also a legitimate issue of the weighted rolls (The dots on the cards), which another reviewer noted and I would agree with that. The probability of rolling anything less than 4 isn't that high with real 2 1d6, but out of the 3 games I have played, none actually had rolled a 2 or 3 and very rarely 6. It was heavily distributed towards 8, 10 and 12.
Otherwise, it's a Settlers of Catan PC boardgame version. It plays as it should and there's nothing really for me to complain about, except that maybe the dice rolls could also have an 3D effect. I also cannot really review the expansions or other micro transactions, because you cannot look at those as a free to play player. I'm often very anal about UI, responsiveness and optimization, but this plays just right and I haven't encountered any bugs. There's also a plus point that you cannot be matchmaked against people you have blocked. If you always wanted to play Settlers of Catan on Steam, then this is probably for you.
