You have three days and nights to deal with a monster called the Rake. And boy, does this game know how to make their monster scary. It could be ANYWHERE. Though it has some predictable patterns, it's difficult to shoot, nearly impossible to escape, and as the game progresses it proves just how much of a monster it really is. And it's
There are boars and deer as well, which will startle and run away from both you and the creature. These two animals are terrifying in their own rights in this game, though I don't think that was intended.

This game does, of course, have a couple bugs. But it's playable - in fact, I can't STOP playing it. If you like horror, particularly Creepypastas or cryptid tales, this game is worth more than the asking price.

Oh my goodness. Let me first say that I have been dreaming of a game like this.
It's not just set on switching between cameras or collecting pieces of paper out in the woods, but it's a game that takes multiple elements from those other common horror titles.
The game starts you off in a parked rv, within the middle of a woodland clearing, giving you the necessary items to start your night's hunting. Yes, hunting is actually a part of this game. No longer do you have to be 100% victim to the elements or creatures that surround you constantly. In fact, you get a firearm as well as other protective items. These other items can be placed conveniently to hurt your enemies as well as to lure them to intended locations.
One of the coolest features of this game is that you can set up a minimum of five cameras around the map. The available placement spots for these cameras are pre-determined, highlighted areas on the sides of specific trees.
A black & white night filter is the only way you can visually see the environment through these cams. This is not a problem though seeing as how the filter does not seem to make trouble identifying things whether day or night. The availability to turn your cameras left or right in limited space is a neat little thing that Rake also offers.
Despite being made in the Unity engine, most affiliated with poorly made indie games, it is actually fairly decent in functionality and its playing mechanics.
The scares are great ranging anywhere from seeing these deadly creatures appear through security screens to the dreadful sound of fast running feet followed by immediate attack. I cannot describe how bad my heart attacks were from witnessing these things first hand.
Sounds make this game. The night sounds exactly how it would in the actual woods, the security feed buzzes and woops are oddly addictive to listen to, the animal sounds are loud and jolt inducing at times, and the little music that unexpectedly plays is reminiscent; in a good way; to Slender: The Arrival.
Now that I've listed all of the things that I love about this game, I will carry on to state the few issues I've had with it.
The monsters that attack you are, more often than not, way too fast to react to. If you were running around in the woods and you hear the quick moving feet of your impending doom, you're most likely not going to know where it's coming from let alone land a shot before you are stuck in a scripted taking damage scene. Please find a way to fix this. Maybe something like a faded bar of light that emanates from whatever side the monster is coming from could help. This along with the attack timing. Just give the player at least a few more seconds to respond. This is all to suggest that you are keeping this hit and run formula. If you plan on replacing the current attack script with a more advanced/realistic trigger event, then that would be even better.
Another thing on the monsters is the models. I'm pretty sure everyone has noticed that the implied different monsters of  the night have literally the same exact same model but reskinned. At the very least they have different sound effects, but the cloning of the monster designs just takes some of the fun out of the mystery and wonder of what they could've looked like. I hope that intentions are to change the models out for better and uniquely scary representations of what they're supposed to be. Please correct me if I'm wrong on the whole model thing.
An obvious would be the graphics. Yes I know that graphics don't make a game seeing as how I'm rating this game positively, but it would do this game such an amazing service. This game is already, for a majority, rated very positive. This is a good thing for a game based off of an internet story abused over and over for the use of rushed "COLLECT ME!" games. If you can get a positive following for a game that doesn't even have impressive graphics, then think of what will happen with the same game touched up with detail! This would also improve on the already great atmosphere!
Also I would find it hard to imagine you defending the graphics here.
I would not take you seriously if you complemented the hills/mountains in this game.
I have not found many bugs playing Rake, but I'm sure you can all agree that you've witnessed the "I can hear the cameras turn while I move side to side" bug. It's pretty funny to be honest, but it does not do anything to improve gameplay let alone atmosphere. To find it, all you do is press your inventory key "i" while in the cameras. Then get out of the camera view and move around. You'll hear what I mean. Bet you this would be a quick and easy fix. Another bug I've noticed, which is actually detrimental to your game progress, is a specific event at a house. Despite mentioning all this stuff, I do not want to spoil some of the little neat things. Short and short, the game freezes there. Fix that please.
Multiplayer seems currently broken. I started a multiplayer world by myself, and my inventory was not accessible at all.
I could see a health bar at the top of my screen, and could not use any items. I thought maybe I'm the monster, so I ran out into the woods only to be killed by that lanky Rake. I know this is all work in progress, but it did not make a good first impression for match making. In fact, I would've given this game a negative review if the only part of this game was online. On a side note, it seems like there are newer models for items in the multiplayer mode.
Why are they not in single player instead?!
Last thing to mention here is the menu screen. Don't get me wrong. I actually find the menu screen cool with the whole window blind moving side to side and equipment lying around everywhere thing. What I don't like is the buttons. I don't know why, but pressing the buttons on screen makes me feel like the game is going to crash. I believe it because of how low resolution the text is on screen. Often, I mentally associate badly made games with low res menus. So when I see these blurry white boxes on screen with text in them, they give off the wrong feeling. Funny enough, the loading times actually fuel this minor fear even more. It reminds me of how DayZ loads with it making you wait and then having you be in the world already yet with text still in your face. It just makes the processing feel awkwardly slow. Maybe it is though. All I'm saying is that it would be good to have the button displays clearer and somehow make the loading times feel quick and responsive. I know just asking for it doesn't make it happen immediately,
but I'm just stating the issues I've noticed.
Hope this review is helpful to those who are interested in purchasing Rake,
and I hope it does some good to the developer.

Apotheon is one hell of a Metroidvania game. Really great execution, for the most part!
Look at the game. I don't think I need to say much else. Sure, the game itself is awesome, but the visuals are a big part of what makes it stand out.
The biggest strength in the combat is how the game is physics driven, but not like most of the lazy games that use a default physics engine with no consideration for gameplay. No no no, Apotheon uses physics almost perfectly, making the combat feel very impactful, and the general game is very satisfying to play. Platforming is cool, but above that is how you can break virtually everything, and the corpse ragdoll effects are really fun to play with!
Beautiful lighting system! Simple, but it's still very nicely done. And it's used as a gameplay tool as well, so it's not just something to look pretty.
Regarding the visuals, I think they went a bit overboard with the visual effects. Most of them were unnecessary and actually taken away from the whole "ancient pottery" aesthetic it has going for it. Looks a bit too polished and sparkly for pottery. But hey, it's still really unique!
I was a bit disappointed with the story... It was very linear, and... "original". In this case, however, original isn't good.
Drawing for mythology, there are tons of stories worth telling. What they've done, is simply to draw from the pantheon and some of the Gods' relationships, and made a betrayal/revenge story of their own, about a human who kills Gods... meh.
Honestly, I expected things to be a bit different. Oh well.
The combat can be a bit clunky, at times, because physics. Still feels very nice to send corpses flying around and throwing javellins at innocent Gods.
Definitely give this one a go! Could have been better, story-wise, but the game itself is brilliant. Lots of different approaches and little mechanics that are barely used, but that you're free to explore.
Awesome game!

Let's be completely honest right out of the gate and admit that there are server issues currently present with this game and that as a result many of us (including myself) have been unable, or at least very little of the time, to get into the game servers. Watching the developers on their twitter however leaves me to believe that this will be fixed by the end of the first week. With that out of the way lets get into it shall we?
Pros:

So I finally finished the infamous Amnesia. I have recently been really into horror games, so I suppose it was only a matter of time untill I got to the game which spammed recommendations to everyone in 2010-11. And don't get me wrong, Amnesia is a fantastic game, a true testament to the potential of indie games and shows that Frictional Games has the capability to make the best horror game, if given the time and resources. But, it is nowhere near as scary as I was lead to believe.
Pros:
+ Amazing Atmosphere. With relatively light graphics, it's amazing how the game is able to create such an immersive and creepy atmosphere. Throughout the game, it always felt like I was actually in a castle, especially with the exellent sound design and lighting.
+ Story. The story of Amnesia is by far its strongest point, especially with the way it's told. Like Bioshock, you understand much of the story through notes and diary entries you find when exploring, and it is clear they put a lot of thought in the story. I also like how it plays on a narrative trope (convienent protagonist amnesia) by, instead of brushing it off as a plot device, makes the causes of it and integration into the story feel so natural.
+ Puzzles. While Amnesia is a survival horror, I found its best gameplay aspects to be the brilliant physics puzzles. Each of these puzzles requires a great amount of thought and the only clues you get is notes you have to search for which don't always give the full solution, and are often in dangerous areas.
+ Physics. Its a small but great detail. The physics in this game really help with the immersion. While they may seem clunky at first, they very quickly blend into the world and allow manipulation of the physics in gameplay.
+ Sanity. While it isn't the best addition, I found it to be a great concept with potential for implementation in other horror games. Basically, staying in darkness or witnessing unsettling events drains your sanity, which makes gameplay progressively harder. but the most creative part is that it drains quickly when you look at enemies. The scariest thing in horror is always fear of the unknown, so this mechanic keeps you in a state of uncertainty and ensures you don't even know what the monsters look like fully untill a while into the game.
+ Soundtrack. The Music in this game complements the atmosphere perfectly and never feels out-of-place.
+ Character Design. While it's not that big of a Positive, the characters in this game are all really well designed.
Mixed
~ The Light Resource. This games' primary survival horror element is the Lantern. While it is a interesting and competent addition, it felt annoying later on as I only found around 1-2 oil pots  in each area, leading me to stumble around in the dark with a constantly draining sanity. Ultimately, I didn't really mind it by the end. But even then, for a game all about immersion, I found myself sprinting everywhere just to save lantern oil, sometimes breaking said immersion.
Cons
- Character Animation. While you won't witness it much, when you do, the animations (especially on monsters) are noticeably stiff.
- Monsters Themselves. The single worst part of this game occurs to you when you realize just how incredibly stupid the monsters are. I discovered this first when I realized that when one appears, you can just duck into a dark corner untill he despawns, when you are essentially invisible. I am fine with spawning/despawning enemies in a horror game, but at least make them actively a threat. Not only that, but they have some of the worst AI I have seen in a while. I literally walked right up to one with my lantern on, AND HE DID NOT SEE ME! I actually managed to black out from sanity loss before he even noticed my existence. When I discovered just how dumb they are, much of the horror from the game almost completely faded.
- The Multiple Endings. [No spoilers] The problem with the multiple endings is that only one of the endings are satisfying. One of them is just flat out abrupt, and the other is so confusing it will make your brain melt out your ears.
- Death. There is little to no penalty to death, to the point that the monsters even despawn if they killed you. The only thing resembling a penalty is your lost Lantern oil.
Verdict:
This is a one-of-a-kind horror game that I think anyone a fan of the genre should experience. Now, looking back on all of this, I could almost give this game a 9/10. But I think the aweful moster AI and letdown multiple endings just drag it down. That being said, I applaud you Frictional, and I hope you will be able to make the perfect horror game. (SOMA might be that, but I haven't played it yet.)
Final Rating:
8/10

First of all, I got this game from an online store where I could have Steam and DRM-free version for less than a dollar. Since it's a puzzle game, I want the one that focuses more on solutions and not on time-lapsed or "steps-taken" approach.
Interestingly enough, Hook is way more than I expected for.
It' s a minimalist puzzle game. White background, some bits and pieces cluttered on the screen. No in-game menu. No clock ticking in a way that you feel like in a hurry. No record for how many steps you take to finish a level. You can press Esc button to quit the game and that was all.
This minimalist approach to me presents some advantages and disadvantages as well. You feel calm when playing the game. You can absolutely concentrate on how to find a solution. You are not bothered with some learning curves at the beginning of the game. There's no tutorial. But I do feel confused when running this game for the first time. All I got was a text "Hook" and an object under it which looks like a circle, a thread and a nail. They just stay there. Funny how I thought the game is still loading and comes to the point it hangs up. I press Esc button to quit it, load it again and click anywhere on the screen until I click on the circle and that's when the game starts. To compensate the absence of a tutorial, I strongly suggest that there should be some kind of arrow or pointer and some texts that tell a player what to do at the first level of the game.
Do I mention some "bits and pieces" before? The objects on the game are grey circles or  "buttons", some "nails" and "hooks", "switches" and some thin lines or "wires". The objective is simple but deceptive. You have to release the nails and hooks from the screen by setting the wires and pressing the button so as to not tangle other objects. What seemingly as easy tasks at earlier levels turns into huge problems at later levels. You will deal with many wire interjunctions of nails, hooks, switches and buttons. Last week I was playing Homeworld, and it reminded me of how often games reuse the same story elements again and again - In that case a highly advanced ancient extinct race, which is also used in games like Mass Effect, Neverwinter Nights etc. etc. I mean it is simply tiring and boring and I expect more from story-heavy games like that.
Of course the idea of transferring or copying your consciousness is not new, but I haven't seen that before in a game. And they really put you in some interesting situations that explore the concept in the way pretty much only a game can.
I typically don't like horror games because they just make me uncomfortable and nothing more, so it feels one dimensional. After an hour or so I typically stop and then there's a small chance I'll continue. But this one somehow guided me in slowly and got me invested in the world first and it slowly turns up the heat, until it really gets to you. It scared me in some original and funny ways I did not expect to see. There are also parts where it slows down and you can relax which is perfect.
There are some puzzles, and they're really cool and sometimes innovative. Some are easy but sometimes I get frustrated and think I can't figure it out, only to figure it out a minute or so later. So nothing that'll stop you for continueing but also not without a challenge -- perfect.
Any way, beside all those things: It looks good, it sounds great, and I didn't see any bugs or anything frustrating. Go get it!

The "Endless Runner" genre of games owes it's livelihood to Canabalt. Without this humble little flash game taking the internet by storm, we would have never seen the creation of Temple Run and other classics (Jetpack Joyride, Rayman Jungle Run, etc). While some people may not care for that style of gaming, there is a simplicity within that makes the game extremely addicting and furiously challenging.
The goal is to simply survive as long as you can. The level is always randomized and will get progressively harder as you stay alive. The speed picks up and new obstacles are thrown at you. You have mere split-seconds to react or die. The simple controls give you enough dominion over your character to make every move; the only thing keeping you back is your reaction time.
That would be about it for a review, but this Steam version includes the updated port that was released on mobile devices a few years back. With that, you get some "3D" graphics and a 2-player mode with challenges. The 3D is pointless as the sprite work in the original is gorgeous. There is no need to even bother with the remixed visuals.
As for the 2-player mode, it is a nice touch. I can't say the game is preferable with 2 people, but it certainly is a nice addition for the truly addicted. Challenge mode is where the real thought went. I like how each level is basically a set of stipulations that require you to still react to random levels.
The only problem is that 2-player mode makes a joke of those challenges. As far as completion goes, you just need to reach a set distance and you've finished the challenge. Since 2-player doubles your score (as long as both players are alive), you end up doing each challenge twice as fast.
You can up the ante and play both players by your lonesome. It does make for some intense situations where one player drifts away faster than the other. Your brain has problems reacting to two different objects and the outcome is often fatal. Still, I feel like challenge mode could have been expanded for 2-player.
Either way, this updated port is great. It may be a bit late to the game, but nothing is truly wrong with this version. I guess it wouldn't hurt to ask for some more content with challenge mode, but the rest is basically as good as it has ever been.
The price isn't even bad, either. $3 might seem like a lot, but you will definitely get your moneys worth. If nothing else, the Humble Bundle edition from a few years back came with a Steam key, so you may even own this without knowing.

I couldn't bear to give this bad feedback as I like and support it. But right now it's a click-farm. Keep clicking, get resources, and buy upgrades that let you click more.
It's fast-developing, and the devs are listening to people - which is normally good. I'm certainly going to check back in again in a few weeks to see how it changes. What I think is going wrong at the moment is that they have taken away some things that the community said were frustrating. In the version I first played, my bunker-family spent ages waiting for rain, and when they were on their last legs it finally rained, but it was poison rain, so they had to wait for it to be slowly filtered while their health was creeping down. Drinking it would have risked radiation poisoning and using up virtually irreplacable meds. The parts to make gas masks were also so rare that I'd be left with choices like everyone can die of hunger, or we could dismantle the water supply so that somebody can make a mask and leave the bunker and find some food. Or maybe recruit somebody else that we can send on a suicide mission into the wasteland without a mask.
But since the last update, it rains all the time. I think I read that it rains at least once every 4 days. This predictability lets you gamble all the water on long foraging missions. Gas mask parts were a daft limiting factor (IRL you would only need to replace the filters not the whole mask), but now that they are more common it's like there is 1 limiting factor too few. Life is sustainable with the starting furniture, and it gets progressively easier.
I had a similar gripe with Fallout 3. Like in that game once you can recover health and reliably access uncontaminated water and food, half the thrill goes out of it.
Everyone always has an angle on what to do about stuff like this in early access games. They might add gangs or mutants to wear you down from outside, or they might change it round so you start with the good furniture and the game gradually wears it down, or they could give you bigger resource stockpiles and lower usage rates but make the replenishment very unpredictable, or they could put in a loyalty system so that when you add another person to the bunker they can forage for you, but they might also murder you in your bed. They could add in Sims-like interaction between the bunker people so that arguments and fights create some risk. Or they could make it that foraging gradually becomes harder as time passes after the initial fallout and food supplies decay, offset with the radiation/dust lessening.
A unique and odd aspect was you can customise the family. I like a lot of people based them on me, my wife and our kids. But I found that it made me want to not turn the game on if I knew they were all doing okay! It was like "bunker family are okay, let's leave them be rather than logging on and risk watching them starve to death or having to eat the dog".
Clicking on people five times a day so they can drink, sleep, eat, wash, poop and mend something is a tedium I haven't experienced since Tamigotchi. I'd have preferred to be able to *stop* them doing things to conserve resources... Water running low? Family meeting. Dog's drinking too much. Bye-bye dog. That sort of thing.
Keep an eye on this game. Wait a bit and see what happens as they are changing it all the time. I'm not sorry I supported it, it is just that as of right now it could still easily follow the community feedback into a route of having tons of new weapons and enemies and other periphera, but still be a click-farm underneath it all.

Basically, it's a simplified version of Frozen Synapse. It's tons of fun and very well polished for a mobile port. Most things in this game are done right, but there are a few huge flaws about that keep it from greatness. First off, there's no multiplayer mode... Really!? A turn-based strategy has no multiplayer gamemode!? Secondly, the camera controls are a bit wonky. You'll get accustomed to it, but it just feels off. Finally, there isn't a story. You're just dropped into singleplayer missions. There are 3 game modes and about about 95 missions in all, which will give you about 15 hours of game time, but they dont have much replayability, so once you play them, then they're done... I got it in the humble bundle and I can say it was easily worth that price. If you enjoy games like XCOM: Enemy Unknown, Frozen Synapse, or Jagged Alliance, then you have no excuse to not buy this game.

+Good AI (on Hard and up)

Cons:

-No multiplayer (Seriously?!)
-Missions can get repetitive
-Is a mobile port

I've only had a short time with Nether, but I find it quite enjoyable. I highly recommend you play this game with friends. It is a harsh, unforgiving world to play in. Allies are few and far between. A run from one outpost to another can be dangerous on highly populated servers. You never know who is friend, and who is foe. All of these elements come together to create a constant feeling of paranoia as you trek through abandoned buildings. That is why I think this game shines. This game is not for everybody. It is a "Hardcore" gaming experience. But if you are willing to brave the wasteland it is a very emersive experience as well. Realism plays a bit part as you never know who you can trust when it comes to player characters. In truth, most of them will try to kill you. Working together is the best way to survive. Join a tribe, and stick to the insides of building when traveling. Invest points in stamina to run for long distances. I look forward to future updates and will more than likely be playing this game for a long time. I suggest it to any person that enjoys a survival experience filled with a feeling of dread and true helplessness. It is not easy. Good luck.

Okay, so. This game is still receiving updates even though it isn't Early Access any longer. As far as a full game goes, it's not the best experience in the world, but I would pay $5 for it. Fortunately for me, I got it on sale day before yesterday for $2.49.
I spent a few short hours in this game before I had been given the peak experience of the game. You play as a scientist in the mountain forests. There's wild boars and deer wandering around the map to add some life to the world. Although, they don't do much. The boars may wander into a trap at your camp which will allow you to place a camera on their heads to track their movements while they wander around the woods.
You can place up to 5 cameras in the woods, equipped with moton sensors to track the movements of both wildlife and The Rake within view. This is nice, but watching cameras can be almost unbearably annoying at times due to the amount of "flickering" the cameras do. It's like an older VCR effect where the screen has some horizontal splicing. If it happened less often, I would be much happier with the camera system.
The Rake was creepy enough for the first few hours and he has a tendency of sneaking up on me, which provided some mild jumpscares. However, what I've seen of his AI turned out to seem a little bland. The Rake seems to wander the woods idly until he spots a reason to come after you or run away. I was able to find a deer stand overlooking an open swamp. It was there, I waited for two nights with my shotgun and sniper rifle. The Rake would wander aimlessly into the open where I would shoot him and he would either run away or sprint towrds me until I shot him a second time. Every time I did this, within two minutes, he would come back for more.
Deer Stands are a nifty feature, providing the player "Invisibility" to The Rake's eyesight. However, I'm not sure how The Rake interacts with players while they are within the safety of a deer stand. I don't know if I'm ever going to see The Rake while I'm in a deer stand because I don't know if he walks in my direction while I'm standing in one. Making it almost frustrating to stand in one and wait for him.
You have the ability to pick up animal feed and traps in the world. You can access them in your inventory and place them on the ground for an added "hunting" effect. However, these features seem rather unpolished, ad boars will completely ignore the feed and I've yet to see The Rake go after any of my animal feed piles. Once I get The Rake to walk over one of my traps, I will deem my experience with Rake complete.
Should you pay $5 for this game? I'd say it's up to you. Different people may receive different experiences with the game depending on how they play, so the game could not be worth the $5, while others will find it worth more than $5. I would say, as far as $5 goes, it's worth the experience, as short lived as it is, because this game is multiplayer and is still being updated. Who knows what will change in the future? I've provided a list of pros and cons I experienced while playing this game. Features I liked, versus qualms I had with existing features of the game. I won't include features that aren't included because they may not be in the game for good reason. (Jumping, crouching, etc.)
===Pros===
-The ability to view cameras and track the movements nearby your camp without actually going outside.
-Cameras detect motion, so the buttons on your screen will turn red when something enters view.
-You can place traps and feed down to "attract" animals and The Rake.
-The binoculars and sniper scope are well-made and, when used with your flashlight, can be used with a sort of night vision effect.
-The Game has good atmosphere, with an array of wildlife and ambiance scattered throughout the woods.
-The jumpscares are enjoyable. Not too obvious, not too weak.
-The game escalates well over 3 days as The Rake gets progressively more aggressive each night.
===Cons===
-Camera screens flicker so much, it makes them very annoying to watch. If you can decipher what you're looking at, it still makes it very hard to see.
-The motion sensors on the camera are very sensitive. They were picking up things that were very far away from view or that I couldn't see at all.
-The animal feed doesn't seem to work as advertised, as far as my experience has shown.
-With animal feed not seeming to work, traps may very well be utterly useless as they are right now.
-The Rake AI seems to wanter aimlessly, seeking out any excuse to attack the player. It's as though his soul reason for existing is to scrape your knees, judging by the amount of damage he does.
-The Rake does a very little amount of damage to the player. This made my experience wear thin very quickly. I was no longer scared of The Rake before too long.
-The Rake has an absurdly large health pool. I had first aid kids and enough shotgun shells to blow up the moon. I don't think it would have been enough to kill The Rake over the course of 3 nights.
-Boar AI seems rather .... dim. I would trap a boar, scare him away, and he'd follow the same path into my tent and right back into the trap every time.
-In the back of the map, where the Sniper Rifle is located, there's a boat located there in the swamp. It has no collision model and I can walk right through it. This can break immersion very quickly.
That's all I have for now, but as future updates come out, I may change my opinions. Is this game worth your time? for $5, I'd say so.

“Amnesia: The Dark Descent” is, without a doubt, one of the best horror experiences I've ever had. However grudgingly, I must admit the game ranks up there with the first two “Silent Hill” games and “Fatal Frame.” “Amnesia” is truly a masterpiece of horror.
That having been said, the game will not be for everyone. It's slow to start; at the thirty minute mark, I was thinking I'd probably wash out of the game. Another ten or so minutes in, things started to 'click.' The immersion came together and I was able to better appreciate the pacing and presentation. Simply put: if sounds don't spook you, check out another game (as this one leans primarily on creepy soundscapes). Also, if you want a more active (read: combat-oriented) tone, “Amnesia” is not for you. Yes, there are monsters but you won't be fighting them. Avoidance is your default solution here, with running and hiding being the only feasible back-up plan.
Much of the terror in “Amnesia” comes from ambiance, specifically with sounds and music. Many horror games focus on jump scares, or frightening monsters, or disturbing images and gore. They rely too much on the visual, trusting that the graphical rendition of a thing is the best way to shock or revolt the audience. Even when this is the case, whatever a person sees can hardly ever be as terrifying as what is imagined. Audio mapping is the best way to help find fear and “Amnesia” makes full use of sound. Haunting music. Monster growls. Creaking doors. Panicked breathing. Amplified by all that time alone in the dark. Glorious.
Inventory management is a stroke of genius: light rationing. Not only is this necessary to mitigate the player's sanity mechanic, but it lends an unparalleled level of tension to the player's decision making process. There are a finite number of tinderboxes (the item that activates light sources) and a limited amount of oil for the lantern. When and where you 'turn on the lights' suddenly matters, especially when you're in a large room or long hall. But be careful: those lights can be blown out by a gust of wind... or allow a monster to see and follow you, 'cause light works both ways. If you'll forgive the phrase, it's brilliant.
Lastly, puzzles. What foray into interactive horror is complete without them? The game has several, ranging in difficulty from child's play to somewhat obtuse. Periodically, it's necessary to complete a puzzle in order to move on with the game. When those challenges are completed, there's a blue-tinged flash on the screen to inform you of your success. There's also a restorative effect on your in-game sanity (“Heart pounding and hands are shaking” is reset to “Crystal clear”, for example). It is worth noting that a few of the puzzles are made more difficult in rather contrived ways. For example, several puzzles require you to turn valves and on one such occasion, I had to ask myself: is the challenge here to determine the correct location for those weights? Or is it simply getting the weights to move at all? Frustrating to say the least, all the more so because such behavior ruins an otherwise clever, well-constructed puzzle. Fortunately, these incidents are few and far between.
8/10. If you're looking for something truly different and you can muster the patience to let the game come into it's own, “Amnesia: The Dark Descent” is a hell of a trip. Lights off, headphones on and enjoy the ride.
P.S. Don't forget about the "Justine" DLC. Instead of selecting 'play game' from the menu, choose 'run settings', click 'Justine' in the lower right corner. It's brief and must be completed in a single pass; no saves or do-overs. Enjoy!

I may only have 30 minutes play time in this game - but trust me when I say that my review has reasoning.
I LOVE Friday the 13th. When I was a kid I would watch these movies with my dad all the time. When I heard there was a game coming out from an indie developer - I was so excited. I've spent the last year tracking this game's developement. Hell, up until I bought it today I would watch tons of people like Cryaotic stream it - and now that I've had my chance to play personally, I'm left feeling empty.
Don't get me wrong - the attention to detail is amazing. I feel like I'm watching a Friday the 13th Movie. But that's the issue - I'm only watching it. I may be in control of the character - but the game has so little in it I felt the only interesting thing to do was to wait to see how Jason would kill me. I had zero enthusiam to actually try to accomplish escaping: and here's why.
Escaping may be fun and difficult - but you have about 4 ways to do it. Call the police and wait five minutes, fix a car, fix a boat, or wait 20 minutes for the timer to run out. Now, I understand that it being the late 70's in a secluded camp, it would be difficult to escape or call for help. BUT, when you make a very small amount of options on how to take on a situation - the game begins to feel empty. I only played one match - and I realised that every match afterwards will consist of me trying to turn on a car while a guy playing Jason who can teleport will try to kill me. That's not fun to me, maybe to you, but not to me. I never got a chance to play Jason, maybe he's actually fun to play. But, hoping you're lucky enough to be chosen as Jason to finally have a 20 minute match of fun, isn't a good time.
The match I played was a public lobby. Apparently playing a private match with just your friends can be a whole lot more fun. The only issue is finding 10 friends who can afford to buy this 40$ game and also have computers capable of running it.
The game just feels empty as of right now. It's an amazing digital take on Friday the 13th, but it's more like an artshow/kill cam than it is a challenging game - and that is why I'm refunding it.
I say, save your money for a rainy day when this game is on sale - by then a lot of bugs will have been worked out and there'll be more content in the game.
Thank you.

If you are considering this game because you have enjoyed other horror survival titles such as DBD, I would recommend looking elsewhere.
Horror
- Jason is not scary.  He is powerful, has some interesting talents, but nothing about him is scary.  The animations are cartoonish, especially his run...which is what he does 90% of the game.
- The counselors faces are ridiculous.  The look of 'fear' is so exaggerated it's laughable.  Again....not scary.
- The executions are actually pretty cool, although having played for a couple hours they were getting stale already.
Survival
- Compared to the fast pace chases in DBD, the survival aspect of this game is clunky and boring.  If you get caught outside a cabin you are dead.  If you get caught inside a cabin you can juke for a while, but you're not going anywhere.
- If you get lucky and are not focused, you have a good chance of making it out.  I don't have a problem with a low survival rate, I understand what the dev team is trying to accomplish by making Jason overpowered.  The issue I have is that it never feels like an accomplishment to survive.  You either get lucky and don't get focused, or you die....there is really no 'earning it'.
- There were a few instances of juking and competitive gameplay when trying to make it to the police, but this is very situational.
The game does seem to do a good job with the F13 lore, and I'm sure fans of the series will get a kick out of seeing easter eggs peppered throughout the game.  However, if you are looking for a competitive survival game, this is not it.

The game rests on a fun plot and sharp dialogue in a beautifully recreated Hill Valley, with terrific voice acting featuring many from the original cast, yet ultimately, it's sadly let down by lightweight in-game puzzles that lack invention and complexity. You're stranded on a hostile alien world, everyone else is dead, and you have to destroy an alien overlord before they invade earth again. Time to bunny hop over everything.
Quake II is a release sequel to Quake but an actual sequel to Quake Wars but also a prequel to Quake 4. It's also older than both of those.
The Terran Coalition of Man embarks on Operation Alien Overlord, a counter-attack on the alien race known as the Strogg, who apparently invaded Earth some time prior. The Strogg are a cybernetic race that fuse biological material with advanced technology. They apparently wanted humanities sweet succulent man meat for their own use. Oh baby.
But humanity did not want to give the alien invaders their man meat, and instead fought a war with the Strogg to save themselves from wiggly robot fingers.
You play as Bitterman, the most bitter man in the universe. Bitterman's drop pod is knocked off course, which saves him from being destroyed or captured by Strogg and their really big gun. I'm serious, it's actually just called “Big gun.”
Now, because Bitterman is a FPS protagonist, he becomes stronger with the less friendlies there are around him. So if lots of friendlies= COD protagonist, then Bitterman is somewhere along the level of  Lo Wang or Sam Stone.
I like Sam.
Depending on who you ask Quake II is either a step down or step up from Quake. But if you ask me I would say it's a...Nice addition, I guess.
Quake II does a lot of things better than Quake. Many of the guns are crunchier and have more punch than the Quake counter part. But at the same time the level design kind of took a hit, even if it makes a little more sense this time around.
This game also has one of the best shot guns I have ever had the pleasure of using. It's just so useful in basically any situation and mulches almost every enemy you come in contact with. Quake II also has a lot more ammo to come across, so you get to use more of your weapons than just the grenade/rocket launcher and your two shotguns.
Quake II's enemy design are some of my favorites from any game. With the Strogg chopping up people and using their parts to make more soldiers. Everything you run into is so macabre and grotesque. Even with their low poly count they're still just gross to look at. Their weapons are usually grafted to their body with little care for hygiene and appearance, so you get disgusting mix of human flesh and steel, which gets even worse when you take a look at some of the later enemies like the Parasite or the flyers.
Like the original game, Quake II also has some different ways to play. There were a few console ports that ranged from “goofy lookin'” to “Pretty good.”
The PS1 port plays like mud, but the N64 port is actually pretty passable. There was also the Dreamcast port which is apparently the definitive edition to play if you somehow don't have this on PC.
You can also get some source ports that improve textures and graphics if somehow you can't tolerate those sweet sweet 1997 textures. Q2Pro is the most popular one, it's also the one I'd recommend.
And just Quake 1, there are two mission packs that were released at a later date called “The Reckoning” and “Ground Zeroes” if you just can't get enough Quake II action.
Like Quake 1, Quake II also has a very competent multiplayer. Quake II took a lot of the features from Qauke 1 and improved on them such as rocket jumping and bunny hoping, it kind of worked as the framework to what would be perfected in Quake 3. And just like Quake you can always find people down to play a few round of Q2 multiplayer.
Quake II is also good, I'm just going to go ahead and tell you to play it. So go ahead and do that.

Sure, you might hate some of the restored parts (damn that Nar Shadaa part was tough as all hell)... but overall it certainly adds to the experience.
KOTOR II is one amazing sequel that also works great as a standalone game... and that may be my biggest problem with it as well. Sounds odd? Well... for the most part of the game I just felt kinda disconnected from what happened in the first game. Most characters are gone, some of them you'll only meet once (and one of them is just a vision/cam-recording)... most of original KOTOR's story is being retold in this game, but it feels way more distant than it should given this is taking place just 5 years after.
This game's start might feel a bit more... dry and boring compared to first game, but it really does pick up pace later on. And whilst first KOTOR has amazing characters, it's story is rather simplistic compared to this. By the same playtime you were finishng first KOTOR, you still have no idea what the hell is going on in KOTOR II. Story is way more complex, as are the dialogues. Overall vibe is darker and more serious tone than in first game adds to story's weight and in the end it's going to feel a bit more satisfying.
I think that as of pure gaming quality, KOTOR II is definitely a bit better than original game (which was already extremely high benchmark), but on the other hand I can't deny that it lacked a bit of it's predecessor's magic.
Nevertheless KOTOR II is one amazing game and a must for Star Wars fans. If you haven't played first game, start with that.

I was fortunate enough to have this gifted to me - I had been eyeing it for a while now.
If you are into squad-based tactics games, then this should suit your tastes. The tutorial covers the game mechanics very well, although the gameplay is a bit lacking in depth if you are used to more hardcore tactics games.
As you plot waypoints for your 4 squad members, you can click on any gridpoint in their routes and switch where they are facing, effectively allowing you to cover maximum area and actually "check corners" as you move. The action points come in the form of your "speed" rating for each character, as seconds are passing throughout the stage. The game captures the intensity of what I would imagine a real "breach and clear" situation would be like pretty well. If your "turn" is over and bullets are still flying, the game will enter slow-motion and you will even see characters in the process of falling to the ground if they've died.
The character level progression is pretty fast, and you can repeat/grind levels fairly easily.
The length of the game is decent, there are 3 game modes (terrorist hunt/bomb defusal/escape) for each location, and each location consists of several stages.
The customization in terms of gear is not too expansive, but still very nice. You will unlock weapons as you beat stages and earn "star" rating points (up to 4 per level), but all the other equipment is available to purchase immediately.
Something I like to do over and over is click the "replay" button after I've planned out and executed my moves for the round, watching from different viewpoints.
Aesthetics are nice, nothing too fancy. Using cover is easy as the shield feedback will immediately tell you what level of cover your character will have. The "undo" button allows you to cancel any waypoints/actions you may have planned out.
Overall, the game is very fun if you are into this type of gameplay. Price-wise, I don't think you would miss out on too much if you wait for it to go on sale, however, I think it is worth the current price.

TL:DR; Steep Learning curve. Old Graphics. Buggy Mess. One of my favorite games.
So I want to start off by saying if you're interested buy this version of the game and only this game. This is a stand alone game, and it is the most up to date - bug-free version. Also, getting the MegaMod pack doesn't hurt either, adds a lot to the game and fixes a bunch of bugs.
It took me 4-5 times on separate occassions to get into this game. Until I finally found my stride and went deep in, and man I feel like I was missing out. If you've ever played Civilization games you know the term 'one more turn' - well this game gives you exactly that same feeling.
Top Pros:
- Ever played Runescape or Eve Online? If you ever enjoyed how authentic the economy was then you should have an appreciation for this game. The economy is authentic by AI & you, there is real supply and demand, and the AI naturally imports and exports from city to city. Your business decisions will depend on local supply & competition.
- Much like CK this is a family dynasty game - not a city or statist game. You will find your wife/husband, live and die, then subsequently control your family as you desire (up to 3 can actively be controlled)
- Politics are hard to get into and can be a bit too shallow in places but deep in others. You can try to gain favor of your fellow towns people, and get high enough social stats and take public offices - and then use your public office to not only make more income but to destroy your competition. Trying to get my dynasty to control the city has been a blast.
- You can bring other people up to charges on various crimes, or be brought to court by others (very common place if you play a rogue. The dialogue is pretty lackluster, but it gives a good incentive to play politician so that you have a naturally high favor of the courts - else you'll suffer the fat of my first rogue and go to jail for 5 years.
- You can hire thugs to spy on your competition for evidence of your competitors then use that evidence to black mail them or bring them to trial. You can also have them firebomb their buildings, although if they catch you - you can suffer through the courts. Very fun system.
- When you start you pick one of 4 classes. Patron (food & inns), Crafting (mining & crafting various equipment and jewlry), Scholar (Churches, Hospitals & crazy magical artifact making), or Rogue (Theving, Whoring, Pirating, & Plundering). For your first time I'd say Patron or Crafting is best.
- I haven't played it but I feel like I need to mention the fact that this game does have multiplayer similar to the single player. This setup seems to be MADE for drinking games with the buddies.
Top Cons:
- Watch some vids online as well if you have the time. I liked this guy:
- If you optomize it correctly it takes about a day to court to marry someone. The depth really goes as far as telling the person to follow you and every couple of hours clicking on a random social interaction as cool downs go. The social aspect of other villagers are also similarly shallow, though you get a few more options through politics & items.
- Likely due to the fact that you're running a similation of hundreds of people, businesses & local economies, the game can run pretty badly. Luckily Guild 3 seems to be fixing that issue, Guild 2 wont run well.
- So many bugs in this game, though a whole lot has been fixed with a recent patch (update to latest game) and mods. Be aware you'll have a lot of non-game breaking bugs and a few game breaking ones here and there.
- Mentioned in the pros section, there is a lot of sections that are so shallow in certain aspects. Social, politics, & court has such potential.
- Hard to explain but there are certain quirks to the UI that are difficult to work around. When you're running dozens of businesses there is no real way to manage the trade routes without memorizing them or following them. The business management on the right can't be customized or rearranged - very inconvenient when you have to scroll up several businesses in order to just send a cart to the market. This may be my biggest personal Con.
- Having to due with the Bad UI, the family management system is pretty bad. You can only control 3 people at once but if you don't control people they don't live their own lives to my knowledge.. So you have to switch them out if you remotely care about your virtual children..
Simply put - this game is for people who are looking for a game that scratches a certain itch. For me it I've been looking for a solid realistic business game, for others it may be a local political simulator, for others it may be a dynasty game. If you think this game will scratch it and you have a solid day to dedicate to learning a new game. Give this a buy. Just curious about this game, give it a buy!

This is by far the most underrated game I own on Steam. I can't help but praise it, it's a great game. You play as a character who's goal is to eliminate all other dynasties on the map by running businesses, running for office, commiting murder, etc. You get married, have children and expand your monopoly as much as possible. The game has 4 classes: Patron, Craftsman, Scholar and Rogue or as I call them: Farmer, Money Machine, Priest and Serial Killer. You can end up having one of each by marrying someone with that profession or by sending your children to school.
My favorite thing to do in this game is to start my own unofficial city. You save up enough money, build a home in empty land on a road between two cities and spam bombard towers. Meanwhile, your competitors will try to trade between cities only to have them raided every time. They will eventually take matters into their own hands and march over to your "city". That's when you murder them in cold blood and become an outlaw for the rest of the game. It's your way or the highway and you own the highway now too. Want to try this? Start as rogue and take over a mine as fast as you can. Selling gems will make you rich and you can start building. Try and take over most or all the mines after that if you can.
It's difficult to learn how to manage businesses at first since you need to supply them, sell products to the right market and upgrade them. You can set your business to automatic but I always preferred manual until I have too many to manage. It gets fairly stressful but that all goes away once you snowball your profits enough. You end up having too much money to know what to do with if you play it right. I recommend this to anyone who enjoys strategy and roleplaying games. You get a lot of freedom in the way you work towards your goal and it gets better if you have friends to play it with.

The Isle is not what I expected when I bought it. I couldn't have guessed how in depth this game was. And the kicker is it's so simple as of now.
There's no weapons or ammo or reloading or talking sh** to the other team. In fact, you can only chat with other people playing your same species. You can't hold grudges on other players because you usually can't identify them unless you're in a pack/herd.
The focus is all on survival. You have claws or spikes or teeth or size, but your best survival tool is the sounds you can make. There are 4 sounds, as well as the sounds of your attacks, that you can use to communicate and body gesture. It is very intuitive, you can understand people's intentions and what they mean even if you can't chat with them. You can threaten, call for help, roar over a great distance, and signal for peace. And it all is sewn seamlessly into a beautiful landscape and soundscape.
The devs are very active and in tune with the community, I hang out on their Discord they made for the public. There have several updates in the short time I've had this game. I've met a good bunch from the community.
TL;DR spend the 20 bucks. it keeps getting better and it's hard f'n core

Not a fan boy of the F13 series, never even watched a movie. Not some toxic brat screaming on the forums for a refund. This is just my current opinion based on what's actually here in the game FOR NOW.
The developers made the game to be a "non-competitive" "fun for all" type of game which is why Jason is hugely overpowered (not just because he's jason). The idea is that Jason's to toy with people and not just try to go with a stereotypical speed-run/tryhard gameplay style that most games these days have, which in theory is great until you realize you're trusting someone to follow that kind of unspoken/unwritten guideline and they're just going to run with the fact that because Jason can do this, it must be the intention the developers have so there's nothing wrong with it.
Generally you can stick together with people and if someone gets caught off, it's not entirely hard to save them. A simple smack to Jason frees that counsellor and all is well. At this time there's nothing stopping Jason from just spamming his basic weapon swing and clearing groups of people within the first minute or two of the game. The stealth system kind of counters this if you're alone, but in public matches there usually tends to be someone who just sprints all over the place (usually close to you) which attracts Jason, so it has its flaws.
The game is fun and most of the people playing and not spewing venom on the forums are pretty enjoyable to play with, but I feel the gameplay lacks in comparison to the fact that there's not much balance here with the idea that "people will just know that it's boring if you rush and kill everyone". There's likely going to be tweaks to come for this, and as I've said this is just a review from the first week of the game being released. But at this time, with the slightly aggrivating lack of balance and the somewhat clunky game mechanics (mostly with doors and windows), I don't feel that the game is worth purchasing

I remember Quake II as the first PC game I owned as a kid. I must have been about 11 years old and had previously played Doom & Doom II together with my dad (I was in charge of pressing the fire button).
The suspense of fighting the evil Stroggs on every corner of their military facilities is an experience that always stayed with me.
It was also the first time I tried to make my own levels and got enthusiastic about the possibility of creating my own games some day (something which later became my profession).
The one thing that really stood out for me about Quake II was the atmosphere. The game's aesthetic may not be a hit with everyone, but for me it was, and still is. The bleak rusty environments effectively instill feelings of dread and despair.
The decision to go with organic/machine hybrids for the enemies is a smart one. We are able to identify enough with the characters because of their organic aspects. We can still recognize the humans and creatures they may one day have been. Yet at same time we are reminded of their cold and mechanical other-worldliness. As a plus, the modelers could get away with a lot more blockiness.
At some point I tried the Berserker mod, which updated the game with modern HD graphics, but while being prettier in a 'technical' sense, the graphics lost their consistency as the models remained blocky. In the end, it damaged the believably of the game world, rather than improving it. A lot of the bump maps were really noisy and didn't make any sense material-wise. They attracted attention to all the wrong elements. It ultimately made me realize how well the graphics were done in the original and how important it is to have a consistent aesthetic.
The levels are well designed, with tons of secrets and some smart use of back-tracking. The weapons and enemies are iconic and well placed throughout the maps.
The sound FX and music for this game are simply amazing and I remember I would put the game disk in my stereo player, just to listen to the soundtrack. Which brings me to the rather disappointing fact that the music is missing in this Steam release.
Despite this, it's still worth picking up this classic!

TL;DR: I can see loads of potential in this game. If they will add features to the combat system and include factions or organized gangs, this would be close to 10/10 in my books.
Review:
The premise is a post-apocalyptic world where resources are scarce and the surface is more or less hostile to human life. The art style is pixelated which I personally quite like.
You start by creating a family of four persons: two parents and two kids. You stumble across a shelter that has some basic equipment in it like a radio, crafting table and a life support system (water and oxygen filter). You can occasionally send an expedition team of max. two persons at a time to explore the surroundings for resources like food, water, crafting materials, weapons etc. You will also need to keep the place clean, because rats will start to appear and they will eat your food. Medicating your survivors in case of radiation poisoning or infection is also vital.
You can upgrade your shelter with the crafting table and even upgrade the crafting table itself to allow yourself to manufacture more advanced items.
Resource management is important, since your survivors need to eat, drink, sleep, shower and go to the toilet every once in a while. Showering and going to the toilet consumes water so the game requires you to plan carefully. Expeditions also require water, the further you want to explore, the more water you will need. You can upgrade the maximum capacity of your water storage by building more reserves. You will also need a pantry to store all the food, the bigger the better.
You will meet other people in the wasteland. Some will knock on the shelter door, looking to either trade or join your shelter, and some will appear when you are out on an expedition. Recruiting other people can be useful but I wouldn't recommend getting additional people if the shelter supplies are running low. Trading systems doesn't use any kind of currency (like bottlecaps) which is ok for me. Instead items have a certain value (Nail=1, Sand=2, Shotgun=200) and you can trade something in equal of value.
The combat system is pretty basic, but I wasn't bothered by it too much. My only wish is that the developers would implement some kind of percentage system in the combat. In many situations I wasn't sure if I should stay and fight or just flee. It would be nice to get some odds on my chance to hit or counter an attack. You can improve your character's combat stats (Agility and Strenght) by making a punching bag.
Also it would be pretty awesome (in my opinion) if the game had gangs or other factions or if you could form a faction of your own.
I'm looking forward to the final version!

I see many people writing about how this is a terrible PC port of a mobile game, or about how the gameplay gets repetitive or stale. At one hour into it so far, this game has become one of my top ten favorite strategy games for several reasons. Not only does it have a huge bevy of missions to choose from, it has a large section of gameplay devoted to customization as well as (optional, sadly) PERMADEATH - my favorite aspect in any "hardcore" game.
The gameplay is easy to learn; I was able to figure out how to play in roughly 15 minutes. The problem comes with tactics - in true to life fashion, what can go wrong WILL go wrong, and the came is fairly unforgiving. On the base difficulty and the first mission, I still lost a squadmate after he got shot in the face for getting a little too hasty, which, ironically, is what cemented this game as a favorite of mine.
If you like games that challenge you, like strategy, or enjoy blowing things up, I heavily recommend Breach and Clear as an excellent choice - especially during the Steam Summer Sale, while it's half off.

This game's graphics are obviously not great. And it appears to be poorly translated from some other language. But overall, the atmosphere is truly terrifying. Here is the story of my first night in Rake:
I had spent the day setting up trail cams. I had four set up a good distance from each other to get fairly good coverage of the forest. I even had one attached to a pig that aimlessly wandered in and out of my camp. Then when night came around, I sat in my trailer and monitored my cameras. It was mostly uneventful: I would stair at the screen and switch cameras whenever I saw a motion sensor go off, but it was always just a deer or a pig that had triggered it. However, the whole time I had this unending sense of being watched and found myself constantly checking the windows of my trailer to see if anything had wandered into my camp. I would even occasionally hear footsteps as that pig wandered through my camp again. But then, I saw one of my motion sensors go off again and clicked over to that camera. When I saw that thing shambling off into the woods and making some unholy moaning noise, I immediately began to question my decision to play this at 11 o'clock at night.
The game is honestly pretty scary and has a sort of Five Nights at Freddy's meets Slender feel to it. Definitely worth trying if you get the chance!

If you enjoy management, simulation, and RPG games, good... This game is all three of those rolled up into a fat burrito.
The problem with this delicous and savory burrito, however, is that every once in a while you will bite into a squirmy little bug. Some of these bugs don't taste that bad, and the burrito is tasty, so you hammer down and continue eating. Untill you find a ugly nasty bug that makes your drop your burrito (straight to your desktop (wink)).  But "darn it", you will say, "this burrito has so much potential for fun! I'll presevere through these bugs. Heck, I think I'll share it with a friend!"
And you do, you share it with your friend. The burrito tastes even better with a friend (or even multiple friends). Everyone will have fun and enjoy it, but eventually, you may bite into a bug so gross, that it will make you forget where you were eating the burrito so you'll have to start over from the beginning... which, after eating that burrito for a while, doesn't sound as appetizing.
Ultimately, this burrito is a wonderful burrito, with much thought and care put into. The burrito allows for you to eat it in whatever way you see fit.  You can find yourself eating this burrito for hours, trying to find the best way to consume the delicous ingrediants. The bugs, and perhaps some uncooked peices of chicken (trade routes), can make it a little harder to swallow.
If this burrito is on sale and you are interested, purchase it and eat it.
If not, maybe save your money for Burrito 3 (due in 2017).

For Honor is some of the most fun I've had in a fighting game in a very long time. I'm not going to do a typical bullet list and break down the pros and cons because frankly, if you like fighting games you'll like For Honor regardless of the cons.
The two primary issues people seem to have with the game are the combat mechanics, in some instance & the connectivity issues.
Combat Mechanic Solution: "Git Gud". As with any competative pvp game, there are a huge percentage of players that don't want to spend the time or effort to become familiar and intimate with the combat mechanics. They have a weakness and when it's exploited by another player (as it should be) they automaticaly call the game broken and unbalanced. That's the typical load of BS. There is nothing broken about the combat in the game and anyone that puts in the time and effort will be enjoying some intense melee combat and duels by the time they get their first favorite character leveled up. I strongly suggest people take the complaints with a grain of salt when it comes to balance issues because the game really has none. Every class has strengths and weaknesses.
Connectivity Issues: I'm not sure where all of these complaints are comming from. I've had the typical minor issues you have in ANY game, particularly one that hasn't even had its first patch yet. Once in awhile there are disconnects or issues joining a match, but they are so few and far between (for me, at least) that I hardly call it a problem. The one issue I see that's worth complaining about is that if a player disconnects mid-fight, they are replaced by a BOT with full health. That is an issue being fixed in the first patch so it's hardly worth listing.
All in all, the game is easy to get into and challenging to master. The mechanics and balance is solid and it's got tons and tons of playability and things to unlock for all the classes. There are NO pay-to-win features and the variety of cosmetics, effects, executions and emotes are all pretty good. Plus, it can only get better the longer it's out. The game is still brand new.
Bottom line is, if you are thinking about getting this game, you are a fighting game fan and you have decent internet, brush aside the standard whiners and their negative reviews and get this game. You will be doing yourself a favor.

In each match there is one person randomly selected to play as the killer Jason Voorhees. Jason’s goal is to kill the camp counselors. The counselors have to work together to escape or survive. You can play in quick play mode with random people, or do custom matches with your friends.
When I first started playing Friday the 13th in beta, I didn’t understand the mechanics, and I admit I found the game to be annoying, and not very enjoyable at first. Since release, I have figured out how to be a much more effective counselor, and I have escaped or been the sole survivor numerous times. The more I play Friday the 13th, the better I get, and the more I enjoy it with every match. With that being said, the game has a lot of bugs, and sometimes server connection issues where you can’t connect to play.
The game has a progression system, where you level up to unlock different versions of Jason, and different counselors. The different Jasons and counselors have different abilities and stats. As you play and complete tasks in game or full matches, you also earn currency to buy different executions for Jason, or craft various perks to customize your counselors loadouts. The perks are randomly generated, and offer small bonuses for counselors.
When playing as Jason, your goal is to kill the other seven camp counselors before they can escape or the 20 minute game timer runs out. Jason is extremely powerful, and a decent Jason feels very, very OP. This is how the game is designed, and even though Jason is OP, it doesn’t mean he will kill everyone. Jason has different abilities that give him huge advantages. He can morph around the map instantly, he can sense enemies fear to stalk them and find them easier, and his most notable ability is called shift, which is his fast moving teleport-like ability. Using a well positioned shift and then combining it with grab can be a one-shot kill more often than not. Jason can grab survivors any time he’s close enough and execute awesome and gruesome fatalities, or he can just hack players to bits with melee swings.
When playing as Jason, you’ll need to be attentive to audio and visual cues to hunt down your prey. Breaking windows, and lights can strike fear into your victims that makes them easier to find with your sense ability. The longer the game lasts the stronger Jason becomes as his rage meter builds up.
When playing as a counselor, knowing that the odds are stacked against you makes you feel incredibly vulnerable. Even though you can fight back to distract and stun Jason, it’s best that you try to avoid him completely, and work together to escape. Counselors can juke the grab, or break free if they’re quick enough. There are three different ways to escape: you can call the police and wait for them to show up at one of the exits, or leave using the motor boat or a car. All methods, require you to find specific items in order to make the escape. In addition to finding the required items, you’ll spend a lot of time searching houses for weapons, or other utilities to help you stay alive and escape Jason’s clutches. In Friday the 13th, running at the wrong times, and wasting your stamina will get you killed. You need to know when to move quickly, and when to just stop and hide, all while keeping your fear levels down by using your flashlight and other lights, and avoiding Jason.
It’s absolutely terrifying when Jason is nearby, and then the fact that he might morph to where you are at any given time keeps you in a permanent state of suspense and unease. By working together, you can actually save your allies by stunning or distracting Jason. Making use of windows, traps, and barricades to slow Jason down while you find a place to hide plays a key role to successfully evading Jason if he does find you. There is a way for the counselors to kill Jason, but it is very difficult to set up all the necessary factors, and typically isn’t worth the effort.
When counselors die, they remain in the game as spectators, and have the option to wait out the rest of the game for significant bonus xp or they can just leave with the xp they’ve already earned. Those who stick around, have a chance to come back as Tommy Jarvis to help others.
Overall, Friday the 13th is quite enjoyable once you figure out how to play well. Yes, there are plenty of bugs still, and sometimes server connection issues, so the game is by no means perfect. All-in-all though, it’s a fun game if you enjoy the survival horror genre. I do wish it had been slightly cheaper since it still needs polish, but I have no regrets with the purchase.

WIth a price like this, especially on sale, you're either a complete Scrooge or your wallet is totally dead from all the other things to pass up a little gem like this. Frankly, I don't know why there are negative reviews at all, considering how cheap this is. Are you really gonna find a game better than this for the amount you're paying? Hook is surprisingly complex for a minimalistic game, and while no level is impossible, it takes a few tries and you'll always hear that satisfying "click"  as the last lock unravels at the end of a level. Difficulty wise, again the curve is fairly maneagable as the game slowly introduces more complex mechanics over the 50 levels, and the introduction of the "three strikes/lives" is a nice help later in the game where it gets to the point where it's almost impossible not to make a mistake. Length wise, it took me about 45 minutes to finish, no walkthrough required, but I was getting into a rhythm and just steam-rolling through at times. It really depends on your approach to solving these puzzles. Some find it fun to do it completely in their heads, others might trace the wires around. The ambience is really nice and I found myself getting into the zone, where despite the sheer amount of different "locks", it was still possible to figure out which line lead to where without too much effort, and the super minimalist design does Hook justice here.

Better than the first one, less the (unfinished) ending and a few game-breaking bugs with event scripting.
How so?
More engaging characters and plot--the dialog is phenominal, even if a bit heavy. Perhaps a few too many wall-of-text expository scenes, but still amazingly well done.
More original story that KOTOR1, and that is truly a compliment because the original was no slouch in that department.
Better loot & crafting systems.
The ability to train NPCs as Jedi.
More feats, force powers, and classes--plus some rebalancing of a few existing powers and feats.
Dark side characters felt much more insidious and evil rather than just selfish/greedy.
Blaster characters are actually viable at endgame.
If you are the modding type, available community content "fixes" the ending, event scripting, and other problems.
Overall I was not disappointed with this game in any regard. Just keep in mind that in its unmodded state it was a rush-job from Lucasarts, and definitely grab the Restored Content Mod to enjoy as close to the "as intended by Obisidian" experience as possible. Totally worth it.

I couldn't play this game for more than an hour despite my love of post apacolyptic survival games.
Starting with the options menu:
There is almost no options menu excluding some music and SFX adjustment bars that don't do much and a resolution selector there isn't much here. This isn't much of an issue except... You can't change the keybinds at all. While this isn't a huge issue it is a bit inconvenient.
Moving on to character creation:
It's alright nothing special, nothing worth mentioning. I really do not like the fact that you CANNOT set your own stats instead you have to use presets which are mostly heavily one sided towards a specific skill.
Gameplay:
Tutorial- the tutorial really needs a big overhaul to cover the controls, objectives, how to feed and shower your characters and pretty much anything you would need to know to play.
Goals and Direction- The game while not linear in any way does a very poor job in guiding you to do anything at all, it's a lot of micromanagment and a lot of unexplained stuff that you have to just guess at. Playing this for the first hour may leave you frustrated.
Overall- Overall excluding all the issues the gameplay is pretty straight forward. Your goal is to survive that is it so good luck.
Conclusion:
I didn't enjoy this game at all and unfortunately I think this game will need a lot of work to be worth the price. Yes it's only $15 but I've seen a lot of other games that may warrant your $15 more so than this. This is only my opinion though and maybe I'm being a bit hard on this game, but the issues I'm posing are still real issues that need addressing and I believe the developer should consider overhauling a large portion of the game and make it easier for the player to actually interact with and explore the world. As of now I feel that my time is spent better with Bethesda's Fallout Shelter.
Thank you for reading and again this is just my opinion :)
