If you have a bunch of free time and love to spend it playing video games, this is the perfect game for you. This will review will cover the basics of gaming reviews: Fun factor, gameplay, graphics, sound, and replay-ability. Fun factor is clearly necessary for every game, if a game isn’t fun than it isn’t worth playing. While some of these points can be more important than others, gameplay, graphics, and sound have become some of the most important assets to include in games. Replay-ability can be one of the most important assets to a game, this factor will also be tied with the amount of in-game content. This is the difference between a good game and a great game. If a game makes you come back to replay it again and again, you know you’ve found a gem.
Star Wars itself is a huge franchise that has spread the globe. It’s an easy topic to talk about and just about everyone can get into a conversation about Star Wars. Since their huge boom, they’ve certainly made a lot of video games and most of them have been less than stellar; however, anyone who’s played Knights of the Old Republic I can attest that it’s nothing short of fantastic. Knights of the Old Republic II is nothing short of that. The fun factor I felt was raised from the previous game. Something that stood out was the fact that you could control your party more. In KOTR I (Knights of the Old Republic I) you could control your party but it felt very limited to what you could do. Depending if you chose light or dark would change some events, but nothing very drastic. In KOTOR II you can control the alignment of some of your party members. You can grow and develop a relationship with all of them compared to just Ballista, or at least more so in this game. *SPOILER* You can even help some of your party members to become jedi’s and can use the force. That’s huge in comparison to what the first game offered. This is game is nothing short of fun, and certainly more fun than the previous game.
Just like in KOTOR I, the gameplay is DND style (DND being Dungeons and Dragons). You pick a character you want and then build off that, choosing your stats, the abilities you have what you specialize in. You get more access to other powers than you previous could in the previous games and there are more weapons available as well. Gameplay wise there is no different with KOTOR I than there is in KOTOR II. You right click enemies and use the numbers or mouse to use abilities. Movement is simple and the simplicity of the combat makes the game that much more fun. Granted, there are a few frustrations. There will be levels that are insanely hard and will require multiple attempts to beat. Saving a lot is recommended. It is necessary to make sure your party also is well equipped, they will be put on missions without your main character, and they will suffer if you don’t level them up and give them the time they need to succeed. Once you get past those parts, you can continue having a blast demolishing and wrecking everything in your path, granted you took the time to make your character strong. Some thought, strategy, and time will be needed to beat this game, but overall the game is addicting once you get started.
KOTOR II was released in 2004, a vastly different time from today. Compared to now, the graphics and sound aren’t up to part with the quality we expect today; but you can’t compare this game to today’s standards. Back then, the game was the cream of the crop when it came to sounds and graphics. After playing the game multiple times you will have a hard time finding issues with the graphics or sound. Clipping textures or obvious faults of the game are little to none, you can play the game multiple times without finding a single issue on the graphics side. The sounds and music are great as well, they flow well with the game and you’ll never find a point where you’ll get annoyed. At worst, the repeated lines the aliens use will ruin the immersion and/or get annoying. It’s a minor issue and isn’t one worth concerning yourself over. The music itself is also grand and fantastic. Thankfully if you do happen to get annoyed with the music (I have that happen to me too.) you have the option to turn of the music entirely and focus on the marvelous sounds the game provides via combat and conversation.
The pride and joy of games like these have two HUGE compliments. One is the fact there is enough content to let you play the game again and still not be able to view everything the game offers. The second is the workshop, steam has a workshop for this game that allows you to add mods to the game. Meaning you can add more custom content and expand the game further than you could without the mods. For a truly satisfying experience of the game it is highly recommended that you download the restored content mod. The original game is fun, but then restored content mod allows you to truly experience the game in its rightful place. The game will leave you with an empty feeling in the end if you do not install the mod. Thankfully there is nothing wrong with playing the game first, then playing it again with the restored content mod. Most people will be able to play the game twice, one as light side, once as dark. Hardcore gamers will find the ability to play it even more than that, discovering all the secrets as well as delving into the lore of each personal party member even further than the regular casual can. Clearly, the game offers much more than meets the eye.
Is this game worth getting? One-hundred percent it is. You will find yourself coming back to this game in the future to see if there was something you missed, or even introducing the game to a friend. For a summary and a TLDR, the fun factor will last you through at least two playthroughs of the game. The controls and gameplay is simple and easy to understand letting anyone jump in, and allows the time for the user to build a strategy that will allow them to become unstoppable. The graphics and sound are high quality and you shall not find a problem as you play.
Rankings of each category:
Fun factor: 9/10
Controls and gameplay: 9/10
Graphics and sound: 10/10
Replay-ability: 7/10, mainly since you must go over some unnecessary levels in order to get to the meat of the game.
The game is easily a solid 9/10.

A simple tactical game. Dont go beyond that. Does not come close to its competitor Frozen Synapse, but delivers what  promises in parts, getting impossible not to compare each one.
Despite having a description on page extremely tempting, promising a highly tactical and complex game, is hardly so.
Strategies and options are simple, basically limiting the positioning of soldiers and their handling in each phase. You simply enter the room and see the shooting happen. You can break down doors, throw tactical devices like grenades and flashbangs, and choose which way to look. Nothing else. The game is an infinite looping entering the room, get lucky for the soldiers first shoot the enemies and start all over again.
A typical game for mobile phones that was poorly ported to PC. It is very clear looking at the layouts and menus of the game, very badly adapted.
Some soldiers have certain specific skills for each class, such as locking doors and having improved reaction time but also by the structure of the game such skills make little difference in the time of action.
The graphics are typically mobile. Few animations make the game boring (like terrorists falling in the same position) and the sound effects are amateurs.
Despite being a mobile game badly ported to PC it's a little amusing. There are options to purchase equipment and a wide customization possibilities. Probably as the game grow with their development (giving more respect to the pc's users) it can become better.
Briefly comparing the competitor, are almost two different games. The complexity and tactical strategy are much deeper in Frozen Synapse.
I'm not recommending the game, I suggest you wait more to spend your hard earned money and go for Frozen Synapse.

Prepare for the longest review I will probably ever write. Mostly because I can, it's an enjoyable foray, but needs serious work.
[Warning; sailor talk and potential (minor) spoilers below]
(As of 10/20/2015,) I'm giving this project a very tentative yes and thumbs up. As has been said before, and I completely agree, this game has a lot of positive elements going for it right from the start.  For so little content, the idea is extremely fetching, and the replay value is surprisingly high, even WITH the ending being what it is (without bothering with detailed spoilers, beating the game in its' current state should result in a chuckle, smirk, or at least a raised eyebrow).
Observing the (fictional) cryptid in the dark of night with limited range night vision cameras and nothing but the otherwise-calming sounds of nature to comfort you, or a wide-angled, convenient set of.. well, a magnified monocular, which when paired with a flipped on flashlight, mystically becomes wide-reaching suitable night vision mode. *shrug* Having Rake scramble from the dark to knock the crap out of the cameras provides good tension and a startle or two.
Finding this critter's den, or traces of it's prey, be it hominid or otherwise, stumbling a little too close in the daylight only to get ♥♥♥♥♥-slapped to the ground by the thing before it takes off because you will quickly learn that it is an absolute virtuoso premier in dickery, is all good stuff, and offers immersion.
So I had some difficulty in figuring out precisely what the goal of the game was.  It is clear you were intended to be armed. It was also fairly clear that you are immediately encouraged to deal with your closest forest friends, (pigs), who like archangels at the wings of Saint Michael, ... are sent forth into the dark calamity of hostile woodlands, blind and dumb, but with cameras attached to their necks so you can sit in your camper and watch with intense interest as they wander aimlessly, keep getting caught in your trap (which has no feed in it), and occasionally saunter into the unlucky spot where the Wendigo is watching, who sprints by and slaps the life out of their poor, succulent, delicious bacony bodies. I am unsure what sordid pleasure the protagonist gains from this viewing, but I admit to partaking in it a few times. While you can catch a pig, there was no indication that you could catch Rake, and furthermore the magic journal which I will mention, makes no mention itself of 'capturing' Rake as a priority.
You are given a fair amount of gear, at least that I've found, to work with. Several traps, a scoped rifle with an awkward two-round built-in magazine, roughly forty shotgun shells for your starter 'rifle' [an over and under model], (Sort of a misnomer considering shotguns don't usually have rifling), and, ah of course, unlimited amount of piglet feed!  Lovely. Absolutely smashing.  The piglet feed and cameras will respawn after each day. But that is where the limitless supplies end. You're also given a kind of PDA/tablet, which functions as a map and indicator of where cameras are placed, and nothing else.
You are lent a magical journal beside the desk of your interior camper, which updates itself automatically day in and day out, as though it is tied directly to the plot and your actions have no bearing on it whatsoever. Not that it would help enormously, as it's written in utterly heart-warming broken English, just like the controls setup menu. Bear with us.
There are several hunting blinds scattered across the map, and to my knowledge they affect an invisibility cloak over your character such that you can throw lead at the Rake without fear of his dreaded, horrifying open-hand slap. (I learned this from reading it, not trying it out, as it seemed rather stupid to me to detach yourself from your camera read-out hub in the trailer to stand around for a half-hour in some stubby, four-cornered, windowless tower to wait for Rake to appear).
Going into Rake combat..
You see, it seems dickery is key to the Rake, in a certain sense. It is difficult to kill, not because it is just so frightening that it's presence is unbearable, nor because it is all that powerful, or excessively intelligent. It is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥because it's means of committing to mortal puglism is by sprinting by just under mach one (that is 766 miles per hour for you dare devils out there), open-hand slapping you as hard as you can upside the head, and trotting merrily away (at a leisurely 75 miles-per-hour) joyous and content in the knowledge that, should he die soon, he (I assume it is male) shall be projected straight to the Valhalla of frat boy♥♥♥♥♥♥butts, where he will serenely paint the faces of his drunken passed out peers with phalluses for the rest of eternity.  'Rake' is indeed a master of the cheap shot to the temple.  He ensures that after you've just been smacked to the ground he is well on his sprint to a nearby tree, after which, with perfect night-vision, he will commence masturbatory celebration as he watches you hold your aching head and glare angrily into the dark. At least, this is the kind of place I imagine that lank freakshow that I just killed would like to call heaven.
What I mean to say is that this fella is a hit and run fighter. It would seem also that a fair name for the creature could also be Wendigo, considering its' speed on the ground.
To run down the usefulness of each bit of gear, I take issue with what you're given and it's functionality. Cameras are only useful insofar as they function to take note of where the Rake is. Cameras are not numbered either. You have to use that noggin of yours to recall where each camera was placed and in what order, maximum of five. After they're destroyed they are, obviously, useless and lost until the next respawn. Being that at least half of the game involves setting up cameras, the limited use of them is something of a bother. Not that I expect auto-turrets, but some kind of intelligent system that allows an affected camera to sound out a short alarm, or for your otherwise-useless tablet to be able to remotely connect to the cameras.. that would have been nice. Instead if you want eyes in the night you have five cameras to look through, but only from the confines of your trailer, or your own naked eyes with assistance of a psuedo-nightvision monocular, or a narrow sight on the scoped rifle. Not very promising, really. And considering this Wendigo is lightning-fast, you aren't intended to be able to easily hunt him with eyes and luck alone.
The 'rifle' is handy more because of the amount of initial ammunition you are granted for it then it's lethality.  At something like 40 rounds, you may have just enough to kill Rake if you make every single shot count. Otherwise, you can easily see yourself running dry while the gangly little hooligan still breathes.
You're given a 'sniper rifle', which while I understood the purpose of, could not really bring myself to use since I knew of no definite way to lure the Wendigo into a long narrow passage about 60-80 meters away from me in a straight path, which is really the only locale under which I would personally find this rifle useful. The forest is too dense and full of sight-blocking brush.  You can't move when aiming it, which is fair, but as of writing this review, aiming the thing is tough enough due to the amount of awkward sway the scope lends at the slightest movement. The central sight will overshoot the actual point of aim quite easily, so in a sense you have to aim it in short bursts and hold it there to check where the actual point of aim is.  Not a great mechanic.  The protagonist also holds the sight much too far from his eye, as though it's a reflex sight and not a magnified scope.  Oh well.   A big issue with this weapon is it's finite ammo and two-round capacity.  If I recall correctly, you can find about 18 rounds with this weapon.

As much as I want to love this game, i cannot recommend it yet because of several gamebreaking issues!
The animations and the combat mechanics are hands down amazing. BUT there are several issues that just ruin the game for me:
1. Matchmaking: I didn't experience that much of connectivity issues but from time to time you get matched into a full game which is complete nonsense. The bigger problem i have with that matchmaking system is that it "ranks" you into categories based on all your characters ranks i suppose. E.g. I got my valkyrie to prestige 2 and wanted to try out different heros. I ended up with the conqueror and the peacekeeper (because i played her in the beta and i was really enjoying her playstyle). The problem is that I, as a complete beginner on that particular hero ended up getting matched with guys who just beelined one char into prestige 6 and were, typically for a fighting game where you just have to invest time to get better, just impossible to beat. Getting steamrolled all the f*king time just ruins the game for me. That leads us right to the next problem:
2. The Gear-System: Ubisoft WTF! The idea of that is that you get gear items as you progress in ranks (they are btw also kind the "cosmetics" in that game). You drop them after battles or you can just open crates to get some items. The BIG problem with that is that you can recieve a HUGE advantage with them because you can basically specialise your char (which is a nice thing in my opinion. It allows unique builds to occur) but the benefits you can get from these are just too big. You can basically just max one attribute, trade in a uselss one, and suddenly deal triple the damage, that you normaly would without specialised gear. Currently the meta is just maxing out your revenge stats which allows you to run around basically 15 secs in an ultra-mode AND only having to block like 4-5 times before getting the next revenge mode. Now coupled with that broken matchmaking you get matched against guys who have gear lvl 108 (which is max) and me as a beginner on a hero has maybe just dropped 3 equips on basic lvl which really don't benefit me that much. So i don't have the damage to kill a revenge guy in time and when he triggers the revenge mode (by pressing Y while i am attacking) i get knocked to the ground. He is then basically in a position in which he can 2 shot me. GREAT THINKING ON THAT ONE UBI!
3. Guard Breaking: Or better counter-guardbreaking. It is so freaking hard for a person who does not play the game constantly since release to counter a guardbreak properly. You really need to put in much practice to finally get the timing right. Take the orochi as prime example: He can chain a succesful guard break into a quite powerfull heavy attack which cannot be evaded at all. Countering the guard break is much too hard and there is just way too much damage that one can deal just by pressing X on the controller. I understand that this is less of a problem in the higher skill levels but for beginners it just ruins the game! You end up being in a match with one orochi who guard breaks you into oblivion. In my opinion the countering of a guard break should be much easier and really only be a viable option to catch a player when he is actually OFF GUARD or maybe out of stamina.
4. BUGS: I don't even know where to start... Shugoki can unblockably strike twice draining you at least 1/2 of your hp bar. The Peacekeepers stabs don't count as stabs that actually inflict bleeding. Just to name a few.
5. Balancing issues of some classes: This just really gets me upset. The thing with the orochi is one problem which is rather a general problem.
Another class which is way too powerfull is the berserker. That guy just deals way too much damage for being that evasive and quick in attacking but thats just personal opinion.
The light attacks of the peacekeeper are also too fast. Some classes can't even change their block stance in time before the next attack strikes.
Environmental Kills are way too easy to achieve: Pick a warlord and shove some poor soul into the abyss or kick them into spikes or fire just because you can literally throw people 20 meters. Especially in 1v1 or 2v2 you always see people doing that and winning duels like this. In my opinion thats just cheap! 1v1s are supposed as a showdown of playerskill with different classes and shoving someone off somewhere with litterally the first move doesn't seem very skilful to me...
To sum it up: For Honor is currently an unbalanced and buggy mess. Out of 10 matches i find 1 which is really enjoyable, because its a close and exciting match. 4-6 of them are rather "meh..." and the rest is just infuriating. I really find that game hard to enjoy even if i really want to. And thats a huge shame.

This game is pretty great. It gives you a true suvival experience where food and water is always an issue. People will die, you will eat them.
It seems similar to fallout shelter at first glance, but really is not like it. Fallout Shelter is all about constant progression, its not a challenging game just a fun one. This game proves to be difficult and remain that way. You will make many morale decisions and is not for the lighthearted. The main thing I liked about this game was you ARE constantly progressing and unlocking things, but basic survival always remains an issue, it doesnt get to the point where you have a massive stock and its never a concern (at least not for a while)
Pros:
- Challenging, and remains that way.
- Very dark, it feels realistic for a survival game
- Somewhat detailed
Cons:
- Interaction between characters is mostly nonexistent, people don't argue or fall in love or question your morale decisions
- Combat is stale, random events seem to end roughly the same. Run, recuit, or trade. Ive never died from combat and I've seeked it out frequently
- Other than food/water your base is safe. No random attacks or traders trying to trick you
- People you recuit ACT like they might try to return and raid your vault, but they never attempt to decieve you
- Managing people can be annoying when you have a lot, telling them to do EVERY basic action from sleeping to using the bathroom. I understand letting them do it freely could waste resources, but a feature could be added to mark toilets to "free use" or something where people auto use them whent he bar fills up
Overall, the survival aspects are very solid. Other than some slightly clunyky controls, the biggest drawback is the lack of ionteraction between players. It would be nice to have to analyze what people say and determine if they are trustworthy, or ever just interaction between your vault members. Such as the morale implications of eating a dead child causing certain people to leave, etc. With not having to focus on that, and most people being the same, the experience can seem stale at times.
Another idea: raiding other shelters could be fun and rewarding.

The one thing I personally didn’t like that much was the backtracking, I much preferred the more linear approach in the original. There is also an issue at one point where a security pass isn’t dropped where it should be, not sure what may have caused this but I don’t recall it being a problem when I first played it.
The multiplayer is also active and in my opinion superior to the original, furthermore there are many mods for singleplayer and multiplayer available. One of my all time favorite is Action Quake2, however it seems only servers in Europe are active.
Steam version of Quake2/Mission Packs do not include the original Quake2 soundtrack, for best experience you will need a more modern singleplayer client like Yamagi and to download the soundtrack elsewhere in OGG format. For multiplayer Quake2 use Q2Pro.

Back to the Future: The Game is a humorous (move&)point&click adventure game in which you take control of Marty McFly, who has to go back in time to save Doc from early demise. In so doing the timestream pretty much gets wrecked up and Marty has to fix things in several places (and times) to restore the original timeline. Actually, if it wasn't obvious: the game makes so many references to the Back to the Future movies that I'd pretty much make it a prerequisite to have watched them to appreciate all the details and humour.
It has been separated into 5 parts, all of which take some 2-4 hours of play depending on your urge to explore and how swift you're at completing puzzles (I reckon there are no truly difficult ones anyway). Gameplay is at times weak, for the camera moves and changes directions often, which results in the movement requiring some time to get used to. There are sound glitches in some places and fire glow sometimes stays burning despite the consumable disappearing. One could also speak to an invisible character inside a phone booth. These glitches were in times amusing and sometimes annoying but nothing gamebreaking. After all, several original actors from the movies make a comeback (especially Doc), and the most important factor, the story, is true to the movies.
There are car chases, crazy science experiments, made-up-names for time travellers, ridiculous escape schemes and of course the-ever-so-present danger of changing the timestream. The story flows seamlessly, and whenever you got stuck, you can always check your present goal and, if you'd like, get a hint within the game on how to advance further. Tension and surprise is maintained well until the end. All in all this game is a very nice sequel to the movies.

I wasn't sure I'd like it, to be honest. I got it over a year ago because I was almost done with my first playthrough of the first KOTOR game. But as I continued to delve deeper and deeper into the plot, I realized that this game may just be better than the original--I know, sue me; it's just so good. So what made this buggy, old, rushed game so good?
Graphics: 13/20; (per 2004, 18/20 on high settings): The engine from the first game was still relatively nice looking at this point, but I can definately tell the difference between the two games. By today's standards, the graphics kinda suck, although they aren't too distracting, becuase it isn't the focus of the game.
Gameplay: 19/20: Okay, now when I started this game, I detested the gameplay; it was one of the reasons that I didn't complete it for over a year after buying it. It's hard to get used to, but once you do, it's quite endearing. Second playthrough, still loving the gameplay. Again, though, not the focus of this game.
Sound: 20/20: Like literally some of the best voice acting I've ever heard; even after 35 hours, I was not tired of the voices. Music was good, too (Star Wars, you know), but my recommendation is that you turn it down, becuase it's kind of overpowering if you don't personally set it.
Story: 20/20 (Considering giving it 21/20): Now... now, young padawans... let me tell you that this is the Creme de la Creme of all games I've ever played, save maybe TLoU or TWDS1. This story--side quests and main quests--is amazing. It makes the entire star wars saga look like it was designed by a child. This dark, sinister story... I could go on and on, but instead I'll give you the gist of it. The theme of the first game was redemption and being true to one's self. This game is about betrayal and loss. I can't go on without revealing too much; I just can't say enough to do it justice, either. I've never been so obsessed with a game. I couldn't stop playing. Sadly, Finals were the next week, so I had to stop playing. Seriously: get this game just for this.
Lasting appeal(Characters and world): 20/20: The characters are what make the story; the world is what makes the characters--domino effect. If it weren't for these characters, their dedicated roles of voice acting, and the expanded universe of Star wars being explored, this game wouldn't be as good; it would still be good, but not as good. Since this is a star wars game, most players don't need too much explaining to understand ("Jedi, sith, What are those?") if they've played the first game, so the story is the main focus.
Cons: Bugs... lots of bugs; more bugs in this game than in a Vegan Naturalist's hair. But it's worth it; the bugs can be endearing, most of the time they're just plain annoying. If you can get over bugs, this game is worth it; just get to know your computer and remember that most of the time, just an alt+tab will fix it; if not, try reloading your last save; if the game freezes, you'll need the ctrl+alt+del. Only significant complaints. (P.S. I used the Restored Content Mod, so probably most of my issues came from mods, but if not, try these things.)
TL;DR Graphics: 13/20 (2004: 18/20); Gameplay: 19/20; Sound: 20/20; Story: 20/20; Lasting Appeal (Characters and world setting): 20/20. Lots of bugs, but amazing game underneath all the issues.
OVERALL: 97/100 Spectacular. Seriously... Great game. Get it. RPG or star Wars fan, don't miss this. Get the first one, as well, even though I don't think it's as good.

The game has a lot of flaws but is pretty decent nonetheless. They really drive home the point that this is a sniping game by giving you a very small amount of ammo for your tommygun and pistol. It means that 95% or higher of your kills will be by sniping. It makes it frustrating at times because you have to face off against a squad of guys, ten to twenty guys usually, and snipe them all down. It is not hard at all, just that sniping gets old after a while. The bullet cam is one of the cooler ideas that I have ever seen in a game but unless you turn down its frequency in the options then you are going to be seeing it hundreds of times in the game and it gets old real fast. The realism is entirely absent and the game is highly inconsistent. What I mean is that sometimes a bullet through the chest of an enemy will kill him but a lot of times it just does 50% dmg to him and he stands there like nothing happened to him and fires exactly the same as before you shot him. Tanks also have external gas tanks on them that blow the tank up when shot. Gee, if only it were that simple in real war. Enemy snipers also are psychic. They are magically aware of your exact location and pull off pinpoint headshots on you even when you are somewhere that they should have no idea about, even when you have only snuck around a corner into view without making any noise and they are very far away across the map. The AI is also dumb as fk. They stand up out of cover and stand out in the open the entire game, making snipe-killing them a cinch. Snipers are somewhat hidden but when you see where they are they make almost no effort to re-adjust when you fire their way. They just stand and fire in a snipe battle with you until you quickly kill them. Use your tommygun and pistol ammo very, very sparingly, as you get such a small amount and there are usually no places to get any more ammo during a level until the next level starts and you are magically at full ammo again.
I tried the MP briefly and I have to say it was fun. And surprisingly it still has enough of a fan base that you will find games to join. It has all the classic game modes too: dm, tdm, and ctf, and several co-op modes.
The game has more of a arcade feel to it than an actual sniping game but it is still a pretty decent game that is optimized pretty good and runs smoothly. It can be fun for a once-through, but it is only about as good as the average professional review of the game which was between 60 and 70 out of 100.

One simple word, one simple game, the absolute best FPS on the planet: DOOM
Straight out of 1993, Doom was a game made simply because the group of 20 something year olds wanted to make it. It's a game where design splashes with creativity, something you don't find in almost any modern game today.
The game is simple. Get to the end of each stage. That's it. You also need to kill the literal thousands of demon hellspawn along the way so don't forget about them either. The monsters range from simple zombie soldiers to demonic goats that shoot rockets at you. The games monsters all revolve around the notion of avoiding projectiles, or hitscans.
The maps are designed with absolute love and attention. Each episode was made usually by one person, and you really can feel that distinction when you play them. Some maps were mazes, some maps were collosiums, some maps used more of a certain ammo type, thus limiting your approach, but most of all, the designs of the maps are interesting and fun to play.
Doom is a testament to the 90's, and a bit to the 80's. The loud metal induced music, the overall design, the action and horror of films such as Aliens. Everything is combined in such a perfect, uniform way that nothing feels out of place.
Doom is in a nutshell, just a game that feels right to play. Not a single aspect about the game feels wrong at all, and thats something you never see anymore in games. The attention to detail and gameplay is absolutely amazing.
There is not one single game I've ever played that did everything as perfect as Doom did. The monsters, the maps, the design, the gameplay, the mechanics, the feel, is all so perfect, that you really need this in your library.
Being a game from 1993, the game runs on DOSBOX. If you don't like that, there's plenty of source ports out there, like ZDoom, Zandronum (which focuses on multiplayer as well), and for a faithfull recration of the game, Chocolate Doom. There's also literally millions upon millions of custom content for the game as well. Some wads I could reccomend include classics such as Alien Vendetta, Memento Mori 1 and 2, Hell Revealed and some new ones such as Back to Saturn X, Doom the way id Did, Doom 2 the way id Did, ZDoom community map project 1 and 2, and the PSX Total Conversion, and anything by mapper skillsaw (Ancient Aliens is a blast).
Doom is a game I will always see myself coming back to, even when we are in 2047 playing games on a display device in our brains.

For three days and three nights, my world has been a slow-burning terror. I just wanted to kick back in the forest. Sunbathe on the warm rocks. Mingle with the gentle deer and playful pigs that roam the valleys. Until the monster came. Soon, I was being spied on every moment. I could no longer luxuriate nude in the green grasses. I could no longer ride the pigs for amusement. It arrived in the belly of a metal beast. It's glassy eyes spread throughout the woods. It raided and stole from the many places I had once frolicked. It lured and trapped my pig friends, only to bind more all-seeing eyes upon their delicate heads. At night, it would watch for me. Waiting so that it might make sport of hunting me.
The first night, I wanted only to fall into slumber outside its many invasive eyes. I destroyed them as they hung suspended from the trees. Perhaps if I could make it understand that I only wanted my peace and privacy, it would leave. But alas, my efforts were in vain. By the next night, all damage would be repaired. The eyes continue to watch.
I met my once-friend pig in the woods outside the monster's encampment. My dear friend had succumbed to the monster's evil. Its eyes stared dumbly back at me, even as that all-eye watched from atop a tortured head. I had no choice. I had to set my once-companion free. I whispered gently as I held his head in my arms, stroking the matted fur. I whispered of times now past. Of romps through the forest and friendship now gone. I twisted then, violently. His head came away in my arms. I wept bitterly, my tears salty in my throat. I left the body there. I could not bear the sight.
The second night, the nightmare was born anew. More dumb stares. More friends gone to the tortures of the thing hiding in the metal beast. I stared into the glass eyes of the metal beast, catching glimpses of the villain. My rage grew. I took the heads of my friends, determined to send a message. I would not back down any longer. It would not break my resolve. My friend's deaths would not be meaningless. I mounted them. I left them standing proudly upon pikes. Accusing eyes leveled at the hidden monster. To greet it when it emerged with the morning. To haunt it as I was now haunted.
The third night, I knew what had to be done. I could be passive no longer. I would confront the evil that besmirched my woods. I would cleanse it from the earth. It had set traps for me. Metal teeth digging deep into my vulnerable flesh. I screamed in pain. But I remembered my pig friends. I remembered their pain. Their sacrifice. I pressed on. I could see it inside. I leapt.
A resounding boom. A hot, heavy pressure hit my chest. My ribcage shattered with the force. I fell backwards. The metal beast was opening, but I could not see through the haze of my pain. I could only taste the copper in my mouth. Feel the burn spreading through my body as my life ebbed away.
The monster was standing over me. I looked up at it as the last of my life left me. I wanted to ask it. Why? Why did you torment me? What pain did I ever cause you? What pain did my beloved friends ever cause you? It looked down at me without pity.
There was another blast. The sound seemed to split my ear drums. Then nothing. Only the blackness.

A game with a lot of potential, but a terrible failure in execution. If done correctly, this would have beaten any Paradox game in terms of depth and immersion, but what you get is a buggy and unstable "simulation" that will make you lose support and get anti-capitalist riots if you dare to lower the taxes, where attacking terrorists that hide in the town with several fighters would cause the people to revolt against you instantly, and where things like private education or healthcare are unthinkable. Overall, I would love for this to work. I love the system of interaction with A LOT of different characters - politicians, governors, military men, secret agents, famous people like writers or athletes or even your wife and parents. This could have been insanely good, especially after years and years of constant development, but failed miserably. Don't buy it, unless maybe on -80% or -90% sale. It's not worth 10$ and will make you furious when you lose your save for tenth time in a row and have to start all over again.
1. The great system of organizing meetings with different people, even though it gets repetitive after a while and there are not that many things to say.
2. Military stuff is alright, not nearly as good as Paradox's games or even Supreme Ruler, but it's alright.
3. Diplomacy is done alright and makes sense, but I would never call it "realistic". On realistic setting, in just a month, Afghanistan attacked Pakistan and Syria attacked Iraq. Almost every time.
4. Map is alright, and I love how there are many different regions, like all the US states, although the regions are too random at times - I don't like how in Syria the regions don't cover the Kurdish areas so you could create a realistic Kurdish state.
5. You get Wikipedia links to articles that describe issues that you have to decide on. That's a nice touch.
6. The revolutions and riots inside your cities that you have to take care of are a nice touch.
1. The price and the DLCs. The game is WAY overpriced and the DLCs are really pathetic - the in-game editor that breaks your game after a while, every single time, and a modding tool that is buggy as hell and mods are usually unstable too. All that for a price of an AAA title. Go figure.
2. 3D models of characters - there are just a few of them, excluding the leaders and in some cases some important politicians - you get Jeb Bush for example, but not Rand Paul, for example.
3. Too few political ideologies - there are no proper libertarians, greens, and terrorists' ideology is "royalist". Seriously?
4. Economy is broken. Signing like 50 good or decent contracts with other countries and lowering the taxes a bit will easily get you a 60% GDP rise in a month, which is hard to stop and makes your inflation fly off the charts. What's more, most of my contracts were simply to sell my pharmaceutics across Europe as the US, along with maize, pork, beef, and some other stuff, while getting resources that I need - steel, bauxites, robots, coal, fuel - I negotiated reasonable prices for each good, which I guess simulates the international trade fairly well, but no - doing that will destroy the balance and make the game extremely gamey. Why even bother with the contract system then?
5. For whatever reason there are no real names and mods that allow them are buggy.
6. There is no private initiative in most areas - no private education, healthcare, research, insurance - you get stuck with public one and high taxes. Not really good if you want to try a more conservative or libertarian approach.
7. Unrealistic reactions of your voters - almost every tax reductios ends in popular unrest of anti-capitalists that somehow managed to get multi-million organizations in the US, and that can co-ordinate unrest accross America, you can cancel reimbursing people for doctor appointments and hospital visits almost entirely, but as long as you spend some more money on handicapped, emergency services and maternity care, it almost evens out. Bombing a town in the middle of Afghanistan with a few planes will result in an instant revolution. Is that "realistic"?
8. Bugs and terrible stability - your game will crash often, especially if you want to use the god'n spy DLC. You basically pay money to destroy your game. Classy.
9. There are very few character models which means that every military chief and intelligence officer look exactly the same - even uniforms are the same, and they don't even look realistic.
They couldn't make it work many years ago, they can't make it work now. It's an overpriced trash.
Even despite all that, I till hope that this can some day become the next Pride of Nations - a great game with a lot of depth and an amazing military system, but one that was once unbelievably buggy and unstable, and was so sluggish on a high-end PC that it was impossible to play. It's a great game now and easily beats Paradox's famous Victoria and Victoria 2 in pretty much every category. I'm going to preface this review by saying that if lack of bugs is an important quality in a game for you, then you will probably hate this game.
I have played every iteration of The Guild 2(as well as the first game). Since it was first released, I have played much of this game in various forms long before purchasing it on Steam. Renaissance is, by far, the best form of The Guild 2 that there is. If you had played the earlier forms of the game, you would understand why I love Renaissance so much. Is this game bug free? Absolutely not. It has had a rocky development and maintenance history. It has been more or less abandoned on more than one occassion. Yet, it's still here, and people are actively developing mods for this game. That's because the gameplay concepts presented are an absolute home run. While it's basically meant to be business sim and rpg, it succeeds by offering diverse ways of playing the game. Sure, you can buy materials, make them into a finished product, and sell your finished goods at a profit. Absolutely. You can also use those finished goods to arm mercenaries who will extort money from passersby. Or you can use other finished goods to improve your chances of gaining political office. You could also rob a plump, plentiful shop for your income. And wouldn't it be nice if you could use your politlcal influence to gain control of the city guard and prevent guards from patrolling near that shop you want to rob? Yes, you can do that, and that is what makes this game great. It's worth noting that that is just the possibilities offered by one class, the Rogue.
Honestly, what makes this game great, for me, boils down to the fact that you have a lot of different things that you can do. In most business sims, materials and goods are just icon swaps for each other with different numbers representing their utility. In The Guild 2: Renaissance, the utility of goods extends beyond simple, numerical values. Have a rival Dynasty in the same business as you in your city, constantly beating you to the punch by selling in your city's market and lowering the economic value of your goods? Sure, you COOOOULD just sell your goods at a different city's market. IF YOU'RE A COMMUNIST. Instead, show them whatfor by setting off a stink bomb in their firm. They can't very well sell goods they haven't made, can they?
Now, here is where reality bites. This game is buggy. Buggy to the point where I simply won't run the game without installing a modpack. Lucky for you, there are many great mods available. To make things even better, you have two great options for mod packs. Fajeth's Mega Modpack and McCoy's Legacy Modpack. Both of these are great. While they both include a lot of similar mods Mega Modpack is geared towards adding more item options, and Legacy Modpack is geared more towards improving the multiplayer experience. On the latter note, if you're looking for a good multiplayer experience, this game is a mixed bag. On the one hand, multiplayer is awesome. On the other hand, multiplayer was poorly implemented in this game. Legacy Modpack has made a lot of improvements, but even with that and following all advice offered by the community on avoiding them, you still may end up with OOS errors. And the advice goes pretty far. Last I checked they even mentioned playing with the same exact video settings (turning most graphics features off). If you can get a good group going, the multiplayer can be extremely fun and rewarding. Mario Party has nothing on this game in terms of ruining friendships.
I recommend this game if you're a patient person who is okay with having to deal with bugs. You have a lot of fun ways to play the game, and its particular blend of gameplay concepts is unique. The game offers a lot in terms of actual roleplaying, and it charmingly begs you to immerse yourself in its quirky world.
EDIT: I can't wait for The Guild 3!

Firstly. my review mostly lists the problems I had, since you're probably already interested in the game for whatever reason and wondering what might be bad about it.  I definitely played the game all the way through and enjoyed it, especially the boss fights.  The art style is brilliant, and the story is interesting enough (although I don't expect anything epic from a platformer).  I played with an Xbox 360 controller and the movement and controls are mostly solid.
The combat was a bit awkward.  It's just impractical to try to aim your weapon AND shield properly with the right thumbstick at the same time while moving around with the left.  I never got used to it.  The weapon switching with a controller is a joke too.  It's impossible to accurately choose one of dozens of weapons with the d-pad in the middle of combat.   You have to pause the game and switch in the inventory screen if you don't want to be carved up while finding the right weapon.  The being said, the combat does take a little bit of brains to know when to attack and with what against whom.
My biggest problem was the weapon/shield breaking mechanic.  Some weapons are more useful against a lot of foes, and some are kind of niche.  You tend to want to save the useful ones for potentially harder fights because they break so fast.  This means sometimes you're using terrible weapons against certain weaker foes just to hold onto the good weapons.  Shields break way too fast for you to be blocking with any regularity as well.  You do get a fair bit of replacement weapons, but you never know when the next good weapon or good shield is coming up, so I tended to try to conserve, which threw any battle strategy in the trash (there are so many health potions you can just keep healing instead of fighting well).  I feel like it would be a lot more fun if at least shields (and preferably weapons) were indestructible, because then you could use the weapons/shields to fit the strategy per enemy instead of playing resource management.  It's not unplayable by any means, just a moderate annoyance.

--------
Apotheon (gr. ἀπο przez/od+ θεος bóg, ἀποθεοῦν przebóstwić - ubóstwiony, "który wstąpił na boskie wyżyny").
Iście obłędny pomysł i realizacja. Na poziomie mechanicznym jest darksoulsowa walka z charakterystycznymi dla każdej broni timingami windupu i strefą zadawania damage'u, opierająca się w dużej mierze o tarcze i przewrotki oraz zastosowanie mikstur; pewną rolę odgrywa światło, którego źródłem jest pochodnia, albo emanacja niektórych przedmiotów. Genialny arsenał broni z takimi pozycjami jak doru, xiphos, sagaris :), oszczepy, proce, dyski, maczugi, trójzęby - w bród i bardzo zróżnicowane, i wszystko z epoki (nie licząc może niektórych zbyt skomplikowanych mechanicznie pułapek). Nie samą walką gra stoi, trochę jest to taki RPG z eksplorowaniem świata i znajdowaniem sekretów; przy czym łupiestwo i rzezie niewinnych ofiar bardzo celnie trafiają w homerycki klimat.
W warstwie prezentacji uderza przede wszystkim grafika nie do pomylenia z niczym innym, nawiązująca do malarstwa wazowego, przede wszystkim stylów czarno- i czerwonofigurowego. Uzupełnieniem są charakterystyczne kanciate animacje 2d utrzymujące w pełni ten styl, a więc twarze postaci z profilu, ciało zwykle w rzucie "półbocznym". Spodziewam się, że to te animacje w połączeniu z charakterystyczną walką są dla wielu głównym kamieniem obrazy, no bo jak to: ktoś śmiał podporządkować płynność mojego gameplayu stylowi gry. Ale tu właśnie tak jest, i mam do twórców ogromny szacun za konsekwencję. No i fabuła bazująca bezpośrednio na greckiej mitologii, przewrotnie i sprytnie; sięgnąłem znów po "Mity greckie" Gravesa i zacząłem zgłębiać. Wydawało by się że to otrzaskany temat i wszystko jest tu wiadomo; otóż nie, okazuje się że ledwo dzwoni w czaszce.
Elementy mitologii są głównym źródłem dla level designu. Tak więc zgoła inny gameplay spotkamy w Hadesie, niż ścigając zwierzynę w lasach Artemis. Takoż i z puzlami: od zręcznościowego kontestu pijackiego z Dionizosem, po test pamięci przy przekraczaniu Lety. Despite not usually enjoying platformers or the "Metroidvania" style of games, I found Apotheon a real treat. The visual presentation of the game is enough to recommend the game by itself -- the art style and animation are really something. The story is interesting, and blends elements of Greek mythology while creating its own narrative. Sound design and music are both quite good, as well. The combat is basic, but engaging enough -- the various classes of weapons each have their strengths, and fights are all about timing and range. With one or two enemies it can be a bit tactical, but when more start piling up it can start to become a bit of a tangle, where you're not certain what (if any) effect you're having.
That's a minor quibble, however, and the game's length means you'll be finished with the epic (and for a nice change, that word is appropiate!) story before they start to detract from the experience. The absolutely beautiful art style combined with fun exploration, some interesting puzzles (I particularly enjoyed Athena's challenges), and decent combat gave me a enjoyable experience that I would recommend to others.

If you like turn based shooters, this may be a game for you. Breach & Clear is a simulator and straightforward. The marginal story only serves as a simplistic backstory to why you are in one country or another. It doesn't matter; you are there to eliminate terrorists. The story only serves to support that.
The levels are well designed and compact. Graphically the game is simplistic but they serve well enough to set the stage. The locals are diverse and enjoyable, though I found myself employing the same strategies on most occasions. Yet I suppose that’s realistic, whether it is some Russian compound or an office building the principles of clearing a building are the same. Even though the game can feel repetitive I always found myself reloading the game and coming back for more. I still am. I hope they add more maps later on. I know it is wishful thinking but it be endless fun if they added the ability to make your own scenarios and show them to your friends.
There are a handful of game modes to partake in. Such as bomb disposal, hostage rescue, and the generic eliminate all threats. There are also a handful of difficulties to take part in to test your skills.
There is also a large amount of upgrades you can do to your characters. There is also a store where you can buy new weapons, accessories, clothing, helmets, and vests. Despite the wide array of options available I never felt that my characters had unique skills that affected my gameplay substantially. I found myself using characters interchangeably regardless of how I loaded them out.
The UI is simplistic but allows a decent amount of diversity. I do wish they had a mechanism by which you could delay a characters movement. It would have been rather helpful. Overall the game has been enjoyable and I hope to get another five-ten hours out of it before I’m done with it.

What Can I say about Sheltered?
...
Sheltered is the latest in a long line of survival games that pits you more against the elements and random encounters than zombies and monsters, you start the game by generating your Nuclear family from a list of cookie cutter options that all have strengths and weaknesses, while this would feel limiting in a lot of games it works well in Sheltered and adds emphesis to the role that you have for each character on building new gear, maintaining your dwelling, seaching the wastes for new gear and resources and the interactions you have with others.
Characters gain experience over time and slowly level up there stats the more they are used (this feature still seems to have a few bugs, but hey, it's early access.) which allows you to work more effectively and keep your family alive longer.
you will have opportunities to meet new people, trade with them, recruit them into your shelter, attack them and ultimately when one of your beloved family members bites the big one you can bury them or... *dry heaves a little* "Harvest" them to help maintain your rations.
Ways to die in Sheltered are numerous, Beaten to death, Shot, Starved, Dehydrated, Food Poisioning and Radiation poisoning just to list the ones I have discovered.
so... Is it worth the price of admission?
Pros
-Fun Game play in a randomly generated world.
-Sense of achievement when you unlock the next tier of crafting items
-Ability to eat the corpses of your Kin
-Currently a steady flow of updates (3 content updates in the first week of release)
Cons
-Early Access means bugs and some semi broken features (game on a whole plays fairly smoothly though)
-Some of the UI needs to be improved upon, I.E. when a character has food poisoning or rad poisoning it can be difficult to realise (90% of my character death was rad poisoning...)
At $14.99 I have spent more money on worse game.

is a horror game, so the first question is how scary it is.  To which I say, I don't know, I was too busy hiding behind the sofa.  Yes, the game's reputation is deserved.  It knows how to use sound and the environment to build an atmosphere of dread.  Most importantly, it knows how to build anticipation and threat, and even manages to follow through reasonably well once the monsters start appearing.  I remember after dying a couple of times thinking that this actually made the monsters
scary, now that I knew what the worst that could happen was; but later areas like the Choir disabused me of
notion.
That said, there were a number of issues I had with
that make me pause before recommending it.  The gameplay can basically be divided into two types: panicked running and hiding from the monsters; and puzzle-solving.  The former is well-done, even if many games now have used the trick of giving you no way to fight back to build fear.  The designers wisely limit how often you have to face monster-heavy sections, to build anticipation and keep the threat special.  Hence the puzzle sections.  But these feel to me much less integral to the game.  None of the puzzles are especially hard, and most just involve lots of exploring areas to find the one thing you need.
Also, the game's story is not the greatest; not bad, just okay.  The pacing felt a bit off on my first playthrough, taking too long to get me fully invested.  It seems that I've been playing a lot of games recently using the "random documents" story telling element, and the execution here was merely adequate.  I did like the use of flashbacks, though.  The biggest let-down is probably the climax, sadly.  The final confrontation is underwhelming from both a narrative and gameplay perspective, not to mention being one of the least frightening sequences in the game.
None of which is to say that
is a bad game, exactly.  It's just that in a number of places it's only okay.  But to go back to my starting point, the game sets out to scare you and is pretty good at that.  If that's what you're looking for, you should find it here.

Wander no More is quite a good read - the story is interesting and the main characters, the ronin samurai chased by his former companions and a teenage girl who he took in his care after discovering her in a razed village, are quite relatable and compelling. It's short and ends a bit awkwardly, but the main plot is good enough to make it satisfying and deliver a few fresh ideas.
The visual assets and voice acting are a bit more problematic - voices of support characters were cringy enough to make me mute voice acting completely (the whole experience seriously felt better that way), even though the main pair wasn’t that bad. The artstyle is not ugly, but the proportions on the sprites and in CG were distorted to the point that it often felt grotesque. Neither of those issues killed my enjoyment of reading through this VN, but they didn’t help the story much either.
In summary, if you like kinetic novels (no choices, just linear story), this one isn’t half bad, but if it wasn’t free, I don’t think I would recommend buying it. A decent freebie, but nothing more than that.

In the interest of being as helpful as possible in explaining what youre getting into with this title, I'll first try and explain why you might want to play this game in despite of the bugs and poorly fleshed out gameplay mechanics...
The guild II Renaissance is absolutely worth playing if you're the kind of person who's seen everything the genre offers and is looking for something new. The way this game handles strategy feels very unique. Yes on the surface its a business management/tycoon style game but this is a game where you also get to throw the legal system at your opponent which was something that I found to be pretty awesome. So in addition to your standard 'right click' to attack commands, you also can also instruct your goons to follow anyone and see if you can witness them comitting a crime so as to take them to court and force them into one of a varriety of punishments...
The various classes you can play in this game play out very differently which is also somewhat of a small saving grace. The patron handles food production and the survice industry while the craftsman can do production of more valuable finished goods as a focus. The rogue and the scholar however are very different. The rogue can perform extortion, rob from merchant shipments, pickpocket, and all manner of general thuggery. The scholar can build churches and banks etc and are particularly good at handling court proceedings.
You can run for various offices in government, each giving you unique powers you can use to mess with your oponents. You also need to find a wife and have kids to ensure your dynasty stays healthy. The game simulates courting your would-be wife as well... which just adds to the depth.
So having said all that, yes its a buggy game. I havent seen a game breaking bug yet though, the game just sort of feels unpolished in a software sense sometimes. In addition to that, its definitely unpolished in the character animation sense... Sometimes the animation is good and sometimes its "WOW how did that not get fixed" bad.
I also said that its true that the gameplay mechanics sometimes feel a bit overly simplified... I want to be clear here, this game is very broad in its offerings but I think due to that, some of those offerings seem a bit minimal. Take courting a potential wife for example: Your options after you single someone out for courting are: Compliment, Gift, Hug, Beguile and Kiss and with the exception of 'gift' they all do basically the same thing unless youve used the same command recently, so effectively the challenge is to remember the last thing you did until she falls in love with you.... (Man, if only! Am I right guys?)
Take the court system. Awesome idea, very fun, even though it too is simple. Essentially while your skills play a big part, all you can do in court is present your evidence and recommend a suitable punishment. So there could have been a whole lot more done with this but it does serve its purpose in basic function.
I should also mention that I jumped into this game for the first time just recently and I found that it plays quite well for an old title, I'd say its aged well given that I was way off in my guess as to how old it was.
For anyone looking for similar games, I'd strongly suggest checking out Partrician 3 or 4 - as well as Railroad Tycoon 3 specifically for interesting strategic mechanics... I was ultimately let down.
The introduction is great, the mood and tone of the game are well set. As a fan of point and click games the puzzles in
are incredibly lacking, where the majority of them require the player to hit button, flip switches and, when that fails, to figure out how to re-enable these switches in order to open up the path ahead. If I'm not the one solving these puzzles then there are triggered scenes that do it for me. There's a little bit of item combining going on with the inventory system but the final parts of the game don't make much use of this mechanic. There soon came a point where I realised just how many of the game's monsters hold no threat to my character, where I could essentially forfeit to them and simply respawn without losing any progress. I find it especially insulting where, as I'm expected to run away from these monsters, one section of the game requires me to be caught by them and fail in order to progress.
There is, of course, a gimmick where the lantern constantly requires oil as a means of fuel, although it never seemed to run out during my play through. Nor did I exhaust my supply of tinderboxes. These two options are required to keep the protagonist's sanity from dropping, in spite of this fact I never did meet my demise through my insanity, nor did I through environmental damage so I have no idea why these systems are in place if not to be an inconvenience to the player. The reason Hook works so well is because of it's cut down and simplified design. In other games you might complain if something had been reduced or "refined" but in Hook it's been done to reduce the pressure and potential annoyances that are common in other puzzle games. What you end up with is a short, sweet, simple, relaxing and fun step-by-step logical puzzle game.
Everything in Hook from the lack of menu and loading screen to the lack of music and fancy animations exist to serve a purpose. Even simple things like the exact number of 50 levels are symptomatic of the design of this game: Less is more when it's well designed.
The simplicity and reduction in Hook means it's only about thinking and proceeding and everything is natural, there's no need to think about controls or options, which servers to relax your mind and make it a joy from start to finish.
My only concern with the title is the short length or lack of content. Hook excels as a simple and relaxing game to play when you have spare time and want something mellow. So not to be able to come back and play more when you're in those moods is a real disappointment.
Hook is priced smartly and correctly. Most games priced under $1 are aimed at being impulse buys and don't feel well polished or lack a lot of what you might expect. Hook doesn't oversell and it's just a plain simple short puzzle game sold at a fair price any time you need something to do for an hour.

SOMA for me was an experience, rather than a game.
Similarly to Frictional's previous babies Penumbra and Amnesia, you are a defenceless mystery just waiting to be revealed. In true form, the prose is brave, deep and wholehearted, with a hard veer towards real-life situations, personal conflict and philosophical tragedies. We've all got somewhere to be, games to do, so I'll try to keep it simple.
SOMA stands out for a lot of reasons; namely we have a protagonist who we can empathise with. A lot of people are conflicted about Simon, but I think given the situation that he's in, we can forgive his bouts of vulnerability, fear and black humour. We also gain a valuable companion in the game who offers generous insights not only into the situation that Simon has been casually tossed into, but also about the nature of human beings, what defines them and our relationship with each other. (Which is really as simply as I can put it.)
Despite all of these things, SOMA truly commits to the sense of isolation within a hostile and dark environment, relying on telltale signs dotted across all levels. (Mr. Akers, anyone?) Amnesia and Penumbra may have has this too, but SOMA uses it to its advantage.
With its deep storytelling, talented actors, intense horror, astounding graphics and elegant gameplay, SOMA is a treat for every gamer and a delight for horror fans everywhere.

If I had to describe Apotheon in one word, it'd be fun.  Plain and simple, good ol' fashioned fun.
Don't come into this game looking for an immersive novel-like story---it's just not there.  But like a beautifully illustrated children's book, Apotheon shines in its simplicity, style, and sense of adventure.  It's fun to play, and fun to watch.  The controls are simple and fluid.  The scenes are beautifully rendered in the style of Greek art.  It's truly a joy to behold.
The soundtrack doesn't disappointment either, with a host of tunes that totally immerse the player into the environment, and convey the excitement (and sometimes anxiety), as you pit your mortal self against the mighty gods of Olympus.
It's a must for any fans of Greek mythology, or anyone who enjoyed the Iliad or Odyssey.  Fans of simple, but fun adventure games will also find a lot to like here, as well as anyone who can appreciate games as art.
To be fair, the story narrative could have been better integrated into the entirety of the game.  At times, it comes off feeling slightly arbitrary, or disjointed.  The side-plots also feel a bit confusing, and it's not clear most of the time how they fit in.  But, on the whole, the story is cogent, and it works for what the game is.  Again, in keeping with my earlier metaphor, think Chris Van Allsburg, not Leo Tolstoy.
My final grade for this beautifully rendered Greek odyssey:  B+.

One of those classic FPS titles that I've been wanting to come back to for ages. So I did. How does it hold up?
The graphics are 1997. Really cool then (PARTICLE EFFECTS!), pretty basic now, but the art direction is mostly fine so it's not unbearably hideous. Unless you really can't stand low poly models with blurry textures.
One thing I don't like that can't really be excused by the game's age is the uninspired enemy design. A lot of enemies look really similar and bland, even the final boss just looks like some of the other stuff you've been killing for hours.
The environments aren't particularly varied either but I can live with that because a) it's a military compound, those are typically not built to look fancy, and b) they had to account for the hardware limitations of 1997 computers.
The audio design is a bit heavy-handed, with the then-standard enemy alert lines (which are always the same, too), narration by Microsoft Sam and the lines of your captured comrades being so repetitive and annoying that you'll probably just kill them so they shut up (and hey, they even drop items sometimes). Most guns sound (and look) powerful, making them satisfying to use.
The Steam version has no music for some reason, which is a shame.
The storyline (if you can even call it that) is simple - you've landed behind enemy lines and your job is to infiltrate their buildings and disable their crucial defence systems so the cavalry can come in safely. That's about all there is to it.
The gameplay is mostly what you'd expect from an oldschool shooter: run around, grab a lot of physically impossible guns and singlehandedly take on an entire alien army.
Some enemies are fairly challenging but if you observe their behaviour you can figure out how to deal with them efficiently.
This game hits just about the right amount of health and items in levels so it's not unforgivingly hard but you still need to be careful. You can (and should) use most guns quite liberally without running out so that's nice too.
There are secret areas in most (maybe all) levels, some easier to find than others. The stuff you get from them is not always that great, often you'll just get a new gun that you'd get your hands on two minutes later anyway.
In compliance with the 90s' standards for FPS games, the level design is a bit maze-like in places, sometimes you'll have numerous places to go and no clear indicator of where you should go first (other than a vague objective in the F1 screen), but it's not terrible. Levels are divided into interconnected maps, similarly to Half-Life.
I must say the final boss was really underwhelming. As long as you've saved up enough ammo (and hopefully quad damage) it's business as usual - dodge and shoot until it dies, no advanced strategy or anything. He doesn't look or act substantially more dangerous than most other late-game enemies.
So to sum up, it's a 1997 game with all the pros and cons of a 1997 game - dated graphics, somewhat awkward audio design, intense action broken up only by hunting for switches and keys. If you're into old FPS games and for some reason haven't played this one, go for it. If you prefer streamlined modern shooters with HD graphics, don't.

Great little game, lots of fun.
The concept is simple enough, you manage a small family of four that managed to not only survive the apocalypse, but also happened across a small bomb shelter. You will need to manage your precious resources, expand your shelter, build what few comforts you can, explore your surroundings, trade, recruit, and kill to survive as long as possible.
Currently the game is still in Early Access but you will quickly see that the dev team is very involved and regularly adding in new updates. So if there is a mechanic you hate, or one you would like to see implemented its not too late to bring it up. Also having bought into many an Early Access title I too have been burned more than once by a dev team that got in over their heads or decided to cut and run. I don't get that impression from these guys, so if your hesitant about buying into a game that is still in Early Access out of fear of getting an unfinished game that will never get completed, don't worry about it with Sheltered. Its pretty clear that these folks have every intention of finishing what they have started.
Now yes there are a few bugs and minor issues. nothing that is game breaking that I've encountered so far. Just some things that won't close when you click on them so you have to hit esc. Things like that. And considering they just did an update this morning, I can see they are still adding in content and fixing bugs. And new content is always fun.
All in all yes I recommend this. Its fun, and addictive. The team appears to be very dedicated. There is a small learning curve and the tutorial needs some work. But after you play around with things for you first couple families, you'll have it down and will be expanding from a family into a post-apocalyptic, underground, community.

Kotor II is a mixed bag. The mechanics feel pretty good for the most part, but the plot and character development leave a lot to be desired.
There are numerous improvements made to the power/feat selection, compared to what was available in Kotor I. Blaster-wielding characters are more viable, classes can spend feats to remove cross-class skill penalties, and the upgrade/crafting system has been greatly expanded. In this respect, this game is better than its predecessor.
The story, on the other hand, feels like a step back, at least in my opinion. There are some iteresting characters with interesting perspectives and goals, but the plot itself seems... absent for much of the game (especially for the first 10 or so hours).
"Rough" is the word that best describes Kotor II. It isn't a bad game, but It has enough blemishes to make it difficult to recommend.

Got this free on Steam. You should have done so too. This isn't entirely realistic, but it's one of those games which strikes a balance between realism and fun. It's challenging too. The story, however, is not very engaging. You are an OSS agent in WWII trying to assassinate German scientists before the Russians can get them, so not only will you fight German soldiers, but also Soviet soldiers. And there's was a lot of room to make a decent story; you are a secret agent carrying out missions that "never happened" after all. But anyway, on the the gameplay itself. As said already, it's great. Since you are a sniper, close combat is discouraged, and even though you have an SMG, it has limited ammo. For the best experience, I recommend you set the enemy skill to "Veteran", realism to "limited", and tactical assistance "off". Lower settings to me make the game too easy. That said, you have to praise Rebellion for making customizable difficulties. And the main feature of the game: the X-ray cam. It show just what a sniper bullet can do to your body. Can be quite satisfying, especially when fighting difficult enemies. This is cinematics done right. Fortunately, if you are squeamish, you can turn it off. Also, never underestimate a single foe: he can kill you easily. Speaking of the enemies, while they can pose a challenge, the AI could use some improving. This is evident when you see German and Soviet soldiers fighting each other; they will have no problem trying to kill you, but they seem to not cope well when fighting each other. The campaign has a decent length: 8-10 hours. And a second play-through is worth it. Multiplayer is quite fun too, you are all snipers. Element of surprise and awareness play an even bigger role here.
So do I recommend this game? Yes. But you should have got it when it was free. Right now, it's $30, and I don't think that's a good price. If you didn't get a free copy, wait for a sale: this game is worth $20 to me.
