Nether has a nice post apocalyptic atmosphere and some really interesting ideas (tribes, capturing and holding points, missions, crafting, announced events etc.) but...oh my, it is close to unplayable.
If you start it, you'll see the server list. And you can enjoy that view for some minutes because, well, you can't even move your mouse. Don't panic and don't kill the process, just wait, after soime minutes you can move your mouse...maybe. Sometimes it really freezes...or maybe it doesn't and it still loads after 5 minutes?
Anyway, sometimes (or after some time) you'll make it to click on a server (which don' show ping/latency or anything besides names and playercount) and click connect.
And here the....waiting begins again. You can fly around the world and explore it a little bit, while waiting to get into the game. This actually is a nice idea but after 5 minutes of flying around it gets odd.
And if you do it on 3 or 4 servers in a row you'll get a bit bored. Eventually the game freezes here gain and you have to kill the process, but you are used to that soon.
But there is a chance that you encounter the character screen and are able to make a new one. (if you already have one you will start as that one) And start the game. Well maybe you'll get back to flying around or the game freezes, but you know, you can kill the process.
Maybe you see your hands and your "butter knife". And that's the moment you can start playing. Well, if you know how. But I wont complain here, hardened by DayZ and other games I just try until I figure it out - and it's not that hard. W-A-S-D moving, left click attacking, "I" for inventory (and access to the other tabs like character), "M" for map.
After some trying you are able to crouch and go prone (C and Z) and sprint (shift).
So, what now? Well there is a little wheel that states that I'm getting hungry...or thristy. So maybe start looking around and loot a little bit. Hm, it feels a little bit...slow. Fast check - yep, 15 fps. Hm...no, after a swift check, it's not my pc (which can run most games fine), it's the game. Well, better avoid other players or creatures, maybe they will drop my frames further...
Wait there is something that moves? Another player? No it's a creature that...well...spits oil it seems. Afraid of having to start the game again you attack it and kill it, but suddenly another thing...this can teleport and hits you....but you fight it off as well. And try to loot "Hold E" ok...well,  it had a gun in its guts it seems. Nice. But no ammo...well not unusual for such a game.Level up? Really, level up. Hm...Shooting? Melee? Survival? Stamina? Well lets go for melee this time....hm...I can block now...if I find something to block with. Ok, thats great. (careful: no reset option)
So you move on, fight, flee (while watching your stamina that drops fast but you can recover it fast as well), and the AI, well let's call it....nah, don't call it. Calling it "AI" is honor enough. And you continue your journey to loot, get back to trade stuff in...and get sometimes shot by Snipers that camp areas.
Sometimes you see messages popping up regarding events (items dropped, safezones under attack etc.) that lead the players to an area. Oh, and you have  tutorial item in your backpack - but you don't know that when you start ;) And the tutorial mission was bugged for me (did not start).
And suddenly the game freezes (or you can't pick up anything), you can't even exit it...but you know, you can always kill the process.
Besides all of the technical problems and the hackers (that seemingly are a serious problem), Nether is a interesting idea.
It tries to take DayZ and mix a little bit of Metro (or Fallout 3) and a "normal" MMORPG to it.
The problem (that DayZ and Rust are also facing) are the players: No communication, only premade groups are able to survive (but will sooner or later also run into campers), KoS (Kill on sight) and well...PvP is for sure part of the game, even a core machanic - but it's far too present. PvE servers? I don't think that those will work out, since, like DayZ the most tension is when you meet another player. But unlike DayZ I have not seen nor heard of any interaction aside from premade groups - kill or be killed. and for new players that play alone it is very often "be killed" because your butter knife has nothing on my Mag DR-15.
And on top of that:
Oh my. I don't like where this might be going...
And for sure, if your character dies the items bought with real money are gone....
It doesn't deserve one now. Well, for 2.79 € you can buy it and wait and hope (or maybe get the 6€ pack with some "nether gold"), but at the moment, from my prespective, you shouldn't play it. A huge load of technical problems (really DayZ 0.39 was smooth and polished as hell compared to this), an horrible, hostile playerbase and an ingame currency that might (or might not) lead to P2W.
I'll try it some time later more and maybe I can recommend i then.

Very seriously the best Star Wars game and one of the best PC RPGs of all time.
You don't have to have played the first Knights of the Old Republic to follow what's going on here, but if you did, you'll notice that when Obsidian took the license from Bioware they put out a game that just viciously dunks all over its predecessor. It's damn near disrespectful how much better KOTOR 2 is.
KOTOR 2 freely gives away things that would qualify as major plot twists in the first game because its most important reveals are so much grander. It repeats archetypes from the first game and sometimes even grabs characters themselves from the first and says "hold my beer; THIS is how to write them correctly." I'm on my fourth play through (I'd played it twice before Steam existed) and I'm *still* discovering new things because there's just that much depth. Where the first KOTOR told your typical humdrum legendary hero Bioware story with "moral choice" amounting to being a boy scout or orphan-murderer, KOTOR 2 goes deeper. Is light always right? Can dark-sided actions be morally necessary? Are there unintended repercussions to simple acts of charity and kindness? Is anything worth believing in or fighting for?
You don't *have* to delve into these questions. You can play it straight forward and ignore so much of the dialogue and character development if you really want. You can speed from start to finish obliterating enemies with Force Lightning and ignore every hint of story. But KOTOR 2 will gladly reward you for the time and attention you put into it. And it's so very worth it.

Because of lots of features, realism, uniqueness in its genre (political simulator), the game CAN'T be discriminated because of bugs and a terrible UI.

Regarding bugs (as of 6.30 patch): screen tearing, crash after almost an hour of gameplay, slow UI under certain circumstances, infos disappearing.

Games like Power and Revolution should be constantly updated with world and scenarios enhancements/bugfix.
Like other reviewers said, Everism needs to build from scratch a better and almost bug-free simulator.

Guild 2 Renaissance is unique in its time, like all other Guild series. It's actually quite complicated but it will hook you for very long hours once you know all the commands and actions. You are born into one of the four classes namely Patron, Scholar, Rogue and Craftsman. Each class is special and has unique abilities.
If you choose Craftsman, your job is to make things out of raw materials and sell them to earn a living. If you are a Rogue, you can rob, waylay or kill a person for money or infamy. However, you can be sent to court and get hanged if found guilty. You are not alone in your line of work. You can also hire workers or goons to assist you.
As you perform your job, you gain money and your reputation grows. With both, you seek to buy bigger homes and increase your social status until you reach the pinnacle! You can get married, have lots of kids, and when you die, you take over your kids' roles. Along the way, you will encounter resistance from other noble families. There are many ways to get rid of them, of course...
There are many scenarios to choose from and there's multiplayer function! I have yet to encounter major bugs but the graphics is a bit outdated but still acceptable.

Overall, I give this game a 115% satisfaction for its complexity and fun!

I have always had a mild interest in Greek culture, or more specifically, its mythology. It is some of the richest that I know, and some of the most entertaining, and this game does every bit of that storied culture proud. As far as I can tell, the setting described within this game is as spot on as one can get in regards to something first created thousands of years ago. The art style is amazing, I feel as if I  am fighting my way through my own Greek epic, my own legend, and the music captures that feeling even more, and honestly, the whole display would not look at all out of place on a urn or carving in a museum. When just wandering Olympus, the sound of Pipes and Lyres fill the world, but when Xiphos and Doru are drawn, out come the horns and battle drums, not to mention a chorus to build up the tension. While the style and display are among the best I have ever seen, the actual gameplay and writing technique fall slightly short. The writing itself is fine, but aside from our silent hero Nikandreos, there are few, if any, returning characters to beef up dialog. When your home village of Dion is attacked, there is little impact to seeing a Greek village engulfed in flames. Characters run around screaming the same few lines over and over again, and even the characters that do speak rarely show up again, and if they do, it is unlikely you will remember any of them. Even the Gods themselves have little to say, barely a paragraph in some cases, Hephaestus and Aphrodite being the most notable in that regard. Some gods have  more substantial amounts of dialog, mainly Zeus and Hera, but the rest talk before boss fights, and that is about it. I remember distinctly (spoilers to those who care) breaking Helios out of Prison, and expecting to see him again after I had done as he asked, but I never saw him again. He just ran off after giving me the requisite three things to blow up. The actual game portion of this game fairs slightly better, though it is also flawed in it's own respects. It is a two-dimensional brawler, with a focus on inventory and clever usage of the tools at your immediate disposal rather than special attacks. Your attack options include tossing various bombs, javelins, darts, or any weapon you happen to be holding at the time, (Hey you! Lets play catch the pike! You first!) blocking or bashing with a shield, over hand and underhand attacks, a faster but weaker stab, healing items for when you are terrible at dodging, at a roll command. Occasionally you can blow something up in the background, usually lanterns and sometimes specific urns, but for the most part that's it. This is improved somewhat with the generally very competent AI, which will attempt to use their superior numbers against you, flanking, dodging attacks, or constantly backing up so they can continue tossing infinite numbers of spears. And finally you have boss fights, when all have their own little quirks to keep them interesting; Apollo shuts off the lights, forcing you to sacrifice your shield for a torch, or else blindly fumble in the dark, Artemis takes turns hunting and being hunted by you, Poseidon attacks your ship at sea, knocking it around trying to knock you overboard, and various monster bosses have their own weaknesses and tactics. This is all well and good, but the combat fumbles a bit with the the combination of an absurd number of weapons at your disposal, and a cumbersome method of switching weapons on the fly, which leaves you vulnerable as you frantically scroll through your six different clubs to reach the hammer you want to use. The Dodge button is also rather finicky, with enemies often hitting you regardless of your efforts to dodge attacks. At the end of the day though, this is a beautiful game, with a wonderful world, with mostly entertaining combat and a mildly lackluster story. In short, I would give this game a 8/10, and a hearty recommendation.

Ingame you have a health and a sanity level, hiding in the darkness decreases your sanity but makes it harder for monsters to spot you, staying near light or lighting your lantern stops your sanity from decreasing but allows monsters to easily spot you, solving puzzles and progressing increases your sanity if you have lost any, but looking at monsters decreases it as well. Once you have gone completely insane you break down on the floor and can't move for a few seconds, this makes it incredibly easy for monsters to get you if there are any around, after getting up again your sanity will be restored to the best possible level. Being hit by a monster or environmental hazard decreases your health which can be refilled with Laudanum, a chemical you can rarely find ingame. Besides Laudanum there are multiple other things you can find, those things include tinderboxes, which can be used to light light sources, notes, which can be read, oil, which can be used to refill your lantern, and various other, mostly puzzle related items. The monsters wander around the levels searching for you, they are attracted by light and sounds, so you should be quiet and avoid lights around them. You'll know when they're around though thanks of the grotesque noises they make. If they spot you they start chasing you, so you better hide quickly because they're faster than you as well! There's also another type of monster that behaves completely different than the others, which you'll have to find for yourself if you do decide to play the game!
The gameplay mechanics above result in the game being hard but balanced, you can hide in the dark but if you stay there for too long you'll have to suffer the consequences, using your lantern gives you a mobile but limited light source which can be turned off if necessary, but staying near a light source lit by a tinderbox or a natural light source will not consume your precious oil but could put you in a more dangerous situation. While there are a lot of parts where these horrifying creatures hunt you, sadly there are also a lot of boring parts where not all that much is happening, it would've probably been better if the different creatures appeared more often, especially during puzzles, although that could just be me.
Another thing that this game is quite popular for is its amazing physics engine which allows you to interact with almost any object by either taking and throwing it around (small objects), by pushing/pulling it (larger objects) or by opening/closing it (doors and drawers). This results in many precious items being hidden behind a few barrels or inside a drawer and is required in many puzzles. Additionally throwing a box at a monster can give you precious seconds in an intense chase as it stuns the monster for a short period of time.
The story is very deep and interesting and I never skipped a note thinking it would not be worth my time reading the note. The notes generally explain the story very well and pretty much everything is explained throughout the game. I won't go into much detail describing the story itself as that would ruin the fun in exploring it yourself, the store page already provides the necessary story elements. There are three different endings.
Atmosphere is probably one of the strongest elements of this game, not only will the soundscape give you goosebumps but the tension you feel when being chased by a monster or the fear you feel when a monster is walking by is unmet by any other game I've played.
The puzzles are always challenging and interesting and solving them feels satisfying. Especially good are the puzzles you have to solve while monsters are around, these puzzles, besides the atmosphere, are one of the greatest elements in Amnesia. While the puzzles are definitely not easy they are never unsolvable and never break the immersion, you'll always have an idea of what you have to do and if not then a little looking around will give you the hint you need.
While the graphics are definitely dated they are still quite acceptable and especially the light effects look very nice. The monsters look disgusting and really give you the creeps.
The price of 19.99€ totally justifies the average completion time of 10 hours, especially considering the general quality of the game in addition to the free "Justine" DLC and the "Remember" story collection (both of which I will take a look at later) packed with the game. Besides that, due to the freely available in-house HPL 2 engine which the game uses, players are able to create and distribute custom storys which others can download and play, these are officially supported and can be loaded ingame, this allows for infinite horror!
(spoilers ahead)
The DLC is quite different from the main game, it is much more linear and it doesn't have the same atmosphere as the main game, nonetheless it is still interesting and the fact that you can't save the game at all is a nice twist, even though it is still not that hard to beat considering the average playtime of 30 minutes. While the atmosphere is not that good the last chase scene with the third suitor Malo de Vigny (who wants to eat your flesh btw) is definitely the most intense moment in the whole game which will definitely have you drenched in sweat at the end!
While the monsters in the main game only emit animalistic noises the three suitors can speak and despite them having the same model they all have a different personality. The three prisoners have their own personality as well as a story which Justine explains after you've decided their fate.
Remember is a story collection containing 5 stories that explain the backstory of Amnesia a bit more, they are nicely illustrated and while it is probably not interesting to a majority of players it is definitely a nice read if you are interested in the story of the game. I think it would've been able to reach a broader audience if it was slightly animated and narroated or even turned into small levels like some flashbacks in the main game but I understand that that probably would've required too much effort to be worth it.

Zeus really is kind of a windbag. Now we can add yet another incident to his already long list of misdeeds. By his decree, the gods have turned their back on humanity essentially condemning it to oblivion. Someone ought to pull that lightning bolt out of his butt one of these days. But humanity has a wildcard in the form on Nikandreos who, with a little assistance from Hera, ascends to Mount Olympus to confront the gods and Zeus himself face to face. Not all gods agree with their King and will be more than happy to help you out, but you’ll also face some of them in direct combat.
Apotheon is a 2D side-scrolling action adventure game with open-ended design. The first thing that you will undoubtedly notice is the fantastic art style, it basically looks like a playable ancient Greek vase. It’s a game that is always a pleasure to look at. Most of the game has a wonderful orange tone, but some areas use a different color palette. For example, the forest of Artemis takes on a greenish hue whereas Poseidon’s realm is sensibly blue. The visual style is very well complimented by an appropriate soundtrack. The sense of atmosphere is heightened further with excerpts from classic Greek literature most notably Homer’s Illiad.
Nikandreos can wield an extremely wide assortment of weapons and use a ton of varying gear. Aside from classic melee weapons of the era such as swords, spears, clubs and maces, you can also use ranged weapons such as arrows (of which there are multiple types), discs and small oil containers that serve as bombs. You can also use shields and set up traps. There are even some mystical weapons that summon skeletons or wild animals to fight at your side. It all contributes to a varied and emergent combat system. However, the mechanics and the controls aren’t as tight as you want them to be in a game like this. You want pinpoint precision in combat and platforming and Apotheon is definitely lacking in that area. It all feels a bit loose, a bit clunky even.
The level design is really good, there are plenty of areas and they are all quite large and filled with different kinds of loot and secrets. There are also various segments that are a bit on the short side, but they definitely add to the variety. For example, there’s a combat sequence which enables you to fight on horseback, there are multiple swimming and diving areas (one even offered the ability to ride a seahorse). Also, encountering each boss either in combat, puzzle or mini-game is not only different, but is built around that particular god. For example, Artemis and Nikandreos exchange turns where one is the hunter and the other a deer until one hunts down the other whereas Dionysus requires Nikandreos to get drunk at his party.
Even though the gameplay mechanics and controls could use a lot of fine-tuning, Apotheon is a genuinely great game with a lot of variety. It looks amazing, the game world is a joy to explore and it remains thoroughly interesting throughout.
8 OUT OF 10 (GREAT)

I'm going to break this review down into parts.
Gameplay:  Ok.

Fear level: Pretty good.
I found Amnesia The Dark Descent to be scarier as well as Outlast.  Amnesia: Machine for Pigs wasn't as scary as this.
Storyline:  OMFG it's great.
Now this is the reason to play SOMA.   The story here is like partly a fantastic sci fi story concerning what it means to be human.  Part post-apocalypse, and part Twilight Zone.  I don't want to reveal too much but if you enjoy sci-fi/horror that really makes you think, this is the game for you.

Well... kind of.
I'd like to get in a long review and explain point by point, but what I really wanna do is to get people to play this and the dev taking into account what I feel was literally a bad idea. The game DESERVES to be played, as it is really cute and funny, but there are things inexplicably flawed in the design. I hope subsequent versions or even successive games will stray away from these things, as they really hinder the fun of the core game.
Pro:
- it's a nice change of pace from the standard VN, it feels more like a sort of long campaign of Punch-out sometimes ahah, or even some kind of Streets of Rage: Teen Story Edition... well you get the drift. The action part is funny.
- menu music is awesome. Soundtrack all over the game is quite cool. But what about all those noises? We'll get on that later.
- artstyle is cute! Animations are cool, and the artswell. It is simplistic but detailed enough to be enjoyable, and man, what can I say... I wish I could be Red for just one day, she literally shapeshifts inside that suit and becomes totally different from when she's in front of the mirror... but it's all part of the camouflage! XD
- happenings are... realistic. But we'll get on this later.
Con and somewhat-con:
- one of the biggest flaws I found on this is about the reputation system: it is literally faulty. What does it represents? It's not even hinting at a good thing, it makes you seem like you have to build reputation for Honey Rose, to get her sponsorship and let her go all the way to the top, but eventually drops if your parents scold you? Or if you fail to raise suspicion? What the hell? About that meter, aswell.
Suspicion meter: that's exactly how the reputation meter should work. It stays up even after days and does not drop except in rare circumstances. Seems more logical here and I don't get why it was easier to build a "punishment" meter than a guidance one. It really made me infuriating.
- another HUGE con was about the random events. I get that it was to get some replayability, and even fake the "randomness" of life, but really, how unfunny it is to miss one cutscene or some cute dialogue option because we hadn't time to keep checking in certain locations over and over again? Or refused to reload repeatedly?
I liked a lot Nolwenn, actually I was pairing Rose with her in my mind and I'd liked a bit of atleast friendship between them developed but... well. Debug mode says I was in scene 9 with her, and so no cutscene whatsover except that one with Isabelle. It kind of feels weird after the Leslie one.
- the ending: to let the player feel the weight of everything, I think there are a bit of overdramatizatez moments. I feel like the game could benefit from a lighter take from Rose, since until then she was a balanced, preppy individual. I felt like playing almost another character the last days, not only for the gloomy dialogues (some of them were really infuriating) but because some reactions were literally deliberately idiot. Could be a personal point, but I tried watching it from a writer's perspective (I do that for work) and it just miss the mark so much. It kind of deluded me, I'll be blunt.
Now, for the almost-con part:
- the action part could be so much more used. I mean, I get the spirit of the game, but man, wished there would be more matches and it would be more developed, I'm a sucker for these 2D street brawlers!
- the noises with character's reactions. What the hell? I get it was to make it a bit more cartoonish, but there are a couple ones (namely: when people get mad and they "whistle") which are sooo obnoxious... and they are also a lot louder than normal volume, so they really stick out. A con for me.
- artsyle is cool and somewhat consistent... I only found Red's fighting model to be a bit less "curved" of what we see on the mirror when changing outfits... but it's okay, although I would have preferred red's fighting model to be reflected in the mirror. She's a fighter, not a Barbie! Show those muscles :D
- one of the two REAL problem: dialogues. While happenings are somewhat realistic, what makes them feel a bit less realistic is the dialogues. They are written weirdly, they look half-way through your average teen-book and something out of an american movie. A bit cliched, but also a lot unrealistic in some parts, like the parts where your parents talk about sending you to another school as a punishment. The father even laughs that she's being sent. Either he's a psychopath or he's faking everytime we see him getting back home. Someone will be appeased by the cynic writing though, I guess. I like more realistic ones, but it's ok.
All in all I had FUN playing it, and maybe I raised expectations way too high, since everything looks really good, but I think the development took a very long while, and things changed throughout the course of it. I can't know for sure, but one can literally see one point where the development took a darker turn of events, leading to what the game is now.
It is however fun, and even a possible spring for thoughts.
If I get some money soon, I'll be sure to drop something, it sure is a big project. I look forward to next games though, hoping to see more polished ideas!

Taking place in a world inspired by feudal Japan,
is the story of Kouichirou Nabatame. He is a skilled samurai and a member of the Kodokushi, but he abandons that order and his kingdom after becoming disillusioned with their needlessly violent tactics that kill innocent people. After raiding and burning down a village, he comes across a now orphaned girl named Chiyo. He decides to adopt her as his daughter and together they try to rebuild the village back to its former glory.
This game is a kinetic novel, a type of visual novel with no branching storylines. If you listen to all of the dialogue it should take no more than an hour and a half to read.
The art in the game is fairly good, though considering the short length of it there is not much of it. Still, what is in the game serves its purpose well.
I also enjoyed the fact that all of the characters are fully voiced in English. Even though not all of the acting was perfect, it is a laudable effort. I was a bit annoyed with some of the dialogue, though. Despite being in English, there is still the presence of bits of Japanese language in parts where it did not seem very appropriate such as the use of honorifics and words like "nee-chan."
The writing is where this game runs into some issues. I will say that the story at the beginning is an interesting premise and I was quite curious to see where the game would take it. Unfortunately, the answer is not very far. Perhaps because the game is so short there was simply not enough time to develop the story further and really go into details. What is in the game is far less interesting than the premise would have one believe. Most of the story is taken up by banal banter about the task of rebuilding the village or some family drama between Kouichirou and Chiyo. Because of the lack of development, these scenes are never interesting. I really wish the characters were developed a lot more as it could have resulted in a much more engaging story. Instead, Chiyo, for example, is written as little more than a tsundere. It is almost comical at some points, but the game plays it straight. It was difficult to take seriously.
Overall, though the art is decent, I found this game's interesting premise to be wasted on a story that never goes anywhere. It is just a disappointment to see good plot potential wasted. The game is short and free, but I feel there are better visual novel offerings out there if you are really curious.
A unique experience. Get it, now.

This game is a visual novel with beat 'em up game play. Their are 6 total stats you are trying to balance, 3 classes and 3 fighting stats. You can only choose to do one thing per day from a decent amount of options. The fighting is enjoyable and all moves are available from the start, you just need to know how to do them. I liked the story and characters, nothing too disappointing/impressive.
The fighting can become tedious with the amount of times people pick fights with you. Sometimes it feels like events are too random and make it feel like the player has very little control over what happens (e.g. getting sick right before an exam, getting caught out of class when you try to meet up with your friends). The actual randomness would be less than issue if the main character acknowledged that the events where not in their control, but instead the other characters just act like my stats didn't meet the required threshold.
The game is 4:3 and I had to set it to full screen every time on startup because the setting didn't save. The UI, along with some mechanics, need more explaining. I didn't even know i could get sick. You can only see the current month of activities so you cannot really plan for events that are planned for the beginning of a month. Some of the things on the calendar aren't labeled, so you can't tell if it is a match, exam, or meet up.
I encountered a few bugs. I somehow went too far right during a fight and went off screen, i couldn't see my character so i just held left until I got back on the screen. One of the enemies during a fight just stopped reacting to getting hit so i just mashed attack until something happened. During a cut scene, the game glitched and there where 2 Big Blues on the screen for a few seconds.
Overall, I liked this game and there really isn't any reason you shouldn't give it a shot unless you don't usually like these types of games.
The game is free, and you can support it by buying one of the DLC items.

Shallow and greatly unpractical gameplay. The PC version of this game looks like it was made for tablets. Coordinating your squad members' actions proved to be quite difficult and limited. Here are some features of the game:
Your tactical options for each soldier in a turn are:
-Moving the soldier (you can set multiple waypoints and also choose between moving quickly or carefully);
-Choosing on each waypoint where the soldier will be looking at;
-Telling the soldier to hold his position;
-Using the soldiers' special ability;
-Checking intel on the enemy.
So far, your options are quite limited, but that is not inherently bad. Sometimes, a small array of options may be backed up by a great gaming experience. Now that's this game's undoing.
The AI is almost as smart as real person... if said person was blindfolded and told to find a way out of a maze made of death lasers that made noise so they could still be avoided... and even so the person decided to run and hug death.
Coordinating your team's actions proved to be quite the challenge when you can't even tell one of your soldiers to take another soldier's position; you can't tell them to hold fire or to focus one specific enemy; if you tell a soldier move up to a door, he will immediatelly open it! Now THAT'S some real tactical decision right there, phew.
Did you make a mistake while placing one of your waypoints? No problem! You just need to press the undo button and remove every subsequent waypoint you had set untill you delete the single one that was wrong... and now place them all again! (I guess the game does that so you don't lose track of what you had in mind...)
Every time you select a unit, your camera moves up to them, which is simply annoying. You then have to keep moving your camera all over the place because it seems like the game wants you to have full awareness of your team.
"Juarez? You selected Juarez? Here he is, look! Look closer! See? That's Juarez! Want him to move over there? Okay! Lawrence too? Good! But let us just take a look at him! Oh my, how well positioned he is right here! Now go move your camera back!"
This game is quite good for on-the-go casual gaming, but definitely NOT for someone who's looking for some real squad-tactics game. The tactics you employ to win this game are basically, in order of priority: 1-Put soldier behind cover; 2- If enemy is still alive, throw grenade; 3-Win game.
The soundtrack is good, it fits in nicely.
The graphics are fine, nothing to complain about.
The camera movement is "meh". In addition to what's been already mentioned above, sometimes the action camera is badly positioned and you can't really see what's going on, but that's not gamebreaking.
The real problem is charging US$15 for a game that seems poorly optimised for PC and with little replay value. Frozen Synapse costs roughly less than two times this price but brings you four times more entertainment.
Luckily I got this through Humble Bundle though, phew!

Breach & Clear benefits greatly from the same game design that many smartphone games these days profit from; simplistic design, addictive gameplay, and tons of replay value.
Starting out, you can design a four-man team from your Tier-1 unit of choice, including US Navy SEALs, British SAS, Canadian JTF, Russian Spetsnaz, and more. You choose a preset face for each team member, from about 20 preset faces, and then you select their role in the unit; team leader, breacher, intelligence, medic, etc. Each unit gives a special stat bonus (the Spetsnaz give two bonuses), and each role has unique skills that benefit the team, such as the ability to throw a grenade and move in the same turn, to revive allies, or to draw the fire of all nearby enemies so your teammates can move safely. The customization continues as you level up your characters, allowing you to upgrade their skills as you would in a regular RPG, increasing their hit points, accuracy, etc., as you see fit. The final touches on your team comes in the form of gear, such as helmets, that can add health to the wearer, various vests that differ in weight (which affects movement speed) and health bonus, weapons (the game includes a large arsenal of automatic rifles, shotguns, submachineguns, etc. to fit any role.. and oh yea, you can customize those too), and finally cosmetic stuff such as face paint and the clothing that your operator wears. Hell, just playing around with the customization in this game can be very impressive, but naturally the fun doesn't really start until you starting breaching doors.
Breach & Clear scenarios are divided into the standard kill scenario, where you must breach a location and kill all of the targets, a bomb defusal scenario, where you must breach the location, find the bomb(s) and then protect the bomb while it is being diffused, and then an escape and evade scenario where your team is already in the thick of it, and you need to help them fight their way out of there. All three modes are available right off the bat, with higher difficulties unlocking as you receive stars for completing missions quickly, and with minimal casualties.
In order to accomplish each mission successfully, you must effectively utilize your moves/turns, which are commands that decide the actions of your teammates in 5 second intervals, and the general goal of each turn is to do as much damage to the enemy as you can, while taking as little damage in return. Naturally, you can choose to run and gun willy-nilly on lower difficulties, but higher difficulties, and the later missions, require effective teamwork within your unit, utilizing tactics such as covering fire, taking advantage of flash bangs and grenades, and properly clearing rooms in a way that covers all of the corners. In the end, what you have is the satisfaction of planning out the perfect raid, followed by the even more satisfying task of watching the assault play out, and then finally basking in your own excellence as you successfully clear an entire compound of terrorists in under a minute, without getting so much as a splinter from the door you just blew up to take out the first three terrorists you came across.
Sure, the game is repetitive, you don't think actual Special Operators grow tired of clearing the same kill house for the 1,000th time? The break in the monotony comes when you change tactics, when enemies decide to spawn in new places (yea, enemies change spawn locations), or when you decide to change the kit for your team. Want to go all-out stealth, with no armor and silence weapons? Go ahead. Want to go loud, with heavy armor, helmets, shotguns and machine guns? Feel free. So really, the monotony only comes from a lack in creativity. There are tons of ways to go about tackling every single mission in this game, just remember; slow is smooth, and smooth is fast.
Right now, I give this game a solid 9/10, but I would certainly love to see some stuff added to the game to make it even more awesome.
Hopes for future updates:
More military units to choose from (MoH: Warfighter definitely got this right)
A wider range of weapons beyond just rifles and a couple of submachineguns, shotguns and a sniper rifle.
More breach options, please. No bang and clear? Prybar? Having a class that can breach through a wall would be awesome as well (Again, Warfighter covered these very well)
Hostage/VIP rescue missions (grab and extract, or escort)
Stealth missions

Very seriously the best Star Wars game and one of the best PC RPGs of all time.
You don't have to have played the first Knights of the Old Republic to follow what's going on here, but if you did, you'll notice that when Obsidian took the license from Bioware they put out a game that just viciously dunks all over its predecessor. It's damn near disrespectful how much better KOTOR 2 is.
KOTOR 2 freely gives away things that would qualify as major plot twists in the first game because its most important reveals are so much grander. It repeats archetypes from the first game and sometimes even grabs characters themselves from the first and says "hold my beer; THIS is how to write them correctly." I'm on my fourth play through (I'd played it twice before Steam existed) and I'm *still* discovering new things because there's just that much depth. Where the first KOTOR told your typical humdrum legendary hero Bioware story with "moral choice" amounting to being a boy scout or orphan-murderer, KOTOR 2 goes deeper. Is light always right? Can dark-sided actions be morally necessary? Are there unintended repercussions to simple acts of charity and kindness? Is anything worth believing in or fighting for?
You don't *have* to delve into these questions. You can play it straight forward and ignore so much of the dialogue and character development if you really want. You can speed from start to finish obliterating enemies with Force Lightning and ignore every hint of story. But KOTOR 2 will gladly reward you for the time and attention you put into it. And it's so very worth it.

The start of the game is very fun, there's lots of exciting things to do and the game appears to have great potential and the game appears to be extremely deep... first impressions of this game are very good. However, after the early-game, the economy becomes unworkable, your businesses grow so complex that they become unmanagable, and the AI factions will be rising up the courts because of regular mouse glitches making you bribe the wrong people.
The economy system is completely broken. The map will always run out of raw resources unless you (the AI will never do this) set up a business to harvest them yourself, but this costs huge amounts of money to set up - money which you do not have in the early game. As you supply raw ingredients to the market, other factions make use of this raw resource and generate huge profits from very little investment on their part. And even though you have a monopoly on a raw resource, you have no control over the price at which you sell that resource.
The mouse controls regularly glitch, which can be extremely frustrating when you're in court and you have to click and bribe the correct NPCs in a very short time limit. Also, as your businesses begin to grow, you will need to start automating the management of your buildings - this automation is very primitive and is very glitchy and frustrating to set up. Also.. there's no pause... the game just runs very, very slowly...?
The more time you invest into this game, the more you realise how broken it is. This game isn't worth your time.

I started with GPS3 and I don't even want to know how many hours I have into it. I played the hell out of it. GPS4 is basically GPS3 with a recolored/rearranged GUI and a couple new features such as playing as a terrorist organization and city battles, both of which are IMHO unfulfilling. There are a couple extra DLC's which IMHO are worth it. And a couple new cheat codes (Alberteinsteinisalive! and Iamthearchitect!) for fast research and fast building.
Playing as a terrorist is pretty difficult to say the least, and you can only create left leaning terrorist organizations. You can not ban the democrat party, you can not even delete the democrat party in the editor, but every other party you can. Overall it just wasn't very fun for me.
CIty battles are, let's just say, tedious. It can be overwhelming enough just managing your normal military units, but to directly micromanage your military inside cities is just too much for me.
As for the overall game, I play this game for it's depth and it's expansiveness. It is a political game, but it's also an economics game, and a war game, and it delves quite deep into each subject. Deeper than any game that specializes in even just one of those subjects. The depth of this game is not comparable to any other game out there, and I can't emphasize that enough. But, it is buggy as all hell and downright frustrating at times. It will crash. It will freeze. It will hang. The map will disappear and bug out. It will give incorrect stats and do weird things it shouldn't do. But it's worth it. I wish the game weren't that way, but it's a one of a kind game and you have to put up with it because you can't get this experience anywhere else.
I have a rather high-end PC, 8-core overclocked watercooled CPU, 4gb 290x graphics, and the game runs good except when wars occur. Large, extensive wars will make the game unplayable no matter what computer you have. I don't know if it's a flaw in the game engine or simply the over-saturation of military units, but I manage to make it work (for the most part) by commanding my military and then leaving the military view to increase the framerate and it works for smaller wars but if other countries start joining in then time will come to a halt, and it will eventually freeze or crash, if not both. Which is disappointing. But I've still managed to annex over half the world... so it's still fun.
Normally I would condemn a game with so many issues, and I do condemn this game for it but I have to leave a positive review simply because I still enjoy the game, It's frustrating as hell sometimes but I enjoy it for hours on end and there is no other game like it. Nothing even comes close.

While this game takes a little too long to get challenging, it’s very worth it once you get past level 30 or so.  Hang in there and you’ll find yourself quite entertained with this low priced gem.

Ingame you have a health and a sanity level, hiding in the darkness decreases your sanity but makes it harder for monsters to spot you, staying near light or lighting your lantern stops your sanity from decreasing but allows monsters to easily spot you, solving puzzles and progressing increases your sanity if you have lost any, but looking at monsters decreases it as well. Once you have gone completely insane you break down on the floor and can't move for a few seconds, this makes it incredibly easy for monsters to get you if there are any around, after getting up again your sanity will be restored to the best possible level. Being hit by a monster or environmental hazard decreases your health which can be refilled with Laudanum, a chemical you can rarely find ingame. Besides Laudanum there are multiple other things you can find, those things include tinderboxes, which can be used to light light sources, notes, which can be read, oil, which can be used to refill your lantern, and various other, mostly puzzle related items. The monsters wander around the levels searching for you, they are attracted by light and sounds, so you should be quiet and avoid lights around them. You'll know when they're around though thanks of the grotesque noises they make. If they spot you they start chasing you, so you better hide quickly because they're faster than you as well! There's also another type of monster that behaves completely different than the others, which you'll have to find for yourself if you do decide to play the game!
The gameplay mechanics above result in the game being hard but balanced, you can hide in the dark but if you stay there for too long you'll have to suffer the consequences, using your lantern gives you a mobile but limited light source which can be turned off if necessary, but staying near a light source lit by a tinderbox or a natural light source will not consume your precious oil but could put you in a more dangerous situation. While there are a lot of parts where these horrifying creatures hunt you, sadly there are also a lot of boring parts where not all that much is happening, it would've probably been better if the different creatures appeared more often, especially during puzzles, although that could just be me.
Another thing that this game is quite popular for is its amazing physics engine which allows you to interact with almost any object by either taking and throwing it around (small objects), by pushing/pulling it (larger objects) or by opening/closing it (doors and drawers). This results in many precious items being hidden behind a few barrels or inside a drawer and is required in many puzzles. Additionally throwing a box at a monster can give you precious seconds in an intense chase as it stuns the monster for a short period of time.
The story is very deep and interesting and I never skipped a note thinking it would not be worth my time reading the note. The notes generally explain the story very well and pretty much everything is explained throughout the game. I won't go into much detail describing the story itself as that would ruin the fun in exploring it yourself, the store page already provides the necessary story elements. There are three different endings.
Atmosphere is probably one of the strongest elements of this game, not only will the soundscape give you goosebumps but the tension you feel when being chased by a monster or the fear you feel when a monster is walking by is unmet by any other game I've played.
The puzzles are always challenging and interesting and solving them feels satisfying. Especially good are the puzzles you have to solve while monsters are around, these puzzles, besides the atmosphere, are one of the greatest elements in Amnesia. While the puzzles are definitely not easy they are never unsolvable and never break the immersion, you'll always have an idea of what you have to do and if not then a little looking around will give you the hint you need.
While the graphics are definitely dated they are still quite acceptable and especially the light effects look very nice. The monsters look disgusting and really give you the creeps.
The price of 19.99€ totally justifies the average completion time of 10 hours, especially considering the general quality of the game in addition to the free "Justine" DLC and the "Remember" story collection (both of which I will take a look at later) packed with the game. Besides that, due to the freely available in-house HPL 2 engine which the game uses, players are able to create and distribute custom storys which others can download and play, these are officially supported and can be loaded ingame, this allows for infinite horror!
(spoilers ahead)
The DLC is quite different from the main game, it is much more linear and it doesn't have the same atmosphere as the main game, nonetheless it is still interesting and the fact that you can't save the game at all is a nice twist, even though it is still not that hard to beat considering the average playtime of 30 minutes. While the atmosphere is not that good the last chase scene with the third suitor Malo de Vigny (who wants to eat your flesh btw) is definitely the most intense moment in the whole game which will definitely have you drenched in sweat at the end!
While the monsters in the main game only emit animalistic noises the three suitors can speak and despite them having the same model they all have a different personality. The three prisoners have their own personality as well as a story which Justine explains after you've decided their fate.

This game is wonderfully atmospheric and I recommend everyone play some of it. It's one of the best examples of Lovecraftian horror in video games, but it is deeply flawed.
The first few hours is spooky as hell and I enjoyed every minute of it, my problem with the game is that once the monsters actually show up, I find myself bored to death. The one off sections like the water monster are great, but the default abomination is all about tediously hiding from it as it walks in circles until it gets bored and walks away. The first encounter with it is terrifying, but as you realize this is the "default enemy" it loses its novelty.
Amnesia's gameplay loop is a mix of exploration, puzzle solving, and light stealth. The stealth is a really weak link here, especially if you've played Alien: Isolation, which is basically the same game, but absolute perfection. If you're someone who doesn't play a lot of stealth games, it might not bother you, but if you're a fan of the genre, you're probably going to quit when I did.

I think there is little question that if you enjoy survival horror that's not awash in blood and guts and also value a coherent (even pretty dang good) story of Cthulu-mythos oddity, Amnesia is just for you. The developers wisely recommend not to play Amnesia to 'beat' it. Amnesia is mean't as an experience. Having a healthy curiosity will make the experience that much more memorable. So i say - Amnesia is not to be played - its to be experienced.

Apotheon is a fun 2D platformer with a beautiful ancient greek pottery aesthetic. The story follows Nikandreos - a champion of humanity - who rises up against the Greek Gods to steal their powers and salvage the fate of his people. As Nikandreos, you will scale Mount Olympus and challenge the Gods in their respective realms.
+ Apotheon's gameplay is quite solid, with plenty of interesting melee and ranged weaponry (historically-accurate ones included) to choose from, making for healthy variation in playing style.
+ Great attention to detail is also displayed in level and character design, with each in-game location having a different feel and plenty of variation in the appearances of both NPCs and enemies.
+ The music accompanies the game well and gives it great atmosphere, particularly during epic god fights. The lyre pieces, in particular, gives the game an elegant touch.
+ The storyline is average with a cliché god-usurper plot. Nevertheless, it is well-executed.
+ Game length is pretty substantial, well worth its price tag.
+ A healthy level of appearance customization is available for the hero, from leather caps to wolf pelts to the iconic corinthian helmet.
However,
- Combat is slightly flimsy as attacks are completely mouse-dependent and can be annoyingly difficult to control when Nikandreos is surrounded by enemies, which happens fairly often.
- The variety of actions available during melee combat is lacking, being limited to the usual stab or an upwards/overhead swing.
- On a personal note, the amount of armor sets available for Nikandreos pales in comparison to the wide variety possessed by the NPCs, leaving something to be desired for a game so heavily focused on attaining excellent visuals.
Overall, Apotheon is a good game with a composition of 55% style 45% gameplay. Its form similar to the pottery art it emulates: carefully crafted and artistically flavorful. A definite must-try if you dig its aesthetic and love classical history; a worth-trying if you're looking to play a fresh platformer.

I love this game unconditionally. I study history at my university, and I love Ancient Greece especially, and I could not stop geeking out over this game. It looks gorgeous, the story is great, and it is one of the most faithful approaches to the Greek myths I've ever seen. On top of that, it's damn fun. Athena's Labyrinth was probably my favorite zone, with all the cool skill challenges, but I was also a fan of the Underworld. The music and lighting down in Hades sometimes made me feel legitimately uneasy, and crossing the River Lethe was slow and tense without being frustrated. My only complaint is that the controls can be a bit sluggish when fighting, which is a bit of a problem in a platformer. Even then, combat made me feel like a badass. I should note, however, that I only played with an XBox controller, so a keyboard and mouse may be quicker and more precise. Other than that, no complaints. As a historian and lover of myth who loves to nitpick, I only noticed two historically inaccurate things: In the game, the sarissa can be held one-handed and thrown, and the pelta is carried on the arm. Besides the fact that these weapons were introduced in Macedonia several centuries after when this game seems to be set, the sarissa required two hands to use, and the pelta (which was invented to be used with the sarissa) was slung over the shoulder. But I digress. Long story short, play this game. Great story, great music, great history, and all-around fun.

Despite its lack of interactivity, Wander No More is a well crafted Kinetic Novel. Although its plot isn't the most thrilling or unpredictable, its topics are presented tastefully and make up a short story that can be picked up readily at leisure.
The beautiful character models and soft backgrounds in muted colours form a cohesive outstanding art style. The softened features of the male protagonist, as well as some of the male voice acting, may seem a little odd before getting used to it though. Similar to afternoon anime, the voice actors sound energetic and lively and despite the thick American accent, the pronunciation of the Japanese names and words are better than expected. The visuals and audio don't overpower the story that is told but establish an ambience that subtly promotes the narrative. Especially the background music is thematically fitting and never disturbing.
For a change, Wander No More is not a translated novel. Even though, or rather since the story itself doesn't cause any surprises and can be quickly summed up in two sentences, the good quality of the writing manages to keep up the readers interest.
Wander No More is an altogether pleasant, albeit a little lightweight, read.

I recently tried this novel.
It's not an actual game in the traditional sense of the word, but more of a story that unfolds on your screen, as you click through the dialogue and scenes (so there's no interaction whatsoever).
I found the art style very appeasing (especially the backgrounds; i.e. forest), though I needed some time to grow fond of it at first.
This is mostly because the character design is rather effeminate (which isn't necessarily a bad thing, but it didn't really fit the story completely).
This story has to do with samurai (i.e. skilled fighters), and the way they were portrayed in this novel was rather unbelievable.
Like, effeminate young adults (with nasty attitudes) trying to be skilled swordfighters.
Because of this, it's a little difficult to feel fully immersed and take some of the characters seriously.
So I found this aspect of the novel quite glamorized and idealized. Some people may like it, while others may not take well to this.
I fall somewhere inbetween. Though I honestly prefer a certain consistency between what a character looks like, and their role within a story.
I did enjoy this novel nonetheless thanks to the music and the plot and how it was written. The voice acting wasn't too bad either. It sounded good enough. I found the female characters sounding more natural than the male ones though.
There was some (unnecessary) repetition in the dialogues (here and there), and a bit of exaggeration (in regard to the description of the main male protagonist and his skills) but nothing too bad.
The chemistry between the two main characters made up for this. There's something about the female characters that really helped adding value to this novel (at least, for me).
One thing that did impress me was how the voice actors pronounced the Japanese names. That was quite beautiful! :). It sounded phonetically correct, and it didn't sound as corny as I feared it might.
I'm glad this novel was offered for free. It was good enough for me!

Firstly it's important to note that contrary to its advertising and the game's intro, Breach & Clear is not a simulation. The game has more in common with call of duty scenarios than real life counter terrorism operations. Soldiers acquire perks and weapons are only effective a fraction of the range of their real life counter parts. It would also be hard to argue that the soldier classes bear much in common with real life soldier roles instead displaying strange attributes like the intelligence specialist's ability to disappear.
The combat itself is fast paced and interesting. It doesn't often feel cheap except when your squad isn't leveled enough to tackle a map. There aren't any game breaking flaws in the combat system  which is more than most tactical level turn based combat games can boost. The game offers incentives to use fire and movement realistically and the ability to flank and suppress means the player has to keep their team on the move. Perma death thankfully can be enabled which gives a lot more weight to the player's decisions. The game uses a WEGO system for the turns but you'll hardly notice because the AI doesn't move around much.
Enemy classes don't offer huge variation but they do provide enough to allow the designers to create some interesting tactical puzzles. Heavily armoured soldiers can cause your team serious trouble if they can close with them and snipers obviously operate at the other end of the spectrum.
The graphics are quite nice with your soldiers displaying the weapons and gear you issued them with. Everything is clear and easy to interpret except some more obvious fog of war would be nice so players would be provided with some idea of which areas had been cleared. The spotting system is balls, soldiers can see through walls and some items completely negate the fog of war completely. This game certainly could have taken a few lessons from the original Xcom in that department.
The level design is often pretty good but the game's original platform holds it back. Maps are too small and quite clearly were designed with short playtimes in mind. They get better as the game goes on but it feels a bit strange that multi story buildings are absent and the game's attempts to emulate this by making assaults on large buildings take up multiple missions doesn't really feel convincing. The game modes provided are Terrorist hunt, bomb diffusal and escape which are all pretty much self explanatory. They all change up the maps slightly but in the long term aren't enough to keep things from going stale. Bomb diffusal maps feature the ever annoying enemy reinforcement spawns that are the bane of several srpgs but within the context of this game they work extremely well and give the mode a bit more tension.
The game tries to keep the player's interest by offering what seems at first to be extensive customization options, but realistically half the weapons and gear offered aren't ever really going to come in useful. The outfitting screen could also do with some work as no indication is given how prospective weapon and gear purchases differ from what is already equipped(unless you click back through some menus). Unequipping all the modifications off a weapon can be quite tedious as well.
Besides tactical combat, the game doesn't offer much else and what's there feels somewhat lacking. The potential of the system is never fully explored because the maps never really get that big and the squad size stays at four men. Insertion methods never change with rappling and helicopter assaults never making an appearance. This lack of variation results in the game getting a bit stale after a while.
It can feel a bit half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at times too with some design choices(no ability to use smoke is the most glaring one)leading to the player's units taking unavoidable damage in some situations.
That said fire and movement in the title generally works well and dumb tactics are often punished. The market isn't exactly swimming in squad level turn based strategy games so this is a welcome addition.
The main downside is that there is no OST included in this version.

Even though I think Quake is a better game, Quake II is still one of my favorite shooters of all time and one that I played constantly as a kid, putting many hundreds of hours into it on both singleplayer and multiplayer. I recommend grabbing the Quake2xp mod from modDB. The gameplay will stay the same as the original, but the game's visuals and effects are heavily updated to be more modern (there are a few glitches but nothing gamebreaking that I've seen). This is a game that really started pushing the genre into the modern days with enemies who could evade your attacks, levels that had you going to different areas and then backtracking to various "hubs" to proceed to new areas, etc. At the same time though it retains the classic id software gameplay of fast paced combat, lots of gibs, and no reloading.
If you've never played it, do yourself a favor and give it a try, it still holds up very well today.

-Chocolate Doom
Highly Accurate to the original DOS executable (bugs and limits included), while being a windows based port. Great for a more authentic experience without the hassle of Dosbox.
-PrBoom+
Raises the static limitations of the original, options for Modern screen resolutions/OpenGL, and  includes support for the boom/MBF formats. Most maps for these formats are still generally traditional with the gameplay. Compatibility levels for different versions of doom make it good for demo playback.
-ZDoom/GZDoom
Numerous advanced features, and supports Heretic, Hexen, and Strife.  Mouselook and Jumping/Crouching are possible in this engine. Most mods for this tend to be less traditional with the gameplay, and often change things up a lot more. Great for those who want to play gameplay mods, and certain partial/total conversions.
-Odamex/Zandronum
These are basically multiplayer source ports with online capabilities. Odamex for a more traditional approach, and Zandronum for a more modern approach.

Honey Rose is an interesting idea that fortunately pays off.  It's part visual novel, part life sim and part 2D fighting game.  It'd be really easy for such a game to be a complete mess, but HR pulls it off masterfully.
You play as the eponymous Honey Rose, who's a University student whose dream is to become a masked wrestling star.  But, of course, her secret life as luchadora is endangered by her parents' ultimatum of graduation or moving to another town.  It's up to you as the player to help her balance her life to hopefully achieve both goals.
Gameplay is fun and a good balance between modes.  You have to help Honey both by correct decision making and good reflexes in a I-can't-believe-it-works marriage of usually completely disparate gameplay mechanics.  The game does a good job of easing you into it, and I give props for the excellent way options are displayed at the start.
Besides gameplay, the art style also has to be commended.  It's really appealing and not the cliche stuff you keep seeing in games of each genre.  I also have to give an applause for the fantastic idea for payment options.  Though I'd be happy to pay the price if they had decided to sell it normally.  It really is a fun game, and it's worth the time and money.  I've only played it for less than a couple of hours at the time of writing this review, but I can tell you right now I'm going to be spending a lot of time with it.

Geopolitical Simulator 4 aka Power and Revolution is the fourth instalment in the Geopolitical Simulator series.  Power and Revolution puts you in the shoes of the head of a state or a country with the focus of extending your influence on the world.
First of all, let me get this out of the way, Power and Revolution is not a good game in its current state. The game is a shadow of what it tries to be and utterly falls flat on its face. The game starts you off as the head of a particular country and then leaves you to control it.
You are given the options to increase/decrease taxes on various subjects like deforestation. Power and Revolution is not focused on taking over the world by force, though it gives you the option to do that. You have to try and increase the economic stability of your country by doing various deeds and slowly building up your nation.
You can make allies with various other nations, suppress uprisings which are common throughout the world and wage war against other countries. On paper it sounds like a run of the mill game which is supposed to have some real depth but it is executed really poorly. All of the systems felt like a ruse and most of my decisions felt like they were only to bring in more funds for the nation. The game tries to implicate many mechanics which do not actually affect anything.
While you’re at war with any nation, you can control your armies directly or decide to auto resolve it by leaving them on their own. The game’s interface is just so ugly that I never actually controlled my army. Icons clutter up the screens and there is quite a lot of visual noise at every given point which can easily distract any player.
The only good thing I found about Power and Revolution is the senator system. Your cabinet  in this game actually does some work and gives you advice on what will happen if a certain law is implemented or not. What does not work though is the fact that they never tell the long term side effects of a plan. This can easily leave you baffled in many situations and might as well force you to quit in latter game. Power and Revolution is also a very slow game and requires patience from you if you want to pull some enjoyment out of it.
The tutorial is very short and does not explain many of the mechanics included in the game and it is a drastic change going from the tutorial to a new game.
Power and Revolution is also riddled throughout with bugs. There were moments when it forced me to rage quit because some of the ridiculous decisions the AI made. There were constant crashes to desktop and it sometimes started lagging horribly for no apparent reason. And this is not a game which looks like it could ever lag. The loading times are longer than they should be and with the price tag the game has, it is just not worth it.

The game is truly one of a kind, there is no other game that does what this does in as much detail. Your literally a single politician (either President/PM or Opposition leader, or a terrorist/rebel/freedom fighter leader) and you have to keep on to/gain power. Once in the top job, everything is open to you. The game is a simulation of the worlds current economic, political and socio-cultural dimensions- with their problems and potential solutions all in their. You thus can literally try anything and see how it works when leading any country (or insurgency group) around the world. My personal favourite- Trying to turn Saudi Arabia into a secual, economically diverse and education/research driven regional power that has no public debt and extremely high standards of living for its people based on a socialist model (high pensions, high wages, lots of employment laws for protection, limited taxes on everything ranging from pets to deforestation to business turn with non-existent income taxes, subsidized by 'dat oil' and a buddy 'green-tech' industry)- its beautiful...and difficult.
At any turn something that goes against the current wishes of various factions of the people, pressure groups, religious groups, corporate intrests, bakers, lobby groups, Parliament or your own political party (or 'family' as a dictator) can land you in some serious trouble- before your either 'forced on holiday', exiled, lose an election, are shot or lose control of the country....then shot. So its very much a balancing act- With Saudi Arabia i found i had to move slowly, gather support through populist means and with every 'radical change' (particularly in regard to the power of religion over the state) i had to make sure i was prepared with either a powerful security service (love my spies), military back-up and a 'carrot' (reforms on minimum wage and the subsidization of the state relgion- before years later- removing that too). It makes for a very interesting game where sudden changes can literally cause chaos overnight- As Brazil i did a comprehensive series of economic reforms...polled individually they were recieved well supposedly by both Parliament and people- but as a massive group that wasn't staggered in terms of month or year when it came into force they caused major economic uncertainty and a loss of faith by the people- too radical- i was deposed (a common theme for me it seems :P).
Best thing ever- Take 'Gary Cimeron' (Or David Cameron *cough*) or Lisa Fay (Theresa May ahem..) and fulfil their deepest darkest wishes to be authoritarian dictators of the UK...and see if you can get their and stay their, so far more me...nope....But who knows, one day.
All in all, this game is complex, detailed and beautiful to play- there is no other game like it truly. It is expensive, but for my point of view (and again i haven't encountered any bugs or issues thus far) its well worth it.

After extensive play, I need to actually change my review and recommendation.  I'm going to do my best to keep my personal preferences from coloring my review and focus strictly on my observations and best hypotheses from a businessperson's point of view.
I'll include the caveat that I still enjoy playing this game from time to time, and in earlier iterations I absolutely loved it.  However, after learning more about the game, interacting with the community and seeing some of the developmental decisions being made, I have to safely say that I no longer recommend this game.  Here's why.
First, the development team.  While some of them are professional, I've found that this isn't the case for all of them.  I haven't had poor interactions with them personally, but I've seen them first-hand openly attack players for asking simple, reasonable questions, and they are generally rude.  They also appear to be unwilling to listen to suggestions from the community, and will readily ridicule players for not playing their game exactly how they intended (i.e. if you're not killing everything and everyone in sight, you're doing it wrong apparently).  Unfortunately, this doesn't bode well for the future of the game, as this will negatively affect consumers' view and experience.
Second is the fact that the public branch of the game is now the test version.  While I agree that this is a great way to obtain raw data for future improvements, I have a feeling it's going to turn away a large quantity of new players and veteran players alike.  The version out now is just too unstable and unbalanced to be enjoyable anymore.  Whereas I used to play hours each day, I maybe log in once a day or not at all - it's simply too frustrating and you are essentially forced into playing only about three dinosaurs of the choices that are available. Yes, I am aware that this is an Early Access game and bugs of all shapes and sizes are expected, but the game is almost downright unplayable (i.e. herbivores can't even eat on the most common map, and therefore can't heal or slowly starve to death) - I find the "Early Access" argument to not have much teeth in this case.
Third is the direction the game is heading.  Yes, it's essentially a super-hardcore survival game with only a small core audience in mind - that's what the developers want to do, which is their right.  But I have a very hard time seeing the long-term financial viability of this game with what they have in mind.  I understand they want to cater to only the hardest of the hardcore, but ultimately, the end product stands to be too complex and difficult for most people to want to play.  My prediction is that it will not be profitable.
These are just my two cents.  While it is a beautiful game with a lot of potential, my outlook for this game is rather bleak based on its current state.

Hook takes a simple puzzle idea and does it very well, it has you playing around with increasingly more complex circuits that control hooks and rods which must be removed in the correct order to remove every last hook in the level; a bit like pick-up sticks, just virtual, 2D, and with some actual thought, not just throwing stuff on the ground. Unlike pick-up sticks, this game is actually quite good.
The visuals and music are minimalist, but are not boring; in a way, they make it easier to concentrate on the game; the gameplay is interesting enough that interesting music and flashy visuals really just aren't needed.
Although the gameplay is quite simple, the puzzles are built in very interesting and challenging ways, especially towards the end.
Hook most definitely has an exponential learning curve, but this is core to making the game a challenging and fun experience; however, this means that for most of the first half-hour you will be solving very easy and obvious puzzles while new features are being slowly introduced. Towards the end you get very complex levels with tangles of lines that you have to think about a bit to be able to solve, these levels are the most fun IMO, and when it ended I just wanted infinitely more levels that I could play for ever and ever.
The small amount[of levels[50] is my only qualm with this game, however for the price this is quite reasonable. I do think that a level designer and community levels  are much needed additions however.
I would recommend this game, because the concept and the levels are extremely fun and rewarding to play through. For 79p this is absolutely worth picking up. However if  puzzle games aren't your thing, you probably wouldn't enjoy it it.

The game takes place almost entirely on Mt Olympus, and has you visit different areas. There are 2 main hub locations (Agora and Acropolis), and each one contains doorways to a number of other areas. Some of these areas belong to a specific deity, whilst others are just bonus locations. Most of the game's story involves you simply undertaking tasks for each Olympian deity and eventually confronting them one way or another.
This is not just a simple 2D platformer. The game has quite an open world and really knows how to reward exploration. There are tonnes of optional areas and hidden secrets, and a huge variety of weapons to collect, many of which are uniques. There's always some delicious surprise around a corner or behind a breakable wall. The gameplay is very reminiscent of the Metroid style games, so if you've ever enjoyed those, you should have a fun time with Apotheon as well.
Despite the enormous amount of fun I've had, I've also come across a lot of frustration, which was somewhat disappointing. As some people already pointed out, the combat, although fun and enjoyable, can be a bit tricky and awkward at times, because you have to time your swings really well. Not much of a problem most of the time, but it can be a nightmare when fighting fast moving enemies that either jump at you or fly around.
There were some parts of the game where frustration came mostly from controls, such as trying to quickly outclimb the fast-rising flames of river Phlegethon, but most times it was in the boss fights. Although some bosses were a fun challenge, a fair few were frustrating beyond belief and involved mechanics which did not make much sense, like Diomedes being completely invulnerable unless you've thrown a jar of blood at him to stun him, or Zeus somehow being weak to his own lightning bolts, but managing to shrug off blades, clubs, and fire like they were nothing.
Still, despite the frustrating sections, I've had a very fun playthrough. The music is also really fantastic and fits the areas perfectly. The most noteworthy one being the eerie track that plays in Hades. So for the most part, this is a really memorable and unique game. I would highly recommend you check it out if you've ever at least remotely enjoyed 2D platformers and sidescrollers.

It's hard not to recommend this game, and i feel it may be semi biased since I really think it did a lot of things right, however i think at the core of the game, I am just bored and have no desire to continue playing.
The music and atmosphere are there for sure, the voice acting is even pretty decent. But maybe this is just me, but the visual style was just not my thing.
