A simple but interesting logic "puzzle." If you enjoy solving puzzles like picross or sudoku you will probably like it. Essentially, you just set up the hooks so that the free ones will pull and the stuck ones will not pull. It's just a matter of checking to make sure everything is set up right before you click each time. If you like games where you just have to notice a pattern and click the right button, this is for you. Only the later 10-20 puzzles really make you have to concentrate, though.
It is very short. I finished it in probably about 40 minutes -- I have 1 hour play time but in the middle I did stop to eat dinner and make tea and left the game running. $1 for 40-60 minutes of puzzles may or may not be worth it to you -- considering you can find tons of puzzles with a similar feeling of satisfaction online for free, or buy something like a sudoku or picross book for a few dollars and get way more than 40 minutes of the same type of enjoyment from it, it's kind of steep. But $1 I feel was worth to support the developer, and hopefully they will be inspired to make similar games but with more levels.
The game teaches you how to play without language or tutorials, which is a very nice design. New concepts will be added slowly and give you time to fiddle with them to learn how they work without having to consult a guide or make too many errors.
The only complaint I really have is that the entire game is black on white. An inverted option (black background with grey hooks) would have been very nice. Or the ability to select colors yourself by simply editing RGB values or something. Simple menus would be nice. The developer said themselves they were simply too lazy to add a menu, though... So perhaps that is enough to convince some people not to decide to support the developer by buying it.

This is one of my favourite games, yet I'd only recommend it on sale. As others have pointed out, the game is insanely buggy. These bugs aren't just cosmetic, minor issues, they can often be gamebreaking. Characters get stuck somewhere and have to be left for dead, saves get corrupted, multiplayer sessions go out of sync... the list goes on. If you do get the game, save often.
To provide some context for that situation, this game was not created by the developers of the original The Guild 2, yet they were forced to use much of the original code, which was a gigantic mess, and just as buggy - if not more broken - than Renaissance is. The "new" developers actually continued patching Renaissance on their own time, without pay. But of course, they can't re-write the code from the ground up, so the game is still incredibly messy.
When you get past the bugs though, you have one of the most ambitious games you could imagine in front of you. The game is eco-sim, RPG and dynasty manager in one. To start off, you pick between one of the four professions. You can either become a Patron to own farms and such, mostly creating food and other basic materials or running a tavern, become a Craftsman, who processes those basic materials and can gather some basic resources himself (like wood and metals), become a scholar, who either owns a church, brews certain concoctions or lends people money, or lastly, become a rogue, who comes into money by relieving other people of their own.
As you can tell that already opens up a lot of options. While doing that, you gain experience for anything you do, whether you work in your shop/mine/farm/etc. or pursue a love interest. Doing the latter will sooner or later lead to marriage and the foundation of your dynasty. Get funky and spawn lots of children who you should send to decent schools to start them off with more experience and once they reach adolescence, get them a decent apprenticeship to determine their profession. At this point, things open up a lot, because you can have three people in your party at once, which means you can effectively have three quarters of all buildings and jobs available to you, diversifying your income.
What do you earn the money for? Paying for education of your children, buying weapons and armour to fight duels (if you want to), upgrading your residence and workshops and most importantly: politics. By bribing your way into the local council, what stands in the way of you becoming mayor? Or eventually king? For that you will need to pay
of bribes and buy a lot of titles.
There's a lot of nuance and a lot of detail in this game, but as I mentioned, bugs can often stand in the way of those many options presented to you. I remember in one of the games I had (I think it was on version 4.20) the council was so ♥♥♥♥ed up that elections were basically a dice roll. If you think your game is ♥♥♥♥ing up, try the beta patches or if you're already doing that, try playing without them. Your experience may vary considerably depending on whether you use the betas or not.

After 100 hours with the game, I think it's time I re-write my review.
DO NOTE: At this point the game is currently in 0.0.77, features are still incoming.
The Isle is a gritty open world survival game that pits humans versus some of the most impressive creatures to have ever walked the Earth, the Dinosaurs. Though currently in open access, the end result will see intense combat between the primal reptiles and the relatively new rulers of earth, and the inclusion of something in between...
The game is a lot of fun at first, however it loses it's luster, and numerous aspects of the game are working against it at the moment. It's an ambitious project however, and I hope it does well despite the challenges the developers, and to an extent us players, face as we push the game closer to official release.
At the moment the only mode is a free for all deathamatch, players can choose between multiple species, from classics like Triceratops, Stegosaurus, and Tyrannosaurus Rex to lesser known dinosaurs like Diabloceratops, Puertasaurus, and Austroraptor. Each dinosaur plays a little differently, and it shows in how the players use them. Once you spawn in the biggest concern is finding food and water, and depending on the animal, sometimes another player is your food, or you might just be on the menu yourself. The dinosaurs all work well together, however the game is not totally balanced yet, as the devs are planning on adding more dinosaurs and other features before getting down to the grit. There are some issues with this, me personally have found that raptor players are able to exploit the turn radii of larger dinosaurs and pretty much just bite you in the♥♥♥♥♥to death, and you can't do anything about it. A raptor soloing a rex is not cool, and I'll specifically say this is my biggest gripe right now.
There is a chat function that is currently species specific. There is also a WIP groupiung system that currently has little benefit but knowing who you're playing with in your group. The chat can be rather annoying at times, and there can often be trolls or immature players in the chat. People seem to get the idea it's a dinosaur chatroom simulator.
There's not much to the gameplay, and this combined with there often not being full servers can lead to very boring games where you are better off studying the map than trying to interact with other species. But as a survival game this is how they all are.
I play on a rather low gaming quality PC, so I can't testify to ultra settings, but I can tell you how well the game runs on low, haha.
The sounds are great, the devs took a note from Jurassic Park, and molded together the animal sounds from existing animals to create unique vocals for the dinosaurs. They Tyrannosaurus has an intimidating roar, that while is not a ferocious bellow, heralds the arrival of the king of dinosaurs. The Puertasaurus practically sings as it plods it's way across the landscape, the songs of a moving herd are almost like music. The Austroraptor chirps rather ominously in the forest at night, and it'll make your eyes dart across the trees as you move from watering hole to watering hole.
The game does not play well on lower end machines. I actually go into the console and lower my field of view and disable grass in order to reach 60 fps at I believe 800 x 640, otherwise I get less than 30. It's only going to get worse before it gets better, so if you're not at a good spot with your machine, wait until the game drops to see if it's better optimized. The dinosaurs however look great, and I really do like looking at the models move around in the world with their crisp animations.
The menus are clear and easy to understand, and the in game HUD is very nice as well! Honestly there's very few ways to muff that up, so it's a good sign the devs can get that done, lol.
Hoo boy here we go...
Some games just have communities that are great, some not so much. This is a not so much.
Despite the growing age of Dinosaur fans (I myself and 3 years younger than Jurassic Park, and I certainly would not have wanted my mom to let me participate in this game way back in, say, 2003 if it came out then,) The Isle's community is, well, kinda lackluster. There's a great deal of immaturity amongst the players, even myself sometimes. There's constant arguing over game mechanics, among other people constantly requesting that their favorite dinosaur be added. It's somewhat grating. There's also people who will either be quick to criticize, or quick to emptily compliment the developers. Often times in the hub it's a battle of who can write the most sarcastic reply, but that doesn't get anything done, and really actually puts me off. In a community based game that behavior is toxic and does no good.
The developers themselves, well, they're not my favorite developers ever. For an Early Access game where you have to work with your playerbase to see what works and what doesn't they don't seem to want to do much of that. Often times the devs have proven to be callous people, uninviting, rude, acidically sarcastic, and quick to throw out bans and respond to being called any of the former with throwing down the book. There's obviously a lack of professionalism in the dev team (No set dates for anything, not even estimates,) and they've made it hard to actually want this game to perform better than it's competition because they don't seem like people I really want to support, however I've played their game for 100 hours now and have decided it's for the best if we all try to make this project succeed. There has to be a compromise between both the community and the dev team in how they behave and interact both between each other and within each other.
So The Isle is currently a game that is really pulling along and trying to make itself as great as it can. This is crucially because of the interactions of the dev team, and the players giving it feedback.
This is a very strained relationship. Too much criticism and negativity will shut everything down, but too much complimenting and positivity won't critically look at the game and fix it.
But if you think you want this game, and you're reading this to see if you should jump in and get to playing, don't do it. A multiplayer game crucially needs the support of it's community, and the community is too infantile and snide to realize that hey, maybe if they weren't so rude to every person who has a criticism, idea, or isn't generally kissing the backside of the game and the devs, then perhaps more people would feel welcome and would participate. But no, it's a toxic and hostile environment, and you won't want to stay very long if you might think differently from the pack.

You need only look at the reviews to realize how amazing yet terrible this game is. While the game can be one of the most entertaining fighting games you'll ever play, it is guaranteed to also be the absolute worst. Ubisoft has decided to make the Ubiconic move of shooting themselves in the foot by crippling their mostly online game with peer to peer hosting and bad servers for anything non-match made.
Speaking of matchmaking, Ubi has decided that they'd throw in fake matchmaking settings instead of actual skill based mm. This means that launching pvp will typically result in lower level and/or low skilled players being pitted against highly skilled or no-life players sporting maxed gear scores and heavily leveled characters. This is less of a problem in 1v1 and 2v2 match-types where skill is the only factor that determines the winner (aside from Meta move spammers). On the other hand, 4v4 game-types are wildly unbalanced by this, as they take gear score into consideration, allowing that maxed out player on the enemy team to near one hit kill you through the magic of min-maxing.
As for the campaign, it’s pretty good. It’s not incredibly surprising or anything, but it is fun and can be played in 2 player coop. The collectibles are mildly rewarding and finishing each portion of the campaign on the realistic difficulty will net you some (usually) cool cosmetics.
All in all, just wait until it gets the Rainbow 6: Siege treatment and becomes less aggravating to play before you invest in this game.

There are a lot of horror games out there that don't live up to the hype, that are watered down and rely more on the jump scares rather than an atmospheric setting, or even story. Frictional Games have really outdone themselves on this outing, SOMA delivers on both atmosphere and story in a big way, along with some impressive scares. So here is my review:
SOMA throws you into the life of Simon Jarrett, an average man whose life was turned upside down by a car crash, claiming the life of his girlfriend and leaving him with a brain injury, which is slowly creeping up on him. Like any person with death looming over their shoulder, he visits Dr. Munshi, a Doctor experimenting in brain related work, neurology to say the least. After being seated in the good doctors chair and having the machine in place, Simon however wakes up to a strange place, an underwater facility called Pathos-II, this is where the game truly begins.
I have played Underwater games in the past, and enjoyed them but there was one area in particular that stood out and made me feel uncomfortable as hell. You're at the bottom of the ocean, surrounded by nothing but darkness, relying on dimly lit beacons to guide you, whilst the pressure ♥♥♥♥s with your suit and the underwater currents distort your vision even further. I myself don't deal well with the concept of the ocean, an area on our own planet which we have yet to fully explore or know about, it terrifies me, and Soma pulled at that fear. A ♥♥♥♥ up on my behalf in that same area ended up in me having to navigate without the aid of light beacons, aimlessly wandering the pitch black of the Ocean, I can safely say, I never wanted to replay that part again!
The atmosphere is haunting, the music and feeling of dread really stick with you exploring Pathos. There are moments which took me by surprise, I thought I was safe after sneaking past a weeping monster, two seconds later a scripted event led to the monster charging at me. I'll admit, I'm one of these immature players who will pick up a glass or fire extinguisher and fling it at a monster for sheer amusement, but leaving laughs aside, the moral choices and events of the game will make you question what it is to be a human, what's right or wrong anymore and even the ending will leave you with bitter afterthought.
Pros:
- Deep, engaging story with some twists and turns you won't see coming
- A powerful and atmospheric setting, ambience
- Beautiful looking graphics, rivals a lot of Triple AAA standards
- Interesting characters and dialogue
- Variety on Monsters and enemies
- Game Length
- Mod availability
- Afterthought of the game
Cons:
- No inventory system like Amnesia, which would have suited SOMA.
- Don't play this game if you're prone to seizures or getting headaches, the glitching when a monster is nearby or in your FOV can really ♥♥♥♥ with you. While it's made to throw you off, it can be a little over the top.
Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed my experience of SOMA, a beautfilly crafted horror survival game with a deep, dark story and the most atmospheric levels I've played through. Is it worth €27.99? In my own opinion, Yes! And I can see why Yahtzee Croshaw put it in his Top 5 of 2015.

I have played the game for a few hours so far, but I absolutely love it.
This is a post-apocalypse survival 'Sims' style game, with no 'Z' word, and I'm having an absolute blast.
It can be unforgiving, but that's the point of survival games - surviving. If you fail, you start again and learn from the mistakes you've made and the things you've learnt. Water can be scarce, as it currently only replenishes when it rains, but if you plan ahead (Tip: build a second water butt!) the risk of running out can be mitigated somewhat. Food is a little easier to come by, but you don't want to be feeding your survivors when their bar is only a little empty!
Survivors can die, either through neglect, illness, or damage in fights etc. so you do need to take care of them. You can also find/recruit new buddies out in the wasteland (or at your door) and lighten the workload for your initial set, but you do have to further balance already scarce resources!
There are quite a number of things to build, using materials scavenged from the wasteland or traded for with NPCs who pop up (in the field and at your door) as well as upgrades to be done to core systems, such as your oxygen filter, water filter, and generator.
I'm not going to lie and say it doesn't have its issues, both in terms of balance and bugs - it does, though no more than any game these days - but it IS Early Access, and that's the entire point of the process, to have players help find and squash bugs, and suggest balance tweaks.
The developers are VERY active on the forums, and are even open to new suggestions for features. I really can't stress how fantastic this is, and it's very clear the game isn't going to simply disappear and be forgotten about.
At £9.99/$15, it's a good purchase. I have paid far more for far less, and this game will only get better. Get in while you can, help develop a fantastic game and have a metric feck-ton of fun!

Amnesia was, without a doubt, a landmark game. It forever changed the face of horror games and the genre is still feeling its impact to this day. Frictional games truly understands the key elements to creating real horror: Not in having things jump out at the player with loud sting music blaring but with subtlety and mechanics that never allow the player to get too comfortable.
One of the key elements to creating a true horror experience is making the player feel vulnerable. Nothing is scary when you’re armed with a rocket launcher, a minigun, three different kinds of shotguns, and enough ammunition to start a revolution. Amnesia accomplishes this by removing weapons altogether. You as the player have no way to defend yourself apart from running and hiding. The monsters that hunt you are always a danger, from start to finish.
Another core tenet of good horror is that your imagination is always far worse than reality. Hence, you are strongly discouraged from looking at the monsters in the game. If you look directly at any of the creatures, your screen distorts and you begin to lose “sanity”, which will eventually result in the monster finding you. You’ll find yourself on more than one occasion staring at a wall and praying that the lumbering sound of its footsteps is moving away from you and not closer.
The Resident Evil style puzzles offer something of a respite from the more intense portions of the game, following the tried and true formula of “tension and release”.
Really, though, the harshest criticism that I can level against this game is that it was too influential for its own good. Games like Outlast and Alien: Isolation have taken this concept to new levels. Consequentially, I just don’t find it as scary as it once was. If you haven’t played it and you’re enjoy being scared, definitely give this a try.

Amnesia: The Dark Descent is a horror game in which you sneak about and hide from murderous monsters while exploring an old structure. You could apply that description to the majority of horror games, but I actually found this one to be entertaining and genuinely creepy. If you want to kill things, this game probably won't satisfy. I love blowing baddies away, but I find that running and hiding is quite exciting, too, and Amnesia: The Dark Descent does a good job illustrating that.
The enemies look freaky coming at you from the dark, though technically their design is a little goofy. To avoid the player from getting too accustomed to their appearance in-game, the dev had the clever idea of triggering fear in the player character if you look right at the enemies. If you see them, glance away and run or hide, so that you don't suffer ill effets.
It's a pretty short game, but I find that short works better for horror. I really wish that Alien Isolation was half its length, or at least a bit shorter than what it is. I really like that game, but when you drag out horror, it doesn't work as well, in my opinion. I will say that the plot was a bit weird, with a final encounter that was even weirder still. This was a case of a game where the plot wasn't the major driving factor for me, which is pretty impressive, since that's usually a massive part ofwhat keeps me invested in a game.

{IF YOURE GOING TO ARGUE THAT ITS EARLY ACCESS, DONT BOTHER COMMENTING, THEY WILL BE DELETED, EARLY ACCESS GAMES DESERVE FAIR REVIEWS UNLESS THEY ARE FREE, WHICH THIS IS NOT)  Updated review 8/10.2015
I don't believe I have to do this, but if you're one of those many people who want to argue with  my review despite not having it in your library and never actually played it, your comments will be deleted and communication with you will be blocked.
Of course it's early access.  And early access games deserve honest reviews in the state they are in.  This review is for the game it is, not the game it wants to be.  Right now, Mad Games Tycoon, Salt and Dig or Die take up most of my time, all Early Access games which I'd highly recommend.
I want to like it.  I really do.  If you look at my library, I basically play nothing but strategy games.  But at this point, I simply can't recommend it.  Perhaps when things get ironed out.  But it's pretty raw and boring at this point.
I've played the game for about four hours.  A couple of people have said that four hours isn't long enough to give an accurate review which I find to be a non-sensical comment.  You either like the game and give it a fair shot or dont.  Four hours is plenty of time to get used to the UI (which is very clunky and non-intuitive in this game), get an idea of the "realism" the game intends to portray and have an idea whether the game is well put together.
The developer is quick to respond to criticism and throw out ideas, which is good.  He seems pretty down to earth and hopefully will make this a good game.  He's already added many suggestions from the community to make it better.
The game is meant to look the way it does.  Graphics aren't the focus or priority of the game.  But what it does, it does well.  Environments and character movement are very minimalistic but work well with the game.
The sound matches the graphcis.  Music is eerie and dramatic.  Sounds sometimes can be annoying, but overall are well done.
The game certainly has the potential to be an addicting game.
I've noticed very few bugs in the game.  The bugs I can recall have either been fixed or only happened on one occasion.
The tutorial is fairly useless at this point.  The tutorial as far as I can tell helps you get in the front door and turn on the power, then ends.  This about 10 seconds of gameplay.  Some screens have hints that tell you the obvious but don't lead you anywhere.
Controlling your people is pretty hard to do at this point, and very counter intuitive.  Nothing is easy when it comes to assigning a task, or moving them here and there.  The characters tend to stand in front of each other, or in front of something you want to access and you have to cycle through them to move them away.  While one menu might want you to right click, then left click, the next menu has you do the opposite or something completely different.
You have limited space, but the apparent lack of room to place something you need, even though there appears to be a good sized gap to do it is both random and frustrating.  Even reorganizing, there are large swaths of space that appear like they could be used but are blocked.  I was able to fit one extra sleeping bag in after reorganizng.
Many tasks need to be completed once startied which is rather annoying.  I tried to add on a room, which as far as I know, only one person at a time can do.  It's a long, long time before it's done, and the person you assign cant break away or you have to restart buidling the room from scratch.  Someone mentioned that you can find tools which speed up your tasks.  This is true, but the speed is not significant.  Something that takes 24 in game hours, which feels as long as it sounds for gameplay, might go down to 22 hours.  At one point, I had a 30 percent decrease in task completion due to finding tools, and it made very little difference.  To some, this might be a balance issue, but to me it feels like a choice. Perhaps this will be addressed in an update.
The game right now is pretty boring.  Send people to the bathroom.  Send them to the shower.  Clean the bucket you're using for a bathroom.  Occasionally you'll have people stop by wanting to trade.  If you have enough water, you can go explore the area.  You're able to place your characters on automation, but if you fast forward to anything important such as completion of a task (a room, for example) takes so long that it forces you to ignore vital indicators from your characters which has a large negative influence on your game.  Placing them on automation also means you can't control when they use the restroom, shower or drink water and eat (all which consume valuable water or food).
Unfortunately, you're at the mercy of the game to provide water.  When it rains, you get water.  If it doesnt, you wait for it to rain.  Sometimes that takes a long while.  In my opinion, this needs to be changed.  Luck should play some part of a strategy game, but it's far too luck based at this point.   You only are able to store 30 (whatever units) of water, and usually an exploration takes half that. Mabye you can expand how much you can hold later in the game.   Drinking takes 5 each time,  times at least four people.  When it doesnt rain for days, you very quickly run out of it.  And then the waiting game begins....
[[Edit: Someone suggested putting in more water cannisters.  I was up to three in the beginning of the game utilizing all my resources.  It didn't rain for six straight days, and after day two or so I was in the same predicament.  Then, somehow they all died of radiation posioning.  My oxygen filter was good.  The doors weren't left open.  No idea why they all died.  Maybe it was my fault, but without a decent tutorial, I'll never have any idea.]]
[[Edit]]  A recent update made the rains come no longer than four days apart.  This helps, but there still needs to be a way to manufacture water.  Also, the update provided more water from explorations.  This bettered the balance for water but didn't solve the problem.  With more updates like this, it should be a more playable game.  That being said, there are still far too many basic issues that need to be solved before I can change it to recommend.]]
The developer wants to stick to realism, as he said in a forum message, but how realistic is it to send your young daughter or son out in a radiation suit to fix a water or oxygen filter?  Or send them alone on an exploration.  Or have them repair a generator or craft a gas mask?  On the forums, someone mentioned that in a post-apocolyptic world, you do what you need to get done.   However, this is supposed to be the story of an average family that finds a fallout shelter.  And it's laughable that these kids have the knowledge to fix complicated devices like water and oxygen systems that filter radiation.  It's also laughalbe that your young daughter goes out on exploration with a strength rating higher than the men and beat men with pipes.
Someone pointed out in a post that it's also very unrealsitc that you have to repair your sleeping bag, water filters, generator (not adding gas, reparing it), oxygen filter, toilet bucket, shower...everything.....every few days.  If the repairs went quick, it wouldn't be an issue.  But the repair can take you up to a full day if you let them get low, which is easy to do considering the lack of resources you have and the time it takes to do everything else.
Hopefully this games becomes good.  It's not nearly worth the price I paid at this point.

A classic FPS that is an entirely different beast from Quake 1. This game has more realistic weapon physics, which slow down gameplay compared to quake 1, but it still manages to be a fast paced "Run and Gun" shooter worthy of the Quake name. It features backtracking to previous stages, a more fleshed out story than a lot of the older FPS, and mission objectives, which were all new compared to ID's other classics. While having very little relation to Quake 1 and 3, Quake 2's story is continued in Quake 4 with a much more modern take.
The game hasn't aged well compared to many other classic FPS, including even Quake 1. The main issue being that many of the weapons just feel clunky. ID tried to emulate some realism this time around and added a lot delays, cooldowns, and recoil to the guns. It takes a few levels to get a feel for some of the weapons, but they work well enough. There is still a lot to love and respect about this game.
tl:dr It's worth giving a shot if you like classic FPS from the early 3D era, or just want more background info on what happened before Quake 4.

Enjoyable round-based tactics game. It's not an in-depth strategy/tactics game like Jagged Alliance 1&2 and even less complex than XCOM:Enemy Unknown, but it's still a fun game that applies the same principle: find the right mix of weapons, skills and positioning to beat the opposition. Since you can't target enemies and have to rely on your squad to pick the targets, positioning and telling your squad where to look is key. Your options may be reduced, but it's also focussed and does this part really well. The pacing for unlocks is also done in a good way, by completing missions and doing well in them you earn stars which in turn unlock equipment for your team. Since you can jump in and out of campaigns it's a game you don't necessarily need to play for longer sessions, you can just jump in and play for 10 minutes and still finish a mission or two.
The price in comparison to the mobile version is also not as horrible as it seems at first glance since you get alot more content than the mobile base version has.
My main complaint about this game would be the lack of information or tool tips. Some things are left unexplained an you have to figure it out yourself, some information is only available on the loading screens - which you will never get to read on a modern gaming PC, because they pass by in seconds. Some might see that as an oldschool approach to game design, but that doesn't make it any better.
On the technical side this game is a port from a mobile platform and it shows. The graphics are simply outdated, the variety of animations is very limited. On the plus side the optimization seems to be decent, so loading times are swift and the performance is very good, even on older machines. The sound design is okay, too. Balance is ok, music isn't annoying, shots go pop and grenades go bang, some radio communication inbetween. Nothing special, but it works.
In about 11 hours of playtime I have experienced one interface freeze, but no crashes, sound loops or graphical errors. And this also gives you a rough estimate of playtime: if you like round based tactics, this will entertain you for ten to 15 hours, depending on how much you are into unlocks and earnings stars.
Overall this isn't a contender for GOTY, but a enjoyable round based snack for inbetween and at 9€ this was worthy buy.

A preface: I'm very reluctantly not recommending this game. It was a gift, for one, and secondly I really wanted to like it on its own terms. I'm a Classical scholar, and the concept is all kinds of wonderful. But I feel duty bound to be honest to anyone thinking of buying the game, so here we go:
+ The art style is superb. I feel like this game could have been a top-notch animated film. It's not only beautiful but steeped in the iconography and lore of the ancient Greeks. Could not be better.
+ The music, likewise, is evocative and well suited to the gameplay.
+ The concept of an ancient Greek themed platformer inspired by pottery is fantastic.
= The story was simplistic. This is something that could appeal to some but not all gamers.
= If you're familiar with ancient Greek epic, religion, or myths at all, you might have some moments of frustration. I knew the hero was making some really poor choices but, as with any linear game, you have to go along with it. Some might find it a refreshing twist on the old stories.
- What other reviews have said about the combat is, sadly, true. The controls are terrible on KB and mouse.
- Combat feels floaty. There were several moments when enemies killed themselves, threw themselves out of the level including an elite. It is also possible for one boss battle, at least, to become glitched if a required item is knocked out of the level by the boss.
- Boss battles have neat gimmicks but are implemented poorly. Each boss has been less about challenge and working out a strategy, or being skilled, but simply having the patience to grind it down.

This is the 4th Geopolitical Simulator (GPS) game, but in reality it is the 4th alpha. The game has been unfinished for years. The reason is that it is such an ambitious project to start with, and progress is made very slowly with each release. Worse yet, the developer intentionally removes features from the previous release (Example: editor and spy mode among others) only to release them a few months later as a paid addon. This wouldn't be so bad (DLCs are standard practice now) but in this case each new release is practically identical to the previous one with mostly cosmetic changes.
At one point they broke the game in an update so it crashed on startup and when I contacted support they told me that to fix the bug they introduced (deliberately?) I had to buy an add-on. That was a couple of years ago. Since then their support seems to have improved a bit for example when their purchase page was misleading about steam keys, they were nice enough to send me my steam key even after the deadline although I didn't know activating the steam key would stop the non steam version from working, but that isn't a big deal.
Moreover they keep listing as a feature that they update the game to match the governments and faces and names of the real world for that year. This is nonesense. They only update a handful of countries and even then the update is silly. It is president Obama not Ohama and if you play a none super power (say Jordan) the characters will be completely generic. Not only didn't they bother to put the king's face or name similarity, but they just use random arab names for the whole middle east. Pathetic! How many countries are there? How long to research something like this? How much does the game cost? How much does 2 weeks of 1 researcher's time cost?
Another item would be real weapon names? B2? Merkava? Seawolf? Nah eversim is too lazy for that. They just have generic names for the whole world. I mean there are only 10 major weapon manufacturers in the world and for the price of their game, they can spend a couple of weeks researching them for crying out loud.
Then in GPS4 they spend all their time to make close up street level battles and they are not even optional. So you could invade Djibouti as USA with overwhelming force and a single guerilla  unit would hold off thousands of tanks unless you go to street level and manually take over the city. This isn't a Tom Clancy FPS action game. They forgot what the grand means in grand strategy and are turning it into (the sims).
So with all of the above why do I still keep buying this game? Why have I bought every update? because it is the closest to achieving a working simulation of this kind. There is a masterpiece waiting to happen with a game that manages to take the best of GPS (eversim), Supreme Ruler (Battlegoat), Superpower 2 (GolemLabs), Hearts of iron (paradox) and a few others.
It is hopeless for Eversim ever to finish it. They just lack the resources and keep bleeding their customers dry and leading them on with half baked patches sold as full releases. Golem Labs seems to have given up since superpower 2. If anyone can do it, Paradox or Battle Goat Studios can. Let us hope Eversim sells to one of them and finally give the fans what they want.

The AI is bad, so bad that I can't play the game on anything other than easy difficulty with AI allies.  My allies are frequently running in front of my line of fire, letting enemies stand in front of them, and not reviving each other.  They're also frequently separating from each other and not sticking with the player character, which is something I came to expect from this genre thanks to Left4Dead.  Their ability to hit enemies is unreal and animated horribly.  Basically, they can snap to any angle, even directly behind them, to shoot with perfect aim, yet they randomly miss when enemies are moving slowly in front of them.  This kind of programming is probably temporary during testing, but I would expect better behavior after the devs posted about focusing on AI updates months ago.
That said, the actions the AI takes can sometimes be pretty funny and almost lifelike if compared to a really troll-like player or someone who isn't taking the game seriously enough and is eating while playing and maybe taking their time to look at scenery, forgetting to help with mission objectives.  It is quite funny (and aggravating) when the AI revives you to 99% and then decides to stop reviving and run away just because an enemy is approaching.
The enemy AI is less important, because it typically just swarms you and attempts to overwhelm you with their numbers and special abilities, like grabbing you and running away.  Enemies seem to spawn in different locations depending on the difficulty setting, but weirdly, easy difficulty has more enemies in some places.
Playing online is a mixed bag.  The real issue I have is it will throw you into an in-progress mission as a dead (knocked down) character even though there are two alive AI characters.  Those AI characters will not revive you if any enemies are around.  They'll get to 99% revive and just quit and run away like good little trolls.  This is a flaw that the devs could fix with a little extra matchmaking code or the option to swap characters (which would be cool af).
My previous review for this game mostly put it down for performance issues, but that's mostly worked out.  I tested the game on both my old rig (Phenom II 955 with 750 Ti) and my new Ryzen rig (1600X with 1060 Strix) can run the game at low-ish settings with no big issues.  The Ryzen rig still shows some stutter if I run the game at low settings but shows absolutely no stutter if I raise the view distance to its highest setting.  This seems to be an object pooling issue the devs could optimize, but overall, the game is playable.
The video settings have an issue, the AA Quality setting.  If you play it at any setting higher than Medium, it causes artifacts around your first-person models.  Just a heads up.  The game looks great otherwise.
Not all of it is bad.  The visuals are amazing.  Great scenery, very realistic locations, pretty skyboxes, and lots of interactable objects.  I wish more objects were breakable or at least physics-enabled, but we at least get breakable doors.  We also get barricades, which work fairly well, though I wish they could be locked shut.  The guns work well, and everything feels somewhat realistic, but recoil definitely needs more work.  Pistols feel overpowered with unlimited ammo, so maybe some balancing needs to be done there.
For $15, this is a decent Early Access title, but I would only recommend it to people who are already bored of Left4Dead and Left4Dead 2, both of which are games you should play before this one.

Back in the day when First-Person Shooters had not yet become the most oversaturated market in the gaming industry, Id Software created the legend that is Doom. A game so chock full of secrets, monsters, weapons, and good level design that many a young gamer's face was melted off by the sheer quality. Even today Doom holds up astonishingly well thanks to the aforementioned level designs, the likes of which have been sadly abandoned by many modern FPS games. It also has a sizable modding community that is still active.

This is *NOT* the best game you'll ever come across. But it's *NOT* the worst game you'll ever come across.
Gonna' start with the CONS and get them outa' the way.
The game launched just a few days ago at this time, and it's pretty buggy. The servers are screwed up because of the massive amount of people playing and whatnot. The developers *ARE* working their butts off to fix this.
That isn't the only bug, though. Your game has a slight chance of crashing, or getting stuck whenever you roll for a perk, but that's rare. Also, your stats may be *TEMPORARILY* reset to 0. This is normal at the moment, so don't worry.
Now onto the PRO'S!
The game, definitely not the best, is very fun to play. You can't compare this to Dead by Daylight as DBD is fast paced, and F13 is a bit more slow paced.
The game *IS* officially liscensed, which is awesome!
As a counselor you run around one of three maps (They're very similar, but the differences are noticeable, *PLUS* the cabin interiors are randomized I'm pretty sure. I *THINK* some cabins are placed around the map randomly.) Higgins Haven, Packanack Lodge, and Camp Crystal Lake. There are many things to find along the map, such as parts to cars or boats, or even phone boxes you need to repair those items. You have 20 minutes each match to either call the cops, escape in one and/or two cars (Two and four seater) or escape by moter boat. You can also kill Jason.. but that's for you to find out on your own.
As Jason, you can pick from different Jason's from different movies, and a specially-designed Jason by Tom Savini himself. Your goal is to hunt down and kill as many, or all, of the counselors as you can in 20 minutes. You can sabotage escape by breaking the phone box (it's still repairable after you break it. same goes for the other escapes) you can stop the car by smashing the hood/engine (players can restart the car) or you can tip over the boat, and try to drown anybody in the boat
Finally, we have Tommy Jarvis. Tommy is a character from the movies, which makes this person extra-special! :) As a counselor, you can find a CB Radio somewhere on the map. If you use it, the option for Tommy Jarvis to join the game is unlocked. A dead or escaped counselor can be revived as Tommy Jarvis. Your main goal is to stop Jason from nearly killing somebody, by shooting him with a shot gun. (You only have one bullet, which I don't think is realistic.) You are also the only person who can actually kill Jason.
..That about wraps this review up. This game isn't perfect, and it's nowhere near that. It's also not a triple A game by some big company. The team behind it is a small indie team that just so happened to be picked up by the people behind the original F13 movies. Don't give them mercy because of this, but don't be too critical either. They are working hard to fix bugs and other things. This game isn't great, but I love it. It's something i've wanted for *YEARS* now, and its finally here.
I hope you enjoy the game. If you don't, that your opinion.. but I hope you find this review to be helpful.

I love the game, and love the development team, but many seem to forget a few small facts concerning the game in its current state.
That being said, the server issues, and other launch issues going on that are hindering gameplay are not as bad as people make them out to be.  I know that its not working to full capacity, but I know very few games, that ever release perfect.  People are calling this a Triple A title, yet its a kickstarter backed, no huge funding source, and actually, for what it is, its quite well put together.  Its got some things that need to be fixed, and its far from perfect, but I've enjoyed the time I've played the game beyond the small nuances that are currently going on.
Call me fanboy if you like, I've got tons of Friday the 13th merchandise and movies and such from over the years, but in time, this game is going to have the problems ironed out and fixed.  For now, you either jump on and ride the wave, the nostalgia, and the fun that this game provides, or don't play it.  It is what it is.
I'd like to commend the developers for responding and working tirelessly to fix the issues.  For that, I give it a thumbs up, its a fun game, and if you take all the seriousness out of it and just enjoy it for what it offers, its a great title with a lot of upside, even more so going forward.

Great, immersive, old-fashioned sci-fi story which really nails the atmosphere. Remember sci-fi stories that make you think about things? This does a good job of that.
Longer than I expected. I played it solidly for 3 days over two weekends.
The puzzles aren't hard, but do require some thought, and make sense within the setting. Think working out how machinery is operated and then putting it into practise, rather than solving abstract chess puzzles. You feel like you're doing things you'd be doing naturally, rather than contrived puzzles inserted at random points. The puzzles also ensure it doesn't feel like you're just walking from place to place, since you have to work out what to do and how to do it. That keeps things more engaging.
Exploration rewards you with more backstory, and some areas feel large or open but you've never lost or wondering which way to go, and there's usually only one path forward (possibly with some dead-ends and optional rooms or areas; sometiems the dead-ends open up later).
There are moral choices to make during the story, and they are handled better than most games. They're a lot more ambiguous than is typical, and there is no god judging you down there; you play that role instead.
The enemies break up the story and exploration side of things (and sometimes get in the way of exploration), which helps with pacing. On the whole they're a good addition and about right, but there were a couple of times where I wished one just wasn't there so I could more easily look around. However, once you know an area (from sacrificing yourself once or twice), and work out how the enemies behave, they're actually quite straightforward, give or take a couple of moments. (Probably quite hard for the devs to get this just right, since it's hard to know what an area is like for the first time once you know it. If you ever get frustrated, just run around, work out what to do, get killed, then do it again properly.)
Graphics and sound were perfect, really. If you look at a still screenshot or certain areas, the graphics aren't always completely cutting edge (e.g. you'll notice the odd texel or polygon here and there), but when you are inside the game that is irrelevant. They do a great job and the atmosphere is completely nailed, as are the different areas and environments. Some areas look absolutely superb, too.
Game ran at 1080p, 60fps, maxed settings, almost all the time on my GTX 960. Occasional drops to 45fps when standing in particular spots, but never an issue and the adaptive vsync option worked well.
If you've played the great, first Amnesia (and let's not even mention the awful sequel by an unrelated team), this is less scary than that, or at least was for me. The enemies can be scary and some are similar to ones in Amnesia but something about the setting made me less afraid of them, and feel more like they didn't know what they were doing, i.e. didn't mean to hurt me but couldn't really help it. I actually liked that. The game has psychological elements but they're more in the story than the enemies, and while I enjoy the odd 'horror' game I can only play them when I'm really in the mood, whereas this I was happy to play at all hours. I really enjoyed the pacing where there are long sections of story and problem solving without crawling around in shadows fearing for your life. There *are* parts like that, and some enemies that creep you out, it's just not relentlessly like that, and it's better as a result.
The ending is great, too.
Highly recommended.

Before I get started, I want to say that I am a HUGE fan of shoot 'em ups, and I really had high hopes for this one.
Those hope were quickly dashed.
So here's the thing:
While this game DOES look visually stunning and has nice controls, it will murder your ears with the uncontrollably loud in-game static. The is due to a issue with the game. It uses the LAV Audio codec, and it conflicts with people using the K-lite Codec pack or the CCCP codec pack. If you have either one of those installed on your PC, you can't play this game.
IMHO, having to remove a Codec pack which lots of users have today for various things (Video editing being one), and not having ANY way of adjusting the in-game audio (there are ZERO controls for audio adjustment), doesn't justify the price.
I gave this game as much of a chance as my ears could bear, but to no avail. Until the devs can get around to fixing it, which I don't think will happen as this game was released 2 years ago - Save your money.
There are better shoot 'em up games on steam, grab any one of those.

As far as I\'m concerned, no housing bug was found by me. I mean, all manpower was returning in time and I was glad with the result. It\'s probably because some people choose to fix 200k dilapidated houses by splitting it over the country. Also, the text now is way more readable when in Masters of the World or Rulers of Nations. I like it. I guess, some colours could be changed, e.g. in the tab of promises (that red and blue, ugh, nooo). But all in all, it\'s pretty good.
New features like opposition, revolutions and a new system of peace treaties (I\'m talking about the right to demand your enemy to pay you money for years) are brilliant. Well, some things can be done better but as far as I see, it\'s good.

Unfortunately, there\'s no such thing yet. But it was re-done as if it\'s there and it works. If you\'re in a huge surplus, you don\'t need to worry anymore of getting deposed because of using money a country don\'t need (just make sure you aren\'t wasting it, like building unprofitable roads and etc).
So, I guess I sort of liked this game. I\'m not sure if it\'s brilliant in general (lots of improvements and possibilites can be implemented yet, especially regarding to new and in-game organisations, regions managing, currency and stock exchange), but it\'s clear that lots of work has been done from Masters of the World. Personally, I\'ve recommend to play it. Unfortunately, the price is a little to high as it still has many various places to improve. All in all, I say 7.5 is pretty accurate rating to this game.

5 hours into the game I can definitely see a lot of things I like and a lot of things that can be worked on. Keep in mind I'm not overly familiar with the previous games of the Geopolitical Simulator games because the only one I've played was Rulers of Nations, however, I play lots of Geopolitical games like Superpower 2, Supreme Ruler Ultimate, Rogue State, Democracy 3 etc etc. Due to the amount of topics I could talk about and my desire to keep it brief and to the point, I will provide a bulleted list and a "gameplay" video where I explain everything in more detail.
Gameplay Footage and Video Review:
Pros:
-Real Time sim where you play as a "Random" World Leader of any major power in the world today.
-Lots of customization in terms of legislation that you can pass. (Wide variety of laws that will appease or♥♥♥♥♥♥off your populace ranging from freedom of expression, legalization of marijuana or even appropriate rules of war)
- A "Minigame" that involves you controlling either rebels or police units and putting down revolts either violently or through arrests.
-Information is conveyed through "video" format. Cabinet members will explain a situation by "conference call."
-It's fun to mess around with the various budget controls in an attempt to keep people happy but to also maintain a positive balance so that your country isn't swimming in debt.
-It's actually really cool to read the papers and see what people are saying about your administration. After a while, you'll start to see the same things repeated but in general it's interesting how many unique lines have actually been written for the various events or actions in the game.
-It's actually fun to role play a certain play style. For example, become a hugely popular leader and then start to build a cult of personality around your leader... you can be a Stalin-esque character within a Democratic society.
-Terrorism is a major part of the game. Whether you're funding it or a victim of it. Power structures of whole countries can be affected by it and it's shown in a way that few games have... a highly destructive, hard to stamp out pest. Terrorism can lead to the death or injury of your cabinet members, or even full blown wars.
Cons:
-User Interface is rather clunky and the tutorial isn't the best at explaining the various features of the game. I ended up quitting due to a visual glitch and just jumping into the game itself where I learned everything from trial and error.
-Graphics are rough. While it's done well enough to convey it's purpose, it would've been nice to have a cleaner World map. Low res retextures look really weird... especially when some of the cities look like copy/paste bird's eye views of cities.
-THe voice acting is all over the place. Some of it's good, most of it is okay and some of it is comically horrendous. It, surprisingly, doesn't kill the vibe of the game but can definitely use some work.
-50 dollars? Sheesh. I would price this at 30... MAAAAAYBE 35. There is a huge amount of content but the presentation doesn't automatically qualify it as a full priced game.
-The game sometimes lacks solid feedback. For example, an advisor can tell you that by infiltrating a terrorist cell, the percentage of destabilization will increase by 3.78% but what other repurcussions can that have? I can assume that there is a chance of getting caught? Is that chance high? How♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥will a country be if I fund terrorists that are working against them? How does a country feel about me in general? Feedback like this is sorely lacking and I believe the game would benefit greatly from adding it in.
-Some of the music is a bit off too. Not game breaking, mind you... just feels like it's in the wrong game.
In summation, I've really enjoyed my time with this game. I can see myself putting in a lot more time as I learn more of the in's and out's. I will say that the actual "combat" portion of the game, I've yet to see as I've played a purely peaceful and entirely democratic leader... looking for peaceful solutions, even if it undermines my authority. However, with what I've played and how much fun I've had, I feel like I must recommend this game. However, if you're anything but a fan of the series or you're never played a Geopolitical Simulator game before, you might want to hold off until there is a modest price drop.

Rake is a very unique horror game experience so to make this short here are some of the Pros and cons of the game.
NOTE: I am only putting down what I can remember from last time I played, which was about an hour ago so I can't pin point everything I had to say about this game.
PROS:
-Scary (Alot of people are saying that it isn't scary but in all honesty if you immerse your self in the game it can be pretty freaking scary.)
-Beautiful land to explore (even though the graphics aren't the best everything looks great, during the day everything pops and just looks amazing.)
- Not a slender clone ( The dev used a very well known creepypasta/myth to make a game that isn't about exploring in the dark and collecting papers for no reason.)
-Challenging (The game just throws you into the world with little to no knowledge of what to do or where to go)
- immersive (With this game having a very minimalistic hud its very easy to get caught up in what's going on)
I had more but these are the ones that I felt mattered
CONS:
So this game has alot going for it but I managed to find a few things that needed improvement.
-Nights last far too long from what I can tell they last about 30 minutes (unless I missed a way to move quicker)
-Very little instruction on what to do (I'm never actually sure if I should be exploring at night and not just hide in the trailer)
- The game is a tad too dark (I know its a horror game set in a forest but when you can't tell where you're going nothing can really get done unless you have your map out the entire time.)
- Buildings are hard to pin point on the map
- (This is a very minor complaint) The camera static can get really bad at times and make It very hard to see anything.
- Emptyness (there is alot to see but very little to gain from exploring, you can find some really cool stuff like a water fall,   a few abandoned buildings. ECT. but most the time there isn't anything there.)
- Framerate ( its seems to work okay but it doesn't like to run over 50 unless im looking directly at the ground.)
This game is amazing, its probably the best horror game to come out of the indie scene this year, its intense, scary, immersive, and just plain fun. I really hope the dev sees this and fixes some of the issues i've listed so that the game can become a much more entertaining experience. I would recommend this to people who are willing to put some time into a horror game and explore the world it give you. Its absolutely worth the $5.  7/10 (not perfect but good)

I just finished Apotheon, and wow, did I enjoy this game!  It's such a great game.  The art style is obviously awesome.  Unless you hate orange, in which case steer clear.  It's a wicked beautiful game and they nailed the Greek Pottery aesthetic.
The game focuses primarily on combat, and don't let anyone tell you it's anything less than stellar.  Yes, it takes some getting used to.  This is a style of 2D combat that in a league of it's own.  1 part Terraria, 1 part Dark Souls, and yet totally unique somehow.  Once you get the hang of it, properly dodging and timing the perfect devastating blow is incredibly satisfying.  This really should be played on a keyboard and mouse, though, as precision is a big factor in combat.  Also, it's much safer to switch weapons by going into your inventory by pressing "i" instead of hitting a number key and scrolling, while trying to dodge enemies.
The music is perfect, The voice acting is good, and I love the story, because it minds me of all the time I spent reading Greek mythology for fun when I was a kid.  I think the ending is just freaking perfect.
It's got plenty to do.  I spent 10 hours playing, and didn't spend a lot of time exploring and many sections I ran and dodged by dozens of enemies.  So there's plenty of time to spend here if you look for everything and do all the side stuff.
My only real complaint is that there are just too many weapons that you hang onto all at once.  I would have preferred just 2 or 3 melee weapons, and 1 or 2 ranged.  As it is, I just had a lot of stuff that I never needed to use, so there was no sense of urgency.  Also, I realize they were going for an "ammo" feel by having weapons degrade and breakdown ... but I'm not sure that helped the game.  It seemed like an unnecessary convention, and the only time it remotely effected me was when my assassins dagger broke, but I just ran and bought a cheap one from the black market dealer.
Anyways ... I highly recommend this game, and that you take the time to learn and appreciate the combat.  I have a feeling that this'll be a sleeper-hit, and once online multiplayer is up there will be renewed vigor for Apotheon!

In "The Ultimate DOOM" (which it's an integrated expansion of the first DOOM) you are the only human survivor in a Mars station infested of beings from hell and your mission is to fight the enemies level to level, much like Wolfenstein 3D, which was the first game of this genre (FPS). However, technological improvements allowed Doom to be a work with many new elements that gave more gameplay than its predecessor.
Doom popularized most aspects of FPS games. Many people claim it was Doom that created the platform and patterns that other games of this genre were to follow, as well as in terms of creativity, allowed the insertion of the expansions and the same user could create custom levels for the game (the famous WAD files, which created, probably, the first modding community in the history of video games).
This is the reason why this game was the CORNERSTONE for other FPS games that remained for posteriority. For example, a great game like Half Life (1998), probably it wouldn't become possible (at least as we know it currently) if Doom (1993) hadn't appeared first because some of the programmers of that game (John Carmack, John Romero, Michael Abrash...) were the same persons who made Quake (1996). Half Life was created using the GoldSrc engine, which is a modification of the updated Quake engine (known as QuakeWorld).
This game, The Ultimate DOOM (as well DOOM II: Hell on Earth), is for the true FPS hardcore gamer from the oldschool.

This game is one of those games that you find, you start up, and you instantly know it will be awesome. Apotheon has a stunning art style, mimicking ancient Greek art perfectly. The story is not the most creative thing but the mission layout is really well made - each zone has tons of variety and there are always multiple ways to conquer them. And the boss fights - don't get me started on those. Each is unique requiring skill and strategy to beat and they have they're own little mechanics to them as well which can make for a nice change.
It has some basic platforming elements which admittedly can be tedious, and usually involve jumping, climbing, jumping, climbing and more jumping - followed by climbing - but the rage boiling inside me is let free when I get to massacre a group of enemies at the next area.
The combat is reliant on player skill, not character skill, and you constantly need to be switching back and forth between your doru and your xiphos and rolling behind your enemies and lobbing jars of greek fire at them. Despite this, there is a nice system of character progression, and you can upgrade armour, purchase skills etc.
Apotheon has basic stealth mechanics built in, and its nice to sneak into someones attic and steal their coins or shoot a satyr in the back from the shadows.
I did find myself lost and the map can be confusing. Unfortunately, a lot of time is spent figuring out where to go, but the reward makes up for the painstaking navigation.
All in all, despite its flaws, this is a beautiful game that deserves your money. Go get this. NOW.

Apotheon is a 2D action platformer with some (elementary) puzzle, adventure/exploration and RPG elements. It is set in an ancient Greek-like world.
I played the game with mouse+keyboard, on normal difficulty (the lowest), and it took me ~18hrs to complete the game and get all the exploration-related achievements. I don't see me replaying it, unless it gets an important update or a DLC etc. I especially enjoyed the design and challenge offered by the boss fights, which was always tailored to the mythology/lore in question. The game played smoothly and I encountered no serious bugs nor crashes. My only gameplay-related concern was that the physics engine sometimes felt weird, with the hero getting "rag-dolled" when hit by enemies; I can't exactly describe it, but sprites didn't feel as "robust" as they should.
In overall, I believe Alientrap made a huge step forward with Apotheon, compared to their previous game, Capsized. I recommend this game.

Apotheon is a game about defying the Greek gods. They have abandoned mankind, so you must seek their assistance or kill them and gain their powers to save man yourself. The combat in the game is straighforward, as to be expected in a 2D action game; click to attack with melee weapons, which is done with a thrust or swing, and movement is done with the WASD keys. Ranged weapons can be thrown or launched with a bow, sling, or other devices. You can even pick up and throw boulders or stone blocks for massive damage. The difficulty on the default difficulty setting is ridiculously easy, and the next setting really isn't much harder. I think I only died a couple of times. Beating the game unlocks the hardest difficulty, which I have yet to attempt. It's a lot more fun than this simple explanation can make it sound, so I reccomend looking up a youtube video of gameplay if you don't get the picture yet. Also, there is a lot of exploration. There are a lot of goodies to be found if you just look in the right places. There is also not much backtracking, so you don't need to worry if you don't like that sort of thing.
As for the presentation of the game, the art style is done in a Greek pottery fashion. There's a filter that applies to the whole screen, the colors are those that would be used in ancient greek pottery, and the screen will crack if you take too much damage. It is very nice to look at. The music, however, is lackluster. Sometimes it is not even present, and when it is, it does not stand out at all.
So, overall, is the game good? Yes, it's very good. The combat is fun and you will have to plan out strategies for dealing with enemies on the fly. Environments are big and there are many secrets to discover. Honestly, the only nitpick I have is the music. Other than that, though, the game is stellar. Originally I thought I would not like this game, but when I bought it, I was very impressed. A playthrough lasted me 12 hours, and it was fun the whole way through. If you like 2D action games with some exploration in them, it's hard not to reccomend this.

I haven't played a whole lot of this game, but I will say, for what it's worth, my time with The Isle was well spent. In a nutshell, The Isle is Primal Carnage with a survival game twist. As a Dinosaur, you must monitor your needs and hunt/forage for food and water as needed. Humans, to my knowledge, are not present in the game as of yet, but if we are to believe what the devs have told us, they'll play similar to survivors in DayZ or the Forest, mainly crafting and looting for gear and teaming up to defend against and even hunt dinosaurs. There will also be different types of human teams, such as mercenaries, tribals, and cannibals, each with their own playstyle and mechanics. Gameplay is, well, what you can expect from a survival game. As it stands now, Dinosaur gameplay is relatively slow paced and occasionally turns into a game of just walking and waiting for your needs to go down enough so you are motivated to hunt again. As for humans, we'll have to wait and see. It should also be noted that despite the fact you can play as a Dinosaur, they're still player controlled. While Dondi has planned to add mechanics that sort of "train" players to react to certain situations like a dinosaur would, If you bought this game expecting to see everyone behaving like a Dinosaur would in-game as it currently stands, you really won't find it often unless you look in the right place, which leads me to my next point...
The game has certainly come a long way from it's release, but really the excellence of The Isle is it's future plans, not it's current content. The mastermind behind the project, Dondi, has made it clear what he wants for his game and has given a relatively clear roadmap of what he wants to do and create while also not sticking to release dates for content updates, instead just releasing content when it's ready. For this, The Isle has my personal respect, and I can't wait to see what it does next.
- 7.3/10, Gameplay somtimes drags with long windows of time where you don't really have to worry about your needs, but from a wide perspective, as far as survival games go, The Isle does right by the genre.
- If you're frustrated with players who constantly kill on sight or players who "carebear", players who guard other dinosaurs from being killed, and you prefer a more realistic experience as a Dinosaur, find a realism server, such as Isla Nublar.

Great, immersive, old-fashioned sci-fi story which really nails the atmosphere. Remember sci-fi stories that make you think about things? This does a good job of that.
Longer than I expected. I played it solidly for 3 days over two weekends.
The puzzles aren't hard, but do require some thought, and make sense within the setting. Think working out how machinery is operated and then putting it into practise, rather than solving abstract chess puzzles. You feel like you're doing things you'd be doing naturally, rather than contrived puzzles inserted at random points. The puzzles also ensure it doesn't feel like you're just walking from place to place, since you have to work out what to do and how to do it. That keeps things more engaging.
Exploration rewards you with more backstory, and some areas feel large or open but you've never lost or wondering which way to go, and there's usually only one path forward (possibly with some dead-ends and optional rooms or areas; sometiems the dead-ends open up later).
There are moral choices to make during the story, and they are handled better than most games. They're a lot more ambiguous than is typical, and there is no god judging you down there; you play that role instead.
The enemies break up the story and exploration side of things (and sometimes get in the way of exploration), which helps with pacing. On the whole they're a good addition and about right, but there were a couple of times where I wished one just wasn't there so I could more easily look around. However, once you know an area (from sacrificing yourself once or twice), and work out how the enemies behave, they're actually quite straightforward, give or take a couple of moments. (Probably quite hard for the devs to get this just right, since it's hard to know what an area is like for the first time once you know it. If you ever get frustrated, just run around, work out what to do, get killed, then do it again properly.)
Graphics and sound were perfect, really. If you look at a still screenshot or certain areas, the graphics aren't always completely cutting edge (e.g. you'll notice the odd texel or polygon here and there), but when you are inside the game that is irrelevant. They do a great job and the atmosphere is completely nailed, as are the different areas and environments. Some areas look absolutely superb, too.
Game ran at 1080p, 60fps, maxed settings, almost all the time on my GTX 960. Occasional drops to 45fps when standing in particular spots, but never an issue and the adaptive vsync option worked well.
If you've played the great, first Amnesia (and let's not even mention the awful sequel by an unrelated team), this is less scary than that, or at least was for me. The enemies can be scary and some are similar to ones in Amnesia but something about the setting made me less afraid of them, and feel more like they didn't know what they were doing, i.e. didn't mean to hurt me but couldn't really help it. I actually liked that. The game has psychological elements but they're more in the story than the enemies, and while I enjoy the odd 'horror' game I can only play them when I'm really in the mood, whereas this I was happy to play at all hours. I really enjoyed the pacing where there are long sections of story and problem solving without crawling around in shadows fearing for your life. There *are* parts like that, and some enemies that creep you out, it's just not relentlessly like that, and it's better as a result.
The ending is great, too.
Highly recommended.

This game is all about patience and knowing your surroundings and being aware that there are other players. It takes a lot of work in survival mode to get to a higher tier dinosaur and if you're not about the whole "waiting to progress" life then this isn't the game for you. The community is overall friendly but there can be some sensitive players and the common KOS (kill on sight) player or troll. Yet I've made many friends playing The Isle, and I have the patience to play. It's an open world game with different regions either on different maps or even all in one. There's a range of dinosaurs to play from small to large and herbivore to carnivore. Not to mention the assortment of colors they have, whether you want to stand out or rather stay hidden. Some people play for the realism/roleplay in the game, and others play just to talk and have fun. It's not very strict on what you can or want to do, but there are still rules such as no cheating, some servers asking for "no KOS", and the harrassment of other players which is a Steam rule in itself. Overall, it really all depends on what kind of person you are with games. Like to keep things speedy? Probably not the best game for you, since it's slow-paced. I highly recommend watching YouTube videos of gameplay. I'd like to add that The Isle has actually come a very long way from the beginning, and it's a really good game for early access. Highly recommend for people that can handle slow-paced games, like dinosaurs, and enjoy high quality graphics (:
