The beautiful lore, art and writing can unfortunately not save the game from the fact that it is virtually unplayable.
The fundamental survival system is completely broken and unpolished. Due to how enchanting the game seemed after watching it played through twice; spent an hour trying to complete the second level without getting anywhere close to winning. And this is while knowing how the game for the most part works.
Everything is stacked against the player and everything is influenced by random chance. The player has to hide from enemies while both are locked to two dimensional movement. Sounds simple, except; enemies will automatically turn to go after the player if they get anywhere near them. Enemies can box the player into a corner with ease. Doors can close on the player and forcibly box them into a room with an enemy. One enemy is actively faster then the player and thus will always outrun them if the player cannot change floors immediately. Players have to take time to actually generate hiding spots, giving enemies the chance to catch them offguard. Multiple enemies can together box the player into a situation they cannot get out of because there's no where to go.
By far the most amazing one, is that enemies have a random chance of seeing the player where they are hiding, which results in an automatic game over. The fundamental way that players survive, has a random chance of failing and reseting their progress; and players have no control over it. The wikipedia claims this is a ten to thirty percent chance, which is ludicrous; but ingame it seemed to have over a fifty percent chance. Bad. Utterly, amateurish, poor design. Making the primary method that the player needs to utilize in order to play the game, randomly not work. Wow.
It makes no sense, because seeing the game played through twice; the random chance was not nearly this bad. But apparently it suddenly is now, and it makes it virtually impossible to actually win because there are so many specific, unavoidable scenarios where the player can get an unavoidable failure screen that the chances of making it past level two without encountering at least one is extremely unlikely. And because encountering one is all the game needs to say the player lost and reset the level, it's basically unplayable unless waiting for a five percent or less chance of succeeding is acceptable to the player.

I write these impressions as someone who's played the game on IOS and now a little on PC. Perhaps the closest analog to Breach & Clear would be Frozen Synapse's asynchronous turn-based tactical combat, with a dash of XCOM's classes and SOCOM's aesthetic.
Each mission places you in control of a small squad (each country has a small perk, i.e. SEALS have faster reactions). Your team consists of different classes, each with special abilities. For example the medic can heal a soldier or heal himself, the Fireteam Leader can draw all enemy fire to him, the Weapons Sergent can lay down suppressing fire, Intelligence can jam doors. As you level up, your troops unlock new abilities. Your weapons are equally customizable, from optics to grips to gas systems. Limited use gear like flash bangs and snake cams provide more strategic options.
Gameplay wise, Breach and Clear is all about the tactics. Place waypoints, aim line of sights, move to cover, cover your angles. Since enemy placement is randomized, you can never rely on one tactic for each level, instead always playing smart and considering how best to approach a room without leaving a blind spot that could bite you in the ♥♥♥. Don't do that, don't plan well, and your men will die. Your missions will take you across the globe, from Afghanistan and Russia to China and Germany, from simply taking down enemies to defusing bombs and reaching extraction points. Each requires you to play a bit different. The tactics to breaching a room is different than setting up to defend an area while defusing an explosive or moving to the extraction area.
While Frozen Synapse is certainly more complex, I actually prefer the realistic special ops aesthetic and the laser focus on close quarters combat and breaching compared to FS's sci-fi virtual style. And this isn't some crappy port either. The game runs silky smooth, the controls feel great, and the visuals have definitely gotten a nice upgrade. Setting up waypoints and firing angles feels even better with a mouse than touchscreen.
Visually it's not Crysis or Battlefield, but neither was Frozen Synapse. And Breach & Clear makes up for its visuals with cool little touches such as your troopers realistically leaning around cover to fire
I'd definitely recommend Breach & Clear if you enjoy tactical gameplay with a realistic edge.
Edit: PC additions include new weapons and maps, improved visuals, a permadeath setting, and probably some other stuff I'm not aware of

One of the most badass and scary games I've played in my childhood. Period.
Quake II is a classic FPS, which was famous because at the time it supported 3d Graphic Acceleration (the good old 3dfx), the enemy AI was very improved from the classic "runandshootatyou" (enemies had different kind of attacks and behaviours, and the most dangerous ones will crouch to avoid your projectiles), many of them will still try to shoot you a couple of times before dying and... flies will gather around fresh corpses of enemies you've just killed... XD
At its days this game held a huge amount of innovations and, considering the title, one of them was the completely different setting from the previous chapter. No more dungeon-medieval themed levels and enemies: now there are stroggs, cybernetic aliens that create their army by taking enemies corpses and reviving them with cybernetic improvements. Scary enough? Not until you see the levels with your space marine comrades captured, tortured and gone completely crazy. Definitely on a different level compared to Quake.
The arsenal is more interesting than the previous chapter and even bigger, considering there are 10 weapons, and there's a BFG again.
Another huge innovation is the level structure. It was confusing at the time because in certain areas you had to solve certain puzzles in order to proceed, and they required items or explorations in other "dead end-levels".
As a metalhead I can't help but mention the badass soundtrack, something rare to hear nowadays.
Another interesting thing is the possibility to play in Coop the main campaign.
Long story short, this game is the definition of "Old but Gold".

Apotheon is one of these games that mixes defining characteristics from different genres and comes up with a great final experience for the player.
First thing you will notice is the graphics. Apotheon uses the distinct ancient Greek pottery art style to portray ancient Greece and it works excellently. The world is unfolding before you as if you were looking at a genuine ancient Greek vase and with the brilliant use of lighting effects Apotheon leaves an impression like no other game.
Exploration is also a big part of Apotheon. Level and world design are very thoughtful and immersive with a good variety of landscapes, from the lush forest of Artemis where you can hunt game, to the dark, spine-chilling Underwolrd where lost souls crave for your warm blood, the game delivers a fantastic world to discover.
There are plenty of mini-quests and hidden areas along the way to keep you sidetracked and like any respectable RPG, you can enter houses, break vases, steal goods, collect unique weapons, craft consumables and although weapons break, you will always find some new toy to play with.
Second, the game mechanics. Movement is done like any other platform game, you can jump, roll behind enemies, grab on edges and more, while combat is similar to Mount & Blade's. You aim/attack with the mouse and you can change the direction of your attacks by moving the mouse up or down. Also the speed of your character and his position affect the damage done, so gaining momentum before an attack, or hiding behind your shield play a big part in combat.
The combat itself feels very precise and fluid with enough weapon variety to make it satisfying. Breaking shields with a big mace, outmaneuvering them with a long spear, rolling behind them and stabbing them in the back with a sword, pinning them down with a bow or even summoning various creatures to aid you in battle. And although every weapon in the game has it's uses, you can focus on playing with the ones you like and enjoy the most.
Personaly I've never played a game that represents the iconic Hoplite better, so if you crave for some spear & hoplon action, you won't find it elsewhere.

Lastly, I would also like to note the ability to customize how your character looks, something that most games seem to ignore but in my opinion is very important in every game that utilizes armors.
Apotheon has become one of my favourite games of all time and I've been playing pc games since the age that Lost Vikings came out.
To sum it up:
-Enjoyable and dramatic story.
-Unique and impressive art style.
-Brilliant level/world design and compelling exploration.
-Satisfying Combat, good variety of weapons.
-Fair price for what the game delivers.

To start: I used to add a much longer header to these reviews, but since it often made the review too long to submit, I've opted to leave it on my Backloggery.
Gameplay: Let's be honest; it's kinda hard to describe at face value this game without comparing it to Dark Souls. The combat is similarly weighty, the hitboxes are very tight, there's a stamina gague involved, weapons/shields run out of endurance, you can have up to 10 health regen items on you at once... yeah, there's a lot of similarities to Dark Souls in this game. One thing that not a lot of people agree with me on is on the matter of controls: I think this game controls fantastically, albeit not exactly like you would expect. Moving is with the left analog stick; that much you can expect (oh yeah, also I really recommend playing this game with a gamepad), but with the right analog stick you adjust the angle of your weapon, meaning that if you're good enough at seeing the angles, you can very easily critical hit any enemy you run across. Critical hits are headshots, for reference. Blocking is with the left trigger and attacking is with the right trigger. It does take a few minutes to get used to, but once you do, it feels very natural.
As far as the enemies go, they usually have a combination of ranged and melee attacks. They also usually come in waves of four to five, so spacing is definitely something you wanna keep in mind. These enemies are all pretty fun to fight, and it's never an enemy swarm that feels unfair or overwhelming. I will say that the final area could've been one section shorter and have been perfectly fine. As for the boss fights, they're all pretty fun as well. There's plenty in there to keep things interesting, and they usually have their own clever mechanics (even if there are a couple of "giant dude" fights).
This game really doesn't have much of an RPG element to it like the Souls series does. In fact, pretty much the only thing you get in the way of upgrades are armor upgrades or abilities you unlock from defeating certain gods. Apart from that, you've got currency and a rather meager crafting system (which feels kinda shoehorned in, to be perfectly honest) and that's your lot. Regarding the difficulty, I'd definitely recommend putting this game on Hard for your first time through if you happen to be a veteran of the Souls series, as this game can be a bit disappointing in terms of challenge if you're just going on Normal. Even on Normal it does offer some resistance, albeit a resistance of size and not of force, if you understand where I'm going with this. I only died once, and that was because I wasn't paying attention.
Even though my first playthrough only took me about five hours, I could see myself playing this game again in the future (more specifically on Hard Mode). It's a pretty darn competent 2D action game with a pretty good amount of challenge and fun. While not anywhere near being GOTY material, I'd say $15 ain't a half bad price for this. 8/10
Story: I'm not too well versed in Greek mythology, so I can't say with certainty how well this game follows the source material, but from what was presented, it wasn't bad. The writing does feel a bit romp-y at times in that it feels like we're going to beat up all these gods for the sake of beating up the gods (and collecting their powers, of course). The core storyline of the game is, "Zeus is a butt, Hera gets mad, go hit Zeus with your wepon." Dialogue is... well, it serves its purpose and nothing more. There isn't much in the way of twists (at least none that I called from a hundred miles away), so to be perfectly honest, the plot ain't gonna impress you. It does serve its purpose, and it does so pretty well, so I'll give it a 7/10.
Graphics: Well, it's meant to look like ancient Greek bronze art, and it does. The way that the sprites were handled can get a bit silly at times, though. Basically, sprites in this game are jointed together, kinda like what you would expect from Flash animation. As such, sometimes the sprites rotate a bit too far and loop around or separate entirely, and it all just looks kinda silly. On the matter of optimization, I do feel like this game shouldn't be demanding as much from my system as it does. It's by no means a system destroyer, but it does warm my GPU up a bit (about 50degC for my GTX 760), which does seem rather odd for a 2D game. I suspect this is because of the lighting engine. Either way, I didn't have any frame dropping issues or overheating, but I will say that it maybe could've been optimized a bit better. The art is definitely stylish, but the obvious jointing could definitely get a few unintentional laughs out of you, and it does feel like the game could run a little lighter. 3/5.
Sound: Again, the comparison arises to Dark Souls: it does feel like the composer kinda tried to use Sakuraba's style for the boss fights, but they didn't quite match the overwhelmingly anthemic nature of Sakuraba's work in Dark Souls. It's not bad, and in fact for an indie studio an orchestral recording is quite good; it's just that Sakuraba's work exists. The sound design is really, really good on the other hand, as well as the more subtle and ambient tracks this game has to offer. A couple of standout areas are the hunt for the Chimera and Hades. Those areas are very well done. The voice acting is pretty good as well. Nothing that's gonna blow you away, but it's quite a bit better than dev voiceovers. All in all, they did a pretty darn good job here in the audio department. While the boss themes could've had a bit more oomph, the subtleties are all very well done. 4/5.
Overall scores are: 8/7/3/4; cumulative score of 7.3/10. I'd definitely say this game is worth your time if you like games like the Souls series. Just don't expect a Souls game and you'll be fine.

This game is actually very refreshing. It's a platforming hack-n-slash that requires well-timed blocks and a good eye for where to swing. You do navigate obstacles, but the game focuses more on combat. You're often put into situations where you need to juggle between fighting at range and up close. Enemies demand that you overcome their strengths and exploit their weaknesses. The AI is pretty decent, it will strike at you if you leave yourself open, wait for you to drop your guard, and even dodge projecticles if you hurl them wildly. There is a progession system, you upgrade your armor, buy new weapons (which degreade and break after use), upgrade your damage/attack speed with certain weapon types, and purchase recipies for brewing potions (health and buffs mostly). There's a surprising amount of weaponry for an indie game, over a dozen choices. The story is interesting, and while it's not what drives me to play it, I'm definitely interested when the NPCs begin their dialogue. The atmosphere, music, and art are absolutely fantastic; the game does an amazing job aesthetically. The art style is what attracted me to it, but I can say I genuinely ended up enjoying the game; i'd give it a solid 8/10.

The fact that this game has overwhelmingly positive reviews is utterly baffling. The poor graphics and syntax-error laden text are excusable. Everything else that's wrong with the game: not so much.
The creators clearly have vision but lack the talent to see it to fruition. Either that or they're just really lazy. I'm not gonna lie; the concept is really cool but the execution is horroible. The game drops you off in a trailor in the middle of the wilderness without any direction or instruction. (You can find the controls in the setup menu before the game even launches and 3 brief pages of hints found in the main menu give you some vague tips of questionable merit.) Each day you get a new journal entry to read and even if you follow the direction to the letter it's no guarantee that you'll encounter the Rake. So far I can only see it in several locations that trigger scripted actions and give you no opportunity to shoot it (if that is indeed what the objective is) and hanging around camp on the final night. Even if you manage to get a few rounds off before it retreats into the woods, it takes dozens of hits for it to go down. Your ammo is limited so you need pretty high hit-to-miss ratio, which is harder than it sounds because you have no reticle and can't even look down the sights of the gun (the rifle has a scope but you only get 8 shots with that so good luck).
Now let's talk about the cameras: they're worthless. The journal entries stress the importance of setting up cameras to capture footage of the Rake (Is that the objective? Do I even have have to kill it? I really wish the game would let me know) but that doesn't seem to do anything. On the first night, it always takes out two of my cameras. I can see him do it but apparantly getting the video footage isn't actually important after all. You have a map that gives you the locations of all of your cameras, but they're not labeled so good luck figuring out which of the ten or so red marks is the one that the Rake was just at. Oh, yeah, and they all staticy and flicker constantly. I'm sure it's meant to be spooky but all it does is give you a headache.
I bought this game because it promised monsters. Technically it delivered that, but it is far from scary. It's good for a chuckle if you're playing with other people or just showing friends how terrible it is but as a serious game it is among the worst I've ever played. I just hope these can get some better talent in future spooky-monster games because it has potential. This game, however, realizes none of it.

I preordered Apotheon back in May, 2014 for $9.99 and got the game few days before released, as soon as I saw the trailer, I was instantly hooked and pretty satisfied when first playing it.
This is the best adventure game I've ever played, even though it's in 2D, the ancient Greek art style is just stunning and I don't think there's any 3D games could deliever this kind of atmosphere.
Although sometimes frame rate would drop a bit, there's lots of stuff going on in the background, fire, running civs, enimies and allies fighting etc.
Apotheon combines RPG elements with a variety of weapons(all are throwable to attack), shields, training to be more powerful, upgrading your armors, crafting system for potions, traps, and allies(wolf, hawks, undeath... and more).
The game also contains rich Greek Mythology, very interesting to learn about the Gods you're fighting with.
Apotheon comes with local multiplayer with 1 v 1 death match; online multiplayer hasn't in it yet, but according to developers, it's a possible feature.
The story is full of length with lots of stages, side quests, secret passages and maps.
To me it worths every penny so I definitely recommend this game!

After 13 long hours of playing through the game multiple times and getting every achievement (the doppleganger one was the most annoying for me due to rng (random number generation)), I can say that I got more out of this game than I ever expected.  There are many creepy sound effects and jump scares that you don't notice or get your first time playing through the game, so there is some replayability.
Spoilers included:
My first playthrough was exactly as the game instructed, alone in a dark room.  I'm not much of a scary game fan, but the atmosphere definitely made me feel a somewhat on edge.  I found a couple of strategies, one for traversing the forest (holding down), and one for not getting hit on the night levels (staying on ladders).  I wasn't sure what the bar at the top that appeared halfway through the game was before it was too late and I took too much time to complete levels.  I ended up getting a game over, initially annoyed that I had to start the game over.
My second playthrough started off and I was surprised to find that the layout of the house was different, expecting it to be the same every time.  I made it further and encountered new enemies, surprisingly feeling more uneasy this playthrough, now that I know that I'm on a time limit.  Overall, it went a bit better, but I barely got a game over, frustrated at how difficult the game actually appeared to be.
The next two playthroughs I got the two endings, but it felt like I got them out of order, since it seemed like one ending occurred before the other.  At this point, I knew the mechanics very well and  just needed that doppleganger achievement since I was unlucky enough to not encounter this naturally.  It took me an hour and a half to wait for the rng to finally get me what I wanted and it was a bit satisfying.
Overall, I liked how a lot of what happened happened for a reason and most of the rng I saw were things like spawn locations and house layouts.  Some of the rng was a bit too random in my opinion, making certain tasks much more time consuming than they should have been and certain layouts looked very strange and were hard or confusing to navigate.  The story was interesting, I liked how finding out more information was optional and you could finish the game without fully understanding what was going on.  I never did truly figure out why he was going crazy, but there are a couple of different explanations that could make sense.  I liked how long the 13 hours actually felt, usually 13 hours in a game flies by, but there is a lot going on, especially in the second half of the game.  Now that I have 100% completed the game, I do not want to ever play the game again, but I think I'll remember it in a weird way.

Anyone who's ever had trouble sleeping can relate to 'Knock Knock', especially if they live rurally.
Wandering through the darkened house, there is a genuine sense of forboding. Players never know when they open the inexplicably doors locked doors of the home whether or not there will be some ghoul or apparition waiting on the other side. Another great aspect of this game is that as the game progresses, the situation feels progressively more and more desperate. By the later levels, one begins almost to beg for the time to elapse before day break, especially in those situations where you are forced to take refuge in a single isolated room with no means of exit.
Word to the wise, however, this game can be rather frustrating at times. This is especially the case on those occasions where you are inexplicably sent back to the beginning of the level. This is most likely an attempt to explain the philosophical principal that time as an entity is cyclical rather than linear, but even then it can be irritating when you are nearing the end of the level only to have to start over for no reason.
In a nut shell: Is 'Knock Knock' worth buying? Yes. Definitely. Is it for everyone? Not sure. If you're patient and enjoy genre games as an exploration of profound metaphysical concepts then you'll love it. If you just want a no brainer with cheap thrills, not so much.
It really gets under your skin, and not by beeing scary.

When a game manages to invoke fear that leaves you questioning whether or not you want to keep playing, it’s an indicator that the devs have done a good job. Some games utilise jump-scares which will force you to jump at loud noises or sudden movements, but eventually you’ll come to expect them. Creating a sense of fear inside a gamer so intense, it causes you to peek around each corner to check for monstrosities, only to find said monstrosity right behind you, is an incredible feat. Frictional Games take things just that little bit further by making SOMA one of the most scary games we’ve ever played.
You are a man called Simon Jarrett. An average guy, living an average life, working at a comic shop in Toronto called “The Grimoire”. Simon’s life is suddenly changed for the worse in a car accident resulting in brain damage. Simon is still mobile and coherent, but due to this condition, he suffers from bleeding and swelling in his brain, resulting in his life expectancy to be mere months long.
Seeing as there’s not much else to turn to, Simon opts for volunteering in an experimental treatment which includes a scan of his brain.
Everything after this turns Simon’s average life into one of darkness, confusion and pure fear. After Simon’s treatment, he awakens inside a room completely different to the one he initially walked into. The new environment is dark, with unknown technology surrounding him.
It is now Simon’s job to find out what is going on and how he arrived in this terrifying new location.
SOMA is played out entirely through the eyes of Simon Jarrett. You use the usual ‘WASD’ keys to navigate the world you find yourself in, and thankfully, Frictional Games allow us a lean mechanism by pressing either the ‘Q’ or ‘E’ key. If it weren’t for the good old lean function, I would probably have used up more underwear than I own.
The new world in which Simon finds himself isn’t one where weaponry such as fire-arms or melee weapons would be found. You know what this means… there’s no way for you to defend yourself but to run and not get spotted by hostile creatures.
That being said, SOMA has an incredibly delightful system which allows you to pick up pretty much any object you can see. I probably spent a good forty-five minutes in Simon’s apartment alone, opening cupboards, placing pots and pans inside the microwave, turning on and off taps and plenty more. This functionality in itself proved to be incredibly entertaining, but as the game progresses it will also become life-saving.
Creatures that you come across throughout SOMA can sometimes be distracted by picking up an object using ‘left-click’, and throwing it using ‘right-click’ to make noise elsewhere. However, enemies are quite clever and will somehow find a way to hunt you down, forcing that little bit of wee you’ve been holding in to try and make an appearance.
In SOMA there is no health bar, or HUD at all for that matter. If you get attacked, you’ll be knocked out and wake up close to where it was you were knocked unconscious. The only indicator of your health is when your surroundings will become distorted and the screen attains a slight red hue. Simon will also begin limping, causing his movement speed to decrease.
Getting smacked around a couple of times will result in your death, compelling you to start again from the last save point. Unlike some games I’ve played, the save points in SOMA are refreshingly frequent so you won’t be starting again from too far back in your journey.
SOMA contains a massive amount of story to occupy yourself with. As you progress, you’ll learn more about the history of your surroundings, people involved, and even about Simon himself via data buffers, audio recordings and even from the few sentient beings you’ll encounter.
In my opinion, the amount of story on offer in SOMA outweighs the amount of enemy encounters. To some people that might be a bit of a turn-off, but to me it made the whole game that much more enjoyable.
The story in SOMA is what makes it so amazing. The concepts used, such as human preservation, individuality and the like are incredibly well thought out and provide plenty to sink your mind into. Many times did I stop to reflect upon something that was said, such as Simon saying that dying sucks because it makes your life feel more real than ever.
There are times when Frictional Games will throw a decision at you that you’d really rather not make, but by doing so, this opens up the door to replayability. Made a choice you’d rather change on your first play-through? Start the journey again and make completely different choices.
However, making different choices will not affect the ending you come to. There’s only one ending. Or is there?
Story aside, SOMA provides more than enough encounters to leave you biting your nails and leaning over in your gaming chair to try and get a better glimpse around a wall to see what’s waiting for you.
My main qualm is that at times there is a little too much walking. Being one who likes to explore game environments, it was a bit disappointing to not find many little hidden bonuses around these large areas. I was hoping for a few extra hidden goodies like audio-recordings etc.
There does happen to be a pretty massive Easter egg out there which you can see here –
SOMA isn’t an incredibly graphically demanding game but due to the sheer size of the environments you find yourself in, you’d probably need a decent computer to handle the amount of detail found in everything.
Creatures found throughout the game are terrifying and look like something taken right out of Guillermo del Toro’s nightmares. Screeches and roars will leave you squatting in some corner of the game praying that something hasn’t just seen you and is about to sprint over and deal out some punishment.
You’ll find that the music in SOMA heightens your emotions at appropriate times. Music that sounds like it came straight out of an Alfred Hitchcock horror film will indicate something nasty is heading your way, causing your mouse hand to become unsteady as you fearfully flail the cross-hair around to open a door to salvation.
Other times, music will appropriately accompany the sense of sadness you feel when having to make a decision you really don’t want to.
You’ll cry, you’ll laugh (maybe) and you’ll definitely shart yourself in fear at least once. But ultimately you’ll enjoy yourself.
The environments in SOMA are gorgeously detailed and the gameplay is smooth from start to finish. Not once did I come across any kind of progress-debilitating bug which is incredibly refreshing.
Playing through the entire game including reading every email, listening to every audio message etc. will set you back around ten to twelve hours. In my opinion, that’s value for money unlike some mainstream games that provide a four to five hour story and charge you an arm and a head.
The ending will leave you both happy and sad at the same time, but at least everything will be wrapped up in a tight little package. No loose ends here!
If you’re a fan of wetting yourself in fear as you try and escape from monstrosities that’ll probably meet you in your nightmares, or even if you enjoy a story to prompt some self-reflection, SOMA is an absolute winner.

Just like the first one, this is a classic and a must play. The Sith Lords is much darker and ambiguous than the first, and it makes you think a lot more about your actions and motives and the consequences of said actions. It is harder to tell what is right and wrong--your choices aren't cut and dry, light or dark--and with many choices, you will have party members chipping in on what you should have done. Also, your choices really matter as they can even affect what your party members think about you. It is just as immersive and interesting as the first, and the characters are even better and more complex, each with their own interesting backstory, personality, and views, and you don't always know what they will do next. Like the first, the game focuses on the storyline very heavily. It is a really great storyline with many twists and secrets in the storyline, you are never really sure what is going to happen next. The companions with you only make the storyline better. There are also some cool appearances from characters from the previous game and references to it. Granted, it's an old game so the graphics are quite outdated and I don't love the combat system, but I personally think that the other components of the game far outweigh these negatives. Overall, this is a masterpiece and easily one of the greatest RPGs/games ever.

Friday the 13th. Oh where do I begin?
I remember the first time I truly saw anything about Friday the 13th was when I was about ten years old. When my dad was watching TV, I came in at probably the best time for me and the worst time for my parents. It was Jason Goes to Hell: The Final Friday, which was also the first time my dad was seeing it as well. When I came down, I saw Jason being blown up into a million pieces. When I decided to go back upstairs and when I came back down, I saw the doctor eating Jason's heart. My mom was so mad at my dad for watching a movie like this when I was still awake. However, that is just my history behind the first sight of Jason. All I knew was that he was badass.
Skip many years later and I discover a fascination for horror films. I watch the first Friday the 13th, the one without Jason, and even though the story is dumb and lackluster until the last twenty minutes or so, but the blood and gore were still very impressive. I felt the same with the second and forth one, the one that did have Jason as the villan.
Now, why the hell am I mentioning this?
Because this game is truly representative of its movies. I'm dead serious.
One big complaint I hear is that "Jason is too overpowered" and "The camp counselors are too weak" (Notice how I am not making everybody sound below everyone else, as I can see why). I feel everybody is forgetting the true spirit of the movie. In the movies, Jason is this unstoppable beast, who only stays dead for not such a long time. In the movies, Jason was like God, being able to do whatever it wants to do. Also in the movie, the camp counselors are a bunch of idiots, who can barely protect themselves and it seems like the odds are always stacked against them. There is no team work in Friday the 13th that takes down Jason, but a single person. Notice something? The game is exactly like the movie. If anything, he is underpowered, but that should be the least of one's worries. Besides, it isn't extremely difficult to escape or survive the entire round.
However, some other complaints is that the game has too little content, which is true with only three maps, and how there isn't a variety of camp counselors. I honestly wish they had the people from the game and not just Jason. Also, many people are having the database error, meaning we can't play the game that we paid $39.99 (Not $40) for. I can understand the situation, considering it is one of their first games, but I find it a bit unacceptable for a game that is currently only online and not singleplayer
Though, the blood and gore is pretty good, as well as the gameplay in general.
Overall, in this state, I would give it a 5/10, meaning it is painfully average, if not a below average game. I'll give the game a higher score once the database error is fixed and more content is added. I do think one should buy it once it gets to be a lower price, but the amount of content you get for the current price is so bare. Until now, just stick with Dead by Daylight if you want something to fulfill your starvation for hiding or being a killer.

I preordered Apotheon back in May, 2014 for $9.99 and got the game few days before released, as soon as I saw the trailer, I was instantly hooked and pretty satisfied when first playing it.
This is the best adventure game I've ever played, even though it's in 2D, the ancient Greek art style is just stunning and I don't think there's any 3D games could deliever this kind of atmosphere.
Although sometimes frame rate would drop a bit, there's lots of stuff going on in the background, fire, running civs, enimies and allies fighting etc.
Apotheon combines RPG elements with a variety of weapons(all are throwable to attack), shields, training to be more powerful, upgrading your armors, crafting system for potions, traps, and allies(wolf, hawks, undeath... and more).
The game also contains rich Greek Mythology, very interesting to learn about the Gods you're fighting with.
Apotheon comes with local multiplayer with 1 v 1 death match; online multiplayer hasn't in it yet, but according to developers, it's a possible feature.
The story is full of length with lots of stages, side quests, secret passages and maps.
To me it worths every penny so I definitely recommend this game!

Honestly a pretty fun game.  I remember a good year or 2 ago when I first saw it it looked liked a complete piece of trash, but it has come a long ways and is actually quite a fun game.  BRING A MIC, voice chat is pretty crucial in this game and there is no text chat.  On top of that it's also very entertaining as it's proximity based and a lot of players actually seem to use it instead of discord or other programs to chat.  Plus it allows Jason to taunt you in voice!  This can make matches either creepy or pretty damn funny depending on just who's playing via voice alone.
Some of the server issues have been cleaned up and you can at the very least play the game now.  There are some issues that crop up related to servers like sometimes temporarily setting your level to 0 or being unable to buy perks, but you can still play the game reliably now and those other server issues are important fixes on their list.
The main issue when it comes to gameplay is Jason is a bit too strong.  Now I understand why, and if you look at the methods of escape in the game it really is tailored towards Jason killing 3 or 4 people at least.  You shouldn't expect to survive too often, and that's fine it fits in with the movies.  However the game is at its best when Jason is stalking you and always near but you're able to just barely stay alive having JUST enough stamina to make it or placing a trap and running, or getting that baseball bat swing to stun him and running for your life.  The main issue is his Shift move into his grab, and let me explain.
His shift move puts Jason into first person and he moves forward rapidly and entirely invisible.  You can attack or grab directly out of this at any point.  The issue with this being that the move comes off of cooldown fairly quickly (And some of the jasons can get it back even faster), and that while the survivors get a sort of VHS tape error effect on their screen and audio cue when it happens it's almost impossible to avoid against a decent Jason.  Your only hope, especially if you are out in the open, is to zig zag and run back or do a circle or just any sort of move and just pray you avoid it.  Generally Jason will grab you and unless you have a pocket knife you are done for, whether you have 1 composure or 10 composure you really aren't breaking out of that grab if he just wants to kill you.  It takes Jason about a second or 2 to activate his kills that he can do anywhere on the map and it is impossible to escape that no matter what your stats are in time.  He will shift towards you, come out of it and grab and then start the kill animation (Which can NOT be interrupted so once it happens anyone near you can't simple try to hit Jason off), instantly killing you.  Of course he could come out swinging as well but then you may be able to swing at him or toss fire crackers to stun him or something akin to that.  This move almost cheapens the game and has no real counterplay where as, at least, everything else feels like it has SOME kind of counterplay, even if of course you are always at a disadvantage.
Another issue I have is I feel the survivors should have a 10 or 15 second head start from Jason.  I've already encountered several games where I had barely taken any steps and Jason used his map teleport and dropped right next to me, effectively either killing me instantly or eventually as I have nothing to effectively combat him or distract him or stop his grabs.  It does help to just crouch down INSTANTLY and slowly move towards the nearest building, but if you spawned near other survivors and they start sprinting then you might be screwed as they will draw attention.
Overall the game truly has potential to be AMAZING, though the price tag is still pretty steep right now.  It has planned future content for free (Notably a singleplayer campaign type mode), but right at this moment you have 3 maps to muck about in multiplayer with.  Watch a few streams of the game to see if it's REALLY up your alley as it's different and the closest game would be Dead by Daylight.  If anything wait for a sale for the game to be more worth the asking price of admission, or if you just want to try it then buy it and use the Steam refund system after 3 or 4 matches to see if it's really your cup of tea or not.
Edit:  Changing my review to negative due to the Savini Jason situation.  I don't care about the counselor skins, I do care about a different playable character that has his own stats and is arguably the best one.

This game will probably stay in my list of top 10 games of 2015. And that's thanks to the amazing art, beautiful music, solid fighting mechanics, and variety of levels. It's not a long game, but I feel it's as long as it should be. The level designs are wonderful and so is the voiceacting. I'd say that the story isn't all that detailed, but at the same time it's oddly very good and interesting.
If anything, I'd like it if the powers you gained from the various Gods gave you abilities that you would need to get to another God or the very least open up new areas. That said, I do like that the powers you gain acts as buffs so it seems like you really gain that God's power. It also removes the need to backtrack through areas you've already been only to open up new sections of it which can be a bit tedious. I feel they have really found a good balance in their gameplay.
The variety in the levels is another huge plus for Apotheon. You usually have to do 3 tasks before facing off against a God, and they have made each level unique to the God you're fighting. There's puzzles, horseriding, becoming a deer, and lots of neat mini-bosses to fight.

This is little more than a Newgrounds-tier novelty pushed by the sort of hipster that enjoys The Big Bang Theory trying to push a "new kind of gaming" that's "inclusive" and is "transformative media" and other similar buzzwords.  It's not really a game, but the type of crowd behind this non-game titles act like they're trying to be subversive and "push the boundaries" when reality they're just mislabeling things that have some degree of interactivity and labeling them a game for supposedly "artistic" and even political reasons.
It's not that they are bad or awful when standing on their own merits for what they actually are-- Gone Home would be neat if not the intentional insinuations it was some sort of horror game title, and it would even be neater if it was repurposed into an Occulus Rift tech demo; and, (to use another incendiary example) Depression Quest--ignoring the multitudinous editing flaws--may not be so bad if it was labeled as interactive fiction rather than an actual game as it's little more than html pages strung together into a choose-your-own-adventure-book style narrative.
The fact that this was a finalist at a couple of indie shows is revealing of the horrible direction a segment of the Indie games world.  Whereas the hipster types were not content with the damage they had done to the D-I-Y music scenes and the travesties of simplistic and just plain bad art they've produced fit only to line the walls of their local coffeehouses, and unable to accquire enough capital and willing victims to portray in any potential hopeful theater or movie endeavors, they've moved onto gaming as it has expanded in its cultural significance and social acceptability, seeking to inject into it everything from postmodern gags to strange political undertones.
I feel there's some sort of political statement being made with this little flash novelty, but I can't quite put my finger on what it is.  I can't even say I disagree with it.  But this is not a game.  This is interactive digital art.  The controls are deliberately obtuse and infuriating (and not in a OctoDad or Surgeon Simulator way), the "scoring" system is an intentional parody of point-based gameplay, and the overall delivery deliberately obfuscates whether something is supposed to happen if you "do sex" enough times.  It's trying too hard to be edgy, and it's more of a wink and a nod to a certain agenda instead of anything substantial.
Who knew that interactive media like The Graveyard and The Path was actually where a large part of the Indie "gaming" scene actually wanted to go?  It would perfectly be fine for them to go down that route, if they weren't so strangely persistent in trying to push their interactive digital art as "video games." It wouldn't be so bad, if it weren't so painfully obvious that their intent is not only to enter the gaming sphere, but to make a significant change and impact on it in terms of aesthetics, gameplay, political messages, themes, settings and stories in a (in their minds) "subversive) way. I think they have a general distaste for the population that generally games heavily with their political and personal leanings (liberal moderate-to-libertarian, technically adept, usually nerdy male, that isn't a "Sheldon") and wants to break up "gaming culture" to reflect certain other worldviews.
This "how do you Do it?" thing would be an absolutely smashing contribution to Newgrounds, but it has no place on Steam. The simple, pixilated MS paint-like aesthetic and gimmick is well done enough and there's nothing overtly offensive about it technically, but it's not a game and stuck alongside the majority of titles, its presence is absolutely just noise. Valve needs to be more discriminating in its curating (on multiple levels) and not simply allow things on because they did well at some Indie gaming show, because they're trying to trojan horse nongaming interactive digital art into the gaming world that way.

When a game manages to invoke fear that leaves you questioning whether or not you want to keep playing, it’s an indicator that the devs have done a good job. Some games utilise jump-scares which will force you to jump at loud noises or sudden movements, but eventually you’ll come to expect them. Creating a sense of fear inside a gamer so intense, it causes you to peek around each corner to check for monstrosities, only to find said monstrosity right behind you, is an incredible feat. Frictional Games take things just that little bit further by making SOMA one of the most scary games we’ve ever played.
You are a man called Simon Jarrett. An average guy, living an average life, working at a comic shop in Toronto called “The Grimoire”. Simon’s life is suddenly changed for the worse in a car accident resulting in brain damage. Simon is still mobile and coherent, but due to this condition, he suffers from bleeding and swelling in his brain, resulting in his life expectancy to be mere months long.
Seeing as there’s not much else to turn to, Simon opts for volunteering in an experimental treatment which includes a scan of his brain.
Everything after this turns Simon’s average life into one of darkness, confusion and pure fear. After Simon’s treatment, he awakens inside a room completely different to the one he initially walked into. The new environment is dark, with unknown technology surrounding him.
It is now Simon’s job to find out what is going on and how he arrived in this terrifying new location.
SOMA is played out entirely through the eyes of Simon Jarrett. You use the usual ‘WASD’ keys to navigate the world you find yourself in, and thankfully, Frictional Games allow us a lean mechanism by pressing either the ‘Q’ or ‘E’ key. If it weren’t for the good old lean function, I would probably have used up more underwear than I own.
The new world in which Simon finds himself isn’t one where weaponry such as fire-arms or melee weapons would be found. You know what this means… there’s no way for you to defend yourself but to run and not get spotted by hostile creatures.
That being said, SOMA has an incredibly delightful system which allows you to pick up pretty much any object you can see. I probably spent a good forty-five minutes in Simon’s apartment alone, opening cupboards, placing pots and pans inside the microwave, turning on and off taps and plenty more. This functionality in itself proved to be incredibly entertaining, but as the game progresses it will also become life-saving.
Creatures that you come across throughout SOMA can sometimes be distracted by picking up an object using ‘left-click’, and throwing it using ‘right-click’ to make noise elsewhere. However, enemies are quite clever and will somehow find a way to hunt you down, forcing that little bit of wee you’ve been holding in to try and make an appearance.
In SOMA there is no health bar, or HUD at all for that matter. If you get attacked, you’ll be knocked out and wake up close to where it was you were knocked unconscious. The only indicator of your health is when your surroundings will become distorted and the screen attains a slight red hue. Simon will also begin limping, causing his movement speed to decrease.
Getting smacked around a couple of times will result in your death, compelling you to start again from the last save point. Unlike some games I’ve played, the save points in SOMA are refreshingly frequent so you won’t be starting again from too far back in your journey.
SOMA contains a massive amount of story to occupy yourself with. As you progress, you’ll learn more about the history of your surroundings, people involved, and even about Simon himself via data buffers, audio recordings and even from the few sentient beings you’ll encounter.
In my opinion, the amount of story on offer in SOMA outweighs the amount of enemy encounters. To some people that might be a bit of a turn-off, but to me it made the whole game that much more enjoyable.
The story in SOMA is what makes it so amazing. The concepts used, such as human preservation, individuality and the like are incredibly well thought out and provide plenty to sink your mind into. Many times did I stop to reflect upon something that was said, such as Simon saying that dying sucks because it makes your life feel more real than ever.
There are times when Frictional Games will throw a decision at you that you’d really rather not make, but by doing so, this opens up the door to replayability. Made a choice you’d rather change on your first play-through? Start the journey again and make completely different choices.
However, making different choices will not affect the ending you come to. There’s only one ending. Or is there?
Story aside, SOMA provides more than enough encounters to leave you biting your nails and leaning over in your gaming chair to try and get a better glimpse around a wall to see what’s waiting for you.
My main qualm is that at times there is a little too much walking. Being one who likes to explore game environments, it was a bit disappointing to not find many little hidden bonuses around these large areas. I was hoping for a few extra hidden goodies like audio-recordings etc.
There does happen to be a pretty massive Easter egg out there which you can see here –
SOMA isn’t an incredibly graphically demanding game but due to the sheer size of the environments you find yourself in, you’d probably need a decent computer to handle the amount of detail found in everything.
Creatures found throughout the game are terrifying and look like something taken right out of Guillermo del Toro’s nightmares. Screeches and roars will leave you squatting in some corner of the game praying that something hasn’t just seen you and is about to sprint over and deal out some punishment.
You’ll find that the music in SOMA heightens your emotions at appropriate times. Music that sounds like it came straight out of an Alfred Hitchcock horror film will indicate something nasty is heading your way, causing your mouse hand to become unsteady as you fearfully flail the cross-hair around to open a door to salvation.
Other times, music will appropriately accompany the sense of sadness you feel when having to make a decision you really don’t want to.
You’ll cry, you’ll laugh (maybe) and you’ll definitely shart yourself in fear at least once. But ultimately you’ll enjoy yourself.
The environments in SOMA are gorgeously detailed and the gameplay is smooth from start to finish. Not once did I come across any kind of progress-debilitating bug which is incredibly refreshing.
Playing through the entire game including reading every email, listening to every audio message etc. will set you back around ten to twelve hours. In my opinion, that’s value for money unlike some mainstream games that provide a four to five hour story and charge you an arm and a head.
The ending will leave you both happy and sad at the same time, but at least everything will be wrapped up in a tight little package. No loose ends here!
If you’re a fan of wetting yourself in fear as you try and escape from monstrosities that’ll probably meet you in your nightmares, or even if you enjoy a story to prompt some self-reflection, SOMA is an absolute winner.

I don't typically write reviews without playing a game to completion.  However, I also don't typically spend the first five hours of a game utterly lost with no idea how to progress. This was my experience with SOMA. The game couldn't have been more promising. It has a wonderful art style and the premise has a ton of potential. Maybe this premise delivers in the end, but I'll never know. At the end of the day, SOMA is a video game and it has to be fun to play. In that way, by this reviewer's tastes, it falls flat on it's face.
Some gamers might praise a game like this for "expecting more of the player" or "not holding your hand." That is true of some games, such as The Legend of Zelda or Dark Souls. The difference in my view is that those games contain obtuse systems that become incredibly rewarding once you master them. SOMA, on the other hand, is a narrative heavy game that kills it's own pacing and delivery with labyrinthine level design and clumsy stealth mechanics.
Perhaps I will return to SOMA sometime in the future. Maybe then it will click for me. If it does, I'll be sure to update this review to give it a fair shake. For the time being however, SOMA has left me with serious buyer's remorse and to reflect anything else in my review would be dishonest. I regret that SOMA, a game that seemed right up my alley, is my first thumbs down.
+Unique tone and setting
+Promising premise
+Good voice acting
-Confusing level design
-Frustrating stealth mechanics

I've been playing through this game twice a year since release.
Why?
Playing this game feels like what it would be like if the force, the Jedi, and the Sith existed. In the movies they portray the Light and Dark so... blandly. These are GOOD guys, these are BAD guys.

It has some of the best character writing you will ever see in a video game. Your companions FEEL real. They have reasons they behave the way they do. They react convincingly to your influence, whether it be gentle probing or cold interrogation.
You will set out on a journey of exploration. Of people. Of PTSD. Of manipulation. Of the Light. Of the Dark. Of the places in between. Of yourself.
I've only touched the surface of why this game is amazing. I could go on for hours. I have. This is the only game I can legitimately say changed me as a person. It made me really think when I was young, and as I got older there was always more to discover. Some nuance I missed, or now see in a new light. I cannot recommend this game enough.
Thank you Obsidian, and thank you Chris Avellone.

This is a single player review as I don't care for multiplayer games.
I really wanted to like this game. It has some unique mechanics that set it apart from many of the other FPS and 3rd person shooters out there and was fun for a bit till I started noticing the many, many, flaws in it, namely that it tires to be too many different things at once... The biggest problem though, is it suffers from the sameness those games do as well. Pushing the player into corridors and hallways way too often and not giving enough options for strategy or planning of any sort. Being a gun enthusiast in the real world I know a bit about bullet drop, wind, and ballistics and it gets things almost right when it comes to the sniping aspects, for the most part (I could nitpick about lack of penetration namely wood is not bulletproof, and their extreme bullet drop at what are considered normal engagement ranges for battle rifles, but with the limited map sizes it is understanable), as for other weapons? Heck no!
The problem is that for a game called "Sniper Elite" there is very little opportunity to snipe. Bad guys seem telepathic, levels are way too linear and too many corridor shooter parts, too many close quarters combat parts, not enough options for sniping as you are mostly stuck on the ground for much of the game with very few options for good sniping positions... You can climb over some walls but not others even if they are lower than the walls you can climb over! Too many times I thought, "Oh look if I can just get up to that window it would be a perfect sniping position." Nope invisible un-climbable wall that is only 3 feet high! The few levels where you get a nice open map with lots of options for sniping are quite a bit of fun and the only reason I would recommend to get this game but only for under $5.
A big issue I have is with the close quarters combat this game forces on the player way too often... First off, enemies do not spawn until you reach certain trigger points or check points, so in an open area you cleared out, all of a sudden new enemies are swarming you that were not there before, forcing you into yet more close quarters combat because they all telepathically know where you are! There were a few times I thought I had a nice hiding spot and an enemy would actually SPAWN ON TOP OF ME out of thin air! Now that would not be a problem if weapons outside of the sniper rifle could actually hit things you were aiming at, but for some reason an SMG cannot even hit a guy that is 5 feet in front of you! At full auto on the SMGs, bullets seem to leave the barrel at nearly 80degree angles so firing off a full magazine of 30+ rounds you will be lucky if 5 bullets actually hit the enemy 5 feet away. I don't think the people that made this game ever even fired an SMG in the real world because the mechanics of it are absolutely terrible in this game. Some other weird issues, certain enemies’ weapons will vanish when you take them out because the game designers didn't want you to get those weapons too early on, "Oh look he has a Nagant! I want that!" poof vanishes, "Damn."
For a game about stealth and sniping it has some serious drawbacks. The stealth is meh. Also location based body damage is very unrealistic. I thought, "Wow! I love the bullet camera, this is pretty neat! Uh oh I see an enemy sniper's hand! I'll shoot him in his hand and take him out of the battle." So I fire over 5 shots into the enemies hands and he just keeps shooting at me like it never touched him. Or if you shoot someone in the leg they just do a cruddy little stumble animation and then continue firing at you like nothing happened even if you technically would have blown off their kneecaps. Even on hard the AI is terrible... Just find a bottleneck area and the enemies will pour through it even if they see a pile of their dead buddies stacked up there. Relocation doesn't work either, I could run away from a group of enemies to try and pick them off and in most cases, even if I ran halfway back across the map, they somehow always know where I am.
And the final reason for the thumbs down on this game I tried really hard to like.... It is less than 8 hours long and that is even with me trying to explore every little nook and cranny in the game. It does have some replay value for the few good sniper levels, I will give it that.
Bottom line: Sniping is quite a bit of fun in this game, when you are presented with the opportunity to snipe, and the few areas where you can take multiple approaches and the trap setting and strategy can be quite fun when it isn't forcing you down a linear path... But I cannot recommend this game for over $5 because most of the game is close quarters combat with terrible close quarters weapons that cannot hit a thing directly in front of you, the enemy AI is terrible even on hard, for a game about sniping you are more the typical "one man army" type every other shooter game does and sniper rifles feel more like a secondary weapon at that point. If you are going to call a game "Sniper Anything" it needs to have a bigger focus on the whole sniper part.

This game is a little sick, a little funny, and a little weird all rolled into one. Before I begin the review, I would ask that you commune with your personal deity of preference, to insure your soul is not damned to eternity. If the cover art doesn't invoke imagery of a psychiatrists office a few years down the line, I don't know what will.
"How Do You Do It?", is a game of interesting proportions, wherein the player takes the role of a nameless 11 year old girl on her high flying adventure. I can hear you saying to me, "Well Ingredients, everyone loves little girls in video games, just look at Clementine from the walking dead series, or Ellie from the last of us." In response, I would throw a thumbs up at you, while nodding my head profusely in agreement, protecting them is such second nature to us gamers, so much so that America must have secretly withdrawn into a lolita complex we can't identify.
In the midst of America reclining within the depths of said lolita complex, this little gem has arisen, and come to my attention. Girl A, as she will be referred to for the rest of this investigation, is left at home alone by her mother, who is going out of the house for an indeterminate amount of time. When Mother A leaves, Girl A proceeds to immediately rush to her set of dolls, and figure out just what mommy and the man from last night were doing.
Of course, *scoffs* it's up to you and I to help this precious young flower of youth, figure out the depravities of sin and intercourse, by repeatedly slamming two plastic dolls together until she blushes like she finally understands everything one can know.
While, you should understand wailing naked puppets together is only one of your concerns, the other being on constant guard of mother coming home, lest she should catch you unawares, and shame you.
My favorite part of the game by far is its quaint unadulterated ending. Wondering how many euphoric eunuch clicks you produced during your time manifested as a young girl?
Yeah...you know you wanted to ask.
So kiddos, remember to cleanse your chakra stream by embodying the essence of electrolytes after you play this game. And remember not to show it to your actual kids.

Apotheon
~~~~~~~~
Apotheon is a well structured 2D platformer based on Greek mythology.  You play Nikandreos and you have an epic fight ahead of you against the gods. The Greek artwork is really well done and the atmosphere will captivates you in this frantic era.
The levels are fairly large, therefore you will find it extremely useful to use the local and world map to pinpoint where you are. You can also use the map to find ancient writing. You will be able to gather plenty of weapons like spears, arrows, swords, axes and much more.  In terms of protection, armours and shields are pretty much it. Mind you, you can find upgrades for your armours which are often in chests.
Crafting, health potions and fire bombs (Greek fire in the game) are vital to your success.
In regards to the combat interface is actually good but it will take you a little bit of time to master all the different aspects of it. Be prepared to use all buttons on your gamepad. It can be challenging at times.
Positives:
~~~~~~~~

-	Great artwork and atmosphere
-	Large levels
-	Challenging
-	Stacks of things to collect  and do
-	Achievements
-	Trading cards
Negative:
~~~~~~~~
-	Controls a bit challenging at the start (Gamepad)
Apotheon is a little gem. If you enjoyed Guacamelee you will love this game.

I very much wish I could give this game a positive review. It has a lot of potential. Sadly, there is a reason ARK: Survival Evolved just added 200 new XBone servers, and The Isle barely manages to keep one, perhaps 2 servers at peak hours (capped at 75 and 50 players respectively) full.
My review of the game and it's content will be down below, though I can sum it up by saying, the game as it stands is not worth the price unless you're an extreme dinosaur enthusiast who isn't satisfied with ARK, The Hunter Primal, or pretty much... any other Dinosaur game. As I hear it, ARK has a mod that allows you to play as dinosaurs now. And it has a better world map, and lots more gameplay and dinosaur species to offer as well. So unless you're absolutely desperate, I say look elsewhere.
First, I'd like to start off by reviewing what is single handedly the biggest problem of the game.
The Dev Team and the Community.
I wish someone had told me about all of this before I purchased the game... Hopefully someone will find this review helpful, and morally object to supporting these kinds of people. If I can deter at least one potential buyer, I've done my job. ((*note* A couple choice pieces of info will be info I gleaned from other negative reviews and not something I experienced personally.))
The devs are extremely rude and openly admit to being trolls, with great pride no less! They openly mock, ridicule, and attack their community... you know, the people who spent their hard earned money on a very rough early access game. To support their idea. And I don't just mean attack in game. I mean both on their forums and during their live streams.
They openly make fun of players who have physical and mental disabilities (especially autism) and casually use words like the F word for gay people, and it seems like they even use the N word for black people. I myself saw Dondi say something to the effect of "Nignag" in Tyrranosaur species chat during a live stream. There was no one on the server at the time with such a steam name. So I think I can safely put 2 + 2 together here and figure out what kind of person he is, and what he was saying at the time...
Also, during a live stream someone had the nerve to ask if there would be a censor for their human models, like in the game Rust, because they will be naked. Dondi proceeded to show off their models, particularly the genitals, in an attempt to intentionally♥♥♥♥♥♥people off.
You can see we aren't dealing with very mature or professional people here.
Also, don't let their early access game info fool you. Particularly the section about including the community.
I once had the gall to suggest that instead of several small updates daily that push the game from working, to broken, to working, to broken again, perhaps they could wait and do one big update daily. Or maybe even do just a few big updates per week. You know, like experienced developers do?
The lead developer Dondi, proceeded to personally attack me, saying that I was just being a whiner and a cry baby, and that I just don't have the skill level required to play their game. He also said that they ONLY take suggestions from Top Tier players. And those who aren't top tier should just be quiet and quit bothering the poor devs.
How can the game grow if the devs can't take even the most basic of constructive criticsm? And what was the patch that broke the game that I was supposedly martyring, you may ask? It's quite simple. They made changes to the stamina system. Previously, most dinosaurs could run long distances and cover a lot of ground. Then, they randomly changed the stamina values of all species, effectively crippling the speed at which they could travel and making travel tedious at worst and deadly at best. In the next couple of patches, they eventually added both a resting mechanic that helped slightly remedy the issues caused by the first patch, and then a trotting function in a much later patch, which has also helped to ease the blow the changes to stamina caused. But I don't think it was unreasonable to suggest that they add all 3 features in a single patch, rather than add them one at a time and break the game for a few hours. It should just make sense that all 3 mechanics that play off of each other would be added in a single patch. Otherwise, you've basically added bullets to the game without guns...
Sadly, the drama train doesn't end there. Levia Draconia, the skin designer and artist for the game was let go from the project without being paid for work she had already completed. She did quite a lot of stirring the pot. The rest of the Dev team never gave an official response, so we can't really know anything besides what Levia told us, but in response to her complaints about not being paid, Dondi and the other devs completely blocked communications with her, they removed all the skins she had created from the game, refused to allow her to post them on the steam workshop, if and when they added workshop support, and Dondi is on record referring to her as "a leech" and "cancerous". Eventually this issue was settled and it seems like Levia is back on the main development team. But the fact that something like this even happened at all is telling.
The devs also encourage public shaming. After creating a test server, they merely labeled it as (KEEP OUT) instead of... you know... putting a password lock on it? Or something that any experienced "Veteran" Deveopler would know to do. Of course people joined the server despite the "big" Keep out sign in the server name. And the devs responded by creating a "Wall of Shame"
To top the cake, when people reported the thread for the harrassment that it obviously is, the moderator both defended and encouraged the practice.
And lastly (for this section) if it's any indication, the default skins for the game are skins from The Stomping Land (another infamous failed dinosaur game for those who don't know). I'm not really sure how they got their hands on them or what rights they have to them but during their big debacle with their texture artist, the skins from The Stomping Land were the only skins in the game.
During live streams the Devs regularly attack and harrass each other as well. In-fighting amongst the devs could easily lead to them walking away from this project. I really can't encourage anyone to support the game knowing how juvenile and unprofessional the dev tem is.
Oh, and they also have a habit of handing out lifetime bans for anyone they don't like or who disagrees with them. I'm more than certain that posting this review will get me a ban. And if it doesn't well, lucky me?
As for the community, there are a handful who are good people. I've made some good friends and some familiar allies, even though for the most part all we had to communicate were a series of calls and gestures. Unfortunately, there is a disturbingly large chunk of the community who hang on the dev's every word, no matter how bigoted, hateful or heinous. They're incapable of offering any helpful feedback because they accept all of the dev's decisions as if they are from god, and actively attack those who do offer helpful, constructive criticsm in any regard. It is excessively difficult to offer any kind of feed back when the devs ignore it, insult you for it, and the bulk of the "community" are all on their knees playing the blind little fanboy and generally being Dondi's little sycophant crew. As if getting his recognition (which is usually passive aggressive at best, and actively insulting at worst) somehow betters their lives.

As for the game itself...
For the most part it's solid. Though it doesn't run well on low graphical settings or low end computers. Check out the other negative reviews for more info on that. And please, do your research before buying.

The eyes of the Rake and the other animals that inhabit these woods all look the same, so when a deer walks by a camera, you have a startling moment when you don't realize it's just a Bambi's mom. I say Bambi's mom, because, much like the story of Bambi, that deer dies. But instead of a hunter killing it, it's a scary♥♥♥♥♥claw beast. The next day comes 30 minutes later, and you finally think you're safe. You head down to a strange church-like building on the edge of the map. There's a sniper rifle. Then, from the ceiling, the Rake jumps down on you, slashes your face, and runs off. And that's pretty much the game. Rainy nights, cloudy days, and the Rake. Unfortunately, multiplayer (as of this review) has not been added yet, but when it is, I can't wait to kill off my friends by locking them outside.

Jason feels super strong which is how it should be. There should rarely be a game where everyone survives. It feels fun to play as the killer but it also feels really rewarding when you manage to survive as a counselor. Especially if you helped acquire the requirements needed to fulfill how you escape - such as putting the parts into a car/boat yourself or being the person driving to freedom.
Be forewarned, one griefer can completely ruin a game. Either by killing teammates, throwing items into the water or whatever else. If someone is deadset on trolling & making the game a less fun experience for others, it will happen. I've even seen players that will purposely tell their friend that is Jason where everyone on the map is & run around opening/unlocking doors for him. Can really kill the enjoyment. If you can get into private games with friends, I recommend that.
I wish you could skip the game launch opening movies as well as the pre-game & post-game cinematics. It's also exceptionally frustrating when a game first starts and the killer just so happens to teleport to the cabin where you spawned. If you're the first one to die, you have to make the decision if you want to just leave the game or sit there for twenty minutes for the 500xp or hoping that someone calls Tommy Jarvis & that you might get randomly selected to respawn as him. Dying first & quickly really sucks.
The game is fun but I would suggest you wait a week or two to give them time to hammer out some of the issues. It will save you some headache.
