Damn it Obsidian, rushing another promising game...
Leaving us hanging after another phenomenal Knights of the Old Republic game, a game that turned Star Wars in a story... a playable story... a story that was already a story that seemed impossible to become a story, but it is a story so it definitely was not impossible! You guys made it a freakin game as well, a GAME... STAR WARS... A GAME... one where you could mercilessly butcher pretty much everything in your way and still be seen as the good, trustworthy protagonist that totally has no intentions of using them all at your own expense. Nothing lives when you're overlevelled to the point in which shooting lightning bolts out of your hands is as efficient as kicking them in the nuts. Nothing lives, not a damn beating heart.
!! A quick thing, if you're thinking about playing this without playing KOTOR 1, then get off this damn page and play KOTOR 1! You will have no understanding of the story without it, believe me. !!
On the other side of the spectrum, this game captured my heart in many, many, many ways, seriously this game is a beautiful RPG. Even for people who do not necessarily engage with Star Wars, the RPG is just there and it is so pure and so distinct; graphics, sure, they are archaic, but forget about it alright! Ever since that awful MMO became a 'sequel' to this series, KOTOR has been completely shut out of sight **thanks a bunch EA**.
One way this game captured my heart was the ability to be a ruthless Sith, or if you rely on Tampax to fall asleep at night, a nimble Heimskir (skyrim reference) equivalent of a Jedi. Dark; lightning-conjuring, fear-striking, sanity-shredding and just overall "I'm going to tear apart each and every damn moving thing in this game". Or you can be the equivalent of a posh♥♥♥♥♥♥from Oxford. Choice is yours my friend, just be smart with the dialogue. However, I must say I would rather not have my veins on the brink of popping out when I strive down the dark side route. Force self-destruction does not seem particularly safe.
**SPOILER ALERT FOR SAD PEOPLE WHO HAVEN'T PLAYED THIS YET**
A second way this game got me, was the core, dynamic feeling of just STAR WARS... this game is the epitome of what Star Wars is meant to be; the true theocracy towards the Force from both sides, it is such an extravagant feeling that can never been received from canon Star Wars. These are the roots that foreshadow the entire galaxy, thousands of years before the Battle of Yavin. The story is just heartwarming, yet bloodcurdling at times. Squaring off against Nihilus, a guy who LITERALLY EATS ENTIRE FREAKIN PLANETS for breakfast; Darth Sion who just does not want to die and finds the will, through anger, to retain his mortality; Darth Traya (who is formerly Kreia) and also throws a bunch of lightsabers at you simultaneously. The story is flawless. If you're a Star Wars fan and you are proud of it, but you have not yet played this game and you are thinking "HMMMM... should I spend my money on this despite the amazing reviews?" then GET THIS GAME. It will literally impact your life forever. If you have to work an extra shift just so you can afford this (might be exaggerating a little bit), then *DO IT* (+10 points for people who get it) because it is worth every dime... or penny... or button...
The final point I want to make is... you don't have to use a lightsaber at all, as you have various selections of weapons to choose from, although you are slightly nudged towards having a lightsaber. I figured that gun + lightsaber essentially means you are unstoppable, nobody will ever defeat you unless you are truly bad at RPGs. You can nick some Mandalorian gear and pretend to be Jango Fett, except you don't have a jet pack... or a grappling hook... or a ship that you can pilot yourself :(
My conclusion on this amazing, trivial game is just... don't bother reading any reviews (apart from this one thanks guys) and just get the game. It is such an underrated game, it truly is. SWTOR resembles nothing of what this game has to offer, in fact I feel as though SWTOR is just The Sims in space. Pay to play, buggy, ugly, time-wasting and genuinely does not represent what Star Wars should be. KOTOR, on the other hand, is absolutely how to perfect a Star Wars game. Get it, believe me, you will not regret a second of it as long as you can cope with a different style of gameplay.

The result is vagueness; full of potential, but ultimately unresolved.

Amnesia is one of the scariest video games I have ever played. Its chilling atmosphere and dreadful threats make it stand out from its other horror counterparts. On top of that, the puzzles make a tense game all the more intense, but not in your traditional way.
Story: The story in this game is extraordinarily compelling despite not being very original. Your name is Daniel, that's all you know as you pick yourself up from the castle floor. As you make your way through the abandoned corridors you come across a note addressed to you. It tells you of a man named Alexander who must be killed by you in order to redeem both your present self, and your past persona. You are also warned of a shadow that threatens to tear reality apart unless your able to stop it. As you journey throughout the castle you will discover sinister threats lurking throughout the shadows that threaten to prevent you from completing your quest of redemption. These include the omnipresent shadow that pursues your stolen power, the evil and twisted agents of Alexander, and the invisible, water dwelling Kaernks that have gotten loose from their confines. As you progress you will find notes and journals that give you insight into what your former peers and you were attempting to accomplish as well as why your previous self came to hate Alexander so much. By the journey's end you will learn of why you drank the Amnesia Potion, and what Alexander's true intentions were. Then you will be given the options to decide the fate of both Alexander's quest, and your own.
Overall Score for Story: 10/10
Gameplay: The gameplay for Amnesia is what differentiates it from the rest of the genre. As you are told many a time, you are unable to defend yourself from the monsters, so your only options are to avoid detection, and if that doesn't work, run like Bill Cosby is behind you. This experience is made unique by the game's sanity meter. The higher the meter, the easier it is to survive as you'll be harder to detect and enemies will glow blue which will help you to evade them. Having low sanity will cause you to be less stealthy, have a harder time seeing enemies, have distorted vision/hearing, and once it reaches rock bottom, you will crumple to the floor for several seconds in a recovery phase that will attract all surrounding enemies to your area, you can get back up, but only if your not killed. The sanity meter is lowered by looking directly at enemies, witnessing unsettling/supernatural events, or staying in the dark too long. It can be recovered however by progressing through levels and completing puzzles. This makes the game an intense experience as your forced to make key decisions at each encounter with an enemy. In addition to this there are a plethora of physics based puzzles that you must endure to progress.
Overall Score for Gameplay: 10/10
Characters: The characters though few in many are memorable and interesting figures. They all have interesting and engaging character arcs that compliment the theme of the game very well. This includes the protagonist, who despite being silent is a deep and tragic figure, an impressive feat considering the average silent player character.
Overall Score for Characters: 9/10
Graphics: The graphics in this game are quite sharp looking at high settings, but at medium or lower begin to look extremely dated (medium settings look like something out of 2007). Its not too difficult to run at high settings with a steady frame rate so you shouldn't have too much trouble unless your on a DS Lite. The monsters are textured poorly but that's not a big deal, especially since your not supposed to look at them. The lighting is alright, but its no Doom 3. It seems that the lights affect a circular area but don't cast convincing dynamic shadows. Overall, the game looks okay, but isn't phenomenal.
Overall Score for Graphics: 7/10
Soundtrack: The soundtrack is minimal in this game but shows up in all the right places. It truly conveys the intended feeling the game wants you to feel whether it be safe, hunted, or confused.
Overall Score for Soundtrack: 8/10
Sound: The sound design is really good in Amnesia. Footsteps feel full and heavy, monsters make frightening growls, and the physics objects bang and clash and scrape when you interact with them.
Overall Score for Sound: 9/10
This game is great and a very memorable experience. I believe that anyone who likes the horror genre should give this one a try as it will fulfill everything your looking for in a horror game. Please just don't be one of the people who plays it just for scares and ignores the story (you'd be doing yourself a great disservice). Seriously guys and ladies, epic game.
Overall Score for Game: 9.2/10

For honor is an excellent game to me, one that allows you to live in the fantasy of being a fighter who stands far above the common rabble. The feeling of beating someone in a duel and executing them or pushing them off a cliff provides a wonderful sense of satisfaction.
GAMEMODES
For Honor does not boast a large array of gamemodes, rather a simple five. The one they pushed the most to us being dominion, while the idea of capping points, killing grunts and dueling all in a gamemode sounds good on paper, not so much in action. It usually ends up turning into a situation where the more organized team travels around the map ganging up on the opposing team, providing no challenge or honor. The cycle repeats itself until the point limit is reached and all of the opposing team is dead. The vision for this gamemode is both sides being organized, sending each other from one point to another, everyone constantly on the move dueling on points, etc.
Duels and Brawls are what those who love the PVP aspect of the game usually enjoy the most. As it allows for the most balanced environment where both sides showcase their skills. Unlike in the 4v4 game modes, it gives the last player standing a fighting chance since the maximum number of opponents are only 1 or 2 respectively.
Skirmish and Elimination are the final gamemodes in question. While Elimination has potential to be a good field for a team to play together without the capture points. Since everyone spawns encouraging either a 1v1 or 2v2, it also doesn't have the problem Dominion has of a 1v3 or 1v4. It does however have another inherent problem, the buffs that spawn throughout the level. This gives players in specific locations an edge. If this buff was simply a small buff there wouldn't be much of an issue, but we're talking a whole new health bar, immense damage buffs, some health, and a long lasting speed boost. With these buffs, there is no possibility of Elimination being a fair gamemode.
CONNECTION FLAWS
The game has its infamous Peer to Peer connection issues, depending on the internet connection of players and not having dedicated servers brings a platter of problems to the table. Games can be unplayable if someone with a bad connection joins the match, as it affects all other players. It can also cause the game to stop working entirely and try to recover the match if a host leaves, as I've experienced personally.
DUELING MECHANICS
Finally, the block, parry and entire fighting mechanics has its flaws too. The system is easy to jump into and master, but it causes the high skill level play to become dependant on pushing an enemy to their death or using cheesy unblockable move. Quoting Sam (Strippin) indirectly through Totalbiscuit on the co-optional podcast, the perfect defense is achieved by players with high skill. Thus all attacks to and fro are blocked, causing the duel to become a stalemate in that point. It is possible to do damage through a person's block if your equipment provides block damage, though how much of that goes through if your opponents block damage resistance is high I have no idea.
CONCLUSION
I bought for honor after trying out its open beta, and I knew personally I would be hooked and had no intention of playing  any PVP. I enjoyed leveling myself and getting all the cosmetic things while living a power fantasy on bots. As much as I love it, I cannot recommend it until they fix the many issues the game has. And while new heroes are a good way of changing the meta, the dueling system requires some touch ups to raise the skill ceiling while keeping the current simple level of entry.

This is a fun little horror game, with some unfortunate drawbacks.
One of the major issues I had with this game was the pacing of some of the sequences. Basically, the game is played in two rounds - the 'dream' round in which you explore the house and avoid monsters, and the 'dawn' round, where you explore the woods and try to find your way back home. Both rounds are very rich in story and atmosphere, which makes them fun to play, but the 'dawn' sections have a problem - your house does not always appear in the same place you found it the first time. There are good reasons not to enter the house immediately and take the time to explore the forest more, but doing so often leaves you stuck in a loop, constantly just walking around waiting for your house to reappear. This takes away from the frantic action of the 'dream' sections.
There are also some frustrating moments in the 'dream' section of the game. There are times when monsters spawn directly on top of your character, or else extremely close by, which of course makes them impossible to avoid. There are also times when, on the way to complete an objective, the game will lock you out of the adjoining room by turning it into a trap room. You can unlock the room, but doing so puts you in an endless corridor where there is a high chance of having to restart the level. Finally, there's no guarantee that hiding will save you from the monsters - there seems to be a high chance of them finding you regardless of where you choose to hide (although perhaps this is the game's way of telling you that some places are better for hiding than others).
None of these problems are game-breaking, however, and even with these frustrating moments Knock Knock is a really fun, scary game to play. The scares are actually really scary, but you quickly pick up on ways to avoid them so the game becomes more than a jump-scare generator. The player character is very relatable, and you quickly become immersed in their story. You can use different playstyles to complete the game, and there are plenty of collectables to keep replayability an option.
One last thing - it's very important that you keep the sound on. You'll see why.

This game is going to be hit or miss for a lot of people, but if you're as enthusiastic about Film Noir as I am, you will almost certainly enjoy it. You play the ghost of Detective James Renoir, who spends a dark, rainy night retracing his last steps in the hopes of catching his killer. This is done by solving light based puzzles in each area with the help of other ghosts that Renoir is (somehow) able to manipulate. I admit, I'm more into this game for its aesthetics and story more than its gameplay, but I did appreciate and enjoy the puzzles that required actual forethought and synchronization.
Negatives:
-- Lack of puzzle variety
-- Controls can be awkward sometimes
-- All ghosts are male and look exactly the same
-- It's never explained why light is harmful or how/why Renoir can control ghosts
Positives:
-- Classic Film Noir
-- Stellar soundtrack and visuals
-- A wonderful mystery story
-- Interesting characters
-- Creative gameplay mechanic
My love of Film Noir wins out, and at $9.99 the game is definitely worth playing to appreciate its visuals and story. I'm glad I picked it up.

Renoir:
~~~~~

Sitting down with his back firmly rested against his own tombstone, the ghost of James Renoir, a highly decorate police officer who worked in a violent and corrupted metropolis, is eager to find out who put him six feet under. This is the story of James Renoir!
Renoir is an adventure/3D platformer/puzzle game where you take control of the ghost of James Renoir.
First, James has to find a way out of the cemetery. In this level, you will be shown the mechanism of the game as a tutorial part of this level. By the way, the tutorial is rather short but comprehensive.  Very quickly you will gather that ghosts do not like light. In fact, it can kill them. What you will also discover is that you can control other ghosts, which will be extremely helpful to clear upcoming puzzles.
The puzzles are based around the light factor; you have to switch off the lights to advance into the story. In some of the puzzles, there will be other ghosts for you to control in order to help you to solve the puzzle. The trick is to coordinate the movements of the ghost/s to guide them to specific switches, turn them off and clear the way for James Renoir to move forward. Let me tell you that on some occasions, you will wish that you were the one who actually pulled the trigger on Mr. Renoir!
Renoir has a really strong storyline and I am sure you will enjoy the cut-scenes as much as I did!
This game is inspired by the black and white 1940 noir movies and the artwork is absolutely splendid! This is topped by a solid soundtrack which really gets you in the mood of the era. Control-wise, it could have been much more responsive.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Splendid artwork
-	Great soundtrack
-	Good story and well narrated
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Controls could have been more responsive
If you enjoy a good 1940’s black and white crime movie, then Renoir is a must to own!

Renoir is developed by Black Wing Foundation and published by 1C Company. Dev team has been active on Steam for the past two years and this can be seen even in the case of the reviewed game today. It’s both in a polished state and also features the noir subgenre along with some of its tropes. I’m still a fan.

Biased or not, Noir films and literature weren’t always a favorite topic of mine. I guess they really are an acquired taste and it involves some degree of maturity, since the themes present in this subgenre are usually bleak and gritty. Definitely not light-hearted as the vast majority of platformers found on Steam. This is a crucial element of distinction and at the same time, the saving grace of a rather repetitive game otherwise. From the perspective of its story, the game emulates the narrative thread from Murdered: Soul Suspect. In Renoir we also have a ghost detective attempting to solve his own murder. The puzzle platforming genre is sadly more unidirectional than an open world environment. Progression is always to the right side of the screen. Still, between you and your escape door to the next level, is always one constant enemy: Light. Whether we talk of street lamps or windows, apparently your ghostly form can’t pass through light sources and from this obstacle, the puzzles themselves emerge. You can simultaneously control up to 5 ghosts, including yourself and maneuver them towards electrical switches which manipulate trap-doors, elevators and the such.
It utilizes a gameplay mechanic of “recording and playing back” the movements of the ghost you can operate. Pacience and careful planning are both important since getting past some of the obstacles, requires synchronization between several characters at the same time. It gets old very fast and the lack of a more fleshed out tutorial, invites some early moments of frustration. You will keep going though since the story, original or not, still manages to captivate through the intricately detailed buildings (you can’t recreate a proper Noir atmosphere without Art Deco) and outdoor scenery. The cutscenes between levels are presented in the form of nicely drawn comic book-style images which further add personality to Renoir.
A fully 3D platformer that uses grayscale with the occasional highlighted elements in yellow or red. Nothing new on the horizon in neither film nor gaming, but I will always appreciate the subtlety of this chromatic choice. Vivid colors can sometimes express far less than just Black & White would. The soundtrack contains some classy jazz songs which fit the game like a glove, so nothing to complain about that. If only the User Interface segement would be as flawless as the sound selection. The last time I looked in a calendar it was 2016. Why is Renoir’s top resolution option, only 1920x1080? The jagged edges I would notice on some of the assets, locations and characters were only remedied by my creative tweaking within the Nvidia Control Panel, since the game’s video options are barebones to say the least. Massive aliasing issues coupled with the fact that no one replied back to me even after three days of writing on Renoir’s Discussions’ thread about these problems, has left me with a sour taste. Silence is also an answer, gentlemen.

+ Beautiful art style and soundtrack
+ Steam Trading Cards & Achievements
- Repetitive
- Resolution and antialiasing issues
Even with those graphical misshaps which may be a nuisance for you as well or not, I am going to judge this game fairly and appreciate the unique outlook it provides for its puzzle platformer brethren. It is a proverbial “splash of color” and ironically, the very lack of chromatic variation is what makes it stand out. Buy it after it (hopefully) receives some technical support and a price drop.

I've played the crap out of Operation Flashpoint when it came out in 2001 and the same held true for its successors ArmA 1, 2 and 3. Altogether, I assume that I put thousands of hours in it (1000+ hours in ArmA 3 alone).
Arma3 is a military sandbox game, open-world with infantry, tank, air and (a little bit) sea warfare. Missions are highly dynamic, extremely immersive and no playtrough is the same. The maps are very realistic, beautiful and huge and, if you just want to walk from one end to the other, you will have to bring some hours with you. Many buildings are enterable, thus offering unprecedented new types of tactical gaming.
Arma3 improves on many many issues from which its predecessors suffered. For example Arma3 now has a very detailed stance system which allows you to properly position/kneel yourself at a window and to rest your weapon. That said, weapon resting is possible on any suitable object in the world.
You can make your own missions in the offical 3D mission editor or download a ton of missions from the Steam workshop. There are countless high quality mods out there for a game which is highly modable by design and which is one reason for its popularity. For example, the RHS or CUP mods add many vehicles from the cold war era.
Bohemia interactive is one of the few honest publishers where you won't have such things as lootboxes or other gambling-like stuff which we recently observed e.g. in Starwars Battlefront II (Electronic Arts). Their DLC policy is super fair and they even give away platform updates for free to avoid community fragmentation. I can safely say this because I follow every bit of news from BIS since 2001.
Last but not least, I experienced the most immersive and memorable moments of my almost 30 years-long "gaming life" in this game and so I can truly recommend this game to anyone who is into this military type of stuff. But please note: there are even Arma3 mods which have nothing to do with warfare, such as the "Pilot Civillian Air Rescue" mod. Plenty of content for every flavor.

It has a good start, but quickly sours.
Pros:
Good introduction in giving a new tower for each of the first levels
Each level is different
Customization through up to 4 items
In-game shop has items for sale for in-game currency from winning
Tower AI is easy to predict
3 difficulty settings
Cons:
Difficulty quickly ramps up by level 3 to 5, making those extra difficulty settings not worthwhile
Items to equip are RNG and can give you ones you cannot use at the start
Certain equippables are a near necessity early on to stand a chance against bosses
A boss reaching the castle is an instant loss, no matter the difficulty
There are no rewards for losses, so the game incentivizes the grinding of old levels rather than progressing
In-game shop is so expensive, expect to grind an unreasonable amount to buy what you need
Towers do not smart target, so those long cooldown towers will probably waste their long and slow-travelling shots on things about to die
The start button is in the center of the screen, causing early starts
Paths are sometimes very close to the castle
Tower selection is very limited
Tower placement locations are very limited in a snap-to system of perhaps a dozen placement locations.
Wave completion bonuses are unpredictable on if they'll happen at all
Notes if you get it:
Remember to check the Inventory at the level select early on to equip runes.
Arrow towers are not multi towers with items.
Grind early levels for runes to sell and then buy what is wanted.

After twenty hours, I think I can finally make a review on this game.
At the moment, there is very little content for what one is getting for 40$, with the promise of more content on the way, I would suggest that if you don't have 40$ to blow, look elsewhere until that new content has been released.
Friday the 13th is a multiplayer survival horror game in which 7 survivors are pitted against one murderer, Jason. The game can be incredibly fun with the right people, using voice chat in game and having intense matches is some of the fun to be had. This comes with a caveat though, as games online have a tendency to not only have quite a few silent people, but in my experience either connect you to a game that has multiple people from another country who do not speak your language and have high ping, or have them join your game. This server problem is one of the first of many issues with the game.
The game still has quite a few bugs at the moment. There are still quite a few crashes and problems with buying perks (Game will freeze in both these cases and need to be alt+f4'd), People can be stuck in hiding places, unable to leave and jason unable to kill them at all, the prompt just dissappears. The only solution to this is to alt+f4 the game. Another bug which can leave you absolutley angry is that sometimes trying to go through windows won't register if you aren't directly infront of it. This can make escapes feel terrible when you move a step to far and suddenly you cant go out and Jason grabs you. There are more bugs, but these are the most annoying ones.
Another thing plaguing the game right now is the community, there are players who will join a game just to murder other survivors and sabotage there attempts at escape. I've had games where the people with a fully working car hit the man carrying the gas for the other car, get out and take it, then they just leave. This can be incredibly frusturating. There are also people who will leave the game at the round start if they even hear Jason's music. Which makes it so Jason doesn't get delayed at all and now is free to go after more people faster. Then there are the people who leave round start if they don't get Jason. These people will leave you with instead of a full 7 survivors, you'll have 6 or 5 instead. This means Jason has less targets to kill meaning it's easier for him and harder for the survivors.
Speaking of Jason, Jason is at this moment incredibly OP due to being able to use an ability called "Shift" which allows him to go into a army of darkness-esque camera view and move at insanely high speeds while invisible to where he is going. The OP part about "Shift" is that it's only limit is the time you can spend in it. With "Shift" Jason can catch up to any survivor they are chasing and instantly grab them from shift, which is impossible to escape without items which are found randomly on the map. The only way to counter shift is to go into buildings, but the problem with this is that jason can break windows which will damage anyone who tries to climb through them, put traps around the exits, which slow you heavily making it nearly impossible to escape, and then he will smash down the door. This makes it so that escape from jason after he has unlocked "Shift" is nearly impossible if he does not want to leave you, all you can do is delay him and hope an option to escape presents itself. Jason also has access to throwing knives, which he can aim and throw at survivors manually to injure them, 2-3 of these throwing knives will make someone heavily injured, which slows there movement speed heavily rendering them basically dead at that point. It is also nearly impossible to fight a Jason who isn't an idiot in melee, as jason can not only block swings, but grab you mid swing and kill you after a 1 second delay. This makes the game seem so much more stupid during those last ditch effort moments, as Jason will more then likely shrug off whatever you do and just murder you.
There are more gripes I have with the game, but still this game is much better then other games in the genre, and is insanely fun even with all the bugs and imbalances.
TL;DR: 40$ is steep at the moment for the limited content. But it's still an insanely fun game, better with friends. (Good luck getting a total of 7 other people to buy a 40$ game)

You will die.
It happens. It could be a predator that gets you, it could be another of your species or "faction". This game isn't for those who take things personally and/or those who get upset when another person kills them, because it WILL happen. Not everyone is hugs and sunshine with others. On the other hand not everyone is a hyperviolent♥♥♥♥♥♥either and quite a few people are more than happy to trust and buddy up in multi-species groups. A lot of the judgement I'm seeing about the game are based on how the players play, not how the game itself functions. No the balancing isn't that great, but it's not meant to be. It's meant to be an ecosystem, not a game where you can pop onto a rex and slaughter things left and right. Mess with that giant puertasaurus and you'll die. Try to take on an entire herd on your own and you will die. The game isn't meant to be easy, and will only get harder as more content is made and released. That's the point of it. The devs want you on edge, mistrusting others, and wondering just how long you can make it before something gets you. It's meant to be thrilling, and I personally can't wait until it becomes that game.

The First Person SHooter is on of the youngest innovations and new gameplay genres being about 20 years old. It gave some gamers exactly what they wanted from an action relentless fast paced in your face action. ID software set out to change the world with Wolfenstein 3-D and then changed the world for a second time with the original DOOM in 1993. Doom and Wolfenstein brought to the table staples of the genre back in the day:
1. Key hunts
2. Lots of Action
3.Progressivley Harder enemies
4.Secrets
5.Limited health and ammo
6.And your basic loadout of guns
Doom improved upon these with its very open very maze like levels, lots and lots of gore, a crapton more enemies(and a larger variety of them at that) the list goes on and on. But they made one last change to the whole FPS genre that changed what people that the capcity of a shooter was. One word, one single word that shook the gaming world forever. It stoodm for something that would leave other shooters in the dust: "QUAKE". This was the first truly 3-D shooter where the graphics did'nt look like crap. The models and textures were great for the time, each episode had totally different and unique art styles, enemies, and textures. The game had fast paced action and what seemed like ♥♥♥♥ing neverending waves of enemies. Now that's all fine and good but what really made QUAKE huge: ONLINE MULTIPLAYER. It was there in DOOM but QUAKE made it better.
Now what do I think of Quake 2.........HOLY BALLS THIS GAMES KICKS MORE♥♥♥♥♥THEN A DONKEY ABUSER.
Quake 2 had wayyy ahead of it's time graphics back in the day, better multiplayer, smoother and faster gameplay, but it had one thing that even today is still used in every single FPS today and that is a mission structure for every single level. Instead of just finding keys, killing enemies then ending the level. You are now told why you are doing this via a computer menu (can be opened by pressing F1 by default) this gave  some sort of structure to the game that wasn't too offensive. The levels are still fairly open and explorable with some areas not being open until you beat a later level. That's another thing as the game progresses there will be times where you have to return too return to a previously explred area to continue which I found cool.
The music absolutley steals the show with this one. Doom had an excellent thrash metal soundtrack that kicked♥♥♥♥♥and made you wanna rip and tear through all kinds of alien zombie ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s but Quake 2 IMO completley blows it out of the water. With a very head-banging heavy metal soundtrack (that sounds all kinds of crisp because CD based music and shiz) it feels like the perfect soundtrack for a game about a lone marine killing everything that breathes in his general directoin. The soundtrack is what made me pursue this game and is part of the reason why I think this game has aged fairly well.
Overall quake 2 is kick ♥♥♥♥ing♥♥♥♥♥ Great visuals, good enemy variety, AMAZING MUSIC, cool guns, addictive multiplayer, frantic and fast paaced action that keeps you on your toes, and classic key card hunts make this an FPS everyone absolutley has to try. Its not perfect and the visuals have aged but the fast action, high difficulty and great music keeps this game alive and kicking.

If you're looking for a story with a beginning, a middle, and an end, it isn't here.  Instead, it's a hearty chunk of middle with allusions to a beginning and suggestions that it might end.  It's definitely an experience game, and if you go in expecting anything else, you'll be disappointed.  The thing is, it's a damn' fine experience game.
The primary complaint about Knock-Knock is that there isn't enough explanation as to what's going on.  Personally, I found that to be the most interesting part of the experience.  The game plays like a simulator of severe OCD, with the Lodger slavishly serving rules that make sense only to his magical thinking to keep monsters at bay.  Rather than lay down absolutes on whether there's something supernatural going on or if the Lodger's paranoid delusions are worsening, the waters are further muddied by each revelation we get.  By playing strange games, has the Lodger invoked dark spirits, or has he simply convinced himself they're there?  Are the abstract and frightening "reality fragments" the true shape of a changed world, or a chemical stew eating away at the Lodger's brain?  Are the diary pages a revelation of past events, or a story the Lodger wrote and forgot about?  We're never 100% sure, and to me, that's true fear--the constant questioning of reality with no answer to be found, and how easily our perception can be warped into believing our own nightmares.
Knock-Knock is short, it's true, but I've never found that to be a bad thing in a game.  Games used to be long because they were routinely $60 and people wanted to feel like that investment was well-spent, and they were often falsely extended with difficulty or bloated with filler because of it.  Indie gaming has allowed for a full experience in a few hours for less money, and with less time to play as an adult than as a kid, I'm over the moon about that.  If that IS a moon up there...
tl;dr: If you go in expecting a grand mystery to explore every detail of, you'll be disappointed.  If you go in expecting to explore the claustrophobic paranoia of one man and his skewed perceptions, and maybe to question your own reality, you're in for a good time.
ONE CAVEAT: The other primary complaint about Knock-Knock is that it's next to impossible to get an actual ending on the first time through without a guide, and this is completely valid.  You'll most likely end up with an abridged "Game Over" and the "Continue" option doesn't put you back far enough to fix it.  Ice Pick Lodge, for the love of God, PLEASE put a checkpoint in before the last levels.  This is a fixable design flaw!  Until it is fixed, though, know that if you see the bright crack at the top of the screen in the last levels run out, it's time to exit the game and restart--if it runs out and you finish, you won't get a real ending.  As much as the endings aren't the point, it's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ so keep an eye on that bar.

As someone who was born too early to enjoy the '90s first-person shooter craze, series like Doom and Quake were something that passed over me.  Arena shooters (Painkiller, Serious Sam, etc.) were what started my old-school fascination.
While both Doom's and Quake's games are timeless, I find that the Quake series is something more familiar for newcomers than the original Doom games. 3D level design of Quake is hardly something new compared to the sprite-based 2.5D design of Doom.
Even with programs to enable mouselook and higher textures/better effects for Doom, the Quake series feels like a game that has only aged by its looks. Not the core gameplay.
For some technical reason, Steam's version of Quake (and Quake 2) do not have the soundtracks included. Before you go to GOG, you should know that their version also lacks the soundtracks.
If you type in Ultimate Quake Patch (for one or two), you'll find Steam pages where you can download a specific patch just for Steam which will run the game on some other engine with the soundtrack fixed as well as larger font for messages. (It also has controller/joypad support).
I cannot stress this enough: You need that patch. Playing this game without the soundtrack is so boring. Admittedly it feels more atmospherc and horrorish, but having the soundtrack will ease your nerves and keep you going. (The texts also seem more abundant to let you know what to do next.)
The main reason I think Quake is much easier to get into than Doom is not the visuals nor the lack of freelook (without any mods or programs like GZDoom, obviously). No, the main reason is because of Quake's sense of verticality and the 3D level design.
The level design of Quake games are these open-ended, yet linear, maps where objectives require you to move from one place to the next. These involve different transitions to new areas or multiple floor areas with secrets hidden plenty. And backtracking rewards you with finding secrets or alternative routes through the levels.
It's also important to note that these games being linear is not a bad thing. In fact, it's how the game obscures its linear nature that makes it feel rewarding.
The 3D level design makes the game never feel like an 2D labyrinth where you have to exhaust all means to find the exit, and the ways the levels twist-back on themselves makes the levels have a nice sense of cohesion and thought put into them.
That attention is made clear with Quake's sense of verticality. It's not just having multiple floors; Doom has several levels with elevation changes. The game relies on the one thing that breaks Doom: Jumping.
Even if you enable mouse-look for Doom to make it play like a modern game, enabling the ability to jump will break the game itself. Secrets, manueverability around enemies, etc. were built around that limitation, and it feels like an artificial limitation to not use the jump button yourself.
Quake, however, rewards exploration with the mechanic. It enables you a viable means to fake-out the enemies or dodge a projectile. It encourages you to explore above you and below for items you may need.
All of what I'm saying is Quake's demand of the player's spatial awareness goes a long way to distract the player from what is otherwise a linear experience.
The differences between Q1 and Q2 are too numerous to state here. They play similarly enough, yet they both look and feel far removed from each other that you could consider them two seperate games. I think it's personal preference for which is superior.
However, there are several things about Q2 that I think would make it a better introduction than the first game.
For starters, the enemy abilities and telegraphs are much more obvious than in Q1. While I love the Lovecraftian/Gothic Horror vibe of Q1, the Strogg are simply a better enemy type because they all stand out and they all have better visual cues for the player.
Compare the Strogg with the chaingun and grenade launcher hands from Q2 to the chainsaw guys in Q1. It is much clearer to know what to do when the arm with the grenade launcher aims at you than the chainsaw guy's other arm.
A lot of enemies in Q2 have visual cues that you'll learn without having your hand held by the game. The enemies' designs are varied to not become confusing when you have to handle more than one.
Another reason why Q2 is a better place to start is that the game isn't relentless with its enemy mobs. Q1 is more relentless with its nonstop action; Q2 relies on pacing out the fights to guide the player in the "right" direction.
There are also gameplay means to ease the difficulty. Things like the Power Armor (charged by cells for some guns) will improve your odds at the cost of not using up your more powerful weapons.  (And then you have the power-ups you can ration out.)
These will encourage you to not save-scum your way through the game, which will help you get better at other old-school games (like Quake 1).
Backtracking is one thing about Quake 2 that may make or break you, and unlike Doom there is no map-screen.
The game is full of backtracking objectives, but you will more often know where the next objective is if you're thorough with your exploration.
For the most part.
While I have gone into great detail for how Quake relies on the player's awareness for their surroundings, I found one part of the game impossible to solve on my own for my first and second playthrough: Mission 9.
Normally, you can usually check your Mission Objectives to nudge you into the right area to be, and there is usually some visual clue on what you affected with a switch or button. (Besides the text prompts or map names.) And the levels usually feature some visually themed objects or names of facilities to let you know what you are walking into.
Even with a year's difference between my first and second playthrough, I found most of the direction of Q2 intutive and not time-consuming. Except for Mission 9: the Inner and Outer Palace.
This level is an absolute mess of switching forcefields off, transitioning between loading screens, and other means of backtracking. Some rooms feel like Escher staircases, and some rooms will take you to areas you didn't think would be there.
Solution for mission 9: Bring an FAQ or find a video guide to help.
Though not as groundbreaking or "new" as DOOM and not as favorited as the original, Quake 2 is still a well-polished game despite the aging years. Brown-grime color palatte and the lacking Gothic Horror tone aside, Q2 is a classic old-school first-person-shooter that deserves to be played by modern audiences.
It's a game that has not aged well on the eyes, yet it has retained all its vigor in its design.

It combines elements of the Sims, CK2, and X3. You start out as a single person (which I love) and can marry, steal, or trade your way into an empire.
Pros:
+
. Enter any sort of business and make any sort of decision, for better or worse.
+
. Watch your wares move all over town and keep an eye on all your workers.
+
. You start out by micromanaging your single business, but you can start automating each business as soon as you wish.
+
. You may have started out as a tailor, but maybe now your time would be better spent transporting and processing gold and gems? As your wealth grows, you can focus on bigger opportunities.
+
. You empire will crumble if you dont have heirs. Find the perfect mate, have babies, and train them into the perfect person to take over.
+
. Many layers of interactions you can have with other dynasties.
Cons:
-
. This game will seem impenetrable to people not familiar with economic sims. Make sure to opt into the beta so you can access the tutorials.
-
. The pathfinding and some of the behaviors of the automated businesses are not ideal. Sometimes you have to intervene and micromanage.
-
. This is a complex game, and it is a few years old. You will get to a point where you have taken over the map and its time to start over. Perhaps the sequel will support larger map sizes.
Overall, I highly reccomend this to people who enjoyed X3. It might also appeal to people who like CK2, but would like to experience it on a smaller scale with full 3D.

The game that started it all. Wow, its been almost 8 years. We started our favourite night on a laptop that had JUST enough oomph to run this. Our channel on youtube, stream on twitch, and even our website at
was based on a foundation that was this game.
It all began when...
3 friends got together and we played this after work until the AM every saturday, just us since we were off on sundays. We powered this on a laptop and plugged it to a TV. First we would just play the story over and over and laugh and scream and buy pizza! Oh there was pizza...such pizza..and slim jims. The stomach pain was nothing in comparison to the nightmares. We loved it! It was soemthing to look forward to when you work 5 days a week. This game was all we played. then we found it had custom stories. The idea of playing player made levels was INSANE. Mind boggling that the company put this level editing capability into the game...just...wow. Thank you. I never made anything, however I played them all. Zombie escape all the way to a dark night. Each was different and uniqu and some took scary to a WHOLE new level. The campaign, no offense, was like a laugh with some startling moments at most in comparison. All around though, it was why eeryone came over and pile to the sofa to go to what became known as "Amnesia Night". The one night where everyone screamed and was able to open up to anything. If you can scream and show your worst moments of fear to a person, it says a lot. So much easier to break down that wall you build to keep you from society when you just nearly wet yourself next to me.
In the end, we still play it, even now. This game still has a certain level of fear that doesn't compare to anything I have ever enjoyed. Thank you, devs, and thank you to those who bought this and supported it. Especially those who had it on disk way back when. We together have fueled something that has made a great mark on this world. Those who have never played it? Get it now and live a little. Maybe record your reaction. I promise it is very well worth it to laugh at later.

Pros:
- Excellent survival mechanics. Having to manage your sanity and health, while conserving your oil and tinderboxes as you traverse the dark and gloomy castle, all combined to produce a tense, unsettling atmosphere.
- Great scares. I'm hard to scare, and I was genuinely terrified at times. There are jump scares, intense scenes of prolonged thrill, and disturbing overarching themes (which terrified me the most out of anything).
- Excellent atmosphere, sound, and overall tone. Graphics are not the best ever but are nice, especially for a game produced several years ago.
- Great value for what you pay. I got a solid 10 hours of out the game on my first play through.
Cons:
- I love story driven games, and I think what ultimately makes this game suffer is that the plot is pulled in two different directions. There's the elements of straightforward supernatural horror, which I really enjoyed, and then there's another plot involving science fiction/fantasy-ish horror (purposefully not explaining much so as not to spoil) that seemed honestly kind of hamfisted into the game and not developed enough for my liking. I think the plot casts a wide net, and the game was just too short to fully explore, explain, and resolve the two disparate elements of the story. I would have liked it much better if the developers had picked one storyline and stuck with it, fleshing it out completely, rather than the amalgamation we got in this game.
- The scares eventually ran out for me around the last quarter of the game. In the first half, I was absolutely terrified as I walked around the castle trying to explore and solve puzzles. In the last quarter, finishing the game felt like a chore. The horror elements became predictable and I wasn't scared or even creeped out - just bored, waiting to move on to the next objective.
Overall, I think this game had excellent mechanics and atmosphere, but suffered from a plot bogged down by too many unnecessary and conflictual elements. I recommend it, but I was disappointed because for me, it didn't live up to the hype and universal acclaim I had heard about. 6.5/10

One of the best games I've ever played. Mostly in multiplayer. I remember the old times with timeout issues. They are mostly gone, but there are till some bugs. I'm glad developers are still working on it. It even has a fairly big modding community. I've been playing it for a long time, got it in a computer magazine, and I've decided to support the developers once more, so I've bought it on steam. I realise that there were lot of different companies running The Guild since Europa 1400.
This game has a great potential. It's one of the most complex games, but yet it is easy to play, but difficult to master.
It's an economic simulator.
At the beginning you create your character, there are not many options in design, but this is not The Sims. The more important things are the stats and class. You can even chose between 2 religions, protestant and catholic, the only difference in my opinion is that you can only build church of your religion. You can change it in a church.
So to the classes: there are four of them: Patron, Craftsman, Rogue and Scholar.
They are not balanced. The devs and modders are trying to fix it, but it's still not it. I hope guild 3 will be better balanced.
My first try was Rogue (obviously). It was the easiest way to accumulate a lot of money, get rid of concurrence and hold the highest position in the council. In fact, in about 30 years, I've had a huge mansion on a hill and I stopped playing.
That's the biggest problem of the game. In singleplayer, it gets repetitive.
Scholar is second easier, maybe even easiest, because you don't break the law for your job. But you should. Where is the fun? :D
You just build a church and people pay you just to go in there. You can easily make friends and make everybody hate your enemies. I personally like the cemetery, because of all the satanists praying there. Even more than in church.
Craftsman is my favorite, because it has a lot of challenge, mostly in big cities flooded with concurence. The job of a craftsman is to make something from something else. That's different from patron and scholar who just collects their materials, and rogue who steals it.
I don't play for patron much, because I find it boring. So no review of that profession.
Every profession is necesarry in a town, maybe except of the rogue. Without patron, craftsman cannot produce clothes and so on, and scholar cannot make medicine or other stuff. It is probably the most frequent reason of dying or bankrupting. No scholar means no hospital, what almost certainly means death. I hate that AI does'n really have a stock of more expensive medicine.
Overall AI isn't so Intelligent, but in recent updates and modpacks it is more agressive and more complex. I hope that it will be better in The Guild 3.
So I think that's enough for now, nobody is reading it anyway, I will maybe write another one regarding some other features, like marriage, children, burning down your neighbours house or kidnapping your mother in law.
I'm really looking forward to The Guild 3, in fact, I would gladly do alpha/beta testing.

I have finished the game, and let me tell you, I really liked it. This game is the epitome of an indie quality product. The amount of inmertion thanks to the background music and, of course, the outstanding artstyle, makes this a game worth trying. I took 10 hours, wich for the price of this game, is pretty fair. Also, I haven't done all of the game's "sidequests", so I still have more to do.
Something important that I didn't expect from this game (because it isn't stated anywhere in the store page) was the fact that it's open world, therefore, those "sidequests" exists. Altough some are just are kind of dull, they give a change of pace to the game if the player ever wishes for one. But either way, the game changes the pace by itself. For example, getting to Athena is very diferent from getting to Poseidon. And in a related topic, let me tell you, I was surprised by the amount of creativity that the boss fights have
+Pros
1.-THE ARTSTYLE. You can see that the artstyle is not only unique, but well crafted and incredible. It's what convinced me to buy the game, and I wasn't dissapointed. You really feel like you are one big piece of ancient art, and it's amazing.
2.-Greek mythology. Many games think that just because God of war succeeded with Greek mythology, it's easy to abuse it. That has been proven wrong. But in this case, they nailed it perfectly.
3.-The controls. They are very responsive, and once you get a hold of the weapons, you find your own fighting style naturally.
4.-Level design. Once you finish the first level (which works as a good, non-boring tutorial) they give you a bit of freedom to do as you please (but thread carefully). In the levels themselves, the enemies feel in place, and the moments without combat generally serve a purpose, and last just long enough.
5.-Boss fights. If you are like me, and like a good, creative, brutal and old-fashioned fight against a
mighty, fearsome and satisfying enemy, then this is the game for you. The classic feeling stays there even with the large amount of creativity that most boss fights have. Rarely are two boss fight the same, or even simlar, which is impresive.
6.-Pace of the game. The "tutorial" is fun, and gives a good taste of what's to come. The difficulty curve is very smooth (unless you try to go too crazy and go, for example, to Hades before Apollo, you may have a bit of trouble). And as I said before, every boss is different, and also the common enemies tend to vary, so you must change strategies from time to time. This prevents the game for getting tedious at all times.
-Cons
1.-Hitboxes. Sometimes you are sure you hit somebody (or that you got hit) but nothing happens. If youlike close combat, you may find a strange and maybe awkward combat situation now and then. And this is way more common that it should. Most times it is actually funny, but when the game gets harder, it might end in a frustrating moment.
2.- Map design. It's not bad by any means, just that sometimes is a little too simple, and relies on changing "areas" to keep the flow of the game. The again, the inmersion of the game makes it hard to noctice sometimes.

Ah, Quake II. I remember the first time I played this wonderful game. It was a quiet spring day and I got home from school. I immediately booted up my old Windows 98, which was a little slow but for games it worked well. I waited patiently for it to finish loading up everything. While it was doing that, I looked around the messy computer desk to find a game to play when I found a copy of a game with a name that I immediately recognized. Quake II. I had already played the first game. It was one of the first games I ever played. It was a memory that would never leave my head. So, as a curious child with nothing else to do, I popped the game into my CD drive.
I immediately noticed something different with the game. The install screen showed creatures I had never seen from the first game and the backgrounds during installation showed futuristic facilities that looked nothing like the first game. I was confused, but excited at the same time. I could not wait to see what hid inside the game itself. The game finished installing and, as a now very excited child, started up the game. The menus looked and sounded a lot different from the near-steampunk menus of the first game, but I shrugged, set the difficulty on easy (I was a kid what do you expect?), and watched the intro.
The intro starts off with a camera zooming out of a weird structure while weird news reports were discussing the plot of the game. An alien race, known as the Strogg, have invaded earth in a galactic war against the human race. They destroyed numerous cities in their time on Earth. The humans surprisingly shove them back home and now we are going to fight them on the Strogg home planet. Then the camera zoomed out to the Quake II logo. A light suddenly shined behind it and blew up the logo! I was completely speechless. I didn't know what else to do except keep watching.
After the explosion, a ship flies from the bottom of the screen with tons of guns and artillery for taking the Strogg down. The intro then cuts to a bay that looked like a prison, but then the doors opened and revealed what I thought initially were cannons. Next I saw one of these weird things about to be launched. It had the name "Bitterman" on it. I then knew that these were pods about to be sent to take down the Strogg. After being launched, Bitterman gets clipped by some cowboy and loses a little control but gets situated. On the planet, we come to this big cannon looking thing on the planet and suddenly...all hell breaks loose.
Screams blast through my speakers as I learn what happens next. Apparently, the Strogg forces knew the humans would be coming, so they prepared an EMP for them and killed the marines with it. Somehow, getting clipped by that cowboy saves Bitterman, but he overshoots the landing zone and crash lands into a bunker on the left side of the big gun. The screen goes black as the sound of clashing steel fills my speakers. Shocked by the intro I had just witnessed, I had to play this game. I was completely speechless from the intro and I had to see what the gameplay was like.
As soon as the game started up, I looked at where I was and was amazed by the graphics. It looked great! And I loved how I could see the hand that was holding the gun. A nice touch by id Software, and a really innovative thing for 3D graphics in 1998. The look of the levels was really astonishing too! The color looked so much better than the really brown color of the original Quake. I was very pleased with the look of the game.
But when the game loaded, something else filled my speakers. The soundtrack. The legendary guitar-filled soundtrack. This is easily one of the best parts of Quake II. The original Quake had a more ambient soundtrack which did sound great, but I felt that it didn't fit the actions you were doing. Quake II however had a much more fitting soundtrack. It's definitely awesome to listen to. I highly recommend the soundtrack. The sound effects sound really good too. The blaster sounds like I would imagine a blaster to sound like, and the other guns have really satisfying sounds. My favorite sound effect has to be the Super Shotgun blast. It sounds powerful, like how a double-barrel instrument of destruction should sound.
The controls are of course fluent as they should be. One thing Quake II adds is the ability to crouch. It's a nice new action that does help with aiming and avoiding enemy projectiles. It also adds new ways to get secrets in each of the levels that are in the game. Speaking of the levels, I LOVE the level design in Quake II. They are big and wide open with lots of secrets to find. You could play a level for hours just to find all of the secrets! Yes you could do this in the original, but Quake II I feel is a little better at this.
The one thing I did enjoy more than the already awesome single player was the addicting multiplayer. This was the first game I ever played online. I was a child, but that didn't matter to me! I was playing one of my favorite games with other people! I was enjoying all of it! Of course I sucked, but it was fun just playing with others on the internet! It didn't matter to me back then. I was just having fun!
Of course I could only have so much fun with Deathmatch. I did notice however that there was a server with a bunch of players, so I checked it out. I was in for a ride though as I found myself playing what would become my favorite game type in any video game. Good ol' CTF! In CTF, short for Capture The Flag, you are on a team going after the other team's flag and returning it to your base. It was super addicting and really fun. I must have been on for hours just playing CTF with whoever was on at the time! It comes with Quake II nowadays so it's awesome to see that it is avaliable at anytime!
What I also discovered on the CTF server I was on was custom character models to play as in Quake II! Pretty much, a character model, a huge improvement over the skins system in Quakeworld, is a custom-made model of any character you can think of to be used in Quake II to play as. I'm not even joking when I say any character you can think of. There's a huge variety! Beavis and Butthead, the kids from South Park, Fox McCloud, and tons more to choose from! If there's a character, there's probably someone who made them avaliable to play as in Quake II.
Overall, Quake II is legendary. As soon as I was done playing it for the first time, I knew I had found something special. Everything in Quake II is amazing. The graphics, the sound, the single player and multiplayer, everything. It was the first game I tried to introduce to a friend and he got into it really quickly. It was my favorite PC game for many years. If it wasn't for the badass Duke Nukem 3D, this would still be my all-time favorite PC game.
BUY IT NOW!!!!

Alright, jokes aside! The Isle is very much a work in progress. There are bugs, and it can be frustrating at times, but it is steadily being updated and progressing at a rather quick pace compared to most Early Access games.
For a game with dinosaurs, it is the best at this moment in time. The models are great! While not all of them a realistic they cater to the fans of realism and fiction. If you want to be a feathered Rex you can! Soon you can be a scaled Rex (young, sub-adult and adult!)! The same with the eventual addition of Utahraptor. There will be a realistic feathered version and a Jurassic Parkish one. And it is also super fun to take a break from all the butt munching to relax (but not entirely) as one of the many herbivores!
There is not much to do other than PvP right now and because of this the balancing of dinos can seem, well, unbalanced. That is because, in the future, there will a progression system implemented. Where you will start off as the weakest creature of the playstyle you want. Carnivore or herbivore. Which is the base of your tree that branches off into many species.
To get the current super carnivores (Rex/Carno) or super herbivores (Puerta/Trike/Galli/ Shantu) each that is the best at its lifestyle will not be quick or easy. It does say on the store page this game will be hardcore. However, for now, they are all easy to access which means everyone, and their mom is playing as them. In the future, it will not be this way.
Lastly, there will be playable human and human-ish races. Survivors, Mercenaries, Tribals and Cannibals! Each will have their own playstyle. Survivors will, well, have to survive. Mercenaries will be more FPS. They will be able to tame some small dinosaurs, get jeeps and helicopters. Tribals will be the tamers and be able to tame nearly every dinosaur on the island, even player controlled dinos!
In the end, I think this game, with so much versatility, is easily worth the price. However, if you can't stand bugs, do not have the patience to wait for fixes, and take things too personally both in the game and in the discussion I would HIGHLY recommend you wait to buy until the game is finished.
I would also recommend not buying this game if you do not meet minimum requirements (obviously), and you are under the age of 18. While the game is not rated at the moment, it IS a mature game.
Now if you pass all that and happen to like following the development of games and seeing how it grows I can easily recommend it for you!
I hope this helps you to decide on your purchase and I hope to meet you in The Isle!

I've had this dream before. Sort of like a dark version of Bill Murray's "Groundhog Day", where I run and run to try to get away from *something* that's chasing me, and I finally make it to the front door, open it, and... I'm back in my room trying to get out again. That's this game, only I'm sort of like a punked-out Chucky doll in a nightgown and my house is way tidier than it is in real life.
To be fair, I haven't beaten it yet, but I intend to when I can give it my full attention. This game *deserves* my full attention. The sound effects are nice n' creepy, the locations and characters are beautifully drawn, and I'm really digging the plot. The Lodger is appropriately self-aware, and there's something about the twisted Simlish that he speaks in that reminds me of the narration at the beginning of Lars VonTrier's "Riget". I like the mechanic of going into the rooms and waiting for the furniture to fade into view -- it may be repetitive, but that just adds to the dreamlike atmosphere.
This is not an action game. This is not full of adrenaline-boosting jump-scares. This is for when you have insomnia, and need something to make you feel like falling asleep ever again would be a bad idea. It's also great if you want to turn the volume up way loud and make your roommate say, "What the **** is THAT?" And then they take a look at the game and fear for your mental health. It's beautiful, and dark, and eerie, and dreamlike, and wonderful.

Apotheon is a real gem of a game from a very involved developper. The fact that this game managed to pull me in and provide a memorable experience despite the fact that I don't generally like side-scrolling action is a testament to its charm. While Apotheon shamelessly borrows from Capsized (the dev's previous release, which I also highly recommend BTW), it still manages to offer something special. The fabulous atmosphere created by the original art style and music, the highly responsive technical real-time combat, and surprising variety of scenarios and playstyle options make this an overall above-average game, especially for a smaller developper.
PROS:
-Great ambiance with unique graphics, excellent music/sounds and real voice acting(!)
-Engaging story and lore delivered in a non-interfering way
-Simple and responsive controls with high freedom of movement
-No real frustrating/annoying puzzles blocking your progress
-Tactical, real-time combat is fast-paced and satisfying
-Boss fights are well designed and require some quick adaptation
-Huge selection of historically accurate weapons allow some playstyle options
-Good amount of optional content (secrets, extra locations and "side quests")
-Nice variety of locations, objectives and scenarios
-Involved and dedicated dev who actually cares about the product
CONS:
-Fairly short campaign (CAN be a PRO if you're busy and like actually finishing games)
-Limited replay value
-Late game balance is real cake-mode unless switched to higher difficulty
-Some boss encounters can be frustrating until you figure it out
-Somewhat lacking crafting/inventory system feels a bit incomplete
TL;DR - There is very little I can say against this very original and well-executed game: 100% worth the price and time. (Also see Capsized)

The main reason I'll recommend this game is because you get a ton of value for the price if you get it on discount. It's more or less a medieval version of sims♥♥♥♥♥business tycoon♥♥♥♥♥political simulator.
+Many types of businesses you can choose to run in the game, each filling a certain market demand, and your town grows as you hire more employees.
+Interesting political aspect to the game, including elections, where you climb your way up the political ladder for more privileges like immunity from the law.
+Many options to dealing with your enemies, including dueling, defamation, taking them to court, kidnapping, or just plain murder.
And now with the cons:
-AI is terrible at managing certain high level businesses. It’s frankly quite broken and doesn’t do what it’s supposed to do.
-Market demand is non existent for certain products. They will remain on the market  pretty much forever and depress the price. The AI doesn’t know how to utilize some of the higher level items and will never buy or make use of them against you.
-Indicator during politics or court sessions not always reliable at predicting the result.
-AI is more or less passive and relatively peaceful, making it pretty much impossible to be killed by one and thus lose the game. Even if you fast forward the game 40 years, the AI even at their meanest doesn’t go around killing people for the most part and while fighting amongst themselves not one of them will eliminate another. If any one of them is going to die it will be because of the player.
My overall impression is that the game had a pretty good and unique concept, but it was executed somewhat poorly. After all the patching it is pretty playable, but still somewhat buggy. Again, the main reason I’ll recommend it is because if you get it on discount, the value you get blows many other games you can get at a similar price point out of the water. Another thing to add is that the Guild 3 is supposedly coming out this year, so you can treat this game a bit like a preview as to what you may expect from the upcoming sequel.

Amnesia: The Dark Descent
Reviewed by: Weston Fleming Mcnamara
I am both amazed and terrified. My favourite genre is horror and this really pushes the limits for how scary a game can possibly be. I did not know much about Amnesia until a friend reccomended it to me and I am very happy he did.
Overview: You are a young man named Daniel. You awake in Brennenburg Castle with barely any memories left. As you stumble around the castle you find pages of a diary. YOUR diary. You find out that you drank a substance that caused you to forget everything. After uncovering even more diary pages your past self tells you to go to the inner sanctum (An area in the castle) and kill Alexander Of Brennenburg. At first you cant tell yourself why, but as the game progresses it becomes more clear. Alexander is a horrible person. After more diary entries you realize there is a shadow following you. Not just any shadow. One that wants you DEAD!
Pros:
-The scariest game I have ever played and im sure more people agree.
-The creepiest atmosphere in any horror game I have ever played.
-When the shadow is close it can be nerve racking and and scary.
-A great story and background.
-A great choice for horror lovers.
-Completely worth the money.
-You will not be bombarded with jumpscares unlike other games such as FNAF and outlast.
Cons:
-Challenges are not difficult, but looking for something such as a lever or switch can be difficult to find sometimes.
-Items are difficult to find.
-Once the shadow finds you are probably screwed. Once he finds you he wont give up.
-LOTS of backtracking. Once you die you will be tempted to quit.
-Boring ending. It does not feel rewarding for being terrified for a couple of hours.
Final word:
This is NOT for the faint of heart. If you cant take the scare, it will sit in your library forever. Do not buy it if you are new to horror. If you have patience and can take a scare, Throw on your headphones turn of the lights, and have fun...
