Game has AWESOME atmosphere.  Despite the brightness being too high (and hardly any game options so you can't fix it easily), daytime being extremely saturated, and nothing happening most of the time... It still manages to be terrifying.  At least at first.  Most horror games rely on jump scares and constant danger (Outlast) but this game takes a completely different approach.  Now it's just you watching nighttime cameras and not knowing what, if anything, will happen.  The tension this creates is incredible... At least until you start getting bored.
In the end there isn't really much content yet and even when you do see the creature you'll probably be disappointed.  It's not the worst creature in a game but it doesn't match the sheer tension that has built up by the time you see it.  Disappointing really.  Once you learn how the game works and how the enemy behaves, the game becomes incredibly simple.
Overall I see a ton of potential here.  Enhance the enemy AI a bit, make it better animated (and get better textures if you can), and find something for the player to do during the long hours of the night when they eventually get bored.  As of right now it's fun for about an hour then gets stale, but it's also very early access and, in my opinion, worth every cent they're asking for it.  If you enjoy slow paced open-world type horror games, give this a shot.
NOTE:  Below is my story, it's long.  You've been warned.
Day One: It's bright out... Really bright.  Like bad hangover bright.  Other than that the place looks nice enough.  Plenty of gear lying around in the trailer I arrived in so I collect as much as I can and decide to head out and explore.  Five steps outside the trailer and a pig from hell comes darting out of the bushes squealing, probably laughing at my now soiled pants.  Oh well.  Onward!  After placing five cameras near my base I realize there really isn't much to do and if the HUD is correct I still have 25 real life minutes of daylight.  I explore a little bit but am excited to get to the meat of the game so I head back to the trailer and sleep until night.
Night One:  It's dark out and I'm already nervous.  Turn on the camera feed to take a look at what is going on only to realize that Camera 5 is already out somehow.  Did it go out in the day and I just didn't notice?  Or is something already out there?  I spend a full minute trying to work up the courage before finally blasting out my front door with shotgun in hand and running to where the camera was.  Surprisingly it wasn't as dark as I had thought, I could see well enough without the crappy little flashlight I had, but that didn't make me feel much better.  Upon arriving I saw that the camera was indeed gone but didn't hear or see anything else.  No sign of what had taken the camera out in the first place.  After standing there surveying the area for a few seconds I quickly replaced the camera then booked it back to the trailer, slamming the door as quickly as I could.  No idea why I got spooked, but I could feel a chill running down my spine from my little excursion.  Not a bad start.
I finally get back to the camera feed and began switching through the cameras.  Camera 1 kept sensing motion and blinking at me thanks to a pig that kept getting caught in a trap near my camper but everything else was quiet.  Saw a few pigs on the cameras but nothing else.
Ten minutes later I begin to get bored so pull out my phone to watch a Youtube video but make sure to keep an eye on the camera sensors in case anything happens.  Nothing.  Ten minutes left at night and nothing happened.  Starting to feel less tense and with the video over, I start switching through the cameras to try and learn the layout of the land better before I explore tomorrow.
Four minutes later I switch over to Camera 5 again and hear footsteps just out of viewing range.  Probably a pig again, but I decided to wait until it came into view.... About five seconds later the footsteps turn into running and my heart skips a beat.  Moments later the camera goes offline as some ungodly scream fills the audio.
I don't know if it was stupidity or courage but I decided to go out and find this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ while I still could, now that I knew where it was.  After sitting around for 24 minutes I needed SOMETHING to do.
Equipping my shotgun I begin sprinting through the woods, too scared to look around me for fear that the damn thing will jump out at any second.  Upon arriving at the site of Camera 5 I don't see anything but I do hear footsteps further up the path.  I quickly replace the camera then slowly proceed up the path, trying to see what is making the noise.  About halfway up the path I hear the footsteps turn into running.  Running in my direction.  I quickly bring up the shotgun and aim in the direction it's coming from, unsure what to expect...
And then I see it, a horribly animated and textured creature rapidly waddles out of the bushes before I blast it point blank range in the face.  A second later it's running off already, scared off apparently.  Fight or flight kicks in and I decide that fight is the best option, so I follow it.  Turns out the Rake is one of the loudest walking creatures on Earth (actually most creatures in the game are) so it's easy to follow.
I keep a clear area between me and it so I won't get caught by surprise in the underbrush, but otherwise am able to follow it easily.  After about tens seconds of chasing I hear it stop and return to normal walking speed, seems it finally calmed down.  I slow myself as well and carefully approach, trying to keep to open areas as much as possible.  Sure enough, I start hearing it run for me again and so I do what I did before, I wait.  Soon as it appears I fire again and off it runs.  Now it's become a game, with only a few minutes left.  I begin chasing it all over the map, firing as soon as it gets close then chasing after it.  No longer is this a horror game, now it's a funny game of tag.
Unfortunately the time runs out and instead of the sun coming up I get teleported back to my trailer.  Almost had the bugger too...  I had been hit once that night as he ran by me in a panic but my health was still pretty high so I considered the night an overall success.  Now to hope that he wouldn't heal during the daytime.
Day Two:  Exploring.  That's mostly what I did.  I found a few dead pigs (some with their heads on spikes) and a lot of old buildings and hunting stands.  Stumbled across one building where the Rake was apparently hiding out and got hit again as he took off out the door.  Scared the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me but I was more disappointed that I hadn't gotten a shot off than anything else.  Health still looked good, about 80%.  Nothing to worry about.  More exploring yielded an area where FPS dropped down into the single digits, some ammo, traps, and a sniper rifle.  Not a bad haul.
Night Two: Now the game begins again.  I'm watching the monitors just to see where he comes from this time, hopefully it doesn't take all night.  About five minutes in I'm watching Camera 4, one that has a great view of a large open clearing near a lake.  I must have great timing, because I hear footsteps and a second later I spot him approaching the camera.  I wait until he breaks into a run to attack the camera before I exit the feed and take off after him.  No need to replace the camera now, this ends tonight.  After a ten minute game of tag I finally land the final shot on him with my trusty shotgun and am rewarded with "You win!" on the top of my screen.  I should feel victorious, but honestly I feel a bit dirty.  The Rake wasn't really much of a threat after all, and learning his pattern so easily made the game a breeze.  Perhaps future updates will change this.  Perhaps he will become a true threat some day.  One can only hope.

Most games force you to run away from the scary monster, this game forces you to hunt it down and kill it. Rake is an interesting game based off a Creepy Pasta of the same name.
You play as a hunter in the middle of a forest with a hunting rifle and sniper rifle to defend yourself with. During the day you set up digital cameras, animal feed and bear traps and during the night time you sit in your caravan, watch your cameras for movement and try to find The Rake somewhere out there in the darkness.
It's terrifying at first until you realize The Rake reacts the same way every single time, running straight towards you, knocking you over then running away. Once you get a bead on his location it's easy to keep him in your sights and make sure he never gets the drop on you, even if it does take 30 odd shots to put him down.
This is a neat concept but deceptively basic and there isn't all that much to talk about or experience. Like the Slenderman games it seems to hinge more on the popularity it has as a Creepy Pasta, more than it does try to be its own thing. It's not early access but it sure does feel like it at times and Unity engine is at its unoptimized best, dipping into single digits on the lowest graphical settings.
I guess if you have a Let's Play channel this is a no brainer to pick up, everyone else might want to hold off.

Got this game as a gift from a friend of mine and it's been a ton of fun. For Honor is an action/3d Fighting game from Ubisoft Montreal with a fantastic premise, great gameplay, beautiful graphics, and a massive host of issues both major and minor that keep the game from being as great as it could be.
PROS:
- As listed above, great graphics, gameplay, and core concepts
- Gameplay is very solid. If you want a weighty melee combat PvP game then For Honor might have some major appeal to you.
- Decently sized roster of 12 characters (6 more planned for future free release), all with unique playstyles, strenghts and weaknesses that are very enjoyable to learn to both play and beat.
- Tight controls that make nearly every mistake feel avoidable, letting you grow from past failuers and improve.
- Around 6 hours of single player or co-op campaign. The writing is a little silly in places, and the plot goes from slightly confusing in places to blatantly obvious in others, but as long as you don't take it too seriously it's pretty fun, and actually a bit of a challenge on the higher difficulties.
CONS:
- Peer to Peer connectivity is the biggest issue that plagues this game. Constant issues with connection hiccups (from a couple frames of jitteryness to full lobby disconnects) and the security issues that peer to peer usually entails are the biggest things that hold this game from being recommendable.
- Microtransactions in a full $60 game is honestly completely exploitave and deplorable. The in-game currency, steel, can be gotten at a reasonable rate just through playing the game, but steel costs for the higher end cosmetics and buying/upgrading gear can take hours to days to grind towards. The game is relativley generous with steel from daily and bi-daily contracts, but the grind is definitely still there and the option to simply bypass it with tacked on microtransactions makes the grind feel inflated to promote paying to evade it.
- Gear stats in this game are somewhat fair and balanced until you reach the "Heroic" level gear you can start getting for a character once they reach reputation 3. The highest tier of gear gives massive buffs for 2 stats and a minor downside for 1. At the time of writing this stacking gear for base damage, revenge gain, and revenge damage allows players to simply play defensively for a short while, then get massive health and damage buffs to shrug off damage while 2-3 shotting almost anyone in their path.
- The matchmaking in this game is nearly nonexistant. I have a profile reputation of 7 (Basically the conbined number of reputation level for all my characters) and I see a fair share of players in 1v1 duels who are either far below me with reputations of 2 and lower, or far above me with reputations of 12 and higher, which is a pretty big imbalance in player skill and understanding. There are also a bumch of other annoying matchmaking kinks like finding a match only for the game to kick you out because the match you just found was full, or getting into a match and immediately getting softlocked while waiting for the game to "syncronize" for eternity.
IN CONCLUSION;
For Honor is fantastic. I only have so many issues with this game because of the insane amount of potental it has that it can live up to as long as the devs keep on it, which so far seems like what they're trying to do with the transparency from their community managers on the fourms and subreddit. The only concern I have is that the devs will try too hard to please the community, ending up hurting the balance or aesthetic of the game.
All in all this is a really hard game to not recommend, but until some of this real glaring issues are fixed, it's just not worth $60 to roll the dice on whether or not you'll never see an issue or never see the game working properly. Hopefully in a couple weeks I'll be able to come back to this review and completly rewrite it in a more positive light, but until then, hold off on buying it if you're on the fence.

A long wait for this game but so far I'm very impressed. I've also edited down below where I talk a little about the controls. Where to start?
-Level design: big sprawling levels, with various "missions" to complete in each one at your own pace and order. A good variety of different environments and I've barely seen anything yet. Also there is a good variety of missions too, the gameplay is not repetitive.
-Weapons: Very large variety of different weapons. Melee weapons can be thrown and picked back up. Arrows and javelins can be retrieved as well. Really gives you a lot of options when fighting enemies. I even picked up a boulder and threw it on someones head crushing them. Each weapon breaks and discards after so much usage, but they last a good while before they break. And you find them all over, so you're never unarmed scrambling for a weapon to use. For weapons that you can only carry one of(like the sword), when you pick up a new one, it will discard the old one and not allow you to pick it up again. I like this feature because it's one less thing to manage or think about(Whether or not the sword you picked up was the same one that was about to break that you just dropped) I recommend use a weapon only good enough to beat the opponent in front of you, save the best weapons for the bosses.
-Crafting: There is a crafting system, whereby you collect plants, fangs from dogs you kill, etc. And you also get recipes from characters throughout, some they will give you others you will have to buy. You craft healing potions, "Greek Fire," bombs, powder to summon wolf companion, powder to summon Eagle companion to hunt for you. The crafting system is simple, easy to use, and yet there are so many good features it brings to the table(Like the wolf companion). I can't wait to see what else you can make.
-Mythology: Stones are placed all over the world with quotes from Ancient Greek literature. They seem to be relevant to where you are in the world as well. By this I mean they inform the creatures and gods directly around you, so you never really feel lost if you are not a scholar in Greek Mythology. I'm learning and it's fun!
-Various: Gameplay is great, controls are responsive. I've seen some reviews that think the controls are clunky, but this was not my impression. BTW I've only used a 360 controller. There is certainly a learning curve, but after an hour I had the hang of it though and never looked back. There is an endurance bar in bottom left that will drain if you button spam the melee weapon, and it will take you longer to swing slower. You really need to use your shields and time your strikes. Don't just rush in after a group of enemies, but rather strike from a distance, set up traps, and rush in when numbers are thinned.
Really creative and unique boss fights(like Artemis, Apollo, you'll see). Voice acting, music, and sound effects are great. There is even some humor in the game(the satyrs made me laugh).
These are just some of the key points I wanted to highlight. I can only imagine the blood sweat and tears that went into making this. Alientrap did an amazing job. I don't want to say anything definitive about any game before I finish playing but this game has quickly become a favorite, leapfrogging hundreds of games in my backlog I've been meaning to play that will now have to wait even longer. I think we may have a masterpiece here.

I have never felt the need to write a review on Steam, but this game deserves one.
Where do I start...
Apotheon is a side-scrolling action & platforming game. The story in short, something is wrong/corrupt on Mount Olympus, and now you have to whoop some a** to find out why. It is much more in-depth than this, but I do not want to spoil anything. If you like reading, there are also several "vases" scattered around the world to really flesh out the story and even educate you on some of the myths.
Do you remember studying Ancient Greece Mythology? Remember those finely crafted vases? What about the Disney movie, Hercules? Remember when they had segways and story-telling on the side of a vase? That's the art style of this game. In fact, the gameplay is as such as well. The animations completely capture the feel of those vases. It almost feels clunky at times... a good clunky... a clunky that makes sense in this art style. If this is turning you away, don't let it - it needed to feel this way if you ask me. Plus, the enemies experience this as well.
After 10 minutes, you'll realize that this is probably one of the most highest quality Castle/Metroidvania that has come out in a long, long time. You find weapons, buy weapons, pick up weapons off the dead bodies of your opposers. These weapons include: (Melee) Sword, Clubs, Spears, Hammers, Shields (Projectiles) Arrows - many different kinds of them, Javelins, Bombs, and Greek fire. Armor is upgradable. You get special powers from defeating bosses.  There are probably tons more as well, I'm only about 2-3 hours in right now so I have a lot more to see.
The game also covers many popular mechanics of today as well. Like crafting? It's in the game, and it's actually useful. They didn't complicate this game with recipes that require TOO MUCH reagents. Want to make a bomb? You only need 2 items. Potion? 2 items. Not a fan of potions or bombs? You can make traps. Hate traps? You can summon companion ravens and wolves. Hate companions? WHO COULD HATE A COMPANION WOLF?
Anyhow, I think I'm done writing this review now - because I want to play some more. I'll update this is I find anything else that NEEDS to be noted.
TL;DR: Buy it.

I'm not quite sure how to describe it... it certainly is surreal, abstract, spooky, and different, and unlike many horror games (especially the popular ones...), Knock-Knock's scares don't really come from its jumpscares (despite the jumpscares being startling as well), but rather, its ambience and the overall feeling of... dread and helplessness. Knock-Knock doesn't use blood and gore as nightmare fuel. Rather, it takes advantage of your own confusion, with almost unreliable tips from the protagonist (the Lodger), and many enemies that look and behave differently. I don't recommend this game to those who expect total guidance from the video games they play, nor do I recommend it to people who get frustrated from confusion, but I instead recommend Knock-Knock to those who are getting bored of jumpscare-fests and gore, for Knock-Knock's scare factor comes from its subtlety and psychological absurdity. Even if the game isn't the scariest one around, it's worth it for its unique presentation.

Any game that claims to not be a game is throwing up a pretty big red flag right there. Knock-knock does that in the opening splash screen, and if anyone besides Ice-pick Lodge made it, I probably would have taken a pass on it. But the creators of Pathologic and The Void know what they're doing on that front, and the result is an intriguing little journey that definitely has its moments.
You take on the role of the Lodger, a wired little fellow that looks like Calvin ditched Hobbes and took up meth. Something odd is afoot in his isolated home in the woods, and if I get any more specific than that I'm bound to spoil something. Much like all of Ice-pick's games, the actual game is figuring out the rules of the game. You can turn lights in the house on and off, hide behind furniture, force open doors, and advance time with a strangely narcissistic clock. Ostensibly your goal is to survive until morning, but the house and its... inhabitants are randomized every other day, and on the other days you spend a chunk of it in the woods. Even the goals themselves get muddled as you progress, and the game is not afraid of throwing entirely new mechanics at you a few hours in.
Once you understand the pattern to the game, it can admittedly get pretty repetitive. New challenges are introduced the further into the game you get, but the core gameplay of lighting up rooms and wandering the woods does not change. One thing it does do well is introduce new threats over time, and some of them are absolutely terrifying despite the almost cartoony presentation. Information on the story comes from many different places, including the Lodger's diary, notes between days, and the Lodger himself, who talks in a charming nonsense Sims language. Most of the way through the game I'm still unclear on much of the rules and plot, but I admit it's fulfilled its original promise of "interactive meditation" and kept my attention. Definitely worth a look if you are at all curious, but be prepared for the mystery and horror to carry some rather bland gameplay.

Learning isn’t really a popular theme for video games these days it seems. I find that a real shame, as there is not much that can be more immersive than a well-made video game. Being dropped into the middle of a strange culture, and absorbing every aspect of it is supremely satisfying for both spirit and mind. As someone who knows quite a bit about Greek mythology, it’s quite obvious that the team over at Alientrap has done their homework as well. The weapons are all standard fare for the time, and can each serve a different purpose. There are ranged and melee weapons, but in a pinch your can throw your melee weapon with the middle mouse button. Just try not to break them all before you find a replacement. The durability on weapons adds greatly to the survival aspect of this game, but is really only the tip of the iceberg. There is a lot here to be excited about, so let’s get into it and take a deeper look at Apotheon.
The story revolves around a Greek warrior named Nikandreos, who has been sent by the goddess Hera to kill her god-husband Zeus as punishment for abandoning the people of Greece. Along the way you will fight Zeus’ brothers, daughters, and sons. As you defeat them, you will be powered up. Artemis’ Bow will allow you to fire arrows faster, Apollo’s Lyre will illuminate the dark so a torch isn’t a complete necessity. Before you fight the gods, you will need to complete objectives within their realm. These usually consist of “find this” but some are a bit more thought out. Stealthing around a Satyr party to smash all their wine and make them leave is bliss. Make good use of your Assassin’s Dagger, which does 600% damage from behind. It might also be a good idea to craft some stealth potions… Or you can craft a bunch of explosives and healing salves, and just go Rambo on them. The choice is yours, and adds quite a lot to the replayability.
On top of using a different loadout of weapons, there is also an advanced difficulty mode. Enemies have more health, swing faster, and hit harder… I wouldn’t recommend it to start with due to the quick nature of the combat. The aesthetic in the game really captured me, it is all based on the Greek art commonly seen on all manner of decor of the time. When the game goes extremely dark, you might notice that the dark nothingness appears to be made of stone. Major kudos to the guy who thought that one up. I just wish the music was able to keep pace with the graphics, but unfortunately, to me it falls a bit short. It’s not that the music breaks the mood, or isn’t enjoyable. I just found that the songs didn’t really stick with me. Still, the multitude of creatures and heroes and gods that you meet along your path towards bloody revenge would be enough for me to want to complete the story, even if there were no music at all.
There is very little criticism I was able to find in Apotheon. Some of the hitboxes are wonky, which can lead to a comical mid-combat moment of both characters flailing their weapons wildly and hitting nothing but air. The music is also a bit bland, as I stated previously. Overall though, I love everything Apotheon has to offer. The endless struggle to find a useable weapon and shield, the crafting of potions capable of amazing feats, and the terrific speed of the running and combat. The entire game feels very fluid, and comes together to form an experience that I’ve never had before and doubt I ever will again. While you won’t be able to write an essay on the rise and fall of Greece, Apotheon is a great game to brush up on your mythology. Or you can just enjoy it for the experience it is, which is great. But I think the tidbits posted add a great deal. Who doesn’t want to read a little passage about Apollo? And once you’re done learning about him, you can murder him! Huge thanks to the folks at Alientrap for developing something that is so much fun, and even slightly edifying.
Summary: Greek action-adventure peppered with survival elements and lessons on mythology.
Final Score: 8/10 for aesthetic, story, replayability, and education.

This is a clone of Plants vs Zombies, but with some of new ideas. One of them is dividing units onto disposal and non-disposal ones, and two types of in-game currency.
This game looks good, and music is quite good too. But this is only true for the first 2/3 of the game. Last levels are terrible.
And by terrible I mean it's hardly playable - there is too much SH...T happening on the screen and I could barely see what to do.
Also it's getting incredibly hard on last levels. On the last level two large destroyers appear at once, destroying two rows of your defense, and if you build something in their way - they just destroy it by simple touching it.
I had a wish to complete all levels with maximum rating, and I already wasted too much time and effort so I decided to use a trick. I managed to complete last level by slowing the game down to 30% of its natural speed - this way I managed to take many actions per second, and slower enemy movement allowed me to see something in that mess.
Also, note, that to beat second part of the game you  will need to grind A LOT. Top units cost money, so if you can't beat the level - you must grind previous levels for about an hour to purchase more heavy units and make another try. Thankfully, if your disposal units do not die (regardless of winning / losing / restarting) - they remain in your "inventory" and you can use them again.
I hate pointless grinding, so I used hacks to obtain money, and it took me 20 hours to beat the game. If I had to grind money  - it would have taken 50 hours or more, which is too much for a game like this.
And the most frustrating thing... There is a story, it's driven by text description of every mission. But when you complete the last of them - it just... ends. No final video, hell, there is no text, no congratulations - nothing, you just finish the incredibly difficult last level and look at he map but nothing happens. Yon can't even return to main menu - ALT+F4 is the only way out.

is a classic tower defense game. There isn’t much of a story, your kingdom is in danger and you’re a knight tasked to protect the castle. The lack of story or any characters with personalities means that everything focuses on gameplay and I found this boring. If you enjoy tower defense games then you’ll have no problems, but it also doesn’t add anything new or inventive. What it does offer are three campaigns to go on and a total of fifty levels to keep you busy.
Your goal is to defend the castle from waves of enemies. You can erect towers to attack the enemies and the game offers of a variety of different types. They range from a basic tower that just attacks one enemy, a multi attack tower and even ones that can slow down enemies or bomb them. There are different types of enemies, some fly, some are fast or have high defense. The strategy of the game is knowing which type of defense to put up when you need it. Towers can be upgraded in game but there is also a shop where you can purchase permanent upgrades or special attacks. I found the upgrade shop to be the most innovative aspect of the gameplay, everything else is run of the mill tower defense logic.
Graphics are fine, it’s a cell phone app port so they’re colorful and eye catching up but don’t have much depth. The characters are very generic looking and the levels are pretty forgettable. That said, I did like the graphics because they were simple and easy on the eyes. I appreciated that, though the maps are a little small. Audio wise it’s fine, the music is there but not impressive. There is no voice acting and the game could use more sound effects honestly.
+ Relatively cheap.
+ Decent graphics.
+ Simple to grasp gameplay.
+ Steam achievements and trading cards.
- Repetitive gameplay mechanics.
- Port of a cell phone game that is available for free.
- Doesn’t offer anything new or different in terms of the tower defense genre.

In this game you play as a knight who got an order from a king called: King Dragnor. The King told him to ‘fight’ to the invaders of his kingdom. You are not real fighting to them with your classic sword, but you are the person who is building traps to slow enemies down/kill enemies. You play each level in waves, there can be a range of waves from 3 to 10 at a time. This game starts off very easy and you may think that the game overall would be easy to play. But believe me, it gets a lot harder later on in the game. You have to build towers, and you can make them even better! So you start with one that is shooting arrows, later you can unlock more towers and some other nice goodies that you want to have! The game has a big variety of levels and maps, and that is making the game also fun to play! Also there are a few bosses, and some of them are hard to defeat, so the strategy is here to not spill your money.
From a graphical perspective, it’s not that good, the quality of the game is a little bit low, but still nice to play this game! Also if you look at the details, you will see the little things what are making this game special to play, as example the stockpiles. This game has also options to lower the graphics and resolution. I haven’t encountered any bug or fault in this game in my played hours, so the dev of this game has done this nicely.
The sound department of this game is very nice to hear, especially when you start a fight. The most sounds are also funny and they are original. If you are talking to the king or to a boss you aren’t hearing any sound. Some voice acting in their chats would be really appreciated.

For them you just get extra steel (the in-game currency) and earlier access to new content (we will all get it free eventually). $60 would be a steep price for the game if it was never going to be added to, but the devs have said there will be at least 6 more characters to come (on top of the 12 now in game), and probably more maps.

The combat system is surprisingly meaty, rewarding players for proper timing of their attacks, dodges, blocks, and parries, while punishing button-mashers harshly. 12 different classes to choose from, each with their own attack types, feats, and combos, as well as a fairly robust amount of customization for each class, both in terms of gameplay and cosmetics. The story feels somewhat tacked on - which surprises no one, considering the game was designed with multiplayer in mind - and can take anywhere from 4 - 8 hours on average, depending on the difficulty you choose to play on. The story itself isn't going to win any awards, but is still surprisingly good for a tacked-on addition. Going into multiplayer, realize that while the game may be called For Honor, most players are willing to fight without, and will happily toss you off a cliff if it means winning a match. Finally, it should be noted at the time of this review, the singleplayer campaign *is* always-online, and multiplayer is peer-to-peer, which can cause connection issues, among other things. Matchmaking also tends to suffer errors somewhat often, but these make up a tiny fraction of playtime in my experience.

This game is rad. So many melee combat games have tried to find a satisfying balance between simplicity and granular control, and Apotheon absolutely nails it. Being able to toss a javelin, roll between the legs of an opponent, then send a slash up his back while his shield's still facing the other way makes me buzz like nothing else.
Weapons feel distinct from one another and satisfying in their own ways. Though it didn't take long for me to discover my love of heavy-headed polearms, I'm always pleased when a situation calls for something different and I'm rewarded with an entirely different (though no less enjoyable) visceral interaction. There's something to be said for the intimacy of shield + knife.
The world is pretty big, with a solid variety of enemy types and challenges, but what I thought was the coolest is how all if it was informed by Greek mythology. I was tickled when I realized I had to stab a certain enemy in the eye to bring him down.
Also, if you've got a buddy on hand, the local arena mode makes for a fun time. They can try to kite you with arrows all they want, but all it takes is one well-placed javelin... (or a quick roll and slash combo... or a mighty leap with hammer in hand... etc.).
All in all, if you like combat platformers with a dynamic rhythm, Apotheon won't disappoint. Strong recommend.

Essentially The Isle is a open world survival game where you get to choose from different classes of dinosaurs, each with their own perks, and all extrememly well modeled and animated, and try to survive playing as the dinosaur. This game feels REAL. The point is to survive, however, there is now a progression system in place which is brutal but rewarding, so essentially you start out small and choose from lower end dinos/humans and fight to survive, earn points, and work your way up the food chain. This isnt a building/hoarding sim, its raw survival. If you are looking for a building sim with dinos go buy ark, if you want an authentic prehistoric survival simulation (soon with a fantasy twist) you have come to the right game. I have already put over 200 hours into this game in its infant stages, money well spent as is.
Another good thing is that the developers are constantly putting out meaningful, and well done updates to improve gameplay. The game came out early december, and it has already become unrecognizable from the game i first purchased, so ti'm pretty satisfied. We've gotten multiple new dinosaurs, new maps, progression, new content and game modes, and a crap ton more, overall a great game and strangely addicting.
Though you do have to suffer through bugs sometimes after updates, and most of the time they are very irritating bugs, they fix them promptly. Some also complain about the developers being abraisive, which in some cases ive seen to be true when people push their buttons, sometimes they snap. However, I have spoken to the devs on multiple occassions and they have been very helpful and involved within the community. They are only human, and have bad and good days, and can only handle so much stupidity.

As many other reviewers are saying this is a blatant rip off of Plants Vs. Zombies. But that's not necessarily a bad thing. I love Plants Vs. Zombies. Robowars does introduce two forms of currency--power and money. Power lets you build and rebuild towers during play. However you purchase a number of 'money towers' at the beginning and are limited to that number through the current game. Buy too few--too bad you lose. That means you wasted all that money too. SO you get to go back to earlier levels and grind out more money to buy more 'money towers'. And if you're thinking like I did--I'll just handle the level with only 'power towers', Good Luck. Thanks to the very slow recharge of your towers (including 'money towers') and the fast attack waves, you will be overwhelmed pretty quickly. Even when you make headway, one mis-step and it's back to grinding money.
I don't mind a challenge. I like a challenge. But when you're simply overwhelmed with speed, lack of funds and very slow charge rate--it's just no fun.

As it's a horror game the story doesn't matter too much, but it's all about to find a person called Alexander and finish him off before he kills us. When the game starts you just wake up in a castle with no way out. Character's name you control is Daniel.
The game itself is very dark, sometimes you may find candles or just normal lights. While playing you will collect tinderboxes and an oil to a lamp which you get almost at the beginning. This is a "key" item, in many situations you won't be able to see anything either there won't be any light, so having oil is very important. I've ended the game with around 70 or 80 tinderboxes, in my opinion they are just useless, lamp and oil is enough. What's so scary in the game? The feeling of fear keeps being with you while playing anytime. Game is unpredictable and you won't be sure when an opponent is gonna appear. Usually the monster appears when some item from a shelf is picked up (I mean keys, drills and such stuff - excluding tinderboxes or oil). Not just enemies or "unpredictable game" is scary, the music plays a part in it too. Honestly without music the game is way less scary. By moving from a room to another room you will often find collectibles - files. These explain story step by step (but you gotta read carefully). A place you are moving in the game is chosen perfectly (what could be better than a castle left around the forest?). Amnesia is the only scary game that I've played, because of the suspens. Titles such as Outlast, Slender and so on weren't scary at all and it was caused by 0 suspens...
PROS:
Suspens
Soundtrack
Feeling fear each second
Perfectly chosen place
Darkness
As for a horror game the story is pretty nice
CONS:
Too many tinderboxes
Few bugs
AI is a bit too stupid
Overall the game gets 8,5/10.

Camera 5 just went offline and I didn't even see it happen. The monster works fast. Fast enough that a few moments later my pig-mounted camera shuts off as well. This time I switch over just in time to watch it lunge. By now I have a pretty good idea of where The Rake is roaming tonight, so I grab my gun and prepare to hunt the beast down...
TL;DR at bottom
There are many out there who feel that the "found footage" genre of film popularized by Paranormal Activity and Marble Hornets is played out and tired. I do not count myself as one of those people. One thing that, to me, is pretty incredible about Rake is that I kind of feel like the guy holding the camera in a found footage film.
Let me start out by saying you're not randomly trapped somewhere collecting pages for reasons unknown. This is a horror game where you have set out to find the creature in question, and you didn't come empty handed. The bread and butter of the game is the ability to set up cameras which you can watch from your base camp. They rotate at your command, and can be put in a number of different places, and even attached to the back of a live pig. The restriction on the system is that you can only place five cameras at a time, and they aren't invincible. The Rake will go out of his way to destroy hundreds if not thousands of dollars worth of your equipment.♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
You also have a gun. This is a monster that can be killed if you're smart and fast enough. It's not easy, but it's possible.
There's a pattern that I quickly fell into as I played. During the day I set up cameras and traps galore, and when night falls  I monitor the cameras and wait for the beasty to show himself. As soon as he does, I take my trusty shotgun and begin the hunt for the creature. Oftentimes, it feels more like the creature is hunting me. I haven't reached an end state yet, but the gameplay is unique enough where I want to keep trying to best my supernatural foe.
A walking simulator this game is not, which is a relief since most creepypasta based games function in that way. Story takes a back seat here, which is fine since it allows you to make your own stories.
There are some drawbacks I feel inclined to mention. The camera system feels like a missed opportunity. It's not terrible, but you're limited to a select number of trees and angles. I would love to see in the future an update that allows me to mount a camera just about anywhere, as it would make the gameplay far more dynamic. The graphics of the monster are mediocre up close, as it kind of looks like you're being attacked by an even smaller and skinnier Gollum. When it's fully dark and he's sprinting through the brush towards you he's pretty scary, but in the off-chance you encounter him during the day you're likely to shake your head a bit.
Currently there's only one map with static elements. Either a couple more maps or a procedural generation element to it would be extremely welcome. The game is rather inexpensive, and you get what you paid for, but it's just exciting to think what this game has the potential to be.
I'd like to note that I'm rather impressed with Rake's AI for both the monster and the wildlife. I've been scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at night by a boar more than once, and The Rake is pretty good about making sure you only catch fleeting glimpses of him. He's animated pretty well too, which helps sell the experience more.
TL;DR: I've been so tired of the corridor walking simulators that pass as horror games these days. This is the first game in a while I've played that throws wrinkles in the formula, and that in its own right is commendable. For 5 dollars, you'll get a pretty fun game that might warrant more than one playthrough, if only for the memorable mechanics! If you're a horror fan, buy it!

Knock-Knock is a (mostly) perfect example of using atmosphere in horror game to have the player end up scaring themselves with the game's help rather than just using a jumpscare to do all the work. Most of the time you'll be wandering blindly through darkness flicking on lights while hoping there isn't a monster inside with you planning to strike the second you turn it on. It's that split second of fear you get after waking up from a nightmare where you hesitate turning on the light because you think you feel eyes on you, drawn out for hours.
The story takes a few playthroughs and thought to completely understand everything that's going on, but spoiler-free the bare bones of it is you are a scientist waking up in the middle of the night to strange sounds coming from inside you house. Your goal is Amnesia-like in similarity to the fact all you have to do is stay alive until morning and hide from the monsters in your home.
Gameplay is simple: avoid monsters, hide, and turn on (or off) lights to lure creatures to specific rooms in your M.C. Escher layout of a home complete with dead-ends, and turn on special clocks to "move time forward" so you can live to see the sun.

To start off, I think ubisoft made a great game. The combat is always interesting and makes you want to come back for more. Getting enviro kills with Raider is fun, executions are great, and even when I lose, there's something I could try again with. For Honor is challenging at high levels, and developing your fighting style is truly satisfying.
The Story Mode in For Honor is okay. Expect some unstable weapons in the hands of characters, laughable horse and elephant models, and basic dialogue (drink whenever you hear 'wolves').---I will say however there are some amusing moments that I liked --- Your AI allies in the story are more likely to interupt your sick chain than save you from being executed. The voice lines of all other characters don't time out, so you will hear Raider! Impressive! about 50293 times if you're going slow. And you may be going slow because Ubisoft encourages that. Observables and Breakables are things you find in the story, and it may take a few careful run-throughs of every map to gather them all. Observables give small background info that fills out the universe, but in an unsatisfying way (I mean it is too much effort for too little reward). Breakables give you steel (in-game currency), emblems, and boxes. This part I really like because it helps you fill out your "Main's" inventory, but more on that later. The last think I'd like to talk about is the difficulty settings of the story mode. Normal is easy. Hard is easy. In hard mode, often your AI companions will do your job for you, leaving you to wander around looking in trees for a little "o" icon (observables). Realistic is stupid. The Art of Combat system is very similar to Dark Souls, except for the "training icons" that flash red when you should block, parry, etc. In Realistic mode all of this goes away. You are left to guess which guard your opponent is in. In some characters the differences in guards is not enough, and chain attacks will end up with you just trying every position seeing if it is the right one. Also, guard break maneuvers in realistic mode are rough. It is a challenge, one that can be more frustrating than rewarding. Completing the story mode on each difficulty will give you sick loadouts, which I like.
The multiplayer is solid. Enviro kills, ganking, and interacting with other players (abrassively or not) is part of it all. It always gives you an idea of how many players are playing a certain mode. Search times for lobbies are long, and there is absolutely NOTHING to do while you wait. If there was just one thing I could fix, it would be that. People would not be as upset about waiting if they had an elapsed time, expected time, and if they were able to work on their hero loadouts while waiting. This is the number two thing I think they messed up. Speaking of loadouts, is pretty important to have good gear in some multiplayer matches. Gear can up your sprint speed, helping you catch that b-word of an Orochi. Just so you know, the number next to your level on the hero is your gear rank, which is the sum of the level of all the gear you are wearing/have equipped. Since loadouts are so important, it gives pay2win players a chance to dominate dominion. However, the gear you get is limited by how high your reputation is, so you can't go in and day one have a Orochi with level 50 gear, even with all the money in the world. (You could get to 36 easily though).
And that brings us to why I don't recommend this game. I have played a bunch, I've got deluxe edition, season pass, Ubisoft club and sometimes I even buy steel. It has cost so much. For so little. I cannot recommend this game because it is the product a greedy company using a good idea (Art of Combat, in this case), a fun story (vikings v samurai v knights??? sick!), and a persistent world to only make money. There are so many unlockables that you will never have the 100% full game without either playing it for a living or paying out the bum for it. It is entirely possible that you get this game for $60 and that is it. You play it and have fun. But wait. This game is not worth $60 at the moment. PvP matches still have disconnections, the story mode certainly isn't $60, I finished in around 10 hours? Not long at all. I don't want to encourage Full price, Deluxe edition, season passes, and microtransactions to all be in one mediocre game that is still lacking in multiplayer AND story.

tl;dr
Story - okay
Multiplayer - okay
Price and all of the "Now buy this" crap - Not okay.
Still. To the designers/programmers/writers/VA's/etc. of For Honor: Good Job! Thank you for this experience!
To the sellers, executives, and leeches of the videogame industry: Find something better to do with your damn life than make money.

Knock-knock is a deeply unnerving game that manages to succeed at what it sets out to do.
From the start you get to meet the charming Lodger as he briefly teaches you just how things are in his home. From there it's up to you to figure out the rest. You have six days and nights to adjust and learn, and then from there the game really begins. The time limit is pretty strict, so if you haven't figured out what you're doing by then, don't expect to survive. I barely managed on my first time with just a teensy bit of time left. Overall that stress of time and all the things out and inside your home coming after you is something that sticks with you for quite a while. Though the game does begin dull, once things speed up it truly feels like a game and all those horrifying things out there become all the more horrifying. I'd rather not say much since there are some great ideas in place and it's better to experience them for yourself than not. That's what the first six nights are for after all, just experimenting and figuring out the most effecient way of doing things.
There are flaws though, this game is heavy on RNG. Though skill can help you through most of what you're trying to accomplish, exploring the forest on a time limit is a bit much since there's no easy way to find your way home again rather than just go forwards and hope for the best. There's no guarentee that you'll figure out just what you're supposed to be doing out there without a hint or two either, though thankfully there are enough hints to make people explore the forest at least once or twice early on. Even worse, once you enter the night phases, enemies can and will spawn near you and remain there for long periods, often trapping you in a corner. Or worse, a roaming enemy will follow with it. Touching a solitary enemy is a minor time loss while touching a roamer will set you back a massive amount, but even a minor time loss is a lot here. The game's pretty well designed however and you figure out just what you should be doing before long, though there's little room for error so a few hints are always welcome.
So yeah, Knock-knock surprises though you need to give it a bit of time to shine and be patient through the less enjoyable segments. Not recommended for those who are effected by surrealistic imagry as half of this game's horror is based on that with the other half being existence and dementia based. If you think you can take it, pick it up.

Full disclosure: review copy provided by developer/publisher!
In the beginning there was presumably chaos; the cosmos swirled violently, endlessly. But the gods, lazy control freaks that they are, swept all that chaos under the proverbial universal carpet and called it a full, rich day. Eons passed, and little of consequence was done: multicellular organisms developed, terra rose from beneath churning primordial seas, and the very first Waffle House opened to middling reviews. At some point (post Waffle House), the gods grew bored and reached out to indie game developer Alientrap. In a booming and unified voice, they decreed that a game be made – a sidescrolling, puzzle/platform adventure game that would do them honor. Little did the gods know that this particular genre of game would be pumped out with such regularity in the indie community that titans CoD and Madden would blush empathetically. Alientrap, like Sysiphus before them, faced an uphill battle.
They succeeded, and did Olympus proud.
Apotheon is the aforementioned sidescrolling puzzle/platform indie adventure game, and it tells a story as old (and as metal) as time: the gods of Olympus have forsook the cosmic “oopsy daisy” of mankind, and it's up to brave Nikandreos to save what little spark of humanity remains. Sure, roll your eyes. “Didn't God of War do this a decade ago?” Well sure, technically, you stick in the mud. Homer also wrote stuff in this vein nearly 3,000 years ago, and whoever the ♥♥♥♥ wrote Gilgamesh 1,300 years earlier than Homer still! And for what it's worth, the story is very fun. It doesn't break the ancient mold, but the ending still left me surprised and satisfied.
Nikandreos sidescrolls his way up  hub-world Mount Olympus on his quest in stunning black and red figure style as seen depicted on all the best Ancient Greek pottery. Watching people stroll the market, guards brandishing their spears, and satyrs getting drunk is mesmerizing. But at some point you'll have to get to the gameplay, and what gameplay it is. You'll have an array of archaic weapons (purchased or picked up), a variety of shields, a torch, potions and the like. Weapons and shields shatter after prolonged use, so the game regularly forces you to fight in different styles. I was initially put off by this feature but found that it forced me out of my comfort zone, requiring me to learn the unique swings, reaches, and speeds of each weapon. You'll pick up money and crafting items after combat and by shattering crates and barrels, though these activities can bring unwanted attention from Olympian guards.
Over the course of  three acts you'll deal with eight major deities (four optional), and each offers starkly different, fun, varied gameplay. For example, Demeter, Goddess of the Harvest, pities humanity's plight, and would provide bounty. Unfortunately her daughter Persephone currently dwells in Hades' realm making it impossible. You'll have to descend to the underworld, cross the river Styx, and proceed to cross the lesser rivers Acheron, Lethe, Phlegethon, and Cocyctus to be granted an audience with the Lord of the Dead. Each of these rivers provide different platform gameplay tropes that keep things fresh, exciting, and entertaining. And that's just for one “quest.” Dionysus, Hephaestus, Poseidon, Athena... each and every deity provides different gameplay mechanics so the game never gets stale. All the while you'll visit shops to upgrade your attack strength, defense, and resupply on favorite weapons.
And for those of you with a multiplayer itch there's local multiplayer combat, allowing you to test your skills against a friend. This is pretty fun, and the combat (singleplayer and multiplayer) is deceptively deep and tactical. The multiplayer won't keep too many people distracted for long, but between the three difficulties, metroidvania-lite gameplay, beautiful soundtrack, stunning graphics, and varied gameplay, you'll sink at least 10 hours into this little indie game.
This is AAA quality on an indie budget, and you'd be doing yourself a disservice by missing out on this one. Apothoen has accomplished its 12 herculean tasks, and is deserving of a place in the pantheon of gaming.

A fun and underrated CoD-style historical FPS, the first of the Medal series set in the modern era. The story takes place during the initial 2001 invasion of Afghanistan following the false-flag 9/11 attacks (still waiting on that video of a plane hitting the Pentagon), a series of victories and losses seen through the eyes of three soldiers-- a SEAL, an AFO operative and a U.S. Army Ranger (and in one of the best levels in the game, the chopper gunner for an Apache gunship).
Combat is your typical run-and-gun, ironsights, pop off a few shots and take cover formula, though you die much faster from gunfire than in other military shooters, even on normal difficulty. There are only a dozen or so weapons, each with their perks and disadvantages, and I appreciated that I could ask my comrades for ammo any time I needed it (but ONLY if it's an American weapon!) Combat scenarios are the usual variety you find with these types of games: the obligatory stealth mission (that you can be discovered without failing the mission), surviving ambushes, endless waves of enemies, sniping, some vehicle sections, on-rail shooting set-pieces, take that hill, laze that target, etc. etc. but hey, if it ain't broke...
Visually the game holds up well. Some of the facial animations are cartoonish and I would haven't preferred an FOV slider. It's worth nothing that the vistas in this game are just breathtaking. I'm pretty sure they aren't just skyboxes or backdrops; when you're up high in those mountain levels you can almost taste the cold, thin air, and the hilly terrain below you seems to stretch for miles. Other art assets, like the voice acting and music, are also stellar.
It's too short, and ends on a somber note. But it's hard to give a happy ending to a war that hadn't ended at the time of the game's development. 8/10

I had a wonderful time with Rake but you know, I wouldn't have done if I didn't have to suffer its outrageous failings first. The game's weird and obtuse, and that'd be perfectly fine if it didn't have a game over. If you do something wrong, the game will penalize you the same way every other game does, by forcing you restart a section.
What you do in it is avoid ghosts as you go from room to room fixing lights hoping something useful will appear. You win the level after a few minutes elapse. Getting caught by a ghost or hiding from them will force you to wait longer. You may also find a clock that makes time go faster, so you'll have to wait less. The word wait is essential to this game and that may give you a clue of how much fun it is.
The rules are unclear, which is fine, even welcomed, but in the first thirty minutes or so you'll understand them.
The real problem, however, is that enemies may spawn on top of you as you're climbing down a ladder. They may appear with no warning from a door as you're busy opening it. It seems they're programmed to spawn randomly, with no regards to the player's current position. More than once an enemy appeared blocking the only exit, and I had no choice but to be caught. There is some (very little) strategy involved in winning, but it's offset by randomness.
If you're unlucky, you'll have to redo the level. That'd be okay if the core gameplay wasn't repetitive and mechanic. All you do is go from room to room, hold X for a few seconds to fix the light. Then, you may or may not get the choice to wait a few seconds to see if an object appears.
That's it. Most of what you do to progress involves waiting or holding a button for a few seconds. You may also choose to take risks and go to an area where a ghost may be in, but at a certain point you'll have nothing else to do but to venture into these areas and hope a ghost doesn't spawn on your face.
You may also force ghosts to disappear, or objects to appear, by leaving and entering a floor/room repeatedly. Which isn't engaging at all and just feels like you're abusing the game. You can also choose to do everything really slowly and remain in safe areas for as long as you want to wait for the time to pass.
Often you'll see unusual things that you don't fully comprehend, and if you try to interact with them you'll be forced to restart a level. For an instance, you'll see an eye on the wall, the game will tell you how to interact with it. If you do, you'll be taken to a place where all you do is walk, then you'll have to restart the level.
Then there's another section to the game where all you do is fix all the lights and walk in a forest, there's no risk involved in any of it, no challenge either. Once again, that'd be fine. I like walking simulators, I like weird games. But the section just keeps repeating itself.

Class imbalance. The Peacekeeper and Nobushi have special attacks that POISON you and you have to take that nasty damage. Ouch? The Kenshi has too much stamina and too much stamina recovery. The Raider can THROW you off of cliffs. No other class can, but they can push you off.

Creepy.  Compelling.  Confusing.  Cute.  One of the most unusual, original, and hard-to-get-yer-noggin-around games I've ever played.  Even once you complete it, many a question remains, such as:  Why does your bleary-eyed scientist character speak in what I assume to be Russian (since that's apparently the origin of the game designers), while the ghosties who haunt him speak in English?  Why is his voice so high-pitched and squeaky, when he appears to be a grown man (albiet one with a face like an angry cherub)?  And what the ♥♥♥♥ is the deal with that endless corridor you keep finding yourself in, which seems to have no purpose other than to send you all the way back to the beginning of the chapter?!

But by all means, if you're in the market for a game which doesn't seek to comfort you (in a psychological sense) or hand-hold you (in a gaming/mechanical sense), then this is one well worth picking up.  Just make sure you're in the mood for a little insomnia of your own, as the aforementioned "cute"-ness is a Trojan horse and a half.  Prepare to be suitably mind-♥♥♥♥ed, boys and girls...oh, and speaking of which, if you google anything about the ending - or should I say, various "endings" - you'll see a mighty♥♥♥♥♥♥storm of controversy this subject has whipped up.  I won't go into it here, but suffice it to say there's been some "design" decisions made by the lovely folks at Ice-Pick which won't exactly go down well with everyone.  It certainly ♥♥♥♥ed me the first time I played, but I still enjoyed the game enough to just jump straight back in, and managed to get the "good" ending the second time through.  So there ARE rewards - including one of the oddest end credit sequences I've ever encountered - but man oh man, you have gots to EARN them!  Whatever you do, don't expect this game to treat you with kid gloves.  YOU HAVE BEEN WARNED.

Quake 2 is FPS developed by id and released in 1997 for PC, on their new id Tech 2 engine. It's not really a sequel to Quake 1, but instead it was developed as serapate title and then at the end was given such name. It also had PS1 and N64 ports. I didn't play them, but they are probably inferior ones. Though, from what I seen, PS1 has best usage of colors.
So, how Steam version was handled? In id style! Which means no soundtrack for you. It just wasn't included, once again. You will have to track down (soundtrack) CD of a game. And then deal with music looping issues. _inmm software helped me here.
Game also doesn't support widescreen by default. But I am sure you can find a way to tweak it. Or just use sourceport.
It also was stuttering for me by default. Strange enough, once I would go into Video setting and exit, it would get fixed for me.
It also refused to save configuration for me, so I had to change things back on each launch.
Multiplayer community is small but still there. Now, I may not be good enough to tell away bot from human, but I belive that you will at least find one Deathmatch with 5-10 players. Though yea, Free For All Deathmatch is the only gametype you will end up playing. Small.
The plot follows Bitterman as he is one of the marines that were sent to planet of flesh-hungry cyborgs - Stroggs. As offense is the best defence. He ends up being possibly the only one surviving the first human attack on planet and now has to destroy and disable all the important strogg structures, alone.
So yea, sounds like another Rambo vs World. Though, you can actually meet some captured marines in the levels, but they all went insane. It addsa  nice touch to the setting, though it still feels a bit too gamey to see that you can't interact with them in any way. Or just that there are no sane ones, just crawling around.
It also has CGI cutscenes. Which would be awesome, but it's a wasted potential, as almost all of them are nothing but a fancy intermission screens. Hexen on PS1 made better use of them, really.
Manual is nice though.
And well, to be honest, Quake 2 is the last title in Quake series that I played. I heard that it was a classic and heard many other good things. And once I got to play it, I was amazed... at how awfully generic FPS title it was.
I mean, sure, it's better than Quake on theory. Because more realistical levels. Or better enemy AI. Or just better engine from technical standpoint, with smooth animation and colored lighting.
Yet the game as a whole it creates a fairly dull single-player experience.
Setting isn't exactly interesting. It's nice that levels are connected into small hub and that they are bigger. And that you are given missions that explain what to do next. But level layouts are still linear, so it hardly matters. There are very few interesting levels, mostly factory and research labs, where you can see what Stroggs do with humans. Terrifying.
But outside of them they don't have anything interesting going on, while also not being as abstract as Quake or Doom ones. It also doesn't help that game looks awful. Whatever technical improvements engine may have, they all are supposed to just improve art design. And art design here is quite bad, consisting of red and grey. Grey and red. And more red than you will ever want to see. Even Hexen 2 which used Quake 1 engine looked better. Or Quake 1, which still used more colors and it was contributing to gritty atmoshpere.
Gameplay isn't exciting either. It's much more slowed-paced. It makes use of more hitscan enemies attacks. It just feels like it promotes more of cover-based tactics. Sure, there are few different enemy types with slightly different attacks, but in the end it still doesn't make a big difference. You peek out, you shoot, you hide from machinegun bullets back around corner. Or from railgun. Quake 1 had Ogres and Fiends, one would spam grenades around room and was often placed in interesting spots, while fiends were dangerous enemies that easily charged at you, all of which making you strafe and navigate, being more interestign to fight against. Quake 2 is just plain not exciting. Even melee enemy, Berserker, isn't threatening here, being slow, attacks while standing, easy to get out of attack reach with a single step, easy to knock down.
On more positive note, Enemy AI was improved. While they don't provide as much of fun as Hexen 2 ones, they still show more life to them. Mostly just ducking here and there. They get covered in blood as you shoot them down and some of the common enemies can even give the last few shots before dying. Don't worry, they don't aim when they do that, just shoot straight, so it's not annoying and looks awesome. Can always gib.
Not sure what to say about equipment. Yes, you got more weapons than before. They got some interesting ideas behind, I like that recoil on Machine Gun, back before recoil was a common thing. You can also choose whether you want to have weapon on left, right or in center, which impacts where shots come from too (it's in multiplayer setting, but affects single as well). And heck, it has railgun. Which even does extra damage on unaware enemies. It's still feels like you have too much ammo and that weapons aren't too specialized in single. But still, nice.
Quake 2 also adds inventory. It wasn't implented good. There aren't so many items to use. Sure, being able to use Quad Damage whenever you want is nice, radiation suit and rebreather help with secrets. But that's about it. It suffers because developers decided that they have to put weapons you have as inventory items as well, making it harder to navigate while bringing nothing. Even worse is that they put grenades between all this mess that you can't select otherwise.
EDIT: Was wrong, grenade are easily selectable with "G" button. Items have other keybinds, but not something I want to always remember.
Bosses are quite meh. You can quad-damage them anyway.
Soundtrack is quite nice. At least great when you listen to it serapately and some memoriable rock. Or whatever genre this is. It gets a bit monotonial after a while. A nice touch is that music suddenly ends when you complete all goals on the level, showing that you got nothing to do there anymore. It somehow ends up being awkward though, when you still got something to do.
Multiplayer on other hand is a big improvement over Quake. Now, it's still old-school and will not interest many, especially seeing how Quake 3 Arena is out. But you got to say that's it's quite a little fun. It's slower-paced, sure. But it finally got balance in weapons. The one who has rocket launcher no longer dominates whole arena, as other weapons are viable alternatives with their own specialization, mostly range difference. Better for those who prefer a bit more thinking and a bit less reflexes. I do have a bad feelign that railgun may end up being a bit too good, penetrating and killing unarmed players in one shot. But I didn't play for long.
And well, I wrote some bad things here, sure. Yes, I think that this game is generic and missable. But you know, it's still a fine generic FPS. With very few bright spots. It's not something I would call a classic, but you can still have fun with it. And it doesn't do anything way too bad in gameplay. No cheap deaths or such to frustrate you. So, feel free to check it out.

In the beginning there was presumably chaos; the cosmos swirled violently, endlessly. But the gods, lazy control freaks that they are, swept all that chaos under the proverbial universal carpet and called it a full, rich day. Eons passed, and little of consequence was done: multicellular organisms developed, terra rose from beneath churning primordial seas, and the very first Waffle House opened to middling reviews. At some point (post Waffle House), the gods grew bored and reached out to indie game developer Alientrap. In a booming and unified voice, they decreed that a game be made – a sidescrolling, puzzle/platform adventure game that would do them honor. Little did the gods know that this particular genre of game would be pumped out with such regularity in the indie community that titans CoD and Madden would blush empathetically. Alientrap, like Sysiphus before them, faced an uphill battle.
They succeeded, and did Olympus proud.
Apotheon is the aforementioned sidescrolling puzzle/platform indie adventure game, and it tells a story as old (and as metal) as time: the gods of Olympus have forsook the cosmic “oopsy daisy” of mankind, and it's up to brave Nikandreos to save what little spark of humanity remains. Sure, roll your eyes. “Didn't God of War do this a decade ago?” Well sure, technically, you stick in the mud. Homer also wrote stuff in this vein nearly 3,000 years ago, and whoever the ♥♥♥♥ wrote Gilgamesh 1,300 years earlier than Homer still! And for what it's worth, the story is very fun. It doesn't break the ancient mold, but the ending still left me surprised and satisfied.
Nikandreos sidescrolls his way up  hub-world Mount Olympus on his quest in stunning black and red figure style as seen depicted on all the best Ancient Greek pottery. Watching people stroll the market, guards brandishing their spears, and satyrs getting drunk is mesmerizing. But at some point you'll have to get to the gameplay, and what gameplay it is. You'll have an array of archaic weapons (purchased or picked up), a variety of shields, a torch, potions and the like. Weapons and shields shatter after prolonged use, so the game regularly forces you to fight in different styles. I was initially put off by this feature but found that it forced me out of my comfort zone, requiring me to learn the unique swings, reaches, and speeds of each weapon. You'll pick up money and crafting items after combat and by shattering crates and barrels, though these activities can bring unwanted attention from Olympian guards.
Over the course of  three acts you'll deal with eight major deities (four optional), and each offers starkly different, fun, varied gameplay. For example, Demeter, Goddess of the Harvest, pities humanity's plight, and would provide bounty. Unfortunately her daughter Persephone currently dwells in Hades' realm making it impossible. You'll have to descend to the underworld, cross the river Styx, and proceed to cross the lesser rivers Acheron, Lethe, Phlegethon, and Cocyctus to be granted an audience with the Lord of the Dead. Each of these rivers provide different platform gameplay tropes that keep things fresh, exciting, and entertaining. And that's just for one “quest.” Dionysus, Hephaestus, Poseidon, Athena... each and every deity provides different gameplay mechanics so the game never gets stale. All the while you'll visit shops to upgrade your attack strength, defense, and resupply on favorite weapons.
And for those of you with a multiplayer itch there's local multiplayer combat, allowing you to test your skills against a friend. This is pretty fun, and the combat (singleplayer and multiplayer) is deceptively deep and tactical. The multiplayer won't keep too many people distracted for long, but between the three difficulties, metroidvania-lite gameplay, beautiful soundtrack, stunning graphics, and varied gameplay, you'll sink at least 10 hours into this little indie game.
This is AAA quality on an indie budget, and you'd be doing yourself a disservice by missing out on this one. Apothoen has accomplished its 12 herculean tasks, and is deserving of a place in the pantheon of gaming.

TL;DR: only get this if free or heavily discounted. I got it free hence my recommendation.
At times this game had me cheering, cringing or cursing.
Cheering:
- It is immensely satisfying when you line up that perfect shot in a set piece and you watch the impact in that x-ray bullet cam.
- The scripted set pieces (i.e. defending the church, the sniper gallery after retrieving the documents from the soviets) are enjoyable.
- Timing your shots with ambient noise to pick off a squad of enemies one by one without alerting the others feels good and is what this game should be about. Which leads me into the cringing:
Cringing:
- The AI. In some points you can rock full-auto on an MP40 or a Thompson and not alert nearby enemies. Other times you can simply be jogging and every man in the city block will suddenly know where you are. Other times I had enemies round a corner and start shooting at the player character where they couldn't possibly know where he was.
- The Weapons. There are only 2 sniper rifles in the vanilla game that are significantly different enough to be worthwhile selecting for a particular setting or mission. There doesn't appear to be any significant differences between the SMGs worth talking about. You'll probably just chose whichever the enemy in the mission will be using just for ammo availability. There is (at least in my opinion) only one pistol worthwhile using- the Welrod - as it is the only silenced weapon available. This leads me onto the cursing component:
Cursing:
- For some reason, a game that is overtly about sniping forces the player by level design into a significant amount of close quarters fighting, particularly within tunnels and buildings. This means that the player is really limited to a single weapon (the silenced pistol) if they want to keep the stealth / infiltrator feel to the game during these sections of the level. I put this game down (about 75% of the way through the storyline) once I realised that I had spent most of the game using only the Welrod due to level design.
Would I spend more than $10 on this game, no. Would I play it for a few hours if I got it for less than $10? Yes. Which I did - hence I recommend but ONLY at a significant sale price.

Medal of Honor (2010) is definitely an unmissable title. Although the game is now 7 years old, the visuals are still quiet impressive and beautiful and the game often has a very cinematic feel to it. Guns feel weighty and the gunplay is fairly satisfying. Shotguns, snipers and grenades all have the ability to dismember and decapitate your enemy and makes for some some satisfying long distance sniper sequences. Other immersive details in regards to the weaponry is that dust is thrown into the air from gunshot impacts, resulting in a lot of visually appealing gunplay.
The singleplayer campaign consists of a prologue, "day one" and "day two", each with their own number of missions in each. You'll play as 2 different special forces operatives, one US army ranger, and even an appache helicopter weapons operator for one mission. Gameplay ranges from stealth operations to full blown out combat and anything in between. It is definitely a good blend of realism and action with stealth and slow paced sections to break up the action.
The campaign does feel quite short however does give a good range of gameplay experience and is one of the most enjoyable singleplayer experiences I've had with an FPS for a while now. I haven't yet tried the multiplayer and I'm not entirely sure if anyone still plays this online, however the campaign was enough to hook me onto this game.
If you're not quite totally convinced about buying MoH, wait until a sale, or get it now whilst the summer sale is on, like I have. It's certainly a must play.  9/10
