This is the true Masterpiece Star Wars game.
Yes, Bioware's first game is fantastic and fun, but if you look at it closely it's basically a retelling of the original trilogy and is a bit one-dimensional in terms of characterization and plot writing. You fight against the big bad empire and find a way to stop their super-weapon(factory) and discover a massive plot twist truth, and it's pretty much polar opposite paths of pure good and pure evil, with almost nothing in between. Plus, the dialogue can be really corny
For the sequel, however, the gods of writing known as Obsidian were given the power to bring their epic writing ability into Star Wars and thus came one of the best RPGs known to man, and one of the best stories Star Wars has to offer, where the story really comes to life through character interaction and brilliant lines that chill you. A lot of what you learn comes through dialogue in this game, so be prepared to listen and respond
Now, you may be saying: "But it has bugs and is incomplete!" That's because LucasArts got greedy and gave them a year to do this game instead of the three years that Bioware had for the first, it's amazing they managed to create this much material. I highly recommend getting the Restored Content Mod here which does its best to re-create what Obsidian had tried to do with this game -->
So why am I saying this game is so good? Well, here are my reasons:
1. It has one of the deepest and most moving plots of any story, and changes your perceptions of the Star Wars universe. The Jedi are not painted as the god-like saviors and the Sith are not necessarily entirely evil. In fact, the game almost presents the point of view of an outsider (well, an exile of the Jedi) and you can experience the consequences of the constant conflict between the light and the dark. The entire plot is trying to find a way to stop the sith, but you have no help, and you just got back into the galaxy and just re-discovered your force connection. As you progress, you discover just what has happened to the galaxy, how bad the situation is, why you were exiled in the first place, and get to make some very tough calls. Unlike the first game, there are no real bomb-shell plot twists that come out of left field, rather a setting of interesting minor twists that make sense, but feel no less impactful (the jedi council scene on dantooine, for instance)
2. It has some of the best written characters ever witnessed. Case and Point, Kreia, who's practically your twisted female Yoda who lies to you so you do her bidding, but mixes her lies with truths as she shapes your view of the world. She also has some very interesting viewpoints on the Jedi Civil War, and provides context to why the war happened in the first place and why Revan (the main character of the first game) did what he/she did. Other characters also have their own flaws and positive traits, each being actual living individuals, whereas in the first game it was clear that most party members were just a character embodying one viewpoint only (light, dark, comedy). And those brought back from the first game are given even more of a shining light and a deeper backstory so that they become real people. (HK-47, for example, is even more epic)
3. Your choices matter - No, really, they do. Granted, the endings don't play out that differently, but you see the consequences of your actions throughout the game (especially with TSLRCM), and particularly with those you travel with. The way you act changes your followers, and the way they respond to you likewise does so. Again, particularly with the restored content mod, you can witness how your choices play out, and experience the difference in how others react to you (People also note that if you're evil your face looks awful, which nobody notices in KOTOR 1)
4. It feels grounded to reality - It's not just cowboys and spaceships, you actually witness good political drama too in this game. Here, you deal with real people and their problems, not just a grandma needing to get across the street. You also have to struggle with what is good and what is evil, and often times the lines are blurred, particularly when it comes to choosing sides. On Nar Shaddaa, you might feel inclined to help the hapless refugees, but it might cause more harm than good because there is no system to replace the caste they are in. Oh, and by the way, common citizens blame the Jedi for the war, both the sith and the Jedi. In fact, they think they are both Jedi, since they don't actually know what's going on.
These are the ones I have off the top of my head, but look around and you'll find more reasons. This isn't some epic good vs evil game like the first or Mass Effect, so don't go expecting it. Instead, look for a deep narrative that tells a complex story that has a journey that matters more than the destination. There are definite flaws, since the game was rushed out the door by a poor production committee, but if you overlook those flaws, then you'll notice just how brilliant this game is. Truly, I wish that Star Wars resembled what Obisidan came up with more, but unfortunately we won't see that in Disney canon. However, if you want a taste of Star Wars for big boys, come check this out.

To start with a few negative points/those i think ought to be addressed:
- Bloom is way too high, please turn this down
- Some more weapons would be nice but that's more of a side point for sure, perhaps a revolver to add a faster firing but weaker weapon. Oooh and flares, can't have a horror game set innawoods without some flares
- The day/night cycle is pretty stale. Having the day visibly change to night would urge the player on far more
And that's honestly it. This game is truly what I believe creepypasta games should be, that building dread as you fall further into a story, becoming more invested in finding the truth, and then coming face to face with something horrifying. The rake, while not a very attractive world model, is to this game what the Blair Witch was to that movie, an almost intangible horror lurking JUST out of sight, far enough that you fear even hearing it but not so far that you don't want to stop. Adding dead camers was a masterful touch, it gives the player a choice of braving the unknown in search of the truth, or staying where it's safe and knowing nothing come morning.
And when you do decide to venture fourth, my god. The feeling is like those first few minutes of Fatal Frame that I haven't felt since I was twelve. I actually had to stand in the doorway of that trailer, truly apprehensive about going out there. It's like going down a dark halway in your house to see if that noise really was just the dog. You feel true
, whether it's the sound design that is done VERY well for an indie game (blending the sounds of the Rake with those of the pigs is a key point) or the knowlege that the thing is out there, hunting you, every minute spent in the dark is heart pounding.
This game is doing for horror what many years of Triple A titles have fallen short and failed to do. It's made it about the story of the monster, the story of the man hunting the thing, and not about just some thing popping out of the dark with a scary face.
And it's doing all of this with graphics from 2005.
Pretty good game.

Well, that was a rather unusual experience. You usually play with the good guy and your objective is to save the world, right? In this game, it's the complete opposite: Your goal is to take over the world, and then put an end to it. No, you don't really get a chance to choose if you're going to play the good Samaritan role or not. The mechanics of the game are rather simple, in a certain sense it does bring some resemblance to old school games. The graphics are fairly simple, there's not much else to say about them. The soundtrack isn't quite captivating, but manages to keep you entertained while you're playing. The sound effects are basic, but they don't really affect anything whatsoever. As for the gameplay, there's an interesting combination of melee and different spells, which makes everything more versatile. The story, besides what was already written in the beginning, is pretty shallow and, unfortunately, the game doesn't get to explore the personality of the characters. You simply don't really get to feel anything for anyone (anger, empathy, pity etc.). Overall, if the objective of the game, besides providing some fun, was to make you feel as a sociopath and / or psychopath, then it was a job well done.

Evilquest Review.
This is a budget title that game was published on xbox live indie and on steam. The game only costs a dollar 0.99$ in USD but for me as I use CAD its costs 2.19$.
Evilquest is a game where you play as a evil tyrant named Galvis who in a SNES style cutscene goes to fight king jericks forces in battle but then one of your two general betrays you and splits up 1/3 of your army leaving you outnumbered. Then you start the game in a wonderful escape from prison setting.

This is a budget game and I think for its price you get quite a well made game. The game is new, it has challenge but it is unbalanced it takes way to long to grind up levels the level design is very basic, the gamepaly is good there is lots of content the story is interesting and very edgy if you like that kind of story.
Your goal is to destroy the world and kill god and that's fun but its really really edgy i am not joking you kill people for one vauge reason, you rarely decide anything. In the game you can kind of make choices like should you kill the drunken peasant in the windmill? You can decide to kill him or not but if you kill him nothing happens like the town guards trying to arrest you for murder. There is a ninja that seems very interesting Galvis says "he should be careful of him" but nothing happens with it and even if you are Max level you are nearly finished the game, have all items etc nothing happens with him saddly.
The game plays great is perfectly functional good controller and keyboard support that's rare for most budget games it is possible to finish but it is a difficult unbalanced game that takes very long to level up in has lots of content but the interesting parts of the game feel incomplete the music and sound effects I think are nice there is good variety but it is too simple it should have better music if you are going to play it for as long as it takes to level up. The game has a few secrets in the game but they are only in a few levels.

An interesting and very atmospheric game. In this game, you play as the mysterious Lodger, a solo denizen of a cabin deep in some forest or another. As the game goes on, you learn more and more about this mysterious place and the strange apparitions that haunt the Lodger. The question is, what is real? What is a dream? What does the house really look like? Is this all in the Lodger's head? And many more questions besides. The mystery will draw you in, and the simple controls keep the game flowing smoothly.
One complaint I do have is that the game is so mysterious it doesn't even explain itself. Understanding how to get a good ending is not told to you. You are not informed when you are on the track for the bad ending. It just happens. Be prepared to play it more than once. Pro tip? Do not take too much damage to your sanity (when cracks appear in the screen you have taken some). Play smart and play fast.

Do not take too much damage to your sanity (when cracks appear in the screen you have taken some). Play smart and play fast.
I also think this game is appallingly short. You can easily play several times in a day or so. However, on the positive side, the game's shortness works in its favor. You don't have to invest heavily to discover the mystery, but it FEELS like you did when its over.
For all of that, I thus say this game is worth the price. If the price were higher, it might not be a good investment, but it is cheap enough to be well worth it.

Hook is a very, very relaxing puzzle game. Minimalist in its design, with only a white background and black lines and buttons for presentation, you’re thrown straight into the puzzle without so much as a tutorial. And that’s okay, you don’t really need a tutorial. Every time a new item is added to the puzzles,  you’re given a very simple version to solve that teaches you what the new symbols do. The basic idea is that you will remove the items in order, taking care none will hook or get stuck with another.
When I say the game is minimalist, I do mean it’s minimalist: it doesn’t even have a menu. Normally I’d be pretty annoyed without control over the sound, but in this case, I didn’t need it. Hook’s sound effects and backgrounds music/sound are soft, pleasant, and as relaxing as the rest of the game is.
The puzzles themselves aren’t difficult, in fact, the game is quite easy and short with only 50 levels, and only the last few levels are more complicated (because of all the ramifications, and not because they’re actually hard) The game even offers you 3 tries on those latter levels, so that you won’t lose at the first mistake.
The only complaint I had was the windowed mode. Alt+enter did take you out of fullscreen and into window mode, but at the same resolution. I made the mistake of resizing the window on the hopes it would help the resolution aspect, but it only cut off part of my puzzle area; alt+entering back to full screen did not reset this, nor did resizing the window again, so I was forever left with a thin black line at the top and bottom of my game screen that cut off a tiny bit of the puzzles.
Still, it wasn’t game breaking as I didn’t resize it too small (thankfully).
If you like these kind of puzzle games (and even though you might not find a huge challenge in this), if you need something relaxing to play then I definitely recommend it. It’s worth the money.
* Key Provided by Developer

updated April 4th:
after nearly 200 hours of gameplay I am hesitating if I still should recommend the game.
The gameplay is great, I like the graphics and sounds, the different characters build a nice version of rock-paper-skissors, their fighting moves are good, there are interesting combos and there is still a lot to learn for me. The fights can be exciting and set me under adrenaline.
Why am I not enthusiastic, though the game has great potential?
Why do I always leave the game frustrated in the last few weeks though I give it a try every day?
There are a lot of reasons and most of them I pointed out in the original review. And I dont care about the ingameshop and the microtransactions even if I think its a no go in a high-price-game like this (you can unlock the feats, yes, but you still have to earn your gear)
What annoys me about this game is:
- game crashes (game crashed 4-5 times this evening, leaving you with no rewards)
- connectivity issues (if players join or leave)
- that whole p2p-setup fails and there should be dedicated gameservers. those servers also could be very helpful for a better matchmaking.
- matchmaking rarely matches players of the same skill and character level. the matching algorithm is simply bad and fails to create nearly fair matches. The matchmaking takes very long and nearly every time ignores skill range due to a small player base. If you tried out every character and brought it to rep 1 you might be matched with a rep 12 player, who really mastered his character. if there would be servers with special skill restrictions, fights could be fairer and more challenging.
- ganks. there are rarely fair matches. you need to duel (1v1) or brawl (2v2), but in ever other game mode you can expect to just be ganked, even by high rep players, and that is no fun. ganking should be countered by a revenge mode, but that is not enough in my oppinion. if more players attack a single target, their attack strength should be automatically reduced. it is absolutely easy to have the ganktrain running 4 v 1, but it is absolutely frustrating no the opposite side. and no, you cant earn skill by getting ganked unless you already have it. this objections fails.
there are other things, that are annoying, too, but not severe:
- being forced to be connected to a ubisoft server even to play the campaign (which is a good tutorial)
- players that annoy with always the same combos (like bash-hit)
- long loading times even on a good pc
- poorly rewarding community events (no increased reward for those who really engage etc.)
Its a shame, because it really is a good game and i generally like to play it, although it permanently frustrates me. I am willing to learn and try to improve, its not easy for me since I am not used to fighting games, but the general game design isnt satisfying at the moment and I really doubt that ubisoft will listen to the community to really improve it.
I will continue to give it new tries in the next time, though I know that I will be disappointed and frustrated. The game is great and has a lot of potential, but there must be changes in the game design very quickly to improve the situation.
For now I will keep my thumb up, since you always can chose to go PvE, if you dont like PVP.  The game, its structure and its community may have big flaws, but you still can have fun in it, even though it really requires some major updates.

old review from Feb, 24th:
First off: the name is wrong. It is: For Ganking.
There are players who fight with honour, but they are very rare. In the last 30 hours of gameplay i met around 5-10 (with 50-60k online). But since all multiplayer games are unfair as there will never be equal chances from different skill levels alone, you can expect a challenging game from pretty much every aspect.
Despite some big flaws and to my impression bad decisions in the game design, I still can recommend the game.
But be aware: The gameplay itself is a constant well of frustration to me, because i find  it very hard to learn the game. If you are not familiar with this kind of game, it takes forever to learn all the classes and their options as basics. The handling of the weapons requires a good mouse handling and good timing, especially because you cant move your mouse too much to not change your stance to be easily attacked.
The only thing that weighs up all that frustration about the bad things is the rewarding feeling of have won a challenging 1 to 1 encounter in a good fight. This is rare, but possible.
pros:
+ graphics: the medieval settings
+ the storyline is a good tutorial into the different classes. if you never had played fighting games before (like pretty much me), it is useful.
+ small maps with intense fighting possible, but mostly: ganking :( (see below)
+ rewarding feeling of victory
+ character strukture: its quite like rock-paper-skissors: fast vs slow, longrange vs shortrange, heavy dmg vs light dmg, heavy armor vs light armor
neutrals:
~ the storyline itself is narrowly guided from waypoint to waypoint, you have no open world and can only stray around to find collectables. But since the game is about close range player pvp it is tolerable
~/- the ingame store where you can buy all feasts, good equipment and boosters for ingame currency. for most players this kind of microtransactions in a 60€ title is an absolutely no go. it truely is problematic, but if you are really good in the game, you still have a chance, even against extremely well equipped players, because it still comes down to skill in the fighting mode, so i will count it as neutral for now.
cons:
- connection issues: since they host no servers, gameplay connects by p2p which is absolutely annoying
-- on 5 games i play there are 2-3 crashes and disconnects
-- syncronisation problems and lags when players join or leave the game
-- game crashes often when host leaves the game, sometimes you have to restart the game (happens like twice and evening to me)
-matchmaking: despite the p2p problem, you always have problems finding a game
-- matchmaking takes extremely long
-- matchmaking rarely regards your skill range or other parameters, so be prepared to face more skilled and better equipped opponents
- toxic players: always expect cursing, insulting and unfair players like in every multiplayer onlinegame. since there is no report option, you only can quit the game. its a shame that a game, that calls itself "for honor", gives space for so much honourless behaviour, especially ganks
- you nearly have no honourable fights if you're not duelling (and your opponent is of your skill and equipment level, which is quite impossible, see above)
- GANKING
- controler imported game, unintuitive menues, impossibililty to change combos with keyboard and mouse. i suspect players with consoles to be in advantage.
All in all, Ubisoft has published a close quarters intense infantry combat game. whoever likes challenging fights and is willing to invest a good amount of time to learn the game can have a lot of fun in this game. I wont recommend it for casual gamers with no or few experience in fighting games, since the learning of the movements and weapon abilities and be extremely frustrating. Despite of the huge amount of compromises (cross platform menu etc.), micro transaction and the annoying matchmaking it still can be a fun game.

For Honor is a game so aggrivatingly perfect- so many boxes ticked, so much good to say about it, but just ONE IMMENSE PROBLEM that ruins all of it.
It has a decent single-player campaign. Not too long overall, simple to follow story, what you'd expect from a multi-player heavy game like this. The gameplay itself is PHENOMENAL! The dueling feels so personal, the modes are just varied enough to offer enough alternative ways to play to keep your interest. The community outside of Duel Mode can be a toxic cesspool of trolls, gang-bangers and dickholes at the worst of times- but thankfully it's easy enough to give them a taste of their own medicine in-game [they throw you off the cliff, you do nothing but through them off back, etc.]. And the metagame 'Faction War' is surprisingly engaging- you think you won't care about it, but then you see your side losing ground and you kinda start to feel dead inside a little [BTW: if you initially want to care about Faction War, then join the Samurai- EVERYONE joins Samurai, so they gain the most ground every turn without fail].
The ONLY flaw is the disconnection issues. I don't know if it's the Peer-2-Peer, I don't know if it's Uplay, I don't know if it's just poor main servers- but you will often find yourself being disconnected from the others in your game. Half the time the game will just replace them all with bots [who will swarm on you and only you, always, like a strike team of Lu Bu clones- unless they're on your team, then they'll be ♥♥♥♥ing useless]- but the other half of the time, you'll be kicked back to the main menu. If only Ubisoft could find some way to stop this happening and actually have a dedicated server network that can handle keeping people online, this would be a perfect game without question. Until then, I CAUTIOUSLY reccommend this game [and advise you look into getting it on a console instead of through Steam- multiplayer connections are apparently a lot more stable on console].

Rainbow Six is my second FPS that I've played, the first true one being PlayerUnknown's Battlegrounds (and tentaively, Overwatch, if you want to count that). This, in my opinion, far more polished than PUBG and I prefer the smaller maps as it makes the game more exciting.
Being new to the genre, as CS:GO-likes never interested me, I feel like I can bring a different perspective to the table here. If you're not used to FPS like I am, the learning curve can be VERY hard to get over. I'm still learning, actually, and I probably will be for a long while. If you're a newbie like me, and none of your friends play this...you may not enjoy it. Be ready to die a lot and have no idea how or why. Be ready to flashbang yourself a ton if you're used to the delay in PUBG like I was.
At first, I was nothing but frustrated as the learning curve is pretty harsh and you die very quickly. However, 7 hours later and some encouragement via friends, it's a really interesting game and I can't wait to continue to get better. Getting your first kill is SO REWARDING as it feels like that learning curve is finally becoming managable.
Likes: I really enjoy the vast range of operators in this game. Instead of being able to pick up different weapons like PUBG you pick your operator who has a different skillset unique to themselves. This completely changes every time you play, regardless of what map you're on. There are many different ways to "skin the cat" so to speak, so although the maps are FAR smaller than PUBG, they don't get boring because of all the different operators, play styles, and fact that almost everything in the game is destructable.
In essence, I recommend it. It has a steep learning curve that is worth trying to get over, moreso than PUBG, make sure you bring friends. The range of operators makes the game refreshing, instead of kind of stuffy like PUBG. Less "down" time sitting there and camping. I know my review is mainly based off of PUBG, but as that's the most comparable experience I have, I think it is worthwhile to compare the differences.

It's not hard to find games with great ideas and poor executions. Having a great or unique concept is only the first step to translating that into a great game, and the path there is rarely clear or easy. That's what I was expecting going into Skyward Collapse, based on what buzz there was surrounding it. But what I got was something far more engaging than that, something that filled its concept out and gave me plenty to do with it. It's still not a perfect or even great treatment, but it's enough to keep me playing.
In Skyward Collapse you are some kind of divine force, overseeing a world coming together piece by piece. There are two burgeoning societies in this floating realm, pulled straight from tales of Greek and Norse antiquity. They don't particularly care for each other, though, and given the chance they will wipe the other out as quickly as possible. Your charge is to help them BOTH flourish, without annihilating the other... at least for a time.
So yes, the hook here is turn-based strategy against yourself. Every turn you have three actions you can perform for the red side, building structures or casting god powers, and then three actions for the blue side. Once you've taken all your actions the little mortals take over, producing their own militaries from the resources and structures you help them set up, and then marching out to murder each other. You have nearly no control over units once they are produced, aside from some basic rally and upgrade powers. That means the challenge is not found in battle, but in the logistics supplying each side.
The overly clever readers among you may have already raised a finger to interject, supposing that you could just NOT produce soldiers from either side and live in forced harmony. It's not that simple, of course, because each game takes place over three eras of lots of other♥♥♥♥♥♥happening. Bandits, warlords, and monsters can (and will) emerge from the forests and caves of the world to destroy the towns you've worked so hard to grow. There are also woes which strike the world every dozen turns or so, inflicting plagues, disasters, and other horrors that may need a military to deal with. And then from the second era, literal gods descend to the continent to take a hand in matters themselves. Rounding things out is a scoring system that gives points for conflict and destruction, and you have quotas to meet to reach future eras and win the game.
You can't get by without building troops and defenses for your towns, and as situations spiral out of control you can dig deeper and deeper into your bag of frankly ridiculous divine tricks. On a basic level you can upgrade key units, bless your settlements with emergency resources, or lay new tiles of land to benefit the side in need. Once you get more established you can drop mythical creatures like minotaurs and valkyries to bolster your armies, or divine blessings that provide huge bonuses to the troops that reach them (and we're talking like 100x damage or 5x attacks per turn here). And then there are special tokens and god powers with global effects, like cloning every unit on the map, dropping 20 invulnerable minotaurs randomly, or annihilating every unit in existence.
Your insane god powers are the real highlight of the game, and also what illustrate Skyward Collapse's greatest weakness. In my first game I combined those clone and minotaur powers with another one that returned dead units and filled the entire map with mythical murderbeasts over the course of five turns. It was wild and hilarious but obviously I lost the game as they razed all of existence to the ground. And that's the problem... to win, you have to work as hard as you can NOT to let things get that wild. Your score targets require you to foment conflict but not TOO much conflict, lest one side get out of control and destroy the other. To succeed you have to hold back as much as possible, only expanding your forces enough to handle bandits and maintain the balance, and that's disappointing in light of all the ridiculous chaos you could be sowing.
Add to that the fact that most of your time is spend building towns and managing resource quotas, and the game can start to drag once you're taking long turns to plan out new settlements or calculate how to distribute blessings to make a pitched battle a draw. That brings me to my one big knock against Skyward Collapse, that games are just too long for what they are. The standard game length is over a hundred turns, where each one could take five minutes or more to plot out necessary developments. I don't mind the challenge of balancing conflict, in fact that's what sucked me in, but it gets tiresome after three hours in the same game. On the bright side, there are a boatload of options in customizing your games and shorter eras is definitely an option everyone should explore there.
In the end, Skyward Collapse turned out to be a great idea that works well, just not perfectly. Its flaws are big enough that they should give people pause, but specific enough that they won't spoil the game for everyone. It's also a really nice-looking game, with some excellent landscape and building art and decent enough units that make it one of Arcen's most attractive titles to me. The soundtrack is oddly jazzy and relaxing which works better with the theme than I expected, and surely made it easier to while away hours building cities to be razed. Skyward Collapse isn't for everyone, but if you think it might be then it's definitely worth a shot.

As much as I'd like to recommend Nether based on the fun a friend and I had with it tonight after purchasing it, I cannot.
Allow me to walk you through my experience with Nether.
Friend and I are on Skype. We both load the game (after making a seperate Nether account). Server browser comes up...and the game freezes both our computers. Each of us has an AMD octacore CPU and a moderate Radeon GPU but neither of us can load this amazing server browser apparently.
So after the server incident, we both get into the game on a low-population server. I get into the Social "menu" and try to send him a Group invite. Invite sends, no confirmation whatsoever, so we, not knowing we can now group up, start using the map and street names to find one another. This takes about 20 minutes since we both chose the Safe Zone spawn point. Once we find each other, we get the Group thing going and go off into the wilderness on the "Tutorial" quests.
Once in the wild, we get destroyed by a group of Nether. No big, respawn in Safe Zone and find we lose all our starter gear. This kept happening for each step in the Tutorial, so we started the "real" game with just the starter knife like everyone else. It took some serious looting but we eventually found some suitable gear. We get together enough money to take to a Global Trade post and buy some supplies. I get myself a Glider that comes with absolutely no instructions whatsoever. Store all my valuables except survival gear and try the Glider out. Die instantly...from fall damage...from landing in water. Yes, the water de-rezzes your Glider and you take fall damage from falling through the water to the lake bed if you don't IMMEDIATELY jump to "swim".
Basically after that we flailed about for a little bit and killed a Golem with pistols. According to Steam, I have 2.9 hours in this game and I feel like I've seen everything it has to offer. Veteran players say the PvP aspects (which my friend and I didn't see but in a 9/64 server, that's to be expected) are what this game is really about but that doesn't excuse that, in 3 hours, you can experience everything in the game. We had full loadouts (shotguns, a 9mm and a .50 cal handgun, and excellent melee) without touching the crafting system and in a very short amount of time.
I really don't foresee myself starting this game back up and time soon, simply for lack of content. If this really is the final build, then I'm really disappointed in my purchase here.

You may just come up with that ending in your own mind, and it may be more satisying than any other developer could have concluded this trilogy with.

Basically a mediocre Sci-fi themed lane defense. Think of Plants VS. Zombies but with robots. There is nothing really original about this game, the game mechanics are directly lifted from Plants VS. Zombies, including manual pickup of a resource that pops out of the reactor (sunflower). This game feels as if the developers spent half an afternoon wondering which game they could rip off and almost 20 minutes on the story, and 15 minutes coding this.
It tells a lot about this game that the first time I tried this game I was able to break the tutorial level because I did not place my towers exactly in the designated spot and the only way I could exit the game was ALT+F4. The game has many bugs like that where the player is able to break the appallingly poorly scripted "missions" and end up stuck with no other option than to quit the game.
Now, the graphics are not terrible but they are mediocre at best, and the enemies are uninspired and dull. The talking heads narrative is stereotypical and dry, and the dialog is badly written and rife with spelling errors and broken sentences. The story is the typical "They found some magic mineral on planet X and now they are at war!"-tripe and it feels like it was written by a third grader. The grammatical errors in the game are just embarassingly bad and stick out like a sore thumb. While I understand that the developers may not speak English as their native language they should have at least TRIED making an effort.
I think that for the asking price of €12.99 this is straight up robbery. Only buy this if you get it 90% or more off.
TL;DR:
An overpriced, weak, unfinished and buggy scifi-themed Plants VS. Zombies clone.
3/10, would not recommend.

I waited to post a review for Beam.NG because for a while, it was more like a tech demo than a game. I still considered it one of the most fun games I'd played, but it was cumbersome for anyone that wanted to just play a game. The early versions could require as much work as play at times, and obviously a project this ambitious had some problems with performance and optimization.
Now between the mods and the actual Campaigns and scenarios built in, I feel comfortable recommending it without reservation. There is plenty of content right out of the box, and the game seems to scale for lower-end machines much better every time an update drops. I simply cannot speak highly enough of this game at this point. Once you dip your toes into the released content, I challenge anyone not to beg for more.
Luckily, there is an tremendous mod scene. It's not built into Steam (for reasons beyond me, it's discussed on the forums and the official website).
Do yourself a plethora of favors, there is a giant banner that will walk you through the incredibly simple process of adding mods (At the time of writing, there is no built-in manager. Just download and move to the corrrect folder, the game detects them on start-up). Also, anything tagged Alpha or Beta is official content that is just not finished or released into the full game. I have barely scratched the surface and try to stick to official mods for compatibility reasons.
If it runs poorly, wait it out or request a refund :/ I'd recommend a gamepad or wheel for driving but you'll need KB+M for the interface. The latest patch even made it possible to work the UI over Steam Link (360 controller only), as long as I wasn't trying to go to the moon. If it seems too much like work, spend 10m on YouTube and find a decent beginner's guide (the official site also has plenty of great info). I literally cannot think of a complaint about this game, unless it being made so well that it becomes esoteric counts. I don't count it.

Like most other reviews say, it's pretty clear the devs took Plants vs Zombies as a major inspiration for Robowars. So much that it feels more like a buggy reskin of the game instead of its own. The lanes, the resource gathering, multiple types of enemies, even the units are all copied from there, but with hardly the same amount of polish that PopCap used on their title. And to boot, while PopCap is still an active dev, at the time of this writing the dev for Robowars hasn't signed onto Steam in a year. An entire YEAR.
I tried making a profile, made a male one. Wanted to see the female, a text box in Russian pops up. Try entering a name, nothing happens. Game is essentially locked up, had to restart.
Upon entering again, we're given cheap dialogue with grammar errors abound, followed by gameplay that barely explains its quirks and mechanics. There's no details, no stats. No way to tell other than looking at life bars how much damage a turret does. Or how much we heal for.
There's no explanation for how to activate some things, like the tower that supposedly powers up your turrets. Or how long it works. Or if it's even passive. Same with the PvZ Garlic clone; no telling HOW to activate it, so enemy soldiers took it down and kept going.
The windowed / full-screen button is in the level hud right above the Repair / Dismiss / etc functions, not in the actual menus. The pause button is over there, no ESC key here.
There's no reason given for why some units cost money, while others are from the resources you collect. Or if you get them back at the end of the level. Which, if they're destroyed, creates a limited economy that threatens you to conserve them, or just not use them otherwise.
That's a problem in itself, though, since you're barely given enough time to start a defense layout (unlike PvZ where the ramp up was well done) before enemies swarm you. So you HAVE to use your limited use units, from your extremely small (5 cards up to the 9th or 10th stage before I quit) selected hand to take down waves that don't stop.
Eventually you can get up a defense, but at that point the game becomes a Repair spam city as your turrets and units do mystery damage to enemy units whose own details are scant at best. And all of this is wrapped up in a sci-fi military tone too blasé to care about.
Do yourselves a favor, Comrades. Skip Robowars, go get PvZ if you haven't already, and play a good tower defense game.

I like Knock Knock. I like Knock Knock a lot.
The premise is that you're a fellow living alone in a cabin out in a forest. I won't spoil the story, but it's multifaceted, told both from the main character's unsteady perspective, through the environment (and even the enemies), and through a series of diary pages. Each says something different and feeds into the atmosphere.
The graphical style actually kept me from buying the game for a while - not because it was bad, but because I expected something in the vein of Don't Starve, another stylized game with a much lighter atmosphere. I was surprised to find a dark and rather frightening tale of loneliness, insanity, and headless monstrosities in strait-jackets stalking me down hallways.
Sound design is fantastic - the main character sounds a bit like the Professor from Luigi's Mansion (which is a bit of an immersion break), but if you can get past that the horrible disembodied voices of the enemies, the creaking of doors and boards, the sound of distant winds and laughter and moans are all fantastically done.
The gameplay is effectively walking from room-to-room, turning on lights and materializing furniture that you can hide from said monstrosities behind. The game deliberately hides how to play it from you, the player, and thus you must try to figure it out for yourself. To some this may be offputting, but once I realized that this was intentional I became far more positively disposed. The gameplay has been said to get a bit stale after a while, but I myself found that the game mixed things up from level-to-level enough to keep me more than invested. Maybe I'd enter a level and there would be a series of basements in a row, maybe a danger of some sort (trying not to spoil anything) would appear in one room at the other end of the house and I would have to find a way to hide and try to survive instead of driving this danger away myself.
Ultimately, I haven't finished Knock-Knock yet but would recommend it for anyone who's a fan of horror and not being led-by-the-nose everywhere in a video game. It's a unique experience and it only occasionally keeps me from falling asleep at night.
